Resident Evil Requiem (RE9) delivers a masterclass in survival horror by expertly weaving together dual gameplay styles, unbearable suspense, stunning realism, and a deeply emotional story. The narrative connects a modern, personal conspiracy back to the dark roots of Raccoon City, giving the game immense narrative weight which I appreciate. Players experience this through two contrasting perspectives: the tense, first person stealth of Grace Ashcroft and the high octane, third-person combat of veteran Leon Kennedy. This dual mechanics system keeps the gameplay loop incredibly fresh, while resource management and unique crafting mechanics force tactical thinking during every encounter. Enhanced by really impressive lighting and a claustrophobic sound design, the game achieves a terrifying level of atmospheric realism where even the characters hands visibly shake in the dark. Ultimately, RE9 stands as a phenomenal celebration of the franchise's legacy that keeps players petrified and hooked from start to finish. LUX APPROVED!

RE Requiem combines two different approaches to this franchise into one extraordinary experience.   RE2R introduced the modern third-person gameplay while RE7 revived the franchise with its first-person gameplay and now RE9 combines these two in a wonderful remix that delivers both action and horror-survival. The sections with Grace are in first-person and deliver horror while Leons sections are played in third-person and focus more on action. This makes the experience refreshing and adds more variety.   This also affects the story in a good way. The difference between Grace and Leon fits their gameplay but also their narrative. Grace is more afraid and unsure while Leon is hardened by the years and not afraid to get his hands dirty. They both work well throughout the whole game. This culminates in a compelling story that both has action and horror but also a bit of sentimental and emotional bits.   All this culminates in one of the best experiences of this franchise.

Not my favorite Resident Evil game, but a damn good one to be sure.   You play as two separate characters in this game. Grace provides you with a slow-paced survival horror experience where even a single zombie is a terrifying presence, and Leon provides you with cheesy one-liners while you casually roundhouse kick six zombies into a wall before gutting them with a chainsaw.  I'll be up front and state that I'm a total wimp with horror games, and Grace's sections were not really my thing. Not only was the game really slow-paced, but it was way too tense for me. You also need to be really careful about resource management with her sections, and I'm honestly terrible at that. All that being said, I still had fun while playing Grace, and with copious amounts of save scumming, I efficiently cleared through her parts with supplies to spare... because I would re-run sections to make sure I could keep as much gear as possible. I admitted it up front, I'm a wimp, and I'm not really ashamed of it.   Leon's sections were a total blast for me. Not only did his sections deliver a ridiculous amount of fan-service in terms of references to past games, but his gameplay was the exact amount of tension and action that I desire out of these games. While he is nowhere near the pushover that Grace is, you do still need to pay attention to how you are approaching his sections or else you'll get overwhelmed.   I really did enjoy the hell out of the game, despite not being the biggest fan of Grace's sections, and the fact that Grace's gameplay is antithetical to the kind of stuff that I enjoy but I still had fun with it should speak to the overall quality of the experience. If you're someone who enjoys tense horror where you need to conserve resources and approach every situation with caution, you'll really enjoy her sections. I'm an anxious wreck who somehow has made it this far in life, and I still had a lot of fun with her sections.

Overall Resident Evil Requiem is an excellent addition to the series. It is successful in changing the gameplay by offering a dual styled loop that keeps the game feeling fresh. I have some general complaints about the game, that I'll highlight below but overall I enjoyed my time with this game.  Pros: - The game is visually stunning. I have a fairly high end computer at the time of writing, but even still - in the era of Unreal Engine 5 titles -- it's nice to be able to max the game out (including ray tracing) at 1440p and still be at 120 FPS.  - The story is engaging and leaves you wanting to learn more. - The gameplay loop is as addicting as other RE titles (Collecting, space management, upgrading) - The horror/tense elements are here (although lacking later on.) - Having both a FPS/TPS style for character is a welcome addition and makes guns feel great and powerful. - Quick time / Interactive cinematics: These typically are boring to me - but I actually enjoyed them quite a bit in this game. They manage to create cinematics that actually feel like you have some control over - The added variety of how to juggle enemies between Grace and Leon was an interesting loop  The "My opinion / neutral" - I really liked the upgrade / full narrative of the previous two Resident Evils. While I appreciate their ability to create a complex game for two full characters in this title, It left me feeling like the game was even more linear and that the "secrets" that could be found in other games - were significantly easier here. - Film grain: I'm not sure if this is just an AMD GPU thing / or if it looks this way on Nvidia cards but wow - I hated the look of it. I typically don't mind these effects, and I can understand the vibe they were going for here -- but it just made things distracting for me. It made walls look like they were having spasms - Replayability: I've replayed the other two resident evils a few times. I really enjoy new game plus / unlocks. This game also has the option for additional unlocks in spending points. But I just don't feel the same desire to replay this game like the others.   Cons:  - No FOV slider. The field of view for Grace was too zoomed in for me. While i can appreciate the zoomed in claustrophobic concept, in practice it made me feel motion sickness. Thankfully there were mods to fix this. I wish they had offered an official slider - Grace is an annoying character. For someone who is suppose to be an FBI agent, she acts like a scared/whiny/damsel in distress. I can forgive it to some degree, given what she deals with in this game. But we've seen plenty of bad ass characters in RE... Feels like she should be the same.  Overall this is a solid 8 or 9 out of 10 for me.

Requiem felt to me like a best-of mix of the last few more modern Resident Evil games, split between the very different gameplay styles of Leon and Grace. In general, the more stealthy gameplay of Grace felt more fitting to the game, and during Leon's longer segments, the cracks in the very simplistic design began to show.  In general, the game's strongest points were at the beginning, and these sections also looked more unique. I loved how many of the zombies that Grace encountered had their own "personality" and different ways of being outsmarted and avoided. Leon, on the other hand, is this unstoppable killing machine. It is a lot of fun to wreak havoc on these enemies after spending so much time avoiding them and counting bullets. But during the longer sections, especially with Leon, I got really annoyed at how stilted the action gameplay often feels.  On the technical side, I had no issues. I played the game at 3440x1440 with the framerate locked to 60 fps. My settings were mostly on High. I had almost no stutters or frame drops. My only complaint is the sometimes very noisy shadows. I guess a higher ray-tracing setting would help, but that's not possible with my hardware.  The studio also made excellent use of its motion-capture studio. There are so many great animations, especially when combined with the great sound work. But I have to admit that the strongest and most atmospheric sections were mostly in the first half of the game. I loved how much detail there is in certain sound effects, details that weren't even animated, but since those things are mostly kept obscured, you wouldn't even notice.  Story-wise, the game is fine. It's your typical Resident Evil plot with over-the-top acting, cheesy one-liners and comic-book-like villains. It often clashes with the more grounded scenes, but on the other hand, it's also very entertaining.  Resident Evil Requiem is a fine entry in the franchise, but it has shown me more than any other Resident Evil game that it really needs to evolve past this. The framework the developers have built has reached its limits, and I think I've had enough Resident Evil for a while now.
While RE4 shat on what RE stood for and RE7 saved it, now we get Requiem. A happy medium between the two, in the best possible way.

As a Resident Evil fan, I have mixed feelings about this game. It's far from a bad game, but it's not a great game either. It's just... overrated.  Firstly, I should mention that my first playthrough was on the hardest difficulty available at the time, and secondly, I will point mostly the Cons based on my opnion.  As Grace, I liked her gameplay. It was fun and scary, but at some point I felt like the zombies were asleep. Seriously, sometimes I stood in their line of sight for a solid two seconds, and they completely ignored me. Also, it felt like the zombies were stucked to their own designated areas. For example, the main hall felt just as safe as a save room because there were no enemies around. In my opinion, the Kitchen Chef should have acted as a stalker enemy—not as aggressive as Mr. X, but someone who patrols the hospital and can unexpectedly corner you, similar to Lady Dimitrescu.  As Leon, I think his gameplay should have been something secondary, similar to Ada's Separate Ways. I won't lie—in the first playthrough, switching from Grace to Leon helped relieve the tension, but on subsequent playthroughs, it became boring. That said, the hospital section was solid. However, once you reach Raccoon City, things start to decline. For example, the Dust Zombies (or whatever they're called) barely react to pistol shots. They definitely remind me of the zombies in RE3R, where shooting them hardly staggers them.  The reason I think Leon's campaign should have been separate is that it felt out of place in the main storyline. Here are my reasons: after Leon gets inside the walls, we're suddenly thrown into a bike fight bs that feels like it came straight out of RE6. Then we reach the RPD, and everything is extremely rushed. It feels like cheap nostalgia that adds nothing to the story because, within about 20 minutes, we encounter Mr. X, leave the RPD, fight Mr. X, and then end up in a random tunnel where we fight plant monsters.  I won't lie—it's cool af to play as Leon, but I feel Capcom used him more as a marketing tool to sell more. I'm not saying he shouldn't be in the game; I just think the way they handled him was the wrong approach.  I give a rating of 6.8/10, It's not bad, but I completely disagree with the "Overwhelmingly Positive" reviews above. As I said before, it's good, but overrated. I just hope Capcom does not follow the same recipe again, that's why I'm giving a negative review

This game is a lot of fun. I even got all achievements because it was very enjoyable and not tedious. A lot of fan service is nice to see.  From the start I was amazed by Angela Sant'Albano's performance as Grace. Great voice acting, very emotional, believable delivery of anxiety and fear.   Sound design is satisfying. Every footstep adds to the atmosphere and guns finally sound like real firearms - even the weakest pistol sounds like it IS deadly. Props to the sound team, in every other RE game guns sound like Nerf toys.  Leon's battle soundtrack is simple but very intense and fitting.   Key item interactions are fast, no more 15 second cooldown because you missclicked the item, thank you Capcom.  This was the first time I actually ran out of ammo and had to carefully plan ahead. Previous games had plenty of ammo if you explore but this one really creates deficiency.   Insanity mode is actually insane. Somewhat unbalanced because why is a rotting corpse able to take SEVEN bullets to the kneecaps but mostly it was tense in a very fun way. Every single boss is disgustingly easy. [spoiler] The only actual challenge is Victor on insanity [/spoiler] Kinda disappointing.   Now for the two main major things that makes this game suck:  Absolutely not scary. Not a single moment of horror happening in this game. A lot of cringy jumpscares. They try to scare you with a falling item, sudden loud noises, thunderstorm and a BIRD. Really? The Girl is just another annoying stalker. Like, yeah, we've been through this already with Tyrant, Nemesis and Jack. It's nothing new and it's straight up BORING. After RE: Village's psychological horror elements I was expecting something that is at least slightly above child level of horror.  And the worst part of this game is a fact that Capcom is a little drunk off all the money they made with this game and they can't fix the AUDIO DESYNC bug. I've tried every fix known to man but my audio was desyncing during every single cutscene. I have never encountered such bug so I was quite mad at this. It's not a slight inconvenience, no, it is literally 10-15 seconds delay between video and audio - cutscenes are unwatchable. This is my favorite Resident Evil out of the whole titanic franchise of banger games.  I think the 3 most important factors of its quality are:  1) A surgically-designed dynamic between the two protagonists, which elevates the game's pacing to a near-perfect level instead of being a burden to progression like it would be for 99% of other games. The gameplay and factors at play constantly change, and neither protagonist overwhelms the other. I've never seen a game pull anything like this off so well. This really unusual structure befits Resident Evil so well, it makes you wonder how it was never done before.  2) Leon and Grace's gameplay are each extremely good in a vacuum, but the way Requiem constantly introduces new elements with every new section is stunning. There was so much work put into developing an insanely large quantity of compelling, fun setpieces, whether they be one of Leon's several high-action thrills or Grace's more problem-solving-based sections with their focus on puzzles and exploration. This also serves to help the pacing, because you're just NEVER left wanting more interesting ♥♥♥♥ to happen.  3) Requiem easily has the best story of any Resident Evil game, and even if that isn't an especially high bar in a franchise which rightfully prioritizes horror and gameplay quality above all else, it elevates the whole journey and mission of our protagonists so well. It manages to indeed be a requiem to every major game in the franchise, dedicating many of the priorly-mentioned setpieces to really tasteful fanservice callbacks. It also retroactively changes so much of the story of Raccoon City to have more depth, and takes Leon to especially impressive heights as a character.  Resident Evil Requiem is all of the best aspects of its franchise rolled into one, and I absolutely cannot WAIT to see what comes next. It is not perfect, and I think 4 Remake is overall a more balanced and well put-together game, but this one is comparable in quality and speaks to me far more.

I have mixed feelings about this game.  But first of all, I want to give Kudos to Capcom for their excellent use of the RE Engine in terms of optimising the game. This game, like all other previous RE titles runs like a dream without any performance issues or hitches whatsoever and its a testament to how the developers love and care can truly make running games a breeze, a thing which is sadly lacking in most AAA or even some AA games nowadays.  Okay now to the game itself. I felt that the game was too familiar to the style of the RE games I have been playing recently. Basically, the game fluctuates between the story of 2 protagonists, Grace Ashcroft and Leon Kennedy. Grace's gameplay is focused more on the survival horror and inventory management and Leon's gameplay on more action and gunfights.   While playing Grace's section I felt that I was playing a mix of RE 2 remake and RE 7 all over again, which were really great games in their own way, because RE 2 was a punishing game and RE 7 tried something different with the franchise which I appreciated. To have a mix of these 2 games in Grace's section did heighten the tension and created some intense encounters, however the sense of familiarity  really felt flat and repetitive to me after a few hours. Its not bad by any means and I actually preferred Grace's sections more than Leon's, but it felt that I have already been there and done that before.  Now, Leon's sections were clearly inspired by the RE 4 remake and fans of that game will actually love his gameplay the most. But then again, while I love the original RE 4 and the remake as well, I wanted a different style of gameplay with Leon. If I want to play a game similar in style to RE 4, I'll just play RE 4. There were some sections which I expected to encounter more like the open style area of Raccoon City which I found was quite new in terms of an RE action game but sadly, that was just once. But I did like the length of that section and I hope they make more sections like these in future RE games.  In terms of story, its not great by any means, but I liked the characters of Grace and our man Leon and how their stories intertwined narratively. I also liked how the game's story connected with the first game which gets quite overlooked and also loved the hidden easter eggs scattered all around the game for hardcore RE fans to find.  So overall, I would't recommend this game at full price considering the gameplay is too familiar with previous titles but its still a good entry into this franchise. I give it 7 Hip Pouches out of 10.

Resident Evil Requiem is everything I hoped the next mainline Resident Evil would be: tense, atmospheric, and packed with unforgettable moments. It perfectly balances survival horror with modern gameplay, proving once again that Capcom knows exactly what makes this series special.  The atmosphere is phenomenal. Every new area is dripping with dread, and the game constantly keeps you questioning what's waiting around the next corner. Instead of relying on cheap jump scares, it builds tension through excellent environmental design, sound, and lighting. There were multiple moments where I found myself slowing down, checking every hallway before moving forward.  Combat feels polished without turning you into an unstoppable action hero. Resources are limited enough that every bullet matters, and deciding whether to fight or run remains a core part of the experience. Enemy encounters stay engaging throughout, with several genuinely unsettling creature designs that fit right into the series' bestiary.  The story is one of the strongest in recent Resident Evil games. It expands the lore without becoming overly convoluted, and the characters feel grounded enough to make the emotional moments land. Longtime fans will appreciate the callbacks, but newcomers can still enjoy the story without feeling completely lost.  Visually, the RE Engine continues to impress. The environments are incredibly detailed, character models are excellent, and the audio design deserves just as much praise. Wearing headphones transforms the experience into something genuinely nerve-racking.  The only reason this isn't a perfect score is that a few sections overstay their welcome, and there are occasional pacing dips before the game ramps back up for its incredible finale.  Final Verdict: Resident Evil Requiem is a fantastic return to what makes Resident Evil so compelling: oppressive atmosphere, meaningful resource management, memorable monsters, and a gripping story. It's one of the strongest entries in the franchise and a must-play for survival horror fans.  9.5/10 – An outstanding Resident Evil experience that stands proudly alongside the series' best.

Today we're talking about a game from a series that seems to [b] mutate [/b] into a new form with every release a series that demands more and more  [b]fresh blood [/b] to overcome each new evolution and about the project that somehow managed to satisfy fans across the entire Resident Evil community:  [b]Resident Evil Requiem.[/b]  Considering the sheer number of rumors surrounding this game before launch, it felt like it had been assembled, disassembled and put back together countless times on  [b]Dr. Gideon's operating table [/b]. In the end, it inherited many of the strongest parts of its various incarnations although that process certainly wasn't without its side effects.  As someone who's been following this series for a long time, I have plenty to say. My thoughts on this game go far beyond the boundaries of a standard review.(i've removed 13,720 characters from the original review)  [h2]So, is RE:Requiem worth playing?[/h2]   I think Leon's [strike]biceps[/strike] and the way he smashes a closet have already answered that question for me. The verdict is simple it is [b]ABSOLUTELY worth playing[/b]. If only for the knockdown return of the series veteran [b]Leon S[strike]-rank[/strike] Kennedy[/b] to the streets of [b]Raccoonville[/b]. The crowd-favorite is shown in all his glory. And if you are worried that he doesn't get enough [b]TIME[/b], don't be, he has more than enough. And if [b]TIME[/b] is running out, he'll always find a [b]FAST[/b] solution... the one who knows, knows.    Personally, this became one of my favorite games in the entire series and left a huge impression on me. My gallery of  1500+ screenshots and my friend can confirm that. If only you knew how much he suffered during this three months between the opening of pre-orders and the game's release. Then he had to listen to me for another entire month saying [b]SEE?! SEEE!?! I TOLD YOU SO[/b]. BTW that’s one of the reasons why this review took so long to finish i wanted to cool off a little and write it as objectively as possible.    [h3]Visual Direction and Character Animation[/h3]   [b]Resident Evil Requiem[/b] tells its story through two completely different perspectives.   On one side is [strike] Dante.. Oopps i mean [/strike][b]Leon S. Kennedy[/b] - a battle-tested government agent, hardened by countless battles and worn down by years of surviving unimaginable horrors of bio-organic weapons returning to the very place where his nightmare first began,On the other is [b]Grace Ashcroft[/b] - a young FBI analyst, fragile and inexperienced, facing the brutal reality of the world for the very first time while uncovering the mystery surrounding her own origins.CAPCOM has always excelled at creating memorable characters but this time they've outdone themselves.    [h3]Modern Resident Evil[/h3]   There's another interesting trend I've noticed in recent Resident Evil games. Each title seems to filter its story through a distinct thematic lens.   [b]RE7 is pure body horror wrapped in VHS aesthetics.[/b]  [b]RE:Village feels like a dark fairy tale inspired by the Brothers Grimm.[/b]  [b]RE:Requiem continues that tradition by presenting its story almost like a detective thriller.[/b]   It's one of my favorite aspects of the modern series. This approach gives every game its own identity, strengthens the atmosphere and makes each entry visually unique. Overall, the graphics, environmental design, and atmosphere are exceptional. I found myself examining every single asset, every texture, every tiny environmental detail.  [h3]Story Line[/h3]   As for the story the first act is outstanding. The first act was done very well and with great attention to quality. The issues and questions only start to appear from the second half of the second act onward.   While the first act is remarkably close to flawless, the second and third acts raise a few questions. One of them is the lingering feeling that a noticeable amount of content may have been cut during development particularly around the endgame and several late-game encounters. I completely understand why that happens. As developers, you always want to add more mechanics, more cinematic moments and more gameplay systems but every project runs into deadlines. The real issue isn't the missing content itself, it is that the game loses the sense of resistance that drives its narrative. Personally, I think this could have been solved in a fairly straightforward way not by changing the story itself but by reinforcing the gameplay.  Just more resistance. More enemies. More dangerous situations.  [spoiler] At least by the end when Leon confronts the Umbrella squad, you expect to be caught in a hail of bullets but that never happens.[/spoiler]CAPCOM was probably afraid of repeating the backlash [b]RE6[/b] received. Ironically,[b]RE6[/b] was a huge project with multiple unique campaigns and an ambitious story. The problem in fact was not the game.  [h3]Madness Difficulty[/h3]   This issues become even more apparent on  [b]Madness difficulty [/b]. The best way I can describe it is with the [b]shape of a bottle[/b], it is narrow neck is the first act or more specifically the cafeteria sequence. Once you've made it through that section, there are very few meaningful differences compared to a standard playthrough. Every act that follows feels largely the same which is a standard difficulty.    A much more interesting solution would've been to redistribute enemies throughout the campaign, increase their numbers, move some of the third act's encounters into the earlier chapters and tighten the game's resource economy. There is very little challenge in being able to  [b]one-shot almost every enemy particularly throughout the act 3[/b] while  [b]unlocking infinite ammo[/b] far  [b]too easily [/b] and far  [b]too early[/b]. Looking back at  [b]RE2[/b] especially on [b]Professional difficulty[/b] you found yourself calculating every single bullet, every knife swing and every route through the RCPD. You constantly weighed your options where every resource mattered.  [b]Madness difficulty [/b] in both  [b]RE:Village [/b] and  [b]RE:Requiem [/b] feels considerably less refined. It gives the impression that these modes simply weren't fully polished before release. As a result the game's replayability suffers in places. Most notably, one of the story's key characters someone you naturally expect to play a major role in the finale ends up feeling surprisingly underdeveloped.  [h3]NG+ and Progression[/h3]   One thing the game desperately lacks is a proper [b]NG+[/b]. Sometimes you simply want to experience the game again as if you were playing it for the very first time. Unfortunately, Requiem doesn't quite allow that. After completing the game once, part of Leon's arsenal and progression becomes permanently available from the very beginning. From both a narrative and gameplay perspective, those unlocks should have remained rewards earned somewhere around the midpoint of the campaign.  But even in its current state, the game delivers exactly what millions of players love RE for relentless tension, an outstanding atmosphere, memorable cinematic moments, and characters you genuinely care about.   Even when you take every criticism into account, none of them undermine the core gameplay or damage the narrative itself. If I had to point to the game's biggest shortcomings, they'd be the third act of Grace's campaign and the balance of Madness difficulty. As for NG+, I don't actually consider it essential.    [h3]Final[/h3]   What matters isn't that those flaws exist. What matters is that they never break the game's core structure or undermine what makes it enjoyable. Even now, I don't regret a single minute I spent with [b]RE:Requiem[/b]. And if you've made it all the way to the end of this review and you're still wondering whether it's worth playing...    My answer is exactly the same as it was in the beginning.    [b]Absolutely. [/b]

Now now, WAIT, hear me out.  This is NOT a bad game, there's no X out of 10 score on Steam so I just want to go against the grain here a bit.  Someone before me wrote "Did we play the same game?" alluding to all of the overwhelmingly positive reviews - and I agree with them.  To me, this game is inferior to RE2R, RE4R, 7 and 8 - especially story/vibe wise. This is NOT the best Resident Evil, not even close - how in the hell...anyways...  Just to get this out of the way: NO FOV SLIDER...wtf what year is it.  Without mods 1st person was almost unplayable to me. and 70€ (okay I paid 55€) for 15 hours of gamplay at most :s  To keep it short and spoiler free - this should've been Grace's game, and Leon just feels shoehorned in. He was great in RE2R & RE4R, here it feels like Capcom have pushed waaay too close back to the RE6 wacky woohoo character and story writing with him. It was a bit too much after the Remakes of 2 & 4.  Grace's parts were great. 1 particular level was a bit boring with her, but otherwise, great horror experience especially at the start. Awesome if you like RE7 & 8 but the scary bits.  Leon's gameplay initially felt great - but once you get to a certain part of the game, it gets repetitive and kinda boring honestly -> and for some reason, gameplay wise, it feels like a step back from RE4R, not sure how that is possible but I swear it felt worse to play. There is a lot of "member-berries" here, if you've played the older games - which were fun but not fleshed out and a bit over the top.  Also, I'd rather do a  - 1 playthrough Grace (scary/horror/survival) - 1 playthrough Leon (wacky woohoo/action) This was kinda done for RE2R and worked great I think - perhaps they wanted to make sure the player experiences both. Juggling between the 2 all the time was annoying and killed the pace in some of the swaps.  Graphics wise - best looking RE Engine, Capom game to date, the path tracing is gorgeous yet performant enough for this type of game (bare in mind, played on a 5070ti though). Apart from no FOV slider...wtf  The story isn't groundbreaking, nor does it move the general RE story along really, maybe my expectations were too high due to the high praise the game has been showered with.   Lastly, not a fan of built-in ads in games (car & watch) but whatever. If it pushes their game over the finish line, it's fine I guess but it's a slippery sloap that will eventually get over-done in games I fear.

Easily one of the Top 5 Resident Evil games ever made. Capcom has just been cooking with these games ever since RE7. They just keep getting better.   The contrast between Grace and Leon's gameplay is what does it for me. Grace's gameplay is more reminiscent of RE7 or RE2 Remake, but noticeably more easier and forgiving, keeping it fun, and focuses more on survival horror (Hiding and using ammo wisely), whereas Leon's gameplay is more like RE4 Remake and just allows you to absolutely maul through everything. It keeps you on the edge of your seat, and as a result, made me complete the game in one sitting upon release cause of how intense and thrilling the story is from start to end, and it only gets better.   If you already know at least some of the Resident Evil lore, this story just makes you wanna go deeper into the lore, otherwise it's just a really fun game, even for the new fans.   The graphics are incredible. The RE engine is truly a beast with these more linear games from Capcom. I use an RTX 3060 12GB (Watched BenchmarKING's optimization video) and I was easily getting over 80 fps with Ray Tracing Max. If you lock your FPS at 60 and enable Frame Generation, you get around 120 FPS and the input lag is barely noticeable and isn't a disaster like most games nowadays.   Definitely a Game Of The Year contender and is a really good 30th Year Anniversary Gift to the RE fans.

The game is bit too reliant on the tomahawk parry mechanic despite it being a fun melee weapon overall.

tl;dr good game is good.  RE: Requiem is a weird game to review, because it does so much that feels just like a direct predecessor (*cough* RE 4* cough*) and yet feels all its own. But also because it's... kinda two games woven together.  The game takes turns between two characters, Grace and Leon, and their two very different mechanics, styles, and most importantly: focuses.  Grace's (episodes? stages?) are: survival-horror. Low resources, high fear, focus on not being found/seen, odds-against-you stress-fests. Leon's are (if you played RE:4 you'll feel right at home): badass mofo with big guns and bigger one-liner-energy. Cleave through the enemies that terrified Grace with a sassy quip or two.   And I'm surprised that I actually enjoyed both of them... I expected to only like Leon's and hate Grace's but they actully both work really well - as different as they are. They play to their strengths, but do so well enough to be compelling and enjoyable.  The game still struggles with the same old gripes that are by-design from this series: - Leon has the agility and turn-rate of a bulldozer so "dodging" attacks is a fugue-state-dream - Grace has chronic deer-in-the-headlights syndrome and will conveniently freeze or walk into stupid traps for the plot - over-the-shoulder aiming and parallax mean that the closer an enemy is the harder it is to get a good shot on them; this ups the fear-mechanism at the expense of making your character feel like they want to get ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ eaten - Grace's failings are more forgivable at times (although an FBI agent sent to do field work who seemingly doesn't own a cellphone or ever even once consider "maybe I should call for some kind of backup?" and has seemingly no weapons or self-defense training is a bit much to turn a blind eye to...) - I am still angry though that Leon doesn't have the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sense to reload his empty weapons and that's offloaded onto the player like "remember to reload your gun every two shots" -- I'd expect at least him to have an "auto-reload when mag is empty" and not have to manually press to reload after clicking to fire an empty weapon twice [like yes, I get it, as a player you want me to feel that stress or whatever but it also makes me feel like I'm playing a badass who lost his ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ brain. This is perfectly in line with playing Grace - a rando who never actually went through decades of zombie-killing experience -  not Mr Leon "suplexes a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tyrant for cardio" Kennedy...   All that aside...  Atmosphere is great, graphics are very solid (although no ammount of tweaking brightness/etc ever got rid of the "it feels like there's a mild mist whenevr I'm in a non-dark area" uncanny effects), sound design is quite good; lots of homages and callouts to the earlier series games, story is quite satisfying, tension build up moments are mostly very well made.  ...yeah, good game is good. Would recommend.

Resident Evil Requiem, aka RE9, is a love letter to Resident Evil as a whole (but mainly RE2). This is the Resident Evil title that tries to take everything good from every single mainline Resident Evil game (yes, even RE6) and apply it to itself, and I must say, it works really well.  The Leon sections are like playing a mix of RE4R and RE6 Leon, while the Grace sections are like playing a slower version of RE7 and RE2R.  The game takes elements from all the other titles, it is a very "Resident Evil Lore" heavy game, so you'll love it if you're a big RE fan. But that doesn't mean you won't enjoy it or understand it if you're a first-time player, though. Actually, RE9 is a great game to introduce people to the franchise, since it foreshadows all the aspects the series has to offer: horror, action, and the different balances between the two in each game.  If you really want to play the most important game tied to this one beforehand, you should play RE2R. And for those who played RE2 or RE2R (especially those who played them a long time ago) this game will, in a certain way, make you nostalgic.  Honestly, my only complaint is the health system in the Leon sections. It feels like Leon loses health too quickly but also gets way too many healing items, instead of having a slightly more complex health system like the other Resident Evil games featuring Leon. That might just be my opinion, though. Maybe it was based more on RE6's health system. Still, it's a minor complaint.  The action is great, the horror is great, those are the most important aspects of every Resident Evil game, and both excel in this one. On top of that, the game expands the Resident Evil lore significantly, which is also really important on the memorable RE games.  I'd say this is basically a 10 out of 10 game, not just as a Resident Evil title, but as a video game itself.

The Resident Evil franchise has managed to become my favorite game franchise over the years, knocking the Zelda franchise off its throne. I have always preferred gameplay over everything else - story, graphics, voice acting, etc. and that's exactly why I hold RE dear to my heart. The classic RE titles have that Zelda dungeon feel to them that I adore, like the intruiging puzzles, atmosphere, backtracking and strategic combat, as well was adding memorable characters, locations and the overwhelming sense of dread with limited ink ribbons, traps and spooky monsters combined with the fear of the unknown behind every door. This brings me to Resident Evil Requiem.  After finishing my first playthrough of RE Requiem on the "standard (classic)" difficulty, I felt like it was a near flawless experience, with only a few minor hiccups. I have since completed the insanity difficulty, as well as doing all the challenges and getting all achievements, which has changed my perspective a bit. I'll split my thoughts about the different parts onto 3 sections: Grace's sections, Leon's sections and miscellaneous things. [b] Huge Spoilers from here on! [/b]  [h3] Grace's sections[/h3] [spoiler] For me, the first act of Grace's story inside the sanatorium was a 10/10 experience on my first playthrough on classic. Limited resources, deadly zombies, suprises, traps - it was all there. From sneaking around to getting the first flimsy handgun to clutching onto every herb, scrap, ink ribbon and bullet - it was perfect. I adored the feeling of "I want to save, but I don't want to use an ink ribbon yet, but I also don't know what's behind that door" so much, it was everything I wanted from a Resident Evil game. The return of the RE1R crimson heads, or in this case, "blister heads", were so cool and made me anxious about passing by a previously killed zombie, amazing! The blood collection mechanic fits suprisingly well into the gameplay, letting the player make smart choices between crafting ammo, healing or even ink ribbons. Grace was also a pretty likeable and very realistic character, who reacts to all the madness like you would expect someone to react like. The stealth segments with the unkillable Girl were also well done, especially the basement, which felt a lot less scripted than the other two encounters. However, after being done with the basement, the sense of dread vanished, as most of the enemies were gone by then and after getting out of the facility, Grace's part's mostly evolve into a walking simulator outside of the last "Girl" section and the lab section. The last section with the girl was fine, but it was short and also rather easy, since I was swimming in resources at that point .The lab section was pretty interesting at first with the return of the lickers, but it was so short and also way too easy to deal with, because you get more than enough to deal with the lickers easily, that it didn't capture that excitment I had at the beginning of the game. I think RE Requiem could have been enhanced by including some more suprises when returning to the sanatorium, like the hunters in RE1 remake, just something to spice it up a bit. In general though, Grace's parts are by far the best parts of the game and really felt like a true RE experience again, like a blend of RE2 remake and RE7. I'd give Grace a 9.5/10. [/spoiler]  [h3] Leon's sections[/h3] [spoiler] Leon's sections unsuprisingly felt like a reboot of RE4, which don't really try anything new. That doesn't mean they were bad - far from, actually, but whereas the survival horror aspect of Grace's campaign evolves the formular with the crafting mechanics and the modern approach to stealth, Leon's parts feel much "safer" and focus more on spectacle than mechanical depth. With that being said though, Leon's gameplay was fun as hell. Kicking, shooting, parrying, blowing stuff up, beheadings, close-up kills and the gore, my god the amazing gore, were phenominal. It's the perfect reincarnation of the term "stupid fun", switch your brain off and have fun fighting your way through various enemies. Similar to RE4, this stuff is cool, but it starts to wear thin fairly quickly and for me, it set in as early as the RPD, since the gameplay never really changes outside some pretty lackluster boss fights. Also, lots and lots and lots of nostalgia bait. At first it was fine, a few returning lines and situations, but the RPD, hunk, "Nemesis" and especially the return of the Tyrant T103 went a little too overboard in my eyes. The action scenes sometimes reached a level of silliness that I really don't like too much, for example the motorcycle ""battle"" or the subway scenes. As I said, I don't dislike the Leon sections at all, they are great, but I feel like they overstay their welcome a little bit and Leon is far too powerful to even begin to care about any of the enemies. Overall, very fun but repetitive parts of the game. I'd give them a 7/10 overall. [/spoiler]  [h3] Miscellaneous[/h3] [spoiler] There only really is one "miscellaneous" section of the game and it sucks: It's the orphanage. On the first playthrough, it's barely decent, but on repeat playthroughs, it's an annoying, boring and predictable walking sim that offers nothing to the story or gameplay of the rest of RE reqiuem. It's short, but it doesn't feel short, it actually feels insulting to replay, because it pretends to be interesting, but it really isn't. I would not have cared if it was skippable, but it isn't and I don't get why. RE7 had exactly the same unskippable cutscene-like gameplay elements noone likes to replay, so I don't know why Capcom would include more of those. The very first section with Grace also falls into this category, as well as that scene with infected Leon walking around in the end of the lab section or any scene where you're carrying Emily. Gameplay like that just sucks to replay, so either let us skip those on replays, make them cutscenes, or stop including them! [/spoiler]  Overall though, this might be the best entry of the modern RE7-RE9 games. It combines a lot of great gameplay elements from the best RE titles and creates a memorable and fun experience with varying amounts of replayability. The graphics are breath-taking as always, the atmosphere is phenomenal, the meticulous details everywhere are amazing, the story is once again silly, the characters are mostly great and the technical performance is very stable. It really seems like Capcom have come to embrace the things majority of the fans enjoy the most about Resident Evil and have put their all into crafting something artistically memorable, which also runs nicely and looks photorealisitic. I am stoked to see how the Code Veronica remake is turning out and if they can capture the essence of that brutal classic title. Taking everyting into consideration, I'd give this title a 8.5/10. My favorite RE title is still RE1 remake, so let's see if Capcom can outdo themselves once again.

I came for Leon but stayed for Grace. (SPOILER FREE REVIEW)  RE9 perfects the two sides of Resident Evil. Grace's sections were full of dread in the best way possible. I liked how they put effort into making the experience more immersive depending on which camera perspective you used. In third person, Grace can trip while running away, whereas in first person that doesn't happen. I like how the zombies now have personalities because of the T-virus. It makes them feel more alive. Grace is a brilliant protagonist. Her voice actor put her heart and soul into the performance. She feels like a normal person who was thrown in to chaos. She is more emotional and vulnerable then other RE protagonists you can also feel and hear the fear in her voice. In my personal opinion, I felt RE9 did the horror aspect better than RE2R. The care centre was designed so well. The puzzles are simple, but they're fun to do.  After experiencing all that dread, you switch to the main man himself, Leon S. Kennedy. Leon is older in this entry, and you can really tell. He's grittier and has become desensitised to zombies and everything that comes with them. You can tell he's been through hell and back. Don't worry though his one-liners return, and they're better than ever. Leon's gameplay is GOD'S GIFT. Leon is ON SMOKE in this game. He has traded his knife for a massive hatchet, and I'm all here for it. You can literally and I'm not joking PARRY EVERYTHING. Is it overpowered? Yes, but I was having so much fun. Leon also gets executions. To trigger them, you shoot a staggered enemy at point-blank range. These finishers are BRUTAL, especially with Requiem. Also requiem is such a powerful gun when graces uses it the recoil is insane. I enjoyed visiting Raccoon City and seeing how it affected Leon. However, his boss fights were mid. They weren't bad, but they definitely weren't good. However, Leon's set pieces are amazing. I loved all of them. Overall, Leon is a joy to play and a great upgrade from RE4R's combat.  Even though this is a positive review, there are some negatives. First of all, this game isn't that replayable. This is due to the split narratives and that boring 10-minute section. I understand why it was there for a first playthrough, but you can't skip it on repeat playthroughs. I enjoyed the story, but some character decisions were strange. There is one character who is basically an off-brand version of another RE villain. He does NOTHING. NOT EVEN A BOSS FIGHT?????? He was just there... because? The story, at the moment, seems far-fetched, but I'm assuming it will line up more with the new timeline after more remakes come out. Also, there is no Mercenaries mode. We got this Leon Must Die mode instead, but I didn't really like it and would've preferred Mercenaries.  Overall, RE9 perfects the two sides of Resident Evil: survival horror and action horror, with dual protagonists. However, the dual protagonists also become a weakness on repeat playthroughs. The story is passable, but the more you think about it, the less it makes sense. Grace Ashcroft cements herself as one of the best RE protagonists in only one entry.

The modern [i]Resident Evil[/i] can be considered love letters in a way.  [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] is a love letter to the horror genre.  [i]Resident Evil: Village[/i] feels like a love letter to [i]Resident Evil 4[/i].  [i]Resident Evil: Requiem[/i] continues this framing.  Only this time, the game is a love letter to the franchise as a whole, combining the different eras of the series into a fascinating, if sometimes tonally dissonant experience.   [h1]Dual Perspectives[/h1]  [i]Requiem[/i] first places you in the role of Grace Ashcroft, an FBI investigator whose mother was a character in [i]Resident Evil: Outbreak[/i].  Her introductory section, where she travels to a burnt-out hotel, ends with a tense, minutes-long encounter with an infected police officer.  Grace’s sections play out both like modern [i]Resident Evil[/i] games and the classic ones, with an emphasis on slow-burn horror and exploration.  Then you switch to Leon Kennedy, an old-time character who has been in the series since the second game.  My first encounter with an enemy resulted in Leon roundhouse kicking them into a pole and decapitating them with a hatchet.  Needless to say, the contrast between the two sections was jarring, but amusing.  It’s obvious what they’re doing here: the creators are paying homage to the different eras of the [i]Resident Evil[/i] franchise.  Grace’s sections play out like the more modern games infused with the classic style, while Leon’s sections are paying tribute to the [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] through 6 era, which focused heavily on more action-oriented set-pieces with a B-movie flair.  The two different perspectives can feel tonally dissonant at times, with Grace’s justifiable fear contrasting with Leon’s totally over it energy and silly quips.  Considering it’s a tribute to an incredibly storied franchise I can accept that.  But the pacing feels off at times.  Grace’s sections can last upwards of an hour, and then you shift over to Leon for at most twenty minutes.  The two characters are given very different emphasis, with Leon getting comparatively little screen-time.  At least until the second half of the game, where the nostalgia goes into overload as you primarily play as Leon and the series returns to where it all began: Raccoon City.   [h1]Down Memory Lane[/h1]  It was during this section that the game’s themes finally clicked for me.  While the section is a bit overlong, and features the return of an old villain that results in an unsatisfying boss fight, this section is poignant in a big way.  One of the game’s major themes is how trauma can follow people throughout their lives.  As Grace, you begin the game investigating a lead involving a series of serial killings where the only link between the victims is that they were all survivors of Raccoon City.  She’s still coping with the death of her mother, who she feels guilty for not being able to save during an event eight years prior.  As Leon, you face the demons of his past, as he deals with an unknown condition that’s slowly killing him, something tied to the events of his past.  Both of these characters face their traumas as they attempt to find closure.  One of Leon’s most poignant scenes comes when he [spoiler]returns to the gun shop behind the police station in [i]Resident Evil 2[/i], where players will remember he encountered a distraught father coming to terms with his daughter’s infection[/spoiler].  It’s a moment that re contextualizes that scene, and where the game’s themes really hit home.  I do hope that the series continues to move forward, and doesn’t dwell on the past forever.  We can have the remakes of past [i]Resident Evil[/i] games, that’s fine.  But the newer games should continue to look toward the future.  And while [i]Requiem[/i] does firmly try to put a capstone on the past, its ending does suggest that more is coming.   [h1] Conclusion [/h1]  While [I]Requiem[/i] does sometimes feel chained to the past, it is still a blast to play, which is a testament to its construction.  The rouge-like mode they added post-release for free is a neat little addition too that extends the game’s shelf life.  And while I am not a super [I]Resident Evil[/i] fan (I played the original [i]Resident Evil 2[/i] but couldn’t get through it because it felt too archaic to me, although I did finish the remake), I can appreciate how long the franchise has been around, and that a certain amount of navel-gazing is to be expected.  Hopefully the series continues to blaze forward, as its existence has helped define the horror game genre as a whole.  Here’s hoping it continues to do that for a long time coming.

I don't usually write reviews, but this game deserves one.  I've been playing games for years, and I can honestly say Resident Evil Requiem is the best game I've played in all my years of gaming.  Everything just clicked. The atmosphere, the gameplay, the story, the music, the visuals—every part of it felt like it was made with care. I was hooked from the beginning and couldn't wait to see what happened next.  Leon was amazing to play as, and Grace was a fantastic new character. I really liked how different they felt, and both of their stories kept me invested the whole way through.  I genuinely don't have a single complaint. Every chapter had something memorable, and the game never felt boring or dragged on. By the time the credits rolled, I was already thinking about starting another playthrough.  For me, this is a 10/10 masterpiece and easily my favorite Resident Evil game. More than that, it's the best game I've played in all my years of gaming.  Capcom absolutely knocked it out of the park.

Clocking in at around 10 hours, RE9 provides what I see as the quintessential Resident Evil formula: a meticulously crafted combination of absurd violence, cinematic drama, and schlocky nonsense. It offers two takes on the RE experience, those being classic survival horror with Grace, and over-the-top action with Leon, each with their own huge section plus several smaller ones, and I like the way it switches between and weaves together both. And I would say the gameplay, level design, and progression in both is top-notch. That said, there are a couple sections that aren't as good, with one unpleasant, ill-fitting, and disposable segment stuck around the middle.  In terms of characters, it's hard not to love Leon, and seeing Grace develop into more of a protagonist is nice.  Graphics-wise, it's incredibly impressive and performs amazingly where many worse-looking games fall short. No game probably needs to look better with this, and AI could certainly never do a better job.  As for the story, it definitely tows the line of believability and doesn't always hit the mark. It feels like it sets up for a lot more interesting stuff than it delivers on, does some misdirection, and then goes out of its way to cut short the story threads it seemed to open up. It's not bad, serviceable at worst, but I felt like it could have done more.  All in all, I would say it's a really fun game, and what qualms I have with the story do not detract from a very engaging experience. If you're an RE fan or just happy to be up for a thrilling ghost train ride, you'll surely enjoy it.

The mega success of this game ensures we get another installment, but hopefully they take the highlights of this game (Grace and the suspense/mixed with occasional action pieces) and build on that, instead of going full on RE6. Somewhat begrudgingly, I have to give Resident Evil Requiem a recommendation. Capcom has once again proven that they are a premier studio that can deliver a damn good product when they commit to it despite my best attempts to dislike this game. Rhodes Care Center gives the RPD or dare I say even the Spencer Mansion a run for its money when it comes to survival horror level design, and while I don't particularly like playing through Leon's segments, they feel so clean, modern and satisfying that even an RE Oldhead like me can stomach them.  Some context so you know where I'm coming from as a fan: My ideal Resident Evil game is essentially REmake. I love RE2 OG as well as RE2make, while I didn't particularly like 4 or 5. Nothing needs to be said of 3make or RE6. I enjoyed RE7, and RE8 had its moments despite overstaying its welcome imo.  That being said, let's get into RE9. I'm gonna try not to spoil anything, but let's just cover the broad strokes here. I really did not enjoy the majority of the story here. I'm not going to bash it, because that would take me too long, but it's convoluted, contrived, and retcons things that didn't need to be retconned. Yes, I know, I know, RE games never had good stories. I agree, but the difference is the older games didn't really have to try. RE9 bends over backwards to fix things that didn't need to be fixed. Frankly, the 2nd half of this game didn't need to exist, but I like my survival horror games short and I dislike RE4, so you can see my bias. However, the second half is *not* a full-on RE6 Michael Bay fest like you may have seen some people say. There are some really silly moments reminiscent of RE6, but they do not drag and really you won't think much of them after the fact. It's fine; let's remember that RE always had goofy stuff, even when it's pretending to be serious.  Grace Sections: I really enjoy Grace as a new protagonist! [spoiler]Like Ethan before her, Grace injects a fresh experience for veterans and newcomers, but unlike our favorite mold man[/spoiler], Grace doesn't fit the everyman archetype; she isn't a pure vessel for the player, although you could chalk this up to the fact that I played both Grace and Leon on 3rd person mode. Anyway, that's neither here nor there. Grace's sections are my favorite not because of her or her adorable neo-Sherry, but because Capcom decided to go all-in on delivering a tight, truly survival horror experience. I mean, this is the best it's getting without getting fixed angles again, honestly. The Care Center is absolutely sprawling, with multiple routes and ways to clear it out. I probably frustrated my friends watching me more than once with the amount of times I experimented with a route through the East Wing, only to get killed a few steps in. Small aside here: frankly, I hate the extended death scenes. They've been in since RE2make and I get that they're pretty technically impressive, but God, I don't want to be shown my failure for 20 seconds before I can reload my save. Just give me the "You Died" screen and get on with it. Thankfully, you can end the scene early-ish, but it's not as early as I'd like. I guess it's Dead Space's fault. Grace's sections fall in quality after the Care Center, but that's fine. Capcom threw their haymaker and I was floored for the rest of the game. They could have had me punching boulders and I still would have given a recommendation based on the Care Center and its basement. Let's just move on to Leon.  Leon's Sections: If you played RE4make, you're in for a lot of the same. Parrying is really strong, you've got a large inventory, happy hunting. I really don't have a lot more to say; I enjoy a couple set-pieces that the game throws at you, but unfortunately I also hate one of them that reminded me of the damn Capra Demon room from Dark Souls 1. By and far, though, Leon's sections are thoroughly polished to offer state-of-the-art over the shoulder action. You already know whether you'll like it or not.  Final Notes for the future: Capcom obviously put a lot effort into Requiem. They left enough room for Res10ent Evil or B10hazard, whatever they want to call it, but this feels like a final entry to me. I have to say, I wouldn't be too mad about it. More of the same, again.  I feel like I've been playing the same exact game with little to no improvement since RE7 now.   "Does it work? Is it enjoyable? Is it worth it?"  The answers to those questions are, to me, subjective to how much Resident Evil you played, or how much you like eating frozen pizza for every meal.  I was, as usual, excited and reveling in anticipation for the release of another mainline game in the series, specially after the endless remakes which, don't get me wrong, were welcomed as a fresh way to experience the 90s titles, but started feeling pushed when RE4 Remake came out.  I truly believe RE4 to be one of the best and most important games of all time, and was very happy with the remake version, but that does not change the fact that I still viewed it as unnecessary.   RE9 plays safe. It innovates in absolutely no way, shape or form, and tries to appeal to the nostalgia and affective memory of its players. Perhaps, a newcomer to the series or the genre in general might be far more able to appreciate it, as they lack the point of reference and tiredness of having to deal with years of west/east wing pseudo-police stations that require the same strategy over and over, the repeated sewer/underground sections right after it, and the anti-climatic high-tech lab swarming with reused enemies and assets from a bygone era.   "But isn't that what makes RE? Isn't that what fans want to spend their money on?"  Yes, for the vast majority, perhaps it is. This is a personal take, and if you were able to enjoy hours and hours of Requiem without ever having a single thought about all I'm saying here, I'm happy for you. I couldn't, and I find almost insane how much praise Resident Evil 9 has received for doing absolutely nothing more than the past 5 titles did.   My indignation with it goes beyond my opinion on how saturated the brand has become. By itself, I believe the game severely lacks in variety of enemies and encounters, specially when it comes to bosses. A gimmick boss at the end of the first half. A generic giant spider at the beginning of Racoon City. ANOTHER tyrant virtually identical to the one in RE2. Another Capcom giant plant. A completely forgettable bullet sponge of a final boss.  None of these enemies deliver a memorable encounter or a actual challenge.  The attempt on an item store for Leon in the second half also feels like just an excuse to insert yet more allusions to a distant past. Leave the vendor in RE4, move on. Picking up weapons in the world has proven far more satisfactory for this tired formula than just making a bland slicky generic weapons upgrade table.   Honestly, I'm even tired of talking about all of this. There are many other aspects I wish to discuss, but I don't wanna waste even more time of my life writing a Steam Review. My hopes are that in their next mainline RE title, capcom goes in a new direction. As flawed as RE6 was, it tried something new. RE7 was yet another bold move, and it worked, way too well at this point.  Perhaps it is time for one more reinvention.   So in the end, would I recommend you pick up RE9?  If you like survival horror in general, and occasionally plays RE here and there, sure, go for it, you'll enjoy yourself from time to time, maybe you'll have a blast.  If you play every RE title to the max, going for every trophy, challenge runs and dozens of replays, you might feel what I've been trying to say.   Overall, wait for a good sale, 50% would be fair.   I myself will try not to expect much from them anymore.

Resident Evil Requiem is a game that came very close to being my favorite Resident Evil. It has one of the strongest openings in the entire series and a lot of ideas that show Capcom still understands what makes survival horror special.  The game looks absolutely amazing and sounds even better. The atmosphere, audio design, and dark electronic soundtrack create a fantastic horror experience. The optimization is also impressive. Game runs great on PC, supports modern technologies like Path Tracing, and even works surprisingly well on Steam Deck.  The biggest highlight for me is definitely the clinic section with Grace. The exploration, tension, resource management, and especially the zombies are incredible. These are some of the best zombies in the entire series. They still feel like they have pieces of humanity left, creating some genuinely disturbing and memorable moments.  I also really enjoyed the contrast between Grace and Leon. Grace focuses more on survival, crafting, and avoiding danger, while Leon is a full action hero straight out of Resident Evil 4 Remake. Both styles work well, although I think the game could have balanced their sections better.  Unfortunately, the game loses some of its magic later on. Leon's sections become much more action focused, the story starts making questionable decisions, and some characters feel like wasted potential. The final parts also don't reach the same level as the amazing beginning.  Despite those issues, Resident Evil Requiem is still an excellent Resident Evil game. It is brutal, atmospheric, beautifully made, and shows that Capcom can still create memorable survival horror.  It was very close to becoming one of the best games in the franchise, but a few design choices hold it back.  Pros:  + Amazing atmosphere and horror design + Probably the best zombies in the series + Fantastic audiovisual presentation + Great PC optimization + Grace's survival horror sections + Excellent exploration and tension  Cons:  - Second half is weaker than the beginning - Final boss and ending could be better - First-person FOV is limited  Highly recommended for Resident Evil fans and survival horror players.

Upon writing I've just finished the game for the 4th time and unlocked all its achievements. Just when I thought Capcom couldn't think of how can their 9th major Resident Evil installment could get any better, they really sat down and ingeniously designed this masterpiece to play on real phobias.   Spoilers ahead!  ------------------------  Fear of the Dark - The monster in the dark mechanic. In this game, there's a stalker monster that you cannot defeat until its boss fight much like Mr X in RE2R. However, unlike the Tyrant, she is vulnerable to light. Well-lit rooms are safe but all of your objectives are in the dark. Safety is temporary-- but sooner or later you have to step into the darkness in order to leave.  Fear of Blood - There's a lot of blood in this game, I swear. There's even a game mechanic you have to collect blood in order to craft items. Every enemy you take down spews out bloody chunks of their organs, buckets of blood all over the map, a bath tub full of blood, blood transfusion bags, defeated enemies exploding like a blood bomb, a body processing site where your character slides into a pool of blood. A vampire's buffet! veh vev vleh!  Fear of Loud Sounds - There are two enemies that have sonic screaming attacks. It made my ears hurt because I have headphones on and it staggers your character when up too close.  Fear of Undead - Well, it's Resident Evil of course it has zombies HAHAHA  Fear of Spiders - Spider enemies the size of a baby, oh and their big mama spider. At some point of the game I was saying "OH THANK GOD I'M LEON NOW, I'M OUTSIDE, I HAVE GUNS AND THE POWER OF THE SUN ON MY SIDE" and then this giant sunavabich isn't subscribed to photophobia.  Fear of Heights - There's one section where Leon has to navigate through a slanted building and the camera forces the player to look down when he is balancing on the beam. There's also a section where he fights on glass floor so if he's a little too careless, it would be an insta-death when you fall.  Fear of Tight spaces - The corridors of the care center are very narrow, even more emphasized when a big monster called Chunk tries to navigate and fit himself through these hallways.  Fear of Medical procedures and items - A significant part of the game is set in a hospital so there's a lot of that going on HAHAHA and not to mention there's a part where you have to grab those artificial organs and put them inside a dead body 😭 and then body goes online LMAO  Fear of Giant things - Chunk is a giant monster. The Girl is a giant monster. The spider is a giant monster. The final boss in his Nemesis form is a giant monster too.   -----------------------  Resident Evil Requiem is a love letter, a masterpiece and I wouldn't recommend anyone new to this franchise to start with RE9. If you're planning to play this game, it is essential that you finish RE2R and RE4R first. That way, you learn how the modern resident evil games work and appreciate the callbacks in the RPD. Who knows, you might find yourself saying "I remember you!".  Grace's section is a mix of RE2R's survival horror with RE7's psychological terror. While you feel like most of the horror is present when playing as Grace, Capcom made sure to instill a portfolio of fears into Leon's action sections as well.  The game doesn't solely rely on jumpscares to be terrifying, but Capcom designed it in a way where there will surely be something that scares you regardless of which character you're playing-- if not the dark, then perhaps spiders.

The atmosphere is what kept me hooked. There were so many moments where I slowed down just because I had no idea what was waiting around the next corner. The graphics are beautiful. Some areas genuinely made me stop for a second just to look around. The RE Engine continues to impress, especially with the lighting and character animations. One thing that really stood out to me was Zeno. He gave me strong Wesker vibes throughout the game. It's not that he's a copy, but there's something about his calm confidence, the way he carries himself, and the sense that he's always one step ahead that reminded me of Wesker. Requiem does a fantastic job of bringing together so many of the elements and characters that have made Resident Evil so memorable over the years, and it really felt like a celebration of the series without losing its own identity.   And Leon... it's always great to see him. He's still one of my favorite characters in the series, and every time he's on screen the game just gets even better.  It's not a perfect game. There are a few moments where the pacing slows down a bit, and a couple of sections felt like they could've been shorter. But honestly, those are small complaints compared to everything the game does well.  Overall, I had a great time with it. If you're a Resident Evil fan, I think this is an easy recommendation. [b]TL;DR:[/b] Two great games in one box: a genuinely scary survival horror campaign (Grace, first person) and a confident action campaign (Leon, third person). Play it as intended, and turn on Classic mode if you like ink ribbons and suffering. One late-game scene fumbles the story's biggest gut-punch, and it's the only thing keeping this from a perfect score. Recommended, easily.  [hr][/hr]  [h1]My setup[/h1] Classic mode, default perspectives. Path tracing at 1440p on an ultrawide OLED.  [h1]The short version[/h1] This game jumpscared me more as Leon than it ever did as Grace. Grace gets a handgun and a shove, so on Classic I was locked in every second and nothing could touch me. Leon parries rockets, so I relaxed, and that's exactly when the game got its hands on me. My fear demanded my full attention as Grace. Leon made me careless. I don't think that inversion is an accident.  [h1]Grace's half[/h1] Classic-style survival horror with modern teeth. Ink ribbons on Classic mode turn every save into a purchase. The blood-collection system turns gore into crafting supply, including ink. Her hands shake when she aims, her panic bleeds into your inputs, and Wrenwood Hotel in the dark is some of the best horror Capcom has ever staged. The stalker (you'll know her when you see her) tracks you through walls, ignores standard gunfire, and turns your own flashlight into a liability. Rough, in the best way.  [h1]Leon's half[/h1] The palate cleanser. A slower, older, tankier Leon with a hatchet you have to maintain and a parry that works on things parries should not work on. Individually incredible set pieces (the Mr. X rematch and the highway bike chase are all-timers), with connective tissue that's slightly less focused. You're managing logistics more than survival. Raccoon City looks like a corpse because it is one; the drab is the point.  [h1]The one real flaw (spoilers)[/h1] [spoiler]The game hands you the trigger on its most devastating kill, forces the outcome no matter where you aim, lets you carry the guilt for hours, then reveals the death didn't count. A choice that was never a choice, and grief refunded in a cutscene. Give players real agency at that trigger and I'd have nothing left to complain about.[/spoiler]  [h1]Performance[/h1] Clean launch on my rig. Path tracing at 1440p ran great; 4K with PT never held a framerate I could live with. Native 21:9 support, though cutscenes letterbox (a community mod fixes it). No crashes, no stutter worth logging.  [hr][/hr]  [b]Verdict:[/b] Play it the intended way: first person for Grace, third for Leon, Classic if you've got the stomach. Survival horror enjoyers eat first. If you want a full legacy-cast reunion, temper expectations. Everyone else gets survival horror operating with full confidence.  [b]TL;DR:[/b] Two great games, one box, one late-game fumble. Recommended, easily.

Resident Evil Requiem starts extremely strong, delivering a tense survival horror experience that feels very true to the spirit of the series. The opening hours are easily the highlight. Tight environments, limited resources, and constant pressure create a real sense of vulnerability that feels like classic Resident Evil at its best even if the world to explore is very limited.  As the game moves into its middle and late sections, the tone shifts. Survival horror slowly gives way to larger scale action sequences, including more militarized enemies and wave-style combat. These parts are not bad on their own, but they reduce the tension that made the beginning so strong. It starts to feel more like structured combat encounters than survival.  The atmosphere also changes. Early on, silence and environmental sound do a lot of the work. Later, constant (and very repetitive) music reduce that feeling of dread and make everything feel more standard and less tense.   The final section continues this direction. While it does provide closure to Leon’s story, it feels a bit rushed. The pacing is uneven, and the ending is not very intuitive, with choices that are not clearly explained, making it easy to end up with an unintended outcome.  Overall, Resident Evil Requiem is a strong game with an excellent first half, but it loses consistency in its second. It begins as great "modern" Resident Evil experiences, but ends up leaning too much into action and failing to be as consistently engaging. In the end, it is still a good game, just an uneven one.

I've had some serious doubts when I first looked at Resident Evil Requiem. I kept wondering what the series would become after the end of Ethan Winters’ story, and I was genuinely curious about how Leon’s part would be handled. The overall premise felt almost too ambitious to execute well. Returning to Raccoon City is a huge topic, and even after I started playing, I still wasn’t fully convinced, especially with how drastically the gameplay shifted between Grace’s atmospheric, tense sequence and Leon’s one‑liners, which were funny but felt out of place in a modern Resident Evil title. But I kept playing until the end, and to my surprise, Resident Evil Requiem is now, for me, the best RE game right beside RE4.  Separating stealth‑horror and action‑shooter gameplay between Grace and Leon is an incredibly risky decision, but here it’s executed brilliantly. Grace spends the entire game simply trying to survive with minimal equipment, while Leon blasts through anything that stands in his way. This structure allows the game to do something no Resident Evil has done before: create a protagonist  (Grace) who doesn’t follow the classic progression of collecting a ridiculous amount of gear toward the finale. She stays vulnerable from beginning to end, relying on limited tools and pure survival instinct, while Leon handles the heavy combat sections. It’s a bold contrast, and it works astonishingly well.  As of the lore, the game is packed with small easter eggs, clever twists, and genuinely masterful lore writing. After playing most of the franchise, I thought nothing could surprise me anymore but this game absolutely did for reasons I wont get here for the sake of avoiding spoilers. It’s simply genius.  Capcom, this game truly feels like a love letter to the fans. An absolutely outstanding experience.
