Resident Evil has always been one of my comfort foods the same way some people turn to Fast and Furious or Mission: Impossible. It’s my favorite zombie franchise. While most games and movies are about surviving the end of the world, Resident Evil is about stopping it from happening in the first place. It’s sincere, over-the-top, and consistently delivers strong gameplay no matter which entry you pick. Even the weaker games have plenty to appreciate and remain genuinely fun. You can forgive their flaws because new releases come often enough that you’re never stuck with mediocrity for too long. As a fan, I’m willing to roll with the occasional lesser entry.  With all that said, Requiem is certainly an… interesting one.  The game tries to do a lot, and much of it is executed very well though not everything lands. It often feels like two different games stitched together. Both are solid on their own, but neither gets to fully shine because of the other.  Like several entries before it, Requiem features dual protagonists: Grace and Leon here. What’s new this time is how you swap between them dynamically as the story progresses, rather than choosing at the start. It’s also the first time the protagonists play with vastly different styles.  Grace is not a soldier. Her sections play like classic survival horror: first-person perspective, limited resources, and few options for defense. She feels sluggish and awkward in a fight. Leon, by contrast, is older and battle-hardened. His segments are in third-person, gives him a wide arsenal, strong melee options, parries, takedowns, and fluid movement. Even their inventories differ. Grace uses the classic item-slot system, while Leon has the RE4-style grid. These aren’t just two characters; they’re two entirely different ways to play.  And you know what? It kind of works… kind of.  The problem is the constant swapping. Just as you settle into the groove of one style, the game yanks you into the other. It’s jarring to go from playing conservatively as Grace, carefully managing every bullet, to suddenly chewing through ammo as Leon, only to be thrown back into scarcity again. I genuinely enjoyed both characters’ segments. They're fun on their own. What I didn’t like was having them ripped away right when I was enjoiying them most.  On top of that, I’m not entirely convinced the game was originally designed this way. Leon’s sections often feel tacked-on and rushed. You notice little oddities: fences laid out like solid walls even though they aren’t connected to eachother, one random zipline linking two areas, a puzzle that has you collecting gasoline for generators linked to single gates, the armband that rewards kill points for upgrades, a combat encounter where you awkwardly aim under a vent waiting for enemies to drop down. It's a bunch of small things that gives the impression that the decision to make leon playable was added much later in development.  And yet, despite those issues, playing as Leon is an absolute blast. I can nitpick the design, but none of it stopped me from whooping everything’s ass and loving every second of it.  Story-wise, Requiem serves as a solid narrative send-off to the Raccoon City plotline. It wasn’t strictly necessary, but it provides a respectful enough capstone without grand twists or desperate attempts to “kill the past” so the franchise can move forward.  I was initially worried about Grace. She had all the red flags of a modern horror protagonist who reacts to everything for you. While that does happen, it’s far less grating than I feared. I grew to like her, and her voice actress does a fantastic job selling someone who’s trying to be brave even though she’s clearly not cut out for this nightmare. Leon, meanwhile, feels like a natural evolution. The RE4 remake dialed back his quippiness a bit too much; here, his more reserved, dry humor fits a man who’s seen decades of chaos and simply refuses to be fazed without turning into an uncaring jerk.  Requiem doesn’t quite feel like the Resident Evil 6 of the modern era, but it does feel like the precursor to whatever that game might be. It experiments with the formula, and not every decision sticks the landing. If the developers had fully committed to just one style, the game might have been stronger. Still, what they delivered is good enough and I had a boatload of fun with it.

Resident Evil Requiem is a fantastic addition to the series and successfully blends classic survival horror with modern gameplay. From the opening moments, the atmosphere is tense, unsettling, and packed with the kind of suspense that made the franchise famous. Every dark hallway and abandoned location keeps you on edge, making exploration just as nerve-racking as the combat itself.  The visuals are outstanding, with incredible lighting, detailed environments, and realistic character models that bring the world to life. Sound design deserves just as much praise—every distant footstep, creaking door, and terrifying creature adds to the constant feeling of dread.  Combat feels satisfying and deliberate, encouraging players to think carefully about conserving ammunition and resources instead of charging into every encounter. Puzzle design is another highlight, offering a great mix of challenge and variety that rewards exploration without slowing the pacing.  The story delivers plenty of mystery, memorable moments, and connections to the Resident Evil universe while introducing new ideas that keep the experience feeling fresh. Whether you're a longtime fan or new to the series, there's a lot to enjoy.  While there are a few minor pacing issues and some sections that could have benefited from more enemy variety, they do little to take away from an otherwise exceptional experience.  Overall, Resident Evil Requiem is one of the strongest entries in the franchise, combining terrifying atmosphere, polished gameplay, and excellent storytelling into a survival horror experience that's hard to put down. It's a must-play for horror fans.  Recommended.

A really good addition to the RE series, I thoroughly enjoyed it. You alternate between playing as Grace and Leon. Typically, Grace's sections lean more into the horror game atmosphere, where you hide, sneak around, and run away from monsters in down-right terrifying places, while as Leon you play more as a hardened combat machine (less survival horror, more action game vibe). I honestly preferred the Grace sections, since that is the type of game I prefer; I think they were much more tense and memorable. Either way though, the entire game is really good and despite its amazing graphics it runs quite smoothly (i.e., well optimized). My only criticism has to be this childish, modern obsession with 'boss fights', of which there are several. They seem like a pointless chore to be honest, and represent the thing I like least in these types of games (yes I hate Dark Souls and other boss-fight based games). But thankfully aside from I'd say about 5-6 boss fights in total, the game is littered with regular combat that you can approach however you like (and there's plenty of room for creativity what with how interactive things are). Furthermore, these hair and facial expression graphics are getting ridiculously good! Grace and Leon felt properly alive on my screen. Anyway, as a final note: the ending makes it abundantly clear that the series is not finished yet!

Resident Evil Requiem feels like Capcom trying to bring together two different sides of Resident Evil. It mixes the slow, stressful survival horror style of games like Resident Evil 2 and Resident Evil 7 with the more action-focused side that fans know from Resident Evil 4.  The biggest thing about the game is the two protagonists. Grace Ashcroft and Leon S. Kennedy offer completely different experiences. Grace’s sections focus more on fear, limited resources, and trying to survive against enemies that feel dangerous. You’re not playing as some unstoppable hero, you’re trying to stay alive and make smart decisions.  Then you have Leon, which completely changes the feeling of the game. His parts are more action-heavy, with faster combat and that confident “experienced agent” style that fans expect from him. The contrast between the two characters helps keep the game from feeling repetitive because you’re constantly switching between being hunted and fighting back.  The atmosphere is probably where the game shines the most. Resident Evil has always been good at making normal places feel uncomfortable, and Requiem leans into that with creepy environments, puzzles, and moments where the tension comes from not knowing what’s waiting ahead. The ability to play in first-person or third-person also gives players more control over how they experience the horror.  The only concern is the balance. Resident Evil has always struggled with finding the perfect mix between horror and action. Too much action and the fear disappears, but too much survival horror can make the game feel slow. Luckily, having Grace and Leon split those roles makes the idea work better than forcing one character to do everything.  Overall, Resident Evil Requiem feels like a celebration of what makes the series special. It has the fear, puzzles, and resource management of classic Resident Evil while still giving fans the action moments they love.  9/10. A strong mix of old and new Resident Evil. It understands that the series works best when you feel scared first, then powerful later.

RE9 uses elements of RE7 and RE4 by using dual protagonist. I like to play games as the developers intended my first play through. Grace plays in first person and it really gives you that immersive, tense feeling while playing her. She’s not as combat hardened as Leon and you feel it. Things feel scarier when you play as her. Then comes Leon, you’re in 3rd person, and it feels like good, old fashioned, zombie horde killing combat making short work of most enemies. But you’re playing tug-o-war with your feelings as you switch back and forth between the two.  Story ★ ★ ★ ★   RE starts you off with Grace. Resident Evil Requiem is a survival horror game where you play as an FBI analyst, Grace Ashcroft, who’s investigating mysteries surrounding the survivors of Raccoon City with help from Leon S. Kennedy. Out of all the Resident Evil games, this is one that I’ve been most excited about, which made me want to start the series! When people say this is one of the best Resident Evil games ever, I'm surprised because this is literally the 10th game in the main series, and for people to say that is insane. I’m glad that I’ve played all of the main games in preparation for this because this expanded a lot more of the series than I thought. The graphics just keep looking crisper and crisper with each game, as there’s so much beautiful scenery to look at with the amazing design of the building where Grace is, or even the ruins of the city that Leon is going through.   Grace Ashcroft became one of my favorite Resident Evil characters very quickly because of how grounded she is in the reality of the situation, where it’s very clear she has no experience outside the field, let alone inside it, and is gathering up the lore of the game very quickly. She gets scared very easily, and her stutters feel so genuine, thanks to the amazing acting. Leon’s character has a surprisingly large amount of depth, and it’s very clear he's gotten older and more experienced in the outside world. Still, he has some regret and guilt over his past experiences that he hasn’t let go of yet, and he’s trying to make amends with them. I love how it switches up the genre, balancing the horror and action elements perfectly, with so many fun action moments and so many terrifying horror moments. Sometimes I want the game to go back to the action elements because I get too scared to go through it. The action gets absolutely crazy, but it also gets awesome to see how far it’ll go, and make it so satisfying.   The story is very engaging, which I’m glad Resident Evil has been consistent with after Biohazard fixed the story that had been secondary for so long. At first, I thought the lore wasn’t quite as engaging as Biohazard or Village, but once you finish the game and get some extra content, it gave you A TON of it, and it definitely made up for it by giving such fascinating lore that fills in the blank that the previous games either didn’t explore, or didn’t present it in such an effective way like this did. The soundtrack is so beautiful that it’s been a while since a Resident Evil game gave such a memorable soundtrack, and the bosses are so fun to face that I think they are better than those in the previous games.   If I have some issues with the game, it’s that I could use a little more development of the main villains, who have clear motivations that make them interesting, and the story and Grace as a character are not quite there to be among the best villains of the series. There’s also a choice close to the ending that will change based on your decisions, and while I appreciate the attempt, it’s clearly wanting you to pick the definitive choice where the other choice is anticlimactic. Other than that, Resident Evil: Requiem is my second favorite game of the main series, and I felt sad after beating the game, knowing I had made such a huge journey for myself to get through the series, but I know I’ll go back to it and play other games that I’m sure I’ll enjoy because I’m a fan of the series.  9/10

Resident Evil Requiem is exactly the kind of sequel I was hoping for. It manages to capture everything that makes the Resident Evil series special while still feeling like a meaningful step forward. From the atmosphere and level design to the pacing and attention to detail, every part of the experience feels carefully crafted. It never loses sight of what made the franchise iconic in the first place: tension, exploration, resource management, and unforgettable moments that keep you on edge from beginning to end.  One of the biggest strengths is the atmosphere. Every location feels incredibly immersive, with detailed environments that tell their own stories without needing endless exposition. The lighting, sound design, and environmental details constantly create a sense of unease, making even simple exploration exciting. Walking through abandoned hallways or investigating mysterious rooms always feels suspenseful because you never know what might be waiting around the next corner.  The visual presentation is absolutely stunning. Character models are incredibly expressive, environments are packed with detail, and the overall art direction perfectly balances realism with the series' signature horror aesthetic. Every area feels distinct and memorable rather than blending together, making exploration rewarding in its own right.  The sound design deserves just as much praise. Every footstep, distant noise, creaking door, and unsettling ambient sound contributes to the tension. Instead of relying solely on jump scares, the game creates fear through anticipation. The soundtrack complements this perfectly, knowing exactly when to stay quiet and when to build intensity during important moments.  The gameplay strikes an excellent balance between survival horror and action. Resources always feel valuable, encouraging players to think carefully before using ammunition or healing items. Every encounter has weight, and choosing whether to fight or avoid enemies becomes an important part of the experience. That constant decision-making is one of the reasons Resident Evil remains such a satisfying series.  The pacing is another highlight. The game never feels rushed, but it also avoids dragging things out unnecessarily. It alternates between quiet exploration, puzzle-solving, tense encounters, and larger action sequences in a way that keeps the experience fresh from beginning to end. Every chapter introduces something new without abandoning the core identity of the game.  The puzzles are engaging because they reward observation and logical thinking rather than feeling like random obstacles. Solving them feels satisfying, especially when they unlock entirely new sections of the map or reveal hidden secrets. Exploration is constantly encouraged, and players who take their time are rewarded with useful resources, collectibles, and additional lore.  What really stands out is the overall level of polish. Every animation, interaction, and environmental detail contributes to an experience that feels cohesive and thoughtfully designed. Nothing seems out of place, and it's clear that a tremendous amount of care went into creating every aspect of the game.  The attention to detail is impressive. Small environmental storytelling moments, hidden references, clever callbacks for longtime fans, and subtle visual cues make the world feel believable and lived in. These little touches encourage exploration and make repeat playthroughs just as enjoyable as the first.  One of the things I appreciate most is that the game respects both longtime fans and newcomers. It contains plenty of references for people who have followed the series for years while still telling a story that is easy to become invested in without requiring encyclopedic knowledge of previous entries. That's not an easy balance to achieve, but it feels very natural here.  Replayability is another major strength. Higher difficulty settings, collectibles, hidden secrets, unlockable rewards, and the desire to improve completion times give players plenty of reasons to return. Resident Evil games have always been fun to replay, and this continues that tradition exceptionally well.  Overall, Resident Evil Requiem feels like a love letter to everything that has made the franchise successful over the years. It delivers suspense, memorable environments, satisfying gameplay, beautiful visuals, outstanding audio design, and an incredible atmosphere that stays with you long after you've finished playing. It's a fantastic example of how to evolve a legendary series while staying true to its roots, and it's an experience that horror fans should absolutely not miss.

Resident Evil Requiem is an amalgamation of Resident Evil 7, 4, 1 and unfortunately for me, 6.  As far as Grace's campaign is concerned, Capcom did an outstanding job for the most part. Her sections strongly evoke RE1 and 7, with claustrophobic spaces, tight resource and inventory management, thoughtful backtracking and genuine survival horror that forces a cautious playstyle as the roaming enemies can overwhelm you easily.  Leon's campaign, however, I am mixed on. While a lot of players compare it to RE4, to me it feels closer to what RE6 could have been if executed well -on the other hand, if you have played the latter you'll know that wasn't exactly a high bar to clear. If you insist on the RE4 comparison, imagine what a full campaign of the Island section would look like, but with none of the atmospheric horror or enemies like the Regenerators. Classic, formidable enemies like the Lickers are reduced to zombie-level fodder, while the iconic stalker Mr. X becomes a one-time boss encounter that Leon simply bulldozes through.  Regarding the gameplay and animations, the first-person gameplay is smooth and reminiscent of RE Village. Third person on the other hand has an issue that I can only describe as overanimation. Grace stumbles about like a tank during chase sequences. Leon performs an exaggerated zigzag whenever you strafe even slightly. Whenever he drops from any height, it feels like a freight train landing -you'd think the sheer mass of his body would collapse the building. An exaggeration, obviously, but several such animations that drag on for too long ultimately add up to tiny, very frequent pace stoppers. There's a certain clunkiness to everything that RE4R just doesn't have.  Both of their character upgrade systems leave a lot to be desired: • With Grace, you cannot max out her Steroid and Stability bars as the necessary resources do not exist in a single playthrough. You find far more Antique Coins than there are rewards to spend them on, in fact, once you clear the Care Center, the coins become useless. I do understand the intent, the surplus acts as a contingency plan for those that skip rooms and encounters but still, it is disappointing. • As for Leon, you'll upgrade maybe two weapons at most per playthrough and the upgrades themselves don't feel all that impactful. His health comes pre-upgraded (no Yellow herb mechanic), and his attache case has like one upgrade and is massive after it, there will be no need for any inventory management. No colorful items, everything is gray. Treasure hunting is not a thing either; backtracking yields mostly ammo, maybe the occasional new weapon. The merchant is replaced by some sort of electronic box you use "credits" on to buy things. That strongly evokes Revelations or worse, a cheap multiplayer spin-off -a design choice I did not appreciate at all.  The overall narrative is about as mid as any plot in the RE franchise really, well maybe with the exception of RE7 as that game has a genuinely strong premise. The plot seemingly has bizarre gaps in logic: the antagonists desperately want Grace alive, yet they throw her into scenarios where she can get brutalized easily, with no intervention from them. Raccoon City was nuked... except not really, they kind of retcon that. Grace at some point walks away from Leon with her would be captors, just because Leon shot a mutated Emily to protect her -some random lab rat Grace met like a couple hours prior. Except at the end they retcon that too, in what is supposed to be a heartwarming revelation for the finale, Leon reveals "I didn't hit any of her vitals, we can save her".  The character portrayals are fine for the most part, with Grace being an absolute standout; her VA decided to act her heart out in a Resident Evil game of all things, I'll be surprised if she isn't at least a nominee for best VA at The Game Awards this year. Otherwise, I do not appreciate Spencer getting some sort of redemption arc and I find it wild that Zeno doesn't exist in-game outside of cutscenes, he could've been an alternate ending boss.  Leon's campaign aside, my other major criticisms of Requiem would be as follows:  • No proper NG+, they opted for the classic unlocks system where you start a fresh game every time, you just get unlocks in the storage box. I don't find that type of NG+ replayable at all, I haven't felt like returning to Requiem after I got all the challenges and achievements. • Certain things are heavily scripted, the worst offender being The Girl. There will be many instances where she might be chasing you or she might be inside a room in one second, then she'll teleport right around a corner and in front of you the next, that's as immersion breaking as it gets. • The Chloe section is mind-numbing and extremely prone to glitching. I'm generally not the biggest fan of the quintessential RE trope where you are forced to play as someone else for a short while, but Chloe's section is certainly the weakest. • The soundtrack disappointed me quite a bit. In RE games, the safe room theme is guaranteed to be a banger or at least something emotional that invokes some feeling of safety and comfort. Requiem completely failed there, with a barely noticeable, generic ambient background noise.  All in all, despite its shortcomings, I would say Requiem is a good game. Not excellent like I think RE7 and RE4 are, or even just great like Village and RE1, but it isn't bad.  The first playthrough is novel, scary (on Grace's side) and loads of fun, but subsequent runs grow dull fast. I believe that if the whole game had been designed like Grace's campaign, Requiem could easily be one of the best RE games ever made, but as it stands Leon's heavily action-oriented campaign really drags the experience down.  You should expect about 11 hours of playtime for your first playthrough if you take your time, maybe more if you have to repeat sections. There are those that would tell you that full price for Requiem would be fair as RE games tend to be replayable, but as I mentioned before, I found Requiem to be lacking in that regard so I'd say it'd be a solid buy at the 40-45€ price range. If Capcom patch in an actual NG+ system at some point, I'd recommend it at full price.

**Resident Evil Requiem** is probably the best-executed Resident Evil game in the franchise.  I've been a longtime fan, starting with **Resident Evil: Dead Aim** on the PS2, then moving on to **Resident Evil 4**, and more recently playing **Resident Evil 2 Remake**, **Resident Evil 3 Remake**, **Resident Evil 7**, and **Resident Evil 4 Remake**.  What impressed me the most is how Requiem successfully merges the two gameplay styles Capcom has been refining over the past few games. Grace's first-person sections deliver some of the most intense horror the series has seen in years, while Leon's third-person gameplay brings back the fast-paced, action-focused combat fans love.  The world Capcom crafted is absolutely incredible. From the Care Center to the ruins of Raccoon City, every environment is packed with detail and atmosphere. The graphics are stunning, but what really elevates the experience is the sound design. Every hallway, distant noise, and unsettling silence builds tension without feeling forced.  Playing as Grace has a unique feel that's hard to describe. The first-person perspective gives everything an almost analog quality, as if you're physically there instead of just looking through a camera. It makes the environments feel grounded, claustrophobic, and incredibly immersive.  The horror also deserves special praise. It's not psychological horror in the same way *Silent Hill 2* is, but Requiem creates fear in a way I honestly haven't experienced in another game. It constantly finds new ways to make you uncomfortable and keep you on edge without relying on cheap jump scares. Even after years of playing horror games, there were moments that genuinely caught me off guard.  And Leon? He's never been this badass before. Capcom absolutely nailed his portrayal. He's confident without feeling over-the-top, and every encounter makes you feel like you're playing as a veteran who has survived countless bioweapon outbreaks.  Instead of choosing between horror and action, Requiem embraces both and somehow makes them complement each other perfectly. It's the most balanced Resident Evil experience I've played. If this is the direction Resident Evil is heading, I genuinely can't wait to see what's next.

Ultimately, Requiem is a solid entry that offers a fascinating glimpse into the future direction of the franchise. It is, without a doubt, an experience well worth your time, leaving us eager to see how upcoming post-launch content will further enrich and round out the title. W-w-where do I start? Besides the laughable, forced stutter of the main character, Grace's campaign is great, managing to make you feel vulnerable and appreciate even regular zombies as real threats. The "stalker enemy" sections were not as organic/emergent as in other games like Amnesia: The Bunker (which I feel was an inspiration), but still extremely creepy.   On the other hand Leon's interleaved action campaign feels (clearly intentionally design-wise) like another game entirely that I could have maybe lived without, or played standalone. I wonder if this was done to give players a breather, or if Capcom is trying to appeal to every type of gamer in the diverse RE pool at once instead of trying to design a focused experience that can stand on its own shoulders ....After a while I felt jaded, also because the game ends up being very long as a consequence.  I loved the soundtrack, with some tracks mixing traditional acoustic instruments and electronic ones.  Technically speaking it runs (and looks) very well (stable 40 fps) on low/medium settings on the Deck, showing that the RE engine keeps on delivering.

Originally played on release day with an ROG Ally X, which ran the game really well with little to no issues.  I'll admit I just wanted to see Leon in the present day and what they'd do to him since his last timeline appearance on RE6, but I fell in love with both campaigns of this game!  Grace's sections were really immersive and brought me back to the survival horror experience I had with the first titles. The amount of times in which I was genuinely scared were far too many to count, which I loved! Her VA REALLY aided in that experience and really made me love the character that much more by the end of the game and makes me want to see more of her in the future.   Leon's sections were exactly what I wanted from a seasoned veteran of the franchise. No fear, no hesitation, just pure determination and drive throughout the entire game. His more human side continues to actually be shown in this game which I've really been enjoying since RE2RE and it just makes you appreciate his character a lot more throughout the years. Although I originally loved his portrayal in RE4 2005 the most, this game really is a fine addition to the world and the lore of Resident Evil. I can't wait for the DLC to come out already and in the meantime I'll continue to enjoy the rest of the games in the franchise in anticipation for its release. Requiem is, at the same time, a truly unique Resident Evil experience and a culmination of everything that has made the franchise memorable for nearly three decades. It’s both fresh and deeply embedded in RE DNA.  I really wish there had been more gameplay with Grace that resembled the very beginning of the game. Requiem was marketed and conceived as an ode to two distinct traditions within the franchise: Leon's action-horror lineage and the slower style of terror that recalls Village, and especially Resident Evil 7. My biggest criticism is that there is a significant imbalance between these two approaches. The game initially promises a dialogue between different interpretations of horror, but as the story progresses, that dialogue increasingly becomes a monologue. By the final act, much of the experience transforms into a cinematic action game adorned with horror imagery rather than a genuine coexistence of both styles. While I enjoyed the action immensely, I cannot help but wonder what Requiem would have looked like had it maintained the tension between vulnerability and power throughout its entire runtime.  One of my favourite aspects of the game is the incredible variety of its settings. Despite its relatively concise length, Requiem has a remarkable range of environments. Within my personal tastes, the most memorable locations were the beautiful ruined hotel, which was even Silent Hill-esque at times, and the hospital itself. The ruined hotel possesses a distinctly melancholic atmosphere, its rooms like fossilized remains of itself. The hospital is equally impressive, and what makes it effective is its range. It embraces the cold sterility of medical horror while simultaneously incorporating gothic lounges and strangely elegant chambers. It is well known that medicine itself became dehumanizing a long time ago, so of course it breeds fertile ground for a horror setting. Leon’s section in the ruins of Raccoon City contains some of the best post-apocalyptic imagery I've seen. The atmosphere reaches its peak upon entering the R.P.D. I did not play these games as a child, nor do I possess decades of nostalgia for them, and yet I felt an overwhelming sense of it. It was not just nostalgia for my own playthroughs, but nostalgia experienced through Leon. The ARK facility takes the coldness of medical institutions even further by combining it with science-fiction horror aesthetics, and even though that is not my personal niche, it still worked for me. What was very interesting to me is how these settings collectively form a kind of historical timeline of horror itself. The hotel evokes gothic horror, the hospital channels medical and psychological horror, and ARK pushes these anxieties into futuristic territory. Requiem moves through the evolution of horror as a genre while moving through its own narrative.  One of the strongest themes is the exploitation of children and the banality of evil. The villains commit horrific acts that are procedural and bureaucratic in the game, just as they are in real life, of course. The suffering is a variable in an equation. The villains rarely justify themselves through madness alone; their actions are necessary sacrifices in pursuit of progress, knowledge, or salvation. Hannah Arendt famously described evil not only as monstrous but also as banal, something capable of emerging through ordinary systems and rationalized decision-making. Requiem understands this concept very well, so I can say that Capcom uses it effectively for worldbuilding and especially character creation.  The archetype of the mad doctor is done very well. Historically, the mad doctor was always a figure who transgressed moral boundaries in pursuit of a supposedly greater good. Medicine itself exists at the threshold between life and death, so the physician is an inherently powerful and potentially frightening figure. Gideon's design is a brilliant example of this. His long hair gives him an almost prophetic appearance, while his strangely charismatic yet fundamentally uncharismatic personality creates an engaging contradiction. He possesses the confidence of a visionary but none of the warmth required to inspire genuine trust. That being said, I might be biased because I find him extremely attractive.  Yes, I love Leon. We all love Leon. He is as attractive as ever and as unintentionally funny as ever. However, in my opinion, Grace is the true protagonist of Requiem. I absolutely adore Grace as a character. She feels remarkably real to me. Some players may find her expressions of fear excessive during the opening hours, but I completely disagree. Despite her terror, she consistently makes intelligent decisions and adapts to impossible circumstances with believable competence. I cannot remember the last time I bonded with a horror protagonist this quickly. I’ve seen a lot of great fan art comparing her to Courage the Cowardly Dog, and the comparison is cute. Courage was never brave because he lacked fear; he was brave because he acted despite it, and he had HOPE. Grace embodies the same principle. Perhaps that is why I loved her immediately.  I have seen some people online suggest that Zeno exists because Capcom regretted killing Wesker, and I can believe it. The theory is hilarious because it would imply that when they tried to create a new Wesker, they realized the only way to do it was by making an even cooler one. The result? Platinum blonde hair, an earring, and a cigarette. I actually like his character. His stylish, nonchalant evil serves as a perfect contrast to Gideon. Gideon embodies obsessive ideological fanaticism; Zeno represents detached self-interest. Their differences prevent the villains from feeling repetitive and create a contrast between two different forms of corruption.  I find the symbolism of Elpis to be one of the game's most beautiful thematic elements. In Greek mythology, Elpis is often translated as "hope" and remains inside Pandora's jar after every other evil has escaped into the world. We have debated for centuries whether hope itself is a blessing or simply another illusion. Requiem seems deeply interested in this ambiguity, and I love when games don’t shy away from mythical themes and symbols. I would say that RE is actually one of the few games that goes a bit deeper than merely scratching the surface with philosophical keywords, and they really did create a solid narrative. The game title is also very beautiful; I thought so even when the name first dropped. A requiem is traditionally associated with mourning, yet mourning itself implies that something valuable has existed indeed.  The emotional weight of Requiem feels earned, and I wouldn’t say that it becomes excessively sentimental. In the end, Leon looks like he is somehow in his absolute prime, we get jokes about Chris Redfield, Emily gets saved, and Grace gaining confidence all contribute to what is essentially a fairy-tale ending. Horror has always been conservative; it has always been a struggle between good and evil. Resident Evil has never been interested in realism. It has always embraced excess, impossible heroes, grotesque monsters, and spectacle. Its horror is not the horror of inevitability but the horror of resistance. Because of that, the ending feels like the natural culmination of everything the series has always been. It is beautiful, and perhaps a little naïve. But Resident Evil has always believed that people can overcome horror, no matter how monstrous it becomes. For a franchise built upon such convictions, there could be no truer ending.

Another amazing game in the Resident evil series so obviously if you are a fan then it is a must!  Pros ---- - Amazing graphics, level design and lighting work! - Sounds and music also amazing! - Story is good and you also get to visit old places and learn information about the past. - Leon is back! Wiser and kicks ass as usual! - Gameplay wise, Leon is purely action focused (maybe a bit too much imo) while with Grace you get to fell truly survival horror! - Weapons have a good variety and some upgrades. - Extra game mode although I would like something like Mercenaries to be able to play with more characters. - Enemies have a variety and boses are good too, not to mention having some old ones back was a good surprise. - All gameplay elements feel like home if you played the previous games. - Blood system and decals are the best in the series so far! If only it had RE2 gore it would have been peak!  Neutral -------- - Performance having a 3070ti and 32gb ram is good for the most part, although at certain locations the fps drops is too intense even with DLSS on.  Bad ----  - Requiem, tries to mix the horror from RE7 and the action from RE4. Personally I would have preferred playing as 1 style of gameplay for the most part and have a 2nd campaign or a DLC of some sorts. However The whole back and fourth between Leon and Grace gives you a different, unique perspective which isn't bad but you don't get as immersed. Also Leon gameplay feels way more "arcade" at times even more from RE4 or even RE5 and should have been toned down. That being said, I really believe this feels like a RE game purely to Grace gameplay and feeling. I love Leon, but I don't believe the gameplay has been designed properly to do him justice. The "merchant" system also feels off. Obviously having an "actual" mechant wouldn't fit, but it would have been better to just find parts instead of this whole magic box and killing points thing. - Personally especially with Leon I find that shooting enemies feel that they are way too spongy at times and they don't react realistically. RE2 has been the peak with the reactiveness of zombies and the gore. - New "Zombies" were marketted as being "smart" and have unique behaviours etc, but there are only a few patterns. - Had several disappearing bodies within small period time (even with max settings), which felt like it broke immersion a lot.

"Pretty cool, right?"   This game is what I've wanted out of a Resident Evil game since I played the Resident Evil 2 Remake (2019). I loved that game as it was my introduction to these fantastic games. I felt true fear wandering the halls of the earie and overrun RPD, and I had been wanting to feel the same with future games.   Biohazard captured this, but I felt as though I missed some of the action. I wanted a good blend of both the action and the horror. That is exactly what this game manages to do right. It brings in both old and new characters that fit their playstyles perfectly, both with their own set of goals that manage to tie together quite nicely. The game feels scary to play, and yet still action packed when it needs to be.  This is easily one of my favorite Resident Evil games, and I look forward to CAPCOM's next title!

I had been waiting for years to get a proper, high quality mainline Resident Evil game starring Leon S. Kennedy that wasn't another remake. At the same time, I definitely didn't want another disaster like Resident Evil 6. Capcom clearly understood that making a genuinely terrifying horror game with Leon as the sole playable character would be difficult, so they introduced a brand new protagonist. That's how Grace Ashcroft came to be.  I think Capcom has finally found a satisfying balance between action and horror. After all, the Resident Evil fanbase has been split between those two extremes for years. Resident Evil 7 and Village also fell short of delivering horror that truly captured the identity of Resident Evil. Instead, they often felt more inspired by other successful horror titles such as Kojima's P.T. and Outlast.  Both Resident Evil 7 and Village have moments where it feels like the developers simply ran out of ideas and suddenly throw in mindless action with no real buildup or planning. One moment you're unarmed, slowly crawling through a terrifying house or dark forest, and the next you're driving a tank while fighting Magneto.  Grace fixes many of the problems Ethan had as a protagonist. Capcom's original approach with Ethan was to make him a blank slate so players could project themselves onto him, which left him with very little personality until Village suddenly turned him into a larger than life hero. Grace, on the other hand, is immediately engaging and believable from the opening of Resident Evil 9. Thanks to Angela Sant'Albano's phenomenal performance, she easily earns a place among the best characters in the franchise.  More importantly, Grace isn't a static character. You can actually see her grow more confident and courageous throughout the game. It's reflected in the way she speaks, her subtle body language, and the way she reacts to everything happening around her.  As for Leon, there's really nothing left to prove. Even after all these years, age hasn't slowed him down at all. He's exactly the hero fans expect him to be.  Unfortunately, the game isn't without flaws. Most of its issues become apparent during the second half, when Leon takes over. The level design noticeably declines, and returning to the Ark ends up being exactly the kind of tedious late game section that almost every Resident Evil game seems determined to include.  In the end, I'd say Resident Evil 9 is the best mainline entry since the original Resident Evil 4, and it's an essential experience for every fan of the series.

ABOSOLOTLY RECOIMEND  THSIS GAME IS PEAK A Cinematic Masterpiece If you are looking for a game that feels like a massive, high-budget movie, I highly recommend Resident Evil Requiem. The graphics are incredibly stunning, and the overall immersion makes it one of the most cinematic gaming experiences out there right now. The game introduces a fantastic plot centered around a new character named Grace (no spoilers here, but the story is genuinely great), and the controls and gameplay mechanics feel smooth and amazingly well-tuned.  Technical Performance & Ray Tracing To get the absolute best out of this game, playing with High Ray Tracing or Path Tracing is the way to go. It completely transforms the atmosphere and draws you right into the world.  For Mid-to-High End Cards (RTX 30/40/50 Series): If you are running a beefy card like a 5060 Ti 16GB, you're going to have an incredible visual experience. Even an RTX 4060 Ti can probably handle this game beautifully with high ray tracing turned on.  A Quick Modding Fix for Shimmering: If you notice any visual shimmering while playing, the game files are very easy to alter. I recommend manually replacing the default DLSS file with an updated version. Doing this won't break the game at all, and it completely cleans up the image quality.  Incredible Optimization for Older Cards Don't worry if you don't have a top-tier graphics card! The developers did an outstanding job optimizing this game. While the official store page might recommend a GTX 1660, the game is optimized so well that you can even run it on a card that is over a decade old, like the GTX 980 Ti.  Even if you are playing on a mid-range card that can't handle heavy ray tracing, you are still going to get a fantastic, smooth experience.  Final Verdict Whether you have a brand-new GPU to crank up the path tracing or an older rig just trying to experience Grace's story, Resident Evil Requiem is highly recommended. RE9 was breathtaking from beginning to end. I honestly can't tell you how much I loved this game in words alone, but it was easily one of the best in the franchise for me simply based off of the combat and the visuals alone. You honestly don't need prior knowledge of the games before playing this game, though I highly recommend that you do so for the full experience!  Pros: - [b] Combat/Gameplay. [/b] The gameplay was unbelievably smooth and incredibly fun. Since you follow two characters around with different skillsets/items, you get to explore several ways of attacking a problem. Stealth can be your best friend, or you can throw a literal can of gasoline at the zombies attacking you. The choice is yours. - [b] Atmosphere. [/b] The moment you start the game, you are immediately immersed in the story. Grace's side of the story was so eerie and terrifying from the get-go, but the moment you switch to Leon's POV, you somehow feel more at ease. Both feelings are intentional, and it's perfect. - [b] Visuals. [/b] When I was first thrown into the game, I found myself wandering around the street you start on in awe of how realistic it was. It still blows my mind how it felt like I was there in the flesh, rather than just playing a character. - [b] Replay Value. [/b] You can play this game several times and still have new things you can try to do. You can focus on the achievement grind, try to find things you didn't see/notice in your last playthrough, or even try speedrunning the game and see where you land. I managed to do all of these things, and I still find myself coming back to play it again. Plus, with the newly added gamemode, there's even more to go back to if you so choose. - [b] Difficulty. [/b] You don't have to play this game on the hardest mode to get the most out of this experience. If you like the RE modern or classic ways of saving your game, you can choose that specific setting. If you aren't the type of person who likes to grind a game out and throw yourself in a challenge, you aren't missing out on any experiences! Play as you like, and you should end up satisfied.  Cons: - [b] Nostalgia Factor. [/b] If you're a newcomer to the franchise, I would consider this game to be beginner friendly... for the most part. You might miss a few reveals here and there that an experienced fan would instantly recognize, but I don't think that it would take away from your experience. If anything, I think it might intrigue new fans further. - [b] Game Size/Requirements. [/b] It's a pretty big game if you are lacking space on whatever device you want to play it on. When I started playing RE games, it was on my laptop in college. I had spotty WIFI, and my laptop sounded like it was going to take off like an airplane whenever I played any type of game. Do I think my laptop then could play this now? Probably not. Yet, if you have something better than a low-end laptop that was made for schoolwork, I think you should be fine. This is the best entry in the series for a while for me. The game is beautifully grotesque. Gameplay is fun and varied and the sound design is perfect for the environments.  First half of the game is truly survival horror and reminds you of the old games in style. This game is also the scariest game in the first half since Resident Evil 7. The second half is more reminiscent of Resident Evil 4, 5 or 6 (or the remake trilogy) and while fun (very much so!), it does make it less scary and more of a power fantasy in zombie apocalypse.   Grace is wonderful new protagonist that fits the series so well and playing as "normal" human in horrifying environment helps set the horror of her portions of the game. She also brings so much humanity in very dark situation. Leon is tried and true veteran and playing his portions makes you feel that. Everything that was hard and scary for Grace is just target practice for Leon. You get to feel like super solider.  The story is really well done in the first portion, but in the latter half it does bring some plot holes or at least questionable decisions that don't make all sense for the series as whole and I think it's mostly because of the amount of fanservice that game wants to give to series fans.   All in all, the game is great and series fans and fans of horror games should definitely play this.  Gameplay: 8/10 Visuals: 9/10 Audio: 9/10 Story: 7.5/10 Characters: 8/10  Score: 8+/10

Requiem is pretty good Resident Evil experience, but it doesnt change the genre and adds not much new things to the series - feels like they wanted to play safe on re9 and (i guess) it worked, the game steals old fans' hearts.  [h2]What works in Requiem[/h2] - the game looks and sounds phenomenal - details in each room and subtle (sometimes disturbing) sounds in background make the whole playthrough more immersive.  - also, Capcom again proved that they'r GODS in terms of optimization. Like, really, there are 0 fps drops, 0 crashes and 0 bugs that could'v destroyed play (at least in my PC build, while many other modern games runs not that smooth)  [h2]The story we have seen[/h2] Plot in Requiem is like closed box made from many pieces that player gather through the game. At the very end, everything is clear, makes sense and fits in series (it fills in what the previous parts didn't tell).  Also it's a classic RE story, so basically we have seen it many times before: bad corporation(s) trying to take over the world? check. disturbing villain who wants to destroy main character? check. Leon saving the day? check. Little girls? check.  The main problem for me is the game was not really scary, even in Grace's parts. RE7 and RE8 have gotten us used to a sense of unease and fear of looking into the next corner. RE9 introduces some original monsters, but [b]most of the time they are scripted[/b] (RE3 Remake, looking at you) so "horror" parts dont make you feel terrified.  While Leon's comeback is something everyone wanted and he's character is still loveable (even though he is close to retired age and should have been more mature, he still has his specific sense of humor, which works well), Grace isn't that good. I would say she gets more irritating the more we play her.  She fights, then cries, screams and cries again...  ...Aaaand there we came to the most important part of Requiem.  Which is repetitiveness.  [h2]Solid(?) gameplay[/h2] Gameplay in Requiem is divided into action sequences with Leon and "scary" ones with Grace. In both cases the gunplay is really good - feels exactly like every RE.  But. The structure of game is very... Closed? There are no open spaces like in RE4, you just walk on the line like the devs want you to. Also at some point (in my case it was in the middle of story) you feel weary of the monotony. Coz it goes like that: 1. you take part in scary (scripted!) sequences with hiding 2. you must find 3 specific things and use them in specific location 3. you watch longer cutscene 4. then switch to Leon 5. and fight monsters 6. find 3 things... 7. then replay from 1  [h2]Overall...[/h2] Its REALLY good RE game and gameplay gives much fun. But dont expect anything new or series-changing - you have seen it many times before in RE2 (setting), RE3 [spoiler](Nemesis, and other well known characters from other games)[/spoiler], RE4 and 5 (Leon kicking off zombies a***s), RE7 and 8 (atmosphere). A the same time - it is not a disappointment. A nice game that plays safe.  Its [b]Leon aging like fine wine/10[/b]

I think RE: Requiem was a pretty good game overall, with some downsides here and there. The Requiem (which is a high caliber revolver that has massive damage per shot) shone quite well when playing as Grace during the first part of the game, but it loses its shine after playing as Leon, as he gets access to rifles, which featured better and more accurate shots, and faster damage distribution. In Leon's hands, I believe the Requiem should have been changed a bit so that it performed substantially better considering his extensive experience with firearms, and because it would have made it shine much more when playing with him (especially since bullets for it are rare even when playing as Leon).   I did like that Leon had access to weaponry with suppressors on them, so I was able to take a mixed approach of stealth and combat in the parts that allowed it.   Definitely a departure from some mechanics that were present in prior games, for better or for worse. - This game is intended to be played by using 1st person perspective while playing Grace, and 3rd person perspective when playing as Leon. I thought it was done quite well, and it also helped put emphasis on feeling like each character; as Grace in a first person view, you're much more close to the horrors, less aware of your surroundings, and it feels distinctly different compared to playing as Leon who fights swarms of enemies as the awesome rough and tough hero, afraid of nothing.  - The log of notes persists among playthroughs, so the challenge to collect them all doesn't need to be in a single playthrough. I'm (generally) a fan of games treating me like I have an eidetic memory, because otherwise I'd need to write down a bunch of stuff that I had already discovered.  - I'm not a huge fan of needing to use parrying mechanics, or boss fights that force me to use them. For me, the parrying mechanic feels forced in boss fights, and I'd argue that it's not a part of the gameplay experience that makes a "Resident Evil experience". My issue isn't that it exists, but that I'm forced to use it in (some) boss fights in order to avoid massive damage or just to survive.  - The ranked playthroughs system isn't present in Requiem, so there isn't a "beat the game in this amount of time, with no more than this amount of saves, on the highest difficulty" anymore. There is, however, a challenge to beat the game in under 4 hours, which I'm less of a fan of in this RE in particular since it doesn't feel great to do when playing as Grace. - In addition, there's a "Leon must die" mode, which focuses on a 1-life playthrough of the combat sections of the game (exclusively as Leon), and a door that teleports between different sections of the game, giving the opportunity to go to certain areas / fights, or to skip them. You obtain buffs after you (passively) collect enough blood from kills, and then choose from a set of upgrades. This mode is similar to a roguelite experience as you can get upgrades from utilizing challenge points, like unlocking a flaming axe to be able to obtain in a run, to starting with a med injector.

Wow! Incredible game! The best Resident Evil in the series. It's like they took all the lessons learned from the past games to craft their magnum opus.   The pacing is immaculate. From the start of the game to the end you're hooked and it never drags. There's absolutely zero padding or filler here.   The blending of the two distinct gameplay styles of Leon and Grace is a stroke of genius. It's survival horror at it's finest with Grace. Every bullet and resource counts with moments of genuine terror. Contrast that with the Leon sections where it's still horror but you generally have plenty of resources and you're a grizzled zombie killing bad ass. Both gameplay styles hold up brilliantly on their own but combine to make something special. The scariest horror games are a bit too draining for me. It's constant tension and stress so I can only stand shorter sessions. With this blend, you are never in that horror stress zone for too long because you switch to Leon and get to go beast mode on the zombies. This would already be a winning formula even if Leon's action combat was just average but it genuinely kicks ass. The best combat and gunplay in the series. It's just plain fun.  I have a pretty decent PC but the performance was also awesome. I wish Capcom would lease out this engine. Because it looks incredible and runs as well as it looks. I played in 4k with all settings completely maxed including ray tracing with DLSS on quality and I rarely ever saw any dips in fps or stutters. It was above 60fps at all times and rock solid with great 1% lows. You could probably play in native res with a little settings tweaking. I tested it in native and while it does look even more incredible, i wasn't able to hit a solid 60fps so I left it in quality DLSS. But that was to be expected for the settings I had it on and my rig. Overall, very well optimized while looking gorgeous.  I will definitely replay this game again at some point. And I very rarely do that for any single player game. My backlog is simply too big. But I know this one will get a replay somewhere down the line. I'm already looking forward to it.

[b] Quite possibly the best Resident Evil that has been released thus far. [/b]  While less focused on one genre, Requiem combines the best of all worlds in its gameplay. Classic survival horror is delivered in Grace Ashcroft's sections, delivering the same kind of terror and engaging map design as Resident Evil 2 and 7. On the opposite end, Leon S. Kennedy's sections have some of the most satisfying gameplay and action sequences I have ever experienced in a survival horror game, evoking the best memories from Resident Evil 4, 6, and even 8. The story is wild and bombastic, with plenty of nods to previous games in ways that are handled very well. For a game that puts you in consistent terror and dread for most of its runtime, the greater theme of hope served as a pleasant bow to Requiem's rollercoaster of a story. The game is visually gorgeous, and all of the various setpieces Leon and Grace visit each have their own distinct tone, amplifying the sense of isolation or fear. The enemy designs are viscerally awesome, watching the zombies come apart as you shoot them will never not be satisfyingly gross. Overall, this jack-of-all-trades of a Resident Evil game offers one of the most satisfying experiences of the entire franchise, rivaled only by 7 for its horror, and 4 for its action. It somehow performs both gameplay styles near flawlessly, making for a near perfect experience.  I do not know where the developers will go next with this franchise, but I'm unsure if their next product will be as well rounded and consistently enjoyable as this gem of a game.

Spoiler free  Out of all resident evil games, this has the best story. The themes of grief and dealing with failure permeate the story and are well woven into the game. The story has many strong emotional beats and parts that evoke empathy or pity for the characters. The villains are perhaps the most realistic (in personality and shortcomings, not abilities or biology) out of the whole series.  This is perhaps the scariest game I've ever played. Insanity mode as Grace is really tense and unpredictable, even on my second playthrough. It's also really really difficult; hours will be spent on as simple a goal as killing a handful of zombies and crossing a couple of rooms. For added clarification, I don't have infinite ammo and not every bonus weapon, so it could be much easier.  Unfortunately the game does have a major shortcoming, which is that Leon's more action focused gameplay is lackluster for an action based game, especially in comparison to resident evil 4 remake. The stun and melee system is less satisfying, the parrying is very flawed, and the weapon variety and weapon upgrade system gives less effective choices. There are only 3 pistols, one being an unlockable; and all of them are less satisfying and less of a reliable 'work horse' than in resident evil 4. For the most part every weapon category (except snipers) has a clearly defined best choices, and the more niche choices don't change up playstyle at all, which hurts the replayability.

Jako zalety muszę wskazać rozdziały z Grace Ashcroft w roli głównej: przerażający prześladowcy, wyśmienicie dopracowane lokacje, świetnie zbalansowana rozgrywka, wciągająca intryga. W idealnym świecie gra skupiałaby się wyłącznie wokół tej postaci, a Leon pojawiałby się tylko w przerywnikach.  Jako neutralny aspekt wskazuję rozdziały, w których bohaterem jest Leon Kennedy: kompetentna rozgrywka w stylu Resident Evil 4, starcia z bossami "bo jakieś muszą być", fabuła "bo musi mieć powód, żeby uczestniczyć w tej historii". W idealnym świecie ta historia byłaby czymś w rodzaju "Not a Hero" z Resident Evil 7 - dodatkiem dostępnym po zakończeniu głównej fabuły jako uzupełnienie luk w historii Grace.  Jako negatyw muszę wytknąć, że w tej grze jest więcej eksploracji Racoon City niż w Resident Evil 3 Remake, co po prostu mnie frustruje. Zamiast serwowania nostalgii w postaci zburzonego miasta, wolałbym tej eksploracji doświadczyć w 2020 roku. W ogóle troszkę za dużo tej nostalgii, tego powracania do RC. Jeszcze niedawno wydawało się, że seria może wyrosnąć z Racoon City i zapomnieć o Umbrelli (Resident Evil 7, Resident Evil Village), a przynajmniej zredukować ich znaczenie na tyle, by zrobić miejsce dla nowych konspiracji i nowych bohaterów.  Z drugiej strony, może w ogóle należało historię Leona wyciąć z Requiem i oddelegować ją do czegoś w rodzaju "Revelations 3", w którym uczestniczyliby wszyscy ocaleńcy z Racoon City. W takiej historii można nawet iść na maksa z nostalgią i nie żałować sobie nawiązań, easter eggów, cytatów, lokacji i bossów, z którymi w takiej lub innej formie już się mierzyliśmy.  Grę polecam, bo zalety i neutrale zdecydowanie przeważają, jeśli chodzi o sumę wrażeń.

The thing that makes RE9 fundamentally different from other games in this series is the fact that in the campaign you will be switching between two characters with wildly different skillsets and that makes for very different gameplay sections:  Grace is a regular civillian with no combat training and her sections, which are horror-focused play a lot like RE2. Particularly the parts in the Care center (which is most of her campaign) are for me on par with the best that game had to offer. The game recommends you use a first person view for her and that combined with the fact that you have few solid combat options and Grace is noticeably nervous makes for some very tense and immersive survival horror. However, for someone who is just naturally more stoic (not me), Grace's nervousness could potentially be irritating, especially since that persists through almost the whole campaign.  Leon is an action-superhero and plays a lot like in RE4. He is much stronger than Grace in combat and as such he can basically punch his way through any obstacle. His sections take up most of the mid- and much of the late game and although there are quite a few boss fights as Leon to keep the gameplay interesting, they are heavily slanted towards the lategame and in the middle there are some sections which are just a lot of Zombie shooting which can overstay its welcome at times (never substantially so though). Overall switching to Leon is usually a welcome change of pace allowing you some respite from the horror of what you face as Grace and being the Horror for once, although the stark change in tone may be sudden and unwelcome for some, particularly if you much prefer one of the game styles over the other.  RE9 is very much a Resident Evil game and retains most of the (mostly ridiculous) tropes that are common in these games for good and bad nor is it's story anything particularly praiseworthy (it gets the job done). As far as performance is concerned, I never had any issues with an unremarkable PC and graphics card. Ultimately I think this game is great to pick up for anyone who liked both RE2 and RE4 and overall is an excellent entry in the series and as such, well worth getting

Man I cannot get into the hype of this game. The entire first part of the game feels like an attempt to return to classic Resident Evil exploration and progression. Only without understanding the charm or satisfaction of it all. No fun merchants to bring levity, no interesting or unique areas to explore. Most of the things that we explore as the game progresses turn into 'hey remember this from RE2?' 'Hey Remember that from RE3?' The game tries to get by it's lack of imagination by throwing out nostalgia and nods to the rest of the series which doesn't help it's already lackluster and overly convoluted story. A story that adds almost nothing to the overall series instead of attempting to turn everything we thought about the events of Raccoon City on it's head, but instead just feels like a slap in the face to the games we loved. The gameplay itself can feel extremely good. Movement is tight, weapons and animation details are nice, Leon's combat is satisfying. But the constant switching between our two main characters is jarring at best, and frequently in the game, happens too often leading me to feel pulled in two directions rather than getting to fully invest myself in one of the perspectives. On top of that, most enemies in the game are the same monsters. Which is to be expected with a zombie game, but at least in previous entries we are given more unique monsters or elites to kill. I liked it okay, I don't think I liked it as much as 7 and 8. Personally, I feel like going for smaller side stories with stronger individual theming really did the series some good. Resi 7 had that whole southern gothic thing going on, Village had all that hammer horror stuff in Transylvania, what Requiem did was go back to what used to be the bread and butter of the series, Umbrella Corp, Raccoon City, large underground laboratories, Zombies... It's not that I have anything against any of these things and we were probably due for an installment like that, it just didn't feel quite as climactic as I think it should have.  I like the thing the game has going on with Grace and Leon as dual protagonists, respectively representing the Survival Horror and Action legacy of the series and they both play very well. There's also just something very satisfying to the entire idea of it, where after being put into an extended section of being disempowered, you are being in one where you are, if anything, overpowered and get to go ham on the enemies you had to hide from before. I think that's a very effective thing for a game with the tone of Resident Evil to do.  This series has been playing around with the action and horror dials for a pretty long time, I don't think ever quite managing to make everyone happy. I think people tend to prefer them more on the horror end, which I understand, but I think for a series that much into cheesy, over the top action movie conventions, I don't think that's necessarily the only way to go. People have their misgivings about 5 and 6 which are mostly justified but I don't think their tone and gameplay categorically doesn't work.  Requiem tries very hard to find some happy medium, which I think comes at the expense of not quite excelling at either. I think early on it is very strong but its middle third, set in Raccoon City, is... well, it's some of the most 2010 art direction and gameplay I've seen in a while. Which might be intentional but I don't think it quite works. That middle section of Leon in a bombed out Raccoon City hunting for a bunch of items is some of the most early PS3 stuff I've played in a hot minute, particularly because it's not like the story's moving forward much for how long that section is.  The story itself is also just kind of undercooked. It has all the individual bits and pieces of what you'd want from a Resident Evil story but... honestly, I think the main problem is just that the villains lack presence? It's a mad scientist named Dr. Gideon and a guy named Zeno who works for some secret organization and may or may not be a clone or something similar of Albert Wesker. They just don't have a whole lot of screentime and the latter doesn't even get to have a boss fight. Like, you'd think having a duo of villains would culminate in one having a fight with Grace and the other one with Leon at the climax but that never happens.  Now, I know there's probably some limits to how seriously the story in Resi is worth taking but honestly, I liked the more self contained stuff the last two numbered titles did, say what you want about Ethan but at least he had a pair of somewhat interesting stories in somewhat interesting setting with pretty interesting villain ensembles. And then there's the fact that, silly as the setup of the series is, now that, tragically, eugenics seems to be making a comeback, it's more relevant than it has been for a pretty long time. So it's not like now wouldn't be a good time to write stories about rich and powerful elites dabbling in genetic engineering and transhumanist evolution. Just saying.  Overall it was good. Not the best recent Resident Evil game but also not really a dissapointment. I want to see where the series goes from here. Wouldn't mind going back to Chris and having a more action heavy, militaristic setup in the next title again. Or maybe something more akin to an international spy thriller. Requiem was a appreciable effort to tie up the story of Umbrella in a way that's maybe not exactly neat but definitely satisfying enough.

Requiem is a gift to fans of the resident evil franchise! (arachnophobia people be ward giant spider boss) It feels like the makers took everything players liked about previous games and made it in to one so everyone can enjoy it. The acting, graphics, story and gameplay was all absolutely breath taking.   Grace and Leon sections/gameplay If you like the scary, more survival aspect of the franchise; Graces sections are amazing! The stalker enemy in this game is definitely the scariest. Knowing that no where is safe if its dark and she's about makes certain sections insanely overwhelming. They took what made RE7's horror fantastic and absolutely ran with it. The part where you need to escape the facility felt so much like RE2R and exploring the area without much ammo/heals made things much more challenging and I really enjoyed it.   If you prefer more action based titles, than Leon's sections have got you covered! Ample ammo, cool guns and quick movement make his sections feel more like RE4 and RE5 which is a good balance to the fear inducing Grace sections. I played his sections more like a run-and-gun just because it felt right, certain sections (like with the lickers) was so fun to play through because with grace I carefully sneaked around them but with Leon, if you're a good shot you can basically just YOLO your way through them. This carefree-ness in his sections makes the rare jump scare give you a heart attack.  Legacy A lot of this game felt like a direct reference to previous games and makes the 30th anniversary all the more prominent. Obviously, you have Raccoon city from re2 and exploring the after math of that game was so cool. Especially the RPD. God the RPD was so cool, looking around and going "ah I remember what was there!" and seeing things like stars office again was so fantastic! I hope in the future we revisit locations like this again. Something that I personally really liked was the bosses being reference to other games. With the main ones I can remember being a black tiger reference, plant 43 returns, HUNK, Mr X and a Nemesis at the end. I was half expecting Yawn to jump out at the end lmao.  Arachnophobia I have insanely bad arachnophobia and will admit I hated the spider boss with every fibre of my being because of it. Congratulations capcom you've outdone the fear that I felt fighting Black tiger and U8 combined. I understand why it was there, most people are just average scared of spiders and few are like me in the sense of VERY HELLA SCARED AND WILL HAVE HEART ATTACK. Genuinely had me shaking. I wish there was a setting that maybe made the fight easier/quicker and took away the smaller spiders for those like me and so those that don't have an irrational fear of spiders can still play the boss. I copied my strategy from re1 with black tiger which was aimlessly shoot untill it dies and try not to look at it for too long lmao. The sound mixed with the graphics were awful, never before had I wished for a worse PC. Even the small non boss spiders raised my blood pressure! Congrats again capcom for damn near killing me lmao.  Over all extremely good game for new and returning fans! Would recommend (even for my fellow Arachnophobia havers)

This game has it all. If you were a fan of the more horror focused Resident Evil games - like RE7 for example, or if you just like Resident Evil in First Person - then this game is for you. If you like the more action focused Resident Evil games like RE4, this game is also for you.  You can play as Grace in first person - as her sections are more horror focused and feature a tighter level design, and you can play as Leon in third person - as his sections are more action focused and feature a looser level design. All of the sections for both characters are so well-thought out, and they each flow into the story of the game very well. The game also has a lot of mechanics that make for longer playtimes, and often really cool moments. Leon's combat especially intrigued me in this game, his introduction mission was so damn cool.  The story is roughly the same as any Resident Evil story. Its just Umbrella doing more messed up things again. Its still a good story, but I feel like RE games have quite predictable stories at times, and I know thats probably a hot take. But i'm not being negative about the game, I am still really enjoying the story - and the gameplay is keeping me engaged.  There are plenty of easter eggs, collectibles, and things to go hunting and searching the levels for - which is always a good thing for a Resident Evil game imo.  Now, I have GOT to mention the graphics, because holy moly they are so good. Every section of this game looks almost photorealistic; the RE Engine is genuinely insane. I must mention the animations while i'm talking about the graphics too: there are so many animations for the same moments but animated specifically for first or third person with whichever character you want. They basically had to reanimate all of the sections twice over. You can play the game in whichever perspective you want and you will have no issues in the entire playthrough. The animations are also very reactive and realistic, and I even saw a video pointing out the detail of Grace's animations becoming more confident - as told by her change in posture as you go through the game.  I'm still pretty far from the end of the game, and it seems like it'll probably take me roughly the same amount of time as RE4 did. Difference is, I have enjoyed this game so much more. I can probably say its now my new favourite game in the franchise.  10/10
