👍 8.5/10  Resident Evil 9: Requiem is one of the strongest entries in the series in years. Capcom managed to blend the oppressive horror of Resident Evil 7 with the larger scale action moments that fans loved from Resident Evil 4 and Village. The return to Raccoon City feels surprisingly fresh, and the atmosphere is absolutely incredible. Some sections had me checking every corner before moving forward because the game does such a good job building tension. The lighting, sound design, and enemy encounters are some of the best the franchise has ever had.    Grace Ashcroft ended up being a much better protagonist than I expected. Her vulnerability makes the horror land harder, especially compared to some of the more combat-focused heroes from previous games. The story also does a good job connecting old and new Resident Evil lore without feeling like pure fan service.    Pros:  * Fantastic atmosphere and environmental storytelling * Great balance between survival horror and action * Some genuinely terrifying enemy encounters * Strong visuals and lighting effects * Raccoon City is handled with a lot of respect for longtime fans * Solid replay value with unlockables and alternate approaches  Cons:  * A few story twists are predictable if you’ve played every Resident Evil game * Some late game sections feel a little rushed * Certain boss fights rely more on spectacle than challenge * The campaign could have benefited from another hour or two of character development * A few enemy types are underused  My biggest criticism is that the game occasionally feels like it’s trying to satisfy both old school horror fans and action fans at the same time. Most of the time it works, but there are moments where the pacing stumbles because of it. Still, those issues are minor compared to everything the game gets right.  Overall, Resident Evil 9: Requiem is a worthy mainline sequel and easily one of the best modern Resident Evil games. It respects the franchise’s roots while pushing things forward in meaningful ways. If you’re a fan of survival horror, this is an easy recommendation.

🧟‍♂️🏙️ Resident Evil Requiem Review (With Leon Must Die DLC) 🏙️🧟‍♂️  🕹 Length: 18–25 hours (main story) | Much more with higher difficulties and DLC 💰 Price vs. Content: Excellent — long campaign, strong replayability, and worthwhile DLC ⚙ Optimization: Outstanding; extremely well optimized on PC 🎮 Difficulty: Moderate on standard modes, highly demanding on the toughest settings  🎮 Gameplay  Resident Evil Requiem feels like a celebration of everything that made the franchise great. Instead of committing entirely to horror or action, it successfully combines both styles into a single experience, creating one of the most complete Resident Evil games to date.  The game splits much of its focus between Grace and Leon S. Kennedy, and this dual approach works surprisingly well.  Grace's sections lean heavily into survival horror. Resources are scarce, enemies are threatening, and the atmosphere constantly keeps you on edge. These moments often feel closer to Resident Evil 7 or the most tense parts of Village, emphasizing vulnerability and fear.  Leon's sections, on the other hand, deliver the action-oriented gameplay that longtime fans have come to love. Combat is more aggressive, movement feels fluid, and the melee system adds a satisfying layer to encounters. Pulling off melee attacks, chaining kills, and optimizing combat encounters never gets old.  What's impressive is how naturally the game transitions between these two styles. It never feels like you're playing two disconnected experiences; instead, they complement each other and keep the pacing fresh throughout the entire campaign.  🏙️ The Return to Raccoon City  One of the most memorable aspects of the game is returning to locations tied to the franchise's history.  Walking through areas connected to Raccoon City again creates an incredible sense of nostalgia. Revisiting iconic places, including sections tied to the legendary police station, is something longtime fans will appreciate immediately.  Rather than relying purely on nostalgia, however, the game uses these locations to expand the story and show the lasting consequences of past events.  For anyone who grew up playing Resident Evil, these moments hit hard.  🗺️ Exploration & Progression  Compared to some previous entries, Requiem places a strong emphasis on exploration.  You'll spend a significant amount of time:  ✔ Searching for hidden resources ✔ Discovering optional rooms and secrets ✔ Finding collectibles ✔ Unlocking upgrades ✔ Hunting for treasures and rewards  The game rewards curiosity constantly, making exploration feel meaningful rather than optional filler.  The campaign is also surprisingly long. By Resident Evil standards, it feels like one of the more substantial entries in the series, especially if you're the type of player who likes to fully explore every area.  🔫 Combat, Upgrades & Charms  Combat feels fantastic.  Leon in particular has access to an excellent progression system that encourages experimentation.  The weapon upgrade system is deep enough to make each firearm feel distinct, while Charms provide additional bonuses and build customization options that give players reasons to revisit the game and try different loadouts.  The melee mechanics deserve special praise as well.  They add variety to encounters, help conserve ammunition, and simply make combat more satisfying. There are moments where you'll genuinely feel like you're farming aura thanks to how stylish and enjoyable Leon's gameplay can be.  🎵 Audio & Atmosphere  Resident Evil has always excelled at atmosphere, and Requiem is no exception.  The soundtrack does an excellent job of adapting to the game's changing tone:  Quiet and unsettling during Grace's horror sequences Intense and cinematic during Leon's action segments Emotional during major story moments  The sound design is equally impressive.  Footsteps, environmental noises, distant enemies, and ambient effects all contribute to the tension. Playing with headphones significantly enhances the experience.  💻 Technical Aspects  🎨 Graphics: Stunning visuals with excellent lighting, character models, and environmental detail  ⚡ Performance: Exceptionally optimized. With Ray Tracing enabled, FSR active, and running at 1080p, the game can maintain around 120 FPS on a Radeon RX 9060 XT 16GB, which is impressive considering the visual quality on display.  🎶 Sound: Fantastic soundtrack and top-tier sound design  🐞 Bugs: Very polished overall with no major issues encountered  🧩 Leon Must Die DLC  The Leon Must Die DLC is an excellent addition for players looking for a tougher challenge.  It pushes combat mechanics much further, requiring mastery of:  ✔ Weapon upgrades ✔ Melee systems ✔ Resource management ✔ Enemy patterns  Rather than feeling like a simple difficulty increase, it feels designed specifically for players who want to fully engage with the game's systems.  For experienced players, it's easily one of the highlights of the post-game content.  ✅ The Good:  ✔ Excellent balance between horror and action ✔ Grace and Leon complement each other perfectly ✔ Strong story with satisfying pacing ✔ Large amount of exploration ✔ Fun melee combat ✔ Deep weapon upgrades and Charms system ✔ Outstanding graphics and optimization ✔ Fantastic atmosphere and sound design ✔ Nostalgic return to Raccoon City locations ✔ Great replayability and DLC content  ❌ The Bad:  ✖ Some players may prefer either more horror or more action instead of the balanced approach ✖ A few progression systems can feel overwhelming initially ✖ Certain side activities lose importance on repeat playthroughs  ⭐ Final Verdict  Resident Evil Requiem feels like a love letter to the entire franchise.  It successfully combines the survival horror of games like Resident Evil 7 with the action-oriented strengths of titles such as Resident Evil 4 Remake, while adding meaningful exploration, strong progression systems, and an engaging story.  The return to Raccoon City is packed with nostalgia, the atmosphere is phenomenal, Leon's gameplay is incredibly fun, Grace's sections are genuinely tense, and the overall package offers a huge amount of content and replayability.  At first, a 9.5/10 might seem fair.  But after considering the campaign, exploration, combat systems, replay value, optimization, nostalgia, soundtrack, and DLC support, it's hard not to view it as one of the strongest entries in the entire series.  👉 Rating: 10/10 🏆🧟‍♂️🏙️🔥

This game disappointed me enough to write a review for it. It was only frustration that motivated me to finish the game, not the story, weapon progression, challenges, exploration or RE lore.   My main gripe was that combat mechanics was extremely sluggish in every sense (ie shooting, melee, weapon transition). I believe this comes from the decision to deviate away from RE4, 5, and 6 style of combat, which were very snappy and instantly reactive.  Here, you must be more skilled in your shots and strategic in timing of your reloads, picking up items, sharpening your axe (for Leon). I thought the sluggishness was just in Grace's section but Leon has the same speed in everything he does which going around enemies difficult. There's just so much delay transitioning from actions that you can be easily be grabbed if you can be easily attacked if you're not careful.  Surprisingly, it was not the bosses that I had a hard time with but regular zombies, mainly their grab attacks. I think all their attacks (unless they're holding a weapon) is a grab attack. There's whole animation for it which made me incredibly livid every single time. After being grabbed, Leon has to recover (ie getting back up, rubbing his shoulder or whatever) right after pushing them off or when he is hit by a projectile which when all added up, takes an ETERNITY. Parrying bosses is very easy but for regular enemies, that parrying window is small or non existent especially if they're in a group. You will be punished for solely relying on parrying everything which is understandable.   Another majorly disappointing aspect was Leon's melee attacks. In the trailer, it looked like we could perform cool varying melee attacks but Leon pretty much does the same move every time (roundhouse kick) and performing special attacks seem random? For example, Leon will perform a closeup kill with his current weapon and if near a wall, he will crush the zombies head into the wall but triggering these is tricky and highly unreliable. Shooting enemies in the knee or head will let you kick or use your axe regardless if you approach from the front, side, or rear.    I though using the axe by it self can reliably kill enemies but it does so little damage (despite the max upgrades) it's only good for parrying. And again with the action delay, when Leon does his axe attack, there are several moments where he is just left vulnerable to attacks since he needs to finish his animation. Like he will not move until he finishes his spin attack thing.   Shooting enemies also felt underwhelming. Not sure how else to describe it but it is not satisfying to kill them that way (or any way). Not even by carefully aimed headshots, riddling them with bullets, melee, sniper, shotgun, or blowing them up. There's that "pop" that older games have when it comes to headshots that modern games are lacking. I think it comes from the "smoothness" and overly realistic body ragdoll effect. I don't mean I have to feel almighty killing them with infinite ammo, but even with low ammo, no upgrades, no charms, it just felt like I was shooting a bullet sponge regardless of what I use. Playing Leon was like playing grace but I have more weapon choices.  Overall, I think they tried to combine all the RE games' mechanics and came out with something disappointing trying to please everyone. Instead of Grace and Leon having the same unhurried pace in all of their movements, I wish they were separate so we can enjoy two dedicated play styles.

[h2]If you don't have an SSD and plan to play on an HDD (like I did), keep in mind that cutscene audio will probably desync, and they may occasionally freeze. Outside of that, though, the game runs fine.[/h2]   With that said, this is a pretty damn solid game.  The standout for me is the boss fights. They're incredibly intense. The one that stuck with me the most was one where the game gives you a shotgun and tosses you in a cramped space with a massive enemy. Watching it barrel toward you, squeezing through narrow gaps while you try to maintain enough distance to stay alive—but stay close enough for the shotgun to be effective—is beyond exciting. I don't think there are many games out there that nail that feeling of dread and excitement at once.  The gunplay is excellent, too. Executions, or gun finishers, are great and definitely an amazing addition. Every time you get one, you just feel like such a badass.   But those are just Leon's sections.  Grace's sections are good for a different reason.  While playing as her, the game really doubles down on the horror and suspense feeling. I guess it's trying to emulate the original Resident Evil games, and it does that pretty well; combat is hard but doesn't feel impossible, and managing your limited inventory space with ammo, healing, and key items is just as engaging as it is in something like Resident Evil 2.  So, there's something for both sides of the fanbase. If you prefer Resident Evil when it's action-heavy and exciting, Leon delivers. If you miss the series' survival horror roots, Grace has you covered. Neither feels better than the other; they're simply different, and both are excellent.  And lastly, the presentation is amazing. The soundtrack reminds me of some of Doom Eternal's slower, more intense tracks, building tension when it needs to and making the big moments hit even harder. And between the care center and Raccoon City, the setting feels amazing.  Definitely worth playing. I'd give it a solid 8/10.  That should be enough to convince you to buy the game. Everything below is me nitpicking, and why I don't consider it above an 8/10.  [hr][/hr]  Overall, I think Requiem is a step down from Resident Evil 4 Remake. Everything it does is good—but it's just not as good as RE4R. Leon just feels heavier, which makes everything, from aiming your weapon to moving around, feel stiff and slow. It's not terrible, but it's definitely noticeable.  I think the melee combat highlights this more than anything else. Leon's hatchet hits harder than RE4R's combat knife, and sharpening it instead of paying for repairs is both cooler and more immersive. But it still doesn't make up for how versatile the knife felt. Parrying itself feels clunky because Leon just doesn't pull out the hatchet fast enough. It feels frustrating, especially when coming from RE4R, where the knife was instant and just super reliable and responsive.  Another thing is that enemies don't stagger as easily and take longer to kill, which forces you to be much more deliberate with your shots. In practice, this means you'll spend more time lining up your shots and waiting for the reticle to close, rather than actually shooting. Which in turn makes the gunplay feel slower.  My issue with Grace is completely different.  I actually like her sections. The problem is that they're paired with Leon's.  It's not even that I prefer Leon's action-heavy gameplay over Grace's horror-focused sections. The issue is the constant switching. Every time I got invested in Grace's slower, tense gameplay, the game would cut back to Leon. Then, just as I was having a blast mowing down zombies as Leon, it'd switch back to Grace.  The pacing ends up feeling awkward. Every perspective change forces me to readjust how I play, and it never feels right. It's a huge handicap on replayability for me; every time I think about starting a new run, I remember the perspective swapping and just lose interest.

I have a huge amount of love for the Resident Evil series, and while I haven't played all the games and haven't seen any of the movies, I can't help but fawn over Resident Evil Requiem. Though I adore this game, it has its issues. And I want it to be known that I only critique it the way I do because I love it so much. From the very first trailer where I saw the POV would switch between Grace and Leon, I got nervous. Balancing a game between two protagonists is a very difficult thing to do, especially in horror. Nonetheless, between two characters such as Leon, a borderline war-hardened hero, and Grace, an extremely traumatized, anxiety-ridden woman who typically works in an office as a technical analyst in the FBI. My friends and I speculated that you'll play as Leon in a powertrip fantasy, and get stripped of everything, switching to Grace. This wasn't far off; however, the split POV raised a different issue I didn't anticipate. Pacing. The Pacing in RE9 leaves something to be desired; I think Bizly said it best when talking about how the game felt like two very different small games, leaving you wanting more of both. In the second playthrough of RE9, you get the upgrade box WAY sooner as Leon, something I remember feeling slightly rushed about in my first playthrough. Something I think they might've added knowing this fact. I remember closing in on the end of the game, hoping for something to prolong it. RE4 took me roughly 26 hours to beat, which isn't 100%, or just the base game. However, I believe I beat RE9 in about 12 hours. With the campaign running a significantly shorter run time, AND having the POV split, the game goes by in the blink of an eye. Which makes me slightly disappointed regarding such an anticipated release. However, what there is of the game is nothing but to be adored. The first horror section that you play as Grace is easily argued as one of, if not the best part of the game. My personal favorite section is the return to Raccoon City as Leon. RE2 was my favorite game out of the series, and I've gone through more than 6 full playthroughs. So, being able to walk down the same halls in the RPD yet completely dilapidated, had me in the happiest Deja Vu of my life. Also, hats off to CAPCOM for the endless optimization; my rig is considered fairly low-end by modern standards, and I was honestly pretty afraid I wasn’t going to be able to run this game, but I could! It’s definitely not the best, but it’s damn good for what my PC is capable of.

I enjoyed this game a lot and I'd consider it one of the better installments among the RE Engine games (which are all fantastic). Gameplay was great, visuals were great, control feel and customization was the best it's ever been. So much about the player experience for this game was "just right".   The thing I like the most about RE9 was the gameplay and the replay value. I loved the Grace sections in particular because I always liked the stealth sections and Grace is all about stealth. Leon's gameplay is very much like RE4R. Flipping between the two very different character-centric design philosophies was really cool in my opinion.  Difficulty-wise, I certainly felt like this was much easier than RE7 or RE8 on first playthrough. Easy but fun. The enemies are very scripted, so simply by taking your time and watching how they behave, you can find optimal stealth routes relatively easily even on Insanity. Learn to stealth as Grace and learn to parry as Leon, and literally nothing can touch you. At the same time, I constantly hear that people found this to be one of the hardest Rezzy games. I'd strongly disagree, but it was still very fun.  Story-wise, I found it to be mediocre. RE9 is an homage to the original Resident Evil Trilogy, much like RE7 was an homage to horror films and RE8 was an homage to gothic horror. So it was an effective and entertaining nostalgia grab, but it was also one of the weaker stories in the franchise. Also the antagonists weren't that... smart.. (you'll see what I mean). There's a viable explanation for it though, so they get a pass, kinda. I would consider just about every other Rezzy antagonist to be better though.  The Scare Factor? Full marks. The atmosphere, sounds, level designs, perspective... All of it was Capcom's Rezzy team at their best. I was fantastic. There were plenty of jump scares of course, but it was the whole package in creating a memorable horror environment. Wonderfully done.  Overall, I can't recommend this game enough. It was fantastic. You should absolutely play Resident Evil Requiem.

What impressed me the most was the whole experience: the pacing, the locations, the storytelling, and the way the tension keeps building. The game does not rush. It moves slowly, but never feels boring. It constantly keeps you emotionally engaged, with the tension rising more and more as you progress. Playing as both Grace and Leon is a brilliant and very bold gameplay decision. With Grace, you will be scared. You have to run, sneak, stay alert, and carefully choose when it is even worth fighting. With Leon, you can still feel fear, but it almost feels like a different game. Where Grace has to survive and improvise, Leon feels much more direct and powerful. The best example is the blind zombie. For Grace, it was a serious threat. I used the fact that it reacts to sound to deal with several zombies and Chunk. Then, a while later, as Leon, I kicked the same type of enemy in the face and crushed what was left of its brain under my boot in about three seconds. On one hand, I really respect Capcom for such a brave shift in gameplay style and pacing. On the other hand, especially early on, these changes can be so frequent that it is sometimes hard to fully settle into the rhythm of the game. Still, that variety is also one of the game’s biggest strengths. It runs two parallel storylines and mixes survival horror with more direct action in a very interesting way. I saw someone compare it to whisky and cola, but served separately: whisky in one glass and cola in another. And honestly, there is something very accurate about that. The game is demanding, but never frustrating. Every repeated attempt still felt enjoyable, because I kept discovering new details I had missed before. The atmosphere, tension, pacing, and the bold decision to split the experience between two very different characters all work incredibly well. For me, this is a masterpiece.

An Absolute Masterpiece!  This entry brings a completely new atmosphere and a breath of fresh air to the Resident Evil franchise, largely thanks to its brilliant new protagonist, Grace Ashcroft. As an introverted FBI analyst who gets visibly nervous interacting with others due to her dark past, her vulnerability makes her incredibly relatable. On top of that, the addition of Emily completely stole my heart. Every single time they shared a moment and bonded, I found myself getting genuinely choked up and emotional. Seeing Grace finally looking genuinely happier at the end of the game after taking care of Emily and starting a life together was such a beautiful, rewarding payoff.  On the other side of the coin, the return of Leon S. Kennedy brings a massive wave of nostalgia. Sporting a much older, more mature demeanor, Leon delivers that classic tactical survival-action experience through the iconic third-person, over-the-shoulder perspective. The sheer contrast between Leon’s battle-hardened veteran experience with bioterrorism and Grace’s raw, naive struggle to just stay alive creates a phenomenal, emotionally driven dynamic. Capcom didn't just write Leon as a mindless "killing machine" this time; his character arc showcases the raw, human side of a veteran still carrying the heavy emotional baggage of the Raccoon City incident from 28 years ago.  Resident Evil Requiem is a modern masterpiece by Capcom. By seamlessly blending a deeply emotional narrative, the brilliant introduction of Grace Ashcroft, the legendary return of Leon, and a suffocatingly tense horror atmosphere, this game has set a brand new gold standard for the survival horror genre.  A GOTY nomination! 10/10 for sure.

Resident Evil Requiem is a survival horror game set in the classic Resident Evil universe, which means dark corridors, lurking undead monsters, and scarce resources. The story is interesting, the music and graphics are great, and the setting and ambience of the game are on point — very creepy. It is everything players have come to expect from a Resident Evil game.  What marks this game as different from its predecessors is that it is, at least from a gameplay perspective, not one but two games. This game has two main characters that you alternate between as the story progresses: Grace, the jumpy FBI investigator, and Leon, the hardcore zombie-killing, one-liner-delivering veteran, and each character has its own distinct playstyle. When you play as Grace, the game turns into a stealth game with combat elements. When you play as Leon, you play a combat game with stealth elements. This is both good and bad, depending on what you like.  All in all, this is a good game, though I'd probably wait for a sale to get it unless you're a Resident Evil fan.

When it comes to the major franchises, I've always admired Resident Evil's versatility and willingness to reinvent itself more than I've actually loved the games. Sure, when a new one comes out, I play it, enjoy it and typically don't think about it much beyond that. Requiem stuck with me though.  This game is marketed as the conclusion to the story they started 30 years ago in the very first game. Hence it utilizes what makes the series appealing by separating the gameplay into 2 character perspectives. Survival horror through Grace's perspective and visceral action from Leon's. The result is a very refreshing cycle of building tension followed by the cathartic release of combat. It makes for an overall very engaging experience from beginning to end paired with superb presentation, performances and a suited soundtrack.  Really, I don't have much else to add. I know some people have reservations about the story and how it's almost too referential to the lore and relies on callbacks to older games for it's cooler moments and I do get that. But I also personally think RE lore is kinda dumb and is really great at chanelling the camp so none of this bothered me.   Overall, a lot of what I said about Pragmata applies here. It's short but sweet, super replayable and continues the lesson of "less is more". I even have to give it props for ending things on a more optimistic note than I would've expected. This might be my new favorite Resident Evil so it gets my full recommendation.

Absolutely loved this game, beat it 3 times in the first week and plan to keep playing, especially once the DLC releases.  The game manages to compact everything great about every game that came out after 2017 into one awesome package. The Grace sections are tense and unnerving, the Girl is the best stalker enemy in the series by a landslide, the games tight corridors and excellent level design make her a constant threat unlike Jack Baker, and she's used sparingly so she never becomes an annoyance like Mr. X. Modern Survival Horror at it's Finest. Meanwhile Leon's sections are refined, high octane action, without ever devolving into spectacle porn like RE6 (except for one moment but it was awesome don't lie). It's a fantastic evolution of RE4R's core gameplay. The hatchet being repairable in combat lets you stay in the fray of combat without fear of losing your lifeline, and the new contextual finisher moves are so flashy and fun.  That's not to say it's perfect, there are a few complaints I have that hold it back from perfection. The game could have been longer and shorter at the same time. While I have come around on Leon's section of the game a lot more once I figured out how to route it, I still feel like it overstays its welcome a bit, which admittedly wouldn't be so bad if there was more enemy variety more interesting gameplay than "go collect some stuff". The weapons in this game are also a straight downgrade from RE4R. One of the best parts of RE4 and RE4R's weapon selection is that every weapon serves a different purpose, none of them are straight upgrades from any weapon, it's up to the player to experiment and find what they like using best, there's an argument for the use of every weapon in RE4, and yet RE9 fails in this aspect. Many weapons are straight upgrades, selling guns back to box doesn't refund your upgrades too, Exclusive upgrades are missing, and there's far less selection. It's really unfortunate because they're modeled so well and all feel so great to shoot, I forced myself to use the Alligator Snapper over the Silencer9 despite it being objectively worse, just because I always like using the default handgun.  At the same time Grace's section feels like so much more could have been done, I wish the Care Centre was longer with more to do and explore, and I especially wish her final section at the ending was longer, and probably my absolute biggest complaint is she doesn't even get a final boss of her own, give Grace her rocket launcher moment!  The story is also nonsense if you think about it for 5 minutes. The villains need Grace alive for their plan to work, so they kidnap her and drop her in a hospital with deadly monsters and just kinda leave here there, before they kidnap her again to bring her to where they actually needed her, which they probably could've done immediately, but I digress. It still has plenty of charm and camp, and at this point I'll play anything Capcom puts Leon in.  All that being said, I loved this game, warts and all, it's messy at times but has plenty of heart where it needs it. Resident Evil fans are truly spoiled.

How far we've come. From its humble beginnings in the REtro Era, through the high-octane REvolution of the mid-2000s, to the brilliant horror REnaissance Era sparked by RE7, the franchise has reached a new peak in 2026 with Resident Evil Requiem. It easily stands as a modern masterpiece, comfortably locking down a spot in most fans' top 5 games of the entire series and will more than likely find itself with multiple nominations at this year's The Game Awards.  Requiem is an absolute triumph of game design, offering immense replayability, rich lore that deeply rewards long-time fans, and stunning visual animations. The voice acting and mocap performances are stellar across the board, setting an incredibly high bar that the next installment will struggle to clear.  What makes the game truly special is its flawless pacing. The combat encounters are fiercely intense, while the horror remains a slow, creeping, anxiety-inducing burn that never feels cheap, repetitive, or boring. This tension is backed by highly competent enemy AI that keeps you on edge without ever breaking immersion, alongside stellar sound design that makes every creaking floorboard terrifying.  Mechanically, the game pulls off a massive feat: switching between the first-person perspective for Grace's psychological horror chapters and the over-the-shoulder third-person camera for Leon's action-heavy segments feels entirely natural. Giving players the total freedom to toggle their preferred perspective is a massive, welcome quality-of-life addition.  However, Requiem isn't entirely without its flaws, and a few notable criticisms hold it back from absolute perfection. While the exploration is gripping, more variety in the puzzles would have been highly appreciated, as they occasionally lean on overly familiar tropes rather than challenging your wits. And in so many of the cases it boils down to finding a piece of paper with a code on it.  The character progression also feels slightly stagnant; a bit more meaningful "leveling up" or deeper upgrade systems for the protagonists would have gone a long way in making the late-game loop feel more rewarding. Furthermore, the game suffers from an immense, almost artificial jump in difficulty when you step up to Insanity mode—a punishing ordeal that feels damn near impossible to complete without unlocking unlimited ammo first.  And finally, the main package vastly outshines its extra content; the bundled Bonus Game turns out to be incredibly half-baked and underwhelming, serving as a tacked-on afterthought compared to the masterclass standard of the main campaign.  Ultimately, these grievances are minor blemishes on what is otherwise a staggering achievement in survival horror. Resident Evil Requiem successfully honours thirty years of franchise history by masterfully marrying its two modern identities into one cohesive, terrifying package. It is a confident, gripping ride that leaves a massive, echoing hole to fill for the future of the series. It is an absolute must-play for veterans and newcomers alike and a very worthy addition to the Resident Evil Universe.

Grace's sections were by and far the most fun I had in the game, but my favourite RE game is RE7 so it's no surprise. Leon's sections are enjoyable being more along the lines of RE4 and the more combat heavy RE games, and as a de-stresser from Grace's sections (Where I was in terror and so incredibly stressed over no ammo consistently).  This formula was well done for the game, as someone who enjoys both styles, I do hope they attempt this again for another RE game.   The story was a nice wrap up for the early RE story to date, pretty nicely ending the saga for a new story. Grace's development from nervous and freaked, to trying to maintain herself for the sake of Emily was great, her getting better not for herself, but for the sake a child, despite having no connections to her, is moving to me.  Leon being forced to face the past and his failures is a compelling narrative, and the final section of the game is memorable and a standard for RE games.  RE9 is great, it's amazing how well they've pivoted this series compared to RE6.

[h3]9/10[/h3]  [b][EN][/b] [h2]Back on Track![/h2]  Damn, where do I begin? Capcom surely knows how to do fan service: bringing back old characters (friends and foes - some of them in a way), making Resident Evil 2 and Outbreak references and Easter Eggs, bringing back a music composer from the original games, returning to Raccoon City and R.P.D.… The franchise is getting back on its track when it comes to its characters and action. Oh, and speaking of bringing back things, even Mr. Raccoon has returned as collectibles to break, just like it was in Resident Evil 2's remake! It's worth noting that Mr. Raccoon's first appearance was in the Outbreak games, but as merch instead of small breakable statues.  My main reason for getting hyped about this game was the return of Alyssa Ashcroft (but at what cost?). She was my main in both Resident Evil: Outbreak games, her ability to unlock doors was very useful. When I played as Grace and used a lockpick on a drawer, I was like, "Come on, make your mama proud", and as soon as I saw an achievement unlocking in tribute to Alyssa, I had a large smile on my face. Only those who played the Outbreak games would get it.  When it comes to gameplay, I preferred Leon's action-driven gameplay much more than Grace's survival-driven gameplay. I played the game as it was intended to, of course - Leon in third-person, and Grace in first-person. Leon, since he's stronger and has much more experience, is very reliable in combat, has more gun variety, can attack in melee, has a shop to upgrade guns and purchase/sell items, and has a larger inventory. Grace, being younger and hesitant, relied more on strategy and escaping rather than being a direct combat character, but it was fun going stealthy and attacking the enemies from behind with those hemolytic injectors.  The motorbike level was very fun, although you clearly don't have to focus much on riding the bike itself, but more on shooting the enemies. In a way, this phase of the game gave me vibes from Tomb Raider: Legend, but darker and in a post-apocalyptic setting.  For some reason, the sniper's scope was blurry when I zoomed in, even with my DLSS deactivated. I did my research, and apparently, it's normal, so I ended up installing a mod from Nexus that removes that blur. It certainly made aiming with a sniper much better for me. I just found it odd because it's the first game that I've played where this happens.  The soundtrack is just so good, it feels nostalgic and fresh at the same time - it's eerie, yet beautiful. Bringing back Masami Ueda as one of the composers was the icing on the cake, he managed to bring back those old-school vibes with a modern twist.  The story is pretty good, it has some plot twists that I wasn't expecting, like Grace's origin, the Elpis, Zeno (he seems very familiar, doesn't he?), etc.. When it comes to both endings, you can clearly see which one is the good ending and which one is the bad ending - and which one is canon. The bad ending is short and underwhelming, while the good ending is much longer, much more exciting, and comes with a final boss battle. The good ending is certainly the canon one, plus it has a post-credits scene!   [b][PT][/b] [h2]De Volta aos Trilhos![/h2]  Caraças, por onde é que começo? A Capcom sabe certamente como agradar aos fãs: trazendo de volta personagens antigas (amigos e inimigos - alguns deles, de certa forma), fazendo referências e Easter Eggs de Resident Evil 2 e Outbreak, trazendo de volta um compositor de música da banda sonora dos jogos originais, regressando a Raccoon City e ao R.P.D.... A franquia está a voltar aos trilhos no que diz respeito às suas personagens e acção. Oh, e por falar em trazer coisas de volta, até o Mr. Raccoon regressou como item coleccionável para partir, tal e qual como no remake do Resident Evil 2! É de salientar que a primeira aparição do Mr. Raccoon foi nos jogos de Outbreak, mas como merchandise em vez de pequenas estátuas quebráveis.  O principal motivo de ficar com hype para este jogo foi o regresso da Alyssa Ashcroft (mas a que custo?). Foi a minha main nos dois jogos de Resident Evil: Outbreak, a sua capacidade de destrancar portas era muito útil. Quando joguei com a Grace e usei uma gazua numa gaveta, eu fiquei tipo, "Vá lá, deixa a tua mãe orgulhosa", e assim que vi uma proeza a desbloquear em homenagem à Alyssa, tive um sorriso enorme na cara. Só aqueles que jogaram os jogos de Outbreak é que iriam entender.  No que toca à jogabilidade, preferi muito mais a jogabilidade focada na acção do Leon do que a jogabilidade focada na sobrevivência da Grace. Joguei o jogo tal como é suposto, claro - o Leon em terceira pessoa e a Grace em primeira pessoa. O Leon, por ser mais forte e ter muito mais experiência, é muito fiável em combate, tem uma maior variedade de armas, pode atacar corpo a corpo, tem uma loja para melhorar armas e comprar/vender itens, e um maior inventário. A Grace, por ser mais nova e hesitante, dependia mais da estratégia e da fuga do que do combate direto, mas era divertido usar a furtividade e atacar os inimigos pelas costas com aqueles injetores hemolíticos.  O nível da moto foi muito divertido, embora claramente não precisem de se concentrar muito em pilotar a moto em si, mas sim em disparar sobre os inimigos. De certa forma, esta fase do jogo fez-me lembrar Tomb Raider: Legend, só que mais sombria e num cenário pós-apocalíptico.  Por algum motivo, a mira da sniper ficava desfocada quando eu fazia zoom, mesmo com o DLSS desactivado. Pesquisei um pouco e, aparentemente, é normal, pelo que acabei por instalar um mod do Nexus que remove esse desfoque. Isto certamente melhorou muito a minha mira com a sniper. Achei estranho porque é o primeiro jogo que jogo em que isto acontece.  A banda sonora é simplesmente incrível, nostálgica e nova ao mesmo tempo – é misteriosa, mas bonita. Trazer Masami Ueda de volta como um dos compositores foi a cereja no topo do bolo, ele conseguiu trazer de volta aquela vibe clássica com um toque moderno.  A história é muito boa, com algumas reviravoltas que eu não estava à espera, como a origem da Grace, a Elpis, o Zeno (ele parece muito familiar, não é?), etc.. Quanto aos dois finais, percebe-se claramente qual é o bom e qual é o mau — e qual é o canónico. O final mau é curto e decepcionante, enquanto o bom é muito mais longo, muito mais emocionante e tem uma batalha contra um boss final. O final bom é definitivamente o canónico, além de ter uma cena pós-créditos!

This is one of those times that I wished Steam had a middle option review. It's not terrible, but it's not great either.  At the time of posting this, the story has many plot holes and design choices that make zero sense. I will not post these for spoiler reasons. The constant flip-flop between horror and action is annoying, I'd rather it be consistent. They could've made the game more like Ethan's sections of Village, where it was action packed into survival horror.  That said, it does execute both parts very well in their respective ways. Grace's sections are tense, and you're better off trying to only kill the ones who you can't get around. But her crafting system is by far the goofiest I have ever seen in an RE game.  Leon's sections are fun, filled with action, but is basically the same as RE4R, with intelligent fast zombies replacing Ganados, even having chainsaw zombies, so it's just a carbon copy. Even down to having the zombies pull a plaga where the enemy will sometimes mutate after receiving lethal damage, continuing the fight.  The lack of a proper New Game or New Game + after having beaten the game is infuriating. RE5 didn't have one either, I know. But you could  keep everything you collected in previous playthroughs while still finding weapons in the game like your first playthrough if you wanted to start over. New Game + in this game forces you to lose everything, health items, ammunition, discovered weapons, currency, even weapon upgrades, except for the unlocks in the special content shop, where you have to retrieve the items as Grace from the item box and rediscover the other items again, and purchase everything again as Leon.  I give this game a 6/10 Hopefully the DLC will correct some of the massive plot holes, and they'll correct the poorly done New Game + but I won't old my breath.

I'd like to start off by saying I really, REALLY wanted to like this game and heavily anticipated it. I even preordered the deluxe edition and called all my friends so we could pull an all-nighter to beat it! (Spoilers ahead!)  It's... An alright game. Pretty fun although the pacing between the Leon and Grace segments felt more jarring than natural. Would've worked better as two separate scenarios where the two would occasionally meet, imo. The intro made a hella strong first impression and I found swapping between Leon and Grace up until the care centre much more natural than the rest of the game. I LOVED the worker zombies and how we actually got undead with unique personalities despite the degeneration, genuinely felt like little nightmares and outlast combined and distracting them felt very fun and clever.  After Grace gets the requiem the game kinda falls apart... Using a child as a cheap device to get us attached to her and feel bad for her felt cheap and so did the death of a well-loved classic character (rip Alissa, you'll be missed). The puzzles felt repetitive and like they lacked variety and nuanced given how painfully easy they were (well, one's solution was literally on the desk in the same room. What?) plus you get so many resources that after one point we'd cleared the facility so running around and back-tracking genuinely felt like a drag. Plus after a while we realised how similar it looked to the R.P.D. which was a shame, too. At least the R.P.D. had a lore reason for all the art. Guess we can chalk it up to an homage.  Eventually we get to Leon's part after unsatisfying bark and forth between the two with wacky pacing. His section is... Fun, at first! Exploring part of an abandoned Raccoon city is pretty cool and you can definitely feel how much stronger he's gotten. His combat feels like a mix between RE4R and 6, even sporting executions from that game. Sweet. After a while though, running back and forth becomes kind of a chore as well. My main issue with this game in general other than the dreadful plot is that it oftentimes feels like it doesn't give you a real choice on how to play it. The originals had some kind of risk and reward factor depending on whether you were trigger happy or evaded which was neat. In this one however, Grace just... Doesn't have as broad of a weapon roster as other older entries while Leon gets a crazy amount of weapons which still sometimes feels unsatisfying as it feels like the game purposely forces you go go guns blazing. I liked sneaking up on enemies and clearing rooms from a distance but it genuinely felt like the game wouldn't let you at times, whereass with Grace it felt like you mostly had to spam injectors at certain points due to her not having a knife stealth kill option (although I love the fact that you could get certain enemies to kill eachother, it was a great touch). With Grace it's less of a problem, given how you're supposed to run past thing ala classic RE but with Leon it felt like sometimes the game just didn't want you to have fun, probably stemming from first person being an option which meant that they had to have less enemies so they wouldn't overwhelm your POV but make them bullet sponges. It's a shame cause I really liked some segments, like traversing the delapidated skyscraper and shooting glass under enemies plus the vendetta motorcycle sequence but the area just felt boring to explore after you'd seen everything like five times. Thought Raccoon city would be more emotional and actually allow Leon to reflect for once but it was just a short, rehashed boss disappointment (I also got stuck in debris during the Tyrant chase and he couldn't harm me so we were staring into eachother's eyes like two lovers lmao). The villains taking Grace to the R.P.D. makes absolutely zero sense but I admit I was emotional about the notes. umbrella lab and the orphanage felt like Sherry's segment plus was very easy to cheese, particularly during the Hatch segment. The lickers in ARK felt more annoying than fun to deal with, mostly cause my friends hadn't left me any injectors so I had to throw molotovs at the surrounding zombies and pray that they'd drop blood so I could clear the way (except for like the licker down the stairs as it didn't mess with anything at first). As for Leon lickers... Eh, the most optimal way of clearing them just ain't fun. I liked the fact that the virus taking over his body was a mechanic though, very interesting and creative. Also the H.U.N.K. boss wasn't that special and too short for me to say much on it other than the fact that Leon besting him to show his growth was pretty neat, although unsurprising considering Leon tanked Birkin while H.U.N.K. did not and many people forget that. Still cool but H.U.N.K.'s characterisation wasn't for me in this one but then again it's short-lived.  Now for the plot.  The plot is... An unfocused mess, honestly. Leon and Grace's goals hardly ever aline and they have next to no chemistry so it's really hard to connect with the story as a whole. Victor was generally really fun and I was super ready to see him turn into a big serpent given the scales on his face so I was severely disappointed when he literally just turned into RE3R Nemesis' boss. Zeno just... Reminded me of the fact that I could be actually playing a better game with Wesker in it and cloning him just feels like they're back-pedalling on his death because he was the iconic big bad of the franchise. Grace's demeanour makes zero sense paired up with her occupation and the fact that her character development happened in the last five minutes of gameplay was just sad. She was very inconsistent, sometimes immensely sharp while others just coming off as dumb or naive which would work with a civillian like Ethan or Ashley but not an FBI analyst. I'm just glad the whole chosen one schtick wasn't the case in the end cause it would've only made the plot worse. Then... Spencer. Hoo boy, Spencer. He'd shown no remorse until his final years yet the entire point of this game is that he magically felt bad for torturing and forcefully experimenting on minorities and majorities alike and made a cure for many of the viruses umbrella had engineered which was... Predictable, to me. I'm Greek and Elpis meaning hope wasn't very creative, I knew it'd be some kind of bait and switch.  TL;DR To me this game overall was somewhat fun but the lackluster plot and rehashed bosses consistenly pissed me off too much for me to fully enjoy it plus the transitions between horror and action and actually balancing both kinds of gameplay wasn't handled too well for me although I commend Capcom for trying. This game doesn't have much replayability unlike other titles and I could see myself having more fun hopping on RE HD Remaster, RE4 og or Darkside Chronicles than this game. Or maybe 7 and 4 remake back to back given that's what they wanted to achieve. To me Requiem stands as one of the weakest games in the franchise as it doesn't have much going for it other than mechanics done better in different titles and a concept that sounded cooler on paper than was executed. At least with RE6 I can turn off my brain and enjoy it for being "funny bad" along with a buddy plus there's some genuine character growth there which we don't really see in modern REs (except for remakes which have better writing than the newer games imo. 8 was awesome but butchered Chris so I'm not sure what Capcom is planning for the old protags), not to mention it didn't reuse copypasted bosses from previous entries. At least they were all its own. Can't say the same for requiem.  Overall I give this game a... 5.9/10 for effort. Whenever I think of it I just feel sad about what we could've potentially gotten if the game was just left to cook for longer. I feel like it would've been much more fun as a Sherry and Leon dual campaign game or hell Grace and Leon if the story was solid and the bosses unique. This game is cool if your first

Resident Evil Requiem is easily one of the strongest entries Capcom has made in years. It manages to respect the history of Resident Evil while still feeling modern, polished, and genuinely intense. The atmosphere is incredible, the visuals are outstanding, and the sound design makes every dark hallway feel uncomfortable in the best way possible.  What I liked most was how the game balances different sides of the series. Grace brings back that slower, more vulnerable survival-horror feeling, where every enemy encounter feels dangerous and every bit of ammo matters. Leon’s sections add the action, confidence, and classic Resident Evil personality that long-time fans expect. The contrast between the two keeps the pacing fresh and gives the game a lot more variety.  The story is also much more emotional than I expected. It ties into the older Resident Evil lore without feeling like it only exists for nostalgia, and there are plenty of moments that feel meaningful for fans of the series. The animations, voice acting, environments, and enemy design all help make the game feel cinematic and high quality from start to finish.  It is not completely perfect, as a few sections could have had better pacing and some story moments feel slightly familiar, but those issues do not take away from how good the overall experience is. Resident Evil Requiem is tense, beautiful, polished, and memorable. For me, it is one of the best survival-horror games in recent years and a must-play for any Resident Evil fan.

Let me start off by saying Resident Evil Requiem is excellent. I would personally put it in my top 5 games in the franchise at this point. I have almost 60 hours on Steam and around 30-ish on PS5 when it first came out. I'll go through a list of pros and cons I have with the game and then a rating real quick. PSA THIS REVIEW CONTAINS FULL SPOILERS!!!   Pros:  -The story itself is excellent. It introduces Grace Ashcroft as a brand new character connected through a legacy character Alyssa Ashcroft from the Resident Evil Outbreak series. Grace starts off very timid and horrified and develops into a courageous heroine by the end. And Leon's story is just as good if not better for me personally. They continue the character arc they've developed for him in the recent remakes by expanding upon his trauma as a character and how it has shaped him. He is truly dancing with death in the game along with his demons. -Pretty good amount of content and replayability for a modern day release.  -Art direction is incredible. The Care Center in the first half of the game is a treat and Racoon City in the later half gives this feeling of a dying city brought back to life which I love. -Characters are really good overall. Victor Gideon, who I consider to be the game's main villain is great. He is always a joy whenever he's on screen. So much so to where I wish there was more of him than we got. Zeno the other main villain is very interesting. It's hinted he's a clone of Albert Wesker, the best villain in the series. Grace is excellent, she is a very new kind of protagonist for the series and I really enjoyed the approach they took with her character. A few of her scenes had me tearing up they were so well done. Leon as always is just the absolute goat. He's badass, he has sick one liners and most importantly his story comes full circle here. They really emphasize the effect Racoon City had on him 28 years ago and it's a pleasure seeing his story unfold. -Gameplay is very good. Grace is more survival horror and has a very RE7/ RE2 Remake feel to her. Leon feels just as amazing just on the opposite end of the spectrum. He's very action orientated, similar to RE4 Remake from a few years back. However he feels even more powerful here, being able to dispatch almost anything in the game with ease if you know what you're doing. They also included the option to switch between first and third person view in this title which just adds a whole other factor of variety to how the game feels. Both perspectives for each respective character feels very polished and are both worth experiencing at least once. The only complaint I have gameplay wise is for Leon's side of the game.  -Lastly for the pros the game looks and runs very well. This is the best the series has ever looked. I played on a pretty good rig and had very little issues with performance other than one section of the game that I'll mention later in the review.  Cons: -The level design is very fun overall but it never feels like it fully takes advantage of every tool that is given to the player. In RE4 Remake every level felt like a perfect playground for Leon's abilities but in Requiem it took a step back in this regard. -Zeno, who is a pretty sick character only has a handful of scenes and we never get to fight him in actual gameplay which is pretty lame. If you skip all the cutscenes on replays he's almost not even in the game. You'll hear him once as Leon in the RPD. -Game is so fun to it's own detriment almost. Once you've cleared all the challenges there's no real incentive to replay unless you're just up for another run. Thankfully they added a free mini game mode to help mitigate some of this but it doesn't fix the issue completely. -Lastly for cons, in Raccoon City in the later half of the game the game suffers severe frame drops. Once you start fighting numerous enemies at a time as Leon the game would tank from almost 100 frames to below 30 in a few instances. It would stutter so bad the game almost looked like it was running in slow motion. Thankfully there is a work around that people have figured out where if you set the "mesh quality" graphics setting to low and if needed cap the frame rate it almost entirely negates the issue. Just at the cost of the models not being 100% detailed which is a bummer. I will say on my recent playthrough I did a few days ago I didn't experience this issue with the "mesh quality" setting set to standard/normal. No clue why though, hopefully it was finally fixed.  Closing:  Overall I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ love this game, and I'm super hyped for the inevitable story DLC whenever it drops.  Rating: Strong 9/10, long live Resident Evil <3

Capcom has always been good at making you mentally crap yourself at the horrific monsters of the RE world, but this game has more variety in its gameplay offerings than any horror experience I've ever played, even compared to the previous hits in the RE series. The RE3 remake is the only stumble along the way, but other than that, this series has never lost sight of how to make a next-level horror experience. Depending on the game, you'll get two different "types" of horror within the RE games, and this is the first game to combine both inside one.  The first type of gameplay is survival horror, with the sections that follow Grace. This type is inspired by the most recent games in the series, and it's probably the first thing someone pictures these days when you mention RE. Ammo is scarce, enemies take a lot of bullets, and you are fragile, so you need to sneak around every corner and make every shot count. It's restricting, but you still don't feel helpless even in Grace's sections. You have a bunch of room to sneak, so this is basically the game's way of forcing you to use your wits instead of your aim and APM to take zombies down.  The second gameplay type is the more action-oriented horror, and Leon is the main character during these sections. You're still trying to survive and conserve ammo, but the game gives you way more firepower and moves to do it, with a lot of enemies to shoot accordingly. Leon is such a badass, and some of his moments wouldn't feel entirely out of place in a Doom game. They're at their best when spliced in between the longer Grace sections, since they're perfect palette cleansers for that kind of high-stress stealth.  All this to say that this game takes both types of that RE experience and blends it together masterfully. There really isn't a dull moment in the game and I have no trouble remembering many of the sections and monsters throughout the campaign. I think if I had one complaint, it's that the length of the campaign makes me hesitate recommending this game to everyone I know. It's not short by any means, but that $70 price tag is just a tough selling point for a 12-15 hour experience. If this game ever goes on sale for 20% off or so, I would say buy with no question. I think the game crams enough crazy gameplay moments and surprisingly touching story beats for anyone to have a great time, as long as you don't hate the feeling of wanting to jump out of your skin once in a while.

[spoiler]I am not talking about the blisterheads, which are a cool monster and an interesting way to raise tension in cleared areas - I am talking about the normal zombies that just decide out of the blue "yes, ill stand back up and waste more resources"[/spoiler]  This game is also full of scripted ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that makes any tension built up while playing Grace go away, because once it happens once, you realize it doesn't matter what you do. In it you are being stalked by a large mutant girl, called "The Girl", that has been harassing you throughout the game. You need to turn on three power distribution switches. To do so, you must creep along as the Girl searches around this underground segment looking for you. A pretty typical setup for this kind of encounter - cat and mouse search. On all three switches, I got past the Girl and turned it on while tracking where she was. The highlight of the game was the Leon segments, simply because they are a completely different game than the Grace segments. I decided to give insanity mode a try to see how Capcom handled this.  One shotting zombies that 360 attack you when you are sneaking behind them: check. Bullet sponge zombies that take over an entire magazine's worth of ammo in headshots to kill: check. Same slow, irritating, unreasonably unrealistic crawl of movement speed by our main heroine: check.  Grace has a knife. Can she do anything useful with said knife most of the time? Nope. Snuck behind a zombie, but don't have a very specific and moderately expensive item? Can't do ♥♥♥♥. Can't push them over, can't stab them in the back, can't even kick their leg a bit to run by them.  The level of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game put into place as a "challenge" is utterly ridiculous. And the worst part is insanity mode has its own content, challenges, and unlocks. So in order to experience a large chunk of the game's content, you have to deal with this insane and unreasonable level of artificial difficulty that is flagrantly in your face with how stupidly restrictive it is.

10/10. RE9: Requiem absolutely nailed the atmosphere and storytelling from start to finish. The character building was excellent, and Grace’s actress delivered a phenomenal performance. Grace’s emotions, fear, timidity, and empathy for Emily felt incredibly real and made the story hit much harder emotionally. Even the stuttering and fear in her voice made her feel far more natural and believable as a character. Her bond with Emily was honestly one of the strongest parts of the game. Grace seeing herself in Emily’s helplessness and slowly evolving from a terrified analyst into someone willing to risk everything to protect her was handled beautifully. The emotional moments genuinely landed, especially during the darker parts of the story where her guilt and trauma really started to break through. The graphics are insane, especially the lighting and environmental detail. Playing on my setup (9800X3D, 32GB DDR5 CL30 6000MHz RAM, Astral RTX 5090, and a 4K QD-OLED display), the game ran flawlessly fully maxed out with ray tracing enabled. Stable FPS, smooth frame pacing, excellent 1% lows, and no issues with the engine at all. The true inky blacks and HDR presentation on a QD-OLED make the atmosphere unbelievably immersive and genuinely creepy at times. The post-apocalyptic world looks surreal and is incredibly fun to explore. This isn’t me trying to flex hardware either, it’s just the setup I personally experienced the game on, and I imagine the game would still be fantastic on all kinds of systems. Leon is still an absolute badass with 100% aura every time he’s on screen, and his one-liners were genuinely some of the funniest moments in the entire game. They fit his character perfectly and somehow made him even more lovable. I also loved that the switching between Leon and Grace never felt obnoxious or overdone. The pacing between both characters was handled perfectly. One of the best Resident Evil games Capcom has made. Easily recommended.

This is where it all began, and this is where it will all end...  After the *Resident Evil 2* remake, I like that Capcom is moving toward a darker, more realistic style-as much as that’s even possible in a zombie game with B-movie-style action, haha. The dark, disillusioned atmosphere suits Leon perfectly, but he still cracks jokes just like in the good old days :D  This is perhaps the most atmospheric and cinematic game in the Resident Evil series of all, yet it maintains a certain seriousness in its storytelling. I don’t know who wouldn’t like this. Of course, some moments might not be to everyone’s taste, but the developers put so much effort into the game and included so many different “Residents” that even die-hard fans of the series will be satisfied, relative newcomers who joined the series with the 7th installment will be happy, and fans of the more action-packed Resident Evil will be satisfied.  The only thing I want to complain about is the lack of classic puzzles. Yes, you’re always thinking about where to go, how to get past enemies, and what to bring with you to be more effective-especially when playing as Grace, since the number of saves is limited-but there just aren’t enough real puzzles. It’s as if the burden of puzzles and a complex plot still rests on the shoulders of its neighbor, Silent Hill, while Resident Evil, due to its popularity and mass appeal, is still afraid to make players think too hard. Otherwise, it’s an absolutely stunning AAA blockbuster and likely the best action-horror game in the industry right now. This is exactly what big-budget games should be like, and not too long either: 12-15 hours for a first playthrough on the highest difficulty setting is just perfect.  Those who complain about repetition and that “Resident Evil” has become boring probably played ‘Requiem’ right after one of the other games in the series. Personally, I don’t think it’s just a rehash yet-the last time I played “Resident Evil” was three years ago, so…  I’ve also seen people complaining, “Where’s Ada?” Dude, she’s over 50, she’s practically retired-I don’t think a grandma in a red dress is appropriate :D  I also didn’t get all this “bad ending” business-like, what’s the point? I mean, what’s the point? Those who fell for the developers’ trick and chose the bad ending instead of the canonical one got such a shock and a kick in the balls at first-I saw a couple of streams where some people were literally screaming and sitting in shock, like, “How dare they?” This isn’t Joel; this is an even more iconic character with a 30-year history and a ton of games, movies, and other stuff behind him. IMHO, it was a bold move-to kill him off so brutally. I think they did a great job; I even got goosebumps, like, “No way, this can’t be the end of the game.” They’re just awesome. After a moment like that, you immediately go back to play through the game again, and if you don’t go back, the developers’ trick won’t work anymore.  In fact, this is the first slasher game I’ve liked specifically because of its cinematography. The camera angles, the way everything is shot and acted out, the atmosphere, the sound, and the music at just the right moments. In that regard, the folks at Capcom have really raised the bar.  It’s quite possible that this is the first slasher game to win a TGA award.   P.S. It’s really nice to see that the two series that kicked off my (and millions of people’s) gaming lives are still going strong and thriving. [b]Resident Evil Requiem works because Grace Ashcroft works.[/b]  I love Leon. I really do. But this game would not hit the same without Grace.  She might honestly be one of my favourite Resident Evil protagonists now, because she brings back something the series needed badly: someone who actually feels vulnerable. Not another polished, expertly trained badass. Not Ethan stapling his hand back on and mostly being fine. Just a normal person dropped into something disgusting, cruel, and completely beyond her. That is what makes the horror work.  A lot of the time, I was not scared because the game threw a monster at me. I was scared because Grace was scared. The way she reacts, handles weapons, and tries to process the nightmare around her adds real weight to her sections.  But the best part is that she is not useless. Grace panics, but she still thinks. She is overwhelmed, but she still pays attention. She is terrified, but she keeps moving anyway. I really liked that about her. She never felt like the game was trying to force me to admire her. I just did, because she kept proving herself in small ways. Especially that door moment. You know the one.  She feels intelligent in a way that makes sense. Not because she always has the perfect answer, but because she watches, listens, questions things, and tries to understand what is happening even when she is clearly barely holding herself together.  That is what made me love her as a protagonist. She is afraid, but she is not passive. She is vulnerable, but she is not helpless. She is brave in a way that actually feels earned.  Requiem feels like a love letter to survival horror fans, but Grace Ashcroft is what gives it a soul.  I loved this game enough to hunt down every achievement. 10/10. More Grace, Capcom.

I loved Resident Evil Requiem, and I think it's probably one of the best games in the series, easy top five.   When playing a Resident Evil game, I always keep in mind that it's campy horror usually, and the story isn't something you really take seriously. However, this game shines in the story and development of its protagonists, Leon and Grace. Leon, of course, is fantastic in whatever he's in, but this game humanizes him so much. Grace, the new character, is easily one of the best in the franchise. From the get go, she's such a truly fleshed out and believable character that you don't find in Resident Evil often.  Having two different gameplay approaches is also great. While neither is truly the best at what it tries to do, as previous entries have done those approaches better. Grace's survival horror, reminiscent of RE2, is done better in RE2, but still is very good. Leon's RE4 style gameplay feels better in RE4R, but is still very good.   My only real critiques is that it isn't very replayable, unlike previous games. There's a couple sections that really drag and take you out of the action. While they're perfectly fine on your first run, it's a bit boring on your fourth run. The boss fights could also have some more interesting mechanics, but they're perfectly fine as is. The first section of Raccoon city also gets a bit dull at times.   Overall, I really enjoyed Requiem and hope Capcom is able to actually build off of this game, and hopefully this isn't Grace's one and only game.  The 100% is also fairly easy, especially if you get all the unlocks before attempting insanity difficulty.

A solid title with much better pacing and streamlining compared to the last two non-remake entries. While the final portion of the game significantly suffers due to the contrast between playstyles and the area designs, overall the first half of the game is very strong and doesn't overstay its welcome quite like the village hub in the last title. Playing as Grace feels pretty high-stakes, and she's much less capable and therefore the survival kicks in pretty good, and minus her final section (which features some of the most boring area design and annoying enemy layouts), all the main sections of the game featuring her are exceptionally well designed. Leon on the other hand is saved for setpieces minus one final callback, which often feel pretty short in the first half of the game, or cut down in a way that doesn't feel great up until the second half of the game, where you have a whole area dedicated to him which while it's a little obnoxious and his abilities are hilariously more capable that Grace and makes some of the enemy encounters outright much more fun to encounter. The story is a little odd and the game makes a few mistakes of introducing random characters with either bad design or nonsensical connection to the plot is a strange retcon of the series, which we'll probably see some rectifications in the remakes to follow. Overall if you were hoping for a mashup of the remakes and RE7/8, this is definitely the game you will get, and although it's a little lean, and I wished there was a lot more for each playable character to do in their opposing halves of the game, it's still much more worth your time than RE3R, and not quite as bloated as RE8. I feel pretty confident calling this one an 8/10 game with some flaws and never quite reaching its peak due to some weaker encounter designs in the first half for Leon and the second half for Grace. If DLC comes out to fill in those portions of the story and bulk up the content for both of those that rating could improve.

Well, I don’t know where to start. First, I want to split this game into two parts. We can call the part where we play as Grace at the Wrenwood Hotel the first part. I don’t even know how to begin praising this part of the game. No matter how many wonderful things I say, it won’t be enough. It was one of the most incredible thriller/horro I’ve played in recent years. The last time I played a thriller with such admiration was the Coffee World section of Alan Wake II. But here, I found something far more magnificent. Since the early 2000s, I’ve played nearly every Resident Evil game except of 5 and 6. I can confidently say that this game’s first chapter is my favorite among them all. Whoever wrote those zombies in that hotel did an amazing job. I’d especially love to meet and congratulate the person who wrote and came with an idea of the zombie that turns on and of off the lights.  Now let’s move on to part 2. Well, I can’t say it’s bad. I can’t say any Resident Evil game is bad, after all. I don’t play 5 and 6 just than I don’t want to say they’re bad :). Anyway, after all the praise I heaped on the first chapter, I’d just like to say the second chapter is average. We’re way too overpowered. I didn’t run out of ammo once, and I never felt that “I’ll be stuck on this boss all night” frustration. That’s exactly what I expect from an action-focused Resident Evil. Especially on Hard mode, I want it to make me feel like I’ll be stuck on a boss all night, even if I try so hard. Just like Dead Space, The Callisto Protocol, and Chronos: The New Dawn.   We could call the story average as well. It feels like they tried too hard to be nostalgic. While it could have been nice to say, “Oh, this came out years ago,” once or twice, it loses some of its charm when they try to make you say it about 15 times.

honestly... it's one of the best games I've ever played. Capcom created a true masterpiece with a game like Resident Evil Requiem, an obvious evolution for 30 years of RE's existence. it manages so well to balance between classic and modern with phenomenal graphics, attention to detail, the classic architecture and technology that'll clearly remind you of older titles, smart puzzles, lots of items and ways to craft more, unique protagonists and enemies and what I liked in particular: zombies with personality! there are tons of zombie games at this point, but it's the first time I see zombies that keep so much from their past self, making you so curious to follow their actions and hear their mumblings before you make 'em fall rock flat by the bullet.  Speaking about protagonists, I can agree on some players complaining about Grace being too weak or a sissy, but you'll get used to this, she might be an FBI agent, but she's young and less prepared for field work like this, unlike Leon that scatters bullets and hatchets left and right and oooooh my goodness, how fun that is... where you run away and manage bullets with Grace, you take fully head on with Leon that might be the most goodlooking and badass character i've ever witnessed and now I totally understand why he was so...sexy even for the guys (I'd also touch him). I miss a more developed stealth mechanic, especially for Grace, since she's more focused on the survival part. she can't do some kind of takedown even with a knife in possession, the knife serving as a direct defence method for her; the hemolytic injector does the job at disposing enemies undetected. On the other hand, Leon is the antithesis of her, more of a killer, more inventory, more weapons, more acrobatic moves, hell, you'll not even want to try to get unnoticed with Leon. So...yeah, best distinction between multiple protagonists since GTA V, though here you're not changing between them at your will, the game cycles between them as the story progresses. what you CAN cycle as you prefer is the perspective of both main characters. personally I preferred the recommended default: first person for Grace to deepen the survival horror atmosphere and the classic third person for Leon to enhance the action oriented parts. I think the only possible loss for the first person view is that you miss some of the character animations, tho it's a win for Grace, because she'll not stumble every few seconds like she does in third person. Grace, the scared and delicate girl besides Leon, the veteran that saw and fought grotesque stuff before she was even born.  as you massacre zombies in a room, the more red it gets from the blood; the enemies will always surprise you with something, some chase you directly, some just want to be alone feasting on corpses or doing their obsessive compulsive tasks from everyday life, some throw gas tanks, some take you by surprise, some stab you, some will suffer a double T-Virus mutation, where you suddenly see some random corpse convulsing and developing a tumor. it's so entertaining that I couldn't wait to finish it to leave a review. the Capcom guys outperformed themselves, and what started with Biohazard's RE Engine 9 years ago, has clearly evolved and gave us the best game of the first half of 2026. buy it, play it, admire it (and Leon) and never F-ING FORGET IT.

If you havent played many Resident Evil games, or dont really care about the story, this game will probably be perfect for you. Unfortunately, I have played most of them, and I actually care about the lore. With the price being €70, my expectations were pretty high. The game drops you straight into a major situation where you barely understand whats happening or who you’re even fighting against. That can be a great way to start a game, but only if the story eventually explains everything properly and gives depth to the new characters and conflicts. Unfortunately, this game never really does that. After following the Resident Evil storyline chronologically, the series felt like it reached a major culmination in RE5, especially with Albert Wesker, who was built up across 4 whole games. Here, it feels like they tried to create a copy, but without any of the depth, personality, or impact that made Wesker memorable. The antagonist ends up feeling meaningless and underdeveloped. While Spences story is concluded well, and Ethan’s storyline was wrapped up beautifully in Village, I expected Leon’s return to continue the overall narrative in a meaningful way. Instead, there’s very little in the story that actually connects to previous games. Outside of Leon himself and the same repetitive format, the game doesn’t feel like a true continuation of the series larger plot. I honestly think the story would improve significantly if they released even a small free DLC explaining Zenos backstory. For the things I enjoyed. The story and progression of the game as a single game is quite hard to match and was definitely enjoyable. The parry system feels polished and satisfying, the graphics are probably the peak of what the RE Engine can achieve, and revisiting the RPD from RE2 was handled extremely well. The live outbreak happening around you was also a really interesting addition that made the setting feel more intense and immersive. Overall, I just hope Resident Evil sequels either cost less or focus more on delivering a connected, logical, and linear story with villains as memorable as Albert Wesker. I’m still really looking forward to the Code Veronica remake. P.S if youre looking to buy the game, wait a few more months for the discount, its not worth it, go play RE7-8.
