Resident Evil Requiem (RE9) is a bloated, disjointed disappointment that fails to recapture the series' glory days.   After the solid but flawed pivot to first-person horror in RE7 and the uneven, gimmicky Village (RE8), fans hoped Capcom would deliver a true return to form or at least a cohesive evolution for the mainline series. Instead, Resident Evil Requiem feels like two half-baked games awkwardly stitched together, burdened by weak writing, inconsistent design, and a desperate overreliance on fan service that can't hide its mediocrity. It's not the worst in the series—RE6 still holds that crown—but it's a clear step back from what the franchise promised after its modern revival  Leon's parts crank up the action, but they feel like a worse version of the RE4 remake—over-the-top, heavily scripted set pieces with dumb one-liners and enemy swarms that turn survival horror into a cover-shooter slog. The adaptive difficulty and inflated enemy counts often feel unfair or cheap rather than tense. Compared to the masterful balance in the RE2/RE3 remakes or even RE4's crowd control, this just feels exhausting and arcadey.   Inventory management and resource tension—core to what made RE great from the originals through RE7—feel neutered here. Upgrades and crafting lean too heavily into RPG-lite elements that dilute the desperation. Puzzles are underwhelming or overly hand-holdy compared to the clever environmental brain-teasers in RE1-3 or the remakes.   The story writing is where it gets tragic. So much doesn't make any sense and its hard not to spoil in an explanation. I will just say, the writing for Grace segments makes no sense when you find out more information later in the story. I will not share spoilers in this review. I will just say that they didn't put much respect or thought into the writing and you can find others opinions on that online where there are many plot holes that develop. More thought was put into the gameplay of areas than having respect for already established lore, for example. The very sloppy writing is reminding me too much of RE6.   Bottom Line: Resident Evil Requiem isn't a total disaster—there are flashes of good horror, solid visuals, and fun combat highs if you lower your expectations. But as a flagship entry, it exemplifies Capcom's identity crisis: chasing broad appeal with action set pieces and fan-pleasing cameos while diluting the pure survival horror that made RE7 a revitalization and the remakes beloved.   5/10—forgettable Requiem for a once-great series.

Capcom is one of those unicorns that has kept on delivering solid, or even wonderful, AAA titles whereas the absolute majority of other big companies have declined into superficiality and soulless pandering over the ages. So, gods of gaming be praised that we can still experience gigs like this.  During the game, you alternate between playing a frightened FBI female agent who never has enough ammo and for whom even a single enemy is always a threat, and a seasoned evil-disposer Leon whose arsenal and killing moves feel straight out of a proper action flick. The dynamic is refreshing, the idea ingenious. Capcom again... Other than that, it's the usual RE formula: search for and apply adventuring items, solve riddles, decide which monsters to fight and which to circumvent, explore, and pay attention to special ways of solving encounters or accruing rare resources.  Word on the atmosphere. I am a fairly old gamer. I've been around, seen a lot, and as a consequence, I don't really get afraid in games anymore. But this piece sent some nice chills down my spine several times already, and I'm not even nearing the end. So, I call that well done indeed.  I recommend playing it on "Standard - Classic," where saving a game is treated as a hard-to-come-by resource, and you have to weigh the risks of continuing without saving versus spending that resource. The game is fair about hinting when things are going to get tough. Sometimes the hints are subtle, sometimes you know for sure, but they're always there. Moreover, finding a way and thinking on your feet instead of bulldozing through everything is rewarded both through conserving resources and with a feeling of accomplishment. I ended up replaying several sections multiple times — a price well worth paying when it comes to that good kind of risk'n'reward tension. Pinnacle gaming right there.  I should also speak a bit about the technical side. Truth be told, I was disappointed by how the game looked on the highest settings, and by how poorly it ran. Granted, my nVidia 4060 and 16GB RAM isn't some kind of awesome rig, but it should be enough to play even modern games at 1080p on the highest settings. Well, not in this case. 20 FPS and GPU temperatures spiking like never before isn't good by a long shot. I ended up turning off some graphical gimmicks and, coincidentally, the game actually started to look somewhat better (?!). I also got a steady 50 FPS with only very rare stutters, which is more than okay to play with.  I mean, don't get me wrong, I like indies a lot, and I play pixel(ated) games even today. So, I'm no sucker for the best graphics, and I actually like when games look dated or "coarse." In my opinion, a game should look like a game and not a frikkin reality simulator and, contrary to mainstream sentiment, I believe there are only a few gaming sub-genres that SORT OF require near-realistic visuals. But when you do make a game where graphics are one of the main attractions, you should optimize it. That's all I wanted to say on the matter. Other than that, I had zero glitches, bugs, crashes — nada. So that part was handled pretty well, and overall, the performance issues were just a minor nuisance worth mentioning for the sake of transparency.  Last but not least, the game keeps outdoing itself. There were at least several moments where I would've thought, “Finally! That took a while... phew, what a ride," only for the next bit of the story / opening sequence to somehow raise the bar even higher. Games usually tend to lose a bit of steam as they go on. Not this RE. If anything, it does the exact opposite, raising the stakes and your emotional investment. Masterfully pieced together, indeed.  Bottom line: I'm mostly into hardcore sci-fi and fantasy. "Low sci-fi" settings such as the RE world are usually not my cup of tea. But even I recommend this wholeheartedly.

In the fall of 1996, about six months removed from it's original launch day, my young 13 year old self was able to obtain a copy of the original RE. This was no directors cut, or Dual Shock, this was the original vanilla game in all its (censored) glory. The game blew my mind, and was part of how the original PlayStation shaped how I viewed gaming as a medium of art(Final Fantasy VII a year later would do the same thing, albeit in a very different way. I had never played anything like it at the time, and all the nuances from the collectible files that built the words lore, to the clever puzzles were a real eye opener. Fast forward nearly thirty years later, I am now 43, a game of nearly forty years. I preordered this game for myself and my twenty year old for each of us got brand new gaming PCs.  I have stuck with the series through its highs, and its lows(RE6 anyone, or better yet Operation Raccoon City).  This very game even after thirty years has cemented my love, and gave me a brand new yet familiar experience that I had felt before. Its very apparent that I love this game, investing 83 hours in its amazing story mode and now the Leon Must Die Forever game, but the fact of the matter is that this game captures fear and action perfectly.  One of the aspects of the game, that is so good is the dual narrative. The game feels like as if Alien and Aliens were happening concurrently(Alien for Grace, Aliens for Leon). Grace feels like as if you are walking on eggshells, every move crucial, every shot matters. Every decision whether that is to flee, or fight depends. Crafting depends on your resources and even gathering those can be exceptionally dangerous.  Leon on the other while at the other end of the spectrum, with a much easier crafting system, a market place, upgradeable weapons and easily accessible items. But here is the thing, while Leon is clearly more experience obviously from other ventures in previous games, and has a come a long way from the bright eyed rookie of the second game, he can still be vulnerable and it can be very easy to get careless. Leons situations are far more extreme, with everything from zombies jumping on a movie lift to an encounter with an old friend in front of an old haunting spot.  The story telling is brilliant, two characters facing their own pasts in different ways, Leon facing his past so he can define who he is, while Grace faces her past so she can be the person who she wants to be. The files are all interesting, but there are a set of five later in the game, that are utterly heart breaking. Resident Evil Requiem is one of this old gamers top games in the series and I am talking top three. Having loved the remakes(I do need to play VII and VIII), this series feels alive to me. And this game is a truly a love letter for those of us. I mean its the little things, and I close it with this. In the original game, my young self caught onto the fact that when a pool blood grows under a prone zombie that means its dead. Well it made very gleeful to see that little touch return in this game. Fantastic.

English :  Requiem is undoubtedly the most successful formula since the debacle of Resident Evil 6. By combining the best elements of Resident Evil 7: Biohazard and Resident Evil Village, along with the remake of Resident Evil 4, the game delivers an almost perfect blend of survival horror and action. It is a combination that will appeal just as much to old school fans of the franchise as to newcomers.  Visually, the game is stunning at times, especially in the early chapters. However, the quality is not always consistent throughout the adventure. Some sections feel more uneven, with textures that are not always top tier and rendering that can occasionally seem less polished. That said, the overall presentation remains very pleasing to the eye. The animation work is truly impressive, whether played in third person or first person. You can tell that great care was given to both perspectives, regardless of the mode chosen.  As for the environments, I found the game slightly below what the previous two entries offered. You mostly explore urban settings or ruined buildings, Raccoon City being the obvious reason, of course, but it is something that stood out to me during my playthrough.  The sound design is highly successful and does an excellent job of immersing the player in both survival focused phases and more action oriented moments, thanks to music that perfectly complements these sequences. Overall, the audio design is of very high quality, whether it concerns the monsters, the weapons, or the environments.  In terms of gameplay, the game handles things very well. On one side, you play as Grace, whose survival horror focused gameplay is strongly reminiscent of the last two entries, but with far fewer resources and weapons available to the player. It is extremely enjoyable if you appreciate that kind of approach, and some segments offer genuinely tense and anxiety inducing moments. On the other side, you have Leon, whose action oriented gameplay is almost modeled after the Resident Evil 4 remake, with the main difference being his tomahawk, which allows him to slice through enemies instead of suplexing them, all while wielding a substantial arsenal that lets you get revenge on the particularly oppressive creatures encountered during Grace’s segments. This creates a very satisfying dynamic during these phases.  Finally, regarding the story, it is best not to think too hard about it. It leans into full on camp, as the franchise has done many times before, although some scenes are so over the top that they become genuinely funny. Even so, I still enjoyed following the adventure as a whole.  In short, RE Requiem is, in my opinion, the ideal formula for the franchise, successfully blending the best of horror and action into a single experience. I had a great time with it, even though I would have liked more. Expect between ten and fifteen hours of gameplay depending on your playstyle.  While it follows in the footsteps of previous entries, I would like future installments to offer richer content, whether in terms of main campaign length or, why not, by including a Mercenaries mode at launch rather than adding it later through updates. This clear lack of content is the reason why I would not give the game four stars, even though I truly enjoyed it.  ____________  Français :  Requiem est sans doute la formule la plus réussie depuis la débâcle de Resident Evil 6. En reprenant le meilleur de Resident Evil 7 et de Resident Evil Village, ainsi que du remake de Resident Evil 4, le jeu propose un mélange presque parfait entre survival horror et action. Un combo qui fera autant plaisir aux fans old school de la licence qu’aux nouveaux venus.  Visuellement, le jeu en met plein les yeux par moments, surtout dans les premiers chapitres. Mais la qualité n’est pas toujours constante sur l’ensemble de l’aventure. Certains passages se montrent plus inégaux, avec des textures pas toujours au top et un rendu parfois un peu moins soigné. Cela dit, l’ensemble reste très agréable à l’œil. Le travail sur les animations est vraiment impressionnant, que ce soit à la troisième ou à la première personne. On sent qu’un vrai soin a été apporté aux deux points de vue, peu importe le mode choisi.  Concernant les environnements explorés, j’ai trouvé le jeu un peu en dessous de ce que proposaient les deux derniers épisodes. On évolue majoritairement dans des milieux urbains ou des bâtiments en ruine, Raccoon City oblige, bien sûr, mais c’est une réflexion que je me suis faite au cours de mon run.  L’ambiance sonore est très réussie et parvient à nous plonger davantage dans les phases de survie comme dans les moments plus orientés action, grâce à des musiques qui accompagnent parfaitement ces passages. Le sound design est globalement très qualitatif, que ce soit pour les monstres, les armes ou les environnements.  Côté gameplay, le jeu fait les choses très bien. D’un côté, on retrouve Grace, qui bénéficie d’un gameplay survival horror très appuyé, dans la lignée des deux derniers opus, mais avec beaucoup moins de ressources et d’armes à disposition du joueur. C’est extrêmement plaisant si l’on aime ce genre d’approche, et certains segments offrent de véritables passages stressants et anxiogènes. De l’autre, on retrouve Leon avec un gameplay action presque calqué sur celui du remake de RE4, avec comme grande différence son tomahawk, qui lui permet de découper les monstres au lieu de leur infliger des suplex, toujours accompagné d’un arsenal conséquent permettant de prendre sa revanche sur les créatures particulièrement oppressantes rencontrées dans les segments de Grace. Cela apporte un aspect très satisfaisant à ces phases.  Et enfin, niveau scénario, il ne faut pas trop réfléchir. On est sur du bon gros nanar, comme la licence nous y a habitués à maintes reprises, bien que certaines scènes soient tellement lunaires que cela en devient drôle. J’ai tout de même apprécié suivre l’aventure dans son ensemble.  En bref, RE Requiem est, selon moi, la formule idéale pour la licence, qui parvient à concilier le meilleur de l’horreur et de l’action dans un seul et même jeu. J’y ai passé un excellent moment, même si j’aurais aimé en avoir davantage. Comptez entre dix et quinze heures de jeu selon votre façon de jouer.  C’est certes dans la lignée des autres opus, mais j’aimerais à l’avenir des jeux un peu plus riches en contenu pour la licence, que ce soit en termes de durée de vie principale ou, pourquoi pas, avec un mode Mercenaries disponible dès la sortie plutôt que via des mises à jour tardives. Ce manque de contenu flagrant est d’ailleurs la raison pour laquelle je ne lui donnerai pas quatre étoiles, bien que je l’aie beaucoup apprécié.

It's so nice when a game you wanted to be good actually is.  RE: Requiem is the 206th (or somewhere around that number) entry in the Resident Evil series, and you can really feel those decades of development in the game. It ran like a dream on high graphics without even a hint of a dropped frame or visual glitch in my entire playthrough, even though my PC is a good 4 years old now and wasn't anything special when I got it. I also found the game remarkably bug-free in spite of it not having been out for that long; I don't think I even saw any of the usual ragdoll ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you see in nearly every game that has them.  Leon's half of the story is about what you'd expect from a Resident Evil game: an action movie plot, a rugged badass hero with good hair taking on the forces of evil one bullet at a time, complete with battles against giant Kaiju-esque monsters, cheesy one-liners and hilariously over the top motorcycle chases. It's exactly what I wanted it to be, and it's wonderful stupid fun.  Grace's half is, at least to me, far more interesting however. I don't say that because I enjoyed her half of the game more — I didn't. If I had to choose which side of the story to replay, I'd pick Leon's every time because I think the moment to moment gameplay of Requiem is much better when it's being an action game than when it wants to be a stealth game. No, what I found so interesting about it was Grace herself.  Grace, you see, is the most unconventional RE protagonist I can think of. In a world full of spec ops agents and femme fatales, Grace is an awkward, stumbling, stuttering mess who can't hold eye contact with people while she's talking to them, let alone keep her cool in the middle of a zombie nightmare. For most of the game, Grace sounds like she's about to piss herself and cry from terror, and it's honestly incredbily refreshing. The contrast between her and Leon really enhances both sides, because you go from playing Grace to Leon and it feels like you've turned up as the Doom Slayer to take revenge on all the monsters that just finished terrorizing you as Grace, and then you have to swap back and there's this sense of dread to it, like "oh no, now I'm just a person again and I'm in [b]danger[/b]". Leon is so obviously badass that he makes you feel safer for playing him, while Grace feels like somebody you have to save from a terrible situation. Also helping this feeling is the fact that Grace's half of the story is probably the hardest Capcom have tried to make RE feel like a straight up horror game. Dark, claustrophobic and uncomfortable, it's genuinely quite tense to be Grace, and there's some pretty good scares waiting for you in her sections.  If you've played any of the REmakes (or RE7 and RE8 if you're one of them FPS fans), you know what to expect from the gameplay in Requiem. It's simple survival horror gameplay, but it's polished to a mirror sheen and feels great to play. Progression through levels is done in the classic RE style — you're always running around fairly small but dense maps collecting a tool to open a locker to get a key to a door so you can go into the office to find a key for another door so you can grab a mcguffin from a safe once you've found the code to it on the other side of the building. The levels are generally very well put together though, and only on one or two occasions did I really feel like I was doing a lot of backtracking.  My only major complaint about the game is the boss fights. To put it bluntly, they're pretty underwhelming. Playing on standard difficulty, I beat all but one of them on my first try and found that none of them seemed to have more than 2-3 mechanics. It's kind of weird when the most creative fight in the game is the one against just Some Dude. They're also just not very imaginative; I mean really, a [spoiler]random giant spider[/spoiler] as a boss fight? As much as I love it, this series really has to move on from the early 2000s.   Overall, I'd give Requiem a very respectable 8.5/10. I don't think it's a game I'm gonna want to replay over and over again like REmake 4, but I still had a great time playing it, and I'm sure you will too if you decide to give it a go.

*This review contains spoilers of the ENTIRE game*  Another remarkably well-put together game by capcom, resident evil requiem definitely meets my baseline expectations for what a resident evil game would be like. Our two protagonists, leon and grace, are ever so lovable and wonderful main characters, with their contrasting personalities defining the horror and action aspects of the game. The wonderful contrast between their two gameplays makes it feel almost like playing 2 entirely separate resident evil games.   Grace Ashcroft is a remarkably well-made and very realistic character that I feel most people would relate to with how she reacts and responds to certain situations, making her feel very authentic and easy to feel attached to. Her voice actor did wonderful in making her sound nervous or fearful, and her character development reminded me slightly of ashley from RE4 with how her confidence grew as her resolve to save Emily solidifed, yet she still remained fearful of the unknown, but adapted quickly despite being much less equiped to deal with the enemies as compared to Leon.  Leon S.Kennedy makes a miraculous return (aging like fine wine) to the franchise and still has those really extra roundhouse leg kicks, which we all love, along with those corny one-liners, making me glad that he really hasn't changed much. Yet, when he returns to the place where it all begun, we get many flashbacks from RE2 which really highlights how much of the place made an impact to Leon, as his regret of the past and focus on the present push him forward in his endeavours.   The gameplay was rather contrasting, with Grace's sections being extremely nerve-wracking and leon's being a joyride with guns out. A lot of unique mechanisms were added to RE9, I particularly enjoyed the chef in the care center, the many different kinds of zombies in the care center, the girl and the return of the tyrant. Though slightly short-lived, I also enjoyed the section with the soldiers as enemies.  Leon's campaign did somewhat fall short as compared to Grace's since the raccoon city zombies were not as unique and fun to battle against compared to those in the care center, which all had special weaknesses pertaining to their human attachments (E.g: blind, siren, lightswitch and maid zombies), with the rest of the zombies following the care center being rather stereotypical, though somewhat understandable, since Leon's part is more action-based than stealth. It still would've been nice to see more unique or different enemies for leon's section.  Plot wise, having Victor's research be built on merely superstitution did feel like a bit of a joke towards the end. The game also introduced many new sections, which felt slightly underutiliised. Victor's character also had a sudden shift in personality from him being in complete control in the care center, to him getting ridiculed and then tossed off the bridge by Leon, something I found rather disconcerting but brushed aside because well, it was Leon, though the motorcycle showdown did feel goofy, it was entertaining at least. [h1]Resident Evil Requiem does a great job of combining classic survival horror with a more action-driven side of the series.[/h1]  The strongest part of the game is its [b]atmosphere[/b]. The abandoned, post-apocalyptic Raccoon City feels lonely, oppressive, and genuinely haunting. For long-time fans, [b]the nostalgia hits hard[/b], but it does not feel like cheap fan service. It actually supports the tone of the game.  Visually, the game [b]looks beautiful[/b]. The lighting, environments, and level details do a lot to strengthen the horror mood. The sound design and soundtrack are also excellent: silence, distant noises, and music all help build tension.  I also really liked the split between Grace and Leon. Grace’s sections lean more into survival horror, with a stronger feeling of vulnerability and caution. Leon’s sections are closer to action horror, giving the game a different pace. This contrast works well and keeps the experience from becoming too repetitive.  The level design is mostly very strong, especially in Raccoon City. Exploring it feels rewarding and atmospheric. Rhodes Hill, however, felt weaker to me. It relies too much on older mansion-style ideas from previous entries, so it does not feel as fresh.  Overall, this is a strong Resident Evil entry with great visuals, excellent audio, memorable atmosphere, and a good balance between horror and action. Not perfect, but definitely worth playing.  [b]Recommended.[/b]

[h1] Solid 9/10 - The perfect blend of old and new RE [/h1] I’ve spent a lot of time with the Resident Evil franchise, and RE9 honestly feels like Capcom finally figured out how to please both the survival horror purists and the action junkies. It’s a wild ride, and despite a few pacing hiccups, it’s easily one of the best in the series.  [h2] The Dual Protagonist Dynamic [/h2] The standout for me is the balance between Grace and Leon. They play completely differently, and it keeps the gameplay from ever feeling stale. Grace’s segments are a masterclass in tension—her focus is purely on survivability, making every bullet count and every corner feel dangerous. Then you switch to Leon, and it’s the high-octane, action-packed RE we know and love. Moving between Grace’s "desperate struggle" and Leon’s "one-man army" vibe creates a really satisfying rhythm.  [h2] Graphics and Voice Acting [/h2] Visually, the game is stunning, but it’s the sound design that actually got to me. I genuinely got goosebumps just from the voice acting alone, especially Grace in the first chapter. You can feel the panic and trauma in her voice, which sells the horror better than any jump scare could.  [h2]  Lightweight and Polished Performance  [/h2] One thing I have to shout out is the optimization. In an era where most AAA games feel like they need a NASA supercomputer just to run at 60fps, RE9 feels incredibly lightweight. The RE Engine is still a wizard at work here—everything looks top-tier, yet it runs buttery smooth without the stuttering or "heavy" feel that plagues other modern releases. It’s a breath of fresh air to play something this gorgeous that doesn't melt my GPU.  [h2] The Story and Endings [/h2] The main canon ending is great and felt very earned. However, if I’m being honest, the "Bad Ending" path felt a little rushed. It felt like it was just there so they could say the game has multiple endings. I really wish they [spoiler] had included a final Zeno boss fight for that path to give it some actual closure instead of just ending so abruptly.  [/spoiler]  [h2] Map Design and Pacing [/h2] Most of the maps are incredible, but Leon’s section near Raccoon City dragged a bit for me. There’s a part where you have to collect three parts to blow up a door that felt a little "empty" and slowed the momentum down too much. It felt like a bit of a backtrack-heavy fetch quest compared to the tight pacing of the rest of the game.  [h2] Final Verdict [/h2] Minor gripes aside, everything here is solid. I’m really hoping the DLC can smooth out some of those narrative gaps, but for now, this is a must-play.  [b] 9/10  [/b]

[h1] Yes but it's worse than RE4R at combat, Graces sections feel hampened by having to balance combat with Leon [/h1]  8/10  Look there are so many reviews glazing RE9, and I really love some parts of it. Graces section, the Care Centre, is one of the best designed locations in the series to play and learn. But Graces gameplay feels like it's missing something to make it more than a puzzle, and Leon's combat feels woefully unsatisfying compared to Resident Evil 4's 2023 Remake.  Prefacing, I've beaten the game twice on classic difficulty, Insanity is an entire can of worms I'll get into. Requiem marries the classic survial horror of RE7 with the combat of RE4R, and while it's amazing in concept, the first playthrough of Grace feels like it's missing a proper power fantasy. Without alternate weapons besides 2 pistols and one-shot injectors, it feels more like a puzzle game, sneaking around with a weak pistol, than a game with guns. No shotgun, only unlockable hand-held smg post game, it doesn't have that same catharsis as RE7 when you take off a molded's head with a shotgun. And Leon's combat is just not very good  [h2] Grace is puzzle gameplay [/h2] Grace is a puzzle without much combat on the first playthrough, even though it's satisfying to push an enemy into the wall and book it, or to sneak in an injector to stealth, I find myself missing that moment when RE7's Ethan finds a shotgun with 2 shells and decides to use 1 for a headshot pop. I suspect it's to move the action to Leon section for the tension release instead, which sadly was done quite poorly.  [h2] Leon... [/h2] Leon combat feedback. Enemies don't react to your shots much, and seeing torsos of the enemies in RE4R get blown off was a satisfying response to your shotgun in that game. Here, we get some blood decals and the enemy flies back a bit. Shots don't stagger, landing a kick doesn't feel rewarding compared to RE4R's being able to take down entire groups of enemies if the kick sends the enemy into others. The animations of Leon are sluggish. it lacks that satisfying feedback.  Enemies themselves are uninteresting. Mostly just zombies, lickers, and... zombies with guns? They aren't the most fun thing to fight. Compare this to the Knights in RE4R where you need to hit the neck, the Ganado's random mutations and working together, the cultists with their medival weaponry. It doesn't have memorable enemies like that.  And the game is animation city. Shoot a bunch of shots without knowing if the enemy is really taking damage or not because of a lack of feedback, get a stagger maybe you can't really tell when, then press f to watch an animation to kick him, and press left click to watch another animation of Leon finishing the enemy with his hatchet. You're watching Leon grunt and jump and do it for you, more than actually being in control of him, his sections are disappointing.  [h2] The second playthrough and Insanity [/h2] Second playthrough with the unlocked Freya's Needle for grace let me better balance resources with power in the vein of RE7. That section with a newly equipped weapon to balance using resources with raw firepower felt honestly amazing. Grace's sections on my second playthrough felt like playing RE7 again, which is high praise from me.  Lack of a post-game difficulty. I beat RE4R base game multiple times, with 2 professional playthroughs from scratch. That was a rewarding and brutal but fair difficulty.  Insanity in RE9 is more like a masochistic mode, and pretty much [b] requires [/b] using post-game unlocks to get anywhere without banging your head against the wall. Even compared to Madhouse in RE7, this is just insanity. Which makes sense given it's name, and it's like [u] Village of Shadows [/u] in RE8 in the sense that it's just painful. I like replaying Resident Evil games, but the lack of a proper post-game difficulty that isn't just a unfair unbalanced challenge mode isn't here, and I found myself really frustrated trying to make any progress in Insanity. I eventually decided it wasn't worth it and no fun, so I replayed the game on classic again. It definately still lacks the bite of a harder difficulty, but at least it was balanced.  Insanity is fine to exist for masochists. But a lack of a post-game hard difficulty really makes it hard to replay the game.  [h1] The long and short of it [/h1] Resident Evil Requiem is a fantastic game if you loved RE7, even if parts of it on the first playthrough feel compromised as Grace is genuinely quite weak without ever having the tension relieved by finding more powerful weapons, instead opting for puzzle-like solutions to things with stealth and distraction. It's clear to me that tension valve was meant to be released by Leon's action moments. But Leon's lack of feedback from weapon shots, uninteresting enemy designs, and overly cumbersome animations, make the release of tension pretty unsatisfying.

This game takes everything learned from the last decade of Resident Evil games and applies them perfectly. Requiem is a masterpiece.  Resident Evil games are usually a cathartic experience once you finish the game and enter New Game+, you are prepared for what's to come, you've unlocked bonus weapons or abilities, this time the odds are stacked in your favor. What sets Requiem apart is that it takes this (previously) post-game sensation and implements it into the main campaign itself.  This is because the campaign will now automatically switch perspective between two characters who both have a completely different play style. Down to how the save system works. This prevents the game from overwhelming you with its tension and frights and lets you work off that built-up stress in the more action filled sections.  The gameplay, presentation and music are all top notch. The RE engine looks better than ever and delivers impressive visuals in smaller spaces, but it also impresses in larger, wider levels.  Despite all this, performance is impressive. This game is a technical tour de force on every level. I played the entire game on Steam Deck and the indoor sections run at 60fps whilst the outdoor sections run at 40fps. If you have an OLED Steam Deck please turn on your HDR It significantly enhances the experience. Yes, you can turn on the fancy hair effects!  My only wants were a photo mode and for Capcom to implement haptics for DualSense users. But both these things have been added since the last two updates.  It feels like the Resident Evil series has never been stronger, a remarkable feat since it has just turned 30 years old.

as a longtime Resident Evil fan, this one was... good, overall. in some ways it provides us with some of the best gameplay moments and ideas in the series, but in other ways it feels like a meandering retread of Resident Evil 6, of all things.  i maintain that Grace's sections in the Care Centre are the strongest in the game, the infected that all still have individual personalities and carry those on while lumbering around the building is actually an interesting concept, especially since this means each of the infected have different ways of approaching them and consequences for doing so that aren't simply "less bullets/health". Grace as a character is also one I found myself endeared to. her more timid personality fits well with her style of gameplay, i'm aware that her vocal stuttering is quite divisive but for me it added to her character. the Care Centre section is broken up with perspective changes to Leon Kennedy, and at first I was fine with them. i can't put my finger on it but he seems to control a bit worse than RE4 Remake but that might just be me. but the split between Grace's more stealth-oriented, less intense gameplay versus Leon's action-packed sections were a nice touch.  and then Raccoon City happens. what was an interesting dynamic between Grace and her encounters with the individual zombies, and Leon with those same zombies but now wiping the floor with them in that colourful and intriguing Care Centre location instead now turns into Leon killing endless hordes of generic zombie enemies for most of the latter half of the game, with Raccoon City itself being an absolute slog of brown-grey environments for hours on end with your only job being to mow them all down mindlessly while you get to the next bit of brown-grey environment. the game does try to make it less tedious, bless it, by having set-pieces such as that area with the shattering glass beneath you or the motorcycle ride, but it's an absolute shadow of what the game had in that first half. and that's to say nothing of the shameless fanservice that goes on towards the end of the RC section, obligatory due to being an anniversary title. while yes, i'm a fan so i indeed was serviced, it became rather egregious when the soundtrack for when you're wandering around the dilapidated RPD building uses motifs from the original Resident Evil 2 soundtrack... that the Remake, the "definitive" version according to Capcom, didn't even use in favour of mostly ambient pieces of music. so, fans who had never played the original games will be left confused, and ones who did will be left bitter that the only times Capcom remember the original games exist is when they can bank off of nostalgia for them and not in any actually meaningful way.  the game just manages to pull it back somewhat by the time the endgame lab section rolls around, but it's still a far cry from the amazing setup it was doing for the first half or so. i don't hate Leon's sections or gameplay, i just wish they'd have stuck to one style or the other. Resident Evil 4 Remake (i compare the two because Leon's gameplay is obviously based on that game) worked because you were always visiting varied locations fighting many different types of enemies with a solid and focused gameplay loop. Resident Evil Requiem feels like two different games were being developed and they tried to sticky tape them together in the end and it just doesn't quite stick the landing for me.  the Care Centre sequence is so strong that it brings my overall opinion of the game up from where it otherwise would be. and I hate to say that as a Resident Evil nerd, i just... expected more, i guess.

I am not a fan of the series, though I have played RE2's Remake, and remember enjoying it more than that stupid piece of gamedev. It should be made clear that I usually care greatly about acting, storytelling, and the overall atmosphere when I am playing a game or watching a movie, but I still decided to play both of these games.  The voice acting is incredibly bad, not to mention one of the main protagonists literally throws one-liners for the whole second part. "Promise me you'll finish this", Should've worn a helmet", "Sorry, I am not on the menu" - true Japanese entertainment. The interview scene at the very end, which is "suppose to be" a very important plot-reveling-something was the pinnacle example of how poor was the voice direction, with Grace's mother voice being so cold and absent it's clear they just didn't give a damn (spoilers - it doesn't reveal anything). Grace herself stutters unnaturally through the whole game, so I can't imagine anyone who's ever played a game with good voice acting actually think it's some masterpiece.  Of course, it was hard to focus on just that, because the story is a whole different beast of madness. I knew this was a japanese game before I started, so I expected some level of bonkerness, and was still disappointed, or wasn't, if the goal was to make me hysterical every time I tried to turn my brain on, but I usually prefer stimulation of a different kind. The writing was so bad, I actually laughed out loud several times, and couldn't stop for more than a minute. It's clear to me that fans of this series have never read a book after they surpassed teenagehood, preferring manga or comics instead. Even by taking a single example I have already mentioned, the interview part, I can start pointing out dozens of plot mistakes nobody on the dev-team bothered to fix.   Like, why did she wait to the very end to watch it? Before, there were heaps of different laptops, computers or whatever else in the game, any which one could have probably been used to insert the disc she finds in the beginning. Wasn't it "very important" for her to find it behind that painting? So why did she had to wait? The only reason was to make it "epic" when she watches it on that big screen in the final, epic location of the game. Again, truly epic.  What finally melted my brain though, was when in the next scene it is said they still "must", "can", and "want" to... Cure the little girl they found in the hospital and bring her with them? What? That heap of mutant clone flesh crawling around with a bunch of other monsters? A quick list of problems I immediately had when hearing this:   "How would they do that?" By flying a helicopter to that place, and then searching for a monster that looks like her, killing everyone else in the process? It could have been the case, but for what reason was it never shown or even explained?;   "Why would they do that?" Why would they ever return to that hellish place overrun with mutants and covered in blood for an uncertain quest at finding and curing her? Is it really worth it?;   "Why would Grace even care?" She finds out later in the story that Emily was one of many failed clones designed by her likeness or something. Wouldn't that aspect absolutely freak her out instead, or make her attachment less emotional? Everyone she's ever knew lied to her about her past, her mother included, so wouldn't she actually want to just destroy the place? That's the choice I made initially, but little did I know only the game's writers could know what is the best ending.   "How's it even possible that she survived?" Leon said he didn't hit any of her vital parts, but the whole point of even knocking out any monster in the game was to completely obliterate it's "vitals". Did she just fall asleep instead, or pretended to be dead? It should be clear none of this makes any sense, so I'd prefer to stop now. I could write a book discussing this game's disregard to writing, but nobody would read that.  As is usual with something that gathers around a large base of devoted fandom, the most baffling thing is that so many of these "people" are incapable of fathoming that anyone can have any kind of major criticism about it. They think there must be something "wrong" with those who criticize their Overwhelmingly Positive product, as if this game wasn't created almost solely for those that like that specific type of Japanese entertainment. The shooting wasn't so bad, the game wasn't scary but it did have an atmosphere - that's the things I liked! But why can't I criticize it for what it is in the meantime? It's no wonder those who aren't weebs or comic geeks usually stay away from works with such a rabid fanbase.

[b][i] Requiem for the dead. Nightmare for the living. [/i]  Resident Evil Requiem is a love letter to the franchise. With its dual narrative it combines the best of both worlds masterfully mixing survival horror akin to the original three games and Resident Evil 7 with Grace’s sections and the action horror of Resident Evil 4 and Resident Evil 8 with Leon’s sections. While the game is the start of Grace Ashcroft’s story of her new life for Leon this is a story about closure, a requiem to everything and everyone that got him this far.  From the messes left at the Rhodes Hill care center to the sterile floors of the ARK facility I was glued to the screen. From the story to the gameplay, the music to the sound design it was all absolutely enthralling and left me itching for a second playthrough. Requiem has something for both new and returning fans that's certain to leave an impression.

Resident Evil Requiem is easily one of the best survival horror games Capcom has made in years. The atmosphere is incredibly tense, the visuals are stunning, and the gameplay perfectly balances horror and action. Resource management finally feels important again, and some sections genuinely had me stressed in the best way possible.  Grace Ashcroft was a surprisingly great protagonist, and Leon’s return was handled really well. The story kept me hooked from start to finish, even if a few parts in the middle dragged slightly.  Overall, this feels like a proper evolution of modern Resident Evil while still respecting the classic games. Definitely worth playing if you’re a fan of the series.

This game was such a blast to play. From beginning to end, the fun beats never stopped. It isn't the longest game in terms of hours to beat but that's not a negative. The time that you do have with the game is filled with tense and fright filled moments. Unless you're playing as Leon, and then it basically becomes an action packed shooter which reverses the fear onto the poor monsters that happen to come across his path. The voice acting is Resident Evil all the way, for those of you who have played the series. Those who haven't, it's not going to blow you away. Visually the game is stunning to look at and it runs very well. The combat itself is split between crazy hand to hand combat with tactical shooting on one side, with cautious sneaking and avoidance on the other. The story has great callbacks to older games in the series that feel good to relive. This game is a very easy recommendation.

Resident Evil Requiem – a gem in the Resident Evil universe  Capcom really nailed the balance between first-person survival horror and third-person action-paced gameplay. Why? Because you get the best of both worlds. I am an avid fan of Resident Evil 7 despite its difficulty (I probably have PTSD from its DLCs), but I was quite surprised to experience a survival horror atmosphere similar, to some degree, to RE7. I was startled several times during the opening segment of the game.  Regarding the story, I will not dive too deeply into it here, as it is something you should experience for yourself. All I can say is that the game delivers both emotional and frustrating moments, as the story can feel a little far-fetched at times, but that is something quite normal for the series.  Grace Ashcroft – The Bildungsroman  Grace is a fresh face in the series and, alongside Ethan, I believe she is one of the most well-articulated characters Resident Evil has ever had. Her journey and character development throughout the story are quite remarkable, a true “zero to hero” evolution. I am very excited to see what the future holds for her, and I hope Capcom will continue to portray her in a favorable light, unlike what they did with their previous protagonist. I would definitely like to see more of Miss Ashcroft. I see her as a worthy successor to Leon. Hopefully, we will still be seeing her 30 years from now, just like Leon today.  Leon S. Kennedy – The returning face  While Grace is the inexperienced protagonist, Leon is an absolute powerhouse. Even after all these years, he still delivers the iconic one-liners. How can you not love him? The game also allows us to relive certain moments from the past that Leon witnessed 30 years ago.  The performance is quite good overall. The game is well optimized and runs smoothly even on older, yet still capable, hardware. Visually, the game looks fantastic, especially with ray tracing enabled (although I usually turn it off, since I am not particularly fond of the technology and my hardware does not support it that well).  All in all, I definitely recommend Resident Evil Requiem and highly praise it as part of this series. Thank you, Capcom, for entertaining my evenings.

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ “Resident Evil Requiem: The Perfect Blend of Horror, Atmosphere, and Pure Resident Evil Chaos”  Resident Evil Requiem feels like everything great about the series fused into one nightmare masterpiece. The moment the game starts, it grabs you by the throat and never really lets go. The atmosphere is unbelievably tense, the environments are packed with detail, and every hallway feels like something terrible is waiting just out of sight.  This game absolutely nails what makes Resident Evil special: that balance between fear, action, exploration, and pure panic.  One second you’re carefully conserving ammo and creeping through dark rooms listening to every footstep… the next you’re fighting for your life against something that should not exist while your inventory looks like a yard sale of herbs and shotgun shells.  The visuals are incredible too. The lighting, creature designs, sound design, and environments all come together to create one of the most immersive horror experiences the series has had in years. Every area feels memorable and distinct instead of just being “another spooky hallway.”  And the enemies? Absolutely horrifying. Resident Evil always shines when it creates creatures that are both disgusting and fascinating at the same time, and Requiem delivers HARD on that front. Some of these designs genuinely stuck with me after I stopped playing.  The pacing is also fantastic. It knows when to slow down and build tension, and it knows exactly when to throw you into complete chaos. It constantly keeps you on edge without becoming exhausting.  What I love most is that Requiem feels like it respects every era of Resident Evil:  the survival horror roots the cinematic action moments the puzzles the exploration the campy insanity the series is known for  It all blends together perfectly.  Whether you grew up with the classics, loved RE4, or got into the series through RE7 and Village, this game feels like a celebration of everything Resident Evil does best.  5/5 — terrifying, immersive, unforgettable, and another incredible entry in one of gaming’s greatest horror franchises.

I've played every version of REquiem, minus the Xbox version and I personally think this is the best RE game since the OG RE3, which was my previous favorite, and it only took 26 years to dethrone it. The PC version does run REALLY well, but something about the East Raccoon City segment occasionally causes stutters in the flooded parking garage, the rooftop mortar segment, and occasional stutters near the BSAA tent after collecting 2/3 parts, and that's while maxing everything out as much as possible.  The game has plenty of content and can take up to 13-14 hours for a regular run with exploration. Speed running can be much faster under 2-3 hours if you're good enough. The environments and gameplay are also pretty amazing. The movement isn't as fluid as RE4 remake but it does match up more closely with 2 and 3 remake, with some minor fluidity of 4 due to the ever aggressive zombies.  Now let's talk characters. Grace Ashcroft is a welcome addition to the franchise, bringing a fresh take to the REverse that we've never seen. She's scared and alone after being forced to revisit the place where her mother, RE alumni Alyssa Ashcroft of the Outbreak series, was murdered 8 years earlier. Her lack of experience and her genuine fear of what's going on bring new scares to the story, making you fear every corner you turn and room you enter. Leon, however, remains the true protagonist of the game. Even at 49 years old, Leon remains unstoppable despite being in the late stages of Raccoon City Syndrome; A disease that he's also investigating and trying to find answers for. Despite not being the first character you play as, Leons story does take up over half of the game but his story does come with the benefit of revisiting and exploring the ruins of Raccoon City, which in it's own right, is a treat that fans of the series have been wanting to revisit since it's destruction.  If you are a true fan of Resident Evil, then you will love this entry. The horror of Grace's story and the action of Leons definitely made for an amazing game that kept the series from falling stale, and the story of Raccoon City, the Umbrella Corporation, and Ozwell Spencer may blow your mind as we enter this next chapter.

[h1] Simply a masterpiece [/h1]  Going into my Resident evil 9 gameplay i was a bit doubtfull of the implimentation of 2 different game styles, and i wanted to play the game as the devs suggested to, so play first person as Grace and third person as Leon, and honestly in my opinion its one of the best things Capcom did to a resident evil game. The story feels much deeper than the previous resident evil games, its very simple per usual, but its very intresting and it pulls you into the Grace storyline and i really liked how Leon and Grace were not parallel but are more connected and it was such a breath of fresh air for the Resident Evil franchise. The game does an amazing job at not getting boring, you start playing as grace, which is a first person survival horror gameplay. its very atmospheric, dark, eerie and it feels like i was playing re7 again, just scary and heavy stuff, then the game grabs you and throws you into an action packed mode as Leon and it does it at a very good time, they balance perfectly how much they give you of each character, at first they give you snippets and short bursts of what playing as Leon feels like, its gets you excited and pumped, then after a short span of time they throw you back to Grace where a massive feeling of dread and pressure hits you, then they leave you wanting more of Leon and at the right time where it makes sense in the story they give you a generous amount of time as Leon to kill zombies, explore and do the classic Resident evil puzzles. The combat difference between Grace and Leon feels polar, when you play as Grace you have to be sneaky, methodical and you cant just waste bullets on whatever, resources as scarce and you are fighting for survival, its more restricted than Resident evil 7 and imo that makes it heavier. Leon's combat on the other hand feels athletic, action packed and its reminiscent of Resident evil 4, the only thing that i didnt like much is that the combat felt less detailed than Re4 and my boy the merchant got replaced by a.i. The art direction of the game is probably one of the best, its not the best mainly due to some technical problems. Graphics are absolutely goergous, the best looking Resident evil game by far and probably one of the most goergous games in the last 5 years in terms of graphical fidelity, the implementation of Path tracing on a horror game was an amazing idea, it makes everything more realistic and horrific at the same time, the only downside is that Path tracing introduces ghosting and it can gat noticable sometimes, it can be annoying in a couple spots during the gameplay but not to the point where it ruins the immersion, the problem is that you should either go with path tracing or raster since the ray tracing mode doesnt enable Ray reconstruction which cause grainy and a boiling effect that looks dreadful, and the path tracing mode is really, and i mean REALLY heavy, my gpu was getting squeezed and i had to use upscaling and frame generation to have a stable 120fps, so with upscaling you can achieve 60fps and i have a beefy gpu, there were some rare stutters but im pretty sure it wasnt a game problem but it was more of a nvidia driver issue, since it got fixed towards the end when i turned of gsync. Audio in this game is the best in th last decade, it feels so well done and balanced, the wind, the thunder, the footsteps and rattles of chains you hear around you make everything so scary its insane. My only critiques as i said were minimal, i wanted a bit deeper of combat system for Leon and make raytracing a viable option. This game in my opinion will be a game of the year contender and its an absolute masterpiece, enjoyed the game so much that i want more of it, technically speaking this game is better than Re2 but that game holds a very special place in my heart since its the first resident evil game ive ever played, so im biased, so far re2 is still my favourite but i would consider re9 the best game of the series, im curious where will capcom go next.

[b]Resident Evil Requiem[/b] is a bold, atmospheric return to the roots of survival horror while experimenting with modern storytelling and gameplay systems. It feels like a deliberate evolution of what [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] and [i]Resident Evil 7: Biohazard[/i] started — only darker, slower, and more psychological.  The game leans heavily into psychological horror, reminiscent of classics like [i]Silent Hill 2[/i]. Instead of constant action, [b]Resident Evil Requiem[/b] builds dread through isolation, unreliable narration, and disturbing environmental storytelling. A slow-burn story that rewards patience, though it may frustrate players expecting a more action-driven plot.  Boss fights are less frequent but more symbolic and unsettling rather than purely mechanical challenges. Enemy design mixes classic bio-organic monstrosities with more abstract, psychological horrors. Some encounters feel closer to hallucinations than physical threats.  Graphically, [b]Resident Evil Requiem[/b] is stunning. Hyper-detailed environments (rotting interiors, fog-heavy exteriors). Realistic lighting that plays into fear of the unknown. Minimal music, heavy reliance on ambient noise. Subtle audio cues often signal danger before you see it. Playing with headphones is almost mandatory.  [b]Resident Evil Requiem[/b] isn’t trying to please everyone — and that’s exactly why it works. It’s a tense, unsettling experience that prioritizes fear and immersion over action. If you enjoyed the tension of [i]Resident Evil 7: Biohazard[/i] or the atmosphere of [i]Silent Hill 2[/i], this is absolutely worth your time.  [h1]10/10[/h1] DISASTER | BAD | MEDIOCRE | OKAY | GOOD | GREAT | AMAZING | [b][u]MASTERPIECE[/u][/b] [quote] Reviewed on: Win11 Home 64-bit, Intel i5-11600K, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 16GB PRIME, 32GB DDR4-3600 RAM, 2 x Kingston NV1 1TB M.2 NVMe SSD, Internet Broadband 1000/1000 Mbit[/quote] [quote] If you like this review, then please consider giving it a thumbs up. Capcom continues to be on an absolute roll with Resident Evil.   RE is a franchise I grew up with. And I gotta say, this recent trilogy is probably my favorite iteration of Resident Evil as a whole. Especially tonally, these three games absolutely nailed it.  Like every good Resident Evil, the game keeps coming up with new things up until the very end. And its full of great ideas and details.   The stand out feature to me though, is the sound design. You can hear enemies through doors, walls and in some cases, even floors. Think Mr.X in RE2 but for all enemies. Now this feature is pretty much only truly prevalent in the first part of the game, but it elevates that part immensely.   And that's the biggest strength of RE9. All the parts are tweaked perfectly to squeeze everything the devs wanted out of them. Maximum impact.  RE9 also blends survival horror with action like no game I've ever seen. Usually its one or the other, but not both and not both done extremely well. Grace's sections were genuinely thrilling, and Leon's section incredible fun. (I did play with the default setting of Grace 1st person and Leon 3rd person btw).  Gameplay wise, you already know how it plays if you played 7,8, or any of the REmakes. But the progression and constant introduction of new things sets it apart, as well as the significant change in gameplay between the two characters.   And I gotta give it up to the RE engine, delivering amazing visuals with great performance. I played on almost max settings (only ray tracing on 1 of 2 settings, and shadows on high, because ultra shadows were too much of a RAM impact) and the game still ran fluid at 60fps(yes I know I should upgrade from my 60Hz monitor its not 2018 anymore...). And again, it looks absolutely incredible.   If there's ONE thing I would criticize, it's that the villains aren't much of a presence. The game's story kinda runs on its own, without them doing too much tbh. They feel more like the guys you defeat on your way to the evil guy, rather than the evil guy himself. Its totally fine as is, but personally I would've liked a bit more. Especially at the end, where I expected a bit more spectacle given the road leading up to it. But this is not enough to deduct any points for me personally.   Absolutely great experience from start to finish. Can't wait to see where they're going next with RE.

[h1]“Fear changes shape, but Resident Evil always finds a way to make it feel alive again.”[/h1]  Resident Evil Requiem feels like Capcom fully understanding what makes this series special and confidently bringing all of those strengths together into one experience. It captures the tension and vulnerability of classic survival horror while embracing the cinematic action and spectacle that helped define the franchise’s later years, creating a balance that feels surprisingly natural from beginning to end.  What immediately stands out is the duality at the center of the game. Leon and Grace bring completely different energies to the experience, and that contrast gives Requiem its identity. Leon carries the confidence and intensity longtime fans expect, turning encounters into explosive moments of action and control. Grace, on the other hand, brings uncertainty, fear and caution, leaning much harder into the survival horror side of Resident Evil. Switching between those perspectives keeps the pacing fresh and helps the game constantly shift between empowerment and vulnerability without ever losing momentum.  The atmosphere is excellent throughout. Requiem understands how important tension is to Resident Evil, and it builds that tension carefully through lighting, sound design and environmental storytelling. Some areas feel genuinely oppressive, while others explode into chaotic action set pieces that deliver exactly the kind of over-the-top energy the franchise is known for. It manages to feel unsettling, stylish and occasionally disgusting in the best possible way.  Combat is another major highlight. Weapons feel impactful, enemy encounters stay engaging and the game does a great job encouraging players to adapt on the fly. Resources matter enough to preserve the survival aspect, but the game never becomes frustrating or overly restrictive. There is a satisfying rhythm to exploring dangerous spaces, conserving ammunition and then suddenly being thrown into moments of pure panic.  What makes Requiem especially impressive is how replayable it feels. Different playstyles, hidden details, unlockables and alternate approaches make repeated runs genuinely enjoyable instead of repetitive. It captures that classic Resident Evil feeling where finishing the game once only makes you want to dive back in immediately to uncover more secrets or improve your performance.  The presentation deserves praise too. Visually, the game is striking, balancing realism with the dramatic style the series thrives on. The environments are detailed and memorable, character performances feel strong and the soundtrack knows exactly when to stay subtle and when to erupt into something intense.  There are small areas where the game could have pushed itself even further, especially with certain mechanics and puzzle design, but those issues never overshadow the overall experience. At its core, Resident Evil Requiem succeeds because it understands its own legacy without becoming trapped by nostalgia. It respects what came before while still feeling like a confident step forward.  More than anything, Requiem feels like proof that Resident Evil still has plenty of life left in it. It is tense, thrilling, replayable and packed with personality, the kind of survival horror experience that reminds you exactly why this series continues to matter after all these years.

Requiem is effectively a highlight reel of everything Resident Evil fans have loved about its recent series resurgence. I think it's also a natural stepping off point for Capcom to renew the formula.   Here we have Grace and Leon, showcasing the horror and action evolutions both sides of the series have become known for. If they fail to innovate from here, a habit this franchise has fallen into previously, I can see the potential of subpar and repetitive games on the horizon.  That said, RE9 is good fun. I don't think it's perfect. Leons' action is never as sharp or responsive as it is in 4 Remake (which I had my own issues with), and Grace's sections are never quite as puzzle-box delicious as RE7, despite enemy variety improving greatly. The best thing I can say about this title is that it's never boring and introduces new scenarios at an appropriate rhythm. The worst I can say is that all elements combined are less than the sum of their parts, because they don't combine into anything new.  Ultimately, this is a Resident Evil for the fans. Don't expect real scares or highly novel design, you won't find it here. You''ll likely enjoy yourself for about 20 or so hours and if you like nostalgia-bait, you'll get it. This is a review I don't like to write, because I did overall, very much enjoy my time with RE9.  But playing through the new mode added has made a few problems glaringly obvious, both in the mode itself, and things I'd overlooked playing through the game.  To start with, the most dangerous basic enemies in the game are also the ones with the most bulletsponge healthbars. The zombies with guns that will rip you apart if you don't have body armour are, themselves, wearing armour and helmets, making them very difficult to wear down; and with a higher healthpool than most other zombies to boot.   The game's new Unique Thing are these guys with giant blisters on their heads; blisters that aren't any more a weakpoint than the rest of them, that have 4-5x the health pool of the enemy they turned from, and will turn any nearby enemies, alive or dead, into more like them when they die. Did I mention, that these blisterheads have a one hit kill attack that you have to perfect parry, where they roar and then leap at you? But the gap between 'Roar' and 'One Hit Kill Leap' is very narrow, meaning you have to recognise which full body shaking is them screaming, and which is them being about to leap at you. It's not impossible, I DO parry it more times than not, but it's not the kind of attack that should be on the most durable enemies in the game.  And lastly, the mode itself; perhaps the original fight was like this too and I just didn't know because we didn't have Health Bars, but the final boss of the new mode is the final boss of the game, and he has invincibility sections midfight. You'll pick a bunch of perks through the new mode that will give you an excessive damage output, and then all of a sudden your shots start doing zero damage because it wants to do the phase transition attack (the phase has its own, miniature phases) before it will let you start damaging it again. But, if he's already started doing another attack, he will finish that full multi-hit chain before starting the attack that will let him be damageable again.  The core game is incredibly fun, Grace's sections feel terrifying, while Leon's are excellent survival action horror, ala RE4 or Mercenaries mode; his moves feel fantastic to play, and I can only think of a single gun I don't particularly like using, and that's solely because of how good all of the others feel.  But ♥♥♥♥, dude; as much fun as I'm having, every time I hit one of these the fun immediately evaporates, and at that point, I just can't recommend it.

Great game overall, everything is top notch; gunplay, horror elements, tone and story. However, I'll mention a few negatives I had with the game that I don't see addressed a lot:  [h2]Boss fights:[/h2] They are few, and super underwhelming, even by RE standards. Most of the boss fights are dealt with by dealing damage, no special mechanics or anything, and they're super easy.  [h2]Main objectives:[/h2] They are all literally the same quest: fetch 3 "objects" to progress. If you played RE2 or RE4 before, you'll know that there a lot of objectives where it's something like this: Grab 3 batteries / grab 3 emblems / grab 3 statues to open the door and unlock the next area. That's fine and all, but here in Requiem, this is literally the only quest type, and towards the end it felt really tedious. I think RE4 had the perfect balance in this area, where progression was a mix of solving puzzles / fetch missions / survival for a set period of time / mini boss fights, etc...  [h2]Inventory management :[/h2]  it's a severe downgrade from RE4, it's back to how it was in RE2, and even worse in some cases: Mainly, I really freaking hate how main quest items take up space in your inventory! this was the thing I hated the most when I played RE2, inventory management was so painful, and when I played RE4, I was so happy that they changed it so that quest items have their own inventory tab... but here in Requiem it's back to how it was in RE2, No idea why they regressed this change here... inventory management while playing as Grace is so freaking painful, in my opinion this is not added challenge/difficulty, it's just simply not fun. having to backtrack to the storage container every few minutes to store your excess items because of very limited inventory slots is a severe waste of time.

Another Modern Resident Evil, another Really Solid Experience. I can't say the game is perfect, no game (especially RE games) can be, but it feels like this is really the best versions of both styles of Resident Evil games up to this point. If you want survival horror, this game does it great with Grace. You want action horror, this game does it great with Leon. Old characters are referenced or return, new characters are really lovely additions to the series. Writing isn't the greatest, but Leon's quippy so it's good enough. It was also really short, you can get all the steam achievements in 2-3 playthroughs, 4 if you're really scuffed, and since launch there's only been one real big gameplay addition, that being a roguelike gamemode designed to be hyper uber difficult. There's honestly not a ton of game here, that's easily it's biggest drawback for what is a $70 game.  Pick it up if you're an RE fan, it's fine if you're not but you're left in the dark on an awful lot of things so I'd absolutely pitch grabbing it on a sale if your only connection with Resident Evil is wanting to salivate over Leon's pectoral muscles like the rest of us.  I'll also say at the end of this that there was some odd audio issues when it came to cutscenes, mainly the audio paused and desync'd. It seems to have been fixed in the post launch patches, but I'm attaching my specs just in case. I suspect it was because I had it on my larger HDD and not my SDD, but from a brief playthrough with seeing a few cutscenes, it should be fine.

This game overall is a disappointment.  It is massively overhyped.  The writing is probably the weakest it's ever been in the series, not even that it is known for good writing.  Grace is the most annoying character introduced to the series who has zero redeemable qualities and  hardly any character development.  The Grace sections are repetitive hide and seek sections with scripted enemy actions that you have to kite in a very specific way because we can't get good enemy AI in 2026.  Grace is more frustrating than you average female in any given horror movie with her incompetence and inability to grasp literally anything going on around her.  Plot armor is the only thing protecting her.  Speaking of plot, the other half of this game turns into a terrible mix of a Michael Bay and Paul W.S. Anderson mashup.  There's a certain set piece that is so over the top, it's laughable.  The return to Raccoon City falls flat and fails to connect with a majority of fans.  It's a lame attempt at cashing in on nostalgia.    Leon's combat segments are barely enjoyable.  Combat is a tuned down version of RE4R with slower and more sluggish gunplay and bullet sponge enemies that aren't even satisfying to fight.    The villains are also some of the worst.  Super forgettable.  No development, no real motivations for them or explanations for the why.  It's just bad writing that's retconning past events.    Furthermore, there's just no replay value in this one.  The game environments aren't really exciting, the gameplay is sluggish and when you're following around characters that are unlikeable, it's hard to become absorbed into the game.    The game couldn't decide if it wanted to be RE4 Remake 2.0 or RE Village 1.5.  It does neither well.  Gameplay feels like a huge step back for the series.    It hurts more being a long time fan of the series that's been playing since 1996.  I didn't expect this one to be good based on the trailers, but I didn't expect it to be this bad.    As for the Leon Must Die DLC, Capcom phoned it in something some intern developers cooked up.  Boring slop thrown onto the game to try and keep interest alive since there's no point revisiting this title.   This to me is more disappointing than the RE3 Remake and RE7.  I'd skip this one.

[h1]Overrated and clumsy.[/h1]  Requiem is getting a lot of praise which is ultimately what convinced me to give it a try, but I personally feel it's leaning into the worst aspects of the franchise.  I realised this game was going to be silly [spoiler]the moment Leon decided to chainsaw through a metal bolt in a wooden door, rather than the wooden door itself.[/spoiler]  I realised it was actually stupid when it made me carry [spoiler]ID bracelets in Grace's inventory. Bracelets, the things you're supposed to wear on your wrist and can easily fit into any kind of pocket. Each of said bracelets take up as much inventory space as the pistol.[/spoiler]   [h3]Things that spoiled it for me in no particular order[/h3] Early in the game you come to a long, spooky hallway with an open window at the end. The open window is blowing lace curtains around and it looks great. As you approach, however, the curtains literally stop blowing so as not to touch Grace. They actively retreat if you move at them mid-gust. I assume this is to hide the fact that it's a baked animation and not a dynamic softbody simulation. I don't know how that ended up happening but it's massively immersion breaking and pretty shoddy for a game that's largely centred around and praised for its environments. It also feels like the priorities are off when the protagonist's hair seems to have more physics simulation than the rest of the game, and apparently at the expense of a dynamic environment. You'll spend most of the game looking straight past the character and at the environment itself so this strikes me as an odd choice.  Grace's movement speed is really annoying. I understand it's to heighten tension, but it really makes her feel like she's dragging her feet when you're just trying to drop things off at the item box or save your game. It's not normal for a human being, especially a scared one, to move that slowly.  Grace's magic shirt is also a little distracting. No matter how dirty it gets, it's always mostly clean again a few moments later.  It often cuts away so you don't get to see monster transformations (so Capcom doesn't have to pay for said animations to be even be made, I assume because they can't easily be reused). They did this with the RE4 remake and it's cheap and lazy.  I played on the hardest difficulty it would allow and it's still easy. Supplies are ridiculously plentiful and you can essentially kill everything in the game without running short, which feels like it goes against the design philosophy of better RE titles.  Speaking of better RE titles, this one rehashes enemies, bosses, environments and even ideas from the whole series. Prepare to undergo a kind of greatest hits compilation of things you've done and seen before.   The villains also really suck and refuse to [spoiler]kill Leon despite having the desire and opportunity to do so multiple times. They just have to do their long expository spiel which is always long enough for Leon to escape or fight back. It's trite and boring.[/spoiler]   Leon's quips remind me of Mac from It's Always Sunny. He doesn't really have the wit to make it work and comes off as an idiot most of the time.  There's also a very silly [spoiler]motorbike chase with Leon and one of the main villains where he's firing RPGs at you while you fend off zombie dogs. It's off the wall, poorly done and feels like budget Uncharted.[/spoiler]  The main Leon sections have you [spoiler]getting "points" for killing zombies and redeeming them at magical BSA boxes for prizes.[/spoiler] It feels very weird after the more traditional scavenging Grace sections.  Speaking of, there's also a some dissonance with the two inventory styles. In Grace's inventory each item takes up one slot regardless of size. A bracelet, a full stack of pistol bullets and [spoiler]Requiem[/spoiler] all take up the same amount of space, which is odd but on its own wouldn't be noticeable. When switched to Leon's inventory where everything has a different size and shape as you would expect, it sort of forces me to think about how little sense Grace's inventory makes.   [h3]In Summary[/h3] As much as I've complained, there are some great aspects to this game and I've had fun playing it. Grace's VO performance is stellar and the moment-to-moment gameplay can be really engaging. There are many nice little touches and it's clear a lot of people who really cared worked on this game, and the environments are, as always, very enjoyable to explore.  It's a mixed bag, though, and I personally couldn't overlook its silliness, its inconsistency or its tendency to cut corners. It might seem fussy and pedantic, but immersion is absolutely essential for a horror game and I spent as much of my playtime thinking about the weird design choices, rough edges and inconsistent tone as I did actually engaging with the atmosphere. It seems like it's heading back to RE5 and 6 territory, and I personally feel that's when the series was at its worst.  Is it fun? Yes. Big silly fun. I laughed a lot.  Is it a good horror game? I'd have to say no, and ultimately a good horror game is what I want/expect from Resident Evil.
