Resident Evil Requiem is not a bad game, but it's a very disappointing one and probably one of the worst RE games. The first half of the game is very, very strong, with an intriguing hook to the story and fun gameplay as Grace, who is definitely a big highlight of the game. However as the game goes on you play as her less and less, and in the second half of the game you basically only play as Leon. Grace contributes very little to the endgame which makes it feel like she's being sidelined.. in the game ABOUT HER. She's even knocked out during the entire final boss fight. It feels like they wanted to make a new game about Leon, but still wanted to make the spooky first person sections, so they made a new character exclusively for that and then dropped her halfway through.  Beyond that the game is laughably bad in terms of replayability, probably one of the least replayable RE games ever made. Not only is the game extremely scripted which makes replaying tedious, there's an unskippable part in the orphanage that contributes absolutely NOTHING but slow the game to a gigantic crawl, so much so that one of the most popular mods for the game is removing it entirely. The story, even for a series that doesn't prioritize story over gameplay very often, is terrible. Death is undone and means nothing, two new villains are created only for them to both die and ultimately feel very hollow and like neither did much, and they even retcon a lot of things pertaining to the biggest event and character in the series. It feels very disrespectful to the series in a way I'm appalled so many people just don't care about.  The worst part of it all? RE9 had the potential to be one of, if not the greatest RE game of all time. Going back to Raccoon City could be a monumental event bringing many of the series' characters together again, but instead we get a lame, generic sprawling city with almost none of the iconic locations and landmarks. RPD is a 5 minute section and insanely underused/disappointing. Characters like Jill, Claire, even Ada, who are extremely important to the Raccoon City story, are never mentioned. It's fanservice that doesn't even feel like fanservice, it feels pointless. At the very least the game is absolutely not worth full price, there is nearly zero replayability and even the new gamemode is just recycled content with random weapon drops and a shallow perk system.

This one's really special.  Resident evil has had a bit of an identity crisis since 4.  1-3 are survival horror - limited inventory slots, rare ammo, etc.  You really have to choose when to use resources.  4 was a HUGE hit, but a total shift in tone.  Action horror - kill everything you can, an ability to aim effectively, etc.  RE7 and 8 were returns to roots, but RE2/3 remakes were more action horror.  So what would 9 be?  Both.  There are two main characters - Leon Kennedy, star of 2/4/6 and now 9.  He's got his attache case, lots of weapons, martial arts training, and a hatchet you can repair.  Grace Ashcroft, however, is very scared FBI agent who has a gun but isn't confident in how to use it.  She's the survival horror.  You swap back and forth between the two characters at regular intervals.  The game has the classic standbys - overly elaborate doors that need three keys that aren't keys, a big ass chest and a typewriter to save your games.  Lots of goofy zombies to shoot.  A currency system for the action-oriented hero with gun upgrades to purchase.  Achievements give you challenge points you can spend on unlocking the very silly game-breaking weapons, so there's an incentive to 100% that I wouldn't normally have.  I'm now playing my...5th playthrough?  I got infinite ammo for the RPG and super hard mode is still pretty hard, because only leon gets the rocket launcher - Grace still kind of sucks and just never gets good weapons.  There are a couple of jump scares, but that's much more true early on before anything is actually threatening in the game.  Still might be a dealbreaker, ofc.  I think I'd say the best RE yet.  I'm looking forward to DLC or extra modes.  5/5

Resident Evil Requiem is a game I can't really recommend, particularly at full price. Despite a promising start and the prospect of flitting between two characters and two fairly different gameplay experiences, the game just becomes a disjointed mess the more you progress.   Here you play the roles of FBI Agent Grace Ashcroft and Leon Kennedy once more. Grace's portion is in first person and revolves around puzzle solving, stealth and general survival horror which is typical of the series. Leon's parts are more action-focused and are done in third person. These two vastly different gameplay experiences don't blend very well thanks to awful pacing which is far worse in the second half of the game and a conflict of gameplay design.   Playing as Grace, especially in the opening few hours is fantastic. The mechanics are enjoyable as is the setting. Despite some linearity and predictable moments, it's great fun and there are a few really enjoyable puzzles. Leon's fan-service appearance in Requiem actually brings back many woes of Resident Evil 6 and all survival horror elements are out of the window as his gameplay is an exhausting mess of open world exploration filler and arcade-style combat. Items are aplenty and there's no real consequence of death either.  There are recycled boss fights, iconic returning environments that lack impact and some truly diabolical set-pieces. Ammo and medical supplies are far too prominent and the fact you can craft these with ease just kills any semblance of survival horror. Some puzzles and sections feel extremely tacked-on and Leon's later sections are so padded out, you just feel like the game is wasting your time. Despite a short completion time of 12 hours or so, the game seems like it's 4 hours too long.   I really enjoyed the first half of Requiem but it's clear much of the latter part of the experience is rushed and deliberately stretched out. The inclusion of Leon is actually detrimental as a whole and a lot of the nostalgia aspects fall completely flat. Even Grace's part falls to pieces at a certain point as the puzzles become really uninspired and easy. It's a real shame because up to that point, everything feels incredible but Leon's railroaded appearance seems to derail the entire game.   Overall Requiem gets off to a promising start but eventually becomes a convoluted mess of conflicting design, terrible pacing and uninspiring gameplay. It feels like Resident Evil 7 with RE6 slapped on it. This game feels so rushed and lacks a clear directional focus.

Requiem honestly feels like it has an identity crisis, but somehow it works perfectly. Capcom clearly tried to appeal to both old school fans and newer players, and for the most part, they pulled it off really well.  First of all, the game looks absolutely insane. I had to stop multiple times just to look around at the environments. The lighting, audio design, and environmental detail are phenomenal, and visually this is easily the best looking game in the series.  Combat feels fantastic, especially with Leon. Dare I say this might be the best he’s ever felt in the franchise. Every time Leon shows up, the game cranks the energy up to 100 and throws in every badass one liner possible, and honestly, it’s great.  The game also does a really good job building tension and atmosphere, especially early on. The opening sections are genuinely creepy and probably the closest the game gets to true horror. But once Leon becomes more involved, the game quickly shifts toward action, and the fear factor drops off hard. It never reaches the level of terror that Resident Evil 7 had.  I really liked the option to switch between first person and third person perspectives. It actually changes how the game feels instead of feeling like a gimmick. but definitely first person works best for grace and third person with Leon.    The pacing is mostly solid outside of one mission that dragged a bit too long. My biggest criticism is probably the difficulty. Grace is clearly meant to be the more vulnerable, horror-focused character, but I rarely felt in danger. The game is a little too easy, which hurts some of the survival horror tension. That said, the story is fantastic and easily one of my favourite recent Resident Evil stories. Capcom definitely played things safe in a lot of areas, but even with that, this is still a great game overall.  The optimization is also surprisingly good. For how visually insane this game looks, it runs really well overall. I only noticed a few stutters during some of the more intense scenes, mostly in larger outdoor areas with a lot happening on screen at once. Outside of that, performance stayed smooth for the majority of the game.   Definitely recommend.

[h1][b]⭐ Resident Evil 9 – 9.5/10 ⭐[/b] “A masterclass in survival horror where every hallway feels like a threat and Leon still somehow has enough aura to flirt with death itself.”[/h1]  [hr][/hr]  Resident Evil 9 somehow pulls off the impossible. It perfectly balances the slow-burn survival horror tension of Resident Evil 2 with the faster-paced action of Resident Evil 4 without sacrificing what makes Resident Evil feel special in the first place. One minute I’m carefully counting bullets like it’s the Great Depression, the next I’m knee-deep in absolute chaos fighting monstrosities that look like they escaped a government lab funded entirely by bad decisions and human suffering. The pacing constantly keeps you on edge. Just enough horror to make you panic, just enough action to make you feel like the coolest man alive for approximately 14 seconds before something with twelve teeth and unresolved anger crashes through a wall. [hr][/hr]  And somehow, against all odds, Grace manages to hold her own alongside Leon S. Kennedy — which is NOT an easy task considering she’s sharing screen time with Leon “Sex God” Kennedy himself. She never feels overshadowed or shoved into the background. She’s genuinely likable, capable, and memorable in a franchise full of iconic characters. The story is honestly one of the strongest Resident Evil narratives we’ve had in years. It balances emotional moments, mystery, horror, and absurd Resident Evil nonsense perfectly. Every new section feels tense, every reveal lands, and the atmosphere is oppressive in the best way possible. [hr][/hr]  Visually? Absolutely insane. Every dark corridor feels handcrafted to psychologically damage you. Every creature design looks horrifying. Every explosion feels like Michael Bay personally broke into Capcom headquarters and demanded more fire. [hr][/hr]  Is it perfect? Almost. Does it occasionally lean a little too hard into action? Maybe. Did I care when Leon started doing action movie nonsense while I was grinning like an idiot? Absolutely not. [hr][/hr]  [b]Final Score: 9.5/10[/b] — A near-perfect blend of survival horror and action that feels like the culmination of everything modern Resident Evil has been building toward.

While RE Requiem still leaves with a positive recommendation for me, I can't help but feel baffled by the severe whiplash it left me feeling, and I don't just mean switching between Action-Oriented Leon compared to Survival-Horror oriented Grace.  The Grace sections were near perfect on the mark. They took the best parts of RE7 and the scarier elements of RE8 (cough cough dollhouse cough cough) and honed them masterfully. Despite my bias towards RE4 with the original still being one of my favorite games of all time, I find that the Grace portions of this game were by far the highlights. My one complaint is the sheer lack of "Resident Evil" puzzles. I always joked that locksmiths in the RE universe must be some of the most well paid and respected engineers in the world because of the sheer quirkiness of their designs. Rotating shadow puzzles, sliding tiles, weird pattern games, these are all staples of the RE environment... and there just wasn't much of that here anymore, which is a shame.  The Leon sections I left feeling conflicted. I entered the series with RE4, and the RE4make was spectacular as well. Despite the obvious clashes of tones with the Grace section, I was so excited to see the best parts of 4 and 7/8 coming together. At first, I thought it worked well-- Leon passing through areas already explored by Grace, roundhousing and inflicting critical hits with Vicious Mockery like the Bard he truly is. But I feel like everything falls apart when he heads to Raccoon City, which is the bulk of his gameplay time.  To the game's credit, the gunplay and badassery you feel playing as Leon is spot-on, I have zero complaints about how the actual action feels. Where it falls flat is everything surrounding it. From the moment Leon enters the ruins of Raccoon City I feel like it completely runs out of steam. In average gameplay, it basically becomes a horde shooter through various ruinous set pieces with very little visual variety between them (until reaching the lab section anyway, which feels like a retread of the underground lab in RE2). And while that is certainly not unenjoyable given how nice the gunplay is, it becomes quite tedious and feels like it goes on just a bit too long.  Then comes the... odd choices. Giant spiders, mutated plant monsters, that's all fine. Par for the course in the RE Universe, really. But I feel like the game just throws them at you because it didn't know what else to do anymore. In previous titles, these over the top battles are usually teased or eluded to in advance, with a natural ramp up period. You see Del Lago eating corpses in the lake before you are forced to cross it, building anticipation and suspense. You find notes or hear characters hint at the existence of their "latest creation" before later putting a horribly disfigured face to the name. That's just not really here, or it happens so quickly that you barely had time to escalate to that point. On top of this, the complete over the top cinematic action sequences (I think everyone probably knows which one I'm likely thinking about as I write this) just completely undercut the tone. Leon is at his best when his stories are campy, a little corny, but grounded in what I would consider "possible" for a well trained and physically fit human to achieve in the universe that has been set. At this point, his feats are beyond superhuman.  And that's where my biggest gripe comes in. I feel like there is heavy MCU vibes going on in the late-game. Not only by putting him on near superhuman levels and dropping him into extreme over-the-top action cinematic set pieces, but with some of it's "twists". Not to spoil some of the biggest reveals, but many of them are just what we see from the latest MCU movies. Retreading known and safe ground, but trying to one-up itself at the same time, only to faceplant during the attempt. It began to feel like a collage of "remember THIS place?" "Remember THIS guy? Wasn't he SCARY?", and with how well Capcom has been doing (and especially with how well the Grace portions were done), I didn't really expect to contend with a nostalgia-bait slideshow.   It's worth noting that this really only happens in maybe the final third of the game, and to me it smells a little of rushed development cycle. They had put so much into the marketing and development that they were approaching the deadline and had to wrap it up and get it out to market, resulting in some cuts to the story or gameplay in some areas. It's the only explanation for what I feel is such a steep decline towards the end of the game.  RE Requiem does not get booted out my door without a positive recommendation,  but it's like eating an entire pie all at once. At first it's hot fresh and tasty, but as you get further in, the pie gets colder and you get more bloated-- but it's still pie. Even if it's cold and you're a little nauseated, pie is still good.

So...Resident Evil: Requiem...  [b] The Setting [/b] It's hard to decide where to start, so I'll open it with this: this game completely blew me away. Having played Biohazard and Village as my latest RE games, my expectations for this game were way different. Whereas Village was a fantastical setting, this game offers the classic, apocalyptic setting. This is also reflected in the game's use of suspense. Playing as Grace, this game is probably the scariest in the series in my opinion. The zombies are smarter, possessing characteristics from their human selves such as screeching loudly (Singer zombies) or having a fixation with turning off lights (Servant zombies). All I can say about these zombies: they make my skin crawl (which is only worsened by the fact that they occasionally speak). Now, this in itself isn't all that horrible, but when almost every area in the game is devoid of light and your flashlight only reaches about 1.5 meters in front of you, it definitely serves to create one of the most creepy gaming experiences I've ever had. Leon's section is way different from this although it still keeps the dim lighting...Leon's section takes the game back to the serie's roots, because we find ourselves back where it all started: Raccoon City. The city is left in ruins after the bombing and it feels truly surreal to walk through the city that once was full of panic, now almost unsettlingly quiet.  [b] Characters [/b] As someone who struggles a lot with anxiety and has autism (Grace is not confirmed to have autism, but her actions and patterns resemble some it's characteristics) Grace is a refreshing interpretation of a hero. She is not the classic, stoic hero who is fearless and handles everything as if it isn't a challenge at all (Leon), but she's rather faced with a lot of very human problems, anxiety being the biggest. This shows through her stuttering during the cutscenes, the panicking in her breathing and her body language. In many ways, she and I was on the same journey together. Both of us were visibly scared and had to take breaks from it all during certain sections (I never wanna go through the basement again)  Leon does as Leon does.  [b] Gameplay [/b] The gameplay can be split up into 2 different sections: The Grace setting and the Leon section. During Grace's setting the resources are scarce, your weapons are weak and the movement feels slow and sluggish (not necessarily a bad thing). This completely controls the power balance between the player and the enemies. Every enemy feels like a big ordeal and your resources take a significant hit with every enemy you take down. I played on nomal difficulty, but I was still struggling to manage my ammunition. Although it is difficult, managing resources in Grace's part feels very rewarding to overcome and it reminds me a lot of scavenging through Raccoon ciry in RE2 and 3.  Leon's section is a lot different and shifts the focus from survival-horror to a more action-focused genre. The weapons are stronger and a weapon upgrading system (very similar to Village's) is introduced. It serves as a break from the horror, but not in a bad way. It's quite refreshing in all honesty. Whereas I was holding my breath with a racing heart in Grace's section, I was overjoyed with excitement during Leon's.   [b] The Story [/b] It's very difficult to talk about Requiem's story without spoilers, but what I will say: it ties together previous loose ends from RE2 and RE3 together to make a well, thought-out story that is as captivating as it is creepy. This is argueably the game's strongest suit.  [b] Miscellaneous [/b] The sound design of this game is amazing and incredibly dynamic. It can go from loud and panicy, to quiet and nerveracking in an instant. The lack of sound in some areas serves to improve the atmosphere a lot. It gets so incredibly quiet that Grace's shaky breathing seems awfully loud. These things work in tandem with the eerie music that floods in occasionally, darkening the atmosphere and definitely gave me the creeps.  Requiem, much like most other Residen Evil games, has it's fair share of puzzles. It follows the classic formula of a single, main area where the player runs back and forth looking for different key items. It can very easily get repetitive, but much like RE2, Requiem makes sure to add little, unexpected changes that keeps the game (and areas) interesting.  [b] Final Verdict [/b] This game surprised me a lot. From the setting, to the characters and the overarching story that ties together earlier installations of the series, it all comes together to create a masterpiece of a game. I am absolutely in love with this game and what it does with the foundation that is Resident Evil. In my opinion this is the best Resident Evil game (only narrowly beating RE4). It combines great features from the previous game and improves upon them and there's so many good things to say about this game. For the sake of whoever is reading this, I'll wrap this up with my final score, which, to no surprise, comes to a gorgeous score of...10/10!!!!  Pick this game up, either full price or on sale, both are worth it.

I absolutely loved this game. After finishing the story, I immediately started a New Game Plus—which, for me, is the highest praise a game can receive. Having played every single entry in the series (except the first one, ironically!), I can confidently say this has landed a spot in my top three Resident Evil games of all time.   The most impressive feat here is the phenomenal gameplay balance. It perfectly bridges the gap between different eras of the franchise, seamlessly switching between the claustrophobic horror style of RE7 and Village and the high-octane action sections featuring Leon that feel like the glory days of RE4 and RE5. This variety keeps the pacing perfect from start to finish.  The story itself is amazing and kept me completely hooked. The characters are exceptionally well-written, with motivations that make the emotional beats land perfectly. Visually, the game is a masterpiece; playing with path tracing turned on makes the environments look absolutely gorgeous, with lighting and reflections that set a new standard for the series. Whether you prefer the survival-horror roots or the action-heavy titles, Requiem delivers the best of both worlds. It is a stunning, emotional, and thrilling ride that I’ll be playing through many more times.

Love it!  So, I haven't played Resident evil revelations 2, 7 or 8 yet, or any of the remakes outside of a bit of 2, but played all others including survivor, dead aim, (didn't finish 6, though), so I am biased as I really like the franchise. For me, this entry had the perfect mix of what I saw from streams of 7 & village and 4 & 5. With slower, methodical gameplay as Grace, which reminded me of those first hours stuck in the mansion as Chris, on the train as Rebecca or as Leon in the RPD with nothing but a gun and too little ammo to even down a single zombie. With some tense moments and well-scripted jumpscares, I absolutely loved making my way through the Rhodes Hill Chronic Care Center.   The game frequently switches back to Leon for more action-packed sequences. Parrying all attacks with the press of a button and a generous timing, swinging an Axe and chopping off limbs, all while getting constant ammo resupplies for an ever-growing and improving arsenal of weapons felt very cathartic after barely making it through the same area as Grace and this made both characters fun and unique to play.  The sound is excellent, with faraway noises cluing you in on the movement of enemies and the atmospheric background music and ambient noise adding to the tension. The graphics are gorgeous and really show off Capcoms proprietary engine (unless you activate an AI DLSS and ruin it, of course) even on my now-humble 3080. It chugged a little during one more open-world section, but performed very well in all other areas of the game, even a high-speed section.   It took me around 13,5 hours to beat the game, but it has an achievement to speedrun it in 4. The game is packed with jumpscares and action-sets, but I felt with this length it didn't overstay it's welcome and wasn't padded with any boring sections. I felt each part of the game was memorable and the conclusion was as epic as you can expect from a modern Resident Evil game.   My only real criticism is the parry button during Leon's sections. This made almost any enemy, including the final boss, feel trivial as I found nearly every incoming attack could be countered this way. It lowered the challenge for me, which was definitely there during Grace's sections. All in all, I really enjoyed it and Grace's gameplay has wet my appetite for Resident Evil 7 and 8.

Capcom has truly mastered the RE Engine-it looks gorgeous, runs incredibly smoothly, and brings a level of polish that makes other AAA games look soulless. What makes it awesome: The Dual Protagonists: The game handles the shift between Grace (intense survival horror/stealth) and Leon (high-octane action) perfectly. Playing as Grace in first-person feels genuinely tense, while switching to Leon feels like a well-deserved, badass power fantasy. The Atmosphere & Gore: It brings back that slow, dreadful fear of not knowing what's behind the corner, with some of the best enemy designs in the series. Plus, the blood and gore are satisfyingly disgusting. Fan Service Done Right: As a long time fan, returning to the ruins of Raccoon City and seeing familiar callbacks felt incredibly nostalgic without being forced. Excellent Sound Design: Playing with headphones during Grace's segments is a terrifying experience. If you love Resident Evil, you need to play this. It feels like a "best-of" collection of RE7, RE2 Remake, and RE4 Remake all in one gorgeous, polished package. Final Rating: 10/10 - A must-buy!

The game is divided into a Grace section and Leon section. Most of Grace's sections are in the beginning of the game and Leon's major section is in the middle of the game and end. There is some sections in between where they switch on and off in the beginning and end of the game. Grace's section relies mostly on survival horror and jump scares, I just call it how I see it.  Leon's section is pretty much pure action horror, with a bit of survival sprinkled in. This doesn't make or break the game, it's basically Resident Evil 4 Leon but a bit stripped down. The middle of the game will absolutely be a break or make for most people as this is Leon's lime light, where he's shines and comes back to Raccoon City. A few twists that as of right now aren't necessarily answered, that maybe the new DLC coming out will elude to. The music is phenomenal! I suggest anyone who truly enjoys Resident Evil to make sure you can hear the music properly with the emotional impact from the story telling and acting. Without going into spoilers and a few gameplay changes that were un-necessary, it could be a 10/10.  Highly recommend especially if you enjoyed all the Remakes so far. Koshi Nakanishi's Resident Evil Requiem, developed by Capcom, is one I felt I had to sit on for a while. It was the first Resident Evil title I played at launch; the others were bare minimum a year after release. Evaluating what this franchise has meant to me over the past several years has led to a lot of introspection on what it truly means to be a survival horror game. Nakanishi seems to have felt the same way. In many of the pre-release interviews, he discusses the direction of the series over the last three decades and what he identifies as strong suits and potential drawbacks. I went into Requiem, then, with excitement, not merely because Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is one of my favorite entries, but because I found his philosophy to line up similarly to my own. Can one merge the two opposing sides of the franchise: survival horror and action horror?  Apparently so! Not that I ever thought it was impossible, per se, nor does it come without drawbacks even in Requiem, but the attempt here is largely phenomenal and mixes some of the finest of both genres the franchise has seen up to this point. Taking clear inspiration from all over the franchise, as well as cult classics like Siren, Requiem is a heart-pounding adventure throughout. Split between the anxiety-ridden Grace Ashcroft and the battle-scarred Leon S. Kennedy, what you have are segments that feel akin to cold and warm water. The Rhodes Hill Chronic Care Center is one of the best dungeons in the entire series; it feels like every segment has two different Jack Bakers patrolling the area, leaving Grace constantly on edge, which is horribly infectious. The zombie chef, the monstrously large Chunk, the light-hating servant zombies for whom every encounter is a puzzle, and the deaf zombie who can be tricked into infighting with other creatures. You are in constant danger, harkening back to the original Resident Evil, where the most basic zombie represents a monumental threat in the early game. Smaller mechanics, such as Grace's melee attack being a weak push, enhance the fight-or-flight nature of survival horror. After Resident Evil Village turned Ethan Winters into an Eastern European badass, it's nice to play as a proper normal once more. The level design flows and interconnects seamlessly; backtracking is not a nuisance, but rather something I look forward to doing. It feels like with every enemy you kill, every puzzle you solve, you are gaining ground and making more and more of the Care Center your territory. Grace’s gameplay segments never fully allow you to go guns blazing, nor should they, but once you master the levels and fully understand enemy behavior, the way you crawl and skirt around is nearly euphoric. The puzzles are not particularly fantastic - Resident Evil puzzles tend to be on the simpler side and usually serve only as a means of level progression - but aren’t frustrating, and complement the dungeons perfectly.  Leon’s segments, then, are the exact opposite. An old, wounded wolf raging through hordes and hordes of zombies, splattering their histories against the walls. Requiem takes more from Resident Evil 4 than other action horror entries, which is ideal for me, as I felt that period of the franchise grew increasingly inconsistent yet stale. Fittingly, you’re introduced to this style via an incredibly reactive sequence where Leon goes face-to-face with a chainsaw-wielding doctor, whose saw can be shot out of his hands, spinning on the floor, slicing legs before the player can wield it. This level of reactivity is part of what made the franchise’s original leap into action horror fundamentally compelling, and its roots are maintained. Leon can kick, slice, and slam his way through the screaming hordes, his movesets changing depending on where the enemy is and what he can do with his environment. Of course, as fun as this is, they are button prompts that the player is directed to do, which is why a particular moment in Leon’s Raccoon City segment stood out to me. Confronted with zombified BSAA soldiers on a toppled high-rise, the player can combat them normally, but with some ingenuity, one may realize that one can shoot out the glass under them to send them falling to their graves. This, of course, poses danger to the player as well, making the area more difficult to traverse and lending a risk/reward dynamic that is immediately compelling. I often felt that Resident Evil 6 would place you in a straight corridor and ask you to kill whoever got in your way, such flat, lifeless encounter design ruining solid combat mechanics. Requiem’s combat encounters are similar to its survival horror design; each encounter is a puzzle unto itself. That being said, minor pacing problems do exist. The opening few sequences see you moving back and forth between Grace and Leon, not allowing you to get a good feel for either style for around an hour. Further sequences are often not of even length, which gives the minor impression of a series of vignettes, instead of a continuous flow. The Orphanage sequence is particularly bad, with poor attempts at “scary children” horror and dull setpieces.   I had to cut out much of this review due to Steam's review length policy, which is a shame. To cut it short, I liked the story despite some flaws, adored the graphics and art direction, and very much enjoyed the musical score.  Resident Evil Requiem is a step in the right direction for the franchise. Resident Evil Village was very good, and I have nothing but sympathy for Capcom having to paste it together during the COVID-19 pandemic’s remote working environment. In many respects, however, it was obvious corners were cut, and the final product was not the great sequel to Resident Evil 7 I had desired, even if I respected many of its bold choices. Requiem is not without minor flaws (one would lose nothing, if not gain, from removing the Orphanage section), but its near-seamless blend of survival and action horror, phenomenal art direction and technological improvements, a hauntingly effective score, and surprisingly solid narrative, all things considered, elevate it to one of the best games in the franchise. Even with the game’s overreliance on nostalgia and a story that isn’t quite risky enough, I still thoroughly enjoyed my thrill ride through the wretched past and anguished present to save our future.

[quote][url=https://summitreviews.biz/article/65/resident-evil-requiem-review][b]The unabridged version of this review can be found on the Summit Reviews website.[/b][/url][/quote]  [h1]Some Old Dogs Don’t Need Teaching[/h1] Resident Evil Requiem is a landmark title for this long-running survival horror franchise. Ten years on from Capcom’s restructuring, fourteen since the controversial 6th entry that last dealt with the mainline narrative, and thirty years since the series began, Requiem is a celebratory title that refines successfully brings together all of the contrasting elements of the franchise into one quintessential title. While I think 4 and 7 are better overall in how they commit to their specific styles, 9 is nonetheless guaranteed to satisfy all types of Resident Evil fans.  Requiem is primarily a follow-up to the core narrative of Resident Evil 2 and 3 surrounding Raccoon City and its destruction. It sees the timid newcomer Grace Ashcroft team up with everyone’s favourite one-liner machine Leon Kennedy to uncover the mysteries behind a resurgence in T-virus infections, and how this connects to both Grace’s mysterious past and Leon’s previous trip to the city. While Resident Evil is largely known for campy writing without much emotional or thematic depth to it, I think Requiem made great strides towards telling a more substantive narrative that has moments which will stick with you on more than a comedic level.  This is greatly helped by the very high-quality character performances; Nick Apostolides returns to voice Leon after the remakes of 2 and 4, handing in a pretty beaten-down version of the character that still has all of the charisma he can muster, despite being at the most vulnerable point in his journey since the outbreak first began. Angela Sant’Albano voices Grace, and she delivered arguably the most realistic performance in the franchise, of someone who feels completely out of their depth in a terrifying situation. The storytelling somewhat falls off during the ending, but the higher standard Requiem has set here is a great indicator that more time will be invested in it for future entries.  [h1]A Nightmare to Remember[/h1] Requiem’s gameplay covers both of the franchise’s recent gameplay styles in one package through the dichotomy of playing as Grace versus Leon, and both sides of this coin have largely been polished to a brilliant shine.   Grace’s survival horror-centred sections adopt the expected formula of exploring an internal space in order to find items that will allow her to escape, whilst avoiding or eliminating the many dangers which may prevent her progress. Almost every enemy she comes across is threatening and unsettling, and eliminating threats takes careful planning every time you initiate or are forced into an encounter. The default first-person camera adds plenty to the tension, as it puts into perspective how even the most standard zombies are a force to be reckoned with, whom cannot easily be overpowered outside of a sparse shot of the Requiem revolver.   As for Leon, this is the strongest we’ve ever seen him. He’s a bit weightier to control, but still has high manoeuvrability and fast weapon switching that allows you to go from a pistol and shotgun shot to a hatchet parry in an instant. He also has even more close combat abilities this time around, as a contextual melee press near a wall or object will usually cause him to smash his target against them, eliminating them from play on most occasions. Gun-wise, he has few different pistols, SMGs, rifles and shotguns to play with, alongside hand grenades to take out larger crowds at a moment’s notice. It’s not an especially inspired gun roster, but they all feel supremely satisfying to use, and enemies react appropriately whether you want to bring them to their knees by blasting them off entirely, or send a few well-aimed headshots their way.  In terms of how these playstyles come together, structure was a big part of this game’s advertised identity, where Grace’s parts were intended to create tension, and Leon’s sequences would function as the release, and you’d switch back and forth between them in a sort of rollercoaster type deal. And while I wouldn’t say this identity is misleading, I wasn’t anticipating how this structure was going to be executed. Without delving into specifics, one act has you play as one character for 90-95% of its duration, and another act is exclusively focused on playing as someone else, to the point where, in this dual protagonist game, one of them takes a surprisingly extended backseat. It gave me plenty of great horror and action in long stretches, but I would point to 4 and 7 for titles which had a more delicate blend between these two aspects.   However, I do take issue with this game’s familiarity level and how resource management was balanced. No section for either character broke new ground for the formula, and I very quickly had more bullets and currency than I knew what to do with which did considerably reduce my level of tension. Hardcore in 4 felt like pitch-perfect difficulty balancing, whilst in 9, the balance is tilted far further towards the action side of equation than I was expecting, and I think it the game would have felt more rewarding if that balance wasn’t so lopsided in one direction.  [h1]It Feels Like a Million Bucks[/h1] From an audiovisual perspective, Requiem is simply best in class for a single player experience. It demonstrates that we have essentially reached the peak of what is possible for graphical fidelity in a big budget title, as there are no characters, no environments, no small objects in the game which ever took me out of the experience. It paints a pretty dilapidated picture of this world’s state, and only occasionally breaks from its noir motif with cleaner internal spaces which put a spotlight on the few areas that ended up largely unscathed by the apocalypse. Simply put, it’s stunning to observe all the way through.  Audio design is similarly excellent. The gun sounds are the crunchiest they have ever felt for an RE game, where even the basic pistol fires a booming shot that makes you wonder just how many other enemies could be attracted as a result. As the zombies in this game had a tendency to retain some of their last memories, many of them actually say a handful of words relating to the role they had before they were infected, and coupled with their generally disturbing grunts and growls, makes nearly all of them sound completely unique and similarly discomforting.  Requiem took me twelve and a half hours to beat on the Standard Classic difficulty, and I then spent an additional ten hours hopping between save files and starting new runs to clear up all of the achievements, all of which provide completion points to unlock cosmetics and gameplay content, including new weapons and infinite resources. While this was my second fastest completion time out of the modern RE games, it’s hard to complain about wanting much more when it constantly delivered a premium experience in terms of the quality and polish of the content on offer.  [h1]Hope and Requiem[/h1] Resident Evil Requiem feels like the perfect capstone for everything Capcom has been working towards since 2017. Its execution of action and horror is masterful, it’s a step up in terms of character performances and storytelling, and all of this is wrapped into an incredibly well-paced journey with not a single bit of fat to trim. While I think its partial retreading of scenarios and increased linearity holds it back from being the best the franchise has delivered thus far, it is the perfect game to mark 30 years of one of gaming’s most important franchises. [h1]Best Resident Evil game since RE2[/h1]  I was honestly surprised how much I liked it and how well Capcom handled nostalgia features in Requiem. To not spoil specific location, I will say that attention to details while bringing this place back is spectacular. It is hands down my favourite area in the whole game and while exploring it, I had a smile on my face pretty much all of the time. Well done Capcom, I can tell with 100% certainty that they were targeting older gamers, like me. And not only because of nostalgia features and bringing back memories from late 90's...but also because they decided this year to add some tricks to activate parenthood feelings. And it's not one-off coincidence, it happens in two 2026 releases; RE Requiem and Pragmata. One triggers motherhood feelings, the other fatherhood. Who knows, maybe there is some truth to the rumours, that government of Japan was involved in the process, to trigger such feelings in mid-aged gamers. It's a joke of course, but Capcom indeed succeeded if it comes to that in both titles.   Characters. Let's start with Grace - new character. It is always a gamble with established IP's going this route and often new protagonists aren't received as well as well-known and loved ones. In Requiem Capcom did a great job with Grace, to the point, where I like her almost to the same degree as our renowned zombies' worst nightmare, Leon. The way Grace is introduced, with background story, being glued to the desk FBI agent - her reactions to the surprising reality (for her, we are used to the zombies, SHE IS NOT) - all of it was captured perfectly. With time, she's getting more annoyed rather than scared of the zombies and she shows that in her one liners while killing undead. And of course, her relationship with Emily, her motherhood instincts are going "wooooo" pretty quickly and it is normal for a person with her background. On my first run, I've got the good ending, and seeing endgame moments, it brought smile on my face to see conclusion of it. That moment, when Leon said [spoiler]"I didn't hit any vitals"[/spoiler] and reaction on Grace's face - priceless. Okay, Leon now - it will be a short one, everyone knows Leon. Icon of Resident Evil, here is even more iconic. And cheesy too! His one liners while fighting, and fighting itself - brings pure joy. Melee finishers, combos with axe, close combat, shooting from behind with Requiem - everything was just fun. He is visibly stronger than Grace (which is a good thing, brings reality to the table). It shows not just in combat, but also in amount of items he can carry, in comparison to Grace. Well done (again), Capcom. I mentioned cheese, yes, Leon is cheesy but just in right amount. Visiting place from certain, old game makes it even more visible. Btw. try to explore EVERYTHING in mentioned area. Picture found with RRR on the back (not going to explain RRR because of spoilers) made me laugh for a short moment. Also seeing notes from certain characters of the past, and Leon's lines while killing specific zombies in that area made me smile too. What a joy... Also, while being deadly for undead, he is kind-hearted and thoughtful. If you'll get good ending, you will see why. Being in a dangerous situation and targeting (HEAVY SPOILER) [spoiler]non-vital parts of mutated Emily[/spoiler] was a proof of forward thinking, mercy and in general, sign of a good hearted person. Huge love for Leon!  Okay, I was talking enough about characters, and mixed some story bits in it. I will not discuss the story, all I'm going to say - it's executed well and in Resident Evil's terms it's good with usual twist at the very end. I said that at the very beginning - it is my favourite entry since Resident Evil 2, and it means a lot to me. Let's move on to the boring part - technicals.  RE Engine at its best. Capcom have proved, that you don't need Unreal Engine 5 to make the game beautiful with next-gen look. And they proved it twice this year, alongside Pragmata too. One would hope for more companies to go the same route with in-house engines...not going to happen, I know, but at least we do have Capcom. What do we have here? Great looking game with all the bells and whistles (ray tracing that actually works well on AMD cards), well optimised with ZERO stutters. I was playing Requiem on highest settings in 4K mode, without upscaling and without frame generation (both available on Radeon gpu's) and I'm pleased to see stable 60fps, just like in Pragmata. I've played it on Linux based system (Fedora 44), as it gives slightly higher (around 10fps more) framerates than on Windows 11.  Everything in settings was maxed out, and shoutout to Capcom - THANK YOU FOR GIVING US OPTION TO TURN OFF CANCER OF GAMING (depth of field and motion blur).  I left one setting for end of this review, as it is personal and some of the people may see it as irrelevant, but...I'm very happy to see an option to switch between first person and third person gameplay. As an old gamer who played Resident Evil from the beginning on PSX - to me this series always was, is and will be a TPP. No matter how much more immersive FPP mode is. I've played entire game (both, Grace's and Leon's parts) in third person perspective. Thank you Capcom for giving us choice, as I'm not sure if I would pick up this game without this option.   To sum it up: is it the best Capcom game this year? No, Pragmata is (in my opinion). But it is definitely a great Resident Evil game. Most likely it will win GOTY award and if so, it will be well deserved. In this weird era of online, multi-shmulti coop craps, Capcom delivers actual GAMES FOR GAMERS. Games that we want. I don't like numeric scores, but for those who wants it, it would be 9/10. Not as strong 9/10 as Pragmata, but sliiiightly weaker. 8 wouldn't be fair (I really hate numeric scores for reviews). Requiem is a very good RE game, but I’m a bit conflicted, because although there is so much I love about this game, I have some issues with it as well. This game has two protagonists: Grace and Leon. And the gameplay feels quite different for each. As Grace, you are in a survival horror game, emphasis on horror. For Leon, it is an action game through and through.  Let me start with what I love about the game. Grace as a protagonist is fantastic, a perfect choice for a survival horror game. She’s unlike the previous RE protagonists in many ways and that is a very good thing. She’s an analyst, not a soldier and she has severe anxiety and PTSD. Although she is physically weak and quite scared most of the time because of that, I didn’t find her character annoying, because she is very intelligent and grounded. This is reflected so well in the gameplay too. During her sections, you have very limited resources and you are expected to outsmart enemies, instead of shooting through them like a mercenary. I found myself enjoying her sections much more than Leon’s not only because of the gameplay but also the level design and the environments. The Rhodes Hill Care Center section is my favorite part. It looks absolutely beautiful and the close quarters are perfect for horror too. I also really liked the variety of zombies in Grace’s sections that require you to think, which again ties into her personality and intelligence. During the first half of the game, you mostly play as her, and occasionally you get a snippet of Leon gameplay, which is a good change of pace that I enjoyed.   But the second part of the game is mostly Leon and it is 100% the weaker part of the game. Although I enjoyed the more open level design, which fits the action much more, the environments are bleak and just… gray. TLDR; This is an OK game but a bad Resident Evil  I'll start by saying Resident Evil is one of my absolute favorite franchises of all time, I had really been looking forward to this one, and until this one I couldn't honestly decide which one was my least favorite as they all are just so good in their own way. Well, after playing Requiem I do have an answer on which one is my least, and it does happen to be this one. It is still a decent game however! Let me explain. There was a certain amount of...drudgery to this one. I've played 'em all previously and I've never found myself bored, as there's always just so much to do and upgrades to have, gates to unlock and treasures to find. This one seems to be lacking in...all of those things.   First of all, no more treasures to find that are relevant to the style and background of the game (RE8 and RE4 combinables like Idols, Dolls, Jewlery, etc). There are 0 treasures to find at all for selling. Instead that has been replaced by basically a system where you get points for each enemy you kill, and it's like...ok, I usually try to kill every enemy anyways so not really any additional incentive there.   The reason there is nothing to sell is because there are almost no upgrades to be had, at least in comparison to previous games like 4 and 8. Instead of being able to upgrade your shotgun let's say 6 times in damage, reload speed, capacity, and firing speed, you can only upgrade each category twice, and it is not expensive at all to do so. This leads to in my opinion just a lack of depth, customization, and satisfaction of building that perfect weapon. I honestly didn't really notice the difference of upgrading the weapons - it felt that insignificant.   The maps and game as a whole felt much...smaller, with fewer contrasting levels. It felt fairly cramped and closed off in comparison to previous games. And this must be why they SLOWED DOWN THE RUN SPEED. I mean, Jesus Christ you've never been able to sprint fast in a RE game but I mean this was like they were physically disabled to the point where if I had to estimate what the run speed would be in real life on a treadmill, I'd say 4.5 miles an hour. This really added to the drudgery for me. In addition, in the levels it just felt as if there were not as many details or items physically placed to add a sense of fullness to the level. For example, I remember just looking around the library in RE4 just amazed with all the small details, or in Castle Dimitresque at all the gothic furniture and cabinets and just really enjoying the immersion. RE Requiem does not have that same feel. Environmental objects seem...lightly placed density-wise and unadorned texture-wise. It all just felt rather plain sadly.  Graphics-  fidelity-wise, not good. Requiem absolutely was a step down for multiple reasons on nearly every level in its environments and weapons (except facial details and cutscenes as a whole-cutscenes were outstanding). I am playing on a 4k OLED Odyssey G81SF with a RTX 5080 and played the game on DLSS Quality mode, Ray Tracing High and everything max settings graphically and achieved about 95fps avg with frame generation off (though got 130, 180, and 220 respectively at 2x, 3x, and 4x FG). With all that said I have NEVER spent so much time in settings over multiple days of play trying to figure out WHY the game did not look good, and here is what I found.   1. You can't deactivate the forced Film Grain without mods, and man does it make everything look grainy. Unfortunately that grain does not mean sharp. Everything in the game looks...smeared over. Now, obviously recognizing artificing and blur from anti-aliasing and upscaling, I turned off upscaling and switched to Native. And yet...still not looking great? A huge thing is when you examine weapons in your inventory, they literally look like playdough and I'm not even joking. There is some bug they need to fix because it really detracts from the sense of realism, and it's all of the weapons (worst is Grace's second pistol). 2. HDR is so washed out. Playing on OLED with official ICC downloaded from the samsung website I was never able to get a good depth of black on a regular basis and ended up playing whole game on SDR as it looked so much better with nice deep blacks. 3. I switched to RE Village to see the difference and it is night and day. A game from 2018 had sharper graphics and amazing HDR.  So, what was good?  -Facial models were absolutely great. Leon and Grace look absolutely amazing.  -I really liked the bits with Emily. You have such a paternal need to protect her and they really made you feel emotionally attached when you're carrying her around and protecting her. -Reloading animations were top notch - Grace tucks the flashlight in her chin when reloading if you play in 3rd person is really cool, and when you reload you can see the individual bullets in the chamber (even if you're full ammo Leon will open and check). -Story was normal RE quality, not bad but you're not gonna find Silent Hill 2 or Last of Us quality here  All in all, CAPCOM is still one of my absolute favorite developers. Any capcom game that comes out I will buy and I'll support them because they have given me so many years of good games. Unfortunately, this one didn't hit the mark for me but hey I still look forward to the next one eagerly and always excited for their new projects!

I don't know how I didn't write a review until now but here we are. Game is incredible though. This game can feel a bit inconsistent with itself given both characters play COMPLETLEY different. Which wouldn't be a huge issue if it wasn't for problem number 2. Length. This is the one RE title I feel REALLY could have benefited from a longer playtime. Since both playstyles take up about half the game each, it means both characters only get about half of the playtime they would in any other Modern RE title. Which in all honesty just kind of sucks given both styles feel amazing to play. I feel a mercenaries mode and some story dlc for both gameplay styles could help alleviate that feeling a bit for me.  All that being said, game runs perfect even on lower end hardware like mine just like every game RE7 and onward does. Do not buy this game at full price! I beat this game a few days after it launched, but couldn't post a review until late April on account of Steam's moderators acting like 1942 Germans and locking my account down. Do better Steam, anyways, this game isn't worth $70-80. Not even close. There's hardly any replay value here. This game does not have a traditional NG+, when you start a new game, none of your upgraded weapons carry over. The only weapons you start with other than the default ones, are the bonus weapons you unlock for CP. The entire point of RE games and NG+ was to have fun and get revenge with your upgraded gear, so this killed the replay of this game for me. As Grace, you lose all of your inventory space and have to get it all again. I started a NG+ with Grace and with all the charms I wanted I had ONE open inventory slot available! What were these developers thinking? Have you forgot how NG+ works?  The first area you play in as Grace in the clinic is hands down the most detailed in the game. You can tell a lot of attention to detail was given in this area. Once you get beyond the clinic, the game just slowly goes downhill. Which explains why Capcom used all the early game footage for the trailers and gameplay, that's the best part of the game! Raccoon City especially is a huge let down. This area has rushed development all over it. It is NOTHING like the first area. I love action horror over survival horror and even I can appreciate the craftsmanship in the first area better. The developers really depended on bringing back the past in this game for whatever reason. Mr. X returns after clearly being dead. Temu Wesker is here as "Zeno" because why not?   Once you clear out the first area with Grace, when you come back through with Leon you will have absolutely nothing to do. I killed two zombies when I returned as Leon due to Grace killing everything. She's not as combat capable as Leon, but she gets enough at her disposal to pretty much wipe the map. You will start off the first 4-5 hours of gameplay as slower paced, survival horror so if you just want action you're going to be upset. The second half is much more action focused, but the attention to detail is very lacking in the second half. It's like the main group of developers went on vacation and left the interns in the office to finish the game.   Grace's character initially I could not stand, she acts nothing like an FBI agent. She grew on me as time went on and the way her story concluded was really good I thought. None of that matters now because I don't want to start an entire new game if I can't have fun with previous charms/upgrades. Leon's character is very off for some reason. RE4R was peak for Leon. Leon's second half of the game feels like a 2006 arcade shooter with a points system and a small hub to go upgrade your guns at when you're done with a small section. The bulk of Leon's time is spent looking for three pieces to a bomb. You're wandering around a very bland version of Raccoon City. Some of the RCPD elements were cool, but you're only there for like ten minutes. There's only like three rooms to look in.   This game would be a great buy around $20-30 but no more. This could have been so much more and the initial glaze are just fanboys that can't take their rose-tinted glasses off. The game is beautiful at 4k with PT or RT. It even looks good without it if your PC can't run those features. I knew this game was probably going to be this way before I got it, people say "We are getting two games in one!" No, you're getting two very half-baked games in one. You're not getting a RE7 and RE5 in the same game. You're getting what feels like two separate DLCs. The Separate Ways DLC in RE4R was better than this, speaking of Ada, WHERE IS SHE? Get this on sale, solid 6/10 for me. Fanboys, a 6/10 doesn't mean the game is trash so try not to spit on your keyboard reading my score.  I thought the story was well done. I really liked the attention to detail at the main menu after you beat the game how it has Grace and Emily together and Grace and her "mom" in another picture. I am an action horror guy, but I actually ended up liking Grace's section better than Leon's due to it being made with so much more attention and care. I was looking forward to going back through as Grace, but the game took all my upgrades from me and that's just not how a NG+ should ever work.

The entire plot relies HEAVILY on contrivance and extremely lucky coincidences. The villains' actions, or LACK THEREOF, severely contradicts their own words and reasoning.  There are SO MANY plot examples of how the story relies on PLOT ARMOR for both the villains and the heroes, and worse, the characters themselves low-key ACT as if they KNOW they have plot armor. I can list so many of them but it would be spoilers both big and small.  If you really want to look into details of what's wrong with the story-writing, just check some of the active threads in the discussions.  One BIG example I will provide is this, because it happens repeatedly THROUGHOUT THE ENTIRE STORYLINE.   "Grace is vital to our plans. She is THE KEY." - The villains spend every opportunity saying this in one way or another, and yet they dump her in a facility with zombies and death traps, AND DO NOTHING TO RE-CAPTURE HER WHEN THEY LEARN SHE'S ESCAPED HER RESTRAINTS.  Yes, RE plots aren't perfect, but I don't remember another RE where the characters blatantly contradict and/or sabotage themselves the way Requiem does.  Heck, at least in RE4, as goofy as the tiny napoleon zombie leader was, they actually TRIED to re-capture Ashley and have enemies attempt to separate her from Leon and kidnap her throughout the entire story.  If you really want to get this game, hold extremely low expectations for the story. It's written so poorly it's practically insulting you.

***SPOILERS AHEAD***  I can certainly say that this is the best "Resident Evil" game ever. While "Resident Evil 2" tuned it, "Resident Evil 4" revolutionized it, and "Resident Evil Biohazard" revamped it, "Resident Evil Requiem" has perfected it. The seamless narrative blend between Leon's and Grace's chapters give the game an excuse to organically shift tones from horror to action on demand, and both are thankfully at their best in the series' history.  Grace is a highly compelling protagonist and feels like the franchise's best and most cohesively written character in a long time, and Leon accents her timid vulnerability with his campy wisecracking and high-octane action.  Leon's combat segments are unbelievable for the "Resident Evil" series; a parry mechanic!? And it works!? His wide arsenal of weapons and consistent upgrade paths make his gun-play feel fresh while the wide swaths of enemy variety heighten the skill ceiling required to master him, and his lethargic movement style — mandated by his age — adds another layer to the challenge. Leon is also just as vulnerable as Grace for the most part, taking as much damage and being swamped as easily as his anxious counterpart, but he's given more tools to pull himself out of situations in creative, skillful ways.  "Resident Evil Requiem" is the series' absolute best in all departments except one: the final boss feels a little undercooked compared to the rest of the game's polish and thoughtfulness. Other than that? A perfect game. Runs smoothly, looks absolutely gorgeous from both fidelity and art direction standpoints, and eclipses the franchise's previous peaks.

It’s an all-too-familiar story in the games industry to see studios behind long-running franchises eventually stray from their roots. They double down on gameplay nobody asked for instead of listening to their fans or refining the core formula that made the series great to begin with. Looking at you, Ubisoft.  So when a studio as big as Capcom drops the ninth Resident Evil; a game clearly crafted with meticulous care, reverence for its roots, and a deep respect for what players actually want; you can bet I’ll be singing its praises from the rooftops. It may very well be the best entry in the entire franchise to date.  The game masterfully balances tense, heart-pounding horror with high-octane action. Grace is portrayed as inexperienced, timid, and cautious; a feeling conveyed through her gameplay segments rather than just cutscenes or dialogue. This makes playing as Leon feel that much more cathartic. At this point in the series, Leon is a hardened veteran, and his gameplay emphasizes his experience, creating a perfect contrast in mechanics and a natural break in pacing. No ludonarrative dissonance here IGN.  In an era where many franchises are losing their way, Resident Evil: Requiem stands as a defiant exception. As a long-time fan, I can confidently say this is one of my favorite entries in the series, and it has me more excited than ever for the future of the franchise.

I've gotten all of the trophies and have basically 100%'ed this game so I think I can make a pretty confident review. This is one of the best first experiences I've had with a resident evil game. My first playthrough was an absolute blast with awesome and terrifying moments. The story is a pretty typical story from this franchise but you get to see an interesting split between the more horror side of the games as well as the b-movie action side. I also really enjoy Leon's gameplay and progression. I think he has a very well fleshed-out combat groove and the upgrade system really helps enhance the gameplay.  Overall a very fun experience. The flaws in this game however appeared after that first initial playthrough. There is no ng+ but there is also no way to fresh start without deleting your save files in your file manager. So you kind of get the worst of both worlds. Leon now starts with the upgrading system so you can get points and purchase stuff at the start. Problem is, all of the weapons that you find in the game are now just in the shop so if you don't purchase them, you'll be missing them where you wouldn't have in your first playthrough. Also, my most replayed RE games are either one or the other style. I prefer a consistent playstyle through an entire game so my enjoyment of this game on replay diminished a lot faster than past titles. I had the same problem with RE8 and this is kind of a repeat. I think a better way to have gone about this style of game is to allow the player to skip either sections of the game so you can play your favorite parts without having to go through the other half of the game. For me, I am a much bigger fan of the RE4 style of games so I would like to just play as Leon but I'm forced to go through the early sections to get to that part. Not to mention, the Leon heavy gameplay doesn't even come until the 2nd half of the game.  Overall, I think if you are a big fan of this series and have a lot of nostalgia for the older games, you will absolutely love this game like I did. I also feel that if you are not a big fan and are trying to get into them, I recommend trying the older games first. I would say the RE2 and 4 remakes are a great place to start. I do recommend this game but it is not without it's flaws.  I'd like to add a little section for the new Leon Must Die Forever mode. It is genuinely one of the worst modes in the entire franchise. It is horribly unbalanced, especially with the red and blue enemies. What makes it even worse is you have to use the axe to be able to defeat those enemies but you can't repair your axe normally, you have to find a drop to repair it. It breaks after like 3 parries and then you are completely exposed. The chef is literally the most unfair enemy in the entire game. He breaks your axe after 2 swings but does 4 attacks even if you perfect parry him so he is almost impossible to kill. I downloaded a mod to be able to repair the axe to try and make it better and while it is, it still sucks balance wise and is super repetitive. It is basically all of the scenarios of the main game but in a weird rogue-lite format. Trash mode, should have been mercenaries. I'm bored of it and haven't even put 3 hours in.

This is, without a doubt, one of the best RE games ever made. If not, the best. I bought and played this the day after it came out, but decided to review it a few months after, to avoid recency bias. I never really got confused, or lost on where to go, which is the problem I found myself having with some of the earlier games. I like being able to not only pick and choose when to use your flashlight but also being able to pick and choose when to play in first or third person. I played through the entire game in both first person and third person and I can say that both of them feel great, despite me thinking playing the second half of the game in first person would ruin it, it did not. Speaking of the second half of the game, combat has never felt so damn good. Every single shot fired, every single tap of the keyboard, feels rewarding. When I died in this game, it did not feel like jank, but rather as if every death was my fault. Every single boss fight in this game was so much fun. I love every bit of this game to death, and I would 100% it again in a heartbeat.

What can I say?   This was an incredible experience for me. The graphics are just next level, even on normal settings. The RE engine is incredibly optimised, and this can run well with great graphics on probably most mid-level PCs.   Level design is *chefs kiss*, you can tell a lot of attention was put into details. Atmosphere in the first half of the game excels, and the game took me much longer to complete than expected. I reached a point around the middle of the game where me and my girlfriend thought it was over and were quite satisfied, then the credits didn't roll and I was amazed with a whole second half of the game.  This game features the best of both generations of RE games; the more action oriented games like RE4-6, as well as the more classic survival horror gameplay of the older games and the recent RE 7 and 8. The only issue is that if you don't like one or the other, some sections of the game might drag, but there's something for most RE fans here. There is also a metric ♥♥♥♥ ton of fan service here, so you'll find yourself in awe of some of the cameos (if a little controversial).  I recommend playing on Classic your first time, using ink ribbons. I played it on Modern with my girlfriend for a more casual experience which was great, but you can get away with a lot of save-scumming which can make it a bit too easy and carefree at times.  There's a lot of quality content here, and a decent amount of it for full price. You can definitely get a few replays out of this. You're paying for quality here, not insane quantity in my opinion.

In a word: wow. It's the best of all of them. I've loved this series since the mid-90s and I've played all but a couple of spin-offs. After RE6 i wasn't exactly sure where this series was going to go and honestly wasnt thrilled with the idea of first person. Then RE7 hit and I was genuinely scared playing it. I loved RE5 and RE6 because i could play with a mate but they weren't exactly scary games. RE7 and RE8 (on VIllage of Shadows), and RE9 brought back something critical to Resident Evil that hasn't been much of a thing since Code Veronica: ammo value. Games like Outlast and Layers of Fear are really cool but the danger element dissipates because you have no weapons therefore there is a way around all dangers. But here... you HAVE to use your weapons and the possibility of literally not having enough ammunition to get past a section is a very real dread and it's fricken AMAZING. Was that Requiem shot really necessary? Did I waste too many bullets on that pack of zombies? Did I REALLY need to kill that one zombie just because they were extra creepy? Did i need to repair the armour or should I have increased stopping power so my armour isnt getting smashed up so much?   And the pacing switch. Jesus. The two characters are so distinct you really feel drawn into both. They are so different and it's VERY rare for a new character to make a good impression on players like me that predate the Gulf War. The story is really interesting, the character dynamics are fantastic.  The tragedy of Raccoon City is really brought to the fore and as a long time fan I never expected RE9 to shine this brightly.   (For newbies: RE2 remake will provide the best backstory for this game}.

I was deeply worried about the decision to split Requiem into 2 halves, because it would likely cause a rift in the game's focus from slow methodical horror to fast paced action. I was certain I would tolerate Grace's horror and eat up Leon's combat but it ended up being the other way around.  Grace's sections are fantastic horror, some of the best I've seen in the series since RE1. Rhodes Hill Care Center is one of the best maps in the series. The talking zombies are creepy, extremely threatening and memorable, each encounter feels handcrafted and gives the ward a unique fingerprint. Grace's stuttering scaredy cat personality makes her stand out amongst a cast of invincible super heroes. I really love the first half of Requiem, I wish I could recommend this game for this half alone, because it's truly special. It's game design I want Capcom to keep refining.  All of this praise Im giving to requiem goes right down the drain when you take over as Leon. I *hated* playing him. He feels like a complete downgrade compared to 4R - he is slower, clunkier and has worst aim. For a Power Fantasy character, I found Leon really frustrating to control and I felt the call to just replay 4R instead. The UI is ugly and overly simple, the maps/world are linear, dull, gray and boring (especially in Raccoon City), and the OST is completely forgettable.  Zombies are tanks with hyper armor, so handguns/machine guns felt like pea shooters, lacking stopping power. The reliable firearms end up simplifying down to the shotgun/rifle/requiem. Combat boils down to shoot from a safe distance (because they walk through standard gunfire), melee/axe after a stun, and axe parry if they try to grab. It sounds awesome on paper, but in application, it becomes tedious really quickly. There just isn't enough variety of enemies. You're shooting the same types of zombies room to room.   Truthfully, I just stopped playing at the Ark. I just don't care anymore and playing the game felt like a chore. When I realized I was *putting off* continuing the game I had to admit to myself I didn't like this game.  Leon feels like a lack of confidence in Grace, as if most audiences would not try Requiem if Leon wasn't included. It certainly feels this way because when Leon takes over, it feels like a incomplete different game,  and stapled on.   It doesn't feel like he belongs here. Leon feels like a last minute inclusion to drive sales.  I wish this was Grace's game with a focused vision start to finish. I don't know what the next RE game will be like, but I hope its more of her.  If split gameplay, frequent cutscenes/walking cutscenes, scripted sequences, and forced gimmick sequences don't bother you, give Requiem a shot I guess. Wait for a sale for at least 50% because only half of this game is worth playing.

I have played 3 playthroughs. This is a tentative recommendation. If you're not a Resident Evil fan, do not drop $70 for this under any circumstances. The high moments are high. There are portions that range from bad to mid. The characters are good, but the story is horribly written. The horror is handled well- at least on the first 1-2 playthroughs.  For me, the beginning part of the game felt like a better version of 7 from a gameplay perspective. The Leon parts are a worse version of 4 remake, but still enjoyable. Even though I think the split characters are handled decently, I still think it was ultimately the wrong decision to make the game this way.  There are aspects to the game that make it worth replaying a few times, but the "insanity" mode is mishandled. The difficulty bump from the hardest initial mode is jarring at first, but once it becomes manageable there is one core aspect of the game missing- consistent melee staggers. This aspect unlocked the survival horror aspect as Grace, giving a solid and satisfying additional evasion technique. It continued 4's enjoyable gameplay loop of: shoot, stagger, melee- often resulting in crowd control. The difficulty bump becomes bullet spongey enemies. Without the stagger, parrying becomes almost mandatory to play efficiently. They took out variety for the sake of artificial difficulty.  In conclusion, I have a hard time with this game. Overall I enjoyed it a lot, and I think they handled Leon's character so well. There is such a lack of focus which results in missed potential. I don't think this is the masterpiece most say it is. I think I enjoyed it more than I think its a well made game overall. I don't think it will age well- especially because almost all of its ideas are nostalgia bait.

*NON-SPOILER REVIEW* What a GOATED game. Resident Evil Requiem/ RE9 manages to bring a fresh new entry into the mainline games after a remarkable release of remakes the past few years and Capcom still manages to deliver the horror, the action effortlessly. It introduces us to Grace Ashcroft , someone who is an FBI analyst and a shy person who has anxiety issues and PTSD from previous events in her life, yet throughout the game we watch her grow from this shy character to someone more confident by the end of the game and playing as her during the horror sections reminded me of my first experience playing RE7. The chase, the suspense, the limited inventory space paired with all of the systems in the game (her hemolytic injector and blood collection mechanic) brings a fresh gameplay perspective after a long time.   Then we turn over to big man rugged daddy Leon S Kennedy with his intro sequence and the first part of Wrenwood being the most aura farming iconic gameplay we have seen in so long, even adding new finisher animations and introducing the hatchet as his new toy. Requiem finisher animations, his hatchet finisher animations are so fking amazing, paired with great animation work done by Capcom. His portions in the game reminded heavily of RE4 remake and every action sequence has been ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fantastic.   This game was definitely worth the full price, and adding a great amount of replayability with its difficulty related achievements such as Insanity, which I feel the overall experience is really challenging, its harder than RE4 Remake Professional difficulty, and RE3 hardcore difficulty but on par with RE3 Inferno, Grace sections being the most difficult of them all whenever you play as her. I did not use any infinite ammo for Insanity run. RE9 also has good pacing, exchanging between Grace and Leon's gameplay back and forth throughout the playthrough.   However, one little nitpick I have is that I think the general zombies that we see throughout the entire game have some variations, if i recall 3-4 enemies that you'll face in the game, followed by a couple of enemies that only appear in certain sections, I think its quite little compared to RE4R, but as a package when you are experiencing this for the first time, the enemy and boss designs are cool and you might feel its already a fair amount of variety.    Overall, Capcom has outdone itself again by combining the horror elements of RE7 and action of RE9 into a new entry mainline game  , with great pacing, no lagginess whatsoever throughout the entirety of the game I didn’t feel bored whatsoever and had an amazing time! This was definitely worth my money with how polished the game came out and Capcom still delivers after all this years, Resident Evil is fking great. I can't wait to see what the next mainline Resident Evil entry will be.   Rating for this game: 9/10, possible GOTY contender 2026.
