I wish I could give a mixed review, but given the overwhelmingly positive rating the game already has, I think it should balance out.  Resident Evil: Requiem is a bipolar experience that varies greatly in quality in both objective and subjective ways. How much you will enjoy this game depends heavily on why you play RE titles, and how much nostalgia affects you.  Without any spoilers, the game is split into two halves, both for gameplay and story. Playing as Grace during the first half of the game is some of the best Resident Evil I have ever experienced, easily up there with the original trilogy and Remake 2. The mansion-esque level combined with the most interesting form of zombie the series has presented, it's top shelf gaming. Leon appears infrequently, counter-balancing the intense and oppressive survival horror with bursts of all-out action similar to Remake 4, allowing you to bend the tension over backwards and show it who's boss for a brief stretch.  Meanwhile, the story keeps a sparse, but intriguing presence, giving you just enough breadcrumbs to keep interests high and theories forming. It's clear that Grace is the protagonist, with Leon being a supporting character, and that works perfectly for the story being presented. Unfortunately, the game cannot keep this pace.  While RE titles are no stranger to losing steam part-way through, this is one of the sharpest drops in quality I have seen in the series, nearly topping RE7's tanker level. Instead of playing as Grace with bursts of Leon, you now have a six hour Leon segment in gray and brown post-apocalyptic concrete jungles filled with the same three enemy types, and while Leon's gameplay is quite enjoyable, even the best will wear thin without variety. This is also where the story takes a nosedive.  I can't really spoil this section of the game, since nothing of consequence even happens. What I can say is that they went all in on nostalgia, and while it makes some sense given the setting, certain parts are leaps and bounds above logic, jumping straight into absurdity with the hopes of blind nostalgia holding your interest.  [If you want to go in completely blind, skip this paragraph.] It's hard to put into words how poor the story is overall, let alone in the last half, but just know that none of the mystery actually matters, it retcons multiple characters (bordering on character assassination), does a poor job of utilizing Grace and Leon, has possibly one of the worst villains in the series, and never answers half the questions it brings up. I don't wanna say this the worst RE story, but it definitely feels the most slap-dashed of recent titles.  Despite a poor story, I can forgive a lot if the replays and gameplay are enjoyable. Unfortunately, RE9 has some of the worst replayability, nearly topping Remake 3. You have the usual suspects with infinite ammo, infinite durability for melee weapons, and some special weapons, but upgrades don't carry over from Leon, and the weapons are really just pre-upgraded variations that you'll use against the same gray enemies. Meanwhile, Grace only gets one special gun that isn't particularly good or interesting. To be frank, this is utter ♥♥♥♥. On top of this, the idea of replaying this game makes me shudder with the sheer quantity and duration of scripted story sections that act as cutscenes with death animations. No, they didn't learn their lesson from RE7 or RE8 and how much people complained about their protracted openings.  Overall, I can't say I didn't enjoy my time with RE9, but there were a handful of points in the latter half where I almost quit, and replaying it for completion became a chore rather than a joy. I can tentatively recommend this game to RE fans, but anyone looking for a quality story, strong replayability, or a solid entry point for the rest of the series, look elsewhere.

[h1] A good game ultimately, a bottom 3 installment effectively. [/h1]  [b]It feels like an exclusive sequel to RE2R, but decided to leave out 90% of every single detail not named [spoiler]Sherry[/spoiler] or Leon.[/b]  RE9: Requiem is an excellent game, yet an EXTREMELY LACKING numbered Resident Evil installment. While I do recommend this game to all fans new and old, the more older fans play it, the more they should take notice to issues revolving around this game's approach to memes, and single-dimensional writing. There is A LOT MISSING from this game. Even the writing makes no sense from Leon's perspective for so much of what's missing.  If you're new to Resident Evil, this isn't the best place to start, but it's actually a good one to get you to explore earlier titles afterwards. It's very fun, modern and accessible to new players, even if you're scared of everything.   Resident Evil 9: Requiem thrives entirely on fan-service. It has a very misunderstood attention to detail of what made RE2 so great to begin with. It's like a delicious steak, the sinfully unctuous marbling, and they just hand you a tray of rendered fat in a pool of oil and nothing of substance to bite into. It's an unbalanced mess that thinks it's giving you what makes meat a high-grade, with no understanding what what the eater wants or has always enjoyed of it.  There's so much deliberate design to the first and third person schemes that enhance gameplay from either perspective(third-person for Grace you can run much faster during certain sequences, but you trip, and from Leon's end, first person is extremely smooth transitions when you go for kicks, and executions). There's clear love and care for hyper-specific animations and interactions, and yet all this attention to detail just to neglect the core basic concepts of old school RE. That it just feels like bells, whistles and jingling keys, which is an insane statement to say after they made RE2R in 2019.  Grace's section is excellent for the first locale, the rest throughout the game feel SO MUCH WORSE. The first location will have you looping around for a couple hours to put a key here, a lockpick there, an enemy spawns on your backtrack. It's very true to the RE formula of running back and forth however, every section after the first location is completely 100% linear...? Grace also gets... no gun variety whatsoever??? How in the world did we go from RE7's John "Everyman" Ethan with a full loadout to Grace with 1 pistol the entire game.  Leon is extremely overpowered(fun) and armed to his teeth. He makes me goo-goo gaga at just how rigid and seasoned he's become but they've eased into his one-liners and memes so much to the point I'm completely prepared for Capcom to make Chris just say "Leon ♥♥♥♥ my sister and continue the bloodline". We have no "fun" guns, no dart launcher, no bolt-thrower, no Chicago typewriter, no PRL-412, no striker, no minigun or sparkshot, no quad-missile, no flamethrower, no grenade launcher.  We're stuck with this strange affection with hatchets all of the sudden(this becomes more apparent when you play the game).  The enemy variety from both ends is extremely unremarkable. Just run-of-the-mill zombies virtually the entire game, no dogs, no regenerador, no mid-boss or elite enemies, like I'm not saying this to sound like "DAE MEMBER RE4/5/6/7/8 ENEMIES" like genuinely there is 0 enemy variety barring like 2-3 extremely specific encounters that last 3-5 minutes and the occasional BIG unit that's completely non-threatening in every way. The entire game not so much as a [b]SINGLE NAMEDROP FOR ANY OF THESE CHARACTERS???[/b] Even when you beat the game Leon doesn't so much as even say "hey please make sure my friends / Claire, Chris, Jill please receive a dose of this cure, BECAUSE YOU KNOW, THEY WERE HERE TOO??" If Resident Evil Requiem is anything like what it’s teasing to be, we’re in for another round of “why did I agree to go into this place?” energy—and honestly, that’s exactly what I want from this series.  Even from what we’ve seen so far, it feels like Capcom is leaning back into that slow-burn dread the franchise is famous for, where every hallway feels like a bad decision and every sound makes you reconsider your entire build. You know the vibe: low supplies, high anxiety, and the constant suspicion that something is absolutely about to sprint at you from off-screen.  What I’m hoping for is that classic Resident Evil balance—tense exploration, smart puzzles, and combat that makes every bullet feel like it costs you emotionally. And if they keep leaning into modern presentation like RE7 and RE8 did, it could be another “turn off the lights and regret everything” masterpiece.  Also, let’s be real: every Resident Evil game needs at least one moment where the protagonist says something like:  * “This can’t be happening…” * “Okay, nope. Absolutely not.” * or the classic internal monologue of *why am I still here?*  If Requiem delivers that mix of dread, chaos, and occasional absurdity the series is known for, it’s going to hit hard.  Only downside? I’m already mentally preparing to pause the game just to stare at a door for 30 seconds before opening it.  Overall: cautiously hyped/10. If it sticks the landing, it could be another unforgettable entry in the series of beautiful disasters that is Resident Evil.

Excellent addition to the RE series.  It's a tricky knife edge they walked merging Leon's action packed gameplay with Grace's slower, more traditional RE style but the devs managed it.  Capcom did something similar to what Valve did with Half-life in using action and puzzle sections to control the game's pacing and avoid fatigue from either style of play. With that said, it's not as perfected as Half-Life.  There are moments in both Grace and Leon's segments where they pacing feels off.  Some of Grace's parts can drag on a bit too long and a few of Leon's earlier segments can feel too quick. It has lots of wonderful callbacks to the original RE games that are done well and don't feel like pandering.  Capcom is still using the adaptive difficulty in this one which can cause some mild confusion or frustration when it comes to getting a feel for how much damage you are doing and how much you can take.  However, it does feel like it has been adjusted a little and the difficulty creep for skilled players is not as sudden as it was in RE2R. The story is pretty good for a Resident Evil game and Capcom has continued their trend of more naturalistic dialogue that started in RE2R.  It makes the story feel a little more grounded and mature.  Story tension is well done, feels like writer took a page out of Jurassic Park's book on how to create and hold tension. Overall it left a rather unpleasant aftertaste. If you feel like you won’t be able to resist buying it because of the marketing hype, I’d say wait for a sale—or go back to older RE titles depending on what this game offers that appeals to you (RE2R or RE7 for Grace-style gameplay, RE4R or even RE6 for Leon).  Despite my disappointment, I don’t want to undersell the game entirely—some phases of Grace’s clinic and cell block sections, the strong opening, and the way past gameplay experience and craftsmanship have been partially recreated with visible effort deserve some credit. Yet evaluating with the rest, this game absolutely does not deserve the level of praise and attention it’s getting, and I think it represents a step backward for the series.  I don’t even know where to begin. Let’s start with the dual-character structure and the overall presentation. Some spoilers ahead.  Grace’s sections start with strong momentum but gradually lose it. It devolves into a loop of collecting blood from the environment and crafting equipment to kill enemies, while also hiding from stalkers and waiting them out. This creates a contradiction with how Grace is portrayed in the story. If you’re even a moderately skilled player, Grace turns into a female Rambo—popping stabilizers like performance enhancers, blowing everything up with infected blood syringes, and mowing down nearly everything except unkillable stalkers. Yet in cutscenes and scripted moments, her voice keeps trembling.  Grace, you just calmly hunted and killed an entire clinic full of people under the logic of survival—why are you still shaking or tripping while running? And why are you still so obsessively fixated on Emily when her condition is obvious? What about everyone else in the clinic?   Sure, Emily is a child and you have a trauma bond—but at some point, like Leon shooting down abominations, you should be able to “let it go.” As it stands, Grace comes off as weak, irrational, overly emotional, and reactive in every situation. It makes you question how she can be so cold-blooded and efficient under player control while being so inconsistent narratively.  This also creates pacing issues with Leon’s segments early on. When you switch to Leon, there’s barely anything left besides loot that only he can access. He deals with a few extra enemies at the beginning or end of his segment, then you’re thrown back into 2–3 hours of dragging gameplay with Grace. But as I said, this isn’t really survival anymore—you’re not prey, you’re the predator. Grace clearly has a Lara Croft buried inside her, but the game never reflects that in her character development or dialogue. It’s a strange disconnect.  You can’t really say you “play as Leon” until the story shifts to Raccoon City. Much like Ada in Separate Ways, Leon gets promoted from side character to main character there, and the second half of the game is largely his. Unfortunately, his sections feel very generic. Aside from a few cinematic moments—like navigating a collapsed skyscraper or escaping a rooftop filled with mortar-firing zombies—the Raccoon City quarantine gate and RPD areas feel sterile and industrial, very much like RE3R. They’re repetitive, linear, and frankly empty. It feels like leftover assets from an early multiplayer/open-world development phase—especially the final Umbrella Ark Laboratory, which looks like reused RE3R lab content.  With Leon, you can upgrade gear via a military-style electronic supply box based on kills and wristbands collected. But compared to the Merchant in RE4R or the Duke in Village, the system is extremely limited and soulless. The UI isn’t user-friendly either—it feels like something ripped from a futuristic online FPS, but stripped of depth.  As for Leon’s combat: while the parry system somewhat resembles RE4R, the overall feel sits awkwardly between RE6 and RE4R. Weapons don’t evolve meaningfully over time. His handgun feels slow and weak—even after upgrades, it only becomes mediocre. Other weapons suffer the same issue: they fire sluggishly, almost like they’re jamming.  In short, aside from bolt-action sniper rifles, none of Leon’s weapons feel as powerful, weighty, or responsive as in RE4R. They’re closer to RE6—and worse, enemies are spongey and unresponsive, again like RE6. They rarely get stunned, making Leon’s added melee finishers and combat moves mostly pointless.   Remember that flashy clinic showcase where Leon pulls off all those cool moves? That’s pure marketing illusion. That’s basically the only segment where those mechanics are used effectively—and there are no additional animations beyond what was shown there.  Another issue: in RE4R, resources were always scarce. Here, unless you’re a terrible shot, resources pile up. This kills tension. I constantly had +10 shotgun or sniper ammo, and even when those ran out, I still had +200 SMG rounds.  As a result, every boss fight became trivial: parry, then spam shotgun or SMG for 2 minutes. Tyrant/Mr. X, Commander, Gideon—they’re all extremely underwhelming.  The writing and story are shockingly bad—even by RE standards. It contradicts the established universe and undermines it with unnecessary retcons. The character roster is barren, which is surprising for a series known for memorable personalities. Expecting villains like Heisenberg or Dimitrescu? Forget it. Strong female characters like Ada, Jill, Claire, or Sheva? Forget that too. Grace doesn’t count—she’s bland and poorly written.  The voice actress does a good job, but the character itself is inconsistent and illogical, as explained earlier.  The retcon of Spencer—portrayed as having a conscience and sabotaging his own legacy—is completely out of character. It’s like claiming Wesker was secretly a good person. The newly introduced elements—Raccoon City Syndrome and Elpis—are equally damaging. If viral bioweapons are neutralized, what even remains of the RE universe?  The writing is so careless that it contradicts itself within the same game. At one point, Sherry claims the Pentagon never ordered the destruction of Raccoon City—but later, Grace’s FBI report repeatedly states that the U.S. government did it under pressure from bioweapon lobbies. Which is it?  Even worse, the government denying past wrongdoing makes no sense when the FBI—under that same government—has documented it. And this was already established lore: the city was destroyed to cover up Umbrella’s actions. Replacing T- or G-Virus with Elpis doesn’t add anything new—it just creates inconsistencies. If Elpis existed, Ada in RE2R would’ve been after that instead.  These retcons don’t expand the lore—they clash with it. The “new Umbrella facility under Raccoon City” twist is especially lazy.  And with something like Raccoon City Syndrome in play, it’s absurd that only Sherry is treated while others just wait around, and Leon goes on a suicide mission while infected. It’s clearly written to push Leon into the spotlight, reducing others—including Grace—to mere tools for his character.  Maybe I should give it a 6/10. But ultimately, gameplay and design matter most, and despite its flaws, the game stands on the shoulders of past experience.  If this were a movie or book, I’d give it a 3 or 4 out of 10.  Like every RE game, does it still make you feel like you’re playing through a horror zombie film? Yes, it does. But overall, it feels like a sterile, overly commercial product that takes the series backward.  A disappointment for me.  Imo, it doesn’t even come close to RE4R. 😀  If you want action-horror with Leon, play RE4R. If you want survival horror like Grace, play RE1R, RE2R, or RE7. All of those execute their focus better than Requiem.  Buy this one on sale.  At this price, it offers an 10 hour campaign that feels like two RE3R-length runs. Replayability is low, pacing is uneven, content is lacking, and there’s no extra gameplay mode to this date. Meanwhile, RE4R Gold Edition offers two excellent campaigns plus a rich Mercenaries.

I didn’t expect Resident Evil Requiem to feel this… personal.  At first, I thought it was just another entry trying to balance horror and action like the series always does. But the more I played, the more it became clear that this game is doing something a little different. It’s not just about surviving—it’s about ending something.  What really stood out to me is how the game handles its two playable perspectives.  Playing as Grace is honestly stressful in the best way. Her sections lean heavily into slow, creeping horror. You’re constantly low on resources, the spaces feel tight and oppressive, and there’s this lingering sense that something is always nearby. It’s not just jump scares—it’s the kind of tension that builds quietly and doesn’t really go away. I found myself moving slower, checking corners more, and just feeling uneasy the whole time.  Then the game shifts to Leon S. Kennedy—and it’s such a noticeable change, but in a good way. It almost feels like a release of pressure. You’re still dealing with dangerous situations, but now you actually have the experience and tools to fight back. The combat feels solid, and instead of pure fear, it becomes more about control and survival under pressure. It doesn’t turn into full-on action, but it definitely gives you room to breathe.  What impressed me the most is how smooth the transition between the two is. It never feels jarring. The pacing just naturally shifts from Grace’s anxiety-heavy sections to Leon’s more controlled gameplay. That balance keeps the tension going without ever feeling repetitive.  Story-wise, the title “Requiem” really fits. There’s a sense throughout the game that it’s wrapping things up—especially when it comes to Umbrella and everything tied to it. It feels reflective, like the series is looking back at its own history while slowly moving forward. By the end, it genuinely feels like a closing chapter, but also the start of something new.  Overall, I think Resident Evil Requiem does a great job respecting what came before while still pushing things in a new direction. It’s tense, well-paced, and surprisingly thoughtful.  If this really is a send-off for that part of the series, then it’s a pretty strong one.

RE9, to me, feels like a very ambitious entry to the franchise, making so many new cool mechanics and features, all while it still contains the core fundamentals of earlier titles. The story is nice, I would say on par with the better RE games, and the characters are enjoyable. Leon is great as always, but the performance of Grace is easily the best in the game, which adds to her already amazing segments in the story.[spoiler] I do wish she got more spotlight near the latter half of the game.[/spoiler]  I won't say much, but the first section of the game is one of the best RE experiences of all time, it feels so refreshing and dynamic, and it offers a perfect balance of difficulty without being an annoyance. On top of that, switching between Grace's horror segments to Leon's more action-like gameplay is perfectly paced in this part of the game, and there's no better joy than absolutely blazing a room that was horrifying an hour or two ago.  And speaking of it, the combat in the game feels really good. I wouldn't say it's as good as RE4R or RE6, but it holds up on its own. The sounds definitely improve upon it, with the game having maybe the best sound design in RE, as well as any horror game I've played.  The game is perhaps one of the longest in the game (which I think is a good thing), and while it feels pretty linear at times, there are a lot of segments that reward exploration.  My main issue with the game is one very prominent bug that I have seen discussed by many, which is that cutscenes will VERY frequently have audio desync, which ruins the immersion immensely, to the point where I'd have to watch YouTube clips of them every so often. This likely won't be a problem if your PC is relatively new, but if your computer runs on duct tape and vibes like mine, then beware this issue.   With that being said, gameplay performance, on the other hand, was great, I was able to stay at 60fps with very minimal stutters, which is great for me. I hope CAPCOM can continue their hot streak of optimization, and I really hope they fix this audio bug early for any newcomers to the game.

!!!! SPOILER REVIEW!!!!!  Ich sag’s direkt: Resident Evil 9: Requiem ist für mich ein Meisterwerk. Ich habe fast alle Resident-Evil-Spiele gezockt, ich kenne die Reihe, ich liebe die Reihe – und trotzdem hat es Resident Evil 9 geschafft, für mich alles zu übertreffen, was davor kam. Das ist kein kleiner Satz, weil Resident Evil schon über Jahrzehnte zu den stärksten Namen im Horror-Genre gehört. Aber Requiem hat bei mir genau das geschafft, was nur ganz wenige Spiele schaffen: Es hat mich nicht nur unterhalten, sondern komplett gepackt, überrascht, mitgerissen und teilweise regelrecht emotional erwischt. Für mich ist das hier nicht einfach nur ein starkes Resident Evil. Das ist aktuell mein persönliches Game of the Year.  Gameplay und Combat: 10/10 ohne Diskussion  Das Erste, was mich komplett abgeholt hat, war das Gameplay. Resident Evil 9 fühlt sich nicht einfach nur gut an – es fühlt sich so an, als hätte Capcom ganz genau verstanden, was dieses Franchise spielerisch so stark macht, und dann alles auf ein neues Level gehoben. Der Spielfluss ist brutal stark, das Pacing sitzt, die Steuerung fühlt sich direkt an und das gesamte Spiel erzeugt permanent dieses Gefühl aus Spannung, Druck und Kontrolle. Auch der Combat ist für mich eine glatte 10/10. Jeder Kampf hat Wucht, jeder Treffer fühlt sich passend an und man hat nie das Gefühl, dass das Spiel sich irgendwie träge oder unsauber spielt. Es ist genau diese Mischung aus Überlebenskampf, Druck und Präzision, die Resident Evil schon immer gebraucht hat – nur hier wirkt alles noch sauberer, stärker und intensiver. Es ist nicht einfach nur “gut gemacht”, sondern so gut, dass ich wirklich sagen würde: So stark hat sich Resident Evil für mich noch nie gespielt.  Atmosphäre: So viel Angst hatte ich noch nie  Und jetzt zum vielleicht wichtigsten Punkt: die Atmosphäre. Ich habe wirklich schon viele Horror-Spiele gespielt, auch viele harte Sachen – aber ich hatte noch nie so viel Angst in einem Horror-Spiel wie hier. Und das meine ich genau so. Resident Evil 9 schafft es, dich konstant unter Spannung zu halten. Nicht nur mit billigen Schockmomenten, sondern mit echter, unangenehmer, schwerer Horror-Atmosphäre. Das Spiel baut Druck auf, ohne dass es ständig laut werden muss. Es erzeugt dieses Gefühl, dass jederzeit etwas passieren könnte. Räume wirken bedrohlich, Wege wirken unsicher, jede Ecke kann falsch sein. Genau das ist für mich großer Horror: nicht nur erschrecken, sondern dieses ständige Unwohlsein, diese Nervosität, dieses “Ich will weiter, aber ich hab eigentlich keinen Bock, da jetzt reinzugehen”. Und Resident Evil 9 macht das auf absolutem Top-Niveau.  Story: Besser hätte es nicht sein können  Ich übertreibe hier nicht, wenn ich sage: Die Story hätte für mich nicht besser sein können. Gerade bei Resident Evil ist das immer so ein Punkt, wo die Reihe manchmal zwischen Camp, Kult und echter emotionaler Wirkung schwankt. Aber Requiem hat mich hier voll erwischt. Die Geschichte funktioniert nicht nur als Rahmen für Horror und Action, sondern trägt das Spiel wirklich mit. Sie fühlt sich wichtig an. Sie fühlt sich groß an. Und vor allem fühlt sie sich so an, als würde sie genau das liefern, was man sich von einem Titel dieser Größe wünscht. Für mich war das kein Fall von “Gameplay stark, Story halt da”. Nein – hier war auch die Story auf Top-Niveau. Das macht das ganze Erlebnis am Ende noch stärker, weil es eben nicht nur spielerisch knallt, sondern auch emotional hängen bleibt.  Hunk-Bossfight: 11/10  Ein riesiges Highlight für mich war ganz klar der Hunk-Bossfight. Und ehrlich: 11/10. Anders kann ich’s nicht sagen. Das war einer von diesen Momenten, wo du als Spieler einfach nur da sitzt und dir denkst: Ja man, genau dafür zocke ich sowas. Der Kampf hatte Präsenz, Druck, Stil und genau diese besondere Energie, die einen Bossfight von “gut” zu “legendär” macht. Solche Momente bleiben hängen. Nicht nur, weil sie spielerisch stark sind, sondern weil sie sich groß anfühlen. Besonders. Bedeutend. Genau so ein Fight war das für mich.  Leon im RPD: Einer dieser Gaming-Momente  Und dann kam dieser Moment, der mich komplett gebrochen hat: Als Leon das RPD betreten hat, musste ich wirklich weinen, weil es so schön war. Mehr muss man eigentlich fast gar nicht sagen. Das ist genau die Art von Szene, die zeigt, wie stark ein Spiel sein kann, wenn es Gameplay, Atmosphäre, Fanservice, Emotionen und Inszenierung perfekt zusammendenkt. Dieser Moment war nicht einfach nur “cool” oder “nostalgisch”, sondern wirklich emotional. Er hatte Gewicht. Er hatte Seele. Und genau solche Szenen machen aus einem sehr guten Spiel ein unvergessliches Spiel.  Technik und Performance: Besser als gedacht  Technisch war ich positiv überrascht. Die Performance war besser, als ich erwartet hatte, und gerade bei so einem Spiel ist das extrem wichtig. Horror lebt von Timing, Stimmung und Immersion – und wenn die Technik ständig nervt, reißt dich das sofort raus. Aber hier hatte ich deutlich mehr Vertrauen ins Gesamtpaket, als ich anfangs gedacht hätte. Dass so ein atmosphärisch dichtes Spiel dann auch technisch ordentlich läuft, hebt das Erlebnis nochmal deutlich an. Es sorgt einfach dafür, dass man sich komplett auf das konzentrieren kann, was wirklich zählt: die Welt, die Spannung, die Kämpfe und die Story.  Was war das Beste am Spiel? Ganz einfach: alles  Normalerweise kann man bei einem Spiel sagen: Das war der stärkste Part, das war eher schwächer, da gab’s kleinere Hänger. Bei Resident Evil 9 ist mein ehrlicher Eindruck aber: Das Geilste am Spiel war für mich das gesamte Spiel. Das klingt erstmal übertrieben, aber genau so hat es sich angefühlt. Es gab nicht diesen einen Aspekt, der alles getragen hat. Es war das Gesamtpaket. Das Zusammenspiel aus Gameplay, Combat, Horror, Story, Bosskämpfen, Fanservice, Emotionen und Atmosphäre war für mich einfach so stark, dass ich am Ende nicht sagen will: “Ja, das und das war besonders gut.” Ich will eher sagen: Das ganze Ding war eine Wucht.  Fazit  Resident Evil 9: Requiem ist für mich nicht nur ein fantastisches Horror-Spiel, sondern der beste Teil der Reihe. Und das sage ich als jemand, der fast alle RE-Spiele gezockt hat. Dieses Spiel hat mich spielerisch komplett überzeugt, atmosphärisch zerstört, emotional erwischt und mit einzelnen Momenten beschenkt, die ich so schnell sicher nicht vergessen werde

I enjoyed the game a lot. The graphics are amazing, the sound is great, the English voice acting is top, and the character, monster, and environment design are peak.  I’ve known the RE genre for a while, but this is the first game I played myself. I usually have motion sickness when playing games, but I was super happy that I was not forced to play in first-person perspective. That helped a lot, and overall I had no problems here with that, so great job!  As I said before, the graphics are outstanding, and you don’t need a 5k gaming PC to run this game (of course not on the highest settings if you have a potato PC, but the game still looks awesome even on low settings). The models are really well made, with great textures and rigging, and didn’t give me any uncanny vibes (besides some enemies, but this is probably on purpose, it is a horror game, lmao).  I played the game on normal/easy because I just wanted to enjoy the game and have fun with exploration and lore. I never felt negatively stressed by the game. It had a lot of action with Leon and some scary parts with Grace. The split between these two was a really good gameplay decision, so everybody gets a piece of the cake. But I am a bit sad that Leon’s parts didn’t get as much playtime. At the end, yes, but at the beginning I wish I could fight way more, because it was super fun to kick, shoot, and fight through stuff. The gameplay was so dynamic, it was so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ entertaining!  I liked most of the puzzles. They were pretty understandable, and even though the game is not open world, it was still a lot of fun to explore every corner. So many details in the environment, so many puzzles. But to be honest, some of them gave me RE7 vibes, where they didn’t make much sense. For example, why do I need three cubes with symbols in a hospital to open a door? Maybe I could find three special keycards from each doctor or something, that would fit the modern setting better. Also, I need to give props to the person who designed Victor’s room. The DNA asset mechanism was really great, a small detail, but really well made. I liked it a lot.  The gore in the game is also really good, parts are falling off, monsters are melting, and you can see all the details. Technically and artistically, really fabulous.  Also, the skins are worth it, they look really pretty!  I also love the fact that the concept art is kind of free, you only need to pay with in-game currency that you get from playing. Sadly not common these days anymore, pretty often behind paywalls. I’m happy that it is free here. A lot of free art I can look at, I love seeing the concept art.  This game feels like a good mix of action and horror, kind of like the best parts of RE2 Remake, RE4 Remake, and RE7.  Me recommend!

Grace feels a bit conflicting between the game wanting her to be a combat adverse character, while on the flipside, giving you everything from weapons, ammo, crafting, and upgrades to make her combat capable to the point 3-4 shots will can kill an enemy, good exploring and resource management will keep you well off, especially with the heavy pistol. Sure, you can play the game on a harder difficulty where you are given less items, less resources, enemies do more damage, and have higher health, but I always feel that a character is either A or B, not A or B on the basis of what difficulty you choose. There isn't really any horror/tense moments that occur naturally like you'd expect from something like Silent Hill, The Evil Within, Dead Space, ect. Like when I played the SH Remake, I found myself often having to pause and just take a break, and sometimes it wasn't even because of an immediate experience but the atmospheric sense of dread and horror and the unknown. Overall Rating: 7/10  I think this is a solid entry in the Resident Evil franchise that brings back a lot of the best elements from previous entries with the two main character mechanic. Having Grace work as a first person stealth horror game (especially on Classic difficulty which I highly recommend) while Leon gets to kick ass is a perfect balance of the two kinds of gameplay the franchise is now known for. Grace feels very weak in an at-times genuinely scary way, and I think they did a great job making Leon's combat feel weighty and brutal, but still precise. I do think some of the Leon sections feel a little sluggish towards the end, but I have always been biased against that kind of gameplay which I know some others really like (i.e. big fans of RE4-RE6). The story here is as convoluted as other entries but it doesn't bog down the emotional moments too much, and there are enough mechanical flourishes tossed in throughout to keep the combat and stealth feeling fresh and exciting. I will say that I think the first half of the game feels a little stronger, because as things are revealed the story doesn't fully capitalize on the tone set up in that first act. But it isn't enough to drag the whole experience down, and I still appreciated the (somewhat egregious) fanservice that happens later on in the game. I hope they take this entry as a starting point for future games in the franchise and continue to work on melding stealth and action-adventure gameplay like this.

Resident Evil Requiem is a solid entry to the series. I wouldn't say the best, but it's a pretty great all-around experience.   The game is separated into 2 playstyles: Grace and Leon. Grace's sections are classic survival horror, more precisely the type of first-person survival horror Capcom developed with RE7, but with the foresight of that game in mind. Leon's sections are more action-horror oriented, very similarly to the RE4 remake.   Both are fun, but as a survival horror purist and big fan of the first 2 entries of the RE series, I vastly prefer the Grace sections. Every move you make feels methodical, the gameplay pace slows down, and you feel the need to experiment with how you play the game. What weapon should I use? Do I heal now? Should I go back and get this? Should I even use a weapon at all? This is what makes the early games, along with 7, so challenging but rewarding to play. All this to say that the early Grace sections in and under the care center are probably the best parts of the game. It's some of the best Resident Evil ever.   I don't hate the Leon sections, though. Resident Evil 4 is probably in the top 3 for me, but that's because of how well-crafted that game is. It's all this more action-oriented approach that's less horrifying than the games before it, but definitely still scary, with the added bonus of being genuinely a ton of fun. With Requiem, the swaps between styles mostly work, but you'll soon realize that the Leon sections feel somewhat less thought-out. I liked the Raccon City bits, but that one area with the tent felt especially drawn out and kinda dull in all honesty. It doesn't help that the environment is a lot more dull too, with lore reasons, but still. At least there's the lab at the end to sort of bring things back. And bring back the final Grace section that's arguably too short.  Story is serviceable, making connections with previous entries and expanding with Grace. It's nothing crazy, but the story is the envelope for the gameplay in these games. I would say all survival horror, but Silent Hill exists. For the next game, I hope they stick to one gameplay style, to be honest. I completed this in 15 hours, and 7.5 hours of each respective gameplay felt a bit short, even if I'm not typically a good game = longer game sort of person at all. My dream would be that an RE10 would be a first-person game. But I know action makes seemingly more money for Capcom. Still happy I chose to start playing Resident Evil remake 4 years ago.

Resident Evil 9 is something of a loveletter to the long-time fans of this venerable franchise. It's a highly polished, well-crafted package of pure, unashamed fan service and, as someone who's been with the series from the first game, it left me with a huge grin on my face the entire time.  The game perfectly balances the all-out cheesy action of 4-6 with the genuine dread and terror offered up by games like RE 2 and 7, switching between the perspectives of series newcomer Grace and grizzled veteran Leon S. Kennedy. Grace, rightfully so, is terrified the entire time and her sections rely on classic Resident Evil sneaking, resource management, map backtracking and light puzzle-solving to survive. Leon, meanwhile, has been here before. He's seen it all and he's an absolute tank of a man, destroying hordes of zombies with enough guns and one-liners to go toe-to-toe with any 80s action hero.  Although not quite as refined as RE4 Remake's incredibly well-tuned combat sandbox, there's an extremely satisfying weight to Leon's attacks and movement. He's older and feels slightly slower but far more hard-hitting.  Guns are extremely meaty with excellent audio-visual feedback and melee attacks are slow, purposeful and create a real sense of connection and power.  Grace, meanwhile, has far more limits imposed on her to heighten the fear factor. Her shots take longer to line up, her movement speed is slow, she's fragile, she has to scavenge for pretty scarce resources on higher difficulties. We all know at this point that Capcom are masters of tension and release survival horror, terrifying you before lulling into a sense of safety as you feel yourself mastering the challenge, only to hit you with new scares and surprises.  Grace's sections very much feel like that formula has been honed to its sharpest edge yet.  The story has proven pretty divisive, largely because of the sharp turn from personal stakes and trauma in the first half to grand conspiracies and classic supervillains in the latter half. I understand how this change in tone could be jarring, but personally I felt the rapidly escalating stakes of the main plot still did a fantastic job of centring the protagonists' personal journeys at their heart. Grace is haunted by trauma and self-blame, and by finding the courage to take these huge events head-on she begins the process of healing and self-forgiveness. Leon, under all the confidence is a man wracked with guilt and sorrow over the lives he couldn't save. In confronting the ghosts of the past and helping Grace, he finally achieves some sense of closure.   This is the most human Resident Evil game I've played.  The human cost, both to the two leads and the countless lives destroyed by greed and hubris in the series, is always front and centre. The game deals with the way the mistakes of the past still haunt us and how we can only move on if we dare to believe in hope. For me, although you might be able to find some individual flaws in the plotting of the game, this thematic backbone is handled wonderfully and makes for a Resident Evil game that genuinely provoked some introspection and feels.  I won't go as far as to say this is the best of the series. For me that will always be a tie between the first game, RE2 remake and RE4 remake. But Requiem easily takes pride of place among the greats of the franchise and delivers everything you want; nostalgia, genuine horror, tightly-crafted action setpieces and a deeply human story about loss and the mistakes of the past.  Capcom have done it again.   9/10

Just off of my first playthrough vibes in Classic mode, where saving as Grace requires ink ribbons. For reference, the only other RE game I've personally played is RE4 Re.  I think this game is a beautiful amalgamation of the gameplay concepts Capcom has introduced in the Resident Evil series. We went from, early on, horror-based stealth and resource management gameplay, to more run-and-gun gameplay midway through the series, then looped back to said horror-based stealth gameplay in the more recent installments.   This game mixes the both, but specifically by making you play out two different storylines at the same time. You get the slow paced, careful, and stealth-based gameplay of Grace, and the fast, guns-blazing gameplay with Leon. I greatly enjoyed both, being able to relive the badassery of Leon and the slow burn horror of Grace. Notably, I'm terrible with horror games, but the limited amount of agency you get as Grace greatly helped balancing the experience.   Grace's section is amazing. The horror elements, extremely limited resources, and first-person immersion made for extremely tense gameplay. The ink ribbon shortage mainly came from balancing crafting those versus consumables. I didn't really experience a *problem* with the lack of ink ribbons, but if you aren't crafting a bunch, you can come really close to running out of them.  Leon's section is very fun, but admittedly a smidge lackluster. I miss the unique quirks of each weapon that you unlock when you max-upgrade them. The customizability of your build is lacking in this regard. The guns do feel good to use, but I wish we got more of them.   Additionally, Leon's movement feels very momentum-heavy. When running, sharp movements are always accompanied by some of your initial momentum. Takes getting used to, and feels a little less responsive, but that may just be the intended gameplay experience.  The resource management is... as usual. There are no Red or Yellow herbs, but outside of that, most things are par for the course. I do believe that my exploration efforts were insufficient to find attachments, as I barely found any, but I don't know for sure that I missed a bunch of them. Thus, you don't really tend to find many permanent upgrades, which felt... weird, to me. Purchased, yes, but found, not really.  Overall, it's peak, 9/10. Will go back and play Insane mode(with Grace's section in 3rd person, I'm too much of a baby).

RE9 feels like a game that’s constantly borrowing from better entries in the series without really understanding what made them work. The setup has potential, but it quickly falls into a loop of predictable story beats, paper-thin characters, and twists that feel telegraphed long before they happen. By the time the game tries to surprise you, it’s already too late—you’ve seen it all coming.  The gameplay is competent but never exciting. Combat works, exploration is serviceable, and the pacing is decent enough, but nothing stands out. It leans heavily on familiar mechanics without adding anything meaningful, so it ends up feeling more like going through the motions than actually surviving a horror experience. Even the set pieces, which should be highlights, feel recycled and oddly safe.  What really drags it down is the lack of identity. It doesn’t commit fully to horror, action, or psychological tension—instead it awkwardly sits in the middle, never pushing far enough in any direction to be memorable. The atmosphere has its moments, but they’re fleeting and often undercut by cliché dialogue and predictable encounters.  It’s not a bad game by any means—it runs well, looks decent, and fans will probably find some enjoyment in the familiarity. But that’s also the problem: it relies too much on that familiarity. In the end, RE9 is the definition of average—a polished but uninspired entry that plays it safe at every turn and leaves very little lasting impression once you’re done. Resident Evil 9: Requiem pushes the franchise into its most ambitious and refined form yet. Developed and published by Capcom, the game blends psychological tension, cinematic storytelling, and modern survival horror mechanics into an experience that feels both nostalgic and groundbreaking.   Visually, the game is breathtaking. Every environment — from decaying gothic architecture to rain-soaked ruins — is rendered with staggering detail. Lighting, facial animation, and environmental effects reach a level that genuinely feels next-gen. It’s not just technically impressive; it’s artistically unforgettable.   The boss encounters are a standout highlight. Each major fight feels distinct, and thematically tied to the story. There’s a strong sense of nostalgia woven into these encounters — subtle callbacks to earlier titles without feeling repetitive. It strikes a perfect balance between honoring the series’ legacy and delivering something fresh.   Gameplay is simply outstanding. Combat feels tight and responsive, resource management remains tense, and exploration rewards curiosity.   The pacing is masterfully handled, alternating between slow-burning dread and explosive, high-stakes confrontations. Unlike some previous entries, the mechanics continuously evolve, keeping the experience engaging from start to finish.   Narratively, this may be the strongest Resident Evil story to date. Emotional beats land with weight, character arcs feel meaningful, and the themes of loss and reckoning give the game surprising depth. It builds on decades of lore while remaining accessible and cohesive.  Overall, if you like survival horror, this is a must-play.   9/10   BossHub

First Resident Evil game that I played, and honestly it completely pulled me into the series. I didn’t expect to get hooked this hard, but everything from the atmosphere to the gameplay loop just works so well together.  The tension is constant. You’re always low on something like ammo, healing, or just confidence and that makes every encounter feel meaningful. It’s not just about shooting your way through enemies. I enjoyed replaying the game multiple times because each run felt a bit different trying new strategies, improving my routes, and just getting better overall. Overall, this game didn’t just entertain me it made me want to go back and play all the other Resident Evil titles. Definitely a great entry point into the series.

Resident Evil Requiem features a well-known split of Leon and Grace.  Grace, like myself, is a newcomer to the series, Her gameplay section is represented through horror and stealth elements. Leon is a famous veteran, and his gameplay section is represented through action and combat elements.  Generally the back and forth works well, although Grace's sections are often a bit annoying from the gameplay perspective due to the sometimes finicky controls combined with the relative helplessness. Leon's sections often feel better from a gameplay standpoint, but will sometimes fall a tad flat atmospherically compared to Grace's.  The callbacks to previous RE games, as far as I can tell, are somewhat questionable. Leon still angsts about Raccoon City after all these years and never moves on, and [spoiler]Spencer being redeemed towards the end of his life[/spoiler] flies in the face of what every previous RE game featuring him has suggested. The ending decision is also played up rather suboptimally in that regard, with one of the final villains [spoiler]unceremoniously being tossed aside in the good ending for the other one - if you make the decision that flies in the face of everything you've been led to believe for 12.9 RE games so far[/spoiler].  Overall, I think the game works, but the game seems to lean more heavily on nostalgic callbacks (and Leon) than strong, fresh storytelling. Still, I could imagine worse first forays into a series.

This is the most linear, newcomer-friendly, simple, and immersive Resident Evil Capcom has ever made. It’s not exactly a criticism, but I had higher expectations for this title in terms of puzzles, the integration of key information needed to progress the story, and even the path toward completion/plat, all while staying consistent with the game’s linear structure.  As for the gameplay, I believe many mechanics already introduced in previous entries have been refined in this installment. However, I’m not a fan of the default FOV it feels too narrow, almost as if you were playing on a console. Customization is basically nonexistent. At the same time (and I still don’t fully understand why), there’s the “freedom” that was reintroduced with this title: the ability to switch between first-person and third-person perspectives. This feels like a feature aimed more at console players rather than PC gamers, where the innovation started with RE7 and RE Village. In a way, the expectation built around the first-person direction that rebooted the series with RE7 feels slightly undermined by this option. Of course, this is a personal take, but it does raise some doubts and questions for me regarding future DLCs and sequels from Capcom.  A special mention goes to the outstanding performance of Angela Sant’Albano, who helped bring to life a character like Grace Ashcroft. Her portrayal adds depth and humanity, highlighting vulnerability in a way that feels grounded and relatable even for an ordinary person thrown into endless horror. This is exactly what the game needed to achieve, and Capcom delivered on that front.  I can’t give completely positive feedback. The game is full of easter eggs, references to previous entries, and nostalgic moments where you can already guess where things are going. BUT what prevents it from being fully enjoyable are these very elements, which alternate between the two storylines for most of the game. Fortunately, Grace’s storyline prevails, providing a sense of closure to the overall experience, without it, I probably wouldn’t have even taken the time to write this review.  I’m still hopeful for the upcoming content announced by the developers. Don’t disappoint me!

[h1] Resident Evil Requiem - Messy, unfocused, wasted potential [/h1]  [h2] TLDR - Why the thumbs down? [/h2] Ultimately, I think splitting the game between a tightly focused classic survival horror experience and a Resi 4 style third person shooter harms the game more than helps it. I was riding a (scary) high for the first 60% of the game, and struggled to drag myself through the final 30-20%. I think Capcom should have doubled down on Grace to deliver what could have been a decade defining survival horror experience and saved Leon's part for the next side entry.   [h2] Backstory [/h2] I've been a huge fan of the Resi franchise since 2005 with Resident Evil 4 on the PS2. I've been there for every major mainline titles and most side titles. I've also gone back to visit all entries before then. This franchise has been a staple for me, and Requiem was a letdown.   [h2] What's good? [/h2] A lot actually. The visuals are beyond stellar, and it runs rock solid on my specification. But the gameplay is why we are here, and that's where it gets complicated.  Capcom's whole unique selling point for this entry was spitting the campaign between two different characters, newcomer Grace and seasoned veteran Leon. You will no doubt already know this from the marketing around the game. Interesting idea, but I think this experiment has failed and provided a weaker game, which I'll address (alongside Leon's section) further down.  Grace's section, set in a new care home is great. it delivers a classic survival horror experience in what might be the best map design in the genre we've had in a while. It's moody, interconnected and a real treat to navigate your first time through. It's the usual gig; resources are very scarce early on while you're killing and running from zombies and other monsters and solving puzzles. I was creeped out sufficiently with the atmosphere here, so points there as well.  In fact, this part of the game was so good, I wish we had more. I wish long before shipping, Capcom went back to the drawing board, cut Leon's section out entirely and doubled down on Grace, expanding with a second map and part to her story, and just committing to a classic, complete survival horror experience.  Before I drag Leon's section through the mud below I want to be clear: the combat on offer as Leon is fun. Often it's very fun. If you've played the Resident Evil 4 remake you know the deal here. It play's great, but out-stays its welcome, and dilutes the package as a whole.  [h2] What's not so good? [/h2] The dual protagonist experiment. Grace's section is so finely tuned for the most part that Leon's section drags, and especially towards the end, really drags. Leon's gameplay had become stale due to a lack of enemy variety and a weirdly speed up weapon economy (more on that below) that had me begging for it to end. The design of Raccoon city is weird as well, open in a way that feels like a chore to slog through.  As mentioned above, Requiem has a not so great weapon economy. Due to Leon's section lasting 4-6 hours depending on personal playstyle and/or difficulty selected, Capcom rush you through acquiring new weapons, as opposed to the more steady drip feed of most other games in the franchise. So within a few hours you've sampled all the toys on offer, adding to the dried out fun by the end.  The story is frankly non-sensical garbage, the primary antagonist is a nothing-burger and the secondary antagonist (featured on the marketing materials) is interesting at first but goes nowhere. In fact the story as a whole goes nowhere. The Raccoon Police department section was nothing more than a nostalgia tour that provides nothing meaningful.  Replayability is [b] severely [/b] hampered by the shorter lengths of both the Leon and Grace sections resulting from the dual protagonist split and an un-skippable story beat about halfway through the game.

Resident Evil Requiem é ok.  Há pontos positivos e negativos nesse game, mas acho que seu maior defeito é a falta de personalidade. Requiem não sabe o que quer ser: survivor ou ação? Nem os devs parecem saber, porque os dois pacotes são tão rasos que ao final do jogo fiquei com a sensação de que estava com um produto incompleto.  Vamos lá: as primeiras horas com a Grace são fenomenais e ali tinha tudo para a gente ter um dos melhores jogos da franquia. O hospital tem um design excelente, e tudo que envolve a sua exploração foi muito bem feito. O problema é que não há aprofundamento; são quatro boas horas de survival, mais nada. A experiência vai decaindo no decorrer da história, há pouco de variabilidade, não há nada de criativo.  Com Leon, temos a base do RE4 Remake, mas também de forma muito superficial. São poucas armas (a maior parte bloqueada na primeira run), há basicamente uma única seção de exploração, não existem puzzles, os inimigos não variam etc. É meio que uma DLC do RE4, mas talvez até pior que a Separate Ways.  Requiem não é um jogo ruim, só não tem nada de especial. É até difícil de avaliar algo tão raso.

[h1] Arguably the best Resident Evil out there [/h1] [hr][/hr] Resident Evil Requiem is Capcom's latest installment in the Resident Evil franchise. A survival horror featuring dual protagonists in a single playthrough where you play alternatively as Grace Ashcroft, an FBI analyst and Leon Scott Kennedy, a DSO agent. This game takes place 28 years after the events of Resident Evil 2, where the protagonists are investigating murders related to the Raccoon City breakout as its survivors are dying mysteriously. Below I talk about some key points about the game and what I generally liked.  [h2]Dialogues, Acting and Cinematography[/h2] This game was pure cinema, every scene felt out of a well made action thriller movie. The voice acting (mocap too) was really well done and a special mention to Leon's one liners. Gotta be my fav genre xD. Not a single one made me cringe lol, it was either funny or badass.   [h2]Graphics[/h2] This has surpassed my top most-realistic-looking-game-ever list, overthrowing Black myth Wukong. Yes, the graphics of this game is unreal as to speak, I know Capcom has delivered bangers with their RE engine but seriously this game looks scary real. Gorgeous looking characters too (Capcom has mastered the art of good looking characters).  [h2]Mechanics[/h2] The game more or less shares the same formula of game mechanics as its predecessors. Smart bullet usage, puzzle solving, exploration and inventory management being the primary ones. Except those are mostly for Grace. Leon is busted since the very beginning and you can shoot all you want ( I suprisingly never ran out of ammo, if anything I had to discard to make space ), so I played him like a third person Doom slayer. He has an axe for melee damage and parrying and oh boy, bro is almost close to becoming Sekiro with how he parries almost everything. The parry timing was very generous making it easier for people to progress and not focus on learning enemy patterns like a souls game.  There were settings to choose from third person and first person view and this was a very intelligent mechanic to scale up the horror feeling.  [h2]World design and Theme[/h2] The world design was good (very resident evil-ish but good), looked insanely real. Especially when you reach Raccoon city it looks AMAZING and its post apolocalyptic setting looked very convincing. The details in the world looked nice (like RPD and Kendo gun shop), including that tofu easter egg lol.  Grace's part of gameplay was mostly the horror theme and it was successful in that area. Since she trips a lot while running it definitely gives you anxiety while escaping enemies lol, not to mention its mostly dark when she is playable. Leon on the other hand is our older depressed zombie killer who is not fazed by anything and throws one-liners at his problems instead. His part is more of a third person shooter with some elements of jumpscares.  [h2]Plot and lore[/h2] The game's setting is 28 years after the outbreak in Raccoon city (RE2 plot), Leon is old and Grace is an FBI analyst sent to investigate murders related to the survivors of the said outbreak. This game heavily uses the lore built up until now in the REverse and explains the real reason behind nuking Raccoon City.  Gotta say the plot holds up fine, the moments of nostalgia and heartbreak we feel for Leon when he enters RPD were set up very well. Some details definitely bring tears and makes you wonder what would have happened if Leon's first day in RPD was just a normal evening of a rookie joining his welcome party.  [h2]Bosses[/h2] There were not many bosses in the game and that's fine. This is a survival horror and not a soulslike, but I would say the boss fights were designed perfectly. With the exception of the Hunk and Tyrant boss fight which were more parry and shoot (and my fav fights btw), rest all the bosses or elite enemies were a very traditional resident evil-ish style setups. Leon fights most of them anyway so they weren't super difficult but it was fun fighting them regardless.  Of all the Resident Evil games I played, RE4 remake was my favourite due to its length, environment, dialogues and ofc ADA WONG. But despite those pros, this game now sits as my favourite RE game ever. Capcom has cooked hard in this game and it shows. This studio rarely disappoints and I am glad I played it so soon. I played the previous RE games last year so I never got to be part of the hype when it came out.  Resident Evil lover or not, play this game. A solid 9.5/10 from me.

Without spoilers — it’s dark, emotional, and surprisingly layered. It respects longtime fans while still being accessible to newcomers. The characters feel grounded, and the narrative actually sticks with you after you finish the game.  What makes Resident Evil Requiem stand out is its confidence. It knows exactly what it wants to be — and executes it flawlessly.  Pros:  Incredible atmosphere and tension Perfect balance of survival and action Stunning visuals and environmental design Top-tier sound design Engaging and memorable story  Cons: – Honestly? I think the Rhodes Care Center is the best that modern Resident Evil has ever been. Everything about it was fantastic, from the zombies holding on to latent memories of their jobs and personality, to Chunk's design as a roamer, it all fit together perfectly. And coming back as Leon going on a tour of destruction, taking out all the enemies you had trouble with as Grace, is a perfect way to cap that section off. But I think everything after that was just pretty good. Leon's more open section in Raccoon City was fun the first time, and the skyscraper setpiece was fun, but visually everything was just so boring, it felt like I was playing an RE4 Remake mod that stitched together a bunch of bombed out Call of Duty maps with sand and dirt everywhere. -The fun merchant's replaced with a sterile container with no personality -The only recognizable area in Raccoon City was retracing the steps of the RPD. Why not have a section where Leon explores the RC streets from RE3R without creating a weird setpiece street that loosely connects everything together? -Lots of time spent wandering around in dark hallways with no zombies to justify the scale of Leon walking up and down the Raccoon City block -Grace's second and third segments in the lab and basement are way less interesting than the Care Center, with all of the zombie AI being generic instead of being able to use the environment or their tendencies to make your way around -Once again, the RE devs thought that putting a 10 minute, unskippable story segment where you play as a character with no weapons was a good idea. Sat on this review for a while. Mulled over it for hours, talked with friends, and read and watched other reviews. As with others I wish there was just a "meh" option for Steam. First half is great, classic RE survival horror mixed with RE7's modern take on it. Story is intriguing enough during this half and kept me thinking about what would happen next. Second half is meandering and does nothing special. It is a remix of RE4R's gameplay with nostalgia galore combined with bland environments. Story takes a nose dive in favor of key jingling said nostalgia. I audibly groaned at some parts, mainly Tyrant/Mr. X and Zeno ([spoiler]literally just Wesker jfc[/spoiler]), as it felt so dumb. RE stories are usually pretty dumb but this one felt extra stupid. It could work but I think the first half of the game is way too serious for it to. Shoutout to Gideon though, best part of the story.  Subsequent playthroughs were fun but felt lacking compared to other RE games. Ended up dreading playing through the Racoon City every time. It has the same unlockable system as every other modern RE game which is fine. No letter ranking system still which is a huge waste. Insanity difficulty with no NG+ items is what I enjoyed the most. If you're a fan of the Resident Evil franchise, this is a MUST PLAY!  While newbies to the franchise can definitely find a lot of enjoyment here, Resident Evil Requiem is overflowing with callbacks and fan service that will tug at the nostalgia strings of veterans. Despite that, the game does a lot of new things that make the experience feel fresh.  Historically in Resident Evil, the games have fallen in to one of two categories:  1. Slower pace, low resources, and death waiting around every corner (Gotta be sneaky and smart, avoiding fights when possible)  2. Faster pace, lots of action, emphasis on upgrades (Gotta whoop some ass)  In Requiem, these two distinct gameplay styles are combined into a single experience through the dual-protaganist system. Grace is timid - she shakes while aiming her guns and often stumbles while running. Leon is an absolute chad (He's become a straight-up action hero by this point). The contrast works well.  The story is pretty interesting and there's a few twists along the way. I got every achievement (49/49) and I still plan on playing more. If you're a fan of Resident Evil you'll love the game!

Resident Evil Requiem 8.5/10  The biggest flaw of this game is the replay value. I’ll never be able to put 300 to 600 hours into Requiem like I have with RE2R and RE4R.  It’s been years since we’ve had a Resident Evil like this—this one truly feels like a continuation of the classic games, aside from a few over-the-top action moments with Leon. Even though Resident Evil 7 is often considered the franchise’s savior, the truth is that Requiem is the real one, because it brings back Raccoon City, zombies, and Umbrella.  From 2017 to 2026, I can confidently say that among the newer titles, this is the best one, standing on the same level as Resident Evil 2 Remake. Even though Requiem has some issues that made me dislike certain parts, I can still say it’s better than many of the games Capcom released after the original Resident Evil 4.  Requiem is truly the game that saved the franchise—we want zombies, Umbrella, and if you can throw Raccoon City into the mix, it’s perfect. So to sum up my review: there are things I didn’t like, and at times it feels very similar to Resident Evil 2 Remake, but I can tell you that among the new generation of Resident Evil games since 2016, this is one of the best, standing alongside the classic trilogy, Code Veronica, Revelations, and Resident Evil 4.  Resident Evil Requiem was one of the best new games in the franchise. Before, Resident Evil 7 was my favorite, and Village was a Resident Evil I didn’t like. So, among the newer titles (not counting remakes), Resident Evil Requiem is a masterpiece—especially for bringing back the true star of the franchise. And I’m not talking about that overrated Leon, haha—I’m talking about Raccoon City. Seeing what the city looks like after the missile is something every old-school fan like me always imagined.  This really feels like a true Resident Evil game: puzzles, escape-room elements, zombies—yes, zombies, not that werewolf nonsense, haha—Mister X, an Umbrella member named Victor, and even a supposed Wesker clone. Capcom really nailed it with this one. I played 66 hours on PS5 and even bought it again on Steam to experience better graphics on my PC. I really liked the game—but not everything is perfect.   Biggest plot hole in this game:  [spoiler] Spencer’s Redemption  Anyone who has played all the games knows how evil Spencer is—the experiments he conducted on Lisa Trevor, his obsession with becoming an immortal god, and what happens in the Resident Evil 5: Lost in Nightmare DLC. He experimented on children for years. Sorry, but someone who did that for so long can’t just “repent.” The reality and morality of a person like that are fundamentally broken—he genuinely believes he’s doing the right thing. There’s no way someone that deranged would suddenly feel remorse.  A lot of people are saying that Spencer could repent, but no—anyone who truly knows the story understands that Spencer was a maniac obsessed with becoming a god. Someone like that would never regret his actions. So yeah, this is the biggest plot hole in the game.  The only plausible explanation for all this redemption narrative is that Elpis was actually Spencer’s final act of revenge, and you can clearly see that Gideon interpreted it that way as well. Wesker’s betrayal, The Connections, everything that happened afterward — and in RE5 Lost in Nightmares, Spencer remains arrogant until the very end. He literally tells Wesker that he wanted to become a god moments before Wesker kills him.  So when you look at it from this perspective, Spencer never truly regretted anything. Maybe he only told Grace those things to keep her safe, because if he were assassinated, people would eventually go after Grace, especially since he constantly implied that the girl was “special.” And in fact, she carries Elpis inside her body, which is why she doesn’t become a zombie.  Victor Gideon even says: “How brilliant, my master… he gave us anarchy.”  And honestly, that line changes everything. All those B.O.W.s that organizations spent years trying to perfect, only for Spencer to create an antiviral powerful enough to destroy the entire concept of bioweapons itself. It’s almost like Spencer’s final message was:  “If I cannot become a god… then nobody will.”  Of course, if you study even a little virology, the idea of a universal antidote capable of neutralizing every B.O.W. virus is pretty absurd, exaggerated, and almost comedic. It’s basically like inventing a single vaccine capable of curing every type of cancer.  But honestly, that’s my interpretation of the ending. [/spoiler]  Gameplay Criticism:  Leon using a chainsaw, Leon riding a motorcycle like John Wick—why? It’s way too over the top. I did enjoy Leon’s gameplay since it feels similar to RE4, but Capcom needs to understand that if they push beyond RE4-style action, it turns into RE6. Having some action is great, but they need to be careful not to fall back into RE6 territory. I’d advise Capcom to keep this balance between action and survival horror, but not go further than this.  Another issue is Victor’s care facility—it feels extremely similar to the RPD: a main hall, two entrances on the left and two on the right. I think they could have leaned more into an urban atmosphere, like in the original RE3 Nemesis (because the remake is terrible).  Even with these criticisms, nothing really harms the overall experience. The story could have been a bit better too, but let’s be honest—Resident Evil has never really had an “absolute cinema” story, and that’s okay.  I do recommend that you buy it, and I appreciate Capcom for making this game. It really feels a lot like the early Resident Evil titles—at least Grace’s section does. Leon’s part, on the other hand, feels much more like RE4.

Resident Evil Requiem is a culmination of all the talent and lessons Capcom has taken in over the past 30 years in making the games from the series, and needless to say, they absolutely did deliver on this title. I really enjoyed playing through this game, however I really wish they did certain things differently.  While some sequences were executed masterfully, most of which being in the later half of the game, and boy are they done AMAZINGLY for I LOVE every single second of those parts, and they certainly flipped my initial negative position on this game on its ass (it is my 3rd favourite re game now),  certain others fell short. There are parts of this game which will make you feel "Why am I still here?? Can we just move on already?", and it doesn't happen just once.   Not only, but I feel like Grace's background could have used a little more care. She is arguably one of the best RE protagonists but her being an FBI Agent really doesn't match her demeanor. Not only, but the FBI feels like a throwaway name as their involvement in her mission is quite literally zero. You're telling me they're living in a world where BOWs exist and they send a frantic woman to investigate a homicide in an abandoned and dark ass hotel where she got her trauma, where zombies could be involved, with no backup or additional gear to defend herself? It just makes the FBI look dumb, but that's just me.  Other than that, the survival horror gameplay is brilliant. You feel isolated, you have no idea what's coming next, and you have nothing but a few tools to make it through the nightmarish areas throughout the game. The Requiem also doesn't feel like an immense power spike because of the scarcity of its bullets. It's strong, but never enough to save you fully. Leon's gameplay is insanely satisfying and just pure perfection, though I wish they brought back the RE4 upgrade system. Even then, performing executions and perfect parrying give you a rush no drug could ever give you. It's just plain awesome.  Anyway, peak game. Buy it when it goes on sale and just enjoy the madness of this game!

I assume this is because the combat is intended to be built around parrying, but Grace can't parry, so you spend the entire first half of the game not being able to use the parrying mechanic: by the time I was Leon for more than a few minutes I completely forgot that mechanic existed and ended up only using it near the end of the game.   Despite my mild grievances with the gameplay the game is overall an excellent experience. Grace's sections feel like a true modern take on the classic survival horror roots of the original games and the sections with Leon feel like the more action oriented games (4,5,6). Leon is a sassy little middle aged man and his overpowered action hero combat serves as nice relief for the stress of playing as the dainty and anxiety ridden FBI agent.  The pacing between Grace and Leon made me appreciate Leon a lot more; I used to be pretty salty about Leon going from a more relatable character to a pretty boy special agent that drops corny one liners, but I'm coming around to the character after this game

tl;dr 7/10 to 9/10.  So what is RE9 like? RE1/RE2 and RE4/RE6 combined. Grace is basically the epitome of a helpless woman stereotype written into her.  Her parts in this game are basically RE1 and RE2 - sneaking and avoiding enemies whenever possible. Her abilities to eliminate threats are limited and depends on her environment and limited tools. [spoiler]Said tools are crafted with blood![/spoiler].  Leon, being the badass he is, is now capable of parrying almost everything he can see, provided the player has the skill(s) to match. Leon is basically himself from RE4 and RE6, plenty of shooting action and capable of taking down all threats coming his way with his hatchet and guns. Also Leon is around 50 now? RE9 28 years after RE2. And like Life Imitating art, as with many Americans, Leon is getting to his middle age and no health insurance would cover him with his pre-existing conditions.  SPOILER ENDING: [spoiler]Leon dies in an ending if Grace is Hopeless.[/spoiler]  I actually struggled A LOT with grace's parts of the game in my first playthrough. Unlike Jill (or her RE3R incarnation), she lacks the training/starting tools and agility to solve things and dodge enemy attacks. It was very difficult to handle her running and stumbling early on in her hyperventiliating-panicky state. And I don't think I've seen such a wimpy "melee attack" from an RE MC until now. Put simply, if one was expecting roundhouse kicks or foot-stomps from Grace to finish off downed enemies, she [b]can't[/b] do it.  [spoiler]And it is very troublesome when some big red heads starts rising up.[/spoiler]  There were some lines about a "Captain Redfield" towards the end of RE9... And I hope we'll see a proper closure to our now old RE heroes and heroines from 1990s.  7/10 - Wow I really hated early game Grace, but her perspective of the game definitely put a ton of tension in the early game that has been missing for a long time. (I do not own nor have I played RE7/8). 9/10 - I think we're getting ready to say our good byes to our RE men and women from the 1990s. Leon is getting there and Chris should be retiring soon. We'll see if Jill still has any superhuman virus left in her to prolong her stay. [hr][/hr] Keep in mind Ada is older than Leon, so players should temper their expectations if she will ever make a reappearance.

Requiem is one of the better Resident Evil's in modern times, with a strong focus on polished gameplay and location design that makes Resi 9 highly replayable.   Grace's sections are my highlight, with survival horror being the games strong point. You've to avoid combat with powerful zombies while trying to obtain puzzle pieces and card keys to access new areas and escape the horror.   Leon's sections focus more on combat and Resi 4 style interactions with enemies.   Both fun, but besides personal opinion being that of survival horror is more fun than action, I believe the Grace sections are more polished, focused, and created with more care.   The story is fun, but you can feel the shift towards late game where rewrites happened and the overuse of fan service grows tiring. The final two or so hours of the game lowers the overall opinion I have for Requiem, but that's not to say the game stops being fun. It just stops making sense if you're interested in the story and lives of the characters.   Speaking of; Grace is a fantastic addition to Resident Evil's universe, as well as a another character you meet alongside Grace. Grace is a fresh face with a lot of potential.   Where as I feel Leon's story never mattered much, a random Tuesday for him. Not because he's a vet that's seen it all, but because his addition to RE9 added nothing ultimately. You could remove him entirely and the story is still similar. Switch him with someone else and the story is unchanged.   There's a number of fun bosses and cool set pieces, and the game's length is very nice. Not too long, and not too short. I'd love if the original plans for the final boss weren't scrapped, because it sounds much better than what we ended up with.   Overall, i'd give Requiem a thumbs up, but a 7/10. It falls short of becoming a masterpiece both in gameplay and story. Back in 2005 Resident Evil 4 revived the series' popularity with its revamped gameplay. I find Capcom have been holding onto that style since, but haven't managed to capture it perfectly. Closest being RE5. At this point I believe Resi needs a new style away from roundhouse kicks to dull the sense of "been there, done that", or "RE4-Lite".   I look forward to seeing what the upcoming story DLC has to bring to Requiem both in terms of story and gameplay. I'm not expecting it to alter my overall view of Requiem, but more of the game and some story elements being cleared up is very welcome.
