After some time of thinking about this game, I came to the conclusion that, while it is a good game worth playing, it's time to accept that Resident Evil has stepped away from the things that I loved about it. As I played through it, something kept nagging me at the back of my mind and I think I finally know what it is.  Previous to all this, I'd gotten a steam deck and decided to give emulation a go. Of course, I got all the OG games and that's when it hit me.   Gone are the days of small details that gave the series it's personality. No more "RESIDENT EVIL [NUMBER]" after pressing start. No more eerie and haunting music, instead replacing it for ambient sound such as footsteps. Menus following the game's style have been taken out in favor for sterile, soulless, neat & modern designs which are now applied to all the new entries. You no longer have to carefully think about when and where to reload while sweating bullets hoping to get that one shot in time since you can turn off your brain and parry literally everything. I could keep going.   The first three original titles took themselves seriously but always allowed for moments of levity. The original Resident Evil 4 stroke a balance with its comedic quips, only letting Leon loose during cutscenes. During gameplay, he never spoke a single word. Ever since the remakes, he became a one-liner machine that never stops talking as if he was a character in the MCU. I had hoped that since he was older in this entry, he wouldn't be as yappy but that is not the case.   Regarding RE9 proper, the game is fine. It plays great, it has a serviceable -- although uncreative and revisionist -- story. This entry decided to combine the old with the new, offering two distinct gameplay styles, sure to please both types of fans. However, Resident Evil 2 or 3 this is not. No A/B stories.  Truth be told, I have no problems with Grace's gameplay or personality. The option to use ink ribbons to save boiled down to an Inconsequential gimmick for the game showers you with enough materials to craft as many ribbons as you like, at least in normal.  Grace is a likeable character with great moments and her gameplay style is what I came to enjoy the most.   Where my main problems lie are within Leon's side of the game. Enjoyable, yes, but I would have liked for something else rather than what we ended up getting. It may sound harsh but this story, out of all the others, seems to be the most creatively bankrupt. It makes no effort to hide the fact that its calling back to RE2Remake and RE4make. You even visit the RPD and fight Mr. X once again. There's a part in the game where Leon's memories flash before his eyes and it only shows cutscenes from the remakes, as if ashamed of its roots. How cool would it have been to see footage from the original 2 and 4? Hell, maybe even 6. It would have shown they care about their past and are proud of what they've achieved. Gameplay-wise, Leon is focused on action, similar to the remakes. Just like in RE4Remake, there is no longer the need to precisely time your reloads or worry about your positioning because your trusty hatchet can just parry literal missiles. To remedy this, enemies are now tougher and can take more punishment. Though I will admit I absolutely loved the re-introduction of crimson heads. The shooting feels great and all but... idk.   But I understand. It's trying to appeal to the demographic that has never and will never play the originals -- whether that's because they are old or "clunky" and if to appeal to a wider demographic that doesn't care about your past you must sacrifice your personality, so be it. Now that RE4 remake became their highest selling title ever, things will only continue to go down this way. I don't hate it. I'm just sad that this is the way thing have to be.

I'm gonna be very honest in my review and while I enjoy this game I think I should bring up a few things I can't let go.  Good points: +Grace is a really awesome characters, and a fresh new addition to the series. +Her gameplay section throughout the care center was really tense and actually kept me on edge. Reminded a lot of the original game mixed with something from Outlast. +It's good to see Leon as well, his section are really fast phased and more action focused. +It overall feels like a story of facing the past and moving on.  +Visually I also think the game looks pretty amazing, I almost felt the rotting smell of the areas and if you ever smelled an animal cadavar you know how that feels. +The ending is actually quite wholesome and sad depending on your choice (even though it's kind of obvious what to choose).  Flaws: -Leon's section could've been a lot better as the earlier ones are over very quick and just when I seemed to get the hang of it, it was over.  - I also didn't really like the Raccoon City level, it reminded me a lot of New York levels from Wolfenstein the New Colossus, and even that's my least favorite part of the game. It drags out too long, there's not a lot of interesting things to find and you do it all for a lousy detonator. Also for a ruined city you find more ammo than what you'd find at an army base. If anything, that would've been perfect for a more survival focussed level for Leon.  - There's not a lot of replay value unfortunately, once you've found things like the Charms you keep them if you start a new game. That's honestly something that Capcom should've altered or atleast give you something to do the puzzles in the RPD again.  - My least favorite part was the final chapter and the whole thing with another lab inside Raccoon City as that's almost the exact same plot as in the movie Resident Evil: The Final Chapter, it even has a motorcycle chase with Lickers, and I hated that too. Come on Capcom you can do better than that.  - The deluxe edition is a bloody rip off, two ugly weapon skins that look like they come from Payday 2/3, two ugly character skins, charms that are like microtransactions, a mini sidequest with a useless reward, audio that only plays in the RPD. DO NOT BUY THAT!  Overall though, I give this game a 7,5/10, it's fun but not something you'll keep coming back to soon.

REVIEW & CRITIQUE AFTER THE HONEYMOON PHASE  TL;DR child of RE2 & RE4. if RE2R was a 9 and RE4R was a 9.5 on a scale of 10, this one is a solid 8.25  if you've played the previous games: get it  if u haven't: play the older ones first and get this one during sales in the future  REVIEW & CRITIQUE AFTER THE HONEYMOON PHASE  the good parts have already been praised a million times, so i’ll focus more on what could’ve been better so the next game can be even stronger  Gameplay, Mechanics, & Design:  - grace’s first section (Rhodes) feels premium and really enjoyable. the last two sections (finding 3 spark plugs / turning on 3 generators) aren’t bad, but they feel very similar. it starts to feel a bit samey, like repeating the same idea in different layouts. the boss fight after restoring power could’ve used more gunplay and utilizing the light mechanics instead of ending too quickly  - combat overall is solid, but after shooting, there’s a slight delay where the character stays in the aiming animation. it makes things feel less smooth compared to RE4R  - inventory and leon’s shop ui feels a bit too dull with the grey-black theme. i get the tone they’re going for, but combined with the already dark & ashy environments (RC), it just feels a bit lifeless  - very few puzzles this time around. re without puzzles??  - RC part 1 and some ARK sections drag a bit. they could’ve been tighter, and that extra time could go into more puzzles or expanding RC part 2 (RPD)  - lickers feel overused, and their AI isn’t great. they end up feeling more like cheap annoyances than actual threats  - leon’s weapons and gunplay still feel better in re4, where each weapon had more identity and combat, especially the gunplay is very smooth  - axe parry and finishers are cool, but light/heavy attacks can feel a bit sluggish at times. also, parrying feels a bit too strong (parrying an RPG is kinda wild)  - leon’s sections are way too easy. the only challenging section was the HUNK fight  - the gap between 'standard' and 'insanity' difficulties feels too extreme  Writing:  - some moments feel like cheap fake-outs. it could’ve been handled better. it feels like they avoid committing to major consequences but still try to tease them, which weakens emotional impact  - one long-time character makes a very out-of-character decision without enough buildup. there’s some explanation later, but it feels too little compared to how big the shift is. especially when their previous appearance (RE 5) showed the complete opposite. some fans defend it with small hints or speculation, but it still feels underdeveloped  - grace gradually losing her stutter could’ve been shown more clearly. it’s there, but not as noticeable as it could be. her voice acting was (super) great  - some of grace’s dialogue feels a bit too obvious at times (“you can’t see, can you?”, “he’s dead”). it could’ve been written more naturally. she’s clearly an intelligent character, so moments where she states or asks obvious things feel off. even small things like the braille puzzle could’ve been handled smarter without changing the story

This is a fantastic horror game. The game follows the perspective of two main characters. FBI agent Grace's side is survival horror gameplay, where you need to employ stealth tactics and ammo conservation, whereas detective Leon's part is action movie-style kicking in doors with an arsenal of weapons. The game perfectly blends in various components from earlier Resident Evil games. The chronic care center map layout reminds me of Resident Evil 2 Remake's police station with East and West side areas connected by the Central Hall. The Grace part of the game feels a lot life Resident Evil 7 while Leon's side in this game is kind of like RE4 Remake with all the action going on. The UI in RE Requiem seems similar to Resident Evil Village.  The puzzles in this game are mostly pretty straight forward. There are a couple quality of life improvements made to the UI of the game, for example a shortcut key to your paper note archive when solving puzzles that have code combinations. Grace has the ability to collect blood from the deceased and use it to craft useful items. The game appears to be quite standard RE stuff in terms of gameplay length. According to the in-game clock, I finished the game in 11 hours.  The only downside to Requiem for me is the uneven tension in the game. The first half of the game, where you roam around the chronic care center hallways, is brilliant. It's an absolute joy to play that classic horror part. Unfortunately at around the halfway mark the tension starts to sag a little and the game doesn't feel as thrilling as it did in the beginning. But this doesn't ruin the game. There still is that nostalgic Resident Evil vibe to the game that carries the player through.  Overall, Resident Evil Requiem is probably 2026's best horror game by far and a must-play for survival-action horror fans. It takes the best elements from the series' previous titles and throws at you a captivating story and thrilling gameplay. 10/10 highly recommended

Resident Evil: Requiem genuinely surprised me—in the best way possible. From the very beginning, it feels like a confident evolution of the franchise, blending classic survival horror tension with modern gameplay refinements.  What impressed me most was the atmosphere. The game leans heavily into dread and psychological pressure rather than just cheap jump scares. Every environment feels meticulously crafted, with lighting, sound design, and pacing working together to keep you constantly on edge.   Gameplay-wise, it strikes a strong balance between action and resource management. You’re never overpowered, which keeps encounters meaningful and forces you to think before acting. The controls feel tight and responsive, making exploration and combat satisfying without being overwhelming.  The story also stands out—it’s engaging, darker in tone, and does a great job expanding the lore without feeling forced. Characters are more grounded, and their motivations feel believable, which adds weight to the experience.  Overall, Resident Evil: Requiem left a strong impression on me. It feels like a bold step forward while still respecting what made the series iconic. If you’re into immersive horror with substance, this one absolutely delivers.

[h1]One of the best Resident Evil games[/h1]  I've played a lot of games in this franchise, but [b]Resident Evil Requiem[/b] really stands out as one of the best for me. What truly makes it a masterpiece is how well they nailed both the horror and the action. The game brilliantly splits its identity between its two protagonists, giving fans the best of both worlds without it ever feeling disjoined. [h3]The Horror (Grace Ashcroft):[/h3]  Grace's chapters are pure terror and horror. The resource scarcity, the fact that she's not a trained soldier like Leon so you have to utilize stealth,  the environment and other tactics to get past enemies rather than fight them, the way her hand is trembling on the gun whenever she aims, all of these things contribute to making the game feel as atmospheric and as authentic as possible. It does a really good job at showing how a regular person would react and behave in a situation like this. [h3]The Action (Leon):[/h3] Then the game flips the script with Leon, and you no longer feel helpless like you did with Grace. Going back through the areas you previously survived as Grace feels completely different. Now, instead of being scared, you're having fun killing every zombie you can find. Instead of hiding and running, you get to fight back and do exactly what you couldn't with Grace, which feels incredibly rewarding and cathartic after hours of being terrified. [h3]Final Thoughts:[/h3] By perfectly balancing the vulnerable, atmospheric dread of classic survival horror with the highly rewarding, high-octane action the series is known for, [b]Requiem[/b] delivers an unforgettable experience. In my opinion the game is an absolute must-play 10/10.

Fun: 5/5 Style, Design, Voice Acting: 5/5 Atmosphere: 4/5 Gameplay Mechanics: 3.5/5 Nostalgia, Lore, Story: 5/5 Challenge: 2/5 Replayability: 3/5 Bonus content: 5/5 Really great game -if you like Resident Evil 2 and 4 (and who doesn't?) then you should play Requiem.  RE: Requiem is fun, looks and sounds beautiful, with a gratifying story and S Tier voice acting. It's nostalgic with nods to previous games (especially the magnificent RE:2) and it satisfyingly carries the story forward, introducing some great new characters and reviving the mighty Leon Kennedy. If DLC drops, I would purchase it.  It artfully combines 2 characters with distinct approaches to their experiences in a way that RE:2 might have been trying to accomplish years ago. Whereas in RE:2, you basically had the same combat mechanics, strengths and weaknesses shared between Leon and Claire as they completed their individual storylines, the differences between Grace and Leon in Requiem really solidifies them as different characters -with the terrified Grace relying more on strategy, stealth and crafting, vs Leon's "God of War" style approach, as he mows down legions of zombies and monsters while making funny quips and sharpening his hatchet. It really works and the switching back and forth between characters keeps the playthrough fresh and exciting.  My main criticism is that the difficulty -both in puzzles and combat, is pretty low (on "Standard: Modern" setting) -to the extent that Requiem feels more like an "experience" than a game at times. Combat is generally fluid and almost always fun and satisfying but Requiem's combat doesn't live up to the standard set by Village or RE:4. Requiem also struggles a bit with pacing and maintaining a tense atmosphere in the mid-game, but the combat and puzzles are good enough to keep a player engaged through the mid-game doldrum.  Requiem is almost as good as RE:2, RE:4 and Village, which is high praise. Wherever it comes up short, it makes up for it by being consistently fun, beautiful to look at, and with outstanding voice acting. Thumbs up!!

Before I start: If you haven't played Resident Evil, stop what you're doing and play RE7 and RE Village - they are cheaper, modern, and a more cohesive experience (more on that later).  Recommending this game is easy. In a world where AAA single player video games are seemingly under the threat of unrealistic capitalistic desires, I find a joy in seeing these games still being made and succeeding.  When I come to a Resident Evil game, I'm expecting certain things from them. This is a 30 year old franchise with a very particular tone in the horror genre. It's easily the most popular and critically successful "survivor horror" video game franchise in the industry - something of a darling child. While the franchise has changed for better AND worst the past 3 decades, you can reliably expect some creative monster designs, some laughably campy and outright bad dialogue (literally no one talks like this), sine genuinely creepy environments to traverse, absurd puzzles involving gems and furniture, and at some point ending in some clinical lab that always conveniently blows up.  The franchise is so damn old, that it has its own tropes.  But the appeal of Resident Evil games, aside from what you kind of always will expect to see, is this question of "what setting are they going to place me in now"? The reason people still get excited the 2-3 years between releases when they see a trailer, is that we all really want to know what is the mood? Am I in a vampire hotel? Will I be in a lab the whole time? Oh! I'm in a hospital mansion.  And in this regard, Resident Evil Requiem delivers mood, interest, fear, and excitement in spades. The segment that you play as Grace (arguably 2/3rds of the game) is oozing with excellence. One small detail for example, is that the zombies now remember a portion of their past lives - and so you may run into a zombie that used to be a hotel service worker, and maybe now he's weirdly obsessed with ensuring the lights are turned off ~ or maybe one used to be an operah singer, and she haunts the hallways singing the last tunes before her infection.  If the game were to only be Graces segment, I would have been happy with this release.  Unfortunately, at some point the game fully pivots into you playing as Leon - the bad boy heartthrob of the franchise since RE4. And with that pivot, so goes the soul and mood so effectively delivered to you when playing as Grace. Leon is there as essentially a super human with guns, able to kill just about any threat with ease, and quips to boot! And the hijinks (yes, hijinks) that Leon gets into are on Hideo Kojima levels of absurd - you'd be forgiven for even forgetting what the hell you were playing before you got to Leon.  Let's linger there - the tone change is so strong, it makes you forget Grace. We were just glazing Grace's segment. And while all of Leon's high octane nonsense is fun - it effectively causes both portions of the game to suffer. Leons portion of the game does not compliment Grace in any way - in fact I would argue that the blandness of environment and tone in Leons segment is only allowed to exist because the Hospital Mansion portion of the game with Grace carries the experience forward. It almost feels like I went to watch a full fledged movie at the theater, and then half way through, the movie changed to a straight-to-dvd release. It's jarring.  With all of that said - the industry does not make games like this anymore, and even with my gripes, I had a great time playing this game.  I do recommend playing this game. But I also strongly condemn this idea of mashing together Survival Horror RE with Action Leon RE moving forward - its a bad idea that should have dies at RE6 - and now that we're done with this experiment, please let's move on to the next Virus.

Incredible game. After three playthroughs, I feel like I'm done, at least for a while. I beat the game normally once, one speedrun and one no-heal run. The first playthrough took me around 14 hours, while the others were obviously much quicker due to skipping unnecessary exploration.  Grace's sections, [b]especially the first big area[/b] are probably the best classic/horror Resident Evil ever. There are some genuinely scary parts, inventory management is mandatory and the puzzles are fun (though a bit on the easier side). Resource management is also important at the beginning, but it quicky becomes a bit too easy. The biggest criticism regarding Grace's portion of the game is that the big pursuer monster [spoiler]The Girl[/spoiler] feels very obviously scripted, and she's super easy to play around when you have seen it. Other than that, it's phenomenal.  Leon's parts lean heavily in the RE4-like action and (un)healthy amounts of fan-service. Level and encounter design is nowhere near the level of Resident Evil 4 (neither original nor remake), and these parts are also quite easy at least on Standard difficulty, but it's a lot of fun regardless. These parts give a nice break from Grace's horror sections, but I would have hoped that the balance between the characters was a bit better. At the beginning, the balance seems fine, but at the latter half of the game, it's definitely more of a Leon show, which is a shame, not because his parts are bad, but because Grace's parts are so awesome.  On the technical side, the game runs well and looks really good. The only gripe I have here is the heavy film grain that you cannot turn off without mods.  As a whole, I would argue that this might be the best Resident Evil game so far, despite the criticisms. Some may find jumping between the characters a flow killer, but most of the sections are long enough to avoid too frequent switching.

This was the final entry to Resident Evil. I finished RE2, RE3, and RE4 before playing this one. This game was a perfect hybrid between horror and action, especially with the switches between Leon and Grace.  It was super fun playing as Leon — they gave the guy five different guns to use, and all those flashy finishers and moves were cool as hell. I also loved the fact that we fought old foes in the game. But honestly, Leon is just a demon — the guy can fight anything, it’s amazing.  This game was a solid combination of action, thrill, horror, and emotional moments. The only annoying part was when I got to Raccoon City and had to figure out navigation to get specific quest items. But that’s more of a problem on my end rather than the game itself. Out of all the Resident Evil games, this was by far the most fun one I’ve played.  I’ll definitely have to spin back to these games later in the year. They’re quite short, so replaying them doesn’t take too long. That’s the main downside though — the price tag can feel a bit high since the game is usually under 20 hours long. However, I know people replay on higher difficulties, do speedruns, or even no-save runs to make it more challenging. That does sound interesting, but it’s not really my playstyle.  Overall, this game is a solid 8/10. I would recommend playing it.

After Village, I was a little worried about the direction this series was taking. Biohazard was a fresh, new look at the series and genuinely a very well-made game. But Village, halfway through, felt tired and uninspired. This is quite the opposite. I really appreciate how this series is trying to constantly reinvent itself. And as much as I love Biohazard, I don’t play RE games for a first-person experience. I want to be Leon, Chris, Jill or some type of action hero against an overwhelming, seemingly unkillable horde of zombies.  After the success of the 2 and 4 remakes, it seems that Capcom has realized how much fans love playing as Leon and the type of shooter that character offers. Every second I played as Leon, I had an absolute blast. I felt powerful, but not too powerful. I felt like I was a John Wick-style action hero, but still in a scary, unpredictable world. Grace, on the other hand, made me feel powerless, alone, and afraid. This was clearly the point Capcom was trying to make, and I really appreciate the courage to switch between these two perspectives. But I couldn’t help but just want to get back to Leon every time I played Grace. Grace just wasn’t an interesting character. I didn’t feel the development or feel like she truly became empowered by her arc. Whereas Leon, felt like a perfect arc for who he is.  The game is scary, full of action, with interesting weapons, incredible reloading animations, and I think it’s well-paced and a proper length for a game like this. Easily one of the best Resident Evil games, even with my complaints.   4/5

I think when it comes to first-time playthroughs, this might probably be one of my favorite Resident Evil experiences in a long while. I love most RE Games, even some of the bad ones...and I think it's safe to say this is definitely up there with the greats for me personally, especially in terms of more recent RE titles.  GAMEPLAY:   Let me just once again preface that this is based off of my initial playthrough, as I have not done any full repeat playthroughs yet. I've only been trialing for a speedrun lately...which I think I have my own gripes about, but that's for another time to talk about.  I think RE9 is a perfect marriage of the identities that have shaped the franchise, both in the survival horror and the action horror aspect.  GRACE: (Enemy-type spoilers ahead)  Grace's gameplay takes what made RE7 and classic RE titles good by giving you a character who has little means to defend yourself in the beginning, and have designed enemies that are just fundamentally more difficult for Grace to handle, given her lack of combat ability--often having her rely on smart positioning, crafting and utilizing hemolytic injectors to help permanently remove enemies that might become a greater obstacle as you progress through specifically the Rhodes Hill portion of the game. Resource management becomes front and center once again as you struggle to find scraps and collect blood to craft items, ammo, or healing items that all mostly share the same components.   You'll often find yourself trying to decide what is best to bring for a specific stretch of gameplay, and until you can get more inventory space, that might include the tradeoff of having safety items like knives to help you escape from grabs in order to pick up key items or other resources you might need like ammo, upgrade items, or herbs. Things feel more tense than they did in say, RE2 Remake or even RE7, and I believe part of that--on top of the resource management is the atmosphere and the uniqueness of some of the zombies in Grace's section. Where RE7 had the Bakers, RE9 kind of plays into that same idea of being more than just zombies or BOWs like your usual Hunters and Lickers. You have these zombies that almost seem stuck in these habits uncharacteristic for infected humans in the franchise, as if they still have a bit of humanity left in them. The cleaning lady, the singing zombies, the chef, chunk, the guy who freaks out if you make too much noise, and they're all very dangerous in their own way. While you can absolutely kill them as Grace, her gameplay is very cat and mouse-like. You are not meant to as you are very weak, and if you do, you better be sure you have a plan or the resources to do so.  LEON:  I'll keep this one short and simple, it's RE4 Leon combat but to me it feels more visceral. Aside from being able to switch from aiming to parrying with the hatchet being clunky in my opinion, the combat just makes you feel like you run this show, and it only makes me wish for an RE5 Remake or an RE6 Remake (one done right would be crazy) with this similar kind of combat. Mercenaries would be so fun with RE9 Leon's combat.   CONCLUSION:  I kind of want to skip over the story stuff as to not really spoil anything major, but I will say it was pretty enjoyable just from a casual standpoint. I'm sure folks have some reservations on certain things, but I enjoyed it for what it was, and that was a fun little story that was kind of about facing the past and overcoming trauma. Performance was great until like the open sections of Raccoon City which had these weird frame drops, but that was only in certain places. Never figured out what the reason for it was.   Gameplay again on a first time playthrough was phenomenal, and seeing Alyssa again made me want Outbreak back, either as a port or as a little B-Team side project with the new gen RE gameplay, but better executed multiplayer unlike Resistance or ReVerse. It's a tangent but Capcom's attempts at multiplayer seem so random...I hope the failure of both of those projects don't discourage them from doing something good with a proper Multiplayer Resident Evil game.  Either way, if you love Resident Evil, or even want to get into it, sure some callbacks might be lost on you, but I don't think it's necessary to be able to enjoy this game. I think this game is definitely worth getting into. I really can't wait to play the next RE game they're making. I hear it's a Code Veronica Remake, that one's a guilty pleasure of mine, and for them to pull off a proper remake that everyone can enjoy--that would be really nice.

Capcom sets Resident Evil Requiem, or RE9, apart by providing, namely: Dual protagonists, dual genre (survival horror and action horror), and dual camera perspective (can be changed if desired). All within a single very well-paced campaign. The first time through the campaign was especially rewarding. I couldn't believe what I had experienced. They packed in so many varied gameplay mechanics, set-pieces, and playstyles throughout its runtime, that it just felt fresh, and like the developers were not resting on their laurels from the successes of their other recent RE titles. When my first playthrough ended, it hit a sort of euphoric note for me, as I tried to look back on the exceptional overall experience. Honestly, Capcom be flexing.  This was the first RE game where I completed all achievements and challenges. Just for the lols. Because why not? The game was satisfyingly challenging on the Standard (Classic) and Insanity difficulties. Some of the boss fights in the Insanity difficulty were mental (looking at you, "Commander"), but satisfying to beat. Further playthroughs on Casual difficulty with unlocked weapons/cheats (the devs want you to let loose after your first few stressful playthroughs, clearly), specifically to blast through the game, repeatedly, for achievements/challenges, was nice too. Of course, it plays very differently during these latter playthroughs, but that's the point. It makes you appreciate the stellar design of the Standard (Classic or Modern) and Insanity difficulties in retrospect (if you somehow didn't appreciate it in the moment itself), still tests your knowledge of the game and its circuitous lock-and-key environments, and gives you enough space to breathe and chill as you rack up the achievements/challenges. I was a bit worried about the speed run challenge, but I ended up completing it with plenty of time to spare (~1 hour left) on Casual difficulty. So, don't be afraid to give that one a shot.  I'm a late-arriver/enjoyer to appreciating the franchise as a whole. While I played RE2 OG for a bit in the 90s (only played the beginning, before stopping, don't remember why), and Alone in the Dark OG (different developers, same genre, the initial inspiration for the RE titles), I only really started appreciating the franchise after the far more recent entry, RE7. So far, from the RE games I've finished, I'd rank them as follows: RE2R, RE9, RE4R, RE7, RE8. I still really enjoyed RE8, so that says something.  RE9 also performs reasonably well on a modest PC without raytracing: Ryzen 5 3600 (35 MB Total Cache), RTX 3070 (8 GB VRAM), 32 GB RAM. Heck, at that point, I didn't even need any upscaling/DLSS. Although, the low CPU cache of the Ryzen 5 3600 results in worse traversal stutters, likely when the game needs to send new meshes from CPU Cache to Main RAM (cache miss and stutter at large asset volume) to VRAM. And the low VRAM of the RTX 3070 results in you needing to reduce the graphics options that require high GPU memory. I still didn't mind these issues, given that I understand the limitations of my aging system for what RE9 is putting out.  As of this writing, the game is sitting at 95%+ overwhelmingly positive on Steam, and a Metacritic Critic/User scores of 9.2/9.4. That's insane! It is well-deserved. The quality of the game is exceptional. Kudos to its developers.

I shall refrain from writing an entire book on why I love this game, so here's the short version;  This game feels like a love letter to the franchise and the fans. The locations, references, music, characters, topics... all of it brings the old games to mind. I felt such painful (but good) nostalgia at times. I loved older Leon, seeing just how much he's changed since 1998, his iconic one-liners. I also loved Grace, she's an amazing addition to the franchise and I adore her character, her VA/actress did such a great job. The animations and graphics are phenomenal as well. Also, the difference between playing as Grace and Leon, one having such a small inventory compared to the other, and one truly feeling like a survival horror game while the other is straight up action horror, is just so much fun. The horror was amazing, I was actually terrified of continuing at times but the story was too interesting to fully stop. And the action with Leon?? God, I felt like John Wick, and that's an AMAZING feeling. The hatchet melee weapon and being able to finally pick up and wield a chainsaw from the enemies was such a great idea.   Now spoilers:  [spoiler]Returning to Raccoon City???? Seeing the RPD, and having it be just recognizable enough to remember the places and moments from the RE2 Remake??? So genius. Also the music that plays when you enter!! Having Leon open the gates he closed so many years ago, like a metaphor of him finally facing his trauma and memories of this place head on. Him opening the door to where Kendo took his daughter... I just cannot praise it enough. Amazing. It also genuinely hurt to see Leon in his late stages of infection, but it was so well done. And to see him and Grace interacting so much near the end, her helping him and him opening up to her and being so gentle and sweet made me so emotional. I'm also so happy about the good ending, that Emily could still be saved, because I felt incredibly attached to her.[/spoiler]  Not everyone will feel the same as I do obviously, and I also have a bit of criticism, though it doesn't change how much I enjoyed the game. I do think the addition of [spoiler]Zeno[/spoiler] was unnecessary, since we already had Victor, who then sadly got sidelined for a longer while. I did like the concept and think it had a lot of potential, but it and he as a character did not get explored enough to really justify his presence. Also it does feel like a lot of moments and fights are taken directly out of the other games, either as "nostalgia bait" or because it worked well the first time and was recycled and re-used for this one, like the [spoiler]final fight with Victor just being the nemesis fight from RE3, or the whole section in Raccoon City and fight with the Tyrant, though I really personally enjoyed that a lot. Also the fight with Hunk was basically the same as RE4R knife fight with Krauser, though I also liked it a lot. Leon's infection and him slowy dying could also easily be compared to RE4R, and again I liked it a lot, but it did feel like a copy/paste story- and gameplay wise.[/spoiler]  However, despite all that, I still love and recommend this game. I like what they did with Leon's character and Grace has to be one of my favourite additions thus far, and I hope we'll see more of her.  Thank you, Capcom. Amazing game. I am in love. Thank you for listening to the players.

I felt truly in the grasp of the game almost every step of the way.  The game gives you different POVS and they feel truly unique and necessary. I would argue there are 3 different play types that are displayed when playing the two characters. The timid and scared Grace, The "I will kill everything in my path" Leon, and "this isn't so bad" Grace. I would explain what I mean but it is really difficult to which is why I recommend playing to truly understand.   The story was really thought out and very cool. Action sequences mixed with the good type of dread full horror gave a nice mix. I felt like as soon as I had enough with the horror It switched to action and pulled me back in. The villains are very cool, a bit predicable but well structured and great personalities. Puzzles are simple as to not throw you off too much and not be entertained.  Guns are sweet and felt great!  Performance was maybe its biggest downfall, which is impressive and let me tell you why. With my specs I was able to achieve 4K 30 FPS Quality Upscale with path tracing enabled. That is not how I played it. But I have this gripe with the gaming industry as a whole.   The replay ability is extremely nice. As in all RE games. I even looked through the art and lore, which is suprising because I usually don't. This game is so beautiful on any setting.   The 17 hours I put in this game felt like a journey, A journey that felt like years and did not want to end. The story mixed with gameplay will throw the majority of gamers into a trance that they too will feel the same. Requiem. Is. Amazing.  The first thing that hit me was how confident the game feels in what it’s doing. When you play the game you'll start to realize it's not horror or action, it’s both, and it blends them way better than I expected. The dual perspective between Grace and Leon isn’t a gimmick, it actually defines the very experience. Playing as Grace feels tense in a very real, human way. You’re cautious, constantly thinking, hesitating before opening doors, checking corners. It’s slow, but never boring. Then you switch to Leon, and everything shifts. The pace picks up, combat opens up, and you feel more capable. It’s not mindless action because there’s still pressure, definitely reminds me of the old RE games.  The contrast between these two characters kept the game fresh the entire way through. Every time I felt like I had settled into one rhythm, the game changed it on me. This might be one of the most immersive Resident Evil games ever made. The environments feel alive in a disturbing way. Not because things are constantly jumping at you, but because everything feels wrong in subtle ways. Lighting, sound, level design, it all works together perfectly.  The level design deserves a lot of credit too. Nothing feels randomly placed. Every room, every item, every path feels like it was designed with purpose, especially Racoon City. The reminiscent feeling that instantly grew over me the second I stepped into Racoon City and further into RPD. It's magic. I myself am a huge fan of RE games having played almost all of them and seeing this genuinely made me value this game so much more.  Gameplay is very smooth and I'm not even hyping ts up. At the same graphics settings, it runs noticeably smoother than most modern games with higher and more stable FPS, barely any stuttering, and super consistent frame pacing. It’s not even about lowering settings to make it playable because the game just performs really well and you can tell a lot of care went into optimization because it feels polished no matter what system you’re on, which is honestly rare these days with AAA titles.  Now for the story I actually really liked it  It feels like a proper continuation of everything Resident Evil has built over the years. It doesn’t just throw references at you rather it builds on them. There’s a sense of weight to everything that’s happening, especially with how it connects back to past events. For me, Leon especially stood out to me. He’s not just the confident action guy anymore, you can feel the experience, the exhaustion. After everything he’s been through you'd think a man his age would give up, but no this guy is built different. The character of Grace was also a great addition. She brings a completely different perspective, and her sections genuinely made the game more intense. What really surprised me though is how balanced the entire experience feels. The pacing was never slow for me, rather I'd say it's perfect.  The shifts between horror and action kept things thrilling.   To sum it up,  It has the tension of the older games, the gameplay refinement of the newer ones, and the confidence to mix both without losing its identity. By the time I finished it, I didn’t feel like I had just completed another game. I felt like I had gone through something. And that’s what makes it special. If you’re a Resident Evil fan, this is absolutely a must-play. And even if you’re not, this is one of those games that shows exactly why this series has lasted this long. Genuinely loved every second of it.

Too much was taken away from both genres in order to make the room, and it shows.   The story is barebones, with fun POIs and fan service (WAY too much) to distract from the cracks that are blatantly obvious. I did enjoy the first half of the game from Grace's perspective, the effective utilization of survival horror, and the brief interspersions of Leon, his action, and his quips; darkly delivered due to his affliction. However, the halfway point signaled the beginning of the end of enjoyment for me. Without wishing to delve into spoiler territory, I found Leon's chapters a frustrating change of pace, with very little joy to be had.  By the time I had gotten to the end, I could not care less about the story, and found myself literally skipping the ending cutscenes (after the obscenely easy last boss battle), just to roll credits, collect the achievements, and quickly uninstall the game. I can easily and honestly say, I will never play this game again. And to think, out of the main entries, I used to think RE6 was the worst, and it holds the current record of never having been completed for me (yet). At least it was honest in what it was; kind of like the Last Jedi of the Resident Evil games. Which make this, ironically, the Rise of Skywalker of Resident Evil games. Bleck.   I may install RE6 and give it an honest go after this.

[h1] I would recommend RE9 (Requiem) [/h1]  Resident Evil: Requiem is my first full on Resident Evil experience. My previous experiences were the demos of RE2 and RE4 remakes. I have not fully played a resident evil game before, but this game has inspired me to try out other games in the franchise. As of writing this review I have 29 hours and have played through the whole game twice on Standard (Modern). I intend to play this game on Standard (Classic) eventually, and possibly even Insanity if i become good enough. (edit note: I now have 63 hours and have 100% the game aside from the new Leon game mode)  What I liked: I loved the two different perspectives of Leon and Grace. It prevented the game from getting too samey. An issue with long horror games is that the longer you spend in the game the less scary it becomes, and it is somewhat solved by this. Grace is traditional horror with big monsters, sneaking in dark and small spaces, while having limited resources. Leon is essentially an action hero and his sections make him feel like the monster, not the enemies themselves. Having these breaks of changing perspective allowed me to become reenergized to play another horror section. Having endless horror with no breaks causes me to feel exhausted, so having these switch ups to action sequences as Leon allowed me to recharge. Also, this game is beautiful. I played on low and medium graphics, yet it still looked stunning and incredibly impressive. The environments felt real and lived in which I really appreciate.  What I did not like: In some of the bosses, the gameplay did not always seem friendly to me, the player. It was hard to learn what the game was asking me to do to dodge certain attacks. Particularly parry with the ax in a certain fight. Spoiler: [spoiler] I really hated The Commander boss fight. I enjoyed the majority of this game, however this one boss fight felt really random and out of place. [/spoiler]  To conclude, I really like 99% of Resident Evil: Requiem. Aside from one particular boss fight, i thoroughly enjoyed the game and would recommend it. If you do not like horror, do not play this game. Also, if you are sensitive to gore or violence, do not play this game. This game is wonderful, but I would not recommend it to everyone because of those reasons. If you are unsure about getting the game, I would suggest getting it on sale because the full price is expensive. It is a very good game, but I would not want someone to waste $70 on it if they hate it.

I`ll start saying that the game isn`t bad, played through it 5 times, 100%ted it, did all challenges. However, the game is deeply flawed, and the amount of praise the game is receiving is concerning to me as a long time fan. If there was a Mixed option I would have picked that, but I cannot in clear conscience give it a positive review to add to the praise.   Now, let me preface saying that I have a very low bar for Resident Evil writing. I enjoy the campy and the B movie tier and even some of its inconsistencies. However, what Requiem pulls goes beyond that, it is just not bad writing but a very cheap attempt at nostalgia bait that ignores basic storytelling structure in favor of awe. Awe that gets old really fast.  I could make a very long breakdown, because there is a lot to talk about that would make this into a book, so I'll keep it short.   The decision to split the gameplay into two different types did not do Requiem any favors. I think the first Act is pretty strong, but the second Act feels short and rushed. There are a bunch of references for older games but they feel tackled in and not really thought out. They are there for the sake of member berries, and nothing else. I like easter eggs and references, but RE9 makes them feel cheap, and those should have been handled with more care.   I appreciate the idea of the T-Virus having a side effect long term incubation, because it gives an answer to the long time question of if the characters ever got infected. However, I feel that we should have had a game dedicated to setting that up, instead of setting it up and resolving it right away. Leon being infected and Elpis being the cure all that solves that problem feels very cheap. Plus we never hear about many of the people that should be suffering from the same syndrome.  Zeno is pointless, he should have been the final boss. But his presence not only makes The Connections seem pretty stupid, but also just makes him a stand-in for Wesker without bringing Wesker back. Just "An imitatiioooon"  Gideon is the best character in the game, made into a very poor final boss fight. Capcom once again nailing a villain, underutilizing it and then discarding it right away. It is a common trend, I shouldn't be surprised but I am, because what a waste.    Racoon City feels pretty bad, I was super excited to go back there, and instead we stop at a wall that apparently serves no purpose outside of giving us a cheap puzzle to solve considering there are zombies and giant spiders outside of it. So in 28 years no one saw anything, the creatures never wandered away, nothing. Also it is all brown and rusted with cars, cars everywhere, despite the fact that in 28 years it should have been mad overgrown. Even if the bomb was nuclear (it wasn't), it would still have been overgrown. Plus the bike section makes RC look bigger than it has ever been, remember that this is supposed to be a town with former 100k habitants, and yet it looks like a megalopolis. The distance Sherry tells Leon in-game is about the distance it takes to cross my city from one point to the other. A city that has 700 thousand people!     Grace is important to The Connections and yet she is loose with things trying to kill her every step of the way. Gideon's plan seemingly was for her to come with them willingly, and so the whole Emily/Girl/Leon part seems to have been planned so she would do that. But man, they sure had a lot of trust on a meek and shy girl to survive your zombie infested care center. Had she died, what they would do? Try cloning again?     Also she was bitten in the first 5 minutes of the game, and then we are informed that she is in fact just a normal person. Surely she would have turned.   I said I would keep this short and I am betraying my words. I feel like mechanically the game is amazing, but the split and short sections and half assed references and plot did not help the game, at all. We should either have had a full Grace game with an expanded care center with more areas. Or there should have been more care on handling RC. Leon should've gone through it on foot so we could experience more of the city and past locals, and the day should have turned into night time so we would have at least a bit more horror on his action section. RE4R pulled that off, why RE9 couldn't? RC and the RPD should have felt like a super trip down memory lane, but it is so short and unrewarding. Why Zeno even bring Grace there anyway? It is just one of those things that is just a setup to nostalgia bait, Zeno and Grace had to be there so another Tyrant could show up to remind us of Mr. X... I think we could have another Tyrant added to the game in so many better ways. But things just ended feeling extremely patronizing.      Game is too short, and the whole thing falls apart on multiple playthroughs. With some of the worst writing/plot, retcons and filler I've seen in the mainline entries, and those are plenty across the games, so yeah, it is bad.  RE9 makes me appreciate RE8 so much more, because it had the B writing but they were still consistent and trying something different, had good setting and level design and puzzles, plus released with at least some bonus content. In contrast 9 is a game you can beat in under 3 hours without being a professional speedrunner and has very basic puzzles, minimal backtracking, and no bonus content on release whatsoever.       But I digress, or I'll keep yapping, as again, there is a lot that I could be covering here. But I'm not mad, I'm just... disappointed. It could have been so great, and sometimes it is, but the sum of its parts leaves a lot to be desired.   Will wait for the DLC and see what can be salvaged.  Edit post LMDF - New minigame is alright, has some replayability. Had enough fun to feel like doing all Challenges.  My review stays as it doesn't really affect the main game. If anything it just reinforces that the game should've picked a lane and had either been a full Grace game or a full Leon game.    Now to wait for the next DLC.

I have 100%'d this game on PS5 and I am currently in the process of doing it again on PC, this is my thorough review of this game: I have played and finished every single mainline resident evil game (excluding nemesis and CVX, which I am getting around to) and I can safely say this series is very special to me and playing this game felt like a culmination of those feelings with Resident Evil 2 being my first experience of the franchise, in certain parts I was holding back tears because of all those memories flooding back, a lot of people will complain that the fan service is cheap to which to an extent I would say that some of it could have been executed better.  Grace's sections are peak survival horror experience, and the care center reminded me a lot of the puzzling hallways of the spencer mansion, and I found myself constantly on edge especially in the basement although it does begin to feel like a hog to get through on 2nd playthroughs, resources are not as scarce as the original games however you WILL burn through a ton of ammo and heals without even realizing.  Leon's sections are perfected visions of RE4 and RE6 combat, with the developers managing to make a satsfying experience with finishers interacting with the environment and an actual good melee system, some people will argue that RE4R combat feels a lot better, to which I agree to some extent, my complaint of leon's combat is that it was never really given time to shine, though I suspect we will get a mercenaries mode in the future. The detonator section felt a bit too dragged on at times, with us being placed into a random urban part of RC outskirts instead of memorable parts of the downtown or clock tower from RE3N.  RPD is perfect in every way, so many callbacks, the music, my biggest complaint is how underutilized it was, so much more could have been done with it, but I understand to have it shorter due to pacing sake.  The music in this game is REALLY good, one of the more memorable OSTs of the modern resident evil games.  replayability is not as fun as RE4R, I would compare it a lot more to RE3R with the bonus item shop, not something I'd really complain about since the game has a couple DLCs on the way.  The performance is pretty optimized, I am on a decently high end rig and I played the game with path tracing which looks absolutely amazing, but for my friends who have played the game on bit more dated rigs they had a pretty smooth experience, the only issue is the lack of ability to turn off film grain and other camera effects that just hurt the eyes.  the story is very nice, people have issues with the retconning but I think the future remakes will tie into that since capcom seems to be changing the lore and canon as we know it with said remakes, that said it did have a bit better writing than usual for these games.  overall I really enjoyed this game, a lot more than village, I think it is one of the best modern resident evil entries and how it was recieved says a lot, I think I will continue to sink time into this game especially if they release a mercenaries mode and how good the DLC expansion coming will be, I give it a 9/10.

There is a lot of nostalgia in this game, referencing to Resident Evil 1 to 4. In fact so much that it almost gets TOO much. But it's still on the positive side. Especially if you've lived through the times when the originals were released (1996, 1998 etc.). The new character, Grace, is introduced well, and not like sometimes in movies or games, arrives as completely superior at everything compared the beloved original characters, talking down to them and the usual tropes. She's a noob, she's scared easily, but pulls her weight and never actually treats Leon bad. She's likeable and I am happy to say that I'm looking forward to a game that features just Grace. She can definitely pull her own weight.  Leon on the other hand, the grizzled, 50 year old veteran, is barely impressed by what's thrown at him, and the game takes on a much more action oriented approach than with Grace. For him the inventory is more like in RE4. There's no item boxes and no typewriters, and he gets bonus points for kills, that he can use to upgrade weapons or buy more items. For Grace its more a horror focused approach with the traditional Survival Horror mechanics such as limited saves and item box.  Some people call this game "creatively bankrupt", and I have to partially agree. There is A LOT from previous games that makes an appearance in one way or another. Characters, areas to explore reminiscent of previous games, mechanics... But to have a Resident Evil game that harkens back to the past is not a bad thing in my book. For the next in the series I would like something new. It would be interesting to continue as Grace in a completely different mission, where she can gather more experience and we can witness her becoming more of a hardened Resident Evil character. It is a blatant copy of Resident evil 2 that does almost everything worse. Story does not make sense, weak villains and weak second half. The graphics are gorgeous, but you cannot interact with environment around you at all. Everything is staged, you cannot even shoot a glass bottle. Remember the RE2 ridiculous gore, where you could turn zombies into pudding with minigun? Here, once something dies, you cannot interact with it in any way (apart from some weak blood splats).   In the end, the strongest parts are the main duo of protagonists who are likeable, and amazing first half that is the essense of everything that makes RE games so good (metroidvania-like maps where you start weak, but slowly gain resources and solve puzzles, until you are able to take on every challenge in your way).  I recommend this, but wait for a deep sale. Or just play RE2 and RE4 that are superior in every way.

This was quite the challenge considered I've never been a huge fan of Survival Horror or Horror games in general. I had already beaten several Resident Evil games such as RE4 (2005) RE2 Remake and RE7 but this one was definitely the scariest of them all (yes, even scarier than RE7). Before playing this game never did I think a videogame could get me to be startled in real life after playing, but Resident Evil Requiem did exactly that, mainly when it comes to the Grace sections towards the beginning of the game. Playing in first person definitely added to the scare factor so I had to change it midway to keep my sanity if I was ever to finish this game.  The simple explanation as to why I, someone who doesn't enjoy horror, keeps playing these Resident Evil games is just because they're actually super fun when it comes to gameplay and I think Requiem is another clear example of that, it never feels overly repetitive, the sceneries are beautiful in their unique grim way and the gunplay in the Leon sections is actually very enjoyable. I know some people didn't really enjoy a flashback part in the latter part of the game but I think it's so small that it doesn't really retract from the overall rating for me.  In all honesty I do have to say that one of the main factors as to why this was so enjoyable for me is that I had the pleasure to play this with someone else which is my prefered way to play these games as misery really enjoys company.  I'm happy to have bought and played through this game and I can't wait to see what this franchise has in store for the future.

[h2] Summarized Thoughts: [/h2] The care center is interesting and engaging, the rest of the game is recycled story elements, characters, and a two-hour filler section in the middle for the sake of fan service. I did have fun playing through it with the bonus items and completing the challenges, so get it on sale if you do at all.  [h2] Extended Review (Spoilers Below): [/h2] Resident Evil games all have silly or ridiculous story elements that are easy to overlook because the overall narrative is interesting, and the games themselves are so much fun to play. For example, Grace is a young FBI analyst who the Bureau decides to send to a dangerous crime scene (where her mother died) completely alone. Probably not at all realistic, but who cares? Easy to look past a little detail like that because we’re here to have fun.    Village had so much to offer: new and interesting areas, characters, weapons, and gameplay. So much so that the goofy Capcom dialogue and story choices just added to the game’s charm for me personally.    My problem with RE9 is that the second half of the game isn’t engaging enough to keep things fun and interesting when the story starts to fall short. The entire middle section of the game when Leon first arrives in Raccoon City feels like filler. Wandering around collecting detonator parts is just boring, plain and simple. On top of that, it’s not very appealing visually or sonically. There’s hardly any ambient sound beyond the repeating combat soundtrack, and because of the nuke, everything is covered in the same dull brown palette. This is all made worse moving forward by the recycled character and plot elements from previous games which make the story feel predictable and uninspired:   Leon’s arc in this game feels almost identical to RE4. He deals with guilt over lives lost in Racoon City, searches for a cure, almost dies, and ultimately survives. It’s like he never moved on and needs to repeat the same arc again in a new game to do so.   There also happens to be another even more secret lab that was here the whole time we didn’t know about, so Leon must fight his way through the lab under Raccoon City...again.    Albert Wesker is back yet again in the form of Zeno. Why not focus on developing new and interesting villains in place of bringing him back for the 3rd or 4th time?  I'd rather spend the time getting to know Dr. Gideon more.  I think this game just leans way too much into nostalgia and fan service. Wesker is back, RPD is back, now Mr. X is back, etc. The first half is a new and unique experience, which we get pulled away from that so Capcom can take us down memory lane. It ends up feeling pretty weak, and I would avoid paying $70 for this one personally.

RE9: Больше, чем финал.  Прохождение Resident Evil 9 стало для меня не просто игровым опытом, а глубоким личным потрясением. Это первая игра, которая смогла пробить мою броню и заставить плакать в финале. И дело не в сюжете, а в том, кого я увидела на экране.  С первых секунд, с того самого тяжелого вздоха Леона в машине, я поняла — это я. Его усталость, его пауза перед ответом «да, я здесь», его взгляд, направленный в пустоту — это состояние человека, который выстроил вокруг себя крепость и не хочет из неё выходить. Я увидела персонажа, который, как и я, не подпускает к себе лишних людей, оставаясь верным только себе и своим принципам.  Для многих финал стал поводом для пустых споров о паре с Адой, но для меня сцена с кольцом — это сакральный момент. Леон надевает его не ради кого-то другого. Он надевает его как символ своей выжженной земли, как обет верности своему пути и своей памяти. Он надевает его в тишине, на пепелище, и просто уходит. Это уход человека, который ни о чем не жалеет, даже если остался один.  Я сама убирала людей из своей жизни, и, поверьте мне, я знаю цену этой тишины. И видеть, как Леон проходит этот же путь до конца, было больно, но в то же время целительно.  Если вам кажется, что я сильно глубоко копаю в обычный вздох или секундную паузу — что ж, я — тошнотворный аналитик. Я вижу суть там, где вы видите просто картинку, и этот финал принадлежит мне и моему отражению на экране. Я не просто пробежала игру, я прожила каждый его жест. Я видела его эмоциональное выгорание в микро-интонациях и взглядах. Пока толпа «жужжит» про шипперские теории, я вижу человека, который выбрал одиночество как высшую форму честности.   Эта игра — мой Реквием. Леон Кеннеди в ней — не просто герой, а моё зеркало. И этот финал я навсегда оставлю в своем сердце как доказательство того, что быть верной себе, даже в полном одиночестве — это единственный правильный путь.

[b]Verdict: Not Recommended[/b]  [b]Performance & Graphics[/b] [list] [*] [b]Stable Rasterization:[/b] The base engine is actually stable. I was able to hold a locked 120fps at 1440p without the drawing too much power. If your rig is properly tuned. [*] [b]The Ray Tracing Scam:[/b] The RT/PT marketing is deceptive. The game is mostly lit with flat, pre-baked global illumination anyway. Turning on hardware-accelerated ray tracing just spikes your power draw for a handful of reflective puddles and a mirror here or there. The performance hit completely ruins the frame cadence for practically zero visual gain. Leave it off.  [/list]  [b]Pacing & Level Design[/b] [list] [*] [b]The 80-Minute Walking Simulator:[/b] The first hour and twenty minutes is just unskippable slow-walking and scripted cutscenes. It completely kills any desire to replay the campaign because you are forced to wait instead of play. [*] [b]Severe Tonal Whiplash:[/b] The game awkwardly glues two different campaigns together. You spend two hours carefully sneaking around with zero ammo as Grace, only to get interrupted by a brain-dead five-minute shooting gallery as Leon. It ruins all momentum. [*] [b]Lazy Fetch Quests:[/b] Every single level uses the exact same "find three items" structure (three cubes, three plugs, etc.). It forces you to backtrack constantly through empty, already-cleared rooms just to pad out the playtime. It's an artificial spatial chore, not puzzle-solving. [*] [b]Fake Action Scenes:[/b] The set pieces are basically on-rails. In the motorcycle chase, you don't even control the bike. You just point the crosshair and click. [/list]  [b]Combat & Horror Mechanics[/b] [list] [*] [b]Broken Melee:[/b] Leon’s hatchet parry is ridiculously overpowered. The invincibility (i-frame) window is so massive that you don't even need to think about positioning. You can parry a massive biological weapon exactly the same way you parry a base zombie. [*] [b]Punishing You for Being Good:[/b] The game uses hidden Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment (DDA). If you do well and save up ammo, the engine silently turns standard zombies into bullet sponges to drain your inventory. A clean cranial shot that should be an instant kill registers as minor damage. Weapons completely lose their kinetic punch and feel like laser pointers draining a health bar. [*] [b]Zero Tension:[/b] You are never actually scared because the game throws way too much ammo and healing at you. Your DPS easily outscales the enemies. Plus, the lighting is way too bright, totally exposing the goofy, high-poly enemy models and removing any fear of the unknown. [*] [b]Boring Stealth:[/b] The stalker enemies aren't dynamic. You just crouch in a corner and wait for a localized timer to tick down while the invincible AI walks its hardcoded path. It induces mechanical boredom, not terror. [*] [b]Camera Penalties:[/b] If you switch Grace to third-person, the game artificially throttles your movement and makes her stumble constantly to offset your wider FOV. It makes the controls feel like sludge during chases. [/list]  [b]Audio Design[/b] [list] [*] [b]Forgettable Soundtrack:[/b] Aside from the main menu, there isn't a single memorable track. The game completely lacks any musical buildup or thematic tension. [*] [b]Robotic Audio Triggers:[/b] The combat music is just a generic synthetic loop that abruptly cuts off the exact millisecond the last enemy's health hits zero. It sounds incredibly cheap and highlights how bad the campy dialogue and monster sound effects are. [/list]  [b]Summary:[/b] You are paying full AAA price for a game padded with tedious fetch quests, high-TTK bullet sponges, and unskippable wait states. The base rasterization runs well, but the actual gameplay loops are functionally bankrupt.

I played Resident Evil 9 on both PC and PS5. Between the two versions, I spent about 32 hours with the game and completed all of the challenges on my PS5 copy.  Overall, I would give the game an 8/10. I can echo a lot of the positives that other players are mentioning, but mainly in the first half of the game. The second half is where a number of issues start to appear that keep this game from becoming the masterpiece it could have been.  Things I loved - The personality of the zombies. They feel distinct and unpredictable. - Exploring the care center. One of the most interesting locations in the game and the series - The core gameplay. Combat and movement feel great throughout. - The ability to switch between first-person and third-person. The red dot sight was a personal favorite. - The intro. One of the craziest zombie openings I’ve experienced in a game. - The story buildup. I really enjoyed the mystery surrounding Grace and Elpis. - Grace’s characterization and voice acting. (Yes, I didn’t mind the stuttering) - Leon’s axe. It was incredibly satisfying to use. I actually preferred it over the knife from RE4R.  Things I disliked - The second half feels less fleshed out. There are fewer puzzles, zombie personalities mostly disappear, and the Raccoon City section feels a bit bland. - Overreliance on nostalgia/fan service. I prefer references in smaller doses, though some players may enjoy it. - No standard New Game option. You’re forced into a somewhat lackluster NG+ structure on subsequent playthroughs. Can't mimic a first playthrough unless you delete a save - The story conclusion isn’t as satisfying as the buildup. Some characters end up feeling underused or wasted. - No extra modes at launch such as Mercenaries or Raid Mode.

Finally, I got 100% in this game, and I have some thoughts about it. I remember when it was announced back in summer 2025—it was my most anticipated video game ever. I love the Resident Evil series, so believe me, I was counting the days until I could play it. This was the first game I ever pre-ordered, and it did NOT disappoint.  First of all, this game looks amazing. This is probably the most realistic-looking game I’ve ever played, and it’s crazy that the RE Engine can look this good while still running well. It’s true that you need a pretty powerful PC to get the best experience—this is obviously the most demanding RE game—but from what I’ve heard, it still runs pretty well on older systems too, which is mind-blowing. Personally, I had a great experience performance-wise. The only thing that felt a bit slow was when I skipped cutscenes (especially while speedrunning), as it sometimes took a while to load into the next scene. But overall, it ran really well for me.  You might think this game is too expensive, and fair enough—$70 is a lot for a video game, especially one that’s only about 15–20 hours long. It’s not the longest game, but trust me when I say those 15–20 hours are amazing. This is a quality-over-quantity kind of game. It’s straight fire and doesn’t drag like 80% of modern AAA games. That alone makes it worth it in my opinion.  The pacing is smooth and straightforward. The game doesn’t really have puzzles per se—you mostly run around collecting items like keys, ID cards, etc., like in any RE game, but they’ve toned down the puzzles. Honestly, I think I prefer it. It keeps the game moving, and you don’t have to stop and think too much—you just keep going. I get that not everyone will like that, though.  The changes in this game are huge, especially with the two protagonists: Grace Ashcroft and Leon S. Kennedy. Grace plays more like RE2 and RE7, while Leon is more action-heavy like in RE4. You probably already know that if you’ve heard anything about the game—it was a big part of the marketing, but it really works. Not only is their gameplay different, but their HUDs are too. When you play as Grace, you can’t see your health on the screen—it’s only in your inventory, like in RE7. With Leon, you can see it on the screen. It’s a small detail, but I love stuff like that.  The amount of work that must have gone into this game is insane. You can also switch perspectives between first-person and third-person for both characters. The game suggests playing Grace in first-person and Leon in third-person, and I agree—that’s probably the best way to experience it. But on my last playthrough (on Insanity), I switched it up and played Leon in first-person and Grace in third-person. That made me appreciate the game even more. They didn’t just lazily reuse animations—they actually created unique animations for both perspectives. That level of detail shows how much they cared about players who want to experience the game fully in either perspective.  The enemies are fun too. I’m glad they went back to classic zombies instead of werewolves or mold creatures from earlier games—it’s a breath of fresh air. I also like how they behave more like humans—they talk and continue doing tasks they were doing before they turned. The mini-bosses are great as well, like the Girl and Chunk. I actually love Chunk—most people probably won’t agree, but I think he’s hilarious. You can even kill him as Grace, which I didn’t realize on my first playthrough. On my second run, I figured out it takes three shots from the Requiem gun to take him down. Enemies like Chunk and the Girl feel more like actual monsters, and I really appreciate that.  The story is pretty solid too. For me, Resident Evil has never really been about the story—the lore is interesting, but I usually care more about the gameplay. That said, I was actually invested in this narrative, and it felt satisfying overall. I even got the bad ending accidentally, lol. I also liked the new characters they introduced. I’m still not sure how I feel about what they did with Spencer, but we’ll see where that goes.  You also get to go back to Raccoon City, which I loved. Some people have said that section felt a bit boring, and I get that, but for me it was a lot of fun. Farming points and taking down enemies felt like a physics-based sandbox, and I really enjoyed it. Going back to the RPD was crazy, and it didn’t feel forced at all—it makes perfect sense for Leon to go there. They even brought back the Tyrant and a giant spider. The whole Raccoon City section felt like a great tribute to both the original and newer games. There was one flashback segment that felt really boring and unnecessary, but aside from that, I don’t have many complaints about that part.  It took me 55 hours and 6 playthroughs to get 100%. Some people say this game doesn’t have much replayability, but I completely disagree. It feels pretty standard for a Resident Evil game—I usually replay these games around 5–6 times anyway, and this was no different. Also, I don’t know about others, but I found parts of the game pretty challenging, even on normal difficulty—so don’t expect a cakewalk.  Anyway, yeah—they made another banger. I can’t wait to see what’s next for the Resident Evil franchise. This is my GOTY for 2026.  9/10

Though admitedly with the game effectively offering two vastly different games within itself, I'd say Leons sections slightly suffer more from that split. Combining the best of RE7's solitary survival horror as well as the goofy as ♥♥♥♥ RE4 action segments, Resident Evil Requiem absolutely excels in synergizing the best parts of these games. I love the tense horror, but I also love the goofy nature of the RE storyline, so I was a really happy fan with RE9.  Capcom spent a lot of time making sure that both parts played well off each other. Both Leon and Grace, our playable protagonists, have very different feels to their gameplay, but as its both happening at the same time their segments serve as a "two sides to the same coin" for the plot of the game, similarly to RE2. Gameplay-wise, it's your standard Resident Evil game: your puzzles aren't too difficult, your combat involves either a lot of shooting with bigger and bigger guns (Leon) or fighting for your life in the dark against a stalker enemy (Grace). There's a lab level (of course), a cool mansion level, and lots of backtracking.  And despite this, each area still feels uniquely distinct and alive and fun to travel through. The addition of the zombies now displaying distorted behaviors and goals based on who they were when still alive is really neat, distinguishing them from previous RE zombies.  This game is heavy on the callbacks/fanservice, and it's really fun seeing these in game during Leon's segments. However, I don't want to discount Grace's segments either - for a new addition to the series and a new playable character, Grace has shot up the list to be one of my favorite RE characters. She's very human in her reactions to the events happening around her, and in certain ways I think she's Capcom's response to the lack of character development they did with Ethan for RE7 and RE8.  The story and villains were straightforward and serviceable, but for a really bold and narratively interesting story decision (such as what is revealed near the end of the game regarding one of our protagonists), there are also ridiculously dumb details thrown in ("missed vitals", huh? That's not how I remember it going down, Leon...).  Performance-wise, this game looks amazing and is very well optimized. My system isn't the newest nor the strongest nowadays, but I was able to get great performance from the game without compromising visual fidelity. Based on the spec testing I've seen online, across the board, this game runs well across a variety of system specs.  For a fan, this is recommended. For a horror experience and a newcomer to the series, you may struggle to understand certain aspects of Leon's segments, but they do throw in flashbacks here and there to help newcomers a bit, so it's not too daunting to get the gist of what's happening. It's a shame there's no demo available, so if that bothers you I do recommend a sale - otherwise, I'd pay full price for the experience, as I thoroughly enjoyed this game.

Resident Evil Requiem is a very entertaining entry in the long-running series, blending together the best elements from previous games into one cohesive and varied experience. It successfully mixes tense exploration, puzzle-solving, and action-packed combat, creating a gameplay loop that constantly keeps things fresh. One of the standout additions is the character-switching system, where players alternate between two protagonists. Grace delivers the classic, nerve-wracking horror segments, where every sound matters, all lights seem to be broken and resources feel scarce, while Leon brings a more action-oriented style with intense combat encounters. This contrast keeps the pacing engaging and prevents the game from becoming predictable.  That said, the game isn’t without its flaws. While most of the experience feels carefully crafted, there are a few moments that fall flat and disrupt the immersion. Certain sequences, such as the motorcycle chase, feel overly scripted and out of place compared to the rest of the game. Similarly, the section set in the orphanage with a young Grace drags on longer than necessary and lacks the tension seen elsewhere. Despite these weaker moments, Resident Evil Requiem remains a highly enjoyable and varied installment that both honors its roots and introduces new ideas to keep the series evolving.
