Boy is this disappointing. It seems like Capcom is going down the path of spectacle over substance again, and while I'd be fine with that for a modern RE (I am NOT forgiving you for Wilds, Capcom), why, precisely, do you BACKLOAD the spectacle? It feels like they tried to give that feeling of earning your fun that you get from the classic RE games  (and 7 and RE2make) but accidentally turned it into the 2nd half of the game instead of the ending portion. Makes me think of an overstretched setpiece, like playing Chris in Village but somehow intended to hold up as a central part of the game.   The good:  The first half has you on your backfoot, stuff's spooky, it's that good old RE charm, you're trapped in a puzzlebox and health and ammo are pieces of a puzzle you lose out on for skill issue, there's neat things to do and you discover new recipes and tools, is good...  The bad ...for about 2 or 3 hours. And then you start offing enemies in 4 or so safe and easy headshots. And then Leon's sections begin and I don't feel catharsis. I don't feel happy about bashing that one SPECIFIC plain zombie that pissed me off too much by alerting his blind mate. I just feel a very distinct feeling of "oh wait, we're finishing? This soon?" as I realize just how little I actually ended up doing in what feels like the most intricate part of the game.   The Legacy I was GENUINELY expecting something akin to an Amnesia: the Bunker Lite but I got the equivalent of a theme park ride through REmake. I genuinely think the castle Dimitrescu segments in Village (itself middling and shallow compared to its predecessor, but in the end enjoyable) pulled off the mixture of modern and classic RE far, FAR better. Grace's part just feels so fake, in hindsight. Maybe Castle D doesn't have the peak of the early game, but it's at least sizable and consistent.   I didn't really hate my time with it. I won't speak on the story as I am currently only about 30-40% through the Raccoon City part, but the gameplay is not really bad per-se. The problem is this game costs 70 fat ones and the moment I look closer at the experience I start to get annoyed. Why did I have so little of the actually challenging part? Why did I get safety wardrobes for leon only so I don't accidentally starve myself of resources from playing as grace? Why does so much of leon's combat feels like it tries to make me feel cool like (OG) RE4 instead of just letting me be cool? I genuinely feel like the best way I can describe this game is "RE6 but not awful" which is NOT the description any game should aspire to.   Conclusion  I didn't hate my time with it, but I feel like even at this point I've got most that I will get out of it. And this is a AAA-priced game. Grab it for an RE fix at a sizable sale.  Post-finishing the game:  The member berries were surprisingly alright. It was cheap nostalgia bait, sure, but I'm not excessively nostalgic for the 2nd game (original or remake) and I enjoyed the tone carried through the parts referencing it. The inevitable lab at the end was actually well-paced for what it was and I didn't dislike it (something that was the case with a few prior labs such as the RE3make, even compared to the prior game I mean).   I guess if I were to sum up my opinion on the game, it'd be "Death by a Thousand Faint Praises".

Resident Evil Requiem is possibly one of the best games in the franchise. I've always been a fan of the original trilogy. I never liked the original RE4 because it changed too much, and RE6 was so bad I couldn't even force myself to play it. Then RE7 brought the series back for me. After that came the remakes: RE2 was good, RE3 was meh, and RE4 was an absolute blast. To me, RE9 feels like a mix of RE2, RE4, and RE7, with maybe a small sprinkle of RE6, because at certain moments it gets a little too crazy for my taste.  The story kept me interested from start to finish. Graphically, it's demanding, but it looks really good. I also liked that the lighting and environmental design do a lot of the visual guidance naturally instead of relying on obvious paint marks everywhere. Grace's sections were easily my favorite: slower, more tactical, and more methodical. Leon's parts were more action-heavy, which makes sense, although a few of those moments were a bit too over-the-top for me.  The enemy design is great. I liked that many zombies felt more memorable than the usual generic cannon fodder. The atmosphere is strong throughout the game as well. The Raccoon City section wasn't really my thing, though. It felt too gloomy, too gray, too post-apocalyptic, and a little too action-focused for my taste. Still, for pacing reasons, I get why it's there.  I completed the game 100% and still wanted more, which says a lot. The combat is fun, the story is interesting, and the whole thing feels like a very strong Resident Evil package. It also helps that both characters can be played in either first-person or third-person, which gives the game a bit more flexibility depending on what kind of experience you want. I personally chose third-person for Grace.  Overall, I definitely recommend playing it. For me, it's one of the strongest modern Resident Evil games. I'm just a bit less enthusiastic about some of the more explosive, action-heavy parts. Still, it's an easy recommendation from me.

I just finished playing RE: Requiem and had a good time.   The game is split into 2 parts where you play as Grace and Leon.  Grace’s parts are much more horror focused. Optimization - Surprisingly well-optimized even for my old, dying "gaming" laptop. Initially, I was a bit confused on why RE9 had fewer tweakable in-game settings compared to other relatively similar RE Engine games like RE8 and DMC5 (which allowed you to control Rendering Resolution to very specific percentages, for example). Had to rely on NVIDIA DLSS 4 to make the graphics look crisp without sacrificing too much on the performance side. Never encountered any major problems or game-breaking issues at all during my 33 hours (as of this writing) and third playthrough.  Gameplay - It's generally fun. The marketing was spot on when they said the player would feel cathartic while fighting zombies as Leon after mostly running away from them as Grace, although it's also hilarious if the inverse happens. Leon's parrying mechanic is also very interesting as you can deflect virtually a lot of enemy attacks, and it invites replayability just for experimenting what you can do with it. The game also blends exploration with one-and-done setpieces, so there are areas where you'll be spending a lot of time on, but there also short parts where you can go "Wait, that's it?". Lastly, the game truly opens up after you've beaten your first playthrough, there are various things to unlock that do carry over, but there's unfortunately no "true" New Game Plus, which can be disappointing coming from RE4 and RE8.  Story - Grace Ashcroft is a nice addition to the RE cast, but I also have to say that (without spoiling too much) one's enjoyment on the latter half varies depending on how you're already familiar with the overall Resident Evil universe. Obviously, it's fun if you can recognize all the references, easter eggs and call-backs to previous RE entries because this game has loads of them (and yes, if you squint or compare stuff enough, it even includes stuff from the Milla Jovovich movies). Otherwise, the references can be easily missed, but this invites the curiosity of trying out the previous RE entries (which I did as I also sank myself deeper into the RE rabbit hole after this game).  Bought this game at full price just to support the small indie billionaire company Capcom, and in the end, even with more specific nitpicks, I didn't regret my purchase. The Lady Dimitrescu outfit alone makes the Deluxe Edition worth it. There are also more content updates planned post-release, apparently including a Story DLC and a mini-game (perhaps the classic Mercenaries Mode), so there's still something to look forward to in RE9.

After playing RE2 remake, RE3 remake, RE4 remake, RE5, and RE6 back-to-back, I can confidently say that, for me personally: this is my favorite Resident Evil game. I know there is still a lot I am missing out on in terms of playing the other games, but at the moment, I think this is the best Resident Evil. As trailers dropped for this game, each one was actually making me more and more excited to play it, despite not playing any Resident Evil games or knowing a single thing about the series. All I knew was my friend loves these games and he wanted me to check them out. After seeing some Leon gameplay for this, I thought it was time to play some Resident Evil games in preparation for this and man oh man, I was not disappointed in the slightest (except for RE6). I tried playing through the main games that would be plot relevant to this one and got really sucked in, falling in love with Leon's character in general and finally playing this game for the first time was something magical. Maybe it was because I was fresh off of RE6 but my enjoyment of this game was at another level.  To start, I have no real complaints about this game. Nothing I would personally change and nothing that made the game bad. I really only have positive things to say about this game. Starting off with Grace. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is this game scary. I don't really like playing scary games because I just find them to be too intense for me. Scary games can be TERRIFY and this game is exactly that. Playing as Grace is just an amazingly awful experience. Every room, every enemy, every event, and that scary ass lanky ♥♥♥♥♥ are just terrifying. Never have I been so afraid to play a game and venture into any room. If it was a game I had no interest in, I would've turned it off extremely early. But I had to see what happened next. Likely one of the best first play through experiences I've had in a long time. And Grace herself was an incredible character. I know people complain about it, but I genuinely think the actress needs to be awarded for her voice acting because JESUS CHRIST was it good. From the way she was nervously stuttering to trying to calm her breathing, it simultaneously made her feel like a real life person being thrust into this petrifying world and actually making me even more tense and nervous. Grace was fantastic in this game and actually one of my favorite protagonists despite not inheriting many badass qualities.  But LEON ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ KENNEDY was the highlight. Grace is one of my favorites but Leon IS my favorite, especially after this game. Although it's debatable which version of Leon is the best, I think Leon in this game is the best version of himself we've seen. From the moment you can control Leon, you know this game is going to make you feel SO good. The music, the quips, the weapons, the gameplay, Leon's sections are something magical, especially for a fan of the games (new fan at least). He is every bit as badass as he's always been, with a little bit more thrown in there. As Grace, you actively avoid engagements and run from enemies. As Leon, you seek out and kill everything in your path with extreme brutality. His finishers in this game are easily my favorite in the series, his whole character design is up there too, and he just has an incredibly strong charisma to him. The weapon system, guns, combat axe, and the Requiem made this game really stand out. You just feel good playing as Leon.  Between the two characters and game sections, this game blends horror and action so well, making you afraid to fight enemies as Grace to being excited to wipe them all out as Leon. On top of phenomenal characters and incredible gameplay, the story I think is fantastic too. Both characters have such an endearing story, with both branching plotlines really getting you invested. On top of that, this game is just such a big love letter to Resident Evil fans. Without spoiling anything, they do certain things in this game that will make you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ giddy with joy and excitement. References and call backs are welcome surprises in this game.  Overall, this game might be one of my favorites I've played in a long time and I personally want to see this get game of the year, if not, at least seeing it get some awards. There are tons of other things I haven't mentioned like graphics, story beats, atmosphere, quality, polish, and how buttery smooth this game ran. Just know this game, highly recommend for both Resident Evil fans and people who haven't played a single RE game before.

Resident Evil: Requiem may be in my Top 5 for the series. It blends together the gameplay style of RE4, and RE7 seamlessly. Playing as Grace gives you the traditional experience of survival horror. Some of them hold different weapons, act differently, and perform different tasks since they have retained some of their humanity, which makes every single encounter feel unique.  The game looks beautiful, and runs great. It's extremely well optimized and has a ton of options such as being able to switch between third and first person for each of the playable characters to better suit your preferences. ((MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD))  Where do I start...  Is this a bad game? No. Is it peak Resident Evil like everyone's saying so? Hell no.  Gripes with the gameplay: Leon. His gameplay feels like a more watered-down version of RE4 remake, as in there's no real cost of using the hatchet. That meter goes out? Just back up and press a button, and it's good as new. In RE4make, you had to completely change up how you play until you find the merchant. It made you feel almost naked and vulnerable not having the ability to parry or stealth kill, which was a fun challenge at higher difficulties. Aside from the hatchet, not much has changed to Leon's gameplay to really pique my interest. What we have for him feels like a step down from what we had before.  Gripes with the story: Two thirds of RE Requiem feels like fan service without much substance. Capcom seems to have made the decision to follow the trend of digging up familiar faces and places to capitalize off of nostalgia, which comes off as lazy and key-jingley. For example: Zeno. My first reaction upon seeing him were rolling my eyes so hard that they touched the back of my skull. Let's all be real, we all thought he was Wesker there for a minute. He could've had any other design for him, and Capcom went with going to knock on the coffin of an old villain. Many of the other returning characters received a similar reaction from me, too, maybe even more with the T-00 and the Hunk bossfights.   Some things I liked: GRACE. I REALLY liked Grace's section in the care center. That part of the game felt like a return to form, having to barely scrape by with scarce ammo and ink ribbons. The whole mechanic with having to collect the blood for crafting felt fresh as well, and the ability to craft ink ribbons was a helpful addition. Gideon was also an interesting villain, being someone that had connections to people earlier in the timeline, but still someone original enough to be a fresh face.  Overall, RE Requiem feels like a disappointment. The developers tried to play it safe and bring back old characters and refuse to expand on the action-oriented gameplay instead of doing something new and innovating. Capcom, you can do better.  6/10.

The one complaint I've always had about horror games was best put into words to me by the Youtuber Scruffy.  The two things that make a horror game scariest is absence of action and absence of information.  Too many games give you FAR too much ability to fight back and the horror suffers as a result.  Resident evil has always been somewhat decent at subverting this but Requiem took it to the absolute maximum.  You have access to guns as Grace, but very little ammo, especially early on.  As you explore the areas, you learn the map layout and discover new items to aid you, while also getting a feel for opportunities where you can avoid conflict.  With the expansion of information and action, the horror elements ease off, allowing the player to feel comfortable and confident.  Requiem lets you keep this comfort for long enough that you don't even think about the horror until you're thrown into a brand new place with no information and minimal action.  In-depth analysis aside, the monsters and the atmosphere in this game genuinely made my heart race constantly, and I was having more fun than any other horror game I've experienced. I have come to realize that we normalized lack of creativity and original art direction. Capcom is doing to this what SEGA did to Sonic - and I'm not even a Sonic fan!  After I beat this game, I went and streamed Resident Evil 6 to my girlfriend to show her the older games that were a part of my childhood, and it just stunned me to see such a significant difference with not just the gameplay, but mechanics. The attention to detail with combat, and so much versatility and responsiveness. ♥♥♥♥, even the attack reactions in RE6 felt more natural than the combat system in RE9! The graphics may have not been the best looking, but it was engaging. At least Capcom is still somewhat loyal to image clarity today. If they had forced TAA and upscaling, I would have avoided buying this game outright.  I found myself frustrated with the combat and mechanics in general, not because it's hard, but because a lot of them are mostly implied and don't work the way that you expect. The trial and error kept me guessing to the point where I just stopped trying. For example, there is a certain distance where zombies can auto-grab you, and you would think that it would be inches away, but no, it's when they initiate a lunge within a certain range. Perfect parry windows are limited, too. When you hit a zombie with the axe, it's a gamble if they flinch, and the momentum of the hit slows significantly before the recovery window kicks in and leaves you open to be grabbed. I feel like you're much more likely to be grabbed when you turn away from a zombie even if you think you're far enough. All they have to do is lunge.  The thing that infuriates me the MOST was how LIMITED the game makes me feel when I try to be creative. You would think that if you made the singer zombie scream near the sound-sensitive one that he would attack her, but that can only happen when you hit her with the bottle... EVEN if I do that, I have to TIME it so that the sound-sensitive zombie hears it, runs over, and THEN initiates the swinging to kill her, but she moves too fast for him to keep up. You can only guess which enemies will actually do damage to others, and if it will even be worth it with the already limited inventory you have. I'm finding myself defaulting to shooting and shoving the zombies out of anger than having fun and using all of the environment and tools to my advantage. Don't worry, though, the glass bottle is just as useless with lickers, too, and they don't even care if the zombies bump into them. I guess lickers have a built in emo-dar or something... The game, however, will prompt me to be careful with glass on the ground because it makes noise and attracts them :) How helpful. SPEAKING of that... At the ARK, I had a fully upgraded Silencer 9 and shot at a licker from above and FAR away. It knew where I was instantly, and it didn't matter if I crouched and moved away, it STILL zeroed in... never mind that all his friends were nearby and heard their comrade screech and scurrying. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, is a little thoughtfulness with the mechanics and how they're communicated too much to ask?  If I were to compare RE6 and RE9 Leon, the only areas that RE9 Leon beats RE6 Leon in is wisdom, grit, and character development. Everything else is just hype. What's more insulting is that the cinematics and parry sequences show that Leon is MORE than capable of quick and deadly exchange of hands, but during the actual gameplay, his movements are all watered down and sluggish. Yes, he's infected with the T-Virus, yes, he was physically and mentally worn down, but it's no excuse. He's a highly trained gunman and seasoned fighter, and I think Capcom can make this more believable. For ♥♥♥♥'s sake, my girlfriend just mentioned to me that at the beginning of the game, Leon essentially ran up a wall and did a backflip, but never again was that seen. I didn't even remember that. It comes to show how unmemorable this version of Leon is, but I still LOVE him as a character. His witty remarks, one liners, and the lore from all the older games is what kept me going, frankly.  I will hand it to Capcom for mixing the older and familiar RE gameplay elements (UI, inventory management, and POV types) with the newer ones, and I can safely say the whole game was put together well ENOUGH that I could keep my attention on it and at least appreciate the story. It started to show it's cracks with Grace. She grew on me quick because I am an anxious person, and I can relate, but it feels like the anxiety personality was played a bit too hard. It just grew stale over time. It didn't feel cathartic when it came to [spoiler]Emily's death[/spoiler]. For god's sake, she barely knows the girl, and never had any kids. It was like she had lost her true love (if she ever had a romantic partner to begin with.) On top of that, who the hell just decides "Yeah, I'll go with the bad guys who want to destroy the world"? I get she was in a pretty bad place, but man, how can you brave visiting a haunted place all by yourself, but be just fine when one of the masterminds who is never around until the last 3/4 of the game politely asks you to go with him? To top it off, the dude is just a player two variation of Wesker who was an absolute pushover in the final battle.  All that being said... we really need to raise the bar... back to where it was before. We're rewarding publishers for making mediocre games, and diehard fans are having to take the brunt of this. Take this from someone who ISN'T a diehard fan. I don't notice as much details compared to my bud in Australia who is a talented artist and knows so much more about video games than me, and I have been playing games SINCE I was 8.  This is an example of what the current standard is. I have noticed a significant shift to making games look as realistic as possible, and as a result, it feels more like the visuals are prioritized over gameplay, story, and mechanics. It's pretty clear to me that either nobody is paid enough to care about thoughtful design, or these publishers have taken to hiring yes men who are willing to do their bidding rather than challenge the norm and use all the resources and time to make something wonderful. I'm gonna vote on both. I won't stop you from buying this game, but if anything in this review stands out to you, I seriously recommend taking your money elsewhere, or if you wanna risk it, get it on sale. I wouldn't pay more than $30 for it.  Thank you for your attention to this matter.

This review is purely focused on the technical failure of Resident Evil Requiem to run correctly on the flagship NVIDIA hardware and Surround Gaming setup it claims it was designed for. It is not a review of the gameplay because I never got to the gameplay.  I recently purchased a 5070 ti and this game was included with the card. The redemption process was a huge pain in the @$$. It's a highly irritating multi-stage process that involves installing the NVIDIA app, linking your Steam account, authenticating with NVIDIA, and redeeming for your account, and it is especially frustrating when NVIDIA consistently fails to authenticate all attempts to link your accounts. I get that they're trying to stop people selling keys but this is just ridiculous. It took over half an hour just to get the ****ing game I paid for. Not a great start, but it would soon get worse.  I installed the game and the very first thing I noticed was that the game was natively vert minus. Yes, in 2026, a flagship game meant to demonstrate high technology was vert ****ing minus with no built-in way to correct it. I also noticed the HUD and UI was not correctly centered on the screen. How do you even advertise a game to be a premium Surround Gaming experience and not get this most basic of functionality correct? After installing REFramework from github and spending another hour tweaking it to get the game to properly display on my Surround setup I finally started playing the game... and immediately realized that the game was incorrectly culling objects right in front of my face. Take that guy that drops the box at the back of the car right before the alley: the box was missing 2/3 of its mesh while he was carrying it and when he sat it down, but only if I was looking at it within my forward field of vision. Moved to beyond about a 45 degree angle to either side of my screen: POOF the box popped fully back into view.  I spent the next 3 hours over several sessions of troubleshooting to attempt to fix this problem and never fixed it, not even with the help of forums, searching, or AI, and I tried everything, from custom lua scripts in REFramework to nuking the graphics settings completely in the game. The irony of all this is that I don't even like the Resident Evil series! I was only willing to give Requiem a shot because it was free with my graphics card and it had so many overwhelmingly positive reviews. But I never even got to the initial alley scene successfully because the game is such a massive technical failure for Ultrawide/Surround users.  On the bright side, nothing I saw during my 3-4 hours of attempting to get the game working made me want to play it. The engine isn't particularly pretty and the gameplay didn't look any different from any other Resident Evil game I've ever seen or played. So apparently I'm not going to miss much. But I really would have liked to find out for sure for myself, because, you know, I kind of deserved to find out considering I own the piece of ****.

I just finished Resident Evil 9: Requiem for the first time and honestly… what a game.  I went in expecting something similar to the latest RE titles, but this one really managed to mix the classic feel with the modern style. The atmosphere is heavy, that constant tension where you don’t trust anything around you. There were moments I literally stopped before opening a door like “yeah… something bad is about to happen.”  The story caught me more than I expected. It’s not just about scares, there’s a lot going on behind the scenes, connections to other games, and that feeling of “okay… things just got serious.” I still have some questions after finishing it, but I think that’s part of the charm.  Gameplay feels well balanced. Not too easy, not unfair either. Resources are limited just enough to keep you on edge, especially in tighter areas.   Graphics and sound are insane. The sound design especially… sometimes it feels like the game is playing with you. Footsteps, doors, noises in the distance… everything keeps you alert the whole time.  If I had to point out something negative, maybe the pacing drops a bit in some parts, but nothing that ruins the experience. Overall, I really enjoyed it and I’ll probably play it again to get everything.  If you’re a real Resident Evil fan, this one is 100% worth it.  8.25   Your Friend, Datmann

I absolutely loved this game.  I'm not very good at survival horror games.  I did play this on Standard Modern.  It was still a trip.  And I'm playing a second playthrough on Classic until I get enough nerve to try Insanity...  I think the opening part was well put together, and I loved figuring everything out in the care center.   A lot of people think the game fell apart after the care center.  But I still loved everything after.  Even if some of the Leon parts aren't for everyone, I still think Capcom did a fantastic job blending Grace and Leon's playstyles into one game.  As for Grace's parts, it was very satisfying when everything started falling into place in the care center, as in figuring out the flow of the place and what solutions worked into each segmented problem/puzzle.  I use "puzzle" loosely because I'm aware there aren't really any classic-style puzzles in this.  But the Grace parts are essentially a puzzle in itself.  Figuring out the routes of each stalker or zombie.  Figuring out who to stealth kill with the Hemolyte injectors, so they don't come back as Blister Heads later... Do you wanna throw a bottle at that maid zombie to aggro that blind guy with a headache to kill the maid zombie?  It's insanely fun.  I still run a toaster for the current day with only a GTX 1660 SUPER and 32Gigs of RAM... Run most settings on Medium, and it still looks gorgeous.  The music in game is typical for the franchise, but there are a few standouts for me.  I love the main menu music and the music you get for the main menu after you beat the game.  It's nice to listen to on loop for ambience.  As well as a certain member berry part Leon wanders in to ... [spoiler]that has little chimes from the Front Hall theme in RE2 mixed with newer age grim synthwave sounds that gave me chills. [/spoiler]   I thought the suspense was wonderfully crafted, and the action was very exciting.  I am so happy I bought this game on a whim.  I'm easily entertained though.  I think this game was trying to have something for everyone.  I'm easily entertained so even if I had to "switch modes" in my brain whenever the game would switch over, I'd still have fun.  If it wasn't for the fact that 5 million (and counting) copies were sold, I'd encourage anyone to play this game.  But I'm sure a good chunk of the 5 million sale are already hardcore RE fans.  I can't say I had any problems with this game.  I absolutely loved it, as an on-again off-again RE fan.  But this game makes me want to explore RE even more.

Grace and Leon each represent a different type of survival horror gameplay, with Grace’s sections harkening back to the classic Resident Evil games with pure survival horror requiring careful resource management, while Leon’s sections focus on the thrilling action horror of Resident Evil 4, RE5, and RE Village. Each playable character gets about half of the game’s worth of playtime (my playthrough was 12 hours, so 6 hours each) and I enjoyed how frequently we get to switch between the two of them.  Grace’s sections are tense, sometimes incredibly frightening, and very cleverly designed. There’s some great puzzles and interesting mechanics related to the environment and enemies in her sections, particularly in the “Basement” section of her portion. I love the aspect of the zombies in her main section retaining their old personalities; this added a lot to the game and even made me feel sorry for the zombies often. Grace also gets access to a new type of crafting system for the series that was interesting but felt a bit underutilized.  Leon’s sections are balls to the wall fun with buckets of blood and gore, but a particular section has a more somber, almost reverent feeling to it…you know the one (hint: it’s on the box art!) that I felt was really special as a story sequence. Leon’s gameplay is an expanded version of that in the RE4 remake, with some really cool new mechanics like axe sharpening, environmental finishers, using enemy weapons against them, and multiple perspective switching with dot sights. I loved Leon’s gameplay so much and I hope we get more of it in future DLC.  The story is fun and typical RE cheese, but it had some really excellent moments in it that stand out amongst the story in the rest of this series. Leon gets a complete character arc at the end of this game which was nice to see; I hope this isn’t his last game in the series!  The ability to play in third or first person for BOTH characters is also an amazing addition. The first person animations in this game are some of the best I’ve ever experienced, and that extends into third person as well. I plan to do 3rd person Grace and 1st person Leon playthrough at some point. Only thing I wish the game had was a quick toggle or hotkey for perspective shifting: having to go into the menu to change perspectives is a bit annoying.  The main critique I have of this title is that the sense of progression the RE games are known for isn’t really here due to the dual protagonist structure. Grace never gets a lot of new items during her sections, mostly having the same things she starts with, and Leon gets a much more stripped down version of the RE4 merchant. You basically get to experience the beginning of a regular RE game with limited ammo and just a pistol as Grace, and then the end of a regular RE game where you’re fully decked out as Leon. There’s nothing wrong with this and it works well, but more traditional campaign progression would be cool to see in any DLC we get.  This is now my third favorite RE game, behind RE4 and RE1.  A must play! Resident Evil Requiem feels like a natural continuation of Resident Evil 7 and Village — and for me, that comes with the same strengths and the same problems.  In Resident Evil 7, Ethan was just a regular civilian, vulnerable and often forced to run. By the time we reached Village, he had already turned into more of an action-oriented character. Requiem follows that exact same path.  On one side, you have Grace — a new character who is genuinely likeable and still unfamiliar with Umbrella-style horror. Her sections feel more tense, uncertain, and closer to what I personally want from a horror game.  On the other side, you have Leon. As expected, he’s cool, experienced, and completely unfazed… but also so battle-hardened that he ends up blasting through waves of enemies without much sense of fear. This shifts the game once again toward action rather than horror.  Even Grace’s sections aren’t free from repetition. The “unstoppable stalker” mechanic returns once again — something the series has already used multiple times with enemies like Mr. X or Nemesis. At this point, it no longer feels fresh, but rather predictable. There was definitely more potential here from a gameplay perspective.  Technically, the game is excellent. The visuals are impressive, and the atmosphere is especially strong in neon-lit city areas or darker interior sections. The sound design supports this very well and helps create some genuinely tense moments.  In the end, Resident Evil Requiem simply doesn’t fully match my personal expectations. It has strong moments and high production quality, but leans too much into action and relies on familiar mechanics instead of evolving them.  This is one of those cases where I’d really prefer a neutral rating option. As it stands, it’s a cautious recommendation — depending heavily on what you expect from a Resident Evil game. Overview Resident Evil Requiem has some really high moments and some weaker ones. The game starts very strong and easily hooks you in during the first few hours. The atmosphere, story buildup, and presentation are excellent. It looks cinematic and the overall mood is great.  The game is split between two characters. You start mostly playing as Grace with a few Leon sections in between, and later the focus shifts more to Leon. Because both characters play very differently, the experience changes a lot throughout the game. Overall I enjoyed it, but some parts are clearly stronger than others.  Gameplay as Grace Grace’s sections are easily the highlight of the game. This is where Resident Evil Requiem feels like classic survival horror.  Resources are limited and enemies feel dangerous, so you constantly have to think about how you approach situations. The areas are tight, the atmosphere is strong, and encounters can be intense.  There is also backtracking and some puzzles along the way. Resident Evil games usually feel their best when you explore areas, unlock new paths, solve puzzles, and manage your resources to survive. Grace’s gameplay captures that feeling very well.  If the entire game was like this, it would easily be a 10/10 survival horror experience. Gameplay as Leon Leon’s gameplay shifts the game toward a more action focused style. In the first half this actually works well. After playing tense survival sections with Grace, Leon’s gameplay feels more relaxed and fun.  However, the later half of the game becomes less interesting. Even though Leon has many weapons and tools, most of them feel optional. You can still handle most situations with just a pistol or rifle.  Enemies also start to feel repetitive, especially during the Raccoon City section. The boss fights are not very memorable and the final part of the game feels a bit flat.  I still enjoyed these sections because Leon is a great character, but they are clearly weaker compared to Grace’s gameplay.  Gameplay in General There are still some great moments in the game. The chainsaw sequence from the trailer is a fun set piece and Grace’s encounters with the large enemies (Girl, Chunk, Chef) are very tense.  The puzzles are decent but not very complex this time. Older Resident Evil games had stronger puzzle design in my opinion.  Combat with Leon is still satisfying. Shooting enemies, performing counters, and finishing them with Leon’s axe feels good.  The game also lets you switch between first person and third person camera perspectives. Grace feels more immersive in first person because it increases the tension, while Leon feels better in third person and gives strong Resident Evil 4 vibes.  Graphics The game looks fantastic and is easily one of the best looking games this year.  https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3674735001  The RE Engine continues to impress with detailed environments and excellent lighting. The game is also well optimized. If you have a strong PC and enable path tracing, the visuals look even better. Even with DLSS the game still looks great.  https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3678100469  https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3674735203  Overall the graphics are excellent.  Pros Excellent survival horror sections with Grace Strong atmosphere and presentation Very good graphics and optimization Some memorable set pieces and encounters Leon is still a fun character to play  Cons Leon sections become weaker in the second half Enemies start to feel repetitive Boss fights are not very memorable Puzzles are simpler compared to older Resident Evil games  Final Thoughts Resident Evil Requiem has both great moments and some weaker ones. The Grace sections deliver an excellent survival horror experience and are easily the best part of the game.  Leon’s gameplay is fun at first but becomes less interesting later in the game with repetitive enemies and weaker boss fights.  Even with those issues, I still enjoyed the game a lot. If the whole game maintained the quality of the Grace sections, it could have been one of the best Resident Evil games. As it stands, it is still a solid and memorable entry in the series.

So here it is, RE9... very anticipated except... meh, I waited a bit, wasn't in a rush to dive in to this... and I mean, with good reason, it's the Resident Evil 6 we all wanted but never got and had to wait 15 years for... turn 9 upside down, get a 6... that's the way I think the developers were looking at it.  After multiple failed RE games and pointless ones to boot, it's a return to form. RE: Requiem blends everything you love about the RE2 and 4 remakes and just mashed them in a blender for your gaming pleasure sensors. I don't get what all the hype was about though because a lot of this game is a copy pasta job... including models and backgrounds etc... I mean it's super familiar and nostalgia bait so if that's the reason for the hype... meh.  I enjoyed the game play because it was familiar at least, it's also one of the most casual RE games ever made, doesn't require as much heavy memorization and there's a lot of moments you can cheese with the right strategy. Best part is, there's no ranking screen after you're finished, so you don't have to feel like you've been sh|t on by the game after going through hell and back, so that was a plus.  All the content is fairly easy to unlock, mostly grinding, and although there isn't a proper NG+, anything you unlock carries over to a brand new game you start. This means you have the option of using overpowered gear and infinite ammo when playing on harder difficulties... of which I would recommend, as they really beefed up the enemy A.I. in this... If you make a mistake, you're toast.  That being said, the Challenge Point distribution in this one is kind of abysmal so make sure you strategize and unlock the good stuff first. You earn the mass majority of your points for beating Insanity mode as well as solving some REALLY insanely cryptic puzzle the dev's threw in, it's actually ridiculous when you read up on how to actually solve it properly.   In the day of computers and data miners, it stayed a secret for about 10 seconds and was then reverse engineered and solved. Unfortunately this isn't the 90's anymore so stuff like this is almost pointless to bother with... it's almost a bit too much at times... like this game is just a triple decker layer of nostalgia, like everything about it is like digging up a time capsule.  The one thing I must say about this game is that it feels like a giant f*** you to the o.g. fans as well as a love letter at the exact same time, so I'm a bit torn honestly... the entire time I played this I was thinking, they're literally telling us to shut up about how great Leon and RE2/4 was and get over it and by doing so, they're literally making us kill off all the past RE villains all over again... I mean heavy spoilers here but this game goes Reservoir Dogs on everything... like they bring everything back just so you can kill it again.  At the end of the day, it's a mid entry. It's safe, which is fine I guess... I was sick of all the side quest crap and dumb new characters like Ethan, his girl friend, their daughter....etc... couldn't stand any of it... the vampires, the were wolves, whatever the f*** they decided to do to change up the formula... Zombies and mutants are Resident Evil, period... not eurotrash fantasy creatures.  If you enjoy the old school RE's like 0 all the way to C:V, as well as the Remakes of 2 & 3, you'll enjoy Grace's gameplay, but of course, RE4 Leon is here with his attaché case so it's full on action mode when playing as him. It breaks up the monotony of being locked in to one style of game play but it can get a bit bipolar when doing a speed run, like it's actually kind of jarring flip flopping back and forth with the different styles.  Without spoiling too much, it takes a bit too much from that RE2 remake and those sections are highly obnoxious to say the least. In the end, it's too little too late really... it's a game that should have been figured out and created over a decade ago. This game is definitely an "everyone wins" style of Resident Evil but in a good way, not in that RE6 kind of way... which was just insanely stupid and lame.  I'd say it's a solid 8/10 for game play, but with kind of a weird retcon plot honestly... The writers were trying to just switch stuff up all of a sudden. It's such a weird departure, considering the content of all of those files at the end of RE: Village, mentioning Spencer and how much of a crackpot and evil person he was... but I guess that's the way it goes in the RE universe.   Anyone can just change the narrative to keep everyone guessing all the time. They could honestly do anything with this story and it wouldn't even matter because everything is so convoluted and contradictory at this point. It's like who even cares really? None of it makes any sense anymore. LOL I give the plot a 5/10 it's pretty weak honestly and just does that whole Saw retcon crap where they insert characters that didn't even exist in to past time lines, it's kind of whack, not going to lie.  Either way, if you enjoy RE2/4, this one's a banger for the style / gameplay. I hope they keep going in this direction and bring back some of the O.G. characters like Claire, Jill and Chris because honestly, I think we get it... Leon is a one man wrecking crew and he's pretty much unkillable at this point... give someone else a chance. Contains spoilers.   Wait for a sale if you absolutely must have this game. Ever since RE6 I haven't paid full price for an RE game because of how disappointing it was, and the positive reviews fooled me into thinking it was worth it this time. It isn't very long, and the second half of the game is especially bad. After the Care Center, it gets worse and worse in terms of gameplay and story intrigue, and it ends up being disappointing at best.  The good: The first half of the game where you primarily play as Grace is okay, and feels a little bit like previous RE games with some resource management, exploration, generally avoiding combat, etc. The scary parts will probably get you the first time. The horror setpieces are pretty good. Graphics and sound are good. On a technical level, this is a good game. Also, you get to kill HUNK, the most overrated "I am a cool guy because I am cool" character in the franchise. That's all I can really think of.  The meh: There are no puzzles to speak of. The challenge: "The Final Puzzle" is really "The Only Puzzle" because everything else you need to figure out is explicitly told to you in a file/note. If you are literate, you can solve everything. There are no environmental puzzles or clues spread across multiple areas. Pick up a note and it will have the combination to open a box you need to progress. Since the original RE4 I actually preferred the shift towards action, but they made the Leon parts of this one so bad that I ended up having more fun as Grace.  The bad: Gameplay: I genuinely don't get why people say you feel more powerful as Leon. Grace is WAY stronger. Early on, Grace gets access to an item that can 1 shot every common enemy in the game and can be crafted with abundant resources, even on Insanity. She also gets the Requiem that can kill multiple enemies with a single shot (line them up in a hallway or something), and her knife attacks do the same damage as Leon's axe at base level. She also gets items that can boost her health to have the same amount as Leon. She can alternatively take 'stabilizers' that make her gun handling BETTER than Leon. For some reason, many enemies won't attack or will delay if they aren't on screen. Combine this with the fact that Grace is intended to be played in first person, and you can pretty safely ignore the majority of enemies by looking at the floor when you need to run by.  Leon, on the other hand, has access to a lot of weapons, and they all feel terrible to use. The axe is useless as an offensive weapon on every difficulty, even when fully upgraded. It doesn't stun common enemies when you hit their head with a 'heavy attack', does pathetic damage, and has a narrow hitbox. It's only good for parrying and finishing stunned enemies. The guns all suck in their own ways. A headshot with a shotgun at close range often doesn't stun or knock enemies away. Machine guns are purely decorative. On standard difficulty a full magazine isn't enough to kill or even stun a single common enemy. The rate of fire for all guns (aside from useless machine guns) is painfully slow, even when upgraded. I don't know who needs to hear this at Capcom, but semi-auto guns can fire as fast as you can pull the trigger. Also, for some reason, there's a ton of camera movement while aiming, but ALSO reticle bloom? Both of these are supposed to simulate shaky hands when aiming. Pick one or the other. Defensively, Leon gets the axe. It has a generous window to parry attacks, and you can block pretty much anything in the game. You better get good at it too, because blister heads can 1 shot kill Leon on Classic difficulty, many attacks knock him down and will lead to unavoidable followup attacks, and they brought back enemies with guns for some reason. Gun enemies in RE have never been fun to fight against and it's more of that in RE9. They can stunlock you to death on standard difficulty. The boss fights are boring. For all but 1 of them you can just run back and forth across the arena, waiting for 'your turn' to attack a weakspot. For the HUNK fight it's basically an extended QTE sequence. You parry his melee attacks and break out of his grapple attacks until you get a prompt to kick him. He parries your melee attacks, and like most enemies, doesn't react to your gunfire. It's literally a worse version of the first Krauser fight in RE4R.  Story: It's trash. It is internally inconsistent, has no meaningful buildup/payoff, and has to retcon previous games to force itself into the overall RE narrative. We get to see Alyssa from Outbreak for about 10 minutes before she's killed off, and her legacy of being involved with Daylight (the first time Capcom showed us a cure for T Virus) is completely ignored. Hilariously, this story culminates with ANOTHER cure to ALL viruses, so I can't wait to see how they undo that in the next RE game(s). The villains are very stupid, as usual for RE. They're peak stupid in RE9. This review is already too long so I'll just give a couple of examples. Victor stalks Grace for her entire life, kidnaps her, and takes all of her stuff, EXCEPT for the giant floppy disk she's carrying, that she just picked up 5 seconds before getting kidnapped. This critically important disk never comes up again until the end of the game. Victor and Zeno had access to other similar disks that had info about Spencer and never thought to check if Grace had one. Then there's Zeno, who injects himself with a decades-old vial of who-knows-what that might or might not work since there are new viruses/mold/plagas discovered since Spencer created it. Also, Victor thinks that curing the worlds most dangerous and unpredictable bioweapons will make the world MORE chaotic? Even for RE villains, these guys are dumb and forgettable.  TLDR: Wait for a sale, watch your favorite YouTuber play it, or just skip this one. While it may be technically impressive, it is not fun to play and I wish I had saved my money.

The survival horror of Grace juxtaposes Leon's high octane action segments so well. The time each character gets is very fair and their narratives intertwine appropriately.   The only gripe I have with the game is Insanity difficulty. I understand that, as the hardest difficulty, it's supposed to be difficult, but playing through Insanity had me incredibly frustrated at times. The large amount of damage taken each time you're hit isn't really that irritating, but enemies essentially become bulletsponges as their stagger resistance is turned up to the MAXIMUM.   Blisterheads are easily the most annoying and dangerous enemy on Insanity because they get a huge speed increase as well as being nearly impossible to stagger if you aren't using the Tac 990 and aiming for legs or centre mass at point blank. Hatchet finishers are the only really reliable way to kill them. It is definitely designed for infinite ammo in mind but there are a few mods out there that rebalance stagger resistance which you can simply download if you don't feel like shooting NERF bullets for several hours.   Suffering through Insanity however was worth it for Infinite RPG, the revenge run afterwards is 10/10 catharsis.

This game series feels like a love letter to fans of the franchise, while also offering an engaging experience for newcomers trying it for the first time.  The story introduces a new character, Grace Ashcroft, as the lead, alongside veteran legend Leon Kennedy as they investigate an old case that begins in Wrenwood and leads to Raccoon City. The narrative is very solid, with a well-balanced pace that never feels too fast or too slow. It’s easy to follow and manages to answer several lingering questions from previous entries. There’s also a strong sense of nostalgia when returning to Raccoon City.  The gameplay itself is divided into two perspectives. Playing as Grace feels very similar to the second and seventh entries, with strong survival horror vibes. Resources are scarce, environments are tight and dark, and since Grace is an analyst rather than a field agent, her gameplay requires patience and precision when dealing with zombies or escaping certain monsters like The Girl, who relentlessly chases her throughout the game.  Leon’s gameplay, on the other hand, feels like an evolution of the fourth entry, but more refined. Despite being older, his strength and abilities are significantly enhanced, from powerful melee attacks to satisfying finishers. The axe weapon stands out, as it can be sharpened repeatedly to become extremely powerful, useful for parrying and executing enemies. His combat feels fresh and polished, especially with the wide variety of weapons available.  In terms of performance, the game runs extremely well. It can be played on high to ultra settings without noticeable FPS drops. Combined with beautiful visual from cityscapes and hospitals to the apocalyptic Raccoon City and laboratories, the game shows a significant graphical improvement over previous entries. Everything feels well balanced between stability and visual quality.  Overall, I really enjoyed this Requiem series, especially as a fan of the franchise. It stands out as one of my favorite entries, perfectly blending survival horror and action into a cohesive experience with excellent pacing. I’ve completed it twice on Insanity difficulty, it's definitely more challenging, but also more rewarding and fun on a second playthrough. One minor drawback is the lack of post-endgame content. After finishing the game, there’s little to do, no New Game+ or Mercenaries mode, which feels like a missed opportunity considering Leon’s fluid and action heavy gameplay. Hopefully, this will be added in future updates by Capcom. Aside from that, I’m really looking forward to the DLC, as it could expand the story and address some remaining plot holes.

After my first finish of the story I didn't LOVE it. There were great moments certainly and some were ultra exciting and felt like it was leading to something amazing. I don't know why I was so hyped up and my anticipation of the story was so high, but it ended up being a big subversion of expectations, and at first I was far more confused than when I started off (but after 4 extra playthroughs it's a lot more sensible to me now)  The way the story was told wasn't fantastic in some points and were more confusing than they needed to be, like [spoiler] when Zeno was telling Grace she was created (we later find out Zeno had the wrong info and Grace was just some random Ozwell picked up as his last minute redemption), the computer is scrolling through pictures of little girls who were made from Grace's child DNA. Then, we get to play a section where we play as one of those girls at Raccoon Orphanage. Except that orphanage was destroyed after the events of RE2 or something right? 1998? So instead we are playing as some girl called Chloe and all the little evil girls who look the same are just some other clones of someone else? Because it definitely isn't Grace since she was born like 2003 or something like that. [/spoiler] and a lot of people went into that feeling very confused by it. You can't just say "hey it's like this" then we play a section of the game directly after that cutscene explaining things. Obviously people are going to think they are connected right? But then if you know anything about the dates it's like "what? why are they saying this? that makes no sense?" then it's like wtf am I even doing here then. That whole section felt like a waste of time to me and honestly could have been an email or done way better idk.  But I'll admit there are a few RE games I still haven't played yet and Mr Spencer and Alyssa were characters I didn't even know about lol. So I watched a few videos explaining some stuff and it made a lot more sense after that lol. Bit of a skill issue on my end ig. After doing some reading I appreciated it a lot more in my second run and I don't mind the subversion of expectations AS much.  I still hold onto that I was looking for something exciting at the end of the story and there just wasn't anything. I don't feel like there was any great revelations, just setup for another game. [spoiler] Wasn't it so whatever when we find out at the end of the game that Elpis is like the be all end all of all viruses but then it's destroyed and Grace reports that it's highly unlikely anything can be salvaged? Maybe her opinion is not reliable and perhaps it can be recovered, but I don't see how Elpis can narratively exist more in an RE game where it's literally all about the varus and it's devastating effects. It's interesting but it's too powerful anyway. [/spoiler]  I am new to the RE games and maybe I expected too much! But when I played RE2, RE7, RE4, they all had narratives that could be followed pretty well. Maybe that's just because RE7 is a different cast of characters, RE2 is Leon's story beginning (idk if he's in earlier games but it reads like this to me) and RE4 is a continuation of Leon's story. I'm in the middle of playing RE6 so hopefully a lot more will make sense haha.  As for the gameplay itself, the care center is hands down the BEST part of this game in my opinion. It's classic RE2 horror vibes and it's so fun! I like the idea that the zombies retain a bit of their memory and it makes them more interesting to see in the environment. The care center felt like it had the most attention put into it and I enjoyed both Grace & Leon's playthrough of the center.  But like a lot of people, returning to Raccoon city was very ehh. At first I really liked exploring the ruins, I liked the zombie variations but it really was a drag to get through and just went on and on. Over that time seeing the same old bland environment gets really old really fast. It definitely felt like the Raccoon section didn't have as much care put into it like Grace and the care center did. On my first playthrough I thought Raccoon section added some neat environmental mechanics that had points of interest, but they were far and few between compared to Grace's. Even when you speedrun the Raccoon city section it's still a drag lol.  I did enjoy unlocking all the achievements and having an infinite ammo run where you just get wreck everyone with Requiem. I have to admit, Leon's whole parrying mechanic took me SO long to get used to and sometimes was confusing for controlling but again, you get used to it anyway. And you have to learn to use it well if you plan on [spoiler] fighting Gideon on insanity, that fight took me so long and I had to use Mortal REminder or w/e it's called. It is pretty hilarious to me that Leon can parry an rpg rocket and cars that T501 (w/e it's called) can chuck at you. [/spoiler]  I appreciate that they juggled Grace's horror sections and Leon's action man moments. I personally liked it, felt nice to have a breather inbetween the tense areas and get a chance to have that power fantasy. It was something new and I always appreciate when games try new things and it was interesting to me. I don't think it was as catastrophic as some people make it out to be lol.   tl;dr maybe play a few more of the RE games before this one if you care about story, gameplay is pretty fun and interesting though so if you just care about that then play anyway

Resident Evil: Requiem – Review Resident Evil 9 is a difficult game to assess honestly. It's polished, atmospheric, and confidently made—but it's also a Frankenstein's monster stitched together from Resident Evil 2, 3, and 4 in ways both subtle and impossible to ignore. The Nostalgia Problem The early hours feel lifted directly from Resident Evil 2. The puzzle-to-unlock-door structure is a series staple, sure, but the facility layout, the pacing, the rhythm of progression—it all felt eerily familiar rather than inspired by what came before. Then Mr. X shows up. And the Lickers. And the Plagas-infected dogs from RE4. Nostalgia has its place, but at a certain point, callbacks stop feeling like homage and start feeling like a lack of imagination. It doesn't stop there. The villain, Zeno, is Wesker with a different name. Same lines, same bullet-dodging theatrics, same swagger, same stylish outfit, same mandatory shades. The game ends with a Nemesis fight structured almost identically to Resident Evil 3's finale—minus Jill's plasma cannon. Throughout the campaign, Leon is infected again, just like RE4, and once again guided via comms by a woman in an unseen facility tracking his movements. This time it's Sherry filling that role, though nothing in the plot would meaningfully change if she weren't there—same as the forgettable support character from 4 who was never seen again. The originality is hard to find when every major beat reminds you of something the series already did. What Actually Works: Grace The game's saving grace—literally—is Grace herself. The new female protagonist carries the experience in ways the recycled elements can't. Even accounting for the "older woman protects little girl" dynamic lifted from Claire and Sherry in RE2, Grace's arc feels genuinely fresh. She's relatable in a way Resident Evil protagonists rarely are: utterly terrified, stumbling and running in the early hours, visibly struggling to cope with the nightmare she's been dropped into. Watching her slowly find her footing and grow into someone capable of surviving felt earned rather than assumed. The game wisely gives her substantial screen time—arguably a 50/50 split with Leon, with Grace dominating the early campaign. She's the element that feels like it belongs to this game rather than borrowed from its predecessors. Atmosphere & Execution Despite my complaints, the game still feels good. The action-movie energy is intact, the tension lands when it needs to, and the production values are exactly what you'd expect from a modern Resident Evil title. It's a well-made experience from start to finish. It's just a movie you've already seen. Verdict Here's my dilemma: I enjoyed Requiem because I loved 2, 3, and 4—not because it stands on its own merits. The gameplay is solid, Grace is a genuine highlight, and the atmosphere delivers. But the over-reliance on recycled villains, enemy types, plot structures, and character dynamics makes it difficult to celebrate what's here without acknowledging how much of it was already done elsewhere. A good Resident Evil game. A questionable new Resident Evil game. Rating: 8/10 (reluctantly) – Carried by legacy and one standout protagonist.

My 2 Cents (Casual Gamer)  This game is amazing. The graphics look great and I did not encounter a single glitch. The (NPC) enemies played their roles well. Most of them have a reason for being in their respective locations and don't really feel like just target practice when you find a cool new gun. Most NPC enemies actually contribute to the story and horror experience with their classic and unique designs.  The game really shines with its fantastic job of keeping a balance between a FPS horror experience (Grace) and a third person shooter experience (Leon).  The game mechanics are easy to learn and the main storyline is not overly complicated to understand (for new players). The variety of weaponry across the game is refreshing. The game provides weapons suitable to the environment you are in, not too weak and not too strong, to avoid frustration with the enemies or blasting your way through the entire game.  The game does have a few jump scares but none of them feel cheap. The horror aspect is unnerving, unsettling and disturbing. After playing Resident Evil 9, I honestly came away feeling very disappointed.  What frustrates me most isn’t simply that the game is difficult—it’s that the difficulty often feels unreasonable and poorly justified. A lot of the time, I genuinely have no idea what the game expects me to do, and it ends up feeling less like a challenge and more like punishment.  The biggest issue is the terrible resource balance. I already did everything I could to conserve ammo—avoiding unnecessary fights, taking the safest routes, and only shooting when absolutely needed—yet I still kept running into severe ammo shortages.  What makes it even worse is that some enemies regenerate after being taken down, which makes every bullet spent feel almost wasted. When enemies can come back but the game doesn’t provide enough supplies to deal with them, it creates situations where progression feels nearly impossible.  The survivability balance also feels off. Even at full health, with the coin upgrade that increases max HP, I can still only survive about two hits from certain enemies. That level of punishment leaves almost no room for mistakes.  As a result, the gameplay loop often turns into this: 	•	enter an area 	•	die 	•	reload 	•	repeat the whole section 	•	die again 	•	reload again  Over and over.  After a while, it genuinely stops feeling like I’m playing the game and starts feeling like the game is playing me. Being trapped in the same area, repeating the same sequence, and still being unable to progress because of enemy strength and lack of resources becomes exhausting.  I personally love Soulslike games and have thousands of hours in that genre, so I’m not someone who dislikes difficulty. But the problem here is not that it’s hard—it’s that the difficulty curve and overall balance feel poorly designed.  In Souls games, when you die, you usually understand why: 	•	bad positioning 	•	greedy attacks 	•	poor timing 	•	wrong decision-making  There’s always something to learn and improve.  Here, it often feels more like:  you didn’t lose because of your skill, you lost because the system never gave you a reasonable solution in the first place.  That’s what turns frustration into disappointment.  In my opinion, this game doesn’t really satisfy old-school fans who enjoy classic survival horror resource management, nor is it particularly friendly to newer action-oriented players.  If you’re mentally prepared to be stuck in the same area repeatedly, constantly reloading saves, and feeling like the game is intentionally messing with you, then I’d still recommend giving it a try.  But for me, this experience felt less like enjoying a challenge and more like being punished by the game.

Capcom has achieved something remarkable with Resident Evil Requiem. By combining the high energy action of Resident Evil 4, the acclaimed Resident Evil 4 Remake, and Resident Evil Village with the intense horror roots of Resident Evil HD Remaster, Resident Evil 2 Remake, and Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, they’ve crafted something truly special. This game feels like the culmination of everything the franchise has been building toward.  The classic horror elements are back in full force. Paired with outstanding voice acting from Angela Sant’Albano as our new, anxious protagonist, Grace Ashcroft, the experience feels incredibly vulnerable. For perhaps the first time in a long while, I genuinely felt uncertain about the protagonist’s chance of survival. Grace is fragile and scared. That sense of uncertainty stays with you as you move through every corridor of the Rhodes Hill Care Centre, which is one of the most memorable settings in the Resident Evil series.  What makes the game stand out even more is how it mixes horror with the series’ signature zaniness. The supporting cast walks that Resident Evil line perfectly. They are eccentric, intense, and sometimes absurd, but each character feels unique and fits well in this universe.  My only real complaint is the multiple choice endings. While the idea is exciting, they don’t feel as developed as they could have been. Still, this is a small issue in an otherwise outstanding game.  I genuinely love this game and this franchise. I could talk about it forever, but I’ll stop here, at least until the DLC arrives.  Thank you, Capcom. You’ve proven yourselves once again.   We’re truly back.

I just finished Requiem two days ago and here’s my honest review on it.  I’ve been trying to avoid any spoilers for 2 weeks because I genuinely wanted to enjoy the game as a first time player, every reaction would be genuine because I love playing any new game like that, especially a Resident Evil game because it’s one of my favourite series.  I absolutely loved the first half of the game with Grace, the clinic really captures that survival horror aspect that I love. Puzzles were simple but good. There were some things I didn’t like but they were just minor unimportant things that didn’t affect the gameplay at all. One thing that bugged me was that when Grace saw the third puzzle was in braille and she had to go get Emily to read it for her. In reality, she literally could’ve brute forced it within 6 attempts because there are only 6 possible combinations, and then she could’ve just gotten Emily after. So because Capcom went this route, that was the only reason the basement even exists as part of the game, when they could’ve just made it in a different and more logical way. Also I feel like the only existence of Emily was to just get an emotional reaction out of the player for thinking they killed a child, but then at the end the game is like “psyche! Emily isn’t dead, her vital organs weren’t shot”. I mean sure… why not!?  As for Leon’s gameplay, it was fun to an extent. It’s satisfying to melee the zombies and to rip their heads off with the axe, but I feel like the only reason they gave Leon an axe in the game is for that specific reason, because let’s just face it, you can’t rip off a zombie head with a knife in a satisfying way even though Leon has used a knife throughout his entire life. Also Hunk is just wielding an axe too cause why not? But we’ll get to him later.  I would also like to mention that being able to parry almost EVERYTHING in the game is absolutely bonkers (including the mortars in the raccoon city section). I’ve never liked the parrying mechanic in any RE game because it’s a fail safe method for people who play too aggressive. You can make 1 million mistakes but you just have to parry and you’ll be okay, there is no punishment for playing sloppy. Capcom should’ve at least reduced the amount of times you can parry so you cannot rely on saving yourself all the time.  The storyline itself was too boring and they made it in a way so they have a reason to include a Wesker clone and other enemies/characters from previous games as fan service.  Spencer basically has an epiphany at the end and is like “oh what I did was wrong, I want to save lives now cause I’m an old man”, I mean if that’s the route they want to go for, sure, but I’m not a big fan of it.  The second half of the game was where it really dipped in quality. They just did a fan service fest the whole time, they introduce the Tyrant for 5 minutes because why not, and then conveniently, there was a bomb he was holding and Leon blew it up JUST so there is a reason he can turn into Super Tyrant and almost 60 year old Leon just casually kills him within 10 minutes like he is some sort of roadblock… you cannot tell me they didn’t put the tyrant in the game, just for nostalgia and shock value.  Same with Hunk, he comes in outta nowhere (just like Tyrant), and he gets killed within 5 minutes of meeting him. That has to be a joke right? Killing off a character like Hunk in an anticlimactic way and in such a short amount of time is blasphemy.  The only original bosses they put in the game are Marie the Girl (barely a boss at all), The huge spider (I mean it’s a spider, arachnophobia is cool) and Plant 43 (I mean it’s just a stupid plant), every other boss was just a reskin of previous bosses from past games. The final boss Victor is a reskin of final boss Wesker from RE5 and final boss Nemesis from RE3R. You seriously cannot tell me that they didn't make the storyline in their favour just to lazily add all these bosses, just so they conveniently have a reason to exist and to be there.  TLDR; In summary, game is very mediocre and I’ll give it a 5/10, very best I can give is a 6/10. Requiem is sacriligious to the entire franchise, I regret purchasing the game.  Thank you.

The first half of the story in particular made me very excited while playing the game. However, after certain major events, the story started to become mediocre. I didn't enjoy the parts where I played as Leon very much; I think I had difficulty getting into Leon's atmosphere after Grace's gameplay style and story. While Grace was more serious, with dominant horror and survival themes, playing as Leon felt more like playing an action-thriller game.   The game’s disjointed feel stems from Capcom’s attempt to merge two clashing gameplay styles perhaps a late stage decision to appease fans. I think they got cold feet middle of developing the game. I don’t want to spoil the story but Grace and her little companion should have had more meaningful time together. Since the director decided what was going to happen to the character, they should have been able to convince the player of that decision better at the end of the game.  ( [spoiler] Like, if you decide to kill Emily, kill her. If she's gonna magically come back to life, then do it in a more realistic way. Convince me [/spoiler])  The characters develop very quickly in the game, so you don't feel too disadvantaged against new zombies from the beginning But most of the things I disliked in the game stemmed from the Leon route. First of all, you don't need to organize your inventory like in other games because Leon's inventory is like a Black Hole. In "Parry," you don't need to time your attacks. The game usually forgives you no matter how early  press the keys. This killed the sense of challenge in the game for me. There weren't enough boss fights. Also, the boss fights were very easy. I really liked Leon's battle ots, but that also made me realize that the save room music didn't stick in my memory I think the reason the game felt rushed and lacked certain aspects was their attempt to integrate two different gameplay styles into a single game. I even think it was a last-minute decision. It seems like Capcom didn't want to take certain risks at the last minute and included Leon in the project. This led to cut corners: Grace and other pivotal early-game characters were sidelined abruptly, their arcs left unresolved.  Thank you Fungy for gifting me Requiem as a birthday gift <3 <3 <3

I never thought I would see the day we get an RE game better than RE4 remake, but we have been blessed. Resident Evil Requiem is a loving tribute to the entire Resident Evil franchise, even making nods to the less than stellar films and generally, could be the perfect ending note if they truly wanted it to be such.   This is a Resident Evil completely involved in its own identity. There is a part where a zombie without lungs and heart, is completely immobilized until you place artificial organs in it. This is one of several references to the original Day of the Dead, by George A Romero. In the films, the zombies, even without functional organs like a stomach, still operate out of motorized instinct and are eating out of primal programming, rather than any actual desire to. The fact they spread the infection the way they do is simply coincidental and an evolution of this behavior.   In Requiem, the developers firmly state they have left the George A Romero zombie behind, by showing their zombies are fundamentally different. And yet, they also embrace the most contentious part of Day of the Dead, the intelligent zombie with memories of its past. The new T-Virus zombies and in a bit of revisionism, even Raccoon City zeds, all operate with far more articulation and reasoning and personality. The zombies are closer to something from Evil Dead now and honestly, this is a great direction.   Resident Evil Requiem embraces its own genre perfectly. There is something for everyone here. Grace's sections are intense and harken back to original Resident Evils and the RE2 remake, with one of the best locations in the franchise's history since the Raccoon City Police Department. As well as nods to RE1 remake even. And yet, there are still numerous music notes to various games from the franchise, including the original RE2. Most surprisingly, there is a direct, loving nod to the cult classic Operation Raccoon City and with more than just a familiar music sting. And of course, Hunk is in the game and has everyone losing their minds.   But Leon steals the show. Leon is surely and truly, THE protagonist of Resident Evil and the game finally gives him the respect he deserves. Leon is second to no one, narratively or in combat, besides maybe Chris Redfield himself. The game is fan service done right in every way. Those that enjoyed the tense, first person horror of 7, those who enjoys the weighty action of RE4, complete with the gore and damage retention of RE2 and a more proper Nemesis-type tyrant fight, for those disappointed in what we got from RE3 remake.   Love. This game is so full of love for Resident Evil and while the Grace sections will make some replays and speedruns less enjoyable, they still have a lot of value. I actually really enjoy Grace as a character and the plot reveals tying everything together into a near perfect end for the main plot's loose ends, actually works well. All of these plot hooks are invented retcons, but who cares, it tells a great story and provides an even better adventure.   There is something for every RE fan here and the overwhelmingly positive reception is deserved. This game premiered with 660,000 concurrent players on steam, beating out DOTA and only being below Counter Strike in its early days of release. This is incredible and it shows that this game does not just having staying power, it has stopping power. No one will doubt the crown of Capcom's flagship horror franchise ever again.   For those who were bored of the faceless Ethan games, Grace is far more of a character and has far more tension. But you still have some experiences of being completely bad ass with her, once you get competent at the new mechanics. This game feels decently innovative and just gorgeously fun.   The RE engine, unlike Village, here is completely in full form. Great hair physics, the ray tracing is profoundly impacting, the HDR looked incredible on a 77 inch 4k television and the best part above all, the damage retention gore is as good as it has been since RE2 remake with only some exceptions to the enemy physics. But all of this is done for optimization sake and you getting swarmed by dusty old, mummified zombies in the ruins of Raccoon City is fantastic.   The game has great set pieces, surprisingly good pacing and it delivers narratively, all while having one of the best soundtracks, especially for Leon.   Resident Evil is what AAA games should aspire to be.
