After playing through the entire game, I can confidently say Biohazard 9, known to us unclean westerners as Resident Evil Requiem, is a fun game, but not a good one. It's almost as bad as RE7 and 8, which were already overhyped rubbish. And yes, I had fun with all three, but a game being fun doesn't automatically mean it's good.   The story is glued together with snot and nursery stickers. Capcom wanted so many cool moments to get people talking about it, but didn't put the work in to earn any of them, or make any of it make sense, or be good in any capacity. And no, the franchise having over-the-top goofy moments here and there in the past aren't an excuse for lazy and outright bad writing. For example.  -Why did the FBI think it was okay to send Grace, a desk agent whose mother (Outbreak protagonist Alyssa Ashcroft) was murdered, to investigate a string of murders at the same hotel Alyssa was murdered, with no back-up or no combat-trained partner to keep things from going awry? She's not a field agent, and her PTSD would put her in grave danger.  -If Grace is important to the villains' plans, why do said villains routinely put her in danger? -Why does Leon just stand there and gawk when Victor goes on a virus-needle shooting spree instead of at least TRYING to stop him before more innocents are killed, or at the very least, neutralise the infected BEFORE they bite and murder others?  -Why does Grace agree to go with the two people directly responsible for Alyssa's death and Emily's mutation? And why doesn't Leon stop her there and then?? -What the hell was the point of Zeno being in this story at all, if we're never gonna fight him? If he'll just unceremoniously get killed off in a cutscene. Was he just there to shill the next game and foreshadow The Connections villain group? -Why so many retcons? Seriously, they only make the story worse. It's bad enough that this game acknowledges RE2 Remake in flashbacks, despite said remake having an objectively worse story than the original RE2's Claire A, Leon B scenario that was canon for years (with less plotholes than the remake, might I add), but they retconned the central overarching antagonist of the entire franchise, Ozwell E. Spencer, to be a flawed human, instead of the megalomaniacal mastermind behind Umbrella, AKA the pharmaceutical company he used as a front to fund his military ambitions and develop the progenitor virus into a miracle drug of immortality. The one who was supposed to be the final boss of RE4, before Capcom scrapped the idea due to the Gamecube's hardware limitations preventing them from achieving their big ideas. The Spencer that had one of his co-founders assassinated when they became a liability for him.   On top of all that, the game continues to have audio bugs a month later, with music randomly cutting out, and a 50-50 chance of the cutscenes freezing for a second and the audio desyncing when it resumes. Got to love the fact that Capcom thought it was okay to still charge £60 for this version of the game in is current state, a whole month after its release.   Oh, and since I beat the game, I have to ask... Where the hell are my extra game modes?? Where's Mercenaries? Where's Battle Games? Where's anything? Extra game modes used to be a staple of the franchise as far back as the PS1 trilogy, and yet Capcom with their AAA budget, resources and manpower can't seem to manage the bare minimum anymore?? Are you serious right now? £60 for a stripped-down version at launch that MAY have paid DLC later down the line if we're lucky, and a Gold Edition to punish all the early adopters and rub it in their faces when everyone else buying it for the first time later gets everything the base game should've been at a reduced price. Wow.  Oh, and even though a second playthrough carries SOME things over, but not the weapons you collected during your first playthrough (AKA, NG+, a basic feature from RE4, 5, 6, the Revelations games and 8), I hope you didn't make the mistake of sticking with your handgun as Leon, expecting to get the shotgun during the fat man bossfight in the attic, otherwise you're potentially screwed and softlocked out of your progress unless you sell your handgun and all of its ammo for the vague hope of affording the Shotgun. Good game design there, Capcom!  And on top of a painfully-slow run speed that's nigh indistinguishable from the default walking speed, the game still has unskippable scripted segments and walking sections, severely hurting its replay value and making subsequent playthroughs a chore. When is this mentally-handicapped industry and its bottom-rung shills going to realise these segments aren't fun, and aren't a good use of games as a medium? Enough is enough. I don't want DMC6 if it means Capcom will shoehorn these parts into a game you're supposed to replay regularly. No monkey's paw wishes for me anymore.   Some puzzles make no sense when you think about them logically, and compare them to Mikami's RE games, like the organ transplant one. Why not just remove the bracelet manually from the corpse's wrist, or cut the arm off and slide the bracelet off that way? Anything's better than reassembling the corpse so it can awaken and attack you as a zombie, forcing you to kill it and THEN pry the bracelet off its corpse.   Here's everything the game got right: +Graphics are good, though there should be an option to turn the garish filmgrain off since it doesn't add to the horror.  +The core gameplay is fun, even if there are little annoyances that add up throughout. Leon and Grace's segments are fun in their own right, but neither are the best example of their respective subgenres, nor are they greater than the sum of their parts. If one got full focus instead of the other, I believe we'd have a much better game.  +The Requiem revolver kicks arse, and is a perfect way to empower the player while letting them consider carefully when to use its limited yet devastating ammo. Magnums aren't new to RE, but this one's the magnum to end all others.  +There are some genuinely great surprise bossfights during the latter half of the game, including a mysterious character who may or may not be a returning icon, and certain enemy types feel like a no-brainer, which we probably should've seen earlier in the franchise (and would have, if Capcom ever went back to the RE4 castle build idea).   That's about it. It's better than RE7 and 8, but not by much, and I'd honestly consider this modern trilogy to be a regression for the franchise, rather than the "revival" the fanbase touts it as. All 7 did was bring the series back to survival-horror, at the cost of good storytelling, good gameflow and replay value. RE6 might've been action-focused, but at least its gameplay is still great on its own merits (barring the unskippable ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ it introduced), and the story's rock-solid compared to the sloppy mess of the past three mainline games.   I have a hard time recommending RE9 to any fans on the fence, let alone newcomers. It's not worth its £60 asking price, it's not worth £50, and I even hesistate to recommend it at the £40 second-hand bargain I got it for, because I've played so many better games at that price and less. Especially in its current state without a fix for the audio problems. So don't buy into the honeymoon-period hype and recency bias. Wait for a sale if you must, but don't expect a GOTY contender here. And this is coming from a fan of 21 years, since RE4 on Gamecube, whose also played prior mainline games from 0 and 1 to Code Veronica. I'm not lying when I say RE5 and 6 gave me much more enjoyment and fulfillment all these years later than the entire trilogy of 7, 8 and 9 combined. Biohazard isn't dead, but it's severely compromised, and its recent success and fanbase's blind loyalty will ensure Capcom never address the franchise's most glaring issues.

TL;DR: An excelent experience with just enough flaws to make it interesting. Well worth the price.  This will be a critical endorsement of the game, and thus it will be focused on how the game fails. If you are unconvinced of the merits of it, understand that this game gripped me for about 60 hours before I exhausted it.   This is what a game ought to be, from a consumer's perspective. No Season Pass, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You buy the game and get a complete experience.  And that first experience is amazing. It is akin to a rollercoaster, with precisely timed sections of terror and action that gather and release tension. If you get in the mood, the game is genuinely terrifying and tense. And combat is fun and rewarding.  Grace's gameplay focuses on the horror of Survival Horror. Limited resources, dangerous enemies and genuine terror (so long as you get in character. Otherwise it is just pixels on a screen). Her sections are amazing on a first playthrough.  Leon's sections are a release of the tension. You are a far more capable character and you will indulge in a much more aggressive playstyle. The combat is rythmic and satysfiing once you get it.  Everything else? Excellent. Production values, art direction, narrative, voice acting. Truly excellent.  So why do I say that I am critical of this game?  Because you are getting two experiences that are somewhat short and incomplete. You will be left wanting more of Grace and more of Leon. Both sections could've been their own expanded games, and you are getting two experiences that are 85% complete. Leon needs more combat sections and more enemy variety. Grace's sections need to be longer and maybe a bit more challenging.  But this is a compromise. Capcom's resources are limited. This is an experiment on their part and thus it will have some flaws.  But two 85% experiences still leave you with 60% more experience for the price.  Beside this, the only serious issue is the replayability. Some experiences lose their appeal after you've played through them the first time. It is like going through a Haunted House a second time, knowing what comes next.  But that first playthrough? That tension you feel just by moving forward knowing you'll have to face danger to advance? ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ amazing. Going blind through that is just about the best experiences I've had in years.  Well worth the price. The hype is real.

Overall the game took approximately 30 hours to complete the achievements 100%.  + You may switch between first person view and third person view at any time. I played both characters in first person view, even Leon Kennedy, despite the game recommending you to play his character in 3rd person view. The game is highly immersive. + There are many different environments to explore in this game, and they are all gorgeous. Whether you are looking at the wood grain on a railing right in front of you, or looking off hundreds of miles into the distance, everything in this game is super polished. It is evident many hours were spent fine tuning the environments in this game. + For me the game was extremely optimised. The game looked amazing on my computer. I was surprised how polished and smooth everything was. The game feels a bit "next gen" at times. I ran into zero bugs during my 30 hours playtime. No screen tearing, no hiccups, everything smooth as butter. + The sound design is perfect. From monsters walking on floorboards above you, chains rattling, zombies grunting, different kinds of footsteps pattering around, everything is fine tuned to perfection. The voice acting is professionally done and sounds exceptional. + All the enemy character models are stunning. Certain boss characters are extremely well designed. Zombie animations are super life like in the way they move around. The first time I ran into the female singing zombies I got goosebumps. The crawling lickers never looked better. + Many fun unlockables to play around with for beating the game under certain conditions. + Usually I do not enjoy stealth games, but the stealth sections in this game are fine tuned perfectly, and they are tense and scary. + Buckets of blood and gore. Admiring your blood splatterwork all over the walls after shooting up a bunch of zombies is always satisfying.  +/- The whole blood crafting mechanic was not needed, and didn't really make sense. Once again, Capcom proves to the world, that the Resident Evil franchise is one of the best in gaming history. They don't miss with their games, except maybe with RE 3 remake (I still liked it, but it's probably their weakest).   I remember playing RE 1 for PS 1 in a video store when it first came out. I was bad at video games and could just play the first zombie encounter and died over and over again, but the game burned itself into my memory. I'm just so happy to see that Capcom still gives RE so much love and that they still have tremendous success with it.  Now, let's wrap this up and rate the game:  [h3] Graphics: 9.8/10 [/h3] Played on max settings with full path tracing + DLSS Balance (Preset K all the way!) + Frame Gen 2x on a 4070 TI Super. I had constant 90 fps and minimal input lag (Mouse & Keyboard).  The game looks stunning. The only reason I didn't give it a 10, is because I encountered some bubbling/noise with Path Tracing shadows + some flickering artifacts in the first scenes. And sometimes the shadow in open areas looked very very soft.  Oh, and the noise in this game is insane. I don't know why they don't make this an option to disable. They had that in previous games, I don't know why they don't have this in a game coming out in 2026.  [h3] Gameplay: 8/10 [/h3] Leon's part is like RE 4 remake and RE 8. It's all about actually killing enemies. The weapon arsenal is less than previous games, also the upgrades you can obtain are quite easy to get. I maxxed out all my weapons.  I saw that there are more weapons for second playthroughs, but I wished, they would have put them into the game right away. The parry/blocking is great, but normal zombies are exceptionally hard to master :D  RE 2 (+remake) were my favourite REs until I played RE 7. RE 7 is still  my favourite RE to date, so Grace's parts were my absolute favourite thing about the game.  They really did a good mixture of both worlds and combined the strengthes of the previous RE games. Also, I would still love a 100% Grace styled RE over anything else.  [h3] Story: 8/10 [/h3] I love that they still connect everything and that RE is actually not just standalone games, but have a common background story that connects to each game. I think they do a great job at expanding the RE-verse and I'm looking forward to further stories. Maybe some Chris Redfield games next :) Maybe something related to RE 8, who knows.  The core of the stories is not THAT crazy, but they all are solid, the writing is good and seeing the games in context of the RE-verse and how long this franchise is alive, just makes it a solid 8/10 for me.  [h3] Sound: 9/10 [/h3] Grace has a great voice actress, but in the end, imho Grace's nervousness was a bit too present. Other than that, the game sounded awesome. Great sounds when shooting zombies, crazy good atmosphere and especially some mobs scared the s**t out of me when I first heared them.  [h3] Final verdict: 8.7/10 [/h3]

Resident Evil Requiem is a triumphant return to everything that made the franchise legendary while still pushing the series into bold new territory. Capcom has managed to strike an impressive balance between psychological horror, cinematic storytelling, and pulse-pounding action, creating one of the most immersive entries the series has seen in years.  The atmosphere is absolutely phenomenal. Returning to the ruins of Raccoon City feels haunting, emotional, and terrifying all at once. The game’s upgraded RE Engine delivers stunning visual detail, from realistic lighting to unsettling facial animations that make every encounter feel disturbingly real. The environments are dripping with tension, and the sound design constantly keeps players on edge.  One of the game’s biggest strengths is its dual-protagonist structure. Grace Ashcroft brings vulnerability and investigative suspense, while Leon Kennedy delivers the classic action-heavy gameplay longtime fans love. The contrast between their playstyles keeps the pacing fresh and exciting throughout the campaign. The ability to seamlessly switch between first-person and third-person perspectives also gives players more control over how they experience the horror.  The enemies are another standout feature. Capcom clearly put enormous effort into reinventing zombies so they feel threatening again. Their unpredictable behavior makes encounters genuinely stressful, especially during the early sections of the game. Instead of simply running at the player, some infected display eerie remnants of human behavior, adding a deeply unsettling layer to the horror experience.  What truly elevates Resident Evil Requiem is how confidently it embraces both old-school survival horror and modern blockbuster presentation. The game respects the franchise’s roots while still feeling ambitious and fresh. Longtime fans will appreciate the callbacks and atmosphere, while newcomers can jump in and enjoy an accessible but intense horror experience. Community reactions have also been overwhelmingly enthusiastic, with many players praising the game’s immersion, storytelling, and next-generation presentation.  Capcom didn’t just make another sequel — they crafted a love letter to the entire Resident Evil legacy. Capcom delivered a horror experience that is terrifying, cinematic, emotional, and incredibly polished. For many fans, Resident Evil Requiem feels like a defining chapter in the franchise and one of the strongest survival horror games of this generation.

[i]Resident Evil Requiem[/i] is another awesome Resident Evil game, following the trend of recent years. With requiem, it's extremely easy to draw parallels to other Resident Evil games; Grace's sections are extremely similar to [i]Resident Evil 2[/i] remake, while Leon's are a cathartic release much more similar to [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] remake. With that level of variety, it almost feels like [i]Resident Evil Village[/i], but with a story, characters, and performances that are far more engaging to the the longtime RE fan than Ethan Winters was.   Keeping this as spoiler free as possible, the initial main gameplay hub where you primarily control Grace, is one of the best Resident Evil locations ever. Having the zombies maintain aspects of their jobs and routines creates areas where every single enemy feels like a dangerous puzzle to attack or manipulate. When I first played [i]Resident Evil 2[/i] I remember how I had to shift my approach if there was a licker in the room, or Mr. X was nearby; here it feels like nearly every zombie has a unique trait that forces you to adapt in some way. The small inventory and first person view add to the horror of the situation, and each upgrade feels like a significant tool. Simply put, this is one of the best levels I've ever experienced in a video game, it's complex, full of character, detailed, and beautiful; on top of that, the game runs excellently in this area.   The second level is far more open and bland in its design. While it's not uninteresting, it's lacking the intense attention to detail that the first level had. This section's combat is more action oriented which is refreshing for awhile, and every now and then a new element is introduced adding a new level of depth to encounters. I didn't enjoy this area as much, the biggest reason for that was the performance. While my PC is a little older now, the first area ran smoothly at high FPS on high graphics, in this area I put my graphics on minimum and still had a choppy sub-60 FPS most of the time, which made the more twitchy action oriented combat in this section much less enjoyable.   The final few levels of the game are shorter, and have a good balance between what worked prior to that point in the game. While there is less enemy variety, new challenges are presented, and every few minutes there are incredible set pieces, often packed with fan service, nostalgia, and references to prior games. While the story comes to an interesting and entertaining ending, it's a classic Resident Evil story in the sense that much of what happens doesn't make any sense, and multiple scenes throughout the game feel out of character for the protagonists, and are clearly meant to move the story in the direction they wanted vs. being grounded in the moment. All across [i]Resident Evil Requiem[/i] you can see the signs of scrapped ideas, or different directions Capcom was considering with this title, but ultimately they tied everything together well enough, making another entry that's on par with the quality of the recent remakes and Village, while pushing the series forward in significant ways with improved enemy and level design. If you're already a Resident Evil fan, then this is a must-play, for first timers, I would start with [i]Resident Evil 2[/i] at minimum, before considering Requiem.   [b]Highly Recommended[/b]  [i]If you found my review helpful, please consider following my [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/44234346/]Steam Curator page[/url], where you can see more thoughts and recommendations[/i]

Resident Evil Requiem - A Genuinely Exceptional Entry  Rating: S-Tier Horror: S-Tier Action: S-Tier  I've been playing Resident Evil since the originals, and I gotta say — Resident Evil Requiem absolutely knocked me out. This isn't me being hyperbolic; this game legitimately delivers on almost every front.  Let's start with the Grace sections because honestly, they're some of the most *genuinely* frightening moments I've experienced in a horror game in years. It's not cheap jump scares or sudden noise stings — it's the suffocating atmosphere, the way encounters with her feel inescapable and utterly dreadful. Your heart is actually *pounding* during these moments. The tension doesn't let up, and when things go wrong, they go *wrong*. It's that sick feeling in your stomach type of horror, not just "oh, that startled me." These sequences alone justify the playthrough.  The atmosphere throughout those sections is legitimately S-tier. The environmental design, the sound design, the way the game controls pacing — everything works in concert to create this relentless sense of dread. It's suffocating in the best possible way.  Now flip over to Leon, and you get something equally impressive but completely different. The action moments are hands-down the best combat sequences in any RE game I've played. The combat feels visceral, responsive, and genuinely exhilarating. These aren't just "spray bullets" sequences — there's weight to every encounter, strategy matters, and pulling off a perfectly executed combat run feels *incredible*. The set pieces are memorable, the difficulty curves nicely, and you feel like an actual badass by the end.  What's remarkable is how well the game balances these two completely different tones. Grace's sections mess with your head, Leon's sections get your adrenaline pumping, and neither outstays its welcome.  Is it perfect? Nah — like any game, there are minor rough edges. But honestly? They're negligible. This is a legitimately great horror-action game that respects both sides of the franchise. One of the best Resident Evils games ever made. Requiem masterfully balances the survival horror of games such as RE7 and older titles with the action-packed focus of an RE4 and to my surprise, there is more than a little RE6 in this game.  The game terrified me in the first half with Grace's more horror focused sections, sneaking around zombies and trying to conserve my resources, solving interesting albeit easy puzzles, and avoiding this game's take on a pursuer and it was difficult at this early stage and I died a few times. Grace's early sections are fantastic and superbly well paced, and her story kept me hooked with its mysteries. I have to note her actress did an unbelievable job; Grace is a fantastic character and a welcome addition to RE protagonists. Victor Gideon was compelling and featured another fantastic performance from his actor.  The game becomes more action-focused in the later sections, and there is no better protagonist to have for this than Leon. His sections are fast, and RE combat is at its best here with his slick parries, brutal melee combat, as well as tight and responsive gunplay. Exploring some old locations in previous games was fun and it was good to break up from the hospital where the game starts. The story is compelling, with the two protagonists dwelling on past failures, and it culminates in a fantastic final act that brings the whole game together. Leon's actor also did a fantastic job with an older version of the character, still had some great one liners.   The game is not perfect and one of my biggest complaints was that the music was a let down. I adore RE's music, and I feel that since RE7 it has not been as memorable as the older games. I will say, Leon and Grace in third-person did feel a little tanky to control movement-wise, and the game has disappointing boss encounters that I really hoped would do more, they felt quite easy.   Despite those negatives, Resident Evil Requiem is one of the best REs ever made and a contender for GOTY.   9/10

So far, I played Resident Evil 1-8 (1-4 I played the remakes, but also RE4 original on the GameCube) with the exception of not finishing RE7 until after this game. Resident Evil: Requiem is absolutely my favorite of the series now. The split protagonists — Grace and Leon — allow for a unique set-up where you can get the best of both worlds that RE has developed throughout its history. The first set of the games was more survival horror, and shifted to a more action-focused gameplay with the release of the first RE4. Capcom eventually went back to survival horror roots with RE7, and to me RE8 felt like a good mix of the two. RE: R extends this by having a different protagonist for each gameplay. Grace is a new FBI agent who is typically disempowered throughout most of the game, and then Leon kicks the action into overdrive with his high-octane gameplay. Because these two are separate, you never have the issue of becoming too overpowered, but also get the break to let loose and have that empowering feeling. Throughout the game, you will go back and forth between them, giving you a consistent amount of both without having to completely sacrifice the other. This game also has perhaps one of my favorite boss encounters in the series, lore wise. The voice acting is some of the best out there. Angela Sant'Albano absolutely nails the mood whenever Grace is on the screen, and the writing for her has to make her my favorite female protagonist in the series. Her character journey is so real and you experience every bit of her fears and failures and feel such an accomplishment when you conquer a major source of that anxiety. RE: R is on my short list of favorite games of all time currently.

As a fan of the series who has played every single game in the franchise I had high expectations from this game since it's like a closure to Umbrella saga. I can confidently say that the game surpassed all my expectations, there are things I love and some things I don't like about the game. I'll start with what I love. Also want to point out that there will be *spoilers* in this review so beware.  First, as a more of a survival horror RE fan I loved Grace's gameplay. Rhodes Hill Chronic Care Center was very tense and so fun to explore. The zombies in this game keep some of their habits from their past lives and I love this idea and I also love how it was implemented in the game. There are zombies who hate noise who were patients, singer zombies, zombies that try and keep lights closed and maids who still try and clean the place while making a bloody mess lol. And they get angry when you kill a zombie near them thinking you made a mess that they have to clean. These kind of interactions with zombies are so funny and also unsettling. There are some bigger threats like the chef, chunk and the girl. And taking out these zombies don't mean they're gone. They can mutate into Blister Heads and trust me you don't want that. You can stop this mutation by using a Hemolytic Injector. This whole section was survival horror perfected for me. What I don't like about RHCCC is that I think the puzzles were way too linear. Everytime you find a key item you know where to use it and everytime you find something that needs some kind of passcode it won't take long to find it. I'm not saying that it should be so cryptic that you get stuck for hours but it could be more challenging than this. I also played on classic difficulty on my first run and I love the new mechanic where you have to craft ink ribbons with your resources, it adds a lot to the item management.  Then there is Leon's sections and I also loved those. Before I start I want to point out that there are *spoilers* in this section of the review so be warned. The gameplay is basically RE4R but better. It's not so over the top like RE6. Exploring the ruined Raccoon City was a dream come true for me. I loved every second of it, finding easter eggs here and there was so fun and interesting. Right after entering Raccoon City we are welcomed by a giant spider that was missing from RE2R and from that moment I knew that so many more fan services were waiting for me in the city and I was right. From that point on the game literally throws so many fan service stuff in your face. Mr.X, HUNK, Plant 43, RPD, Kendo, Lickers, Nemesis, clone of Albert Wesker and as a fan of the series all of these made me excited like a little kid but the thing is these all happen too fast and feels rushed. Mr. X comes chases you for a few minutes then there is a boss fight and he's gone, Hunk comes to stop Leon has a fight with him and dies in a few minutes, you go through a cave and there is Plant 43 in there and dies a few minutes later. I wish these battles lasted longer and felt more fleshed out.I dont think Raccoon City's potential was wasted at all but it could have been better  The Graphics are amazing and optimization is fantastic I love RE engine for that. In an era of gaming where every game has an issue with optimization this game feels like fresh air. Gameplay is so smooth and fun on both characters and animations are also really good. I've heard there are small bugs here and there but never happened to me so the game was very polished in my experience.  I also loved the lore in the game. Learning the secret behind Raccoon City, what it had to do with Grace, what Elpis is and learning more about The Connections made me so excited. Some details in the story could have been executed better but still it's not so bad.  The game is very replayable. With extra weapons, costumes, upgrades and challenges it gives you reasons to replay the game. Took me around 19 hours on my first playthrough but I took my time a lot. From what i've heard it's around 10-15 hours for most people which is enough with lots of replayability the game offers. The voice acting is also really good especially I loved Grace's voice acting.  Overall, I loved every second I had playing this game and will be replaying it a lot over the coming days. If I have to rate the game I would give it a solid 96. It's one of the best if not the best Resident Evil game that came out since Code Veronica in my opinion.

Perhaps an unpopular opinion, but I think Resident Evil is at its best when it focuses on the survival horror genre. Requiem does that to some extent with Grace, but not nearly as well as its predecessors.  The game started really strong, with amazing first couple of hours. Then Leon was introduced, and initially felt great to alternate between two different approaches within the same game, but not far into his segment you start to feel its undercooked and rushed, giving the impression it was included mainly as fan service for nostalgia.  All of Leon’s section lacked meaningful exploration with too many scenario restrictions. I was excited to revisit Raccoon City, but quickly became disappointed to find that most paths were blocked by collapsed walls. The game creates a false sense of freedom with wide open landscapes, but is ultimately designed so that you follow a linear path. When Capcom announced the game would alternate between tension and action, I was expecting a mix of RE7 with RE4, but Leon's gameplay is nowhere near that. The inclusion of points acquired by killing zombies just confirms the thesis of a rushed segment, in the end giving you the feeling of playing a long session of Mercenaries or an improved version of Resident Evil 6.  After finishing Requiem, I had to go back to Resident Evil 2 Remake to remind myself what makes the series great, and it’s clear that RE2 excels in almost every aspect. Even the graphics aren’t that far behind. The industry is placing too much emphasis on hyper-realistic graphics these days, resulting in an overall experience that feels mostly bland and rushed, lacking the depth and substance that defined the best entries in the series.  While Requiem is not entirely a bad game at all, for Resident Evil standards I would not recommend at full price.

Resident Evil 9 ultimately points to a franchise running out of ideas.   The game begins on a strong note, with Grace’s sections in the Wrenwood Hotel and Rhodes Hill Care Centre delivering a genuinely immersive and atmospheric experience, which is exactly what I was hoping for from the rest of the game. For a brief time, it captures what Resident Evil is all about.  Unfortunately, once you move beyond the opening sections, that sense of immersion quickly disappears, and the game falls into a drawn out, repetitive and boring experience. RE9 feels like a patchwork of ideas taken from previous entries that have been recycled and stitched together without any real sense of originality.  Another issue with the game is the direction of the gameplay which shifts from a tense survival horror to something that feels more like a cheap arcade shooter. Zombies using assault rifles, chainsaws and working mortar artillery finally kills off the last bit of realism that was hanging on by a thread, leaving the game feeling like a joke and far removed from what made the original Resident Evil games so great.   The game also falls apart with the characters and the worst by a mile being Grace. Her constant stuttering is awful and it becomes overbearing and repetitive to the point that it breaks what little immersion is left. It feels overly exaggerated, even in moments with no real threat, and comes across as a poor attempt to create the illusion of fear.  Essentially, as the game progresses it becomes more of an endurance test than an enjoyable experience. What begins as an atmospheric survival horror quickly fades into a repetitive, lifeless and ultimately disappointing game. Overall, Resident Evil 9 fails to deliver on the strengths of the original games, leaving behind an experience that feels forgettable rather than frightening. RE Village has the best story RE4 Remake has the best gameplay Requiem has the best first chapter, and Grace is one of the best-written characters in the history of gaming. I can’t say it’s the best Resident Evil 9 for me because I’m a huge fan of Resident Evil 7 Biohazard and Resident Evil Village, and this one is quite different. But I would definitely rank it in the top 3 Resident Evil games.  Actually, I’d put RE7, RE8, and RE9 in the same category, and all three would share first place for me. However, for someone who isn’t as attached to RE7 and RE8, Requiem will probably be their favorite.  First of all, the optimization is insanely good. The game runs great on pretty much everything. For example, with a GTX 1060 you can comfortably play at around 45 FPS at 1080p on Low with FSR 3.1 Quality, or lock it to 30 FPS on Medium at 1080p with FSR 3.1 Quality and enjoy the experience. A GTX 1650 also runs it with solid FPS. Not to mention RTX 2060, 3060, or 4060, and especially the 5060, which can even handle Ultra settings at 1440p with over 60 FPS (without ray tracing, ofc, using DLAA 4). Meanwhile, the 4060 holds around 50 FPS on the same settings, which is great in my opinion.  4K resolution isn’t that demanding either, so the 4060 at 4K High with DLSS 4 Quality gets around 45 FPS in the most demanding areas, which really highlights how well optimized the game is.  Requiem also has a very, very good story. Without spoiling anything, it’s hard to say if the lore is better than RE7 and RE8. Even though Requiem stands on its own, it still connects to previous Resident Evil games. On the other hand, RE7 and RE8, while sharing a theme, are also strong standalone experiences with their own depth, especially with the Shadows of Rose DLC. I know a lot of people didnt like it, but I personally did. It even feels like Shadows of Rose was a kind of test DLC for Requiem, maybe to experiment with third person gameplay haha.  In any case, if you’re a Resident Evil fan, you definitely won’t miss by playing Requiem. In fact, you absolutely should give it a try.

Resident Evil 9 is a solid addition to the franchise. After the Ethan saga, it feels genuinely refreshing to revisit classic characters and return, in a way, to the roots of the series. Visually, the game is stunning. The graphics are top-tier, and the physics system is seriously impressive. Enemies—especially the zombies—feel more realistic and full of personality than ever. They’re no longer just mindless obstacles; they behave with eerie remnants of their past lives. They mutter phrases, continue repetitive actions, and give off strong BioShock-like vibes in how they blur the line between human and monster. Gunplay is extremely satisfying. Every shot has weight, and the dismemberment system adds a visceral, almost addictive layer to combat. One of the game’s core ideas is its dual-character structure. Playing as Grace leans heavily into survival horror: limited resources, puzzle-solving, and escape room-style level design, reminiscent of Resident Evil 7 and Village. On the other hand, Leon’s campaign is much more action-driven—closer to Resident Evil 4—with large enemy hordes and a faster pace. However, this is also where the game stumbles. Boss fights are, unfortunately, quite easy—especially with Leon. The parry system makes you feel overpowered, removing much of the tension those encounters should have. The biggest issue is that the game tries to do too much at once. It ends up feeling like a “jack of all trades, master of none.” The dual approach is interesting, but neither side feels fully explored. With more time and depth given to each character’s gameplay style, this could have been something truly exceptional. That said, what’s here is undeniably high quality. The experience is polished and engaging—it just feels like it ends too soon. Like playing with an amazing toy that gets taken away right when you’re fully immersed.

I think this might be my first Review of a Resident Evil Game. Strange, since I played Resident Evil Games since their Inception. I wouldn't say I am a Hardcore Resident Evil Fan but still a big fan.  I haven't played many titles that were on some consoles I didn't own (Code Veronica for example or the Lightgun Resident Evil Games and whatnot) since there is a million of spin offs. But I played RE1, 2 and 3 when they first released on PS1, RE: Directors Cut was my first RE Game on PC when it released and I played every single Resident Evil Game available on Steam multiple times.  (Always liked RE more than Silent Hill, even though SH Games are good in their own right. Also super glad that as of writing this Review, Classic RE1, 2 and 3 are now available on Steam - which of course I bought - that were previously only on GoG - which I also bought.)  But I think this might be my first RE Game which I 100%'ed. Not because it was particularly fun but because it was pretty easy and not as annoying as many other Games in the series (purely to 100%, not the Games themselves). To 100% the Game, it took me 34 hours which is not that long. First playthrough was on Standard (Classic; of course with the Ink Ribbons) where I took my time. Second playthrough I did the Speedrun/no heal/no blood collecting in one go, 3rd playthrough on Insanity and a half playthrough on Casual since I missed a Mr. Raccoon halfway into the Game (-.-).  First off let me say that I don't understand how this is the most highly rated RE Game yet. It is a really good Game, for sure, but for me definitely not the best in the series. It is cool that you can switch perspectives from first to 3rd person or the other way around. The ninth mainline game in the Resident Evil series is a great addition to the franchise.  Resident Evil Requiem has some incredible visuals due to it being built around path tracing. The realistic lighting and shadows really enhance the atmosphere of the game.  The gameplay is likely familiar to long-time fans of the series. This one is a mix of the horror exploration and survival action found in some of the past RE games.  The main downside is the usual campy story along with a lack of a proper NG+ mode which makes replays a little less fun to do.  Overall, it's a very fun game to play and would definitely recommend to anyone interested in a quality survival action/horror experience.

🖥️ Graphics & Visuals  ● Overall: This is by far one of, if not the most photorealistic games I have ever played. That goes for the entire gaming landscape, not just this franchise. Turning on path tracing makes everything look absolutely gorgeous, but obviously comes with a massive performance cost.  ● HDR: The native HDR needs some tweaking. It gets noticeably better if you install the RenoDX mod.   🎮 Gameplay  ● The Formula: It follows the same successful "recipe" used in recent titles since the Resident Evil 2 Remake, offering a great mix of puzzles, action, suspense, and horror.  ● Balance: The developers managed to perfectly separate the vibes between the protagonists. Leon's sections brilliantly handle the heavy action, while Grace's sections deliver pure suspense and horror.  ● Pacing & Replayability: The game features incredibly high highs, but also some lower lows, making the pacing a bit more inconsistent than Resident Evil Village. It leans heavily into linear, cinematic small areas, which makes for a thrilling first playthrough but slightly reduces its overall replayability.   📖 Lore & Story  ● Near Perfect: The lore is excellent, not much to say here. It's on par with, or at least 99% as good as, Resident Evil Village. It follows the same trend that started in Resident Evil 7 (and continued in Village), where the ending leaves you with a lot of "dots to be connected" for the future.   📝 Final Thoughts  ● Conclusion: My only real criticism, which isn't even much of a criticism, is the slight dip in replayability mentioned above, and the fact that I wish the game's story had been a little bit longer, with more bosses and special enemies.  10/10

Resident Evil Requiem is a zombie shooter ultimately for so in the style of the new RE 4 and was a very polarising experience for me. I'll start with with Grace the first 4-ish hours of gameplay if I remember correctly and it was honestly a terrible experience. Let me come out and say I am by all means a coward usually for RE games especially when I first played them so to not come close to scaring me is a feat you don't want to be associated with. It fails at the horror for a few key reasons, one is that the game is ridicously easy and two is that the zombies just aren't threatening. To expand on why lets go with the former: I played on classic mode and expected something between the 1st and 2nd games in the series mixed together complimented with the new story. Except the 'limited saves' weren't at all restrictive, I had 12 saves, no yes actually 12 extra saves by the time I beat the game. That goes for all the resources in this game. How I am supposed to be scared of zombies when I realise that "Oh I can just kill every one of them I meet" and have an unlimited amount of ways to kill them or heal myself. Immediately all tension is gone from the game at that for me but it gets worse.  In the latter example it's as it reads, the zombies AI isn't just brain dead, it's formulaic. I was terrible at this game as Grace and there was a weird sense of satisfaction by the end of the chapter when I figured all this out which I think is poorly timed (back to that later). Back to me being bad though, running away from every zombie and gathering my composure in the safe area made or respawning there made me realise on every run through how scripted this games events are and it sucked out any remaining joy. Before in previous titles it was genuinely freightening going over a corpse you killed or a human corpse, not knowing if they'd come back as a stronger foe. But you realise 2 things, dead zombies (even withh a head) almost never come back as blisters and every human is a zombie so I just started shooting everything I saw. Frankly this was actually humilating because I took this game seriously as a horror title. My expactations were matched as well when baba yaga (yes I know her real name but this is what I called here through my playthrough) appeared and whether by pure lucky coincidence I thought it would be funny to turn brightness all the way down through the whole game. Not knowing where she was, going off of sound was blood rushing trying to duke her with bottles or to get past her into the light. That's what makes this game such a tough call for me because the opening segment as Grace is such a spit in the face, such a mockery not just of horror but to the player for having any level of hopes that a RE game would be scary.  Going from that to full Leon initially made me very vexed but I slept it off and beating it all see that yea that was actually pretty good. There's a lot of throwbacks of course to RE Outbreak but also areas that feel inspired like the opening but of course the obvious throw back to RE 2 and the RCPD and they feel tastefully done like it's not retreading ground for the sake of it but also just expanding it with the games interesting narrative. As a whole the environments were all beautifully crafted and atmospheric especially returning to Racoon City where I often found myself simply walking around with no rush taking in the scenery and imaging life before the outbreak or bombing. At the core this is still a RE game so there's a lot of detailed notes that helps fill in the full puzzle, or to find bonus content which is always a treat, but what I'm getting at is if you like previous instalments and can bare a few hours of bad game design this might be worth a pick up(for you at least). Of course there is the high price tag, the fact I crashed 3 times through this and the whole Grace part makes me wonder if this should of been a movie instead of a game, but I'm gonna talk about spoiler stuff now so if you couldn't make up your mind before you have a lot more problems you should probably work to before getting this game.  I really liked the final choice the game presents because it was actually tough to me to figure out what was going on, like was the code made before or after the interview? Even after you find out Elpis is a cure for the T-Virus what was really the best choice? My first choice was destruction as I thought it was a trick question and it was made before, anyway I liked my ending honestly. I think it's poetic how Grace essentially became Leon as Leon passes down his trauma to her but ultimately stopping Umbrella in theory as now there's no investigation as far was we know on the organisation. Irony being there's nothing stopping anyone else doing it again to repeat the cycle with the new 'Leon' to stop them in a loop. Back to the review because I know a lot of people only read them to reaffirm their beliefs so to the people with a hate boner I'll explain what this game could of done better if you couldn't already. I think what would of made this game better would of been to have that really hard start with grace with better zombies and scarcer resources then swapping to Leon makes it more satisfying and conquers any fear in zombies so when you swap back to Grace in Umbrella it feels that more empowering to slaughter all the zombies with guns, acid and so on. Also I don't usually make comments on specific guns but Requiem the gun the game is named after was so weak lol.

Ultimately a very good entry. Though I don't think this is a top fiver in the franchise like many think it is.   The game is gorgeous, 'zombie variety' in the Grace sections of the care centre are the very best the series has ever produced. The strongest parts for me was playing as Grace as I'm primarily a fan of the original classics. Navigating the care center carefully, feeling overwhelmed, backtracking, using the box etc. It all felt very RE2R/RE7. Even the mechanic of using the blood collector was an interesting touch to give players options. I disliked very little about the Grace sections. I'd say maybe The Girl's (stalker enemy) final 'boss fight' was too simplistic and blatantly stolen from RE0. Another gripe of mine is how sluggish she feels in 3rd person. She tends to have this unresponsive inertia type movement going on and she gets stunned by some things in 3rd whereas on 1st she doesn't. But because we have the choice of either 1st and 3rd person, this is a much lesser criticism.   Leon's side on the other hand, although was fun and engaging, felt like a poor man's RE4. Very little enemy variety (the zombies lost their sense of individualism after fighting the care center ones), no side missions, no treasure system, shallow and rudimentary merchant type box and not much difficulty scaling from RC to the end (it felt as if the game got easier if anything). I quite liked the John Wicky moments of fighting the actual humans in the third act though. Felt surprisingly natural. I wanted more from inner Raccoon City. I felt as if we should have had a wider expanse of backtracky gameplay in that sandbox, similarly to how the lake in RE4R gave us a boat to use. Why couldn't we have had full control of the bike?   I think the biggest problem with the game (other than the bad ending which I won't spoil) is that Grace's gameplay has you building her inventory, upgrading, collecting supplies and charms etc. And most of her inventory is rendered almost redundant after the halfway point because we never play as her in any meaningful or significant length of time after the first half. It prevents you from utilizing her arsenal to a fuller extent which feels unfulfilling.   A lot of players felt bothered by some of the retcons in the story but I can honestly say they never bothered me. Of course I won't go into detail but I thought the plot was fine and some elements added layers to previous events which I liked.  What I played was very enjoyable, especially Grace's stuff, but that design choice didn't work for me and on my second playthrough I found it hard to be motivated to finish it because I knew Grace's gameplay kinda goes nowhere. I would have preferred a more fleshed out scenarios based separation of the two styles. Pending DLC, as it stands, the game's replay value seems weak. I think the game is ballsy and brave for making the game like this but alas, I hope that going forward, Capcom stick to making survival horror focused RE games for a while that are split via scenarios like RE1R and RE2R. I usually don't like giving review scores but I think 7/10 is reasonable from me.

[h1]REQUIEM FOR A NIGHTMARE[/h1]  There is a thing that happens when a video game franchise survives for thirty years. It becomes an institution, it gathers ghosts, and Resident Evil, as a series, has a lot of ghosts. We’ve gone from haunted mansions, punching boulders inside volcanoes, swamp magic, tall vampire ladies, and now... we are here; the [u]Requiem.[/u]  Capcom looked at the bifurcated soul of their entire franchise, the slow, creeping dread of survival horror and the explosive, high-octane absurdity of action, and they decided to just do both. And here’s the thing: they actually pulled it off.  [h2]The Ghosts of Raccoon City[/h2]  Nostalgia is a dangerous tool. It can be a cheap parlor trick if you aren't careful. Requiem wields its history like a scalpel, when we finally step back into the ruins of Raccoon City, it is profoundly desolate. The desolation is so much more apparent than in any of the previous games or remakes, you aren't just looking at ruined buildings; you're looking at a graveyard that the world forgot.  And then… there’s the R.P.D. section.  Walking back into the Raccoon Police Department isn’t just a callback. It is a pure, unadulterated nostalgia trip that perfectly captures the essence of "going back" to where everything went wrong. You feel the weight of 1998 in the architecture, it's beautiful, and it fundamentally hurts my heart in the best way possible.  [h2]The Duality of Man[/h2]  The narrative splits its time between our returning golden boy, DSO Agent Leon S. Kennedy, and a new face, FBI analyst Grace Ashcroft. And the tonal shift between the two is staggering.  Let’s talk about Leon first. I put Leon on a pedestal. We all put Leon on a pedestal. And in Requiem, Leon S. Kennedy is operating at his absolute, unmitigated prime. The man's new combat mechanics are absurd, and I love them so much. He is out here parrying axes. He’s parrying blades. He is parrying missiles. It is magnificent. It is the purest distillation of Resident Evil 4 energy, evolved for 2026.  On the flip side, we have Grace. Now, full disclosure: I found myself actively hating the Grace segments; not because of its design, but because they are terrifying. If you, like me, are still carrying a long-running shock from the claustrophobic, resource-starved survival horror shift brought by Resident Evil 7, Grace’s first-person sections will test you. You are vulnerable. You are hunted.  [spoiler]Which brings us to the Chloe segment. I played this part in the dead of night; my chest was physically beating so fast I thought I was going to need medical attention, it was pure, concentrated nightmare fuel. A massive part of why this works is the sound design. The audio team at Capcom found the absolute sweet spots. The way the suspense and anticipation build in near-silence, only to follow up with a meticulously orchestrated salvo of terror? Give them all the awards. Right now.[/spoiler]   [h2]Heartbeats and Hand-offs[/h2]  But underneath the scares, there is a deep, resonant emotional core. Without spoiling the context, there is a quiet moment where Leon gives "Requiem" to Grace, letting her hold it. It was such an excellent decision. It immediately evoked that beautiful, tragic familiarity of Rose from Resident Evil Village. It grounds the chaos. It reminds you that underneath the monsters, this is a story about legacy and survival.  Now, if I can speak directly to the developers for a second, because Capcom, we love you, but we gotta talk about the pacing.  [b]First:[/b] Harry. With everything happening in the narrative, Harry’s screen time felt incredibly short. It gave me legitimate narrative whiplash when his relatively brief exposure concluded. We needed more time to breathe with him, he deserves more time on the screen!  [b]Second:[/b] The difficulty curve. I am not an esports champion; I am a lore-hound. I play on Casual because I want to soak in the story, read the files, and live in the world. But Requiem's Casual difficulty is... a bit on the heavy side. It is punishing in a way that feels misaligned with the intent of a "Casual" mode. Easing up that baseline would do wonders for players who are just here for the history of Raccoon City.  However. For you absolute nuts who crave the pain, the Insanity difficulty is a revelation. I stepped into it thinking enemies would just have larger health pools, but no. The game changes. Encounters are modified. You will walk into a room, smug with your muscle memory, and suddenly go, "Hey, this didn't happen!" It is a brilliant, terrifying way to keep players entirely off-balance.  [h2]The Verdict[/h2]  Resident Evil Requiem is a triumph. It is a game that respects exactly where it came from while aggressively carving out a space for its future. It merges the visceral dread of the modern era with the campy, high-octane heroics of the past.  If you haven't picked this up yet, do yourself a favor. Even if you're intimidated by the horror, the sheer craft on display here is worth the price of admission. Turn the lights off, put on some good headphones, and dive in.  [spoiler]Just... maybe check your heart rate before you meet Chloe.[/spoiler]

During my time with Resident Evil: Requiem, what struck me most is how precisely it controls the player’s emotions.  The Grace segments push survival horror to its limit. Running out of ammo while being relentlessly chased doesn’t feel like a scripted moment—it feels genuinely desperate, almost suffocating. In contrast, Leon’s sections act as a release valve. Instead of running from fear, you confront it head-on, channeling tension into aggression and firepower. This deliberate shift between fear and catharsis keeps the experience constantly engaging and emotionally charged.  The level design is exceptional. There’s rarely a single “correct” approach—stealth, suppression, and infiltration are all viable, and the game consistently respects player choice. Resource management sits at the heart of this system: you’re never truly comfortable, yet the dynamic drop system prevents it from becoming punishing. It’s a delicate balance between pressure and fairness, and the game handles it remarkably well.  The map design, meanwhile, feels like a love letter to longtime fans. From the RPD police station to the Redstone subway, these iconic locations aren’t just callbacks—they evoke memory. For players who’ve followed the series over the years, this blend of familiarity and reinterpretation creates a powerful emotional impact.  Overall, the game stands out for both its content density and its level of polish. Every system feels tightly integrated, resulting in an experience that is not only engaging, but also refined and deliberate in its design.  That said, it isn’t without flaws. The final boss fight feels underwhelming—too short, with limited interaction—and doesn’t fully deliver on the tension built up throughout the game. Additionally, the relatively high hardware requirements may limit accessibility for some players.  在体验 Resident Evil: Requiem 的过程中，我最深刻的感受是——它几乎以一种“精确计算”的方式牢牢抓住了玩家的情绪。  Grace章节将“生存恐惧”推向极致：当子弹耗尽、退路被封、敌人仍在步步逼近时，那种无力与绝望并非夸张的设计，而是一种极其真实的心理压迫。相比之下，Leon章节则像是一种情绪的宣泄出口——玩家不再只是逃避恐惧，而是以愤怒与火力正面回应，将压抑已久的紧张感转化为主动的反击与掌控。这种“恐惧—释放”的结构切换，使整个游戏体验始终处于高度张力之中。  关卡设计同样令人印象深刻。游戏几乎不给出唯一解——暗杀、压制、潜伏，多种策略并行存在，玩家始终拥有选择权。而资源管理则成为这一切的核心约束：你永远不处在真正“安全”的状态，但动态掉落机制又巧妙地避免了过度惩罚，使紧张与公平之间达成了一种微妙平衡。  地图设计则更像是一封写给老玩家的情书。从RPD警察局到红石地铁站，这些标志性地点的回归不仅仅是视觉上的复刻，更是一种记忆的唤醒。对于一路玩过系列作品的玩家而言，这种熟悉与陌生交织的体验，带来的冲击远超过简单的怀旧。  整体来看，这部作品在内容体量与完成度上都达到了系列的一个高点。系统之间的咬合紧密而自然，使它不仅“好玩”，更呈现出一种成熟而克制的设计美感。  当然，它并非毫无瑕疵。最终Boss战略显仓促，流程偏短且缺乏足够的互动深度，未能很好承接前期建立的情绪高度；同时，较高的硬件配置要求也在一定程度上限制了部分玩家的体验。

TL;DR The new Resident Evil looks great and runs superbly, but it feels like three disjointed games stitched together. On one hand, you have the Care Center which has a strong start, focusing on tense survival horror with a Dommy Mom-esque stalker and zombies that still  act out their day jobs. On the other hand, you get Leon, who basically just Kennedys his way through everything with an arsenal of guns and his parrying hatchet, which is super cathartic after having to run away all the time.. The first half is top-tier RE goodness, but once you hit the Raccoon City back half, it falls off hard into a boring conga line of fodder zombies and boss fights that are done and dusted in mere minutes. It’s absolutely worth checking out for that strong start, but since the middle stretches on and the ending leaves you feeling a bit underwhelmed, I’d probably wait for a sale.   Review Proper: It’s been a while since the last Resident Evil game and even longer since the last new mainline installment. I’ve been playing the series since the '00s, with my first title being Deadly Silence on the DS. I’ve played most of the mainline games at this point, barring 6 (which I gave a chance, and I didn’t click with it, to say the least). In more recent years (well, if 7 years is recent, I guess), I’ve played all the Resident Evil games at or close to launch, with RE9 being no exception. So let’s dig in!  We take on the mantle (for now, anyway) of Grace Ashcroft, an FBI analyst who, for some inane reason, is being tasked with checking out a string of disappearances, as well as a body in the hotel where her mother was murdered almost a decade ago. Ignoring the ethical concerns, Grace decides to do it with nothing more than a dingy raincoat and a small pistol. While, uhhh... ”browsing” (in the place where her mom grew a new orifice through her neck), Grace uncovers her mother's hidden journal and a data disk, which gives her some time to ponder that coming here was a mistake before she is attacked by a rotting, strangely well-built scientist by the name of Victor Gideon.  Cut to Leon, who is also on a macabre quest of his own. Infected with the T-Virus, with time running down by the hour (with series oldie Sherry Birkin offering her own support à la Hunnigan from 4), he tracks down Gideon to a shady Care Center, and then, before he knows it, he’s Kennedying every creepy-crawly that crosses his path. I mean, it's what we're here for, anyway.  The game looks great, as always. They’ve been using the engine for nearly a decade, but it really doesn’t seem like it. It still looks really good, with lots of detail in the characters' appearances. Grace and Leon look very lifelike. The series sure has come a long way from those fridge-torso, hazy potato heads of the 5th gen.  It runs superbly as well (with the caveat that my PC is on the higher end with a 5070 Ti, 64GB DDR5, and 9800X3D at 1440p). But even then, Resident Evil games have done a good job of keeping the performance pretty stable even on modest hardware (Monster Hunter, not so much, apparently).  Blasting bio-monstrosities in the third person has been here for over 20 years, so that's to be expected here. Still, they aren’t trying to leave behind the adventure game-like puzzles the series is known for. Don’t expect them to really be brain teasers like back then, since a lot of the solutions are fairly straightforward, with the tools you are to use being pretty nearby where you are. (A pencil that's practically thrown at you must be used on a writing pad. A crank for a machine is a few leagues away.) They weren’t really dull or anything, though.  To emphasize this dichotomy of puzzles, survival horror, and action lie our two protagonists, Grace and Leon. Now, in early Resident Evil games, the only differences between the protagonists were a stupid item limit or access to crazy weapons. In this run, Grace is focused more on survival horror, where enemies really take a toll on your resources, and your best bet is to avoid them entirely (however, you can still fight here and there, and more often than you would think).  Leon contrasts this by absolutely butchering everything that gets in his way, including enemies that Grace couldn’t dream of taking on. It’s actually funny how there is a giant enemy that chases Grace down, and the next time you play as Leon is spent tearing it limb from limb. The Leon sections were really cathartic. Grace largely uses a pistol and a shove attack when enemies are stunned to answer the probing questions of a pushy zombie. Leon has access to a variety of pistols, shotguns, sniper rifles, and magnum pistols, as well as a sick hatchet. Back from the RE4 Remake is the parry mechanic. Leon seemed to have gotten sick of his knives breaking, so he opted for a hatchet. It still needs to be sharpened practically every other time, but it's better than what he had, I suppose.  In the Care Center area, it was cool seeing “unique” enemy types (I put it in quotes because they're not THAT distinct). After 9... I mean... Requiem games, it's surprising that they found new directions to take the franchise while still feeling like Resident Evil games. The enemies are basically zombies, but they really put a unique spin on them. The zombies this time try to continue doing the things that they did when they were “alive” (i.e., a cleaning lady zombie will be viciously cleaning the area, and breaking the various vases used for items will send her into a murderous frenzy; an unhinged patient will scream about the noise Grace makes as she sprints across the place, punishing you for keeping your finger eternally on the Shift key). There is also the Mr. X / Nemesis / Jack Baker / Dommy Mom—I mean, Lady Dimitrescu equivalent in this game known as "the girl." A bellowing figure that towers over Grace and threatens to tear a—  The Care Center part was the best part of the game... now for the iffy and bad.  I try to keep my reviews as spoiler-free as possible, but whatever is in the marketing is fair game (since, of course, they’d expect you to see that). So after you deal with the Care Center, you head out to the ruins of the infamous Raccoon City. You would think after nearly 30 years of jack happening there that everything would have the courtesy to STAY dead, but apparently not. Enemy types at this point in the back half stop being so distinct and kind of blend together. Really, the Detonator segment is the most boring part of the whole game, and I doubt I’d want to replay it, despite how fun the combat with Leon is.  Really, a lot of the game feels disjointed. It felt like three different games were present. The first part with the hospital and sewer (which I thought was where the game was at its best), and then a middle part where you return to Raccoon City, specifically the RPD. There are really cool fanservice moments that I won’t spoil, but they didn’t make up for such boring conga lines of fodder zombies. Bosses were never the series' strong point, and that's still the case. At the very least, in previous games they had a bit of presence, but they are done and dusted in mere minutes, which was surprising.  The game could really use some more enemy variety. The last area in the game alleviates this somewhat, but this is no RE4. I thought the final area was better, but that middle Raccoon City part stretched on a bit too much.  All in all, I would say try to pick this one up on a sale, as I felt a bit underwhelmed at the end of it. It's definitely worth checking out for the strong starting area, but I wouldn’t blame you if you dipped. I don't know how I got to 20 hours, but the game didn’t feel that long, so I’ll give it that at least.

Resident Evil Requiem absolutely nails the feeling of survival horror again. The game isn’t afraid to challenge you — some sections are genuinely difficult, especially when resources are low or enemies start overwhelming you — but that’s exactly what makes it enjoyable.  There were moments where I died multiple times trying to figure out the right approach, and instead of feeling frustrating, it felt rewarding once everything finally clicked. The difficulty pushes you to think, manage ammo carefully, and stay alert instead of just running through areas.  The atmosphere is fantastic. Exploration feels tense, puzzles are satisfying without being annoying, and the sound design constantly keeps you on edge. Even the harder encounters feel fair because the game gives you just enough tools to survive if you play smart.  Not every moment is perfect — a few sequences drag slightly — but overall the challenge adds to the experience rather than taking away from it.  Hard at times, but always enjoyable. If you like Resident Evil when it leans into real survival horror, this one delivers. Great game

There are horror games… and then there are experiences that crawl under your skin and make a home there. Resident Evil Requiem belongs unapologetically to the latter.  From the very first flicker of light against damp, decaying walls, the game feels less like something you play and more like something you survive. It’s a slow, suffocating descent—equal parts dread and fascination—where every footstep echoes like a bad decision and every shadow feels alive. This isn’t just another chapter; it’s a eulogy whispered through broken corridors.  Visually, Requiem is hauntingly beautiful. The environments drip with detail—rust, rot, and ruin rendered so meticulously that you can almost smell the mildew. On PC, especially via Steam, the game truly shines: high frame rates and crisp textures sharpen the terror, making each grotesque figure and subtle movement all the more unbearable to look at… yet impossible to ignore.  The sound design deserves its own standing ovation—or perhaps a moment of silence. It doesn’t just accompany the horror; it is the horror. Distant creaks, breathy whispers, something dragging itself just out of sight… you’ll find yourself pausing, listening, dreading what your ears might confirm before your eyes dare to.  Gameplay walks a delicate line between vulnerability and control. Resources are scarce, tension is constant, and combat feels like a last resort rather than a power fantasy. Every encounter becomes a small story of panic and improvisation. It’s not about feeling strong—it’s about feeling barely alive.  But what elevates Resident Evil Requiem beyond its mechanics is its tone. There’s a lingering sadness woven into the fear, a sense that something has already been lost long before you arrived. It’s horror with a soul—melancholic, reflective, and quietly devastating.  Verdict: Resident Evil Requiem isn’t just a return to form—it’s a transformation. A chilling, artful meditation on fear, loss, and survival that lingers long after the screen goes dark.  9/10 – A beautifully orchestrated nightmare you won’t want to escape… even as it terrifies you.

It made me feel something I haven't felt In a long time. Like the title, It's a truly perfect Requiem.  The way the game mixes all the elements from Resident Evil's sequences, set pieces, puzzles, combat, pacing, etc. All of it is just absolute perfection. Not just in a simple horror/action way, but in a way that parallels, and juxtapositions itself inline with every single title of the franchise from the first Remake of 2, all the way to 8.  The elements are all improved on a technical level and the smoothness is that of butter. In an indirect way, all the elements seem to blend into one form, and the narrative linking all of them makes them sequenced and synced in such a brilliant way of indirect story telling and passive design. The small details of every title, especially in Raccoon City, is retold here in a very tasteful way. While progressing throughout the game, every once in awhile, you get the warm feeling that this isn't your basic fan service type game, It legitimizes every call back to an old moment you experienced before through environmental story telling, and with how both Grace and Leon act.  Rugged and jaded, yet still idealistic and witty. Leon tries with all his heart to break the cycle through sheer will. It grounds him into making him extremely authentic to himself and how past events shaped him, and the game shows you that through its pacing and environment. As I played the previous games, It actually somehow made me feel nearly as jaded as him, but also as hopeful.   Scared, anxious, but still willing to endure. I feel as if she represents the player in a way, to how we were when experienced RE for the first time. But as she keeps enduring and moving, she subtly grows to be desensitized but also learn to be resourceful, to keep her morals and wits about her, due to her feeling powerless. It's a nod to her being the opposite of Leon. In terms of how the players perspectives shift drastically when swinging between the two.   Notable elements of audible expression, ambience, and music are always just a delight from Capcom. The combat Is abysmally great. The way it ties that signature RE feeling, Mixing RE4 and 2/7/8's while giving you the freedom is such an amazing design choice. It shows that with both characters: Grace's feels Impactful, heavy, yet loose. Leon's feels punchy, and gutsy, but so smooth, that it flows like music.   This shows, throughout the grueling trek and struggle, there is hope and solidarity yet to come.  Thank you for making this Capcom. Big applause for the people who made this.

Leon coming back was already enough to sell me.  He’s easily my second favourite character in the series right behind Albert Wesker, so going into Resident Evil Requiem, I was already invested. But what I didn’t expect was just how hard this game would lean into pure horror.  I’m not exaggerating when I say this game had me screaming like a little ♥♥♥♥♥. That hasn’t happened to me in a horror game since the Silent Hill 2 remake. There’s something about the way Requiem builds tension. It doesn’t rely on cheap scares, it pulls you into dread and tightens it until you feel it.  For context, I grew up around the original games, but most of my real experience with the series comes from the remakes and Resident Evil Village. This game feels like it understands both sides of that. The classic survival horror identity and the modern cinematic intensity come together really naturally.  Yeah, it’s short. You’ll finish it quicker than you probably want to. But honestly, it doesn’t waste a second.  Everything that should be in a Resident Evil game is here. Tight resource management, oppressive atmosphere, memorable encounters, and it goes even further with how refined everything feels. The gameplay mechanics are just on point. Smooth, responsive, and never getting in the way of the tension.  What really surprised me though was the contrast between Leon and Grace. It’s not just gameplay. It’s tone, pacing, and even how you approach situations. Leon feels like controlled power-house and I was never frightened whilst playing him, while Grace brings a completely different kind of vulnerability that actually enhances the horror instead of slowing it down.  That contrast alone keeps the experience feeling fresh the entire way through.

Is Requiem a good game? Oh bloody hell... yes, it is.  I am by no means a die-hard fan of the RE series. I’ve completed a fair share of them (1R, 2R, 3R, 4R, 7, 8) and although I had a great time with each entry, I was never the person to get an Umbrella Corp tattoo or ask my barber for the "Leon Kennedy" special.  However, Requiem is something else. Here is a breakdown of why it works:  Graphics: I’m fortunate enough to have a beefy rig, so playing on max settings with Path Tracing was a true "experience." The opening scene with Grace on the city streets is something I’ll remember more vividly than the majority of AAA titles released in the past few years. It’s a visual masterclass.  Protagonists: Grace: Initially, I feared she’d be one of those irritating, "know-it-all" characters. I was wrong, she’s awesome and well-written. // Leon: He’s the peak R4 killing machine, just upgraded. Pure badassery.  Pacing: The balance is perfect. Playing as Grace feels methodical; knowing that any encounter could be your last keeps the suspense high. In contrast, when it’s Leon’s turn, you know it’s time to blow stuff up and watch the body count rise into the dozens.  Mechanics: It feels like a "Best Of" collection, successfully incorporating the strongest mechanics from RE2, RE4, and the modern 7/8 era into one cohesive package.  Quality of Life (QoL): I wasn't a huge fan of the forced FPP in 7 and 8. While I get that the limited FOV adds tension, having the option to play in TPP as Grace was a game-changer for me. Also, as someone with less time for gaming these days, the lack of ink ribbon restrictions made playing in smaller chunks much more accessible.  Difficulty: By 2026 AAA standards? Medium. By the standards of someone who has been gaming since the 90s? It’s definitely on the easier side. It’s a bit of a shame they opted out of puzzles almost entirely.  Final Verdict - Who would I recommend this to?  Everyone. Period. This title does something very few modern games manage to do: it actually meets (and in many areas exceeds) the majority of the hype and expectations.

I was hesitant, Triple A is never worth a play. In this case it definitely is. I've heard mixed reviews but I have to say if you're a fan of either remake and the original RE4 or like the more horror focused gameplay of the more recent entries this game has a lot for you. Without spoilers I would say the default split two style campaign is fun but at times can feel like an after thought, which according to rumors it was. Allegedly Leon got a lot more focus later in development to have more of an active role they also toned down the elements about aging out and any notion of "replacement" which is often where these mentor or gender reversed games tend to go, old white guy is replaced with younger female, that's not at all where this goes if you find those cliches tiresome. The story so far is enjoyable enough and the gameplay fun enough I can comfortably review it without seeing 100%. Only thing I can say is that its strengths can be its main weaknesses with the gameplay, the two protags are diametrically opposed in personality and how they feel to play, which engrosses you well into each but is also vary jarring and frustrating when an enemy you can kill with two shots and a melee as Leon takes literally all of your scarce resources with Grace and this can at some points be a few moments after another.
