TLDR: Great game that rewards long time fans. Leon's section drags on a bit but game as a whole is still fun. 8.5 out of 10.  RE9 was a blast and feels like it pays tribute to all that came before it. It takes the best of everything that came before and mixes it together (gameplay, enemies, plot threads). It also combines the 3rd person action style of the RE2,3, and 4 remakes with the first person survival gameplay of RE7 and 8. You can also tell a lot of the environments are taking inspiration from areas in previous games.   For a little bit I wasn't sure if I liked that the game combines both campy/action Leon and serious/scary Grace plotlines and gameplay. The gameplay and tone of the game felt a tad inconsistent when switching between them. With that said, I do love both gameplay styles and characters. I think as long as Capcom picks a lane (horror survival vs horror action) in following entries this one will be fine being known as "the one that tries to do both".  Seeing plot threads from previous games tie together was pretty nice. The way they call back to old plot points makes this game feel like a natural stepping stone to the threads from RE1-4 and [i]maybe[/i] RE5. As far as I can tell RE6-8 don't really get any call backs but I guess Grace's gameplay is what takes inspiration from those. RE2 seems to have the most relevant plot call backs so definitely play that one first if you haven't already.   Gameplay wise: both characters feel right at home for their respective styles. Leon's large inventory and robust weaponry feel ripped straight from RE4. Grace has a more limited inventory and enemies feel scary since you can't take them down near as easy. I definitely like her gameplay most. My main gameplay complaint is Leon's portion in Act 2 feels like it drags on a bit. I felt myself wanting to revert back to Grace's gameplay to restore some of the horror feeling. Ammo is plentiful for Leon so there was rarely a scary feeling knowing I can blast anything in my path with enough bullets.  This is where I feel sticking with one gameplay style would be preferable in the next entry.   Even if some sections felt stronger than others I very much enjoyed my time with this game. I would rank this game 4th place among the the other mainline REs (behind RE4, RE2 remake, and RE8). 4th place is not me knocking against the game though. Most of the mainline REs are solid games in general. I give RE Requiem a solid 8.5 out of 10.

After getting every achievement in the game, I can easily recommend it. Capcom keeps experimenting and trying to reinvent the series, which this time around, is quite successful.   The gameplay this time around is broken up into two different styles. Grace, a new protagonist, is focused far more on survival horror. You'll have to manage your inventory, solve puzzles, figure out which enemies are worth taking out and which ones you can run past. There's also a fair amount of sneaking around, which I generally dislike in games, but I didn't really mind it here.   And then we have Leon, which focuses more on combat. Inventory management is boiled down to fitting things into a case, since he doesn't get an item box. He can also upgrade his weapons, while Grace can not. The parrying mechanic makes a comeback and it's quite satisfying to pull off. There's also an addition of finishing moves, which during all of my achievement hunting, never got old.   There's also a ton of fan service in this game. Small easter eggs, mentions of details from previous games, references to things you'd find in the past titles. There's so much of it, that I actually feared this is going to be last RE game, lol.  There are a few minor complaints that I could have about this game, so I'm going to briefly mention them here.  First and foremost, switching between different gameplay styles can sometimes be a bit jarring. For example, just when I got into the groove of things with Grace and was ready for more, the game switched to Leon. This could serve as a cliff hanger, but when switching back to Grace, after tearing through hordes of zombies with a massive arsenal of weapons, her lack of fire power felt more tedious.   Then, the replayability... This game suffers on that front, as some of the segments have little to no variation to them in the subsequent playthroughs. One section in particular is just a drawn out hide and seek game, with tons of frustratingly long and boring waiting for things to happen. It doesn't help that the weapons and items from previous runs don't carry over, as the New Game+ is absent.  And finally, the polarizing Insanity difficulty. People seem to get hung up if it's possible or fun to do without using infinite ammo and bonus weapons. After playing through it, I can clearly see arguments for both sides. On one hand, some encounters are far more tense and require a new approach. On the other hand, some enemies are extremely tanky, to the point of frustration ruining the fun. And insta-kill moves are never fun to deal with, which are pretty prominent in certain sections. Reading upon it online, you can parry them, but you have to do it before the animation even starts... I'm not a fan.   And for my biggest gripe with the game... Capcom, please give us a damn FOV slider! On my display, the game was so cramped, that in third person, half of the screen was taken by the character. While aiming, it's impossible to spot some enemies or see attack patterns of certain bosses, because they're off screen. I understand this was done for the purpose of immersion, but the immersion gets broken anyway, when it feels like the characters can't see a few degrees to their left or right.   Overall, despite it's flaws, it's a very good and enjoyable game. I had a great time with it, even though I had my gripes throughout.

[h3]Rating: 8/10 | Recommended[/h3]  [h3]Playtime: 21 hours (100% completion)[/h3]  [h2]TLDR[/h2] Resident Evil Requiem is a solid game, and a good entry in the series. It excels in a lot of aspects, such as graphics, audio and atmosphere, though it falls a tiny bit short of expectations in the story compartment, but it's still good enough.  If you enjoyed the previous Resident Evil games, or you enjoy survival horror games in general, then you'll definitely enjoy this game. Though with the game being as short as it is, you may want to wait for a sale.  [hr][/hr] [h2]Pros[/h2] - Stunning graphics that shows off what the RE Engine is capable of, alongside having good performance considering the level of visuals - Excellent lighting and atmosphere - The character and enemy models look incredible - First few hours as Grace is genuinely tense and scary, especially the basement section - The difference between the gameplay of Grace and Leon is very different and feels refreshing - Gameplay is solid and exploration feels nice and rewarding - The story itself is still good, but it feels underwhelming compared to the previous entries in the series, though it is still good enough - The voice acting is superb, especially for Grace, she was genuinely incredible  [h2]Cons[/h2] - The game lacks enemy variety, though there is more of a variety later on in the game - The boss fights are okay-ish, but not really memorable - The game is quite short (it took me a little under 7 hours to finish my very first run and 21 hours to 100% with 2 more runs) - The puzzles didn't really feel like puzzles, and I feel like they may have streamlined this way too much  [hr][/hr] [h2]Expanded Review[/h2] Resident Evil Requiem is quite a solid game, though disappointing in some aspects. I'll start off with the good things. Graphically, the game is absolutely stunning and really shows off what the RE Engine is capable of, especially with its lighting. The environments are full of details and feel atmospheric. Alongside that, the performance is also good considering the graphics. The first few hours with Grace were surprisingly scary, and I felt on edge a lot of the time, though it quickly disappeared when I had more ways to defend myself. The gameplay loop itself is the standard Resident Evil formula, which is just solid.  One of the areas that I personally found lacking was the story. It was good, don't get me wrong, but it felt underwhelming, especially compared to the previous entries in the series. The enemy variety also felt lacking, since the majority of the time you're just fighting a variation of a zombie. Though near the end you're at least fighting something else other than just zombies, which is good, but wish there was more early variety. Another gripe I have with the game is how short it is. My first run took a little under 7 hours, and then I managed to 100% the game within 21 hours. It's not a bad thing that it is short, but for 70€, it's hard to justify buying this at full price unless you're really into the Resident Evil franchise.

Resident Evil 9 is a fantastic game and, for me, one of the best entries in the series. I had a blast! Here are my impressions, broken down into pros and cons:  Pros + Outstanding graphics that greatly enhance the mood and atmosphere. + Great variety thanks to the different playstyles of the two main characters. While Grace handles the horror parts and has to act cautiously, Leon represents the action. + First-person and third-person camera settings can be adjusted separately for both characters. + Excellent voice acting (the German dub is superb). + Creative and disgusting enemies and monsters. Some zombies still retain parts of their former personalities, making them more unpredictable. + A great mix of exploration, puzzles, stealth, and combat. + First-class sound design. + RE9 picks up lore from older titles and brings some of them to a satisfying conclusion without relying solely on nostalgia. + Multiple difficulty levels and an extra-hard mode to unlock. + Tons of unlockable bonus content like concept art, videos, outfits, and more. + Solid playtime. It took me about 18 hours to finish.  Cons - Leon has a very long segment in the middle. There’s a stretch with less variety, though I didn't mind since playing as Leon is also a lot of fun. - A scripted chase sequence in the middle that is pretty "over the top." I still enjoyed it, though. - Leon drops one-liner after one-liner. For me, this is actually a pro because it made me laugh every time, but it’s definitely not for everyone.   I’d love to see Grace return as the protagonist in the next mainline entry!

Hamsters happily gobble up effects like "OH, THE CLOTH IS FLYING, COOL" completely forgetting that we saw this more than 10 years ago in MGS5. "OH, LOOK WOWZERS RAIN AND TEXTURES". Guys, you forgot about Crysis 3 and Thief of 2014. And finally.... hair strands. Why does hair in Final Fantasy games look better and not cause FPS drops, I ask you?  The game also refuses to use the most basic ragdolls and drops FPS in Raccoon City for no reason at all.  And of course — the monochrome style of the game. It seemed like Crapcom learned how to make colorful games after the 2nd Remake, but no, get used to Monochrome tints, of which there are many here. Yes, I understand, the theme of death and all that, BUT WHY IS EVERYTHING SO DREARY?  [h1]The Resident Evil series we should have gotten instead of the one with Black Wesker[/h1] 🟡Crapcom wanted to please fans with a new cinematic action game. And instead of making a new animated movie, they decided to make a 15-hour game, including 4 hours of cutscenes. Here is a Grace episode, here is a Leon episode, then Grace, then Leon, etc.  I’m not even talking about the plot, it’s full of holes. Not a single question from previous games was answered. Where Rose is — unknown. How Umbrella dealt with a bunch of super strong children? Where Zeno came from?  And in general, shoving new twists into a well-forgotten story like "Well, actually, the T-Virus acts throughout whole life span" and "The Illuminati are to blame for everything" — this is the literal PEAK of absurd.  In short, turn off your brain and enjoy a bunch of cool moments, of which there are many here. Oh, and yeah, there are two endings in the game, but one of them makes no sense. Crapcom JUST wanted to kill Leon to piss off its fans for no reason again.. And after that, the game politely offers to return to the choice of ending, without even letting you fight any final boss. Great.  [h1]RE7+RE2RE+RE4RE[/h1] 🟢Gameplay as a whole is everything that we like. We walk through gloomy locations as Grace, look for loot or quest items. We avoid the undead or try to overcome them with any available means.  However, after 4 hours of gameplay as Grace — you expect to get at least an hour of playing as Leon as a reward (LOTS of REALLY cool action), but no. Through the cleared location(as Grace), Leon simply runs, opens a couple of lockers, lazily kills a few scripted zombies, and the gameplay as Grace starts again. This time, though — we now literally playing Amnesia: The Bunker.  After some time, they will let you play as Leon normally. But instead of "WHAT ARE YOU BUYING" - literal CoD points await us, which we receive for killing everything that tries to kill us.  Oh and yeah, SMGs are "almost" useless.  [h1]Level Design that uses lots of nostalgia[/h1] 🟢Yes, the hospital as Grace was good, it's literally the same as in RE2RE or RE7, both in terms of tension and in terms of deciding where to put items  However, Leon's levels? To be honest, not really good.  Yes, climbing around abandoned buildings is cool. Yes, visiting the ruined RPD is very cool, although ithe game tells me that Im too old for this sh1t already. But the game's level design truly begins to shine closer to the end of the game, when they start to surprise you with some quite unexpected enemies. Unfortunately, the game is already close to its end by then.  [h1]Chinese Copy of Wesker, a stuttering girl failure, and a dying man[/h1] 🟢The main active characters — are memorable in their own way. Sometimes they irritate, sometimes they please. It's a pity that Zeno never became even a parody of Boss-Wesker. He simply — GONE.  As for the enemies — a huge number of Slightly Smart zombies, with a huge number of different clothes and different lines for each of them. There are zombies that aggro on other zombies. There are zombies that SING VERY LOUDLY. There are zombies that hate dirt. Zombies that hate light. And zombies that turn into Crimson Heads... uh, sorry, into Bubble Heads. And that’s basically all. There are, of course, a couple of thicker zombies. Two EVEN THICKIER zombies. A Huge Spider and its children. Lickers. And several Secret Enemies that you should see for yourselves. Trust.   [h1]Very mediocre soundtrack[/h1] https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YJSQ_Qdp6fY&list=RDYJSQ_Qdp6fY&start_radio=1 🟡Yes, Hunk is in the game. Yes, his theme is good. But among 40+ themes, at most 6 are memorable, which is VERY bad. And as for the sound design... let's just say they slacked off here too.  [h1]Insanity was a mistake[/h1] 🟡Yes, past games were sweaty, but quite beatable, because there were several solutions for each encounter. The maximum difficulty of this same game is unforgiving. For all rooms, for all encounters — there is only one solution. A prime example is the second battle as Leon. Forget about the chainsaw — the main features of the trailers - it will kill you here lol. Abuse the axe and the animations of zombies trying to climb to a lower level.  Or protecting Emily — without speedrunner strategies — it's damn hard to survive here.  As for Leon's gameplay — you only need TWO Guns from the entire rather boring arsenal. Oh, and you also can just skip final boss battle by choosing bad ending lmao.  After completing the game After completing Insanity  All that's left for you is to beat the game in 4 hours, not using most of the game mechanics — and that's it, there's nothing more to do in the game. And since the zombies don't behave as randomly as in the  2nd Remake... I'm afraid even a randomizer mod won't help you here.  [h1]7/10 - this game needs DLC. A good one. or even more than ONE DLC - or else its even a 6/10[/h1] 👌Its good - but its FAAAR from perfect sir. Combat is not engaging enough. A TON of scripted events that makes the game not very replayable. Weak story line. Unimpressive visuals with pretty bad performance if you use RTX. And overall mediocrity here and there.  🙄Capcom, tons of money that you dont know where to put again? Should we remind you what happened last time when you got lazy?

All the game really needs is an FOV slider, but I understand it's more of an artistic choice... it was just a bit hard for me to look at at times during Grace's first person segments.  Some may find Grace to be annoying, but I found her very endearing. She's an oddball with a lot of anxiety and her gameplay is perfectly suited for that. I felt a lot of tension and genuine fear during her segments, which is something I can't say for RE8. Leon's gameplay is the polar opposite, and somehow they got both of these styles in the game flawlessly.  There are a few parts in the story that feel a little bit nudged in the direction of making an interesting gameplay moment, but that's still getting into nitpick territory I think because it's hard to blame a game for being a game. I can imagine some people pointing out things that seem like bigger plot holes but I don't think they are... there are multiple layers of conspiracy going on in the story with characters believing things that aren't true in actuality. Things are not what they seem on the surface at all. I don't want to spoil anything but if you play it for yourself maybe you'll know what I'm talking about there.  This really did feel like an homage to all the previous Resident Evil games. You had the ever-expanding layout of a key location from the original trilogy, the over-the-top action of 4-6, and the more overtly horror-centric first person design from 7 and 8. All jam packed into one game in a way that felt really good the overwhelming majority of the time. It's really an all-killer-no-filler kind of game, and at just over 14 hours IGT it's pretty long for that sort of thing.  It's going to be hard to top this one. I can already tell this will likely be my GOTY. Capcom did an outstanding job with it.

Here is my review for Resident Evil Requiem:  Resident Evil is one of my favorite franchises, and I'm happy to say this one is a solid entry. The game plays in two distinct styles: traditional survival horror and killing explosive action. These are the same two genres which split the Resident Evil games. I find this an interesting middle ground between some of these modern games, classic games, and remakes. The game begins with the focus on the survival horror. You're trying to avoid a hospital full of creatures that you are ill prepared to deal with. You're stuck hiding and sneaking around gathering puzzle pieces and tools to get through your tribulations. In the next chapter, you go through the same area with the same creatures, but in an action mode. This is such a cathartic moment because you are no longer a terrified person, you are a well trained veteran and kill everything in your path. Your ammunition is plentiful and your skills are far superior. Those fiends chasing you down for the past few hours, are now your prey. Destroying them all is such a payoff for all that stress and strain they caused. And, I have to mention that the game plays really well. I didn't experience any lag or issues and the controls were quite responsive (though I didn't like the mouse scaling while zooming in).   The story follows to protagonists Grace Ashcroft and Leon Kennedy. Grace is the newcomer to these scares, yet she has to go to a decrepit old building which is the source of her trauma. She gets abducted and then has to escape a monster infested hospital. Leon soon gets to the hospital and blasts away everything moving. You both escape and make your way to the place this all began thirty years ago, Raccoon City. You fight even more freaks and make your way to yet another underground laboratory. There's callbacks to moments in previous games all throughout. Even if some of them seem a bit ham-fisted. But I still find it quite enjoyable.   Overall, this really feels like a love letter to the Resident Evil series for it's 30th year anniversary. I do think it holds it's own without relying on nostalgia; yet, I think long time fans of the series would get such a kick out of this.

7/10 Solid title, but far from the best.  What I liked: They nailed the horror part when you play as Grace. there is a clear influence of RE7, making her an anxious character is a genius choice made by the developers as it increases the tense moments of the game.   Leon's side is pretty fun too, they absolutely aimed for RE4 excellence and for the most part it was fun, the game However is at it's peak when you play as Grace.  I also wanna mention that Leon's Action moves are pretty cool, like RE4 Remake but more badass.  The game isn't too long or short its well balanced in most cases though some parts feel a little dragged out. however, replay value is still excellent once you get some of the unlockable content the game will be much faster to finish.   Story isn't bad its what you'd expect in a typical RE title.  What I didn't like: the graphics are RE Engine level of good but they have some real issues I never experienced playing the previous titles.  I finished the game on PS5 Pro at first and thought it was console limitations which made me purchase it here on steam because RE4 Remake looked like heaven with my RTX 4070 Super.  one notable issue is film grain, it's annoying and it softens everything, and you cannot really turn it off, I tried turning it off from the files and it didn't really do anything, so my guess is just some bad post processing.  Some textures also look weird in some items, like it's noisy when it moves, I also tried using DLAA just to see how it may look which made my PC scream of terrible performance and DLAA supposed to play at native resolution and handles anti aliasing well. it did, however the image still softer than the previous titles in some weird way.  There's a part later in the game when you play as Leon where you have some sort of loot system with points, like (common, rare, legendary...), and that stays with you even in NG+ and a store like the trader where u buy weapons and stuff like RE4.  That, along with some nostalgia parts they went with are major signs of online life-service attempt that they scrapped (I mean, they talked about it before if I'm not wrong), that would certainly explain the lower-ish graphics and the very boring semi-open world part that is unlike what you'd find in RE4 Remake or RE8, it just empty.   I also noticed some heavy reliance on reused assets though they did use many assets in previous RE titles, so I didn't care much of it here.  It's nice to switch from 1st to 3rd person whenever you want. however, I just wish they stuck to one for each character it would've given it more identity but it's no biggie.  in short: Most of the things i didn't like about the game are stuff I also saw in life-service games like COD (lower graphics than previous titles, boring parts, loot system, ability to change between 1st and 3rd person and some glitches upon release that are mostly fixed by now)   At its core, the game is very much solid and fun with Grace's part being the highlight imho.

[b]Gameplay:[/b] 5/5 stars. My first playthrough was on the Standard (Classic) difficulty, and I think they struck the right balance. The gameplay difference between Grace and Leon was handled well with Grace leaning more into managing resources and trying to avoid notice, and Leon being more straightforward action. It’s not easy to design a game that is tailored to two different kinds of gamers—especially when you have both in your fanbase-but they did a great job. If you liked both playstyles in previous RE games, you’re going to have a great time with this one.  [b]Plot:[/b] 4/5 stars. The game starts out with Grace, and it's this establishing section that I consider the weakest part of the game. They moved far too quickly through her backstory, and because of that didn’t make her a very convincing FBI agent. Her boss also appears to be the least sensitive boss in the universe although you can tell they intended to write him from a “tough and willing to push her to be her best” angle. If they’d expanded on that opening scene just a little more and given them each a bit more dialogue, we could have avoided that problem entirely. Having said that, everything else about Grace’s depiction is excellent. She’s dealing with a pretty bad case of anxiety and PTSD, yet she consistently finds her strength to keep on going. That’s the kind of protagonist I like to see. I’ll also say that her story with [spoiler]Emily[/spoiler] was moving, and a big highlight to me.  Leon’s characterization is on point when it comes to the RE2 and RE4 remakes, so modern game writing for him is consistent. I 100% believed this was an older version of the man we met in RE2R. Calmer, completely self-assured, but still holding on to a lot of guilt. Main complaint in the early game is that [spoiler]he somehow failed to save a nurse. I fully believe he was capable of saving her, or at least having an actual reaction to her death-by-chainsaw. :/[/spoiler] It’s only after finishing the game that big questions arise (mostly [spoiler]“Where was the rest of the DSO for this entire operation?”[/spoiler]), but I’m hopeful the expansion will resolve most of those. I’m also hopeful we’ll get more [spoiler]Sherry[/spoiler] in the future; I liked seeing these two get a chance to work together.  [b]Visuals & Level Design:[/b] 5/5 stars. Graphics are beautiful, although I will note that RE4R did a better job at depicting small gestures as you moved around the game what with Leon rolling his shoulders after shooting a larger gun, wiping sweat from his brow, the occasional grunt of frustration, etc. I didn’t really notice Grace or Leon doing those things in Requiem for the most part, which means there’s a bit less personality to pick up on through body language.   Level design was great, although I would have liked some areas to be just a little larger or less straightforward so I could have more to explore. Not asking for open world, just more intricate design.   [b]Voice Acting & Music:[/b] 5/5 stars. Fantastic all around. The voice acting was convincing; it made me empathize with the protagonists, and the villains were suitably unnerving. I loved the direction of the OST as well, and wouldn’t mind if future RE games stuck with it. “Indomitable” was the first track that really stood out to me; it was both eerie and filled me with determination. The save room theme for Leon, “Lament,” also reminded me of something from Half-Life, which was fun.  [b]Misc:[/b] We should be able to name our saves and easily delete them. This is a failing for a lot of modern games, so RE isn’t alone, but the point stands. There’s no reason not to have this feature for users.  RE also continues to have awkward attempts at racial diversity in ways I don’t understand. Surely there’s someone on staff who has brought this up by now? I believe in you RE; you can do better in the future.  I'd prefer an option to turn off the death scenes for our protagonists.  All in all, I think people should have a great time with this game regardless of whether you're an old-time fan or a newcomer. It experimented a bit, and it paid off.

This entry into the Resident Evil series is a love letter to fans of the old and new eras. There are certain aspects that don't quite hit the mark but overall the game is great.  On one hand we have Grace, an FBI rookie with no exposure to biological terrorism who is suddenly thrown into a nightmare with hellish creatures and a mystery that needs to be unraveled with her at the center of it. The other side of the coin brings in Leon, a fan favorite grizzled veteran that has dedicated his life to hunting down BOWs (Bio Organic Weapons) and the people that make them.   The protagonist's journeys eventually collide in what can be described as a rollercoaster of survival and action horror. It can be argued that both characters were not given enough time to shine and as such their progression in gameplay and story can be slightly underwhelming.  Ultimately though I think Capcom did a great job at weaving both styles of Resident Evil gameplay into the 9th installment of this legendary series. I would definitely recommend this title.

Absolutely Outstanding! Game of the Year Contender! Capcom does it again!  I just finished my first play-through of Requiem and it blew me away, even more so than Village (its predecessor). As a long-term Resident Evil fan, I started on Classic difficulty and completed the game in four days (it hooked me from the beginning). I recommend the classic setting for gamers whom have played at least 2-3 first person shooters and/or a previous Resident Evil game. The classic difficulty is the sweet spot - its manageable but there are significant consequences for mistakes and this adds to the anxiety-inducing immersion; this is indeed one of the best survival action horror games to date.  I greatly appreciated the multiple protagonist approach; gameplay progresses from the viewpoint of primarily two protagonists. Each protagonist has different strengths, weaknesses, and play styles. Capcom are best in class regarding the use of multiple protagonists and providing dynamic characters with excellent contrast providing an outstanding gameplay pace and balance – Capcom nailed it! All of the main characters (antagonists and protagonists alike) provide excellent depth and the voice and body language acting is nearly perfect (only because perfection doesn’t exist 😉).   I estimate that this game runs at a ratio of 60% action and 40% horror. The Resident Evil formula just works! One of the monsters, The Girl, is utterly frightening and she is one of the most terrifying antagonists I witnessed in a Resident Evil game. Some minor feedback for future games, I would have liked to see a bit more of the unexpected startling quick scares that I have experienced in classics like Resident Evil 2 and Village – the types of scares that make you drop the controller and have an Oh Sh** moment.  This game uniquely uses dynamic perspective change as one protagonist is better suited for third person view while the other is better suited for first person view. Again, Capcom nailed this and I highly recommend that players not change the perspective but to play the game as the creators intended it to be played. This added tremendous value and originality to the game and contributed to a gripping pace (hence, why I finished the game in four days).  I am not a fond of corporate greed and I am concerned that games are reaching the 69.99 USD price tag - I will not be paying this price often and will be scaling back on annual purchases consequently. However, in all honesty this game provided satisfactory value for the price tag. As you can probably see from my review, I highly recommend this game! All of the following were of an excellent standard: story development, character development, fun factor, action, horror, pacing, unpredictability, and originality. Congratulations Capcom – I have a new favorite first person shooter!  Another minor criticism is that the puzzles were considerably diluted in comparison to previous Resident Evil titles. I was able to solve the puzzles much easier than any of the previous Resident Evil games I have played. I would have liked to have seen just two brain busting puzzles that really tested my patience and attention to detail. One difficult puzzle in the latter 1/3 of each half of the game would have been ideal.  Lastly but certainly not least, there is a twist with the ending that I greatly appreciated (no spoilers here!). Out of respect for the game, I will not go into further detail but yet again, Capcom nailed it with the ending which may encourage subsequent playthroughs.  I am already looking forward to the next Resident Evil title. Keep up the great work!

I immediately purchased RE2 Remake after finishing this. As I am writing this review, I have just finished RE2 Remake's both scenarios and gotten its true ending.  This is the first resident evil game that I completed. I have bounced off of re2 remake and re7 before, playing for an hour or so before dropping it. I never liked horror games, moreso when there's an unkillable monster that you have to constantly hide from. I was ready to quit at the first encounter with the girl. However, this time I stuck around. Maybe it was the Leon aura-farming memes that compelled me to play till his turn came, maybe it was due to my friend who was watching my livestream all the while we were giggling while hiding from the girl or maybe I have just grown up . Whatever it was, I am glad I stuck with it because this is one of the best & most important game I have ever played. There are some games that expands your palette of games, once you complete them you understand why they are regarded as classics and you seek to play more games like them. Resident Evil 9 Requiem is that game for me.  The level design is very fun and engaging with branching pathways, locked doors, puzzles, it is like a metroidvania with inventory management. If you like that genre of games I am positive you'll enjoy this as well. Oh! and I liked the concept of special mini-boss like zombies like the singing lady, goliath & the chef. It was one of the thing I missed in RE2 Remake. RE9 zombies have lots of personalities, if that makes sense.  The gameplay loop of Leon & Grace could not be more different and yet, both of them are very enjoyable in their own way. Solid RE game: jaw-dropping graphics, a perfectly paced story, cinema-level cutscenes, and the same old great gameplay — an immense amount of work overall, and the result is a world-class game. I’m glad the franchise is alive and well.  Leon’s first half of the game is already a meme: John Wick vs zombies. I had a ton of fun feeling overpowered and diving headfirst into hell. Grace’s gameplay is almost immaculate; it gives off RE7 vibes, and I’m all for it.  Now to my personal rant. The second part of the game’s plot turned into a formulaic Hollywood action film with a struggling hero burdened by toxic masculinity issues, descending into darkness, overcoming the final trial with great effort, and walking away changed but scarred, promising to return for more great adventures and deeds once again. It works, but it didn’t necessarily have to be like that. Anyway, I had hoped the return to Raccoon City wouldn’t be melodramatic, but the writers made it exactly that, with cheesy phrases like these (not exact quotes, but close): ‘I couldn’t make a difference. So I am here now’, ‘Never again’, ‘I need to push forward no matter what’, ‘I will stop them’, ‘Leon reporting for duty’, ‘I will kill you as many times as needed’, etc. With the introduction of themes of hope and redemption, the eeriness of the story, the world, and its seriousness were diluted quite a lot.  Victor’s intentions at the end weren’t clear. I was like, ‘Why did he want to fight at all if everything was already fine for him? He could’ve just skedaddled.’ Maybe I missed something, idk. Grace’s ‘It’s all my fault’ felt a bit unclear too. It almost seems like they made it intentionally vague so people would want to replay it or dig deeper into the lore.  I still think RE7 is a masterpiece, but RE9 is such a well-made medley of previous games that it’s a must-play.

It's a good game deserving of a positive review, but given the budget I think it could've been better. I'm not going to glaze capcom just because it met my bare minimum expectations. Of course it was ambitious to have both action and horror, and to try and separate the two playstyles by having two characters, but the end result is, the horror in Grace's sections is not as good as RE2 (rpd tension) or RE7, and the action in Leon's sections is not as good as RE4.   The tension in Grace's sections, especially the "run away" scenes, rests largely on her inability to obey your inputs as a player, which feels BAD. It's gameplay 101 that characters ignoring player inputs feels bad, and capcom should know better. I get it, Grace is a noob, she falls over, she freaks out, blabla, but it feels bad, and honestly just makes me dislike Grace and get annoyed, rather than get scared or sweaty. She pissed me off on multiple occasions especially in the first half of the game, kind of embarrassing that she's an FBI agent but little Emily behaves more calmly and maturely. I think there was a little too much emphasis placed on Grace being scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ because it just ends up being too much, to the point where its not believable anymore. I do think Emily being quite composed in comparison does not help my opinion of Grace.  Now for general gameplay... Enemies sometimes grab you from a lightyear away while they are facing away from you. Zombies throw projectiles that can (a) travel ridiculous distances and (b) go through walls; this happened on multiple occasions in my playthrough. Meanwhile when Leon wants to throw something, he can only do it if they're stood right next to him (this guy has been doing the most obnoxiously badass stuff the entire game but god forbid he can throw an axe more than 10 metres). I dislike these "cutscene" style animations for the pickup throwables as well, there is just generally too much forced gameplay. Many occasions I found myself with two targets, and I want to pick up, say, an axe, and throw it at a particular one. Well, you don't get to choose your targets I'm afraid, you don't even get to throw it yourself. You just press A and watch. I think Capcom could do better than this. The weapon upgrade system is, in my opinion, also a downgrade from RE4R. It got a fancy new UI but the arsenal is limited.  So yeah, it's a game that tried to do everything, and the end result is it did everything alright. But I can't say it really stands at the top of any of the genres it was trying to straddle. It's not even my favourite RE game, let alone my favourite action or horror game. Resident Evil 9: Requiem is a very strong entry in the franchise, and easily one of the best Resident Evil titles released in recent years. It manages to balance different styles of gameplay while still delivering a memorable experience.  Gracie’s section is truly flawless. She is a charismatic and sympathetic character who grows meaningfully throughout the game. Her journey is grounded in fear, resilience, and a developing sense of protection—especially in how she looks after Emily while searching for answers. The setting in the clinic, particularly the basement, is outstanding. It delivers pure survival horror atmosphere, with tension, vulnerability, and excellent environmental storytelling. I genuinely hope Capcom brings Gracie back in future titles.  The story overall is solid and coherent, but there are a few questionable narrative decisions. Spencer’s “regret” arc feels unnecessary, especially considering how complete his storyline already was back in Resident Evil 5. Similarly, the inclusion of a certain clone character feels more like filler than meaningful expansion—there’s no real boss fight or narrative payoff, and it seems to exist only to patch gaps rather than enhance the plot.  Victor, unfortunately, is a weak antagonist. He lacks presence, personality, and emotional weight. With more development, he could have been far more impactful, but as it stands, he feels forgettable.  Leon’s segment is more divisive. I won’t criticize it too harshly because it clearly caters to fans of the more action-oriented side of the series. For those who enjoy that style, it delivers a satisfying amount of combat with some light horror elements. However, for players who prefer pure survival horror, it leans too heavily into spectacle. Leon remains as relentless and capable as ever, but some sequences feel exaggerated—the motorcycle scene, for example, and certain moments where character AI breaks immersion.  That said, the game still shines overall. The survival horror elements in Gracie’s campaign are exceptional: the orphanage is perfectly designed, the pursuer enemy works very well within its intended role, and the resource and weapon management feels tight and rewarding. On the other hand, Leon’s campaign is pure adrenaline—a different flavor, but still enjoyable.  In the end, Resident Evil 9: Requiem succeeds by offering both tension and action, even if the balance isn’t always perfect. It’s a great game, and one of the strongest recent entries in the franchise.  Thank you, Capcom.

Resident Evil 9 is a very good game, but for me it did not fully live up to the huge expectations. I would still recommend it, but in the end I would rate it an 8/10 rather than a masterpiece.  The game clearly peaks in its first half. Grace is a great character, but more importantly, I simply enjoyed her gameplay loop more than Leon’s. The Care Center is one of the best locations in the modern Resident Evil games because it combines strong atmosphere with excellent survival horror gameplay: careful progression, resource management, and gradually dealing with the zombies in a satisfying way. The Girl also works very well as a stalker-type enemy.  The second half is weaker. Leon’s combat is still good, but I expected more, and I still prefer RE4 Remake in that department. The Raccoon City ruins and especially ARK look impressive, but they do not have the same atmosphere or gameplay quality as the earlier Grace sections.  The boss fights were also a disappointment. They are not terrible, but most of them feel too short and lack interesting mechanics, which makes them less memorable than they should have been.  On the positive side, the cutscenes are well done, and the safe room music is excellent. Also, Casual is extremely easy, so I would recommend starting on Standard.  Overall, I would rank it above RE7 and RE3 Remake, but below RE8, and clearly below RE2 Remake and RE4 Remake. Still a strong game, just not one of the very best modern Resident Evil entries.

Extremely good, both as a member of its series and as a game in general.  - Nails the Resident Evil "feel". Splitting the gameplay between RE7's first-person survival horror and RE4's third-person action works really well. - Fantastic pacing. The way the game mixes its formula keeps it fresh and engaging from start to finish. - The game is great at building tension and releasing it at the right moments, nailing the rollercoaster of emotions. - Satisfying gameplay. Weapons feel amazing to use and are well-balanced. New enemy types keep appearing throughout the playthrough, keeping things from becoming stale. - Strong art direction; environments in particular look amazing. - Spotless level design. Each area has its own clear identity, and traversal feels smooth. The game is also far less linear, and thus more satisfying to navigate, compared to RE8. - The plot is simple, but engaging enough to drive the game forward.  What I didn't particularly enjoy:  - Poor performance. As I said, environments look good, but not good enough to justify how demanding the game is. I chose settings that allowed me to stay well above 60 FPS, yet the game still stuttered and dropped FPS multiple times. I think the game is excessively heavy for what it offers, especially when compared to its predecessors. - [spoiler]The fake choice. The game "pulls an RE7" by having a completely pointless decision near the end of the game.[/spoiler] - [spoiler]The motorcycle segment. I can appreciate a game for not taking itself too seriously, but this section, other than feeling needlessly silly compared to the rest of the game, is also not that fun. It gave me RE6 flashbacks.[/spoiler]  Overall, Requiem is an amazing game with very few flaws, and an easy recommendation.

It took me about 51 hours to 100% the game. Overall I liked this game, but not as much as RE2 Remake or RE4 Remake. Or even RE7. The thing is this game tries to appeal to all audiences. Grace has RE7/RE8 style gameplay and Leon has RE4 style gameplay. But unfortunately I found the content lacking, because you basically get two half games.   The replay value is not as good as it could be. There should have been more challenges and items to unlock. This way there would have been more reasons to replay the game over and over again. For example I did not use every weapon Leon gets as there is no challenges like "get x kills with y weapon". I just picked up the most powerful weapons and used them.   I enjoyed the story, but unfortunately won't be coming back to this game any time soon. That being said I believe the RE2 Remake is the gold standard of Resident Evil games and that is how I like the gameplay and storytelling. This game is different and therefore doesn't appeal to me as much.   I suggest you buy this game discounted especially if you are looking for RE2 Remake (or RE4 Remake) style experience.  Edit: At 60 hours I was able to complete The Final Puzzle. This didn't count towards steam achievements, but for good reason I suppose. If you are willing to sink your time tens or maybe hundreds of hours just to treat everything as a clue and to do some crazy experimental stuff you just might solve the puzzle - halfway. As far as I know The Final Puzzle was cracked by data mining, not by trial and experiment. That's how hard it is and I would call it a very unfair puzzle. Solving this puzzle was not fun, it was frustrating. And after I decided to read a tutorial I didn't have an epiphany - I was angry. I knew there was no way I could have solved this puzzle. I felt like this was intended to be a time sink -  not to add replay value.   Oh, and Leon must die forever is a nice add on. Not something to write home about, but I guess I have a reason to revisit the game in future.

Resident Evil (9) Requiem is a love letter to all Resident Evil fans.  Resident Evil Requiem (henceforth "RE9") is perhaps my favorite Resident Evil game.  It is a love letter to all Resident Evil fans.  The next paragraph will go over some of the background of the RE series from my own viewpoint.  Subsequent paragraphs will focus on RE9 specifically.  I will not include spoilers, but will go into some general themes.  I'm a classic RE fan, who was around for RE1.  I think that RE1, 2, and 3 are a great trilogy, and they will always represent "classic" RE to me.  RE4 changed things from "survival horror" to "action horror" and introduced things that stretch one's belief much more than the "scientific" themes of original trilogy of the series.  Some action-oriented people think that 4 is the best in the series, but I feel that it lost its way. 5 and 6 continued to stray from what I feel made RE great.  7 was apparently a "return to survival horror", but the story was not good, and it was too far removed from classic themes.  8 (Village) introduced vampires and witches and werewolves and other fantasy characters that have no place in a series that started from themes of quasi-plausible scientific experimentation.  7 and 8 were also first-person, which I don't particularly like for RE.  RE2 and RE3 REmakes brought in themes and gameplay that are distinctly RE, and they were a breath of fresh air after the series had lost its way.  But they were both remakes, and RE3 REmake cut so much content that was so disappointing, as its core was quite good but just needed to be expanded to include all of the areas of the original.  With that background, I must say that RE9 is the true return to form, but it also gives fans of each RE era what they want as well.  RE9 feels like the 2 and 3 remakes in terms of gameplay and most of its atmosphere.  That said, the game is at least as long as the combination of both of them.  The game starts with Grace, and her game is classic RE perfected.  As the game progresses, you play more as Leon, and his gameplay is somewhat reminiscent of RE4 (which should excite fans of that game), but it's not off-putting to classic fans like me.  There is a certain bit of Leon's campaign that drags on a bit with an environment and enemies that get a bit bland after a while, but it's still worth having in the game.  Grace's part is nearly perfect "survival horror", and Leon's part is the best "action horror" I've seen in the series yet.  As for fan service, this game is rife with it.  I love it.  It doesn't over-do things, but there will be MANY moments when fans will be shocked and overjoyed to see familiar faces and sights.  It is obvious that those who created this game are fans of the series and want other fans of the series to be delighted.  I certainly was!  I won't get into all of the details, but pretty much everything in RE9 is taken from the best of RE.  You can change perspectives for either character (3rd person or 1st person), the gameplay stems from the RE2 and 3 (and a bit of 4) remakes, but improves upon them, if anything.  There are secrets and puzzles like in the original games, and there is also some RE4-like action.  People may prefer certain aspects or areas of this game above others, but I think that both "survival horror" and "action horror" fans will find things to love about this game, and will find that this is either at the top or near the top with regards to pulling it off.  Finally, unlike so many games with microtransactions required to get any extra costumes or other bonuses, this game allows you to earn numerous things (including items to bolster your offensive capabilities in subsequent playthroughs) with in-game credits.  You earn the credits by completing various tasks in the game.  Not only does a desire to complete tasks increase replayability, but the items that you can earn from completing tasks can make subsequent playthroughs unique from prior ones.  The game is long, and is maybe the most fun RE game that I've ever played.  If you like ANY RE game, I think you'll like RE9 at a minimum, or like me, you are likely to love it.  Certainly, if you are an RE fan, particularly of the classic trilogy and their stories and atmospheres, then you are very likely to love this game.  But fans of RE4-6 will also find things to like here, and fans of RE7 and 8 will also find some similarities (including a first-person mode).  Fans of the 2 and 3 REmakes will be right at home, just with a longer game to satisfy them.  If you are an RE fan...or if you are interested in the franchise at all and want an excellent introduction to the RE world, you have come to the right place!  Buy this game!

Where do I even start with this one? Resident Evil Requiem was my true introduction to the series, and wow… what a way to begin. I’d only ever touched RE5 for an hour or two because it came in a mystery bundle, and I didn’t enjoy it enough to stick around. So going into Requiem, I was cautiously hopeful — especially knowing the franchise took a big turn after RE6. And honestly? This game completely surprised me in the best way. You switch between Grace and Leon throughout the story, and the way the game uses their perspectives is just chef’s kiss. Grace’s first‑person sections make you feel small, vulnerable, and trapped in this nightmare, while Leon’s third‑person gameplay flips the vibe entirely and makes you feel like the star of an action movie. It’s such a cool contrast and it keeps the pacing fresh the whole way through. I won’t spoil anything — because this story deserves to be experienced blind — but it is absolute storytelling gold. Twists, tension, emotional moments… it constantly keeps you guessing. Even the classic survival‑horror “find the missing part to fix the generator” moments made me laugh because at this point it’s basically tradition. The atmosphere is incredible. The lighting, the detail, the sound design — everything works together to pull you into this world. And as someone new to the series, the jumpscares felt fair and never overdone. You don’t need to be a Resident Evil veteran to enjoy this game, but finishing it definitely made me want to dive deeper into the franchise. Overall, I’d give it a 9/10, and it’s easily one of my top 5 games of the year.

This game is a bit of a tough one, and I kind of figured it would be when Capcom announced that [i]Requiem[/i] would include Leon and have playable sections for him. On one hand, he’s unmistakably the face of the [i]Resident Evil[/i] franchise (sorry, Chris, but you’re just a bland piece of wood, and there’s nothing you can do to change that anymore), but on the other hand, Leon’s been attached to the series at its messiest. And the series is [i]messy[/i] at this point. I remember being interested in [i]RE9[/i] when it was first shown, but when they revealed that Leon would be an active part of the game, my interest morphed into hesitation. Still, I decided to pick it up, and I’m glad I did, but there are some flaws in the game that my hesitation was right about.   To get the “bad” out of the way first, those Leon sections are functional and tightly designed, but they really fall short when you put them up against Grace’s tense, survival horror parts. For one thing, Leon’s gameplay only really gets going in the second half of the game, and for him, most of that gameplay is spent out in broad daylight, in a bombed-out city, with generic zombies. Yes, the core combat design itself is solid enough, but the game just abandons all of the excellent stress and tension it created when Leon’s gameplay segments really get rolling. What sucks about this is that Capcom has proven they can make a [i]Resident Evil[/i] both tense and action-packed when they did it with [i]RE4[/i], so these Leon segments feel particularly disappointing.   And while I mostly like Leon’s role in the narrative—and as an experienced, collected counterpart to Grace—he’s just too attached to the messy, broader [i]Resident Evil[/i] story that is now in desperate need of some trimming. The series has always been at its best when it can get away from that tangled mess of nonsense, which is why [i]RE4[/i], [i]RE7[/i], and Grace’s parts of [i]RE9[/i] are so good for the most part. When [i]Requiem[/i] started to feel more like, well, a [i]Resident Evil[/i] game, I started to like it less. What sucks the most about that is Leon is [i]so[/i] married to those parts of [i]RE[/i], that it feels like you can’t remove them from his involvement without setting the whole thing on fire.   And, yeah, the story is just so fundamentally dumb. It started that way, too, so 30 years of added continuity haven’t done a thing to clean it up. I get [i]Resident Evil[/i] likes to blend horror and camp, and it does that really well at its best, but there are just some story elements that don’t get covered by the leniency that being a little silly offers. How are Bio Organic Weapons that cost as much as a small nation’s GDP in any way more efficient than just a nice, big bomb? Umbrella has dedicated so many of its resources to absolute nonsense that it just becomes laughable that they still, somehow, manage to have underground labs tucked away in everyone’s basements. There’s silliness that adds to a game’s story and campiness, but this is the kind of silliness that’s begging to be ignored because it just doesn’t work in a functioning narrative.  With that out of the way, there was a lot I did actively like about [i]Requiem[/i]. For starters, I think Grace—the world’s sweatiest woman—is a solid protagonist, and I liked having her drive the plot forward. Her being an introverted desk nerd, but still being a trained FBI agent, makes for an excellent blend of a character who is both in over her head and still competent. It can be hard to make those competent characters come off as inherently vulnerable and sympathetic, and Capcom did an outstanding job with Grace here. Angela Sant'Albano also does an outstanding job of making Grace become a fully realized character.   The survival horror parts of Grace’s sections—particularly her early sections—are excellent. The most important element of making something scary is the element of your protagonist being threatened. [i]RE[/i] makes great use of that immediately by taking away Grace’s flashlight and gun, dropping her in a claustrophobic environment with a freakish abomination affront to God that will rip her head off, and telling you to figure it out. And there isn’t a whole lot more threatening to a 110-pound desk nerd than having her head violently eaten by the kind of sleep paralysis demon you only see coming off a botched dental procedure, so A+ there.   Even without Ms. Sleep Paralysis Demon roaming around eating heads, the regular zombies can still be a handful. Since Grace’s sections are so claustrophobic, more than a single zombie approaching her is fairly threatening. This is where I felt like playing on PC sort of gave me a disconnect from the experience I would have had playing on console. Difficulty when shooting encroaching enemies in the head is just substantially easier using a mouse than it is using a controller, so I was able to get through most combat scenarios with Grace without using too many of my precious bullets, or without losing too many healing items the first time around.   But for the few times I did manage to get caught and killed, I have to give [i]Requiem[/i] credit for its insanely brutal character deaths, which is never a bad thing in a horror game. I never died as Leon, so I can’t comment on anything grizzly that might have happened to him, but they really didn’t pull any punches on Grace’s enemies. Watching a character inherently designed to create sympathy get stabbed in the eye with scissors or [i]agonizingly[/i] cut in half by a bone saw over a few seconds is pretty gnarly, and I say that as someone who has been entirely unbothered by games like [i]Mortal Kombat[/i]. It’s amazing how often that needed sense of threat is completely lost because enemies don’t feel like they’re any actual danger to a character beyond a “Game Over” screen. I don’t need limbs and heads flying everywhere for brushing up against an enemy, but how [i]Requiem[/i] handles it for Grace is very well done.   The main gameplay loop for Grace when avoiding those zombies is solving puzzles, and I’m a little more mixed on that aspect of the game. Bizarre puzzles that require backtracking through your environment are mostly standard for this series, and those bizarre puzzles aren't more or less than what they need to be in [i]Requiem[/i], but I never felt like these added much to the gameplay experience. I guess the game needed something for Grace to do that [i]wasn’t[/i] just whimpering like a sad, wet kitten around zombies, but if anything, I feel like it should have leaned more into that part of the gameplay. Then again, that can also make the game feel like it’s running the risk of having its best aspect overstay its welcome, so the variety was probably needed.   There is a lot of fun to be had in the game, particularly when you’re playing as Grace, and the game is at its peak. That’s when [i]Requiem[/i] is able to successfully build horror and tension without the messy bloat of the additional [i]Resident Evil[/i] canon and context. But there are some major letdowns in Leon’s sections and the broader narrative that did leave me feeling a touch disappointed. [i]RE9[/i] is an easy enough recommendation for the Grace sections alone, but it’s a shame those parts are somewhat bogged down by some of [i]Resident Evil[/i]’s worst habits.

The Resident Evil series has spanned many genres in its lifetime, and Requiem is an ambitious attempt to unite those different and often conflicting elements into a single game. It feels like a sequel to and celebration of the previous entries, and it does a surprisingly good job of delivering on that goal. It's certainly not without its faults, but it's well-crafted and definitely worth playing, especially for anybody that enjoyed the previous games.   RE9 feels a bit like two games woven together, with sections of survival horror in the vein of RE2R and RE7 interspersed with sections of action horror in the vein of RE4R. While it does a pretty good job of balancing the two, I would say that the former is more successful than the latter. The Grace parts feel like a clear evolution of what's come before and offer some of if not the best survival horror in the franchise. There's the familiar gameplay loop of conserving limited resources, weighing options, and planning routes; but added to it is the challenge and terror of maneuvering around The Girl. While there have been unkillable antagonists before (Mr. X in RE2R, Nemesis in RE3R, Jack in RE7), The Girl feels more like the [spoiler]fetus monster [/spoiler] in RE8's dollhouse dialed up to 11. RE9 is properly scary in a way that Resident Evil hasn't been in a long time.   The Leon parts are a welcome break from the tension of Grace's gameplay, but they did feel a little disappointing. RE9 never really reaches the level of RE4R. The controls don't feel as tight, and with a few exceptions, there's a lack of memorable setpieces and enemy encounters. Without RE4R's large hordes of varying enemy types approaching from different angles, positioning and weapon choice feel a lot less important, and the fights aren't nearly as fun. And this unfortunately makes the second half of the game drag on when you play as Leon for an extended period of time.  The two protagonists are both great. Leon is a fan-favorite and it's easy to see why. And aside from a few times where the deeper voice felt forced, it was a good performance that felt in-line with the various tones of the game. Grace is an awesome new addition and one of the best performances in any of the resident evil games I've played.   My main issues with Requiem have to do with the story and the pacing. It feels very front-loaded. The locations in the first half of the game have so much more character than the later ones (although it's almost Resident Evil tradition at this point to start with the best area and then leave it halfway through). The game's opening and first half were incredibly captivating and felt like some of the best storytelling in franchise history, but the emotional climax of that story occurs around the midpoint, and after that, the writing nosedives. I know Resident Evil has never been known for its story, but it felt especially disappointing in this case in light of how good the first half was.

Resident Evil 9: High Quality, Low Focus (Full Review)  The Verdict: A Great Game that Falls Short of the Hype While Resident Evil 9 has received glowing reviews and high scores online, the actual experience feels "inconsistent in its direction." It is undoubtedly superior to RE6, but it fails to reach the high bar set by RE7 and RE8. The main issue holding it back from greatness is the excessive focus on action in Leon’s segments, which thins out the horror identity we expected.  Strengths (Classic Level Design):      Masterful Map Layout: Grace’s segments are the highlight of the game. They perfectly capture the brilliance of the Classic Design (RE1, RE2, and Code Veronica) and the polished direction of RE7 and RE8. The room distribution and interconnected exploration are top-tier.      Crafting System: The resource management and crafting mechanics are excellent for both characters, adding a great strategic layer to the gameplay.  Weaknesses (Why it Lost Points):      Over-the-top Action (Leon): This is the primary reason for the lower score. The game leaned too heavily into pure action during Leon's parts, breaking the horror atmosphere and making the overall experience feel unfocused.      Lack of Genuine Puzzles: A major disappointment for long-time fans is the near-absence of challenging puzzles. What little was included felt insultingly easy, stripping the game of the intellectual challenge and mystery that defined the original classics.      Enemy Design: There was an over-reliance on massive, grotesque boss designs rather than building psychological tension.  Final Thoughts (Score: 8/10): Resident Evil 9 is a solid and high-quality title, but it "didn't live up to the massive expectations" set by the hype. It lacks the cohesive vision that makes RE7 and RE8 objectively better titles without a second thought.  ...While technically an 8/10, I’m giving this a dislike because it is clearly overrated

[SPOILERS] If you're ok with that feel free to keep reading, but if you'd like the TLDR now, good, but overrated.  I'd like to talk about my first experience with Requiem. My first playthrough with the game was great, fantastic even, enough to the point that I thought it was one of the best, but much like every other resident evil a lot of the time spent with these games is on repeat playthroughs since these games tend to be so short in comparison to other games which is ok; it's one of its strengths even. The issue with this game is because the replayability in this game is extremely lacking, as repeat playthroughs only show the bigger design issues with Requiem and how it is less of a game and more of a modern action/horror set piece simulator instead.  The biggest offense is the Grace segments, on my first time through I was like "Wow they really captured everything I love about classic resi! It has pathing, inventory management." etc and it did feel like a great experience, but then you start to realize that it's nothing more than a ghost house with jumpscares to disguise the lack of gameplay. Most if not all enemies have to run a script to set the scene if you will and during this time they are not actually a part of organic gameplay, meaning you can actually just walk past or even use the med injector to kill them during this state, one of the easiest butcher kills in the game is just hitting him with an injector as he rounds the corner.  The game is designed around you never actually interacting with anything and even less so if you know how to path the first cycle. Due to never having to interact with the enemies you never actually need any resources as Grace either, making the blood collecting for her to be an extremely laughable or negligible reward for actually engaging with the combat of the game, and by extension making the stabilizer a complete detriment to your run when you can instead be pumping the steroids to fix your mistakes if so.  If you're reading this there's probably a chance you're going "well that's ok, you can run through everything in classic resi games too!" and I hear you, but that's sadly not even a 1:1 comparison either. Enemies in classic resi while they could be avoided were actual obstacles, they were something you had to maneuver around and were again a part of actual gameplay, not because a script was running and allowed you to. That's also not the full extent of it though as classic games still had scenarios in which you are forced to interact with the enemies or room, for a lack of better term "forced encounters", in which Grace only has technically 2 of these. 1 is the zombies that will eventually block the stairs which you can kill with 1 requiem bullet that the game gives you anyway making it a knowledge check, which is fine, but then you have the room where you're waiting for Emily to do a puzzle due to it being in braille which is also extremely laughable as you're only required to kill like 3 basic zombies.  Speaking of that segment it makes no sense lore wise and could've been a better puzzle for the player too. The reason I say that is because Grace is literally an FBI analyst and can't solve a simple 3 button combo puzzle that she already has the combination to because it's in braille? Now I'm all for my stupid puzzle logic because game is game, but when you make it part of the lore and make it the reason Grace has to endanger a little girl, now you're just being silly as anyone with literally 2 brain cells and not even a high school diploma could pass that puzzle. What's worse is that the machine that has these buttons actually has the same symbols written in braille on the other ones in the facility too meaning even by just looking around you could remove guess work entirely if for whatever reason it didn't let you do guess and check.  Grace removes herself from the game for a bit and goes with the villains for what reason exactly? Because she's done with the situation and would rather go with the evil guys who keep saying she is a "key" and have made their very malicious intentions clear? On top of that the big twist at the end that she wasn't actually a key, while it may blindside the player themselves it shouldn't be a surprise to the antagonists at all. They don't even question how she could be a perfect or original "clone" when she's not even old enough to fit when the clones were being made? She literally wasn't even born at the time of it so how do the villains who know so much about her not know this? The story in resident evil games is never anything truly spectacular, but this is just worse than fanfic writing at this point.  To end off Grace and her gameplay segments I will bring attention to the final stretch of the game ARK. The biggest nothing burger in the entire game as her quest is to get 2 magical mcguffins to proceed to the end of the game blocked by lickers; a well known enemy in the series that has essentially been declawed in this game. In RE2R for example, you may remember how lickers were actual threats that needed to be addressed. Yeah well no more, the lickers in this game can't even harm you if all you do is run and not look at them. Even playing in the 3rd person view as Grace which is slower means they will rarely if ever catch up to you, also giving you even less reason to stealth and grab resources in the final section. Nothing about Grace's gameplay is real, it's all fake up until the end. So fake that the series that originally let you type the password in Code:Veronica leaves that choice entirely down to a binary left click right click option. Are we really so far gone that developers think people can't figure out that the password was the one word that kept being repeated on screen?  I believe it was stated in a dev interview that the original pitch for this game didn't even have Grace, and boy does it really show. Her story makes very little sense and her gameplay is extremely hollow by design. I don't think it's unfair to say that she is mostly trying to take the role of Ethan but instead of being a no faced character to project yourself onto they make her a character that is relatable to most nerds/introverts like myself and probably you reading this.  Leon's segments are action horror instead of trying to be survival horror like Grace. You could easily compare his sections to RE4R, his inventory is a big attache case like 4R/8, he has tons of guns, a hatchet that functions like his knife in 4R as a parry tool while also being your primary method of removing blisterheads. Leon has an actual reason to engage with his enemies and gameplay.  I don't have as many complaints about Leon's sections but there are still some things to note. Gun executions/gun parry while cool, aren't really ever explained to you; a game not explaining it's mechanics is something that RE3R/6 both do in the series as a complaint so I won't cut it slack here. You execute them by being in close proximity to the target with specifically a kill shot. Since this can be done during a stun animation as well I do not wish to call it a parry, your gun can't have a sight if you want to do it for some reason. Due to how the difficulty works in game, this becomes rarer on higher difficulties too making a cool mechanic kinda redundant sadly.  Quick notes since I'm running out of space. There is no real fresh save, new mechanics like the store for Leon will be added right from the start regardless and the weapon spawns that were once there will no longer be, and likewise goes for bonus "unlocks" that are normally in the game like the immortal edge. Insanity has some good choices but many questionable ones. Tons of options which is great, but we lost quick combine in the inventory somehow? Worse bike/turret segment than RE5/6, but gets more praise? Long story short, game with a good base/skeleton, feels unfinished and missing content. Better than 7/8 not better than 2R/4R. (It's mostly hype)

Expect a fair bit of backtracking.  When playing as Leon, RE9 becomes a zombie slaying, campy action game like the films that inspired it. Being able to parry practically everything as well as having unique weapon finishers gives our favorite Raccoon City cop a massive John Wick glowup. Also, he's got daddy energy now. Every gameplay moment that I experienced is an amazing 8 - 9/10 experience.  What stops me from giving this game a 10? It's writing of course (and the annoying music that plays at every encounter as Leon, but that's more of a nitpick)  Capcom, as is expected, couldn't write a solid story to save their life.  So you mean to tell me an FBI field agent with experience out in the field is going to act like a stuttering, babbling mess of a human at every inconvenience? And wtf is up with the director of the FBI in this world, sending someone whose clearly a SUSPECT in this whole strange case without any backup or support whatsoever? "Yeah Grace, go into this spooky hotel that was closed off because of this crime. For me it is a good game but not the best resident evil game. Overall a 8/10.  The good: - Graphics are great as expected from RE engine, everything looks beautiful and detailed, lighting is superb, characters are well animated and motion captured. - Voice acting is great with a minor annoyance of Grace stuttering all the time. - Gameplay is solid overall, especially the Leon segments feel great with a good variety of weapons and the Grace segments having solid survival horror gameplay.  The mixed: - While gameplay is solid, it feels that it lacks focus since the game adopts 2 separate styles instead of focusing on 1 and giving us great gameplay like that. - The replayability is a bit mediocre compared to previous RE titles, while it has unlockables it is missing any bonus modes, I am hoping they will come with DLC or future updates. - Grace highly lacks weapons variety, and while I understand that her gameplay is more horror oriented, she should have a few more options more in line with games like RE7. In addition she only has 1 unlockable gun with NG+ and nothing else which limits the replayability of her segments more than Leon's.  The bad: - The story is absolute nonsense, introducing many characters only for them to do nothing then die, probably one of the weakest Resident Evil stories in the whole series, and that is saying something since RE games are not known for super stellar stories. - Retcons of characters from previous games which is never nice. - Relies too much on nostalgia baiting and member berries, especially in the Leon segments which is not that great.

Resident Evil Requiem review: - There's not much to say about this game! Everything has been positive since its release, even the trailer at the 2025 game awards! Capcom fooled me because I thought this was just a game for Grace, but it wasn't surprising that Leon appeared, making me want to cry!!! Many people think that if this game only featured Leon, because Leon's combat experience is top-notch, and controlling Leon wouldn't feel scary because he's experienced it himself, this is just my prediction before the game's official release in 2025. Regarding the storyline, the direction is excellent, and the gameplay and controls of Grace made me incredibly scared, and sometimes I was startled.  - Grace's gameplay is relatively scary and very engaging. However, Grace's inventory is severely limited, requiring players to strategize strategically, much like Resident Evil 2 & 3 Remake. Grace's gameplay is slightly more challenging than Leon's because she can only survive if she can't melee or parry anything. Overall, I think the director did a great job with Grace, improving her gameplay compared to previous installments. -  Leon's gameplay  is no different from Resident Evil 4 Remake, but Capcom has upgraded Leon's combat and defense mechanics. Leon can now use multiple moves such as melee and parry. Instead of wielding a knife like in games 2, 4, and 6, he now uses an axe to block attacks, even those fired by Victor. The axe's durability can be increased by sharpening and polishing it, whereas in game 4 we had to spend money from defeating enemies to upgrade it.    p/s: The game has been released and has received very positive reviews, including mine ^^. I'm hoping the DLC will be released soon. The game is well worth the money; it costs $70,00, but I don't care. Because I love it. This is more of a "mixed" review than positive. This game is very strange...  The first half in the care center is fantastic, it's creepy, has good puzzles, just all around great survival horror that felt well-paced. But as soon as you get to Raccoon City, things start to fall apart a bit. The pacing becomes breakneck, a bulk of the time you spend in Raccoon City is in the East part of town. It's not a bad area by any means, but it feels more like a prelude section (amplified by it being more on the edge of the city). But once you get to Raccoon City centre, it's just a brief stroll through the RPD, a quick Tyrant boss followed immediately by a plant boss (about 10 minutes after the Tyrant fight), and then you're already in the usual lab endgame part that every RE game has, which itself is over before long. It feels very rushed and unsubstantial, even more so than even the incredibly short RE3R. The first half of the game seems to have had a lot more care put into it whereas Raccoon City just ends up feeling like an unfinished fanservice spectacle. Also, the tone of this game is very strange. One scene at the very end where the villains are fighting has dialogue that is just plain ridiculous, in a bad way. The game is much too serious overall and seem to be completely missing any of the camp of the previous games, which feels jarring coming off of the entertaining RE Village.  I would still overall recommend this game, if only for the care center. the gameplay in Raccoon City is great too, with combat similar to RE4R's, both the good and the bad (zombies inherit the Ganado's spongeyness). Of course it still can't compare to RE4 2005's gunplay, but it's certainly fun.

You’re constantly on edge, but never bored.  The ending theme, “Through the Darkness,” is insanely good.  Grace is annoying early on, but it pays off. She grows on you—literally. By the end, I was on board. I also liked that she doesn’t have access to a full armory, which keeps inventory management meaningful.  Leon isn’t tied to an item box, but if you want to fully use his arsenal, you need one. In practice, you end up running a “loadout,” which feels like a solid middle ground between classic survival and action.  I’ve played RE1–RE5 and all the remakes.
