Firstly, this is what a true resident evil game should look like, as experienced player you will get a lot of easter eggs and fan service. But it's not ruining the impression for newcomers at all. Furthermore, game hooking up new players play more games in the series. Talking about gamplay, it's pure dophamine for any player, you will experience in Grace's part enough horror to feel tension and a lot "hell yeah" action with Leon part  From the perspective of the story, writers nailed it. Pacing of the story in game is well balanced, so you will never feel that game is too short or developers padding it with useless gameplay. No doubt, idea of adding another character in RE franchise, is a bit controversial, as they already have a lot of forgotten characters, but Grace is such aт excellent and well-written character, that fits story perfectly alongside Leon. The idea was definitely to personify Leon's rookie personality in Grace, so you will see perfect match with this two, one is coping with his past, trying to close Racoon City night trauma, whereas the other is confronting her first true trial alongside a battle-hardened mentor.  Nevertheless, as true fan, I felt lack of good boss fight. Where do I even start with this game?  As someone who grew up with Resident Evil and especially Leon, this one hit different. Resident Evil 4 (OG) was the first game I ever played in my life, and I played it nonstop as a kid. So coming into this, I already had a strong connection to the franchise—and this game absolutely delivered.  I played 18.9 hours, finished the story twice, and went all the way to 100% completion, including an Insanity run with multiple challenges stacked together. It was tough, but also really satisfying.  Story & Characters  The story is solid. Nothing revolutionary, but it does what a Resident Evil story needs to do. It sits comfortably around a 7–8/10 in terms of writing, which is completely fine for this series.  Where the game really shines is the characters:  Grace is outstanding. Easily one of the best new characters in the franchise. Great performance, great writing, and just overall memorable. Leon is Leon—and they handled him perfectly. His older design, personality, everything feels right. The performances overall are top-tier. This game deserves recognition for that alone. Gameplay  Gameplay is where this game becomes special.  The balance between horror and action is perfect Playing as Grace feels closer to Resident Evil 2—tense, stressful, survival-focused Playing as Leon feels like an evolved version of Resident Evil 4—more action, more control, but still grounded  The puzzles are well designed:  Not too hard Not too easy Never annoying  Everything just flows naturally.  Atmosphere & Design  This is one of the strongest parts of the game.  The Renwood Hotel was incredible The Care Center stood out a lot The Ark section and Raccoon City aftermath were exactly what you’d expect from Umbrella—dark, detailed, and immersive  The game is not the scariest thing ever made, but it builds tension and pressure extremely well, especially in Grace’s sections.  Technical Aspects No crashes No bugs (in my experience) Performance was smooth Graphics are excellent—the RE Engine continues to deliver Sound design is top-tier Music is very good (not as iconic as RE4 for me, but still around a 9/10) Final Thoughts  I loved this game. I genuinely did.  It’s not perfect, and the story doesn’t reinvent the series, but everything else—from gameplay to characters to atmosphere—is done at such a high level that it’s hard not to respect what they achieved here.  I would recommend this to:  Resident Evil fans (this is a must-play) Anyone who enjoys action-horror games Players who liked RE2 Remake or RE4-style gameplay  Score: 9–9.9/10 Recommendation: Worth full price. If you’re unsure about horror games, wait for a sale—but it’s still absolutely worth trying.  One note: I 100% completed it and immediately uninstalled it—but that’s just me. I tend to move on fast after finishing everything. That doesn’t take anything away from the experience itself.

Resident Evil Requiem is everything I could've asked for... with a few minor problems (Spoiler: Performance is NOT one of them).   Don't get me wrong, I love the game and I love Capcom for still creating a game just like this in 2026.  Something that feels like a love letter to the early 2000's, but with contemporary tech.  Speaking of which - the optimization is insane. The RE Engine is the real star of this game (sorry, Leon). It looks beautiful and it runs smooth and fast (Nvidia 5070TI). I can't remember the last time I played something where I can be in and out of the game in a matter of seconds. (Yeah Kojima, I'm looking at you...).   With Requiem, we get the best of both worlds: The survival horror of RE2, as well as the action of RE4.  The characters are interesting enough and the story is at least entertaining. Awesome voice acting from the whole cast btw. The atmosphere is intense and motivates you to go on with the game at anytime, to be then rewarded with the next cutscene. BUT+ I have to admit that I didn't enjoy Raccoon City as much as I thought I would. Coming back didn't feel as good as it was supposed to feel. Something about this whole chapter felt off, especially in regards of the amazing setting we just visited before. It's... empty. Everything reminds me of the p*ss era games, minus the actual p*ss filter. Back then we had a lot of environments that were just... boring. It almost felt like a break, because everything so far was intense and made you sit on the edge of your seat. It's still fun, of course, but I can't remember that there was a section like that in RE4, where you'd like to enter the next set piece as fast as possible.   I could speak a lot about this, but in the end... it doesn't even matter.  Why?  Because RE Requiem is an amazing game.  It deserves all the praise it gets.   Definitely in my personal Top3 Resident Evil games of all time - at least for now.  The developers hit it out of the park with this one. And since it seems to be a hot topic everywhere: I prefer Grace over Ethan. As much as I do like RE7 & RE8 (both being a rollercoaster par excellence) - those games never reall felt like a true entry to the series. And that's okay, because they were still very entertaining. Requiem however... feels like the essence of Resident Evil. Yes, it has its flaws. But the devs understood the assignment and created an amazing game that delivers exactly what fans of the franchise asked for.

**Resident Evil Requiem – A Thrilling Return to Horror Roots with Fresh Faces**  Resident Evil Requiem delivers an experience that feels both nostalgic and refreshingly new, blending the classic survival horror elements fans love with bold storytelling choices and compelling new characters. From the moment the game begins, it’s clear that this entry aims to deepen the emotional weight of the series while expanding its universe in meaningful ways.  The story is one of the strongest aspects of Requiem, and this time it leans heavily into the legacy of Raccoon City in a way that feels personal and intense. The re-emergence of a mutated strain of the Raccoon City virus—closely tied to the T-virus—adds a constant sense of dread throughout the narrative. What makes it especially gripping is how it directly affects Leon. He isn’t just fighting against the outbreak—he’s fighting against time itself. As the infection slowly takes hold, Leon becomes a ticking time bomb, and that pressure seeps into every mission, every decision, and every encounter. It adds a layer of urgency and vulnerability that we’ve rarely seen from him before, making his journey feel more human and more tragic.  Leon’s return is easily one of the biggest highlights. He’s older, battle-worn, and clearly carrying the scars of everything he’s been through, but this new threat pushes him further than ever. There’s a constant tension in his character—he’s still the capable agent fans know and love, but now there’s a fear that he might not make it out this time. It’s a powerful evolution of his story that keeps you fully invested.  Even more exciting is the return of Sherry Birkin, now stepping into the role of Leon’s trusted partner. Seeing her alongside Leon feels like a full-circle moment for the series, especially considering their shared history tied to Raccoon City. Sherry isn’t just there for nostalgia—she’s a crucial part of the story. Having lived with her own version of the virus—a unique strain derived from the T-virus—she brings both experience and insight into the situation. Her condition gives her an edge in understanding what Leon is going through, and their bond is strengthened by that shared burden.  The dynamic between Leon and Sherry is fantastic. There’s mutual trust, history, and an unspoken understanding that adds emotional weight to their interactions. Sherry often acts as both a support system and a voice of reason, especially as Leon’s condition worsens. Their partnership feels earned and meaningful, and it’s one of the emotional cores of the game, the fact there both fighting the same virus hoping for a chance to rid of it shows the bond they have.  On the newer side of the cast, Grace is an incredible addition. She stands out immediately as a strong, well-written character with her own motivations and struggles. Her backstory is especially engaging, offering a mix of emotional storytelling and intense gameplay sequences. Playing through her past not only adds context to her actions but also builds a strong connection between the player and her journey. It’s refreshing to see a new protagonist introduced with such depth and care.  The Grace and Emily duo is another standout feature. Their relationship evolves naturally throughout the game, balancing tension, trust, and moments of genuine connection. Whether they’re navigating dangerous environments or sharing quieter conversations, their chemistry feels authentic. It’s exciting to see a new duo brought into the series with such a strong presence, and they hold their own alongside returning characters like Leon and Sherry.  Gameplay-wise, Requiem strikes a great balance between classic survival horror mechanics and modern refinements. Resource management feels tight, exploration is rewarding, and every encounter carries weight—especially with the added pressure of Leon’s infection. The environments are rich with atmosphere, constantly reinforcing the sense of danger and decay tied to the virus outbreak.  Another aspect that has me genuinely excited is the upcoming DLC. The base game already sets up so many possibilities, especially with the unresolved threads surrounding the virus and the characters’ fates. I can’t wait for more information to be revealed, because it feels like there’s a lot more story left to tell—whether it’s deeper exploration of Leon’s condition, Sherry’s past, or even more about Grace and Emily. The anticipation alone adds to the overall experience.  Overall, Resident Evil Requiem is a standout entry in the series. It honors its roots while pushing forward with bold ideas, emotional storytelling, and a mix of beloved and new characters. With Leon facing a race against time, the return of Sherry Birkin as his trusted partner, the standout introduction of Grace, and the compelling Grace-and-Emily dynamic, it delivers a memorable and intense experience that leaves you wanting more—and eagerly waiting for what comes next.

TLDR: This is a must play. Don't question it. Just buy it and play it.  I loved this game. I might actually like it more the RE4 and that is by far the greatest entry into the Resident Evil universe. Yeah, it's that good.  So first off, Grace Ashcroft is a fantastic addition to the main cast. Her lack of confidence at the start and fear are completely justified and heighten the fear felt by the gamer whenever having to play as her. But don't let her vocal inflections and lack of confidence get to you. She'll eventually come into her own, although I do wish her stutter had subsided. Then there's the Chuck Norris (RIP) of the Resident Evil franchise, Leon S. Kennedy. My guy is so bada$$ it's impossible to feel fear as Leon. And that's intentional. This story was a blast and perfectly paced. Don't get me wrong there are some negatives and I'll get to those, but there's not enough to make me not recommend it or to not put this in complete competition with the GOAT that is RE4. Do yourself a favor and buy this. No need to wait for a sale, you won't regret this purchase.  So what are the negatives? Alright, some of this is completely nitpicky, but here they are. The fact that there is no option to turn off film grain. Why? Why is this included in every AAA game by default now? It doesn't add anything. It's just ugly and for someone like myself, visually painful. I suffer from a condition that literally makes me see constantly visual snow. It's probably best described as constant film grain. It's quite annoying but I didn't realize it was even a thing I see all of the time until very late in life. I know it sounds crazy but if that's how you saw the world would even ask if anyone else experience it in the same way or just assume that was normal? It is what it is and I've managed to adjust for the most part. It can make watching old films or VHS videos a bit of a challenge, but if the film is good enough I'll put up with it for 2-3 hours. But with that said, I absolutely will turn this effect off the second I can find it in any game. 5-10 hours is big ask for me, so the fact that it's not automatically optional in modern games is absolutely infuriating. Yeah, it's a me problem but it was an optional feature in VII, VIII, 2 and 3 remakes so why isn't it here. Mods to the rescue!   Anyway, getting into character flaws and development. Grace's stutter should have gotten less and less as the game had progressed and she became more confident in her own abilities. I'd be fine with it flaring up the first time she encounters something she's never experienced before, but it got a little grating after the 30th time when she was still just dealing with the same sh!t she had been for the entire first 3rd of the game. I did enjoy the way she went from holding her flashlight like a wand to a more tactical stance almost immediately, so why not make her stutter taper off as well? Like I said, I'm nitpicking but still I felt like that was miss by the devs.   Next, why was Grace, a technical analyst, even chosen to go out into the field? [spoiler]To the exact place her mother died no less.[/spoiler] This one point was the biggest plot hole in the entire game. It not only flies in the face of logic, it's in direct contradiction of FBI policy. So let's ignore the fact that she just wouldn't even be sent their base on her job and the fact that she has a direct connection to the location at all. She would have at least been accompanied by no less than one experienced field agent, plus the accompanying officer would not have left her sight regardless of how secure the site was. But we wouldn't really have the game laid out in the story the way it needed to be presented and probably would have added unnecessary bloat to the story, so cutting some corners is understandable and I can over look it.   Then there's the [spoiler]"she may still be alive" part of the story. Don't get me wrong, Emily's supposed death was gut wrenching, but come one ... "I didn't hit any of her vitals," really? This left me nearly gobsmacked. But eh, it's Leon. Bro could literally swallow a nuke and I'd probably accept it. LMFAO. Plus, it gave us a fantastic ending.[/spoiler]   And that's it really. I'm sure if I really wanted to get ultra nitpicky I could find more, but that's not the point of this review. In the end I absolutely loved every second I had in the game. I couldn't recommend it more and if I could I'd buy all of my friends copies so they could enjoy it as well. Great work Capcom. You've really made Resident Evil into a forever franchise. Now all we need is remakes of Zer0, 1, Code Veronica, and the two Outbreak games.

Requiem is exactly what it sets out to be: a homage to the past, present and future of Resident Evil -  beautifully balanced and cruelly compelling.  Through two converging story lines, Grace and Leon drive a narrative centered on the future of humanity and its resistance to forced evolution. Requiem avoids many of the pitfalls of previous entries and understands when to take itself seriously - an approach welcomed that gives a clear sense of tonal depth. It doesn't overstate its importance, instead striking a balance between the believable and the absurd that the series has often struggled to maintain.  Grace's development serves as a reflection of the of the player's experience. As the narrative unfolds, she shifts from an unwilling participant to a capable and assertive lead, so too does the player - learning when to fight, when to avoid danger and how to use the game's striking visual and sound design to their advantage. Leon's development is equally superb, and it's refreshing to see his vulnerability and weaknesses as his T-Virus infection progresses - a brave decision by Capcom for their franchise poster boy.  While Requiem excels in atmosphere, storytelling, and character development, its pacing can feel uneven. The early game builds tension masterfully, but mid-to-late sections lean heavily into combat, sometimes at the expense of exploration and puzzle-solving. Certain sequences feel repetitive and I found myself hoping I was near the end on more than one occasion. Despite these minor flaws, the game's final stretch regains momentum, delivering a self-referential and introspective conclusion that create a rare sense of poignancy not usually found in a Resident Evil game.  Ultimately, Resident Evil: Requiem is a game that succeeds at what it sets out to do. It balances homage to the series' past with innovative design, offers compelling character arcs, and delivers a tense visually striking experience. While the pacing isn't perfect -- which could even be seem as a subtle nod to franchise's own highs and lows -- and some late-game combat can feel repetitive, these issues never overshadow the game's strengths. For survival horror fans, Requiem is a thrilling and memorable journey that they must go one, and one that firmly earns its place in the franchise.

I had very high expectations after Biohazard and Village and this entry fell flat. While Requiem is by no means a bad game, it just isn't... great. And I believe reviews are going to change once the hype dies down. It's far from being the best RE entry, or even one of the best ones.   The rehabilitation center is just a less engaging version of the police station in RE2. While there were sections I enjoyed and that were genuinely scary, I constantly had the impression that I've seen and done it all before.  I appreciated that during Grace's chapter we had some short, action-packed Leon sections to give us a break from the horror. I hoped that things would get more interesting once the game focused on Leon. Fail. His chapter was grey, repetitive and boring and the level design didn't make me want to explore. I found myself thinking "I don't enjoy this at all" which is sucky when you pay that amount of money for a game. As I said, the genre switching is a good idea and they should have stuck to that recipe until the end.   But even then, this game is just a mid entry in the franchise, because it feels like RE heavily regressed to it's first 3 entries. While Biohazard and Village really showed us how a video game series can evolve and stay fresh, this just feels old and unoriginal. Huge house, sewers, lab... I know this recipe already! I love part 1 and 2 very much, but I was ready for something as original as Village. Combine that with clunky movements, a mediocre story and not a single memorable boss fight and I'm pretty certain in a few years we will look back and rank RE9 among RE5 and 6 or the RE3 Remake, which isn't entirely terrible but kind of meh. It comes nowhere close to RE2, 4, Village or Biohazard.

Resident Evil Requiem is more a remix than a continuation of the main storyline of the other games. It does continue the storyline but it tries to mimic the gameplay, story, characters, and setting of the other games a bit too much. This is both good and bad in a way, since the gameplay isn't as good as the other games. It's like a jack of all trades but master of none. I did enjoy the game for what it is, and it definitely does a good job of representing what RE is to its core, but it fails to succeed at what made the other games so iconic.   For starters, Leon's gameplay from the very beginning is too ridiculous, over the top, and too streamlined, which makes him feel way too overpowered and the game too easy. It's probably a lot more challenging on other difficulties rather than the default, but I feel like the default experience should offer more of a challenge. Grace's parts are more challenging in the beginning which makes the early part of the campaign my favorite, but that's only half of the game. I think the gameplay needs more tuning so that it's more balanced, but it's still an enjoyable experience.  I wouldn't expect to be amazed by the story, as I felt like they were trying to evoke nostalgia from me rather than give an original experience. It does good in excelling at familiarity but not creativity. Even some of the boss fights are remix versions of the past games.  I'm still giving this a positive review because it is a good game, but I would go into this with the expectation of it being a greatest hits version of RE and not an iconic experience. If someone hasn't experienced an RE game before I would highly suggest playing the other mainline games first (or the remakes), this one is a rehash compared to the others (aside from RE6). Hopefully the DLC expands on this in a way that changes my mind.

I have played this masterpiece franchise since I was about 8 years old, back in the PS2 era. It was the first zombie shooter game I ever played. It has elements of horror and survival. The first game in the franchise that I ever touched was Resident Evil 4 on PlayStation 2, which my dad bought for me. I’m glad I had the chance to grow up with this franchise. I love playing every game in it, and many of the characters are very memorable. The gameplay may seem simple, but it is not. Each game always has its own unique mechanics while still keeping the same atmosphere that all the games in the franchise share. The main objective is usually to defeat the final boss, but each boss has their own story. Some games do not show everything at the beginning, so we have to slowly explore and discover it. I think that is one of the charms of this franchise. I also like that some games use a third-person view while others use a first-person view, and I think the choice fits each game well. One difficult thing is aiming and shooting with a controller, but that also makes the game more challenging and fun. The unique design and traits of each character can also lead to different gameplay styles. If you are looking for a zombie shooter game with a survival-horror atmosphere and have not played any of the Resident Evil games yet, I would recommend this franchise. For me, this is one of the most fun games in the franchise because it brings back my favorite character, Leon. He is one of the most enjoyable characters to play because he can kick and punch zombies. One of the pros of this game is that you can play in two styles: gunplay and melee combat, and both are fun. The storytelling is also good and mysterious because we return to the city where the zombie outbreak first began. The graphics and animations can really make you fall in love with the game. The map is large, and the game feels semi-open-world. For me, one con is that some parts can feel a little boring. Also, because the map is big, it is easy to get lost and not know where the objective is. One thing that shows how good this franchise is is that there are 9 main games and the story is still continuing. The first Resident Evil game was released in 1996, and RE9 is coming in 2026. That is a long time, which shows that many people are still waiting for this game and that the franchise has a strong fanbase. Overall, every game in this franchise is good, and I will definitely be waiting for RE10.

The first Leon section in the streets felt great, but when the tired chainsaw gimmick came out later followed by essentially an arena battle, it just made me groan.   Capcom tried really hard to make both the horror and action fans happy and I think they overshot on both accounts. Instead feeling like it has an identity crisis. RE 9 bounces back and forth in the extremes of horror and action when the beauty of Resident Evil was that it's always lived somewhere in the middle.   I usually binge RE games into completion, but I had to put this one down mid way through the treatment center cause it simply wasn't fun. After 3 years of waiting for a new RE game I'd personally say it wasn't worth the wait. The length of the game is pretty underwhelming as I was hoping for it to run WAY longer, and also for the split campaign option after finishing the game for the first time (kinda like how RE6 was) but would that really even matter considering that the best parts of the game are Rhodes Hill for Grace & Raccoon City for Leon and the game just falls flat when they meet in ARK afterwards. It honestly feels like they want to move the future mainline titles to be like The Last of Us Part 1 where you play thru the game once or twice for the story & cutscenes but at that point why even play the VIDEO GAME when you can just watch it on YouTube like all the tourists from twitter that crave to be a part of something + save yourself $70  The story is all over the place and relies on you looking up community posts of people who are giga nerds in the franchise putting the pieces together for it to make even a little more sense, also people are calling this nostalgia bait which is what most games are doing nowadays but Requiem does not feel like it at all.  The gameplay is amazing tho it perfectly mixed both styles of Resident Evil with Survival Horror & Action, if RE5 & RE6 remakes have this level of polished gameplay or even better it's gonna be super ironic that the most hated games turn into the most beloved for the new generation of RE. Some people pointed out how over the top the motorcycle part was which makes me pretty excided to see Chris punch a boulder in RE5make & pretty much the entirety of RE6make  The performance is also perfect as expected from the RE engine, apart from the very first part of the game where you walk to the burnt hotel as Grace (where they are obviously showing off how powerful the engine really is, kinda like RE4R Chapter 5) the game runs insanely good on max settings even on a 6 year old GPU. No frame drops, no lag spikes, and honestly if you have a good rig, just max out the settings and use frame gen for high refresh rate monitors and you'll have an amazing experience  The only thing that can fix the messy story is releasing multiple DLC's like RE7's Daughters, Not a Hero, End of Zoe etc.. I'd love in one of them for Chris to find Zeno in the ruins of ARK (Assuming his body still has some T-Virus in it and can regenerate him since he "died" pretty much a minute after injecting himself with Elpis) and maybe Leon going back to rescue Emily as we see her fully cured in the end cutscene.  Fun Fact: While going for 100% and skipping cutscenes during one of my replays I realized that I completely forgot Zeno even exists as you don't see him anywhere apart from cutscenes and only hear him talking to grace in RPD for like 3 seconds before the Chloe section LOL  6.5/10 (Will update my review and rating after the DLC's)

The new villains are campy and fun, playing as Grace is tense and scary, and Leon is hot - that's basically what you need from a RE game.  Like many other games in the series, the late parts aren't as good as the early ones, as the game devolves into pure action and forgets to be scary, but the beginning is great. Loved The Girl and Chunk as new stalker types, and the new zombies are eerie with their twisted smiles and "personalities." Game looks and sounds absolutely fantastic, with great enemy and environment design and nice bloody effects.

It’s great, but I love one half of it more than the other.   Grace’s sections are the highlight. Some parts of them are legit nightmare fuel, and they featured one of the best decision-making and resource-managing moments in the survival horror part of this series. Plus, Grace is a cutie—10/10.  Two-thirds of the Leon's half are like Resident Evil 4 but slightly worse. This is still a high bar, but enemy variety isn't all that great, later environments look kind of ugly, and all of this contributes to the “slightly worse” impression. Then, the dynamic RE4-light gameplay kind of stops, and the game shifts to semi-cinematic nostalgia pandering. Nothing against cheesy nostalgia in Resident Evil, but can we have all of that without sacrificing gameplay please?  So, the game kind of runs out of steam by the end, but this is pretty much the case with every Resident Evil, so I guess it’s forgivable.

Functioning between dualities, propelled by extremes, “Resident Evil: Requiem” is a disjointed experience both brilliant and horrendous. Initially capitalizing on the best survival factors found in the series, Grace’s opening scenario is an evocation of the Spencer Mansion. Meaningful navigation, resource management and limited saves require thoughtful planning as zombies once again (finally) pose a significant threat. However, “Requiem” second half plays out like a cruel trick. Naive nostalgia glazing tempers mediocrity in Leons campaign. Dominated by a drab colour palette of muted brown aesthetics reminiscent of PS3 games, the same trajectory is applied to the action-oriented loop. Outdated and downgraded compared to previous iterations, combat is dimensional. The trivial arcade nature conforms to bullet sponge enemy's, low stakes engagements and bloated scenarios. The tension and urgency developed within the first half dissipates at the throe’s boredom and creative bankruptcy. If anything " Requiem " erroneously emulates "The Evil With" without competence nor improvement. Despite “Capcoms" investment into RE remakes, “Requiem” struggles to move the series meaningfully forward. Frustratingly caught staring into the rearview mirror.  6/10

As a fan of Resident Evil since the late 90's where I began my journey into the series. The series has went through an evolution. From fixed camera angles and tank controls to over the shoulder third person.  If you are new to the series  and want to understand the lore/story go play the originals (canon games) and then play this.  Graphics are the same as the 2020 /2022 titles, including RE7 and Villiage. With the gore engine, the zombies take damage with enough blasts from certain weapons and it shows in the character models.  gameplay is as you would expect if you played RE7/Villiage including RE4.  Buy this game if you liked the previous installments.

The perfect balance of horror and action, everything you could want from this entry has it. This is Resident Evil in it's purest form.  Requiem is an ambitious title for Capcom and somehow it feels effortlessly masterful. I knew it would be good, I had no reason to believe it wouldn't be with how good the remakes and the most recent mainline titles were, but even with no doubts and extremely high expectations I wasn't prepared for this.   Grace's sections are pure horror and tension, leaving you nearly helpless against all obstacles put in front of you and forcing you to use every little drop of resources you have to their fullest extent. I had some of my biggest scares and tensest moments in all of the franchise during her portions of the game. I also loved strategizing and routing her sections, both in Normal and Insanity, figuring out how to clear an area properly or sneaking past certain encounters felt incredible. Every time I learned a pattern or killed a difficult enemy or traversed an area unscathed I felt *incredible*.  Easily my favorite part of the game.  Leon's sections are action packed and explosive with lots of exploration and skill expression. I've never felt cooler as an RE character even in other games where I've played as Leon than I did in this game. His portions are such a great reprieve for the tension and frustration you build during Grace's sections and being able to take it all out on the same enemies that gave you trouble on her is just the icing on the cake. Parry and execute monsters, dash attack and knock them down, GUN COUNTER ATTACKS, it's all such a treat.  I could gush for hours about everything I loved in this thing but I'll cap my praise off with one more area of the game, the performances. This game has easily the best performance capture of any RE title. Everyone is putting in overtime with their characters and it shows immediately with our lead character, Grace Ashcroft. She is a breath of fresh air and completely took me by surprise with how connected I felt to her through Angela Sant'Albano's performance. I genuinely hope she sticks around for a long time in the series. Nick Apostolides is obviously a great Leon but he really steps it up here and gives the character a fresh perspective that doesn't feel foreign to any version of the character. Leon has been around for a long time and has seen a lot, this is the most I've ever felt that time and experience. Victor Gideon is another standout from the cast. Antony Byrne gives Victor a hauntingly unhinged aura with fun, campy dialogue as well as an intimidating and threatening aura. Nearly every second he's on screen is enjoyable and it added so much to my experience.   A real masterpiece. This game is special and I can't wait to see what comes next if this is the standard. Thank you, Capcom.

This game is genuinely terrifying. I consider each play session as an exercise of my persistence muscle. The writing has rejected any hint of cheese, and piled on the dread and gloom. The "infected" possess a malevolence that terrifies more than previous RE games, especially the earlier ones, where they would shuffle and moan in predictable ways. Here, they have personality.   RE 9 is filled with moments reminding me of Texas Chainsaw Massacre and Hellraiser. The French-chateau atmosphere of the Rhodes HIll Chronic Care Center juxtapose a sense of sophistication with all the macabre gore, making it that much more disturbing. And then Leon arrives!  I would recommend playing the "Grace" sections of the game in first-person view. It ups the sense of terror, which makes Leon's sections even more cathartic.   The RE Engine has come a LONG way since Biohazard almost 10 years ago. The lighting and realism are some of the best in gaming today. This hyper-realistic graphical design encourages you to examine your environment closely as you struggle to survive. The sound design is also excellent, with Grace struggling to breathe as she shivers with fear and grotesque location cues from your enemies. Little touches like that go a long way with a game that emphasizes intimacy.  This is my favorite RE game yet. Capcom deserves accolades for this one.

Let me preface this by saying I definitely think this is a fantastic game and would recommend it tenfold. HOWEVER, it's not nearly what is to be expected after their track record of recent games and I mean that MOSTLY on a gameplay level.   The mechanic of switching characters and gameplay styles sounds amazing at first and it IS pretty fun. However the game is way too short so it kind of shoots itself in the foot. There is not enough time to flesh out the gameplay styles and mechanics of either character since their styles are so vastly different. It ends up a good game in it's own right but there are better Resident Evil alternatives if you want to fully engage in either style of gameplay. By this I mean Grace's gameplay is a hallow version of RE2R and Leon's gameplay is a hallow version of RE4R.   I found myself disappointed that Leon felt so different than RE4R. In this game his movement isn't as responsive, he has a significant lack of i-frames, his gunplay feels stiff and the guns themselves are extremely bland. RE9 gave Leon a ton of gimmicks that don't add much to the gameplay. Gun finishers require you to be very close and the enemy to have low HP and you typically want to avoid being that close so you rarely see those. Useable enemy weapons turned out to be a chainsaw like three times total and some random weapons you can interact with to toss at enemies. Melee finishers are cool but just another form of a mechanic that existed in RE4R.  Grace's gameplay is pretty weak as well. The biggest issue is there is no melee counter when you're grabbed. Meaning you can't stab them (usually using up a significant portion of the knife as a tradeoff) when you're grabbed as a counter as you could in RE2R. Yet she also has a significantly smaller variety of weapons. I will say Grace's sections and gameplay are HEAVILY carried by the enemy and level designs/mechanics. That being said, most of her gameplay is still extremely fun in it's own way due to the levels/enemies and her lack of self-defense (Though I was able to kill nearly every single enemy I came across in my first Standard playthrough with much ammo to spare).  As for the plot, I play games for gameplay primarily so I won't have much to say other than it's pretty poorly thought out. This isn't a spoiler because it was in the trailers, but Leon's whole "infection" plotline is very obviously forced to illicit concern from the player. There are a lot of really strange lore choices that can only be corrected if they decided to remake RE5 and 6 and adjust the plots in minor areas. And the way they incorporated RE7 and 8 into the lore make those games feel like very weird and out of place entries to the series considering this game typically works in loose trilogies. With that being said, RE always has some wild plots that have a ton of issues so I don't really care too much about it.  All in all if you enjoy Resident Evil, this game will be so much fun to you. But if you were hoping for two characters with fleshed out gameplay that give you RE2R and RE4R in one game then you'll probably be better off just playing those games. I will add that this game is graphically BEAUTIFUL. The lighting REALLY makes for some tense horror moments. Grace's sections are probably some of the best horror in the series, matching or even exceeding 7.   And for those of you who like a challenge, Insanity mode is incredibly difficult and up there with RE7's Madhouse and RE8's Village of Shadows.

I don't know where to put this one.  This game felt like a fanfare of a story, but it wasn't terrible. A lot of callbacks to previous games, almost "Hey did you remember thiiiiis?". Not an inherently bad decision, but the cuts between Grace and Leon literally feel like two separate games. Just as soon as things were getting good with our now protagonist Grace, we cut to Leon. Sweet! Finally get to play Leon! For like 5 minutes. Cut to Grace, things just getting good, we cut to Leon. Okay cool, I enjoyed the first little bit feeling over powered as our old protagonist. 10 more minutes of gameplay, and we cut back to Grace.  A few parts in this game too just make running through the game not worth it, let us skip the part where you run from the girls. It adds ZERO gameplay sense, and doesn't even make use of the map later. Zombies feel unresponsive to shoot compared to previous titles, and can end up just being sponges on the harder difficulties, even with headshots.  Shopkeepers which have been a staple in most of the biggest hitters has been reduced to a simple box with an interface that looks like it was ripped from another game. It looks boring and basic without any character. Upgrading you weapons doesn't seem like all that impactful, and you have to already beaten the game once to unlock the third upgrade to each weapon. Makes it useful for Insanity mode, but that's another topic.  The inventory system uses a RE7 style storage for Grace, and a sorta RE4 style inventory for Leon. Grace's inventory system works fine as it does, it can be a little tricky balancing all of the slots, especially in the basement, but that works in it's favor, as inventory management and knowing what to hold onto has always felt like a core component to this series. Leon on the other hand, it felt like his inventory system was slapped on last second. I don't think there was a single time I needed to worry about inventory size in the game. Granted you could claim it's because "Leon got smarter" but it doesn't feel as fun to play.  Speaking of slapped on, the antique coins and shops they had in this game also felt like an afterthought. In the normal 3 difficulties you find way more coins than you'd actually ever use. In Insanity, zombies drop coins, netting you way more coins than you'd use. Near the end of the game on insanity you find a recipe to craft coins into scrap, but by then you'd barely need it.  It sucks they removed blocking for Grace like Ethan had in RE7 & RE8 which made encounters easier especially when dealing with some of the swarms this game straight up throws at you as Grace.  There isn't really anything new in this game besides the story. Most of the enemies are just callouts from other games. Nothing felt original. Oh boy! Another science lab by Umbrella! Zombies with weapons is new I guess, and so is fighting the Elite guard, but that wasn't a fun section. Getting shot at angles that I can't even see.  Two bosses in the game are just recycles of each other.  The part that gets me the most, is I've got about 95% of the challenges completed and put less hours into this the RE3R, which is touted as being the shortest in the franchise.  That's enough about the bad. Let me tell you what I did like, and why I would recommend this game on sale. The graphics in this game are the best in the series. I found it hilarious NVIDA used this game for DLSS5 when this game does NOT need any sort of upscaling. Many scenes in the game pulled me in and made me feel like I was in their shoes. The way the world breathes around you to make it feel like a living environment. The dark environments this game constantly puts you in feels fair with the amount of lights given, using even the tiniest bits of light to catch a shadow of an enemy.  Big Sister is a genuinely scary encounter. The first time you encounter her with the lighter made my heart skip a beat and panic. Hearing the chase not daring to look back. Not many games can capture that feeling.  The story was pretty decent. It felt a little mad at Grace multiple times. Like "Lemme grab the blind girl to solve this puzzle that has NO FAIL CONDITIONS!!!!!! GRACE YOU ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ IDIOT PRESS A BUTTON TO FIGURE OUT WHICH BRAILED BUTTON IS WHICH. Many of the RE games have scenes like this, so I won't hate on Grace too much. It goes to show how impactful the characters became in a quick time frame.   All in all, this game is being WAY overhyped because of all the fanfare put into it. It makes me happy to see so many people excited about the series again, and all the memes that come out of it. I hope Capcom is able to use these funds to make of this franchise. It's still very enjoyable.

Resident Evil Requiem is an incredible game. The hype was real and CAPCOM delivered. It had potential to dethrone RE4 Remake as the new magnum opus of the series, it actually came very, VERY close, but in the end RE4 Remake is still king. Nothing can top that... not yet at least. Requiem, however, became my 2nd favorite game in the franchise. It's an incredible experience which fills you with every kind of emotion. It truly is a game made for the fans. Everything in this game is phenomenal, the gameplay, the story, the characters, the visuals etc. However, like any game, Requiem is not perfect. I bought this game day one and played it like a madman for 2 weeks. After getting the 100%, the hype died down a little and I was able to see the game's flaws. And it pains me to say it, but Requiem has quite a few flaws. There is quite a bit of a read so before I talk about them, I can say that despite the flaws I am about to mention, Requiem is a masterpiece of a game that is ABSOLUTELY worth your money. It's one of the few games that I actually regret not being able to experience it for the first time again.   Now to talk about the flaws:  SPOILER WARNING!!!!  - The game is too short for what it's trying to be.  The game's average length is 10-12 hours without cutscenes. That's how much an average first playthrough is. For a singleplayer game, this length is great. However there is a catch. Requiem isn't exactly a 10 hour game. It's 2 separate 5 hours games that are mashed together. You play as 2 different characters with 2 completely different playstyles. It feels like we are not given enough time with them. Grace's major section is the Care Center, after that is over we do not see her again until the final area of the game where she only has 30 more minutes of playtime. Leon's major area is Raccoon City but we ONLY play as him during that part. We had small Leon bits during the Care Center, we should have had small Grace bits during Raccoon City as well because bro, I sure as heck got tired of Leon at some point and wanted Grace back. I feel like we were given enough time with Leon but not with Grace. Grace should have had one more major area like the Care Center after Raccoon City, maybe the ARK should have been longer, I don't know. This game really would have benefited from an extra chapter, about 2 more hours of playtime. On a first playthrough it's fine, but when you start replaying the game, especially for the achievements, that's when you realise how short the game actually is.  - No proper New Game and New Game+  Honestly my biggest gripe with this game. The fact that there is no proper New Game+ is bad enough but what is worse is that there is no proper New Game either. You can only have a fresh experience ONCE, and after that you are stuck in a combination of New Game and New Game+ that nails none of them. You can only have a proper experience in your first playthrough, after that the story is modified with a NG+-ish mechanic, PERMANENTLY. The only way to have a fresh experience again is to delete your save file but even that is tricky. You have to delete your save file and then play offline, because Steam will attempt to redownload your save from the Cloud.  - Too easy challenges and not enough of them  Every Resident Evil game has difficult challenges that make the 100% a challenge in which you must invest time and skill. Requiem had none of that. Requiem is by far the easiest RE game to 100%. Every single challenge in the game is very easy, even finishing the game on Insanity is not difficult since you can cheese it with the infinite Requiem. Besides the challenges being very easy, there are simply not that many overall. The bonus content you can unlock is also very underwhelming.  - Weakest replayability in the franchise  The RE games are designed to be very replayable, but unfortunately Requiem might have the worst replayability in the franchise. The game feels short, despite having 2 characters with 2 playstyles, there is not that much variety, ESPECIALLY FOR GRACE. Leon has enough weapons, there is enough variety for him, he's got 3 handguns, 3 shotguns, 2 snipers, 2 submachine guns, an assault rifle and 3 magnums, 1 of them shooting rifle ammo. Grace on the other hand ? 2 handguns and a submachine gun that is completely useless without infinite ammo. Every single time you will be using Grace's personal handgun (the one she starts the game with) because the handgun you find in the dining hall is objectively weaker and Freya's Needle barely does any stagger or damage and eats ammo like crazy, it's not worth it unless you have infinite ammo. Grace should have had more guns, at least unlockable guns that were not useless unless you used bonus settings (again, like infinite ammo). Whenever you play as Leon you can choose to use a different loadout for a slightly different experience. Grace on the other hand is going to play the exact same way every single time.  - Stiff and non-fluid animations  RE engine games have incredibly smooth and fluid animations but Requiem does not, for some reason. While most animations are fine, some of them feel very stiff for some reason, specifically Grace's animations when she gets grabbed and Leon's kicking animations. They feel very laggish and unnatural. Compare it to the other RE engine Resident Evil games that have much smoother animations that feel a lot more natural. I actually noticed these animations in Requiem's reveal trailers and I was a little worried about it from the start. While they did improve them, they still feel a little ehhh.  - Performance issues on Nvidia hardware  While the game is INCREDIBLY well optimized and absolutely beautiful, it has performance issues, specifically on Nvidia GPUs. AMD GPUs seem to be unaffected. Some of the performance issues encountered are traversal stuttering, micro stutters, random FPS drops, Frame Generation causes the game to crash, audio desync and cutting off during Leon's segments etc. I am probably missing a few. It feels like CAPCOM skipped on their final quality check that they usually do before releasing their games. Some of the issues are not as bad anymore but they still happen.

After playing [b]Resident Evil Requiem[/b] for almost 50 hours, I still feel like coming back to it — which already says a lot.  This game felt so surreal that I had to sit for a few minutes after finishing it, just listening to the soundtrack in the menu and processing everything I had seen and experienced.  Words can’t fully describe all the emotions I went through while playing this. I was literally jumping out of my chair during some moments, laughing at Leon’s silly (but kind of adorable) jokes, and feeling so much empathy for Grace during her more vulnerable scenes. And yeah… I got the bad ending and cried like a ♥♥♥♥♥, then just sat there in the menu for a few minutes because I needed time to recover mentally.  Talking about Grace, I honestly think she’s really likable. I don’t get the hate she receives, and it actually makes me a bit upset. Her anxiety and panic attacks made her feel real, and I could relate to her. It’s refreshing to see a character who doesn’t feel “invincible” all the time.  There’s honestly so much to say about this game, but not enough words (and probably not enough space). I loved almost everything about it — even though Leon S. Kennedy’s movement can feel a bit clumsy at times and did annoy me occasionally, it’s a small issue overall.  I don’t regret spending money on this game at all — it was worth every penny.  [b]I genuinely wish I could erase my memory just to experience it again.[/b]

It doesn’t just revisit the roots of survival horror it redefines them with a level of confidence that only a franchise at its peak can deliver. From the very first moments, the game establishes an atmosphere that feels both intimately familiar and disturbingly new, blending psychological dread with methodical pacing. What truly elevates Requiem is its mastery of tension. It understands that horror isn’t about constant action, but about restraint about what it chooses not to show. Every corridor feels deliberate, every sound design choice calculated to unsettle. The game respects the player’s intelligence, refusing to hold your hand while quietly guiding you into moments of genuine fear. Technically, it’s nothing short of stunning. Lighting, facial animation, and environmental detail create a world that feels alive and decaying at the same time. The narrative, meanwhile, avoids unnecessary spectacle and instead leans into a grounded, emotionally resonant story that lingers long after the credits roll. Resident Evil Requiem isn’t just another entry in a legendary series. It’s a statement a reminder of why survival horror exists in the first place. Quite simply, this is one of the finest experiences the genre has ever produced.

Resident Evil Requiem Review – 8.5/10  I had a great time with Resident Evil Requiem and would personally give it a solid 8.5/10. From start to finish, it delivers a polished and engaging experience that feels true to the series while still bringing something fresh to the table.  One of the standout elements for me was the story itself. It’s very well done, entertaining, cohesive, and never felt rushed or overly cramped. I was afraid having two main characters would be too much. I was wrong. Capcom really nailed the dynamic between Grace and Leon, creating a strong “one-two punch” that kept me invested throughout. Their chemistry and individual moments both shine, making the narrative one of the game’s biggest strengths.  Visually, Resident Evil Requiem is absolutely stunning and does an incredible job delivering a horror experience through its graphics and sound design. The level of detail in the environments, character models, and lighting is top-tier, creating a constant sense of tension and unease. Dark corridors feel genuinely oppressive, while subtle lighting and shadows are used masterfully to keep you on the edge of your seat. The atmosphere is awesome with every location feeling carefully crafted to pull you into its world and make the horror feel real. Capcom clearly put a lot of effort into the visual design, and it pays off in a big way, making this one of the most immersive and visually striking entries in the series. Rounding that off even further is the stellar performance from the cast. Grace's actress (Angela Sant'Albano) fires on all cylinders here. She really brought the terror and anxiety in Grace to life, and it bleeds onto the screen and in her voice lines. Beautiful! Of course Leon (Nick Apostolides) is back and he delivers the pizzas on time. It is absolute cinema and the bias monster is here. I loved it. He brings a confident, familiar presence that longtime fans will appreciate. Together, their performances add a lot of emotional weight to the story and elevate the overall experience.   Gameplay-wise, everything feels tight and satisfying. The Grace parts are reminiscent of RE2 with a splash of 7. The horror moments shine and it feels like you are saving every round, scrambling through the dark, and trying to survive. Leon is HIM. You get that RE4 action. Get the Dews and the Doritos brother. He is coming in full swing. I swear you'll have enough ammo to destroy every zombie on screen. Parry their souls out of their body and curb stomp their teeth into the wood paneling. It just feels right. Here's the thing... my main drawback comes down to replayability. Compared to something like Resident Evil 4, there just isn’t as much extra content to chase after once you finish the main story. That’s not necessarily a dealbreaker.. it’s still a complete experience, but I do miss the variety of unlockable weapons, modes, and costumes that gave earlier entries more staying power. Those extras were a big part of what kept me coming back to Resident Evil 2 and 4. There are some things to go after once you complete the game, but it isn't as fleshed out right now. With that said, I know DLC is on the horizon! Super excited to see what they add later on ;)   Overall, Resident Evil Requiem is a fantastic entry with strong storytelling, memorable characters, and solid gameplay. While it could benefit from more post-game content.. what is here is highly enjoyable and well worth playing. Whether you are a long time fan or looking for a new game to spice up the weekend.. this one is definitely worth the buy!

I came in to this game as a pretty huge RE fan. My first game was the original RE4, fell in love with that, went back and played all the titles I missed (other than mobile) and have played every title since. The puzzles are a little lacking in this one, pretty much just backtracking with very little actual puzzle work being done. Overall though, I had a great time with my first run and still plan to do the usual and unlock all the challenges, even though the game doesn't quite reach the heights of the series. Definitely recommend if you're already a fan of the series. Might seem a little weird to a newcomer, would recommend starting with the RE1 or RE2 remake first before jumping into this one.

[h3] Pros [/h3]  [hr][/hr]  Atmosphere as the biggest strength. Refined gameplay, probably the best in the franchise. Works like a charm on high settings (RX 6600 + R5 5600). Visually stunning. Top-notch production; looks expensive in cutscenes. Smooth transitions between Grace’s and Leon’s gameplay segments. Grace has the potential to be a solid protagonist in future games. Leon’s one-liners. Design of zombies and their overall uniqueness. Some story elements. [spoiler] RE2 references and the older Tyrant. [/spoiler] [spoiler] Grace/Emily sister-like relationship. [/spoiler] [spoiler] Marie becoming The Girl and the background story around it (trying to keep Emily as a “close sister” and bringing her dolls, as she (The Girl) still resonates as a child). [/spoiler] [spoiler] Grace being born as a product of an experiment. [/spoiler] [spoiler] The bike sequence vs. Victor. [/spoiler] [spoiler] Elpis actually representing a cure. [/spoiler] [spoiler] Emily staying alive in the canon ending. [/spoiler] [spoiler] “The kids” stealth sequence as Chloe can be creepy. [/spoiler] [spoiler] Leon’s ring (our boy is officially married). [/spoiler]  [h3] Cons [/h3]  [hr][/hr]  Could be more horror-oriented. Narrative full of holes and illogicalities (disjointed). Boss fights (poorly designed, unimaginative, and too simplistic in terms of mechanics). Too much focus on using a parry. Unimaginative and poorly designed puzzles (not all of them, of course). Feels too long and becomes very repetitive if you try to explore more (as you should in this genre). Gives the impression of being rushed and unfinished in certain segments (some late-game content feels like padding). Mainly focused on presentation and set-pieces, and because of that lacks in other areas. [spoiler] Panting and loud breathing from Leon and Grace (especially her) become irritating quickly (no, it doesn’t add tension). [/spoiler] [spoiler] Blood analysis sounds cool on paper but is terribly executed and non-intuitive. [/spoiler] [spoiler] The Girl (Marie) is the only boss fight worth mentioning (maybe Tyrant too, because of the RE2 reference). [/spoiler] [spoiler] Victor and Zeno are antagonists just for the sake of it (they lack exposure and development)[/spoiler] [spoiler] “The kids” stealth sequence as Chloe (badly designed). [/spoiler] [spoiler] “Elite soldiers” stealth sequence as Leon (badly designed). [/spoiler] [spoiler] Laughable moment when Zeno lets Grace do whatever she pleases at the end of the game with Elpis (really?!). [/spoiler] [spoiler] Victor’s “blindness” to Elpis being a cure instead of a weapon, despite working on the experiment for 20+ years. [/spoiler]  [hr][/hr]  In short: It’s a good game—not great, but not bad either. It feels like a game you’ll finish once or twice and then forget soon after. Which is a shame. It definitely wastes its potential in the end. It could have been much, much better than it is. Rating it higher than 7.5–8 would be too generous, in my opinion (as most people seem to do).

I played RE9 expecting a good game, and I came out of the experience impressed.  This is a game that treats the player like an adult. It doesn’t hold your hand, doesn’t play the game for you, and doesn’t need non stop action to keep you interested. It’s a game that focuses on tension, pacing, and decision making, and succeeds.  One of the strongest aspects of this game is the atmosphere. It’s not a game that relies on cheap jump scares. I recall several instances where I was forced to slow down and enjoy the atmosphere. I also recall several instances where I was low on ammo, health, and all that, and I had to clutch my way through. These are the instances that make a game memorable.  I also liked the two character aspect of this game. It keeps things fresh:  Grace is all about feeling vulnerable, resources are scarce, the best offense is defense (pure survival horror experience) Where Leon is literally a power trip, Kill everything, nothing left standing. i don't think i left a single enemy alive as Leon, Unlike grace where its completely normal to leave enemies and find a way through them with the many option the game gives you.  My favorite part of this game besides the atmosphere is the zombies, and I know that sounds stupid, but hear me out: Zombies in RE9 retain their characteristics when they were humans even after they turn, and you can use that to your advantage, especially during Grace's parts, which is very refreshing and adds flair.  Technical aspects, this is one of the most beautiful games I've ever played, graphics wise, and is optimized extremely well, which is very rare nowadays.  Overall, absolute cinema, top 3 RE for sure. i still like 4 and village over this.

Resident Evil Requiem is the latest entry in the series and a direct follow‑up to RE: Village. It takes place in Wrenwood, near the ruins of Raccoon City, and introduces a new protagonist, Grace Ashcroft, an FBI agent. The story explores her origins as well as the background of the new villain, Victor Gideon, a former Umbrella researcher. There is much more beneath the surface, but the campaign’s biggest strength is how it lets players experience the story from two perspectives: Grace in first‑person and Leon Kennedy in a third‑person, action‑focused style.  The graphics are mind‑blowing, fully utilising the RE Engine with photorealistic visuals and smooth performance. Combat is fast‑paced, and players can wield weapons such as an axe, rocket launcher, magnum, and grenades. The gameplay feels like a blend of RE4 and Village, keeping the experience familiar yet fresh. The soundtrack is immersive, and the overall presentation is excellent. I also appreciate that after completing the game, you can read Grace’s report, which summarizes the events in a clean, narrative format.  One of the best aspects of Requiem is that you don’t need to play every previous entry to understand the story. Having some knowledge of Resident Evil 2 helps, but you can easily catch up by watching the cutscenes online. On standard mode, the game takes about three days to complete.  Another standout feature is the cast of characters you meet along the way and the reveal of the new villain—MAJOR SPOILER ALERT—Zeno, who turns out to be another clone of Wesker. The zombies, infected with a new variant of the T‑Virus, can even speak using the last fragments of their human memories. The game pays a lot of homage to earlier titles, which longtime fans will appreciate. My only complaint is the lack of a New Game Plus mode, meaning you’ll have to upgrade your weapons all over again on each playthrough.  Overall, I had a lot of fun with the campaign and feel it’s a strong follow‑up to RE4 and Village. I’m looking forward to the upcoming downloadable content scheduled for later this month, which will hopefully address missing features such as Mercenaries Mode. On a scale of 10, I give Requiem a 9.5. It’s the best game in the series so far.

Resident Evil 9: Hollow Filler Verdict: Hard pass at $70. Wait for a sale or DLC.  Atmosphere & Logic: The hotel opening is a glorified tech demo, heavy on graphics, but it trades tension for scripted cutscenes. The RPD section feels like a lifeless museum.  Tactical Failures: For a veteran operative, Leon’s lack of preparation is eye rolling. He should be using titanium chainmail and thermal optics, not a basic pistol and chest rig. Guess he spent it all on his wheels and watch, fell for the status symbols instead of functional items I guess. Furthermore, Lickers remain mechanically rigid and video game janky after 30 years, failing to fluidly navigate surfaces as they do in the films.  Broken Economy & UI: The coin system is a glaring example of poor game design. The world is cluttered with them, yet there is nothing to buy after the first items. The leon's box shop UI is a clunky mess and I much prefer the physical weapon attachments of RE3 2020, replacing grounded realism with a bland, confusing shop menu.  Lazy Design: The "choose your ending" mechanic is a low-effort button press. Between the forgettable soundtrack and on-rails motorcycle sequence that handles worse than the PS2 RE4 jet ski  Missed Opportunities: Instead of rehashing 80s tropes and Raccoon City nostalgia, the series should move toward relevant themes like modern settings of bio-warfare or consumer virus strains.

[h3]This is an excellent entry into the Resident Evil series, and a nearly perfect example of what many gamers want to see in their respective genres.[/h3]  Requiem feels like the developers worked as improvement engineers, not only advancing what you might find in a RE game, but also noticing and implementing refinements from other horror titles.  The two characters offer different gameplay experiences which are both very full and fleshed out.  This intertwining feature also enables the pacing of the story to stay fresh, flow smoothly and maintain a lot of tension and suspense.  I enjoyed the story a lot, nuff said!    Visually the game is incredible, it is definitely a top pick for best looking among releases at this time.  If you are able to use ray tracing and push the options a bit it is a feast for the eyes and will never disappoint.  The character models are intricately detailed and very much help ground the physical performances which are all incredible as well.  It is an amazing looking game, hands down.  One detail I loved is how Leon's tired, pallid and aged look really sells the weight of all the years, not to mention the time bomb of a burden that he and others carry.  Sound is outstanding and very well mixed and balanced.  The music is incredible and will keep your pulse red lining in those desperate moments.  The vocal performances from all the cast deserve attention, and the 2 main leads are outstanding and never get old.  Grace's fledgling venture into this story blends nicely with an exhausted Leon who just won't quit.  There were many scenes where I was blown away.  Everybody involved really sunk their teeth into this one and it shows.  RE typically maintains a level of reality [i]just[/i] a bit dialed up in style, and those moments shine as well.  Gameplay is fantastic.  The stealth and survival aspects feel really good.  Requiem is the best feeling RE title for me for character control and action, and there are awesome contextual moments and tons of details that are great fun.  Combat is really good and very fun.  Standard (Classic) felt like a great difficulty setting to really experience the game for those who are themselves experienced in survival horror.  This setting helps to maintain the power balance between Grace and Leon while not hindering player progress in any unfair or cheap ways.  For fans of horror or Resident Evil in general it's a must play.

The first time I played the Resident Evil games was a long time ago, but I became a fan of the series relatively recently - around the end of 2021. The first release after that was the Resident Evil 4 remake, which I wouldn't call bad by any means, but it wasn't a game I was particularly looking forward to - mainly because the original isn't the first in the series that I'd consider a favorite.  So, it's safe to say that the new Resident Evil Requiem is the first game in the franchise I've truly been looking forward to. And I have to say, the first few hours were like an extra New Year for me.  The game starts off incredibly well. Somehow, Capcom managed to combine the qualities of the recent remakes and original installments, and even add a bit of the over-the-top madness of Resident Evil 6 into the mix. And the result isn't some incomprehensible Frankenstein's monster, but perhaps one of the strongest gameplay segments in the series in a very long time.  The attention to detail is particularly striking, especially at the beginning of the game. Some gameplay aspects were meticulously crafted to be used only a couple of times, but they add so much fun! And surely these small, yet memorable, moments must have cost an inordinate amount of resources to develop, only to be used so little. But it's precisely because of them that Requiem initially feels so magical.  I was personally pleased with the developers' take on the series' traditional concept of a "Nemesis-style pursuer", which I have very mixed feelings about overall (and for example I even consider its execution in Resident Evil 2 remake to be quite mediocre). The approach here is more similar to the (unfairly) disliked remake of Resident Evil 3 and Resident Evil Village: we are not pursued too often, and, in most cases, such moments are scripted scenes or gimmicky level sections. In my opinion, this is a better realization of such an idea and the result is much more interesting than the too "mechanical and rule-based" Mr. X from the Resident Evil 2 remake.  However, Requiem is so much Resident Evil that it manages to replicate a quality that plagues many games in the series. Specifically, the second half of the game is somewhat inferior to the first. It doesn't feel like it received any less attention than the first half, don't get me wrong. The entire game is very well made. But for some reason, the second half of Requiem is simply far less inspired, far less special.  And perhaps the game's biggest "sin", which manifests itself towards the end, is its overreliance on nostalgia. At some point, Requiem goes out of its way to constantly remind the player of "the old days" and bombard them with references, as if constantly asking: "Remember this? And this? And this? Cool, right?" Up to a point, it's enjoyable, but by the end, it simply becomes tiresome and feels a bit forced.  But even with a slight note of disappointment, Resident Evil Requiem, for me, is one of the most impressive entries in the series in a long time. And remember, we're talking about a franchise in which new games have boasted a very high bar of quality for a decade now, seemingly managing to please everyone. This is no trivial achievement. Will the series ever achieve the ideal I personally dream of? I'm VERY interested to find out.

Resident Evil Requiem feels like a love letter to those of us who grew up with the original games, while still being accessible enough for newcomers. You do not need to have played any previous Resident Evil to enjoy it.  Capcom finally found the right balance here. Grace’s sections bring back that classic survival horror tension, with limited resources and the kind of inventory management that actually matters. Leon’s sections lean more into action, but thankfully not in the over-the-top RE6 way. They feel much closer to the best action moments from RE4.  The atmosphere is incredible. Genuinely oppressive, tense, and at times terrifying. Play this with headphones or, even better, a proper surround system. Alone. At night. No phone, no distractions.  The game also has solid replay value, since some of your choices are irreversible and can lead to different outcomes. That alone makes another run worth it.  Final verdict: if you loved the classic games and also appreciated RE4, this is absolutely worth playing. If you are a purist who hated RE4 and everything that came after it, you may want to skip it. Still, if you care about the old storyline and want closure, I would say it is worth trying anyway.  This game is a solid 10/10.

Resident Evil Requiem is by far the best RE to ever exist. I was frankly quite apprehensive at first, but the more I played it the more I enjoyed it.  Let's start with the characters...  I absolutely love Grace. She's a heavily scarred individual that frequently struggles to deal with the trauma of her past. She then has to confront this trauma head-on and it makes her story much more meaningful. I felt a personal connection to her awkwardness, shyness, fear and clumsiness. Her actress Angela is simply fantastical.  Leon is back and great as always. He's got the same wit as in Resident Evil 4 and is the biggest badass ever. I'm glad they brought him back into the story in a way that made sense. He's also got some of his own "baggage" that he deals with and it's cool to see that unveil in the story.  Other characters such as Victor, "Z", were very well written as well but I'd rather not speak too much about them as to not spoil the story.   The visuals and atmosphere are some of the best in the series, this game absolutely nails it. From the Care Center to Raccoon City, the well kept city to the desolation, it's all really visually impressive even without Path Tracing. Almost every place in Raccoon City and whereabouts is extremely cinematic. I took over 500 screenshots through the entire game, it's pretty and runs well on most machines.  The gameplay is extremely fun, however, Grace's sections are a bit lopsided in difficulty when compared to Leon's. While Grace's is supposed to be survival horror, it leans too much on the difficult side and made me switch to "Casual". This switch made Leon's section way too easy taking all of the challenge away from the experience. Still, I had fun.  The game also manages to leave enough downtime when necessary and I truly appreciate it. It lets you take in the sights and the atmosphere when needed and keeps things fresh when combat/horror comes back.  Finally, I think this game is an absolute masterpiece. There were multiple surprises and lots of moments where I was smiling ear to ear on how absurdly fun this game is. From the grounded moments to the crazy ones, this game is an absolute masterpiece. It is worth every cent and is a strong GOTY contender.

Resident Evil requiem is the best of the six modern Resident Evil games, combining the best elements of the first-person horror from 7 and 8 with the satisfying third-person shooting from the remake trilogy (2, 3, 4 remakes.) The devs learned a lot about what works and what doesn't, and they really fine tuned the formula into to a modern classic.  Although the game gives you the option to switch camera perspectives, the recommended default settings are best. Grace's first person segments are meant to make you feel powerless, and using a third person camera diminishes that intent. In contrast, Leon's gameplay is fast paced and works better with quicker camera movement, but it's still scary at times even in third person if you're not careful.  The modern RE games have been full of great voice acting, but the fearful performance by Grace's actor is phenomenal. Some of her cutscenes felt incredibly realistic and made me forget I was playing a game. Leon's actor also did a great job portraying Leon becoming old and tired. The story, though still full of the same old RE tropes, does have a few new tricks up its sleeve to freshen things up. The cutscenes have a more Hollywood movie feel in contrast to prior games. Overall, the production value on this installment feels higher than usual for RE.

Resident Evil 9: Requiem – A Haunting Evolution Rooted in Survival Horror Legacy  Few franchises have managed to reinvent themselves as boldly—and as successfully—as Resident Evil. With Resident Evil 9: Requiem, the series doesn’t just push forward; it reflects, refines, and resurrects the very essence that made Resident Evil 2 such a landmark in gaming history.  From the moment Requiem begins, there’s a palpable sense of dread that feels intimately familiar. Fans of Resident Evil 2 will immediately recognize the DNA: tight, oppressive environments, resource scarcity, and that constant, gnawing tension that danger could be lurking just beyond the next door. But Requiem doesn’t merely imitate—it evolves.  Where Resident Evil 2 thrived on claustrophobic police station corridors and methodical pacing, Requiem expands its world without sacrificing intensity. The environments are broader, more dynamic, and layered with environmental storytelling that rewards careful exploration. Yet, despite this scale, the game never loses its grip on fear. Every shadow feels deliberate. Every sound matters.  Narratively, Requiem is one of the series’ most mature entries. It masterfully weaves psychological horror with the franchise’s signature bio-organic terror. The story doesn’t just rely on shocking mutations or grotesque enemies—it digs into trauma, consequence, and the lingering scars of past outbreaks. In doing so, it feels like a natural thematic continuation of Resident Evil 2, where survival wasn’t just physical, but emotional.  Gameplay is where the connection becomes even more striking. Requiem brings back that careful inventory management and deliberate combat rhythm that made Resident Evil 2 so compelling. Every bullet counts. Every encounter is a decision: fight, flee, or outsmart. But modern refinements—fluid movement, smarter enemy AI, and seamless transitions—make the experience feel fresh rather than nostalgic.  Perhaps the most impressive achievement of Requiem is its atmosphere. Much like the iconic police station in Resident Evil 2, the game creates spaces that feel alive—and hostile. Lighting, sound design, and environmental detail come together to produce moments of pure, unfiltered terror. It’s not just about jump scares; it’s about sustained, psychological pressure.  In many ways, Resident Evil 9: Requiem feels like a love letter to Resident Evil 2, but written with the confidence of a series that knows exactly what it has become. It honors the past without being trapped by it, delivering an experience that is both nostalgic and boldly new.  Final Verdict: Resident Evil 9: Requiem is a masterclass in survival horror—an unforgettable blend of old-school tension and modern design. For longtime fans, it’s a return to form. For newcomers, it’s a defining experience. Either way, it stands as one of the strongest entries the franchise has ever seen.  missed you Leon!
