Resident Evil 9 is the perfect amalgamation of every aspect that made each Resident Evil entry amazing.  Grace's gameplay heavily focuses on resource management, with it being a lot like the originals in that sense, or much like 7. If you have the means to get past a section without using ammo, you take that chance, because it's imperative. Choosing what to leave behind and what to take, having to make extensive use of the item box, all whilst thrown into some of the most immersive and haunting dynamic horror presented in the series yet, with each environment carefully designed to immerse you in the horror of Grace's story.  Leon on the other hand whips you straight back to RE4. Plentiful ammo, gruesome finishers, elegant parrying, and corny one liners. Requiem also introduces new combat mechanics, such as being able to throw fallen opponents weapons to save ammo and get some major damage in, and being able to throw explosive barrels to deal with grouped enemies. Whilst it is reminiscent of RE4's combat, it strives to go far above what RE4 allowed, giving a new level of fluidity and action to Leon's sections.  The environments, however, are by far one of the most impressive feats of this game. As Grace, each room is designed to make you as anxious and petrified as possible, whether it be a coat rack angled like it's a stalker, or smashed glass alerting every nearby monster that you're vulnerable. As Leon, the environment is your weapon, whether it be shooting glass out from under a zombie and watching them fall to their death, or stomping a zombies brain into a banister. The environment's interactivity is a welcome change to the Resident Evil Formula, and makes each encounter feel so much more immersive.   Whilst I preferred Leon's action oriented gameplay, with the original RE4 being one of my favourite games of all time, Grace's gameplay astonished me, as someone who never really gets scared by horror games, because I spent each second of it clenching, and trying to avoid a cardiac arrest. RE9 has by far my favourite monster designs yet, with each monster feeling so akin to that of the monsters you imagined under your bed as a child, so familiar and yet so unfamiliar, the perfect recipe to a panic alt-f4.

I went into Resident Evil: Requiem expecting something that tried to capture the older feel of Resident Evil—and for the most part, it delivers.  What stands out right away is the atmosphere. It leans into that slow, uneasy tension where you’re constantly second-guessing what you hear or see. It’s not just about jump scares—it’s about the feeling that something isn’t right, and that sticks with you the longer you play.  The puzzles and exploration feel familiar in a good way, but they can be frustrating at times. There were moments where I found myself stuck longer than I probably should’ve been, not because it was difficult in a rewarding way, but because it wasn’t always clear what the game wanted from you. That said, when things click, it feels satisfying.  Being hunted is where the game really shines. It creates pressure without constantly overwhelming you, and it keeps the pacing unpredictable. One minute you’re exploring, the next you’re trying to figure out how to not get caught—it definitely gets your attention.  It’s not perfect. The pacing can dip, and some parts feel a little rough around the edges. But overall, it captures something that a lot of modern horror games miss: tension over noise, atmosphere over chaos.  If you enjoy slower, more methodical horror with a focus on exploration and being just uncomfortable enough to stay engaged, this is worth your time.

This is not the best in the series. This game showcases some of CAPCOMs bests, but repeats some of their worsts to new levels of stupidity.  This game isn't bad at all.  I would rank it behind RE4R + RE2R as the third best of the modern RE Engine games, easily beating out 7 and 8; only barely beating RE3R due to having a wider roster of enemies.  This game is two games stitched together. For Grace's part of it, I would rate it a 7: it's bogged down by the same things I dislike 7 + 8 for; in some instances, takes the most annoying aspects from those to new extremes.  Leon's part, I would put it around 8.5; it would be higher if it clearly wasn't made as a sort of apology tour for the state of RE3R.  Resident Evil is a series built on its replay value/unlockables, & that's the first gripe I have w/ this game.  The unlockable content is dire, more limited than RE3R which the same people regaling Requiem derided RE3R for lacking in.  Grace gets a knife & a machine pistol.  Leon gets some cool guns, but pales to just how many RE3R gave.  Insanity too is fairly basic: a few items have been moved & you see certain enemies earlier; it's not Arrange Mode, it's not Madhouse: key items remain in the same place. Replayability in this game is the 3rd worst of the modern series: I would replay it over 7 & 8, but that's not saying much.  1 thing hurting the replayability is no Scenario Select: in future if I want to play the peaks of Leon, Grace's campaign & the later Orphanage become a "oh, that part" that will convince me not to.   Not only are the unlockables minimal, but there are 0 extra modes. I don't know why CAPCOM continues to avoid just making Mercenaries a series staple.   R.E, Grace: I like her character,  I enjoyed her sections for the most part, but where I grew sour on them was the constant unkillable chase sequences with The Girl.  Since RE7, CAPCOM love their unkillable stalker enemies, but since 7, the cracks have been visible: the AI behaves the same in every. single. game.  They only ever patrol Us, Os & linear hallways + will always retreat due to a gimmick or threshold.  If you've played and remind yourself you've played 7, much like the baby in RE8, The Girl won't scare you.  Instead, her ranged grabs and tanky nature will only serve to annoy you & the manner in which she shows up sucks all tension out of the game.  Play an area where you have to turn the lights off? You already know she's going to spawn, you already know you'll have to hide in a corner or blast her with Requiem & move on; it plays out the same every time.   CAPCOM, in 1999 you cracked the formula to a pursuer enemy with Nemesis: even though he's scripted in RE3R, they still got it right that you could dispatch him & have some downtime.  This game has the worst stalker in the series & she's beyond tedious and boring.   Adding to Grace's section, I enjoyed the Zombies having their own personalities, but it was underused & by the time you're in the underground area, the zombies are just basic dudes again; the game had a solid idea it just abandons 1/3 through.  You're incentivised to avoid them but even on Classic in my first run, I killed every enemy as Grace to the point where Leon just had empty rooms later.  Now onto Leon, where IMO the game is at its best.  It's clear playing his sections that CAPCOM wanted to just make another Leon game, & that's a good thing. They should have been honest with themselves from the start & just gone with that, b/c Leon's parts are so very solid.   He's seasoned, he's rugged, he knows his BOW types + how to beat them and so we get an RE6-lite style of gameplay where Leon is a lot more grounded & brutal.   The gameplay shines in the hub-like Central Camp area of Raccoon City: the devs - and I - had a lot of fun with the set pieces, like a totalled skyscraper with glass floors you could shoot out to make Zombies fall.   If I could select only Leon's campaign, this would be up there with 2R + 4R on replayability for me.  We need to stop alienating 4, 5 + 6 like action REs are some ugly disease, when the gameplay feels best when it leans into it, as we saw with the masterpiece that is RE4R.  Though this game has the same DNA as RE6 IMO, it succeeds at striking a better balance.  [Spoilers] Story-wise? I don't have a lot to say. RE story is like the narrative in a porno, but I do like that Zeno went his own way compared to who he was based on, and I enjoyed that Victor Gideon was essentially Ledger's Joker injected with the NTa-Parasite.  What I didn't like however was the retcon that Spencer felt bad about all the child-abducting, torturing and experiments he did all of a sudden: this is the man who bragged he was going to be God in RE5, now suddenly he had an epiphany and wanted to atone. I don't buy it, and I won't buy it unless CAPCOM makes an RE5R and dramatically alters the story, because with only OG5 to go off of, this seems like an absurd retcon even by RE standards. Only a couple years back, we had a file in VILLAGE of him boasting to Mother Miranda about using the mutamycete to subjugate people.   One part of story I have to touch on affects the gameplay.  Like Spencer, this game also seems to be trying to atone in a way for the critiques of RE2R and RE3R.  Plant 42 was cut, so in this game we get Plant 43.  Black Tiger was cut? In this, we get a new giant spider.  Super Tyrant's original boss fight was reduced to an elevator fight? Now you can fight one on the streets of RC.   This is good and all from a gameplay perspective, but it makes me lament that we didn't get this in 2019 and 2020, and furthermore, why is Leon the one going through them, and not Jill or Chris, or even Claire? I love Leon, but there were moments in this game, particularly against Gideon at the end where Leon makes reference to how persistent a Nemesis is, but how would he know? It doesn't feel earned, and it makes that crater-sized hole where Jill SHOULD be all the more evident.  It comes across as very lazy asset reuse that our final boss of this big anniversary swansong game is a reused asset from the worst modern RE remake, RE3R.   Onto performance.  On my machine, I was at a locked 120 (Variable setting, then capped with AMD Adrenalin at 120), 1080p with no upscaling or FG.  Game ran like a dream, as I've come to expect from any RE Engine game that isn't MH or Dragon's Dogma.   Visually, this is one of the most gorgeous games ever made. Even when you reach Raccoon City and the game becomes brown and drab, there's a beauty in the macabre and the gore, character + weapon models and terrain all pop out at you like the most stunning vistas.  It's hard to imagine where we go from here, graphics feel they're at their peak, and complementing them are animations so good they put RE4R, Death Stranding 2 and RDR2 to shame. Leon has a unique animation for all stances, all weapons, all contexts like being staggered holding X weapon, the amount of effort that must have gone into mocapping these must be monumental.  Overall, 7.5/10. I don't regret buying (at 48% off), but it's not what I want the future of RE to be.  RE4R perfected the formula. I only hope the future is more of that, & less of 7, 8 & 9 - because they're obviously made for people who didn't like the older games.  Comments cont.

Resident Evil 9: Requiem, is a fascinating Game. By splitting the narrative between the legendary Leon S. Kennedy and  Grace, the game attempts to marry the series' high-octane action roots with its claustrophobic, psychological foundations. For the most part, it succeeds in delivering a cinematic powerhouse, even if a few choices hit some sour notes.  The Leon Experience: Blockbuster Brilliance Playing as Leon feels like stepping directly into a summer blockbuster. These segments are a masterclass in choreographed chaos, featuring tight gunplay and set pieces that demand quick reflexes. The "action movie" energy is palpable, providing a satisfying sense of power that long-time fans of RE4 will find instantly familiar.  The Grace Experience: Slow-Burn Terror On the flip side, Grace’s chapters offer a stark, effective departure. These sequences are thick with atmosphere, trading explosive firepower for tense, suspenseful exploration. The pacing here is deliberate, forcing players to manage limited resources while navigating environments that feel genuinely threatening. It’s in these quiet moments that Requiem truly finds its horror identity.  The Rough Edges While the gameplay is addictive, a few elements break the immersion:  Vocal Delivery: Grace’s voice acting occasionally misses the mark, leaning into over acting or trying too much to cnvey her fear.  - Leon’s audio design is surprisingly distracting. His penchant for constant grunting and moaning during every physical exertion—from climbing to taking damage even from running —becomes a repetitive soundtrack that wears thin over a long campaign.  The Completionist’s Nightmare: For the trophy hunters and achievement chasers, the requirements for the highest difficulty levels are more irritating than challenging. Rather than testing skill, it tests for patenice .  Final Verdict Resident Evil 9: Requiem is a thrill ride that successfully juggles two very different styles of play. Despite some grating audio choices and a punishing achievement list, the core experience is a polished, high-stakes journey through one of gaming’s most iconic worlds.

A glorious combination of everything Capcom has learned from the beginning of the series and up until its recent retreading through the remakes.  Grace's sections are everything good from RE2 (particularly that first area, which could be amongst the best in the whole franchise) and Leon's sections are everything good from RE4. They nailed the balance between them and it's never shocking or awkward to switch between both characters.  Visually outstanding, with generally great level design, and all the QoL additions make it very easy to get 100% completion (or be very close, at least) if you're a bit careful and check the map often.  The story is along the line of other titles, and it sneaks in a handful of homages and easter eggs from previous entries all the way through as a sort of celebration of everything up to this point, but they don't feel jarring or forced most of the time.  I had a wonderful time with it and I'll absolutely be there for the DLC.

Before getting into how good the game is, I want to point out a couple of technical issues I experienced. For some reason, the first time I launch the game after booting my PC, it crashes. I’m not sure if this is just on my system, but it happens consistently. On that same first launch, I sometimes get strange graphical glitches—similar to when a GPU is failing, with colored squares appearing on screen. After restarting the game, everything runs perfectly fine.  Another odd issue is the lack of a mouse sensitivity option. I spent quite a while looking for it but couldn’t find anything. Because of that, turning can feel a bit clunky at first. It’s not game-breaking, though—you do eventually get used to it.  Now, with that out of the way: the game is amazing.  The optimization is solid, and the combat is easily the best in the entire Resident Evil franchise. I’d honestly rank this as a top 2 Resident Evil game. It was so fun that I ended up 100% completing it just to get all the achievements.  One of the standout features is how differently the game feels depending on who you play. With Grace, the experience is genuinely tense and scary. She’s not as experienced as Leon, so you constantly struggle with ammo and health, and you have to keep your distance from enemies. It really emphasizes survival horror.  On the other hand, playing as Leon flips the experience completely. The moment you step into combat, it feels like the zombies should be afraid of you. It’s that classic Leon energy—like the doom music kicks in and you’re the biggest threat in the room.  There are also some new bosses that I’ve never seen before in a Resident Evil game. I won’t spoil anything, but they’re definitely worth experiencing for yourself.  All in all, I strongly recommend Resident Evil Requiem. Despite a few minor issues, it’s an incredibly fun and memorable game.

The graphics, attention to detail and the cinematography of the game combined with the amazing sound design and music make for an immersive experience which draws you in and keeps you playing for hours. As soon as the first playthrough is finished and all the challenges are unlocked that grant completion points to be spent on fun extras for the game like infinite ammo or new weapons, some of which are necessary to compete the games tougher challenges and difficulties.  All in, this game is an easy 10/10, Capcom have done it once again and I can’t wait to see what the DLC will bring.

Did I enjoy the experience? Absolutely. Did it justify its full price? Unfortunately, no.  I genuinely tried to appreciate what the game offers, taking in the atmosphere, examining the environmental detail, experimenting with the weapon variety, and admiring the character models and overall presentation. However, by the end, it felt like the experience fell short of what I would expect from a full priced RE title.  There is also the matter of post launch support. While a DLC has been announced, it is difficult to see that as a complete solution. Previous entries in the series set a stronger precedent when it comes to additional content. Even RE7 which is often less favored by some players, still offered meaningful extra content. Likewise, RE2 included modes like ghost survivors, and RE4 featured mercenaries. These additions significantly enhanced replayability. In comparison, this installment feels lacking in that regard.  There are also several design decisions that are difficult to overlook. Weapon customization is unnecessarily restrictive. Scopes can be detached, but not stocks. Additionally, the inability to adjust fire modes on certain weapons such as the matilda, limits tactical flexibility, particularly in terms of ammo conservation. Some aesthetic changes, like the model 70’s altered appearance after upgrades, may not appeal to all players.  Customization options are also limited. While there are minor cosmetic options for select starter handguns, the system does not extend far enough to feel meaningful. More importantly, progression systems in new game plus are disappointing. Weapon upgrades and character improvements do not carry over in a satisfying way which undermines the incentive to replay the game.  Beyond these issues, the game is notably short and offers less replay value than its predecessors. With no substantial additional modes at launch and limited incentives for repeat playthroughs, the overall package feels incomplete.  In its current state, the game would benefit from expanded content, improvements to weapon customization, and a more rewarding NG+ system. I do recommend this game just not at it's current price point.

A blend of RE7, RE4, with an attempt at the spirit of RE2 that struggles with pacing. It is an attempted love letter to the distinct eras of RE that mostly succeeds and is still an excellent game.   The strongest horror part of the game, by far, is the sanitarium as Grace, strictly via atmosphere. However, the quantity and quality of puzzles is lower than the RE1, RE2, RE3, or RE7, all of which this game is trying to simulate in that section. The [spoiler]invincible stalker[/spoiler] section has been done before and much better throughout the rest of the series.  The action hero part of the game is like a main story version of Mercenaries a la RE4 and RE8 that is very much enjoyable, but this half of the game loses a lot of momentum to the interspersed Grace sections, especially the forced [spoiler]hide-and-seek[/spoiler] part. Funnily enough, it has the same problem that RE6 did, in that the combat was a blast but kept getting interrupted by, well, the rest of the game.   The story is usually RE fare (that is, corny, tropey horror schlock that's endearing), but Angela Sant'Albano has a brilliant performance as Grace; it's series defining and it's not particularly close.   ~27 hours for 98% completion, including challenge and insanity runs (no, I don't want to do more playthroughs to suck up enough blood for 100%). I'll lump this one in with R3make and RE8: worth it on sale if you're unsure, worth it at full price if you already are invested in the series.

When RE9 launched, I wanted it badly but couldn't justify the spend, so I held off with no spoilers, no playthroughs, nothing. I finally bit the bullet recently and I'm so glad I went in completely blind, because it made the experience hit so much harder.   Grace's introduction alone took me a few hours to get through since I'm genuinely terrified of horror games, but that slow, dread-filled buildup was clearly intentional and does a brilliant job pulling you into the world.   The game does ease up on the pure horror as you progress, but don't get too comfortable as the orphanage section completely blindsided me and I could not get through it in a single sitting. Gameplay-wise, if you've played the modern RE titles you'll feel right at home, but everything feels tighter and more refined, and the pacing between the two protagonists is handled really well.   The story is where the game genuinely surprised me though as I was on the edge of my seat the entire way through, the narrative unravels at just the right pace, and the ending left me genuinely excited for whatever comes next, even if that's another decade away knowing Capcom.   Overall, amazing atmosphere, great gameplay, and a story that actually sticks the landing, one of the best in the series.

To the point ============== Like an expensive cake filled with a poo-filled center, this is a fantastic survival horror experience in the beginning and an unbelievably tedious slog in the end. It's a tough game to recommend, but if you're a franchise fan like me you've already bought it, to anyone else maybe consider a sale or a lore video.  +Cleared on Classic difficulty+ +Some light spoilers ahead+  Good Stuff =============== - Grace, our deuteragonist, has some of the best horror sections since RE7. Very tense and creative while not being overwhelming. I loved all of her scenarios and these are the parts I would willingly replay.  - Early Leon segments in the care center are really fun. They're short and sweet segments that help drive home how different he and Grace's experiences are and I loved getting to play through them.  - The story, for it's MANY weaknesses, hopefully puts a bow on Umbrella references going forward ( thought I doubt it). It would be nice to more deeply explore new antagonists in the future and put the OG aside.  Bad Stuff ================= - Oh boy the second half of this game, beginning with the exploration of Raccoon City, just wore me down. It's ugly, it's takes for ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ EVER and it's not creative. You effectively go from ambush to ambush as Leon collecting bomb parts and it feel like padding in the most generous definition.   It makes all the mistakes of RE6, transitioning away from a horror game and into a straight action set piece with Grace sidelined for Leon. I don't know why Capcom is incapable of making strong second halves for the last 3 games (The ship from RE7, the factory from RE8 and now this) when their beginnings are so strong. Complete disappointment.  - The story is a mess. Introducing characters only to immediately either kill them or have them meander around doing nothing. Emily, and a certain late game character that only exists to aura farm are just some examples.  - "Do you remember THIS Resident Evil Trope ?!" Is something you'll find yourself being asked over and over again by the devs during your playthrough. The game isn't confident enough to tell it's own story so you just get very frequent 'memberberries. Good lord it's so rife in Leon's sections too where I wouldn't blame him if he though he was stuck in a time loop or something.  - Capcom REALLY seems to not understand what made Leon so great in RE4. Yeah he was a wise cracking secret agent but his whole schtick didn't consist of doing Avengers level physical feats in every scene while cracking one-liners. Even a little restraint with him would have made him seem that much better. Hell, they could have even used the excuse of his sickness as to why he's not so crazy powerful in this game but they went the total opposite way with it.  - There are, generously, like 5 enemy types in this game. It's like the Molded from RE7 but somehow more boring. The smart zombies concept is interesting in the first section, but then you fight dusty zombies in the ruins, lumpy zombies in the lab and my least favorite, Commandos in the lab. I had to take a break with the Commandos because ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥...why? The bosses are mostly non-existent and prefer to be portrayed as gauntlet style battles. Oh and the last boss sucks after all the build up.  - I realize how harsh this review sounds but all in all this game is solid. If you're not going in with a ton of expectations like myself, you'll probably like it quite a bit more so take this review as one from a grumpy elder RE fan.

If you're a longtime fan of the series, this may not be the game you're looking for. instead of following in Ethan's footsteps or taking a page from RE2 remake's Leon, Grace's gameplay is a stealth game, plain and simple, while you will have to deal with some encounters head on, for the most part you're staying low and quiet and your resources are best put towards stealth-killing enemies. There are SOME puzzles, but they're certainly lacking. Leon on the other hand has you playing very fast and aggressive. Quick reflexes to parry attacks and quick aim to take out targets, some of which give you small, hard to hit windows later in the game. And while the game does offer a classic mode that utilizes ink ribbon saves instead of modern checkpoints for when you die as something for the classic fans, i recommend against it as the game has what i can best describe as "modern balancing", where as dying has become inconsequential in modern games (no life counters, autosave checkpoints only setting you back to just before the current fight, etc.) the punishment has instead been shifted to making the individual mistakes, and punish your each mistake the will,  with single mistakes being very capable of wrecking you, or even one hit killing you, as this game does seem fond of insta-death mechanics which doesn't take too long to show up for grace and even in the parrying tutorial for leon.  If you're someone who loves this game, more power to you, it's just not for me. so far the biggest appeal has just been the callbacks to earlier games and that's it, it's been more frustration than enjoyment and personally has me questioning if i want to continue with the series, as RE2 remake has been the best RE game capcom's made since the originals back on PS1 and capcom just hasn't been able to follow it up correctly since

I currently own and have completed every RE game that's available on Steam, and my history with the franchise goes all the way back to the original Resident Evil on Playstation in the cardboard long box. Out of all the RE games out there, this very well might just be my favorite. Amazing in concept and execution.   The dual-protagonist campaign is nothing new, but the way it's executed is the chef's kiss. The dichotomy of Grace's first-person true survival horror and Leon's third-person more action oriented horror perfectly portrays the two styles that the RE franchise has always exceeded at.   The graphics are beautiful, the art style is very good, and the audio is simply stunning. From the soundtrack to the characters themselves, and the very ambiance, it's a treat for the ears.   The combat (or aversion to in the case of Grace's story) is very good, I think maybe the best in the franchise. The bosses are unique, but could be more difficult and still be enjoyable to beat.   Finally, this game feels like a love letter to classic RE fans, especially those who have followed Leon's journey since RE2. The return to Raccoon city, and even the fact that Leon ends up opening the very same gate that he closed 28 years ago, hit me hard in the nostalgia feels. There's plenty of that in this game, the RCPD building still has some secrets left.   Replayability is very good, It's not a long game once you know the puzzles, but in the 43-odd hours I've played at the time of this review, I have beaten modern, classic and insanity difficulty modes and gotten all Steam achievements. I have not yet completed the final puzzle, that will be my next playthrough.   All in all, I would absolutely recommend this game to, well, everyone.   TL;DR: Fantastic Game, buy it now.

The environments are beautiful, with a special mention for returning to Raccoon City after the nuclear bombing. The atmosphere is incredible. My favorite scene was, without a doubt, the motorcycle chase with Victor Gideon on the highway through the ruins of the city. The moment when you ride vertically up the remains of a tower and then launch into a glide over Raccoon City after reaching the top… it was just amazing both visually and in terms of sensation.  As for the story, I found it well-written and really engaging. It makes you curious to see what happens next, especially if you’ve played the previous entries in the series.  If I had to mention one downside, it would be those FPS drops in areas where a lot of elements are rendered at once. But honestly, it’s a minor issue compared to the overall quality of the game. Resident Evil: Requiem showcases Capcom's continued effort to stay at the cutting edge of the survival-horror genre, just as they were with the original title back in 1996.  In Requiem, we finally get to see many of the lessons learned since the soft FPS-reboot in RE7 start to meaningfully overlap with both the gameplay and story elements from the classic games.  The RE Engine shows its prowess once again as an incredibly well-optimized powerhouse for modern graphics. It incorporates real-time global illumination and shadows, and even supports full path-tracing if your hardware can handle it.  The game is also longer than most recent entries, which is generally a good thing since some of the previous entries felt on the shorter side. That said, there is a roughly 2-hour section in the latter half of the game where the plot somewhat crawls to a halt.  I'd recommend playing the rest of the "modern" games (REmake 2, 3, 4, 7, and 8) before picking up Requiem. Doing so will give you the best overall experience.

Resident Evil: Requiem is, without a doubt, one of the best games I have ever played. From the very first moments, it pulled me in and never let go. The game is both very fun and scary at the same time, Capcom nailed perfectly action and horror in one title.   The graphics are absolutely beautiful, and every area you explore looks amazing and full of detail. The whole atmosphere of the game just feels creepy, tense, and interesting all at once.  The story builds up in a really satisfying way, that I was always curious to see what happens next. The puzzles are fun to figure out without them being too annoying. The combat mechanics feels good and works well, making every fight feel rewarding. The crafting system is nice, though Grace's part of it is kinda weird, but I don’t mind.  One of the coolest things in the game is being able to pick between first-person and third-person view. The game suggests third-person for Leon and first-person for Grace, and I did played like that and it was the perfect choice for both characters.   I also have to mention the voice actors. Nick Apostolides cooked as Leon, his one-liners made me laugh so much and Grace’s voice actress Angela Sant'Albano deserves an oscar for her performace. Her actiong was so real and so nautral as if they had real zombies on the set. I hope we will see Grace in future RE games.  There are two things I did not like though. The orphanage part of the game was not a good time for me. I think it should have just been a cutscene, and we should have gotten something else to play instead. The game also feels a bit too short, it’s defnetly not 18 hours, I had 12 hours on my 1st playtrough while searching every corner of the map.  Still, Resident Evil: Requiem was a fantastic adventure that I will not forget any time soon. The atmosphere, story, gamepley and acting, it all comes together perfectly. The game starts off strong with a focus on survival/horror that the franchise is known for with a compelling new main character, but around the half-way mark turns into a generic action game which almost makes the action in RE5 look tame in comparison.  There is a noticeable drop-off in quality when this change happens, both in terms of writing and gameplay. When you change over to Leon from Grace, the game starts to feel extremely reliant on fan-service and aura moments.   As for the gameplay, Grace's segment is up there with peak RE with a top tier mansion-esque area to explore, which is oozing with atmosphere. But with Leon you just kind of have a generic open area to walk around and shoot enemies constantly.  Unfortunately, as good as Grace's segment was, I didn't find it to be all that scary due to how scripted the enemies felt. That is my only complaint with her segment aside from it not being longer.   Overall, I would say this is a solid game, but probably the worst of the RE engine games. Interested to see what the general consensus in a few years will be when the hype dies down a bit. Would recommend playing, but not at full-price due to me only liking about 4 hours of the game (took me just shy of 10 in-game hours to complete). Would definitely recommend on sale. Finally, shout-out for a bug free, well optimised experience.  Grace's section(s) - 9/10.  Leon's sections - 5/10.

To the review, Resident Evil: Requiem is a great Resident Evil game, and a great game in general that manages to balance horror and action better than most games in recent years. What I found really impressive is how the game makes the character swaps come with such different [i]tones and feelings[/i]. Playing as Grace is genuinely a horror game as you try to survive in your first playthrough. Playing as Leon is just like a satisfying itch being scratched where you can fight all the zombies you had to avoid earlier. The action, fighting gameplay, and gun controls are good with suspenseful moments. The search and craft mechanics are easy, and fun. The Mansion was easily the best section of the game, with a great choices as to how to make Grace's choices affect Leon's gameplay experience when it was his turn. Racoon City and the City Center were definitely the weaker parts, but they offered such different feelings they felt almost a second game in playstyle in a good way though.  I am on my second playthrough, and one complaint is the challenges that actually provide decent credits require way too much time. Resident Evil Requiem is a disappointing entry in the series.  The game is relatively short, barely reaching 10 hours at best. There is a clear lack of enemy variety, and the puzzles are overly simple and uninspired. The story feels shallow and lacks depth, making it hard to stay engaged.  Boss fights are few in number, and unfortunately, they are both easy and very short, which removes any sense of challenge or excitement. On top of that, there is an annoying visual filter that makes the game look blurry and unclear most of the time.  Overall, the game feels weaker and smaller in scope compared to previous entries—especially Resident Evil 4, which set a much higher standard in terms of content, gameplay, and design.  What makes it worse is that Capcom is charging $70 for such a limited experience. Even more frustrating is the director openly talking about future DLC, which makes it feel like content was intentionally held back just to generate more profit from players.  Let’s not forget the obvious in-game marketing and promotion of commercial products, which further breaks immersion.  Overall, this feels like a step backward for the franchise and not worth the full price.

Resident Evil 9 Requiem attempts to give fans both, a survival horror experience they've come to expect from entries like Resident Evil 7 or the Resident Evil 2 Remake, and the action oriented gameplay they've come to expect from the Resident Evil 4 Remake bundled into one package. And they absolutely delivered!  In classic Resident Evil fashion, there is a mansion-like space to explore in the first part and it does not disappoint. I think it stands shoulder-to-shoulder with Spencer Mansion (from Resident Evil 1) and RPD (from Resident Evil 2) as starting hub areas. They nailed the tensions and feeling of helplessness with the lack of ammo and resources. I was constantly feeling like I'd never be able to make it further.  The actions sections were also done really well. Think of it as a distilled, mature RE4R combat experience. You fight through loads of zombies with the occasional classic Leon one-liner and it always feels super satisfying.  couple minor gripes. some of the dialogue and narrative stuff is a bit corny/hard to listen to, and the intro section with the flashback in the Wrenwood Hotel is annoying to play on repeat playthroughs, wish you could skip it.  This is an excellent entry in to the franchise. The horror sections are great, the actions sections are great, and the fan service is spot on.

This is definitely one of the best games in the series, and definitely one of the best games I have ever played, however it has some flaws, that are kinda important to point out. Before I begin, I just want to point out that I have 100% completion on this game, which means that I  have a decent amount of hours on it and had to go through many playthroughs. Anyway, to begin with, the game has a very good and interesting storyline, which has you hooked and constantly thinking and wondering until the last moment. Also, the characters included in this game are very interesting in my opinion, especially Leon ( but maybe I am a little biased since he is my favouriote). The graphics and the atmposhepre are phenomenal, while also showing tribute to the ogs, and the gameplay feels very smooth and satisfying. Unfortunately, here is where the main problems start to occur. The game offers a 50/50 mix of horror, puzzle-solving and item-managemnt gameplay when you play as Grace, and action-packed, intense and combat-focused gameplay when you play as Leon. During your first playthrough as Grace you will come to realise that the scare-factor and survival horror aspect of this game is perfect, BUT, this only applies to your 1st playthrough. After that, during your other playthroughs, you will come to realise that Graces gameplay feels significantlly weaker than Leons, since you are no longer scared (becasue you already know what to expect), while also having to deal with the fact that Graces arsenal is VERY VERY LIMITED, WEAK and BORING, thus making you spend 50% of the rest of your playthroughs having to go through the same areas with the same boring weapons over and over again. On teh other hand, Leons gameplay is perfected, you are playing as a 49 year old Leon during his prime, using smooth and satisfying melee attacks and axe combos, combined with a very satisfying, but also kinda limited (since Leon doesnt have access to many guns in this game compared to RE4R) arsenal. Despite that, I found Leons gameplay to way more interesting, fun and satisfying than Graces in every single aspect. BUT, another MAJOR Downside is that you cant start a NG+ in this game, which means that you have to gain access to those weapons and build your arsenal from the beginning each time you replay the game. As you can see, the main issue with this game is that it offers poor replayability value, which is a very significant Downside when it comes to RE Games. To sum up, despite its negatives I would so far as to say that this still remains as one of my favourite RE games and it would definitely be at the number 1 spot if it wasnt for the poor replayabilty value (since currently I cant decide wether to put RE4R or RE requiem at the number 1 spot for my favourite RE game). I think you should definitely play this game, especially if you are a fan of the franchise, just beware of the negatives that I just pointed out

German & English Review :D  Von allen Resident Evil Teilen ist es für mich bisher das beste. Die Mischung aus Survival-  und Action Horror ist echt gut gebalanced gewesen, auch wenn ich Leons Parts mehr mochte. Das liegt aber nur daran, dass ich Stealth Gameplay und Stalkergegner hasse.   Grace und Emily sind mir auch ans Herz gewachsen. Sehr cute, was sie für eine Verbindung zueinander aufbauen. Von Leon brauche ich gar nicht erst anfangen, oder? Kann verstehen, dass es gewisse Mods gibt.   In den Ruinen von RPD zu sein hat mich emotional mitgenommen, und das obwohl ich den zweiten Teil erst letztes Jahr gespielt habe (und den dritten noch vor mir). Ich kann mir also gut vorstellen, wie sich die Leute gefühlt haben, die diesen Ort schon seit Jahrzehnten kennen. Und Leons Reaktionen auf die Orte (nicht nur RPD, sondern auch die Umgebung mit dem kleinen Waffenladen) sind so immersiv gestaltet. Ich musste immer mal wieder stehenbleiben, um das alles zu verarbeiten.  Die Bosskämpfe sind sehr typisch für Resident Evil. Daher war auch der Endboss keine so große Abwechslung, aber das sei dem Game verziehen. Allein die Sequenz mit dem Motorrad hebt das wieder auf.   (Kleiner Spoiler zu den Charactern) Eine kleine Kritik wäre für mich die Einführung von Zeno als vergleichsweise kleiner Character. Victor Gideon ist DER Bösewicht aus dem Teil, aber es wäre soo interessant gewesen, mehr über ihn und Zeno zu erfahren. Es klar, dass er ein Klon ist, aber wie ist die genaue Verbindung zu Wesker? Aus welchem Grund wurde ausgerechnet er geklont, und gibt es Hinweise darauf, dass es noch mehr gibt? Hätte man ihn weiter ausgebaut, wäre er als Boss eigentlich echt interessant gewesen. Verschwendetes Potential bei dem PEAK Characterdesign.   Insgesamt sehr empfehlenswert und für mich wirklich eines der besten Games des Franchises!   ---  Out of all the Resident Evil games, this is my favorite so far. The mix of survival and action horror was really well-balanced, even though I liked to play Leon's parts a little more. But that's because of the stealth gameplay and stalker enemies, I am not the hugest fan of that.   Grace and Emily are two beautiful good written characters. The connection they develop is so cute, plus Leon is of course the greatest. I think we all know, why.   Being in the ruins of RPD really affected me, even though I only played the second game last year. Third part is not done yet. So I can imagine how people who have known this place for decades must have felt. And Leon's reactions to the locations (not just RPD, but also the surrounding area with the small gun shop etc.) are so immersive. I had to stop every now and then to process all of it.  The boss fights are very typical for a Resident Evil game. Therefore, the final boss wasn't much of a big challenge, but that's forgivable in my opinion. The motorcycle sequence alone makes up for it.  (Spoiler regarding the characters) My only criticism would be the introduction of Zeno as a relatively small character. Victor Gideon is the main villain of the game (sadly), but it would have been so interesting to learn more about Zeno and their connection together. It's clear he's a clone, but what's his exact connection to Gideon and Wesker? Why was specifically he cloned, and are there any hints that there are more Zenos/Weskers/whatever? I have to say, I didn't find all of the files, so maybe it's explained in the game. But still: If he had a bit more screentime and cutscenes, he could have been a really interesting boss for me. A wasted opportunity given the otherwise EXCELLENT character design. That doesn't mean that Gideon is a bad boss or character at all, I think he was good paced.   In the end it's still one of the best Resident Evil games, if not THE best so far!

Oh. My. God.  Cappy went big with RE9. Like HUGE. Makes sense, really, because it's the franchise's 30th anniversary, but they went so wonderfully big that I really wonder what they have in mind for X, despite the name "Requiem" suggesting this is an end. Not many franchises make it to their tenth entry, but not many franchises get my day-one bucks, either. But after this? Oh, boy, does the next entry have a massive footstep to follow (and it better have Chris and Jill, gat dang it) and it will definitely get my day-one bucks! I should clarify that I'm talking about the lore here, but the game itself is also the next logical step in the post-Mikami RE universe.  First off, the RE Engine, introduced with RE7 and featured in several games since, continues to impress. It has had some upgrades since its inception, of course, but the engine still runs silky-smooth on PCs, even underpowered ones like mine. I'm running a 2080Ti and only my insistence on enabling raytracing has caused hiccups (mostly solved by shutting down my browsers while playing). Though RE Engine has been proven to work wonders on other games like DMC5 and Monster Hunter World/Wilds, what it does best is [i]this[/i]. It really does blow its load in the opening sequence on the Brooklyn-like street in "Wrenwood", but it's still very impressive end-to-end and all of the environments are immaculately built out and believable.  [i]Requiem[/i] (aka RE9) is best described as mish-mashing RE7 and 8 with the remakes of 2, 3 and 4, as demonstrated by its two main protagonists, fan-favorite Leon S. Kennedy and newcomer Grace Ashcroft ([i]not[/i] Ash[i]ford[/i]) as you switch between them to experience the game's narrative. Where Leon's segments default to an over-the-shoulder camera to focus on a more action-oriented experience, Grace's are meant to be experienced in first-person and lean more towards horror. However, in a first for the franchise, you can choose which camera you wish to use if you don't like the defaults so you're not stuck with something you don't like. The two experiences are further delineated by Leon retaining his attache-case Tetris-like inventory while Grace's resembles the ones found in 7 and 8.  On the other hand, if you're coming into this brand-spanking-new - and of course, you are welcome to jump on in - you'll still get a great gaming experience as the gameplay is solid whether you know your RE lore or not. As per usual, you will typically explore locations finding pick-ups and unlocking doors to progress forward. Files are scattered all over the place and reveal insights into the story, but so are monsters and you'll have to deal with them. Grace's sections are rooted in survival-horror where ammo is limited and you're often challenged to find alternate ways of overcoming obstacles and Leon's sections are blast-everything-that-moves as he walks around fully-equipped with a personal arsenal. It shouldn't work, but it does - at least for me. I can see that people might not like the disparity between the two play styles, but they honestly fit each character and it wouldn't make sense to have them swapped around, especially if you [i]do[/i] know Leon's history with the franchise.  And if, like me you are a massive fan of the franchise and have been around for quite some time, then RE9 is an absolute treat. There's no discussing it without spoilers and places like YouTube are extremely dangerous if you want to be surprised, but trust me as a fan - close yourself off and avoid everything until you've played through this once. The amount of stuff they've put into this game is clearly a love-letter to longtime fans. A reward, if you will, for sticking with it through those bumpy years when Cappy tried to pretend Umbrella didn't exist. I've written in the past that I believe that RE4 was a good game that took the story to a bad place, but we're all good now. I promise you. The circle, as it were, has been closed and I can't say more than that, other than that as a fan who has been on board since the very beginning in 1996, RE9 felt like we're [i]finally[/i] back to where we ought to be.  I expect that's mostly because the people responsible for making the games now are fans who grew up with it in the first place and wanted to make something for [i]us[/i]. 30 years of a franchise that hasn't had too many missteps (even in the side games) is nothing to laugh at and kids/teens who first experienced it on the PlayStation are more than likely behind the wheel now. RE9 [i]feels[/i] like it was made by those who love the franchise and wanted to do right by it, not tear it down from the inside and subvert everything to make themselves feel better. This game is for us, the folks who have been around since the early days, who probably own multiple copies of the original trilogy because all them Dreamcast releases were worth double-dipping, who own pristine copies of BradyGames' [i]Resident Evil Archives[/i] and cherish it even though it was mostly invalidated by the sequels that followed it, who bought a GameCube not because Nintendo built it, but because Capcom said that was Resident Evil's new home. There are things that happen in this game that will be completely lost on new players (not that they'd know) yet are incredible treats for franchise veterans.  That said, there are a few blemishes, but none of them impactful enough to be worthy of much discussion. Some segments can feel sloggy and there seems to be a lot more backtracking than in previous entries. Almost anything else is a gameplay adjustment that you'll figure out how to overcome rather than let it drag down the experience. And I found many of the setpiece fights debatably underwhelming on the default difficulty (I have not played insanity mode yet).  The only thing that I would really point out is that Grace's VA does a lot of stammering to demonstrate the character's untested nature, but it sounds very unnatural and she does it [i]a lot[/i]. Once you notice it, you can't unnotice it.  In short, this is a tightly-focused expansion into the Resident Evil franchise, made by whom I assume are longtime fans, and delivered with such spit-and-shine polish that even grumpy old men like me smiled the whole way through. No wasted resources on forgettable multiplayer experiences. No attempts to push the game into weird contemporary ideological spaces. No grand standing or ulterior motives. Just Resident Evil, as it should be, at last.  [spoiler]P.S. Capcom - Hunters are scarier and deserve the main stage next time.[/spoiler]

I usually do not write reviews, or let's say only recently started doing those so I'll just go through what is important for you!  The Game in my oppinion is a good 8/10, it leans towards a 9/10 yet is sitting on an 8 for a reason.  [b]Graphics:[/b] The Graphics are genuinenly amazing. The amount of details they put into this game alone are phenomenal and raytracing really helps elevate alot of it too. Not worth the effort if you got a full on potato PC.   [b]Gameplay:[/b] If you played all Resident Evil Games... I would say this is the perfect mix between Resident Evil 4(Leon-Sections) and Resident Evil 7 and 8 (Grace-Sections). If you didn't play those comparable games, I'll just say, Grace-Sections are spooky the first time and is more typical survival-horror focused, while Leon-Sections are Action-Focused.   [b]Story:[/b] The Story exists certainly, end of the first Story-Arc of Resident Evil (Not End of the Series just the Story-Arc, they will continue making games, don't you worry). Yet this is where atleast one point falls off from my 10/10 and turns to a 9/10 the Story feels a little rushed... or more so... they added too many elements to focus on that they all got not enough time to go through.   [b]The Difficulty:[/b] Not difficult at all if you are used to Survival Horror, especially the way Resident Evil handles it. Moderate Difficulty for new Evil Residents.  [b]Replayability:[/b] Your first run will take something between 8 to 12 hours, depends how used you are to the games, if you are a cutscene-skipper or not, if you read everything etc.   The replay-value exists, bound to as alot of the achievements need you to return a few times. Once you are used to all the Puzzles, the pathing, the enemies the game can be completed in 1,5-4h per run, per difficulty. The only downside being that well, certain sections will bore you to death and or feel like a slog to go through multiple times.   Now while the Replayability is fun the first few times and the Achievement Hunt is simple, the feeling of certain Areas becoming a Slog turns my 9/10 to a good 8/10. That is my personal oppinion.  Other than that I definately can recommend this game.   [b]Have fun![/b] ~Siren

Old man Leon yessir! Your boi didn't age, he just upgraded his plot armor. :)  Leon S. Kennedy. Bro is out here moving like a 90’s action hero who watched Die Hard one too many times. We’re talking backflips off exploding staircases, one-liners, and surviving things that makes you wonder if Leon is juiced up with compound V. It’s WACKY. It’s unrealistic. It’s EXACTLY why it works.  Visually? This game is straight-up disrespectful to your GPU. The graphics are insanely clean, lighting, textures, facial animations I don't know but it hits that “next-gen horror movie you can play” vibe. There are cheap jumpscares sure.. but it’s that slow, suffocating dread where you hesitate before opening a door because you already know something is about to ruin your life.  Then they hit you with the nostalgia bait ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the RPD section. If you’ve been around since the old days, stepping back into that police station feels like unlocking a core memory. It’s like revisiting your childhood home.  And for the real ones? The Tofu easter egg is back. Only the OGs remember grinding for that unlock back in the day, flipping through worn-out tips & tricks magazines, decoding weird requirements like it was some forbidden ritual. No YouTube. No Reddit. Just vibes.  Now… let’s not pretend this is flawless.  The controls? Kinda janky when playing as Grace tbh although I think that's intentional. Sometimes you die and it’s less “I got outplayed” and more “my character turned like a truck in mud.”  Difficulty-wise, it actually hits a sweet spot. It’s not brutally punishing like Resident Evil Code: Veronica but it’s no walk in the park either.   Now here’s the real talk: as much as this game cooks, I feel this is the Marvel movie equivalent of survival horror It’s loud, it’s flashy, and that's okay?   Performance-wise? Absolute chef’s kiss. Running this on an AMD Ryzen 9 9900X3D paired with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080, Smooth frames, no weird dips and no stutters. It looks insane and runs clean, which is rare these days.   8/10 ngl I think this is the 2nd best game overall in the franchise

Resident Evil: Fan Service.  The title might be misleading because I completely adore this game. ​I want to start with the things I didn’t like. One of them is the "nostalgia-bait" fan service, which I understand is meant to attract new players rather than the existing fanbase. The narrative doesn’t make much sense, especially as you approach the ending, but that wasn’t a dealbreaker since the Resident Evil timeline and lore are notoriously all over the place. ​From a gameplay perspective, the experience is simply exquisite. However, the idea of constantly switching back and forth between survival and action horror wasn’t really my cup of tea, as I am a survival horror purist at heart. ​Grace can be annoying at times, as she clearly suffers from severe anxiety, but her gameplay sections are the pinnacle of "OG" Resident Evil. As for Leon, he is clearly showing his age; his gameplay feels stiff and sluggish, though I do like that you are capable of parrying almost everything. ​Unfortunately, the bosses feel terribly underwhelming, at least during Leon's segments. ​That being said, this game is an ode to the franchise—a love letter aimed at both long-time fans and newcomers. Grace takes the crown, as the Rhodes Hills section captures the old RE formula, level design, and atmosphere as effectively as the legendary Spencer Mansion or the RPD. You are constantly tense, and while the enemy variety is small, it is executed perfectly. "Blister Heads" are every bit as frightening as the classic Crimson Heads. ​The ending was 100% fan service, and I absolutely loved every second of it. While it might not be the "best" Resident Evil game objectively, it has easily entered my personal top five.

Great stuff, and by and large an well rounded Resident Evil game. One that, when broken down, plays to both the series' greatest strengths and, at times, some of its weaknesses. It's not always as consistent in quality as I'd like, but that's par for course for nearly every single entry in the series, and the sum-total-of-parts here still exceeds the defecits.  Working to the game's strengths are Grace's chapters and their explicit homage to 'classic' Resident Evil, where resources are scarce, pacing of action is reduced, and engagement with both the location and enemies is more puzzle-like. In its best moments, Grace's progression harkens back to Resident Evil 1's mansion maybe closer than any other game in the series, and captures much of that brilliance. I think the crown jewel here, even if it's underutilised as a whole, is each monster/zombie having a unique identity, behaviour, and presence in the location. The routines and patterns build up upon RE1's emphasis on planned approach and careful movement, and I'd love to see them do more with that in the future.  Leon's chapters are fun by their own merits but structurally and conceptually teeter between Resident Evil 2 remake and Resident Evil 4 remake, drawing tone and prose from the former but action from the latter, yet never excelling at either. Shooting and engaging with enemies lacks the encroaching terror of RE2 and equally lacks the punchiness of RE4. It falls somewhere in between and is fine, is fun, but never reaching the highs of its source material and thus, as a whole, feeling less put together and polished than Grace's chapters. They're the weakest parts of the game. The homages are nice, but undercooked at best, and at worst gaudy. I kinda feel Capcom wanted to capture some "Old Snake returns to Shadow Moses in MGS4" with Leon, and within the overarching context and delicate execution of the execution it instead winds up a bit silly and underbaked.  It's a stupid gorgeous and sounding game too. Audio production is immaculate with fantastic layered environmental cues and excellent positioning. Visual direction is fantastic and path tracing elevates the assets to another level. One of the best looking games out there and an absolute showcase for how future tech like path tracing can be transformative to the overall visual direction.  The story is exactly what you'd expect. Hammy and silly in all the right places, but also an overall nonsense continuation of Resident Evil shlock. It's missing the strong rogue's gallery cast of villains that RE7 and RE8 had, but what's here is still fun. I don't know. I have zero personal investment in Resident Evil lore and its stupid narrative so I'm probably not the best critique here.  All in all, great game, good fun, strong direction, not perfect but few things other than Super Metroid are. Recommended!

Resident Evil Requiem is a fantastic return to form for Capcom's legendary survival horror franchise.  After years of experimenting with different formulas, Capcom finally found a great balance between classic Resident Evil horror and modern action. The game brings back the tense exploration, puzzles, resource management, and atmosphere that made the series famous, while still delivering the spectacular moments fans expect.  The biggest strength of Requiem is its dual-protagonist structure. Grace Ashcroft represents the survival horror side of Resident Evil: vulnerable, under-equipped, and constantly trying to survive against terrifying creatures. Her sections perfectly capture the feeling of fear and isolation that made Resident Evil 7 so memorable. Leon S. Kennedy, on the other hand, delivers the more action-oriented side of the franchise, with bigger fights and more explosive encounters.  The atmosphere is incredible. The environments, sound design, creature design, and attention to detail create some of the most memorable horror moments in recent entries. Capcom clearly understood that Resident Evil is at its best when it combines fear, mystery, and satisfying gameplay.  However, the game is not perfect. The transition between horror and action can sometimes feel uneven, especially when the more cinematic Leon sections reduce the tension built by Grace's slower gameplay. The story also relies heavily on the franchise's past and can become a little too focused on fan service.  But overall, Resident Evil Requiem is one of the strongest modern entries in the series. It respects the legacy of Resident Evil while proving that Capcom still knows how to evolve the formula.  A must-play for horror fans and one of the best Resident Evil experiences in years.

10/10  (+) Capcom has truly mastered this series at this point. The story itself has never been more interesting and although it's still a soap opera with body horror, the storytelling is really well done here. The pacing is completely perfect. The two main protagonists perfectly represent both the survival horror genre that was birthed by the series, as well as the more action packed latter entries to it.   Grace is a truly wonderful character added to the already great roster of lovable and relatable cast. Her emotions were shown and portrayed in a very realistic fashion and the voice actress deserves every praise she can get for her performance.   The combat sandbox is very reminiscent of RE4 Remake - meaning it's perfect. The tiny iterations that were added on top were just the right amount of spice. I always felt that I have plenty of options to deal with the situations I'm presented with and there was not a second of boredom throughout the whole game. This actually made me realize that Requiem was less reliant on actual puzzles to solve, and more on letting you figure out how to deal with whatever challenge you are facing at the moment. The gameplay of it all makes me immediately replay it, and I'm 100% going to in the future.   The level design is worth mentioning as well. This game features more open areas to explore, which was a nice addition this time around. Even if progression is almost completely linear (as always).  Graphically it's the most impressive game I have played to date. The animations are so versatile and fluid that it's just pleasing to look at whatever you are doing. The facial animations are done extremely well, the expressions of the characters never feel video gamey, it's really like watching a movie.   (-) As much as I love this game, it doesn't really do anything new if you have played the rest of the series already. It relies a bit too heavily on fan servicing and nostalgia in it's core elements. I have thoroughly enjoyed the callbacks it makes to earlier entries, but I still wish Requiem has done more to stand on its own a bit more.   The bosses are so... forgettable? None of the fights are that unique, none of them are challenging and I would even go as far as to say that they were predictable. The new villain(s) are well written though, and that matters more to me than a new fancy mechanic or boss arena.   In conclusion: it's a 10/10 game with zero fat - all substance. The characters are amazing, so is the writing. The gameplay is top tier entertainment, and it's super pretty to look at. I'd recommend this game to anyone who has played 2 & 3 & 4 remake as well as 7. Requiem is definitely not a good entry point to the series. Thank you Capcom, it was well worth the wait for this one. ❤

I think that Resident Evil Requiem is a good step toward progressing the series. RE9 feels to me like one enormous love letter to the entire series, and I believe that majority of the people who've played it would agree with me. To put it simply, it's made for the fans. There is no shortage of fan service in Resident Evil Requiem. That's no critique either. The fan service is much appreciated here.  In regards to the gameplay, Resident Evil 9 is phenomenal. My opinion is that Resident Evil 9 features some of the best horror that the franchise has seen yet, rivaled only by House Beneviento. In relation to earlier installments, I'd say that The Girl is debatably the scariest stalker enemy ever, the first couple encounters had me absolutely petrified. What unbelievable enemy design. RE9 does a fantastic job in balancing the horror and action aspects, far better than RE8 did. Grace representing horror and Leon representing action was undeniably the right choice. Depending on who you're playing as, RE9 feels like two completely different games at times. It's a good fusion of elements from RE2, RE4 and RE7. RE9 takes RE4's combat and tries expanding on it. They succeeded with this for the most part, some parts and better and some are worse. The melee combat is most definitely improved, but RE4 still has an edge in gunplay in my opinion. Nevertheless, the combat is what I enjoyed most about RE9. It was a very satisfying experience.   In relation to characters, I liked just about all of them. I very much enjoyed Grace as a main character. She feels very real, like a random woman caught up in these horrifying and traumatizing situations. Leon is back and I enjoy this aged, jaded and more experienced version of him. I'm glad they kept some of his old characteristics though, like his sense of humor for example. I was afraid that Leon would outshine Grace, but I'm very glad that he doesn't. Leon and Grace are only two examples, there are other great characters. But for the sake of the review, I can't cover all of them.  My main complaint is most definitely the boss fights. I feel that all of them except for the HUNK Fight were quite underwhelming honestly. This is because of a few reasons. For one, they were all far too easy. I didn't die once to any boss, and I think that should tell you a lot. There are also not very many boss fights throughout the game. The ones that we were given are not very meaningful nor interesting. On top of that, they're all so short. Not a single boss has a second stage or anything similiar. The boss fights are at best somewhat exhilirating and at worst flat-out boring. I would also like to add that the ludicrously unforgiving parry mechanic contributes to the boss fights not feeling very challenging. You point, shoot and parry if the boss tries attacking you. Resident Evil, historically speaking, does boss fights very well. Therefore, it's quite suprising to me that they managed to drop the ball here.   The writing is fine yet the strongest that I've seen since RE4. Resident Evil Requiem's storyline is among the better ones that the franchise has to offer. Everything felt somewhat logical and planned. The writing does get a bit choppy at times but if you compare it to some of the earlier installments, it does stand out. RE9's storyline is great when compared to other Resident Evil titles, is what I'd say if I wanted to summarize it in one sentence.  Resident Evil Requiem is a very impressive game. It didn't necessarily floor me or anything, but despite that I left feeling very satisfied and impressed. Safe to say I had a lot of fun playing RE9. My thoughts about it are scattered because I don't quite know how I honestly feel about it. Some of it was fantastic, and some of it was disappointing. I feel split between two differing opinions, and that may speak to the magic of the game itself. My opinion in regards to RE9 is undoubtebly subject to change so I'll have to see what I think about it in the future. I feel that an Insanity playthrough will greatly alter my view of the game and maybe even weaken some of my critiques.  Leon doesn't look anywhere near 49, by the way.

Resident Evil is one of those series that doesn't have to deviate too much from its formula to still be great.    Honestly, just about every RE is the same, you start off in a spooky setting like a house, mansion, or other standard building, then work your way down to the super secret lair and fight the big mutated baddy.  Which sounds like a recipe for it to get stale, but because the series generally leans into its flavor and maintains the mechanics that have made the formula work, it continues to work here, again.  Ammo scarcity and horror elements will generally always create a game that keeps you engaged instead of just turning off your brain and letting the slop wash over you like most modern games have become.  Even though it's a standard RE experience, it's not just a bunch of reused situations, there's still plenty of moments that completely surprised me and managed to grip me all the way through to the end, which is saying a lot more than most games these days that just instantly bore me and rarely finish.  They did a great job of utilizing the two characters and making their experiences feel different, justified in their design, and highly polished.  The only downside I can think of is the replayability is not great, it isn't nearly as good as the RE4 remake, for example.  A lot of the unlockables are best to get by completing the game on the easiest setting and blasting through as quickly as possible to then go to "insanity" which I found to be jarring and disappointing.  I'd prefer to go straight into harder and harder settings gradually, but this goes straight from "normal" to "what the actual hell" instantly and is basically unplayable until you go back and do all the "challenges", which is mostly tedium rather than an actual "challenge".  The "final puzzle" for example is just a bunch of doing random things in a particular order over two playthroughs with the help of an online guide to get a very particular value of points to help get the very necessary unlimited ammo perk in order to even consider starting insanity.  But overall, the game is still one of the best games to come out recently.  Definitely grab this at some point if you're any sort of RE fan or even casual enjoyer, sale or full price you'll likely to be happy either way.

For me, Resident Evil Requiem was the ultimate title in the franchise. I have played all of the Resident Evil games available to me including the remakes for Resident Evil 2, 3, and 4 and know enough about what the different styles of the series have to offer. As far as I knew Resident Evil 5 and 6 received mixed to negative feedback, therefore I was not committed to completing either of these games and only attempted parts to see how they compared.  I found the switch in Resident Evil 7 and 8 to first-person perspectives extremely effective because they brought the series back toward leaning into a "More Horror" and made it very immersive. This perspective added a great deal of intensity and immersion.  However, Requiem stands out more due to its combination of this kind of omnipresent inverse horror with an established camera style; these elements complement each other beautifully.  The gameplay is what will stick with me most regarding Requiem. Regardless of the occasional bugs or performance dips, I find that they never detracted from how enjoyable an experience it was. The mechanic feels tight, properly paced, and every instance was meaningful. This is one of those titles that you can restart several times but still want to continue because the core gameplay loop feels ​so satisfying.  In my opinion, Requiem captures the essence of Resident Evil: suspense, excitement, and ambiance. It also has plenty of enjoyable moments. Unlike many other games, Requiem does not depend on nostalgia, but instead provides a complete experience.  Honestly, even with the faults that this game has, it definitely has a lasting impact on me and I've come to consider it my favorite in the entire RE franchise.

Story The story is engaging and well-connected, with smooth transitions between characters.  Gameplay Gameplay is precise and enjoyable, with a good level of variety. However, if you’re a long-time fan of the series, some mechanics can feel predictable at times. Resource management stands out  ammo and items are very limited and carefully balanced, forcing you to think before acting.  Boss Fights Boss battles are relatively easy and don’t offer much challenge compared to older entries. They lack uniqueness and memorable moments, making them one of the weaker aspects of the game.  Horror & Tension There are moments of tension in certain areas, but overall, the horror factor isn’t as strong as expected  especially when compared to Resident Evil 7 and 8. Also, not pausing the game when opening the inventory reduces the overall tension significantly.  Overall Direction The game clearly tries to bring back elements from older Resident Evil titles while blending them with modern gameplay. It works to an extent, but doesn’t fully stand out with a strong identity.  Final Verdict A very good game and an enjoyable experience overall, but it doesn’t surpass the best entries in the series like Resident Evil 7, 4, 8, or 2. Worth playing  just not the strongest in the franchise.

Resident Evil Requiem - это потрясающий survival horror. Многие возлагали на него большие ожидания, учитывая неплохое качество последних представителей серии игр. Но, к моему огромному удивлению, разработчики в этот раз действительно превзошли себя. Впервые за 14 лет они представили нового персонажа, который, во-первых, ЖЕНЩИНА, во-вторых, интересен в сценарном плане, в-третьих, заставляет тебя сопереживать, не оставляет равнодушным. Более того, разработчики спустя 9 лет решили начать работать над ошибками последних нескольких игр серии Resident Evil, а также, очевидно, вдохновляются и успешно заимствуют интересные элементы других игр жанра survival horror, вышедших за последние годы. Повествование от лица двух героев выглядит бесшовным, темп игры бодрый и органичный, геймплей разнообразен, сюжет интригует. Игра потрясающе справляется с задачей как развеселить, так и напугать игрока. На данный момент это, пожалуй, лучший survival horror на рынке видеоигр, которому удалось не только совместить в себе все самые лучшие и запоминающиеся элементы жанра, но представить новые. Это по-настоящему NextGen игра.

Maybe the greatest Resident Evil game ever made?  I love when you play a game and you realize while playing it that you're like having a moment. Combining Survival-Horror and Action-Horror. Grace's sections are just truly terrifying. She's probably the most relatable character in the franchise because she really is just like a normal person. She reacts to everything in a realistic way and doesn't just adapt to the situation like Ethan in RE7. The enemies are like I mentioned before terrifying and especially The Girl. I was genuinely horrified when I saw her in that beginning segment. All of the stalker enemies were great and gave the same vibe of someone like Mr. X. Now Leon's part is where the game really shines in my opinion.  Grace's part is really good, but Leon is just on another level. Leon returns rougher and tougher and delivers the best action in the entire franchise. The action is so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fun! Resident Evil Requiem é aquele tipo de jogo que te pega pela gola e te faz lembrar por que essa franquia é tão marcante. Eu entrei esperando terror, tensão e aquele clima pesado, e o jogo entrega isso muito bem em vários momentos.  A ambientação é um dos maiores pontos fortes. Tem partes em que você anda devagar não por obrigação, mas porque não quer descobrir o que tem na próxima esquina. O som, a iluminação e os detalhes trabalham juntos para criar uma sensação constante de desconforto, e isso funciona muito bem.  Mas o jogo não é perfeito. Em alguns momentos, ele parece indeciso entre ser um survival horror mais estratégico ou um jogo de ação. Isso acaba afetando o ritmo, porque você sai de trechos mais tensos e calculados para sequências que parecem mais um corredor de tiro, o que quebra um pouco a imersão.  Os inimigos também variam bastante. Alguns são realmente memoráveis e trazem aquele medo e respeito clássico da franquia, enquanto outros passam sem deixar muita marca.  Pontos fortes:  Atmosfera muito bem construída Direção de arte excelente Momentos de tensão que realmente funcionam Sequências marcantes Pontos fracos:  Ritmo irregular Falta de consistência na identidade entre ação e terror Alguns inimigos pouco impactantes No geral, Resident Evil Requiem não é um jogo perfeito, mas entrega uma experiência que vale a pena. Ele tem seus problemas, mas também tem momentos fortes o suficiente para compensar.  Eu recomendo.  Não como uma obra impecável, mas como um jogo que consegue te prender e te fazer sentir aquele desconforto clássico da franquia em vários momentos.

Grace’s sections are straight-up horror, dark environments, very limited resources, and a constant enemy chasing you that you can’t even fight back against. Leon’s parts, on the other hand, are full-on action, bringing back stuff from Resident Evil 4 like the case and upgrade points to buy and improve weapons.  The story is interesting, but toward the end, there are some things that don’t really make much sense and even contradict each other. Grace is a great character and a really solid addition to the series. She feels realistic, like how a normal person would actually think and act in a situation like this.  Overall, I think it’s a really fun and entertaining game. That said, I was a bit disappointed that there’s barely any post-game content (like Mercenaries, extra modes, unlockables). Also, the whole “main” idea of the game was going back to Raccoon City, and yeah, you do go back, but you barely get to explore any of its iconic locations. And when you finally reach the police station, it’s a super short section with almost nothing to do.  Another downside is the boss fights. There are very few of them, and they’re extremely easy. They don’t really have any unique gimmicks, it’s mostly just shooting until they die, which is kind of a shame considering how memorable boss fights have been in recent games.

Resident Evil 9 is an absolute masterpiece that elevates the survival horror genre to a whole new level. From the very first moment you step into its world, you’re pulled into an atmosphere that feels both terrifying and deeply immersive. The game perfectly balances tension and excitement, keeping you constantly on edge without ever feeling overwhelming. Every environment is crafted with incredible attention to detail, making exploration feel rewarding while still maintaining a sense of dread around every corner.  What truly makes Resident Evil 9 stand out is how it blends classic horror elements with modern gameplay innovations. The mechanics feel smooth, responsive, and refined, allowing players to fully engage with the experience without frustration. Whether you're solving intricate puzzles or facing terrifying enemies, the game always keeps you thinking and adapting. The enemies themselves are designed in a way that feels fresh and unpredictable, making every encounter unique and intense.  The story is another major highlight. It’s gripping, emotional, and full of twists that keep you hooked from start to finish.
