[b]Good?[/b] Absolutely This game is a love letter from Capcom to the fans of the Resident Evil franchise and it shows. Ultimately, I had a lot of fun playing this game. The two-protagonists shows the two sides of RE; horror and action. By going down this route, I think Capcom was able to satisfy people who missed the horror side of the franchise and those who enjoy the goofy action. However, there are some fundamental issues that did bring down my enjoyment of the game.   The music is great as always. The art style and the graphics are beautiful, so it'll age really well just like RE2 remake did. This game is a split of both action and horror, so if you like either then you'll probably have fun. Satisfying puzzles too, they generally hit the sweet-spot of not being [i]too[/i] difficult. If you're new to this series, you may feel lost since Requiem ties the lore of previous games together especially for Leon. Requiem is tying together the progression of his character from the RE2&4 remakes.   The rest of this review will contain spoilers!  [b]The Villains[/b] Resident Evil is renowned for their memorable villains. Not just early series villains like Tyrant T-00 (Mr. X) or Nemesis but Jack Baker (RE7) and arguably most of the villains of RE8. Lady D, Heisenberg, and the horrifying fetus baby still left an impact on me years after playing Village. The Girl in RE9 is a fantastic addition to these villains. The dark is one of the most primal fears of the human psyche and her segments work amazingly. The use of the dark coupled with the rattle of the Girl's chains builds such strong tension and dread, it was phenomenal!   Victor Gideon was also a great villain at the beginning. He has such a strong character design, the snake-skin lab coat is both hilarious and genius. There revolved this air of mystery around him and foreboding. He was smart enough to lay a trap, and I was eager to see where it went! But unfortunately, there isn't much of a satisfactory conclusion with his character. The chase scene on the motorcycle was fun, but his final form was more squid-like than snake-like. I was genuinely surprised that he didn't turn into some horrific snake monster. That let-down aside, the "twist" of RE9 leaves Victor (and Zeno) looking rather stupid.   Zeno felt like engagement or excitement bait for Wesker fans, but he ultimately... did nothing. It was really disappointing to get a clone of such a memorable, important villain who you don't ever get to fight. His sudden death also means that there's seemingly nothing else to do with his character, unless it's foreshadowing other Wesker (or Alex?) clones in the future? But the biggest problem with Zeno's character is that he weakens Victor's. There is nothing that Zeno did in RE9 that Victor couldn't have done. He hogged screentime that could have been used to build up Victor, but it was instead wasted.  [b]Raccoon City[/b] As much as I loved going back to Raccoon City, like Victor and Zeno it felt a bit wasted. Retrieving the bomb components to bust through the gate was both long and tedious. The only enjoyable part in my opinion was encountering the BSAA zombies for the first time. But Raccoon City (and later the ARK) encapsulates the biggest weaknesses of Requiem: repetition. The Care Center suffered from a lack of a fun monsters outside of the Girl, but it was fine. The Chef and Chuck were obstacles and there was enough variation in the zombies to keep it interesting. As Grace, you had to learn each of their "quirks" to get around them.   Raccoon City, however, has very boring, generic zombies that sometimes evolve into Blisterheads. With Leon's large arsenal of weapons, they're effectively nuisances to kill then run past. At the very least the BSAA zombies had a fun twist of using weapons, but it's not enough to make it challenging or interesting. I had gotten my hopes up that there would be weird big monsters to fight like the Spider but I was severely disappointed. There wasn't even a huge crocodile in the sewers.   The atmosphere of Raccoon City was turned out to be rather boring. Everything is dusty and grey with harsh, oversaturated lighting. I think that this part of the game would have really benefited from creating more interesting but ruined buildings for Leon to travel through. Perhaps like the hospital from RE3, but that leads me to my next issue:  [b]The Kennedy Problem[/b] Leon Kennedy is a phenomenal character. He is admittedly my favorite RE character, so I know I'm part of the problem. Something my girlfriend said while she watched me play Requiem is that she could watch Leon file taxes and it wouldn't get boring. However, Requiem doesn't do anything satisfying with his character.   Leon walking the old halls of RPD is a good way to show his growth as a character. He went from a scared 21 year old who could barely fight zombies to a zombie-killing machine. But the writing of the game doesn't really do anything to explore that evolution or to progress Leon's character. We know that he's depressed, we know that he has severe guilt for not being able to save people like Kendo. But where does that actually go in Requiem?   Leon Kennedy doesn't have a satisfying conclusion in this story. It leaves us wanting more, but he already has three other games that he is in. Not to mention the CGI movies and tv-show. If this isn't his last game, that means that he'll be taking the spot from another protagonist. If it is his last game, then we don't see a conclusion to any of his important relationships such as with Claire and Ada.  We all know that Leon Kennedy will never forget September 30th. But you know who else wouldn't? Jill. Jill feels like she would have fit this game so much better as the action-protagonist because she has a deeper connection to Raccoon City than Leon does. She actually knows Wesker and has unresolved trauma involving him, which would have made Zeno a more interesting villain from that connection. As sad as Leon's experience in the RPD is, Jill actually had friends and co-workers there. She watched as her fellow S.T.A.R.S were hunted down and killed. She actually knew the city residents like Kendo.   This game felt like a perfect fit for Jill, but Leon got slotted in as the franchise's favorite.
You'd think after nine installments the game would lose everything that made the series great.  Everyone behind making Requiem - Give yourselves a round of applause.

Capcom has been releasing absolute bangers the past few years, especially in the Resident Evil franchise. Each new entry and remake has been absolutely fantastic and I've loved every single one of them.  RE4 and 4 Remake are some of my favorite video games of all time and as I was playing Requiem, there were a few moments when I was almost worried it would steal that spot.  After replaying it several time, I can say with confidence that... RE4 still holds that place in my heart BUT Requiem is definitely up there in my love and appreciation of each entry.  I was really hyped for the game for a long time, bought and played it on release and thoroughly enjoyed myself the whole way through. It's a fantastic game overall, had pretty much everything I could have hoped for and more and I'm just very pleased with what I got. Just a good, clean, quality game.  If you're hesitating because you haven't played Resident Evil before, don't. You lose nothing from starting here and in fact, I think it's a fantastic point of entry. It's a perfect blend of horror and actions and has a little bit of everything from the previous games. It's scary, it's dumb, it's fun. There are obviously nods to long time fans but the story itself is self-contained.  [h3]Story and Gameplay[/h3]  The story itself is fine, pretty much what you would expect from any RE games. Nothing mind blowing but there are lots of unexpected turn of events. As always, I feel like the gameplay drives the story more than the other way around and I think that's for the best. The level design is absolutely fantastic and each area is very memorable, distinct and has rooms and layouts that are easy to memorize and recognize.  Pacing is fantastic. You alternate between playing Leon and Grace. Grace's gameplay is more focused on survival horror, with limited resources and inventory space, enemies are genuinely threatening and a lot of moments can be very stressful. Leon's gameplay is more focused on action and being a bad-ass zombie killing machine. By default, Grace's perspective is first-person and Leon is third-person, which works really well for what each character's segments are going for. It's also a good mix of the recent shift to first-person with the RE7 series' reboot and the more traditional over the shoulder from RE4 and the remakes. Alternating between feeling helpless and feeling super strong feels great and gives you a nice break compared to being under constant stress.  The game is fairly short, but it's quality over quantity. Great moments, lots of details, everything looks amazing and polished. It also ran great and I didn't encounter any bugs, which seems like a great ask nowadays even with really high-end hardware.  It felt longer than it was, though. I initially thought I wanted more Leon but after replaying it several times, I think it's perfectly balanced between both characters. If you end up finding his sections too short as you play, don't worry, he'll get his turn.  There is obviously less focus on the action than RE4R even for Leon, but there are a lot of little gameplay addition that makes you feel like a badass. Leon feels stronger and cooler than ever. You do get to play with a lot of different weapons and upgrade them, but there isn't much to it. You get to make your guns a bit stronger and that's it.  RE4 definitely has the most replayability. Subsequent playthroughs in RE9 were... Fun. But I think its first impression is very very strong. A lot of segments lose their novelty the second or third time around, especially when you're trying to speedrun the game for one of the challenges. Much of the game that is supposed to be slow and tense don't really work anymore.  [h3]Difficulty[/h3]  This time around, we're given a choice between difficulties that limit or not your ability to save the game as Grace. I'm not a fan of limited saves / not having autosaves but I do understand that it raises the stakes and makes the game more stressful. Just not my cup of tea. I don't mind replaying the same section or encounter several times. What I dislike is saving then dying stupidly after looting an entire area and organizing your storage and having to re-do it all over again.  Once you clear the game, you unlock the "Insanity" difficulty which is much, much harder than standard. So much so that it almost seems intended to be played with special rewards you unlock after completing challenges. I had already unlocked mostly everything before giving it a shot and heard other people say that insanity was ridiculously difficult even with infinite ammo... I can say with confidence that having a magnum with infinite ammo completely trivializes the majority of the game on Insanity.  There was an odd decision to forego New Game + this time around. But what's even weirder is that *some* bonuses apply to new games and some don't. Meaning you can't start a NG+ but you can't start a fresh save either...  Much like other modern RE, you get points by completing challenges then spend them on special bonuses. Those bonuses are accessible from [i]any[/i] new game... So if you don't want to play with infinite ammo, infinite durability, infinite ink ribbons (to save)... You can turn it off the settings and dump everything in your storage I suppose.  In any case, yes, this means you cannot start a game with your weapons and upgrades from the previous playthrough and cannot start a "real" new game with none of the specials unlocked. There is no ranking system like in RE4R so you can just cheese insanity with an infinite launcher if you want.  [h3]Price[/h3]  Capcom seem to have learned their lesson and didn't release the game a million P2W DLCs this time around. Deluxe upgrade is a bit corny with a 100$ games... But I get it. I was really happy with the game and decided to purchase it afterwards to show my appreciation... But I honestly still wish the extra costumes were unlockable in-game instead. Especially considering there are only [b]two[/b] costumes to unlock in-game... 1 for each character (1 more for each if you consider their jacket to be one). Deluxe gives you 5...  [h3]Conclusion[/h3]  Really happy with how this turned out. Grace is a fantastic character and I hope she'll be back in future games. Game is very expensive but very high quality and I appreciate the absence of microtransactions... I don't feel robbed, I feel like I paid for a premium quality game and got exactly what I asked for.  It's not too short, it's not too long, lots of horror, lots of action. It's very deserving of its success.  Looking forward to the story expansion and I honestly hope they'll add something like the mercenaries... Would love to play more as Leon with more weapons and upgrades in a more "arcade" style mode!  Can't wait for RE10!

"A Frustrating Mix of Missed Potential and Tedious Gameplay"  I wanted to love Resident Evil Requiem, but after finishing it, I'm left with more frustration than satisfaction. Here's why:  The Grace Problem  You spend a significant portion of the game playing as Grace, yet her toolkit is laughably inadequate. Here's what you get:  · A pistol · That's it. No shotgun. No rifle. No magnum. No grenade launcher. No meaningful weapon upgrades.  Ammo is so scarce that most of her sections devolve into running past enemies because you simply can't fight back. There's no satisfying progression—you start weak and stay weak the entire game. Meanwhile, Leon gets all the classic Resident Evil toys, making the contrast utterly jarring.  Who thought it was a good idea to give one protagonist a full arsenal and the other a peashooter and call it a day?  The Chloe Section  Then there's the Chloe gameplay segment—a tedious, unoriginal stealth sequence that feels like a lesser copy of the Sherry sections from RE2 Remake, but without any of the polish.  · It's padding. Pure and simple. This section exists to stretch the runtime. · It's lazy. The mechanics feel recycled and unrefined. · It's a replay killer. Going through this on a second (or fourth) playthrough for achievements is an absolute slog.  The Story Confusion  The narrative around Chloe, Grace, and Emily is a convoluted mess. The game teases a clone storyline, then undermines it with timeline inconsistencies, and ultimately expects you to accept that "the villain was lying" as a satisfying resolution. It's not—it feels like the writers painted themselves into a corner.  Structural Issues  The game constantly pulls you away from what works:  · Leon's sections? Fun, classic RE gameplay. · Grace's sections? Underpowered, frustrating, and you get no meaningful weapons. · Chloe's section? A complete momentum killer.  Instead of building toward an empowering payoff, Requiem keeps you stuck in a state of vulnerability without the catharsis that makes survival horror work.  What Works  To be fair, Leon's gameplay is solid. When you're playing as him, it feels like Resident Evil. The atmosphere is there, the sound design is good, and when the game lets you actually play, it can be enjoyable.  But that's the problem—too much of Requiem feels like it's actively working against the player rather than challenging them.  Final Verdict  If you're a die-hard Resident Evil fan who needs to play everything in the series, wait for a deep sale. If you're looking for a satisfying survival horror experience, replay RE2 Remake or RE4 Remake instead.  Requiem isn't the worst game in the series, but it's easily one of the most frustrating. The non-existent weapon variety for Grace, tedious stealth sections, and confusing story add up to an experience that overstays its welcome

Capcom have knocked it so far out of the park with Resident Evil Requiem. While some complain that it is a bit short, I personally disagree. If this game was any longer, the story would have felt padded and would have suffered from a lack of urgency. It was straightforward without shoving it in your face, allowing you to still deviate from the golden path every now and then - the way that I'd argue it should be.   Visuals and graphics are absolutely top tier, especially with the available Path Tracing options, and performance is good overall if you are willing to switch on settings such as DLSS Super Resolution and Frame Generation. The image quality with these settings is mostly good, but at a few times I could notice artifacts around thin details such as hair or fringing on depth of field. However, this does not take away from the masterful work the artists at Capcom have accomplished. I do feel that the lighting is particularly reliant on ray tracing, as traditional rasterised rendering does make the game take a visual hit in some parts - but if you can run with RT on, I would heavily recommend it.   Gameplay is prime Resident Evil, blending new ideas & the learnings from past remakes into one. I played on Standard (Modern) difficulty and at times, I did feel that the challenge was the slightest bit inconsistent. Some situations came off as extremely easy, and others played out as needing a couple goes or more strategy. Other than the difficulty, the game feels great to play and makes use of an excellent control scheme and UI. The option of choosing First Person or Third is great too.   Overall, I think this is the culmination of Capcom learning its lessons from the previous remakes and sequel games. The result: a very well crafted Action/Horror that oozes great writing, satisfying gameplay and just enough nostalgia to make it properly sit in it's place as a Resident Evil title. Visuals are excellent, cinematography is high end, and the voice acting is enthralling. Absolutely recommended at full price, and furthermore on offer.

Resident Evil: Requiem is a fitting name for the game, it is a celebration of the franchise in its purest form. Requiem wears its heart very clearly on its sleeve, there is something to be enjoyed from every single previous game in the franchise, all combined together to make this experience. The survival horror lovers will feel at home during the tense segments of Grace's gameplay. The action horror fans will find themselves giddy while being an unstoppable force of destruction while playing as Leon. It truly does have something for everyone.  The game itself is absolutely stunning visually, I had just recently upgraded my graphics card, so I got to play the game on max graphics using ray tracing, and it's clearly the peak of Capcom's efforts with the RE Engine. The lighting is perfect, the designs of not only the care centre, but the following areas of the game were clearly given so much care and special attention, it's hard not to stand back and appreciate the detail in every corner of this game.   Audio is done just as brilliantly, each sound made dread fill my body as Grace, yet the electric guitar riffs pumped me up to keep mowing through enemies as Leon. There is also few motifs within some of the OST as a clever easter egg from Capcom for those who played some of the older games, even the originals, which was great to pick up on.   Gameplay is perfected in both halves of the story, it is distilled survival horror gameplay, with its own twist of course. Leon feels better than ever, growing even from his buttery smooth gameplay from RE4R. No complaints here at all.   Requiem for the dead, nightmare for the living - the motto given to Resident Evil Requiem; it ties well into the story, hitting the main themes of the game quite well. Leon still harbours his survivors guilt from the Raccoon City Incident and it is clear it weighs on him. The narrative is up for debate, it has some pitfalls and character moments which are quite strange, but overall I found it quite enjoyable. There is definitely a lot to love here if you have played the previous titles, it is a celebration of the franchise after all, IMO your experience of this game will be greatly enriched by playing the previous games. It does feel like it leans a bit much into fanservice sometimes, but as a fan of the games, I didn't really mind it too much.  For new fans of the series, this is a great place to pick up the game if you want to try out both sides of the franchise, for returning players, you'll be able to witness everything Resident Evil has been building up to for the past 30 years and see it all come together in this experience. It was fantastic and I don't think I'll forget it anytime soon.

[h1] Damn, I feel for any contenders for Game of the Year 2026.[/h1]  There's a lot to unpack here but I'll just summarize the TL:DR now: The game offers substantial gameplay, whether it'd be combat focused or stealth horror, it's the perfectly fine balance between the two genres that the series is known for, and it brilliantly does both; giving it intuitive modern shooter gameplay as well as a hommage to the effectiveness of horror stealth tactics, and since I played it in classic, nothing is left unwanted on both. I definitely rate it [b]9.8/10 [/b]   [b][u]Spoiler Free Segment:[/u][/b]   [h2] [b]Story and Characters:[/b] 9.8 [/h2] The story revolves around a new protagonist and a veteran one; Grace Ashcroft as the meek, innocent and cautious FBI agent with a historical past coming back to haunt her. Her personality [i]gracefully[/i] evolves throughout the game, such a fantastic way to bring a memorable character onto an ensemble of epic characters the franchise already has. I found her more memorable than Ethan, since for Ethan, it was all personal perspective, in action sequences and even in cinematic cutscenes.  Speaking of [b]epic[/b] characters, poster-boy Leon S, Kennedy is back on the trail of investigations, one specifically explores his past as well. His side of the story finishes loose ends the previous games, as well as create new threads to which completely extends his ties to the rest of the franchise. You can't go wrong with his heroic bad-assery, and with years of experience behind his back, the player senses how Leon would act before he even does it, goes to show how respectful the game devs really had on adding him to this game.  [h2] [b]Gameplay:[/b]9.5 [/h2]  The gameplay had always been intuitive, especially when carrying two major genres into the fold and mixing them into something new. Unlike the predecessors of the new remake games and the sequel games, this game blends horror stealth game as well as action survival into one amazing amalgamation. Since both are gigantic improvements of the RE franchise I will critique them separately:  [h3]Action-Shooter Survival:[/h3] [b]Leon's[/b] segments of the game are obviously made to please his fanbase, but also add into the notion that he is no longer in the shoes of our new protagonist grace, instead, his feet are bare and already used to the confrontations of the franchise. Even though there is a slight aim-assist (even when its off on settings), the gunplay is still great. Different ways to deal with enemies with their weaknesses, and there's a segment of the game that adds into the crafting side which I really like AND there was a sleuth of different combatants and also previous ones too. Since I enjoyed RE5 and RE6, the sequences of Leon for this game really felt fun while keeping that slight survival aspect to it.  [h3]Stealth-Horror Survival:[/h3] [b]Grace's[/b] segments of the game is what shines for me, since I was more into the horror genre side of the Resident Evil franchise, and this game matches things I've felt when playing two specific games that are S tier/top of its' genre: Alien: Isolation and Medium. The game has subtle forewarnings before things get really heated and very nerve-wracking. The game's movement in terms of navigating around threats is in similar fashion as the two games I mentioned above, so I found it very very simple. The gravity of suspense and fear of the unknown is still captivated in one of the small portions of the game, that I would've loved to explore more.  [h3]Puzzles:[/h3] Not much is say how different this game does its' puzzles in comparison to the previous games, though it was a lot simpler in comparison to knowing where to go than RE7 or RE8. It was very straightforward, just like RE:RE2.  [h2] [b]Sound Design and World Atmosphere:[/b] 9.8 [/h2]  [h3]The World Building:[/h3] This game shines on creating so much while also self-aware on how it ties to the bigger picture, which is the RE established canon. It leaves room on expansion but also ties loose ends that sort of excuses its' plotholes in terms of story. The environment was extravagant, though it involves being inside a massive mansion like map, theres also Post-Raccoon City, which had amazing details, and gave a very eerie chernobyl-like vibe when exploring.  [h3]Sound Design:[/h3] From the start, I knew the sound design team had fun with this game. Especially in the horror aspects of the game, the gnarling, the sudden movement of objects, ones that you don't even interact with, but gives subtle hints that would help you path your way through certain areas. It's a masterclass of knowing how suspense work, and to be able to build it without giving too much noise, really deepens the fear and terror Resident Evil is known for. And the action sequences had several times blown me away, from how they designed specific impact of different calibre shots, to all of the new bio-infected units and how they sounded in reaction.  [h2]Spoiler Segment:[/h2]  [spoiler][h2] Story had lots to be wanted and explored [/h2] Needed more of Grace during the Post-Raccoon City segment. I felt like the transition of her character from wanting to save Emily, to, going willingly with Victor was too abrupt and there's really no build up or major excuse for her to shift like that. Maybe have Victor offer a chance to subside Emily's infection? OR have her trick that the real Emily is still alive? There's multiple ways to drive a character into willingingly be part of the forces they initially had altercations with while keeping it ambiguous.  I was hoping the Destruction Ending would have gotten Leon to fight Zenos for one last stand, or something more heroic, and not very.. abrupt. (This is a big Joel from Last of Us 2 vibe). Or showing something more to explore things on what happens to the BSAA or Umbrella, in reaction to destroying Elpis, and not just, again, abrupt ending.  [/spoiler]  Play the game. Buy it with an open mind, and you won't regret it. Salute to Capcom for respecting old characters while giving us memorable ones like Grace Ashcroft and delivering an absolute engaging experience that no other piece of media can replicate. I love Resident Evil.

This is easily one of the best modern Resident Evil games. Whether it is your first RE game or you're a series veteran. there is so much to like about this game. To get it out of the way, I would give this game a 9.5/10. Let's break it down:  Pros: [*] Absolutely GORGEOUS game. Capcom is doing magic with the RE Engine and literally every part of this game is gorgeous. [*] The dichotomy between the intense survival horror sections and the action horror sections blends really well for a game that will scare the sh*t out of you while also letting you live out a power fantasy, wasting zombies. [*] The gameplay is super fun. Being able to switch between 1st and 3rd person feels so seamless and that the game was crafted with the option in mind. [*] The story is a nice return after the Ethan Winters saga (for me personally). It was nice to connect back to the original story while progressing the narrative and doing interesting things with a new protagonist, Grace. [*] Like many RE games, the replayability is great. There are so many unlockables to change the way the game is played, as soon as I finished my first playthrough, I was able to start a new one and play it completely different. [*] LEON S FREAKIN' KENNEDY  Cons: [*] Certain sections can feel a little long, not necessarily respecting the balance between the survival horror and action segments. Not a huge problem by all means, but definitely in the latter half, there are sections that may feel too long. [*] The difficulty options are interesting. Departing from previous difficulty options, this game's options do not feel as nuanced. I am such a fan of older RE games and using ink ribbons to save, but this game having it as a mechanic for only part of the campaign just felt odd. And the difficulty difference between the standard difficulty and Insanity is drastic. [*] Bosses. The RE series is known for the bosses and I think this title trends to the lower end in terms of unique and interesting boss battles. They are not horrible, but I definitely find them less memorable than previous titles.  Overall, this game is incredible and worth the hype. Whether you're looking for a spooky game or a fun action packed game, Resident Evil Requiem has you covered. Capcom, you are KILLING IT.

9/10  An amazing horror game and one of the best entries in the RE franchise, taking inspiration from RE7, RE4 and RE8 (and even some inspiration from RE6, in a good way), with only some small flaws.  The game is split between two playable characters, Grace and Leon, and their sections are very distinct from each other: Grace's sections are very focused on horror and resource management, with limited ammo supply and the game encouraging stealth over combat, with Grace as a character also being very nervous, which matches her gameplay style. In addition, she also has a limited inventory, similarly to the inventory system from RE7. Leon's sections, meanwhile, are more focused on action and combat, with the game providing considerably more ammo. Leon is also able to perform stealth takedowns without the need of a specific item (like Grace does), only needing to sharpen his hatchet as it gets damaged from use.  The game does the switching between both characters very well. Even during Leon's sections, the action is done right, not being over-the-top, while also still maintaining a level of horror.  The enemy design is amazing, as most zombies in the game still retain part of their personality - they have limited speech ability, being able to say some words, and they're often seen doing things pertaining to who they used to be: cleaning incessantly, turning off lights, chopping meat, singing, etc. It also means that some zombies carry weapons, going from bottles that they throw to slabs of concrete and even occasionally guns. It all helps to build the atmosphere, specially during Grace's sections.  This is a game that also heavily builds on the story of the franchise, not only filling in some blanks in the story but also leaving a lot open to future entries, so the future of the RE franchise is really promising right now, thanks to Requiem.  The game also both performs incredibly well and looks amazing - even while running the game in performance mode, the graphics still looked great and I had no technical issues at all.  I also didn't notice any bugs at all during the game, which would normally be surprising, but it seems to be par for the course, with other recent RE games also being very polished.  For the flaws, there are really only a few worth mentioning.  The first and main flaw is that the NG+ mode is somewhat underwhelming: you get whatever unlockables you got with points, Leon's chest and tracker are unlocked from the start, and that's it. Guns, items, gun upgrades and inventory upgrades from previous playthrough don't carry over and you have to find/buy them all over again. One of the things I've always enjoyed in RE games was being able to start a new playthrough while carrying the upgrades I had before so I can enjoy a playthrough of steamrolling through enemies (or using upgrades to tackle harder difficulties). Additionally, the unlockable weapons are also somewhat underwhelming - apart from one unlockable pistol for Grace and one for Leon, the rest of the unlockable guns aren't that interesting and they can't even be upgraded, either.  The second is that there is no item box for Leon, in addition to him also getting only one case upgrade. So, unless the player is constantly using their supplies, it means that Leon's inventory is often going to be full or nearly full. Surplus items can be sold, but I think I would prefer being able to stash them and only selling if absolutely needed.  Finally, there is something that happens in the story that is a pretty big spoiler, so I won't provide details about it outside of spoiler tags, but there is one character in the game with a lot of promise that ends up not having that promise fulfilled. Actual spoilers: [spoiler]Zeno is a really good antagonist throughout the game, but ends up being unceremoniously killed during a cutscene, with no actual boss fight involving him. Played through the game 3 times and I can safely say this is tied with the RE4 remake as my favorite of the RE Engine games. A great blend of survival horror from RE2 and 7 and the action-adventure of RE4 (and maybe an appropriately small amount of RE6 in a couple of key scenes).   The game switches between the two main protagonists as you progress through the story. Grace's gameplay is more survival-horror with less combat, more puzzle solving, and resource management, whereas Leon's gameplay is almost all action. I feel like Grace's parts are stronger with the care facility having some of the best level design in the modern series and unique zombie personalities to deal with. Leon's sections are still a blast to play and has some well-designed set pieces, but his half is just not as interesting gameplay-wise as Grace's sections for me. I kind of felt like I played two great halves of two different games, and I just wish there was more.  It took me around 16 hours for my first playthrough and it felt expertly paced. Other than a mandatory flashback scene in the second half that's more annoying than scary, I felt pretty engaged throughout the whole runtime. Like most RE games, there's plenty of neat bonus items to unlock to make the game worth replaying multiple times. My third playthrough was a 3 hour speedrun with infinite ammo which felt like a fun victory lap. Hopefully a Mercenaries/Raid mode is added in the future because it'd be nice to have an extra mode to play after finishing it.  The overall presentation of the game is fantastic, with great visuals, performance, and optimization. The fact that someone at Nvidia thought that this game's visuals needed to be "enhanced" with DLSS5 AI garbage is insane to me (and also insulting to the talented artists that worked on it). Awesome sound design, soundtrack, and voice acting as well.  The story is entertaining for the most part and I enjoyed the main characters and over-the-top villains. It's a fun, campy, summer blockbuster style story, which is kind of the norm for this series. There are some plot points that might seem like nonsense, especially in the second half, but they didn't bother me too much. If you're a Resident Evil lore expert, some stuff might bug you, but for me I still enjoyed my time with it.  Highly recommended!

His charisma and quiet confidence bring a strong emotional core to the experience. Even in the most terrifying moments, his presence grounds the story, adding depth and personality that longtime fans will appreciate. Watching him navigate the nightmare with a mix of grit and grace is one of the game’s highlights.  Overall, Resident Evil 9: Requiem is a masterclass in modern horror gaming—terrifying, immersive, and incredibly fun. It’s a must-play for fans of the series and anyone looking for a truly unforgettable horror experience.  -Wesker

Re 9 is just a pure disappointment.  You have a few hours of something interesting and teasing with Grace, where you explore new locations, resolve puzzles, and search for new clues to finally get the full picture of the story.  The first part of Leon in the mansion feels like a smart distraction, a short break for the player to relax a bit before diving back into the mystery of Re 9... ...But no, there is no mystery left. 1. After the helicopter crash scene, Leon's gameplay style becomes the only gameplay loop (even on Grace's episodes) until you finish this empty shell of a game. After the mansion part of the game, your only gameplay left is to shoot, run, farm points, upgrade weapons, rinse and repeat until the last cutscene.  Don't trust those people or articles which compare this gameplay mix to Re 2 OG or Re 2 R with Re 4 — this is not true!  Honestly, it feels like Resident Evil 5 combined with Resident Evil 6, with rotten enemies taken from Resident Evil Revelations 2 implemented in the worst way possible...  Zone-spawning zombies to kill and clear the area, Cinematic sequences that feel like they were made for QTE, but had QTE removed just before release. Motorbike sections with unlimited ammo and endless enemies until you reach the next scripted waypoint. RPG fired at you while on the motorbike — are you already feeling this nonsense Re 6 aura?  No investigation. No puzzles. No new areas to explore.  2. The areas they want you to explore in Raccoon City are the same ones you have already seen in Re2R and that awful piece of remake R3R.  That’s it! There are no areas from Re 2 or Re 3 OG nor any from Outbreak reimagined in new, remake style.  I could swear, I at least hoped to visit the Raccoon Press building, because our foster mother Alyssa Ashcroft was working there as an investigative journalist. But no, they just killed her in the prologue and that's it. Done. Forget about her. The next time you see her is only in final cutscenes.  Baam! That’s how important character she is. Your mother. An investigative journalist everyone wanted silenced... A few hours later in the game - Ehh... what was her name? Who is this woman?   Back to the locations - yeah, there are none. No real expansion, no depth. The game just mockingly teases you with items like Raccoon City Zoo tickets from Resident Evil Outbreak, as if saying to the player — remember this one? Nope, we won’t do it for you. Eat dirt...   3. The story itself is weak. Very weak. Already in the prologue, just by Alyssa Ashcroft’s dialogue, the scriptwriters keep winking at you that she is not Grace’s mother, and that we, as Grace, are so, so special that the player immediately understands — Grace is one of the successful experiments. And this is confirmed again and again through antagonist dialogue throughout the story. The Leon part of the story - ahh forget it, He and Sherry are both infected with T-virus mutation and in the end it will miracuosly dissappear without any trace as if there were none.  4. Interesting boss battles!? Forget about them. The only boss fight I even remember is killing Chunk, only because you need to use three Hemolytic Injectors (which are rather expensive) right into his ass.  5. The final boss battle feels like the devs saying: "Hey pal, we are tired, we don’t have time, and we actually don’t want to do a final boss battle..." "Ehh!? You are still here!?"  "Here, take the awful final boss battle from Re3R. Eat dirt!"  And that’s all. That’s the whole game. There are no closed areas left or anything interesting to replay after the first run to explore in your next walkthrough.  I hope that I am wrong here, but Resident Evil 9 Requiem is a big success for Capcom and... ... And a gravestone not to the RE series, but to the path.  The path that Resident Evil 7 found on its own, only with a slight look back (over the shoulder) at the original, classic Resident Evil gameplay formula. The path that Resident Evil 7 established to revive the series from decomposing into “just another zombie shooter game” trash completely. The path the studio tried to follow... until now.  From Dev Diaries and Re 9 Requiem itself, it is apparent that Capcom was and still is obsessed with the idea of turning Resident Evil into a blockbuster action shooter for all, to maximize its audience and sales.  Due to Re 9’s success on the market and positive audience response, it’s a clear corporate signal, they found a new “golden” path, and they will push this formula into future RE games wherever possible. On this sadly overcast note, I am ending this epitaph.  Sleep well, dear RE… until your next revival.

Just finished Resident Evil 9 and honestly… I loved it.  What surprised me the most was the story. I really didn’t expect Spencer’s character to go in that direction. Seeing him change and actually want to give hope to the world instead of destruction was really interesting, and the fact that he finds that hope through Grace made the story hit a lot harder than I expected.  At first I thought Capcom might just be bringing Leon back again for fan service, but he actually plays a really good role in the story. The contrast between Grace’s horror-focused gameplay and Leon’s more action-heavy sections works really well. The horror parts with Grace are tense and creepy, while Leon’s sections feel like classic Resident Evil action.  I also really enjoyed the difficulty and all the challenges. The game can be pretty tough, but in a good way, and it feels really satisfying when you finally get through a hard section. My favorite part was probably the section with "The Girl" in the water treatment facility. That whole sequence was absolutely terrifying and easily one of the scariest moments in the game.  Honestly for me it’s an easy 11/10.  If you like story-driven games or you’re a big Resident Evil fan, I definitely recommend it. It’s one of the best entries in the series and maybe even my favorite.  Great game. Great series, if not the greatest.

Capcom absolutely cooked this one to perfection!  TO PERFECTION!! This is an absolute chef's kiss to the fans and the franchise.  Not only do they get what fans like about Resident Evil, they served it across all platforms without needing day-one bug patches for the console releases. For the most part, the PC version is perfect as well, catering to many different setups and age-old graphics cards—1080ti, I’m looking at you! (Can you believe it’s almost been 10 years since that card launched?)  Honoring the Legacy On the subject of anniversaries: some of you know that Capcom is celebrating Resident Evil’s 30th anniversary this year, and they have totally respected and honored that milestone with this game. They have taken what works about every game they’ve released in that time, chucked out the bad stuff, and kept only the good. It is the perfect recipe for a seasoned fan or a newcomer diving into the series for the first time.  I have been playing Resident Evil since day one, so I’ve experienced the good, the bad, and the ugly. For me, the series has never truly "peaked" because with each big release they tend to sidestep and try a different angle—whether that’s changing camera angles, removing puzzles, or introducing new mechanics. Sometimes, it feels like only the first few games actually belong to the same series!  As legendary as Resident Evil 4 was, if Capcom had branded it as a new IP rather than an RE title, I think the series would be buried and gone. It needed that reinvention to keep things fresh, and whenever they put out a new game now, the whole industry takes note.  Finding the "Resident Evil" Recipe Resident Evil 5 was wildly successful and, at the time, their best-selling entry. On paper, high sales mean "this is what fans want," so they doubled down on that for Resident Evil 6, but it was a misstep. It crammed in every action trope imaginable. If that had been a new IP, it would have been a fine, fun action title—but there is a specific recipe that makes a Resident Evil game feel "right," and they finally nailed it here.  They have taken the first-person and iconic over-the-shoulder action and given you a choice. Many fans can’t stand first-person, but after the success of RE7 and RE8, it’s great to see both camera angles featured and polished. (Personally, I recommend Grace’s sections in first-person and Leon’s in third-person!)  Story and Pacing I won’t go too deep into the story as that’s a huge part of the enjoyment, but while it isn't overloaded with backstory, you won't feel like a fish out of water if this is your first game. It’s told in a way that keeps you intrigued, making you wonder how these things happened rather than feeling like you should have played the previous games first.  The pacing and the use of the new character, Grace, act as a great introduction to this horrific world. It carries you all the way to the final scene and leaves you wanting more—to go through it again on different difficulties, earn challenge points, and experience it all over again.  The Horror The zombies are exactly as they should be, but better. They aren't just a "herd" anymore; they have individual characteristics that tap into your psyche. You might kill one zombie who actually says "sorry" for attacking you, while others just want to cut you to pieces! Some hate loud sounds; others will turn off the lights you just turned back on. It’s fantastic, creepy, and unsettling because it makes the setting feel convincing. By the time the gameplay shifts to Leon, you feel absolutely ready to start taking names.  Gameplay and Mechanics Item management is good, pacing is excellent, and combat is superb with many different approaches to every situation. Stealth isn't just an "instant death if spotted" mechanic; it encourages you to sneak to conserve ammo and learn your surroundings before rushing in. Believe me, this game will throw everything at you, and the death scenes are BRUTAL. The world feels reactive—enemies hear your heavy footsteps and your gunfire, which really pulls you into the immersion.  The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ With all that said, there are a few ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I noticed after a couple of playthroughs:  The Puzzles: They have taken a real back seat. A "puzzle" now is basically a fetch quest, and most unlocks just require finding a note with the answer. I wish they had a "Puzzle Difficulty" option like Silent Hill 2. I’d love a mode where items need to be inspected and manipulated to reveal keys, or doors with symbols that require logic to open. They have some of this, but it's more like they just had it for nostalgia sake for one or two things, they also give a self-aware nod to this in one scene, but I wanted more of that classic puzzle tedium that the original games were known for.  Audio Sync (PC): Performance was mostly spot on, except for the sound being out of sync in cutscenes. I think the game struggles to load new assets during transition scenes, causing a delay. Moving the game to an SSD completely fixed this for me, but hopefully, a patch will allow it to run better on standard drives.  The Forced Stealth Section: There is one moment that feels like a pace-killer. I welcomed it initially because I didn't want the game to end, but on a replay, it’s a chore. It’s a "get spotted and die" section that feels jarring once the surprise has worn off.  Conclusion Aside from those small points, this game is absolutely brilliant. It’s a Resident Evil game that has finally stepped out of the "itchy, tasty" closet to declare its brilliance. It took 30 years to get here, but it was worth it. Between this and the potential for RE10 or a Code Veronica remake, I can’t wait to see what they cook up next!  HUGE round of applause from me!!

Resident Evil: The Set Pieces  I don't know how to feel about this outing. It's not bad, but it leaves me disappointed. Overall personally, I definitely feel it's a setback. They're once again slowly drifting toward the spectacle, which is a shame because 7 was the right direction if you ask me. And they're slowly but surely moving away from that. Village overall is my favorite recent game, it's just excellently designed, but it definitely had its out there action moments.  Maybe Capcom are confused as to where to head after the success of the RE4 remake and as consequence they stretched this one apart in all directions. For one it just doesn't have the intimacy and urgency of 7 and 8, which I definitely feel has something to do with the perspective. You might argue, "but you can play the entire game in First Person!" and I did, yet, certain elements are designed for the third person. Leon's idiotic melee attack is a good example; it's the most immersive breaking/video gamey thing I've ever seen in a recent Resident Evil. Just yanks you right out.  Another thing is the cinematics themselves. They were all handled in First Person in 7 and 8. Not in 9. Which removes you from the feeling of danger. You are reduced to a spectator. You know nothing will happen to the character and nothing is expected of you the player. Whereas in 7 and 8, there was the sense that you might have to act at any point. Also I feel it asks way more of the designers, in essence, it demands more finesse in telling an entire tale from the perspective of a pair of eyes only.   Lastly my major design complaint is what others have pointed out. It's too much based on set piece locations. It doesn't feel like a coherent large place that you have to explore and solve. It's mostly, go here, look around, boss fight, go here shooting gallery, go here fight until you find item. Go here turn on all the lights. It's overtly video gamey. Which most games are, but the good ones hide it with subtle flair that makes you forget it.  I realize all this makes it sound like I hate it, I don't. It's a fine enough game, certain elements of the design are sublime (most of the care facility in fact) and it's beautiful to look at. Even Leon's sections of action I'll admit are good, if that's what you want. I don't. But if you like that stuff, it's good.  If someone were to ask me, should I play Requiem? I'd say sure it's not a bad game, but I'd personally start somewhere else. Also I just feel like, well, there are enough "Overwhelmingly Positive" reviews and if I should have my critique reach whatever data collecting aggregator Capcom uses it should probably be pinned under RED Negative Review.  I'm happy people are enjoying this game. I personally can't help but be slightly worried. I don't want this to be an RE4 moment. Because that eventually leads to games like 6. If that's where we are headed, I might as well put my brain into airplane mode and watch some of the dumbass movies they spit out.

This game is absolute cinema. I'm always surprised how Capcom manages to come with novel and gripping storylines in Resident Evil universe. The new character Grace is especially great, but I also liked the return of Leon as the more experienced companion. All performances by the actors are also outstanding. It really feels like a movie at times. The graphics also add a lot to this. Especially with path tracing the game looks stunning and the characters and materials in the game really shine. It also runs reasonably well. Only one section towards the end of the game had some stuttering that was likely caused by the engine not being able to handle the more open environment very well.  You get a mix of two different playstyles that provide a nice change of pace every once in a while. When you play as Grace the game is more puzzle oriented and has more of a Resident Evil 7 feel. There are also some new mechanics that didn't exist in previous titles which make every encounter even more strategic. The puzzle loop has really been perfected here. Playing as Leon is more action oriented and feels more like Resident Evil 4 Remake. Although his part only really picks up after the first ~30% of the game. Overall I liked his sections less since I'm more of a puzzle fan. But you do get to feel quite powerful and there are some surprises that felt really cool.  There are a few minor gripes that I just want to mention because I'd like to see them improved in future titles. The dynamic difficulty can get a bit too crazy at times with the game basically forcing you to die at certain points only to make it easy on the second attempt. I felt like I had couple of unnecessary deaths because I simply got unlucky. The controls can also feel a bit cumbersome at times. Especially playing as Leon in more chaotic fights can lead to some frustration. The game also drags on for a bit towards the end and there are way too many (mini) boss fights. It makes them feel less special and I'd like to see the series go more into the puzzle direction again. But that is of course a matter of taste.  All that being said the game is 100% worth buying. Might even be the best Resident Evil game ever made. You'll certainly have a great time if you enjoyed the series in the past.

First and foremost, [i] Resident Evil Requiem [/i] has been really fun to play.   I avoided most trailers and information about it so that I could be surprised — and I have been; I like the use of different perspectives depending on which story is being played. The storyline feels solid and entertaining; I was flabbergasted to see Alyssa Ashcroft rescued from the not-so-well-known [i] Resident Evil Outbreak[/i] and [i] Resident Evil Outbreak File 2[/i]. I do not feel Grace adds anything new, but she blends in well and does what she is supposed to do — in-game and narratively speaking. However, Emily... If I had not done the first playthrough in the highest possible difficulty at the time, I would have deemed the game [b] too short[/b]. My first playthrough had me checking every nook and cranny, enjoying the slow pace set by the enemies. The second round was way faster, more focused on challenges and speed, then finally the third playthrough showed me that this game might not have very good replayability. Resident Evil has returned to feed us once again with Requiem. Everything we love about the series has been crammed into one tight package, framed through the lens of both series veteran Leon S(ex) Kennedy and series newbie Grace Ashcroft. Together, they make up two halves of a whole, and, amazingly, neither half feels short-changed. Both are fully realized and deliver one of the best executed examples of a dual-protagonist structure in recent memory.  You get the dread-inducing survival-horror of the classic games, with excellent level design and memorable locations and encounters that will go down in series history. You also get the intense action-horror of the later games, and just like Resident Evil 4, the gunplay is among the most satisfying you will find in any third-person shooter. The game is perfectly paced, speeding things up and slowing things down at just the right time before funneling you into the next encounter.  Now is the best time to be a Resident Evil fan. Requiem is an absolute banger and further cements the series as one of the strongest and most iconic in video game history.

Requiem is essentially a combination of the best features from several previous Resident Evil games. Splitting the gameplay between Grace and Leon was a great idea, balancing survival and action horror. Grace has to rely on wit and stealth, while Leon delivers satisfying, spectacular carnage. A seasoned series veteran doesn’t hold back, and taking down hordes of zombies in his shoes provides plenty of brutal, gory fun.  The visuals on PC are impressive, especially with Path Tracing enabled and all settings maxed out. Nvidia technologies like DLSS and Frame Generation are very well implemented, I didn’t notice any artifacts (DLSS Q + FG 2x).  The performances are very good, voice acting stands out, I especially liked Grace's VA.  The story is well-paced, gradually revealing its cards and new secrets, effectively keeping players on their toes; Requiem also serves as a tribute to long-time fans. Grace is a great new character, I quickly grew to like her, and the ending was truly uplifting after the game’s heavy storyline.  The only things I could complain about are that the main story could be longer, although replayability of the game is decent, I achieved 100% completion within 3 playthroughs, and the orphanage section felt unnecessary and rather boring, especially on next playthroughs (no wonder modders made a skip for this part).  Capcom has been in incredible form for the past few years—hopefully they can keep it up for as long as possible! Can't wait for RE9 story DLC and further remakes and instalments!

Resident Evil Requiem – Review (8.2/10)  Ah yes, Resident Evil Requiem—the game that bravely answers the question: “What if we did the same thing again… but slightly shinier?”  To be fair, it does look great. The atmosphere is dark, moody, and about as cheerful as a locked basement with questionable noises—which is exactly what you’d expect. Exploration is decent too, assuming you enjoy backtracking through the same hallways like you forgot your keys… repeatedly.  Combat? It works. You shoot things, they (eventually) stop moving. Revolutionary. Resource management is back as well, so you can relive the joy of asking yourself, “Do I really need this bullet?” Spoiler: you do.  The enemies are creepy at first… until you realize you’ve seen most of them already. Variety clearly took a day off. And the story? It’s interesting enough to keep you going, but don’t expect anything life-changing. It’s more like, “Oh, that’s cool… I guess.”  Performance is solid overall, though you might run into a few hiccups—just to remind you the game is, in fact, alive.  Pros:  . Looks great, very spooky (good job) . Exploration exists and sometimes feels rewarding . Classic survival mechanics are still doing their thing  Cons:  . Enemy variety said “maybe next time” . Story is… there . Minor technical issues for flavor  Final Verdict: It’s a good game. Not groundbreaking, not terrible—just comfortably sitting in that “yeah, I had fun” zone.  Score: 8.2/10

While not the same caliber as RE2/RE4, perhaps the greatest mainline RE games, Requiem is a good Resident Evil game. It strikes a nice balance between survival horror and puzzle solving at the series' roots (like RE1/RE0), and the intense monster smashing action of later games (RE4/RE5).  It presents Grace as a protaganist that is far more a *normal* person that's frightened. Her reactions IMHO, are far more human than most, and the get back up and keep going factor shows the characters strength. We also get a somewhat older and more mature Leon, who is no longer the rookie but the unyielding hero we've come to know.  The zapping system between Grace / Leon in the early part of the game, I think is pretty spectular, and much nicer than either approach in RE2: the original and the separate "runs" of the remake. Both fit well and evolve with their mission, and I believe alternating them this way works a nice better than making them separate campaigns.  Plot wise, I think it works pretty well. Obviously, being an RE game, we have to discount some concepts like physics and technology, but the plot intersects well. In the end, thanks to Grace, I think that Leon finally gets his wish about the truth of Racoon City. I also rather love the idea that Spencer's last wish with Elpis, and how Grace and Emily fit into this, rather than, ya'know, the typical evil villian business. It's far more a Requiem than a Revisit, but it's also well peppered with references to the old games.

Honestly, Requiem can only be reccommended with how perfect this game is. It could've been a tad bit longer, but I won't complain about that much, since we're getting a story expansion soon. The optimization is perfect and I was surprised I could run it on max graphics with around 400 FPS, even though I'm currently running single-channel RAM. Graphics are honestly insane and the entire game is just really well made, including the extraordinary performance of the VA's.   The story is nicely paced, with a good equality of the two main characters Grace Ashcroft and the goat Leon Kennedy. With a perfect balance of horror (Grace's POV) and action (Leon's POV) it's definitely a must play for every Resident Evil enjoyer. For the achievements and 100%ing the game; it's really enjoyable to actually get all the achievements and look around the Rhodes Hill Care Center, or the wrecks of Raccoon City.  So, yes, I can only reccommend this game even for the whopping price.

[h1]⚠️ Long rant + heavy spoilers ⚠️[/h1]  [b]The industry standard must have hit an all-time low[/b] for this game to be sitting at “Overwhelmingly Positive.”  To me, this is yet another example of Capcom’s ongoing identity crisis when it comes to storytelling, game design, and artistic direction as a whole.  It feels like the studio has been recycling its 20+ year-old franchises for decades now, relying almost entirely on them for success (aside from technical achievements like the RE Engine). But when it comes to creating something truly fresh or original, they seem unable to move forward without leaning on [b]nostalgia bait[/b] or stretching a franchise for as long as it remains profitable.  [hr][/hr]  [b]Hype over substance[/b]  We’re living in a clickbait, TikTok-driven era where content is judged less on depth and more on hype — and RE9 is a perfect example of that formula. Even before release, the marketing machine was already in full motion, largely driven by content creators. Many made it seem like we were about to witness the game of the decade. Reaction videos flooded social media for months, especially around Leon, while Grace was barely highlighted.  [i]“We’re back in Raccoon City? We’re so back.”[/i] [i]“Porsche & Hamilton collab? So much aura.”[/i] [i]“Leon kicking the ♥♥♥♥ out of zombies? I can’t wait.”[/i]  And just like that, the hype built itself.  [b]Result:[/b] : fastest-selling Resident Evil title in history, over 350k concurrent players on PC at launch, and 6 million copies sold within a week. The shareholders must be thrilled. But longtime fans? They paid $70 for roughly 9 hours of gameplay. Sadly, the FOV slider wasn’t even included in the deluxe edition — might have to wait for a DLC. s/  [hr][/hr]  [b]Safe, scripted, recycled[/b]  The game takes no risks. Capcom is playing it as safe as possible. It’s overly scripted, constantly holds your hand, and once again falls back on the same formula: narrow corridors, puzzle backtracking (“oh no, the power is out again”), and of course the usual stalker-type enemies.  [hr][/hr]  [b]Grace arc — good idea, bad execution[/b]  Ironically, despite being almost absent from the promotional material, Grace ends up carrying the first half of the game pretty much on her own. But that doesn’t necessarily make her section enjoyable.  The voice acting is decent, but the constant stuttering feels overdone and immersion-breaking (“W-w-w-what t-t-the hell is happening?”). The game director mentioned he wanted players to be scared during her sequences, and that Grace was designed to reflect us, the player. Because she isn’t special, she isn’t trained in combat or gunfights — she’s just a random person, just like most of us (though she's FBI). She is supposed to mirror our real-time emotions, but in reality, the devs end up taking away the freedom of feeling fear by forcing you into what is supposed to be scary and how you should react. It feels like the game is trying to be a movie rather than an actual game.  As a result, Grace comes off as this clumsy character who constantly panics, stumbles, and falls during chase sequences. I’m not gonna lie — when I fell twice in the span of 4 seconds while running away from "The Girl" trying to reach the safe room, I just alt-F4’d the game on my first playthrough and went to sleep.  Level design doesn’t help either. The care center feels like a reused and glorified RPD: a big reception hall as a safe hub, with side corridors leading to key items needed to progress. Doesn’t ring a bell? Because that’s basically the RE2R layout.  Lastly, Emily. At first, I thought she would be a key player in this new storyline, tying the plot together as the mysteries unraveled. But to my disappointment, she was nothing more than a vessel for dramatic and emotional impact to deepen Grace’s character. After her “death,” the cracks really started to show.  Honestly, this feels like the point where Capcom abandoned their original idea for RE9. Grace and Victor weren’t enough to sell the game, so they brought Leon and Raccoon City back (just my theory). The whole post-apocalyptic Raccoon City honestly feels like it came from a canceled project that got repurposed here. And remember, this game was in development for 7 years.  [hr][/hr]  [b]Leon arc — mixed bag at best[/b]  As much as I like Nick Apostolides as our new "Leon", his performance here just doesn’t hit. He lowers his voice way too much, to the point where it sounds forced — like a Discord mod trying too hard to sound cool. Capcom wants him ultra serious, but also forces him to drop cringe one-liners every 5 minutes because people need their new “bingo” quotes.  His early scenes — chasing Victor, meeting Grace — are actually great. He feels mature, grounded, professional. But once the “I’m not on the menu” type lines start, it’s over. From that point on, it’s constant one-liners until the credits roll.  [hr][/hr]  [b]Marketing gimmicks… that go nowhere[/b]  You can’t even drive the Porsche. The Hamilton watch? Barely used outside of a single scene. It could have been a great way to display health or interact with the world. Or wouldn’t it have been cool if we actually had to drive our way to Raccoon City? Instead, it’s just branding. Zero gameplay impact.   [hr][/hr]  [b]Raccoon City — empty in the worst way[/b]  Once we arrive in Raccoon City, it feels… empty. As it should — but also empty from a game design perspective. There is no ambience, no real soundtrack, no memorable audio or SFX. The buildings, colors, and lighting are bleak, but they don’t deliver that emotional “we’re back where it all started” feeling. Leon’s voice delivery doesn’t help either — it just adds to the already sterile environment  Enemy variety is a joke. Whereas the care center staff each had their own personality, textures, and behavior, in Raccoon City we literally have two enemy types (three if you count the spider): dust zombies and BSAA zombies (plus the chainsaw guy, I guess).  Cherry on top : the BSAA soldiers all have the exact same face and hair. Every single one. In 2026. That’s not artistic choice Capcom — that’s asset reuse.  After collecting the detonator parts (which was already a chore), you suddenly get a motorbike section, infinite ammo, wolves chasing you, and you’re shooting Victor Gideon in the ass. RE: Vendetta called, they want their plot back. I thought we were in a grounded, emotional story. Guess not.  [hr][/hr]  [b]Villains and plot — completely lost[/b]  It’s official — Capcom cannot make villains anymore. And that's concerning for the future titles. Not only do they jeopardize already existing ones (Salazar and Saddler in RE4 Remake, Spencer…), they also clearly can’t come up with any decent replacement for Wesker since RE5 — hence Zeno. Zeno is the perfect example of Capcom’s inability to create anything unique without reusing what made their franchises successful in the first place. And the worst part is: we know just as little about Zeno at the end of the game as we did when he was first introduced. By the time the credits roll, nothing meaningful has been revealed or developed about him.  Victor Gideon actually had potential, but gets sidelined for this deus ex machina character. His voice actor is probably the best in the game too, which makes it even worse.  As for the plot… what happened?  Emily not being dead feels like a last-minute asspull. The Elpis storyline had real potential (government conspiracy, erased evidence, cure for bioweapons), but it goes nowhere.  And where are the OG characters? Claire, Jill, Ada, Carlos… nobody shows up or even matters.  It could have led to something interesting — like the original cast going rogue with the cure.  Instead, Leon just hands it over… and that’s it.  [hr][/hr]  [b]TL;DR[/b]  Nostalgia bait, hype-driven game that plays it safe, reuses old ideas, and delivers a short, forgettable experience. At least in runs well, and looks decent.  [b]Wait for a discount.[/b]

This is a masterpiece! I absolutely loved this game right since the first couple of minutes. The story is beautifully woven, with twists and a great climax. The atmosphere is tense, the suspense is true, and the horror is scary to the right measure. Grace's parts with The Girl give you that constant feeling of being vulnerable in the dark. The fear here actually gives you wings - your brain is in hyperdrive and you want to beat odds with intelligence. Leon on the other hand is in full action mode, destroying zombies has become his second nature. The game perfectly captures the gunplay of a seasoned warrior who has been doing this since ages. The gameplay is fantastic! I loved Leon's finishers with the .50 cal executions, the 9mm to the chin, the shotgun in the mouth! Blood and gore are abandunt; you see chunks of flesh mixed with blood; each shot registers as visible holes in the body, and the sound effects satisfy your need for guilty pleasures of R-rated stuff. The graphics comes with adjustible filters and that's amazing. The background score is beautiful - it peaks specifically during Leon's venture in Raccoon City when you take a look at the devastation and ruble and skies silently talking about what they witnessed 28 years ago after the missile strike. Unlocking infinite ammo was tough without medicines and blood collector but the reward is giving me a whole different powerhouse of experience now that I'm in my third playthrough. Enjoy this one!

As a huge Resident Evil fan, I found this installment of the series to be a huge disappointment.  It starts off promisingly, with strong atmosphere, sound design, storytelling, and graphics... but only at first. The hotel section delivers the kind of tense experience you will desperately want the rest of the game to maintain.  Sadly, the game soon starts to feel more like Resident Evil 6, which, in my opinion, is the weakest entry in the series.  Things quickly become bizarre in all the wrong ways. We get blood-sucking elements, and switching to Leon feels like stepping into an action movie rather than a survival horror game. There is little of the usual tension or suspense. Then we get another story involving a Wesker who is not really Wesker. Really? Again? From that point on, it only gets worse. Story will start to make no sense. In fact, none of what we are gonna do will make any sense whatsoever.  I have not even started talking about how annoying Grace is to play as, listen to, or even move around with. It's like Lisa Simpson turning into 22YO anime girl. You can play Trevor GTA VR video and the first moment with the Trevor will be every Grace's dialogue. To-to-today, Junior!  This ends up feeling like the worst installment in the series, made for newcomers and casual audiences rather than longtime fans. I hope Capcom changes course, but I doubt it will.  Resident Evil was the only series I used to preorder, because even when an entry was not great, we still knew we would play it. After this, though, I seriously doubt that will continue.  Capcom needs to wake up. I am tired of seeing them make the same mistakes over and over again, and I am not even going to start on a full Vaas-style monologue about it.  Game sucks.

not only did this became my favorite resident evil game, it became one of my favorite games of all time, and i fell in love with it more and more with each replay.  grace ashcroft is a fantastic new character and i think the awkward, socially anxious crowd can relate to her a ton. her more bottled in scared nature is reflected in her gameplay, which is reminiscent of old school resident evil - simplistic inventory, limited resources and ammo, scavenging and finding items for crafting, and picking and choosing fights with zombies, often finding yourself fleeing rather than engaging in enemies - her sections are true survival horror. the care center and basement are some of the best atmospheres in the game to traverse through.  leon kennedy... women want him, men want [strike]to be[/strike] him. after surviving through grace's anxiety inducing sections, leon's sections are a little reward you get after pulling teeth to make it through with grace. worry less about your ammo/inventory management and more about what flashy sequence of attacks you can chain together between zombies. for the resident evil 4 fans, this is your time to shine - it's the best version of the more action-esque resident evil games like 4 and 5, with carry over mechanics from 4 remake such as parrying, allowing for skill expression for those who truly want to get good at the combat in this game (especially if you wanna try insanity mode, you're gonna be using that parry a lot.) it's a satisfying feeling going through the same areas grace did but as leon, having your chance to clear out the zombies that you would flee from as grace.  i won't spoil the story as i think it's worth experiencing yourself, but i will say this: the story absolutely can stand on its own and in my opinion doesn't require knowledge of previous games to understand what's happening. however, for people who have played 2 and 3, there are scenes that will be ESPECIALLY sentimental, emotional, and overall just way more impactful - if you're able to, i'd definitely recommend playing 2 and 3 before requiem, but if you can't, it's not the end of the world as the game can hold its own without those games. you'll find a surprising amount of heartfelt moments throughout your time playing.  this is my personal contender for game of the year 2026, and it's become one of my top 10 favorite games of all time.

The best *new* Resident evil installment that's not a remake in a long time. It's not to say it's not without some faults, but the positives outweigh the negatives. The average playtime seems to be like 13-15 hours maybe which is decent for the money value depending on the person. If you do more than one playthrough then of course the value goes up.  They boldly blend both previous types of gameplay of modern Resident Evil, being first person horror and third person action, Grace segments including more of the horror, and Leon's segments including more of the action.  After finishing up with the mansion, the game goes from horror and calculated play into something more akin to the Merceneries gamemode to be honest. The second half of the game seems to be what people criticize where you play as Leon. It's not to say it's boring or all bad design, as it's clearly meant to be alot more action and fun for people who want combat.
