Resident Evil: Requiem isn't a bad game. Just like the others before it, it's very solid. Having said that, all the people you see online saying it's the best RE game out there are absolutely glazing the ♥♥♥♥ out of it.  First, let's start with arguably the worst thing in the game and franchise: Grace. Grace is literally the worst character I can think of in the entire RE franchise, surpassing Ashely in OG RE4. Everything you can think of about a character that could make you hate them, Grace encompasses all of them. Firstly, she's the most unqualified FBI personnel out there. Anyone who uses the excuse, "well she just works at the desk", is hard coping. The FBI then sends her to investigate a serious issue relating to her mother's death by herself, knowing she's absolutely incompetent. She stutters just about every single word. I can't blame the voice actress for this, I blame the Director for this for not pointing it out and helping direct the voice actress and making them aware that they don't have to stutter on every single sentence. Top this with the fact that Grace literally have 0 awareness of danger. You're telling me a member of the FBI who attended academy is this oblivious? Come on. She literally will watch someone be murdered in front of her, turn infected, skin begin blackening, and be like, "are you okay?" Get attacked/attempted murdered by someone, "oh hey, are you alright?", and approach situations with no awareness or survivability skills. She watched a little girl turn into a giant mutant baby and legit thought she could save her, got mad at Leon when he shot at the mutated girl to save Grace, and then pulled thee ole, "I'm mad and leaving now", which actually set the rest of the plot in motion where she's tagging along with Zeno (so you can basically blame the plot moving due to Grace's stupidity). Funny enough, you do end up saving the little girl at the end, which makes absolutely zero sense because the end cutscene shows her like she's in a cocoon in the mutant, but the cutscene where she initially transforms shows that's clearly not what happened. Anyways, Grace's only redeeming quality is that she's hot. That's literally it.  When the main characters aren't interesting, you at least look to the villains to be interesting. Instead, we get a Nemesis infected Igor from Frankenstein and Walmart Wesker, both of which are either not interesting or not displayed enough to care about. Leon's still a badass and carries the entire game as far as characters go. In regards to non-boss/important enemies, there's simply no defining ones out there except for giant mutant Babushka.  The level design and environments are pretty solid and it was pretty cool going to Raccoon City again. There's definitely a Nostalgic factor at play there. However, the underground facility was short lived and felt kind of bland in comparison to the underground Facilities in RE2 and RE3.  Gunplay is well polished. Gameplay in general is well polished. My biggest complaint is, just like they did with RE7, RE2 Remake and RE3 Remake, they deviated from traditional NG+ and instead went back to the Challenge Point system. It's not bad, but it's simply not as good as actual NG+. RE7 corrected this issue with RE8: Village, introducing the classic NG+ with weapons, upgrades, ammo, etc., carrying over, which was awesome. Then they completely abandon it in RE9? Makes no sense and is honestly silly, IMO.  Graphics are obviously solid and performance has been fine for me on my 4080 with everything maxed out at 4K (DLSS was on Performance mode though, mind you).   I either didn't pay attention or it simply didn't stick out enough for me to actual care, but in regards to music, it's okay. Creepy atmosphere felt creepy with complementary music, but given that there's little to no actual boss battles with epic boss battle music, it's not really something I'd give a yay or nay on. Oh, speaking of boss battles, Walmart Wesker isn't even an enemy you can battle. They're literally in cutscenes only, and only appear a handful of times before getting merked at the end. Like, what?  The story initially had my interest but turned out to be mid. As mentioned, Grace instantly took my interest out of the story because of how absolutely stupid and timid she is. Top that with a lack of villains (really only 2 main villains, Igor and Walmart Wesker) and the fact that they're uninteresting, and all you really have is the mystery of Elpis, which is an alleged weapon that turns out to be a cure. Good on paper, I'm sure, but executed poorly. The foundation itself was weak with the whole "dormant virus" that survivors of Raccoon City got. It's like they wanted to make another game with Leon, have a purpose to bring him back to Raccoon City, and whipped some random crap from their butts and said whatever, this works.  I'm sitting here talking trash about the game and what I dislike about it, yet slapping a recommended on it, but that's because when you buy an RE game, you already know it's gonna be good and you're gonna enjoy it. So I'm not here to state the obvious. You will play this game and you will enjoy this game. What I'm here to state is simply the things that really jumped out to me that I was disappointed with. Again, I still really enjoyed my time and will be playing this more in the future, it just has some hiccups and was absolutely glazed by so many people when, in actuality, it's a pretty mid RE game. It's a well polished turd that's wrapped in some nostalgic crust.

[b][h2]BLUF[/h2][/b] 9.0/10  One of the best games in the series, with a story and true survival horror formula to match. Appeases fans of both classic and new Resident Evil games, combining the best elements of the two in this love-letter to RE fans. Atmosphere, story, gameplay and graphics are compelling and immersive. A must-play for anyone who's even slightly a fan of Resident Evil or survival horror games in genera.   [b][h3]Overview[/h3][/b] Resident Evil Requiem is a welcome entry into the series, building off of the success and atmospheres of RE7 & RE8, while calling back to the formula that made classics like RE1 - 4 so loved. As with recent Resident Evil titles, the opening few hours and locations are incredibly immersive, atmospheric and maintain the sinister tone throughout. The shift in tempo and atmosphere during the mid-game loses some of this immeriveness and downright horror, however RE9 reclaims itself in the late-game as it returns to the amalgamation of what players have loved from the series' classic titles as well as it's newer icons like RE7.  The alternating between Grace and Leon is a welcome addition to force alternate playstyles and keep certain segments fresh and exciting. As a player who has preferred the newer titles to the originals (a sin, I know), I was originally sceptical of the game forcing me to alter my playstyle while also changing the atmosphere of the game. With Resident Evil 7 being my favourite title in the franchise for its overall terrifying-ness and the way it kept me on edge through my whole playthrough, I was worried that segments with Leon would break my immersion and ruin the atmosphere for me. However, I was pleasantly surprised by how much I enjoyed the Leon segments throughout Resident Evil Requiem, at no stage feeling like his playstyle ruined the game.  [b][h3]Gameplay[/h3][/b] Grace’s segments were my favourite parts of the game, though I admit I am biased, and perfectly replicated the first-person horror elements that made RE7 (and RE8 to a lesser extent) so terrifying. The early Grace segments almost rival the dread and paranoia created by RE7's Main and Old House segments, something that I wasn't sure RE9 would be able to achieve. The claustrophobia and feeling of helplessness, paired with the (optional) first-person view draws you close to the screen, listening intently for the squeak of a floorboard or growl of an enemy while you slink around trying to solve the next puzzle or just find the next save room.  Much like RE7 and RE8, exploration takes center stage with Grace, as you're forced to navigate around each area, finding clues and solving puzzles to survive and progress to the next segment. Resources are limited, making each encounter with an enemy a calculation of whether to run or fight, further adding to the sense of helplessness. Fans of RE7 will be no strangers to this formula of exploring, backtracking, puzzle solving and resource management, all whilst being stalked or constantly checking behind you for enemies. This has been perfected once again in RE9 and is what makes this game so great.  In my opinion, if the entire game was structured in this way and the claustrophobic and eerie level design was maintained throughout, RE9 would be flawless and a 10/10 horror experience. Where I felt the game was let down, however, was in Leon's segments during the mid-game.  These segments are heavily centred on action, melee combat and brute-forcing your way through a section with any weapon you see fit. At first, this change-up is refreshing and just what is needed to compliment the intense segments with Grace. Combat with Leon feels effortless and highly rewarding when you nail a parry and can finish an enemy up close and personal. The pacing, paired with Leon's much faster movement speed and comparitively more open areas, makes you feel like a seasoned veteran and a real action hero.  However, as you approach the mid-game, Leon's gameplay style begins to lose its appeal a little. I would argue that this is mainly down to level-design, lack of enemy variety, and uninspired boss fights. During this part of the game, RE9 falls victim to repetetition with little reward, sending you after three objectives with very similar gameplay loops partnered with the same enemies for the most part. This section of the game got stale rather quick, and was the reason why I stepped away from the game for a few days before coming back to finish it off.  That's not to say that Leon's segments of the game were not enjoyable, rather some of the most memorable parts of the game occur whilst playing as Leon. It's also fun to go ham and put metal to flesh with Leon's hatchet every once in a while, just not for multiple segments in a row.  [b][h3]Puzzles[/h3][/b] A Resident Evil game would not be Resident Evil without puzzles, and whilst puzzles do play a part in RE9, puzzle design is lacking and less intricate than previous titles. Furthermore, after the early-game segments, puzzles feel like they take a backseat and don't feature again as heavily, or at least as intricately, throughout the mid and late game. Perhaps it's because I played my first playthrough on standard difficulty, but I didn't feel as challenged by RE9's puzzles as expected.   I would've liked to see puzzles take a more central role, particularly in the late-game segments, as well as an increased difficulty or intricacy (one that could be scaled through a difficulty slider for players who don't wish to play the game this way).  [b][h3]Graphics[/h3][/b] Resident Evil Requiem is by far the most visually stunning entry in the series, by a mile. Capcom's updated RE Engine has environments looking better than ever before, with greater fidelity, improved ray-tracing and gorgeous textures. Character models are incredibly detailed and are amazing when viewed in either first or third person. If your PC is able to handle the game on maximum settings, I would HIGHLY recommend it, as it undoubtedly adds to the atmosphere and immersion tenfold.  [b][h3]Final Verdict[/h3][/b] Resident Evil Requiem is a standout entry in the series. Grace's segments felt like a true return to the terror, claustrophbia and scariness of RE7. Paired with the action and combat offered throughout Leon's segments, Resident Evil Requiem proves itself worthy of addition into the game libraries of Resident Evil and horror fans alike.  Though the game does have its flaws, I still thoroughly enjoyed it and will definitely be replaying the main story and DLC when announced. Had the level design and quality remained consistent with those of the early-game, RE9 might have been the best in the series. On a whole, it's an entry worthy of a top five placement in the series, but falls slightly short of number one.  9.0/10

I’m about 15 hours into Resident Evil 9 and haven’t finished it yet, but it already feels like one of the strongest entries in the series. Gameplay is dialed in. Movement is fluid and responsive, and combat has real weight to it. Weapons sound and feel powerful and every shot has impact, which makes encounters tense and satisfying. It keeps that classic Resident Evil balance of action and resource management without feeling clunky or outdated with a few twists that is new to the series. Mechanically, it’s deeper than it looks. Systems are introduced cleanly, but there’s enough depth to reward smart play. Positioning, timing, and decision making all matter, which keeps things engaging instead of repetitive when it comes to pulling off those multi kills. Atmosphere is top-tier. Environments are detailed, immersive, and genuinely unsettling at times. When you get to that certain section (you'll know when you get there) it really gives a good punch to the story and brings back good memories. The game builds tension through pacing, sound design, and environmental storytelling. If you're a fan of gore, RE9 turns that dial to 11. The story has me hooked so far. Even without finishing it, there’s a strong sense of direction and mystery to Grace is here for in this story. That said, it’s not perfect. Some sections can feel a bit linear, and there are moments where pacing dips slightly between major set pieces. A few mechanics could’ve been expanded more, and occasional backtracking might not land for everyone. None of it is a dealbreaker, but it’s noticeable. At 15 hours in, it still feels like there’s a lot left, and none of it feels like filler. Everything has purpose. Overall, this is about as close to a near-perfect Resident Evil experience as I’ve played in a while. If it sticks the landing, it’s easily one of the best in the franchise. I’d recommend this to any friend and anyone who loves Resident Evil. This is absolutely worth your time.

The game is challenging but not ridiculous on its standard difficulty for someone who has played vaguely similar games before.   The difference between the two different characters' play style is honestly a lot more fun than I expected, I thought I would get annoyed with that but it actually worked extremely well. The pacing between the scarier sections and the more action-focused ones was phenomenal as well. I'm a big fan of this level of horror game, Dead Space and Cronos being some other favorites of mine. But usually I have to stop and take a break after playing for a while as I get too tense. I didn't have to do that here because of that excellent pacing. Though that did mean that the only thing that could tear me away from the game was the need for sleep for a full day of work the next day.  The game is a little on the short side for the main story, but it has excellent replay value via bonus challenges that can then be used to unlock more weapons, outfits, and other gameplay quirks as well. All in all, I think this is the first AAA title I can recall off the top of my head that I whole heartedly recommend buying if you have even the slightest interest, even at full price.

As a new fan to the series, playing through 2RE, 4RE and knowing the story of 1, Requiem is such a fantastic love letter to the series.  Beyond the callbacks, references and overarching stories, Requiem manages to also be an incredible game. The gameplay of both Grace and Leon is excellent. It would have been easy enough to just copy RE4REs gameplay for Leon and do the same old for Grace as was done in RE7 but they expanded on both beautifully.  Grace's segments are definitely my favorite. The first true open segment for Grace is on par with the RPD from RE2 imo. The constant pressure that builds as you go further through the area is outstanding. Just as you feel safe, they throw the pressure back onto you in a completely unexpected way. All the other sections she has are brilliant and are a delightful mix of heartstopping terror and methodical planning in order to survive the onslaught and complete the puzzles. The introduction of the hemolytic injectors and blood-based crafting is really great. I only wish we got more from Grace's playtime. Not to say it was too short, but it just left me wanting more, especially more areas like Rhodes Hill.  Leons gameplay is similar to RE4RE but a lot is added. Firstly, the hatchet is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awesome. Giving the player a permanent melee weapon that has to be repaired mid combat is just so cool. His segments feel a lot more intense than RE4, primarily because the enemies are more advanced than the Las Plagas hosts. Zombies will not only wield actual weapons, but they will actively dodge your aim. The difficulty never feels cheap, it just forces you to think more. The spectacle of Leon's sections is absolutely one of the highlights of the game. There are so many moments that are there just to make you lose your ♥♥♥♥, and they all work so well. The Requiem hand-cannon itself is so cool. Having something with incredibly limited ammo that you save for extra special moments and are rewarded with absolutely obliterating enemies is so satisfying.  Even though I wish we had more Grace sections, I think the game is a perfect length and offers a lot of replayability which is obviously what makes or breaks a Resident Evil game.  I love RE9 and I really am looking forward to the next games Capcom releases in this series. Fingers crossed for Code Veronica and 0 remakes.  9.5/10  P.S. RE Requiem is a fabulous blending of the best parts of RE2 and RE4. There's a lot of nostalgia, but it's also a genuinely amazing game and so it never feels like empty fanservice.  Grace's sections, especially the Care Center, are immaculately crafted. You play as her in first person and she must be cautious around monsters, so all of the details in the environments have a chance to be appreciated up close. You can really tell how much love and care went into sculpting the world.  I especially love how each zombie seems to have their own personality: they all look unique and have idiosyncratic behaviours you can analyze and exploit. And you'll need every advantage you can get, because Grace's gameplay is tense with limited ammo and resources.  Leon plays like a cheesy action hero in all the best ways. He delivers campy one-liners, perfect-parries enemy attacks, holds five different guns, and roundhouse kicks zombies to the face. He's the perfect release of tension after hours of crawling around in the dark with Grace.  You shift between the characters in a way that feels natural until the story builds to a satisfying conclusion. I was pleasantly surprised to see that the plot never went too off the rails; RE9 remains remarkably well-grounded despite being about "the fate of the world." It's confidently Grace and Leon's personal story.  Everything about RE9 feels well-earned and focused. You can tell that the developers knew what they wanted and worked hard to realize their vision. As a result, playing as Grace and Leon is such a joy from beginning to end. This is an amazing game. I would highly recommend RE9 to you!

Resident Evil Requiem - Lots of Fun for Lots of Money  Performance: -RE:9 Is optimized very well - most reasonably recent hardware can run it well.  -Graphics look beautiful with minimal tweaking  Characters: -Leon is returning along with a Grace - While Leon is going to be your traditional Resident Evil 4 style action gameplay, Grave will be your typical puzzle solving, ammo conserving, sneaking-around gameplay.   Game-time: -If you linger around and appreciate the beautifully detailed environment, you can stretch your first playthrough of the game to between 7-9 hours. This also depends on the difficulty of which you are playing the game on.   -RE9 Offers moderate replay-value. You can unlock Bonus Content by replaying the campaign in multiple ways. This will at least net you between 3-5 replays, which in my opinion is decent, however do not expect your overall game time to exceed more than 50 hours.   -It's important to note that the average player will blast through the campaign in less than 4 hours after completing it for the first time. This is about only good for the achievements.   (Future DLC has been announced but this do not count in to the already expensive base game)   Locations -You will spend most of your time in Rhodes Hill Care Center. This is important because this is 70% of the gameplay that you will be doing with Grace. If you are a long time fan, this will remind you of RE1,2 and 3.  -The rest of the game takes place in a variety of locations in Raccoon City/Raccoon Police Department and the Umbrella Corporation underground labs. -Leon will be your character in the second half of the game where you will be exploring the ruins of raccoon city. The rest of the map looks good, but you can feel that most of the care has gone in to Rhodes Hill Care Center. Raccoon City is sort of just a pretty afterthought.   Gameplay Variety: -The gameplay offers a variety of weapons for Leon - that is important to note because Grace will not be able to use the variety of weapons that Leon has at his disposal.  -With that that said, Grace has a decent variety of crafting recipes which she can unlock for herself. Molotov cocktails, acid, injectors filled with poison etc.   -The gameplay feels different on every section of the map, which contributes to the variety of RE9. The inspiration can be felt from RE2&4 remastered, along with RE7 style first person gameplay in Rhodes Hill.   *IMPORTANT* Price: -The base game sells for 70USD, meanwhile the Deluxe Edition will run you 80 dolans. In my personal opinion, it's best to wait for a sale even if the game is good fun. Better yet, its best to wait until the DLC releases so you can buy it with the main game in a bundle.   -If you do decide to drop money on RE9, it is important to note that the DELUXE Edition of the game comes with a couple of costumes for the characters and some charms that modify gameplay, along with a couple of weapon skins and useless filters which you will probably never even care to play with.   -All of the above listed things from the DELUXE edition make no difference to the gameplay. Furthermore there are a ton of MODS which you can download. These can be used to modify the game to your taste FREE OF CHARGE. Consider this before you decide to opt for the more expensive edition of the game over the already expensive base game.  TLDR: Graphics - Beautiful Gameplay - Very Good PC Requirement - High-End Difficulty - Grace (Significant Brain Usage) Leon (Easy)  Story - Good, decent Fanservice Game Time - Average to Short (Easy to breeze through) Price - Must-buy if you are an avid fan. Otherwise wait for the sale.

The first half of the game, while not perfect, really impressed me with how well it blended short bursts of action heavy Leon segments to "de-stress" with Grace's more classic RE gameplay where the enemies are slightly more threatening and you have to think a bit about resource management, including when to save (I can't imagine playing on any of the difficulties that don't involve ink ribbons). The return of a crimson head-like enemy that gives you more to consider when deciding where and how to dispatch zombies was welcome! Early story beats were compelling enough and Grace is endearing. Gideon was a mysterious and entertaining antagonist and the first half of the game concludes with a hard hitting bit of drama that gets your mind spinning about where these characters might go from here.  Things went mostly downhill for me from this moment.  You're tossed into a very lengthy segment with Leon. Leon is no longer a tasty treat to break the tension but the main course for a good long while. Very little resource management, no ink ribbons, frequent auto-saves, boring and drab level design and enemy encounter design, a shop for upgrading your weapons to trick you into feeling like you're still making choices that matter, and a completely different villain has now taken the spotlight. Everything that had me hooked in the first half of the game is basically gone at this point. Aside from one or two intensely ridiculous (in a fun way) moments this portion of the game really blended together into mush for me.  The game finishes in a way that seems to signal that an era of RE has ended and the series has reached a conclusion (aside from a tease for the upcoming DLC), which feels oddly welcome. I say this as a big RE-head but I think the series probably needs a break, though that doesn't seem to be in the cards given that several more remakes are rumored to be in the works.  As much as I enjoyed a large Chunk of the first half of the game (and a few bits in the back half), there are several things that made me uninstall this rather than dive right back in with a second playthrough. Much like some other recent RE games, Requiem has a prologue that plays out like a lengthy playable cutscene. These are always... "fine" the first time around but tiresome on replays and sadly un-skippable. There's another sequence like this later on involving running from bald murderous children that I'm not eager to play through again.  There's also a serious lack of bonus content aside from a higher difficulty setting that seems to have been at least partially balanced with cheat items in mind if the tips that appear when you die suggesting you buy more cheat items and the fact that you can't attempt it on a fresh save file are any indication.  I might re-install this once the "Gold Edition" is ready, but for now this probably isn't going to be an RE game I revisit much in the future. I wish there was a third option other than thumbs up or thumbs down, but what nudged me towards a thumbs down is this:  - The care center section with Grace feels like a miniature RE game rather than something worthy of a $70 release. This was the strongest part of the game for me but feels like 40% of the total package here. - The Leon gameplay doesn't have the pacing and tight design of RE4 or the combat depth of RE6 to bring me back for more. - The game is constantly defanging itself in too many ways to mention for the sake of a frictionless modern experience. - The plot devolves into complete non-sense, even by RE standards. Normally you'd give this sort of thing a pass but the game presented things so seriously at first that you feel like a fool for becoming invested in anything going on by the end.  PS: Huge respect for the game running well and looking incredible without any ray-tracing or path-tracing, which are incredibly expensive to run but do not offer much visual benefit in this game 90% of the time. The audio is also truly excellent.

Overall recommend, but man it's for me closer to a mixed opinion than I'm willing to admit.  Let me preface this that there is absolutely nothing mechanically or technically wrong about the game itself. Matter of fact the game performs stellar along that often obvious faultline that more than a few games unfortunately decide to break themselves on. My issues in particular stem from some gameplay choices and some narrative choices. Because I'll be discussing narrative choices, this review also contains heavy spoilers.  Let me preface this by saying that I am primarily an action horror fan. The two games I love in the survival horror genre more than any else are Resident Evil 4 and Dead Space. This is critical information in order to contextualize the rest of what I say.  Theres two, maybe three directions a survival horror game takes its role:  You have the Resident Evil 4/Dead Space way. It can have scares, it can have horrors, but most importantly you shoot those horrors until they stop being horrors. The horror is less a persistent scare element and more an environmental backdrop to the action gameplay that takes front and center. This is the direction I prefer.  Then theres the Resi 7/Alien Isolation way. You have scares and you have horrors, but those horrors are additionally inherently scarier because your tools of surviving encounters is more minimal, your ability to juggle more resources at once is less, or both. I don't like this, I've basically almost never liked it.  Then theres the Silent Hill 2 Remake/Resi 8 sort of way which tries to strike a balance. I can't say it's always right on the money but I can't fault it.  I think Resi 9's first issue is the way the game divides and paces itself.  The game is effectively divided into two sections: a Grace part (which makes up roughly one half of the game) and a Leon part (which makes up the second half of the game). Leon exists in Grace's part to break up the gameplay as Grace and vice versa.  At the very start they sell Grace as this sort of character who, at least in my opinion, was perhaps what Capcom originally intended for Ethan to be: Grace is well and truly terrified of most things she encounters, combating enemies is an ordeal and she is overall painted as this sort of fish out of water in regards to the horrors she now has to encounter.  Because of the contrast it gives you with Leon you don't feel like Grace's systems are rewarding, instead it feels like playing Grace every system is designed to waste your time or your inventory space, to remind you how good you have it when you get to play as Leon: you start with limited space and it takes a very long time to increase it noticeably, key items take up a slot and you often carry multiple that you can't get rid of going into an area, Grace's pistol is closer to a peashooter (did I mention the scope of Grace's weapon choices are two pistols and a magnum?), a single basic enemy for Grace is meant to be played with tactical circumventing whereas Leon just obliterates anyone and anything with the amount of power and ammo he gets, I don't understand the need for them to complicate crafting by introducing the idea that you don't have recipes first and need to earn them and make them with blood, craftables do not stack, etc. Grace also has very little pressure from tyrants, and whenever she does it is not naturally occurring but rather there are specific actions you take and specific paths you go through that will cause a tyrant to appear.  By contrast Leon has his classic RE4 inventory style, has a melee option on stagger (whereas Grace only has a non-damaging shove), has a perma-kill attack (whereas Grace utilizes an item you have to craft), a parry option, a vast choice of different weaponry etc. A basic zombie that might take Grace a full magazine or two of pistol ammo to kill Leon can and will dispatch with, at most, 2 pistol shots, a melee kick and a hatchet into the head.  And like I know that theres a clique of survival horror fans that like this, even love this, but it just ain't me. A classic survival horror fan is gonna get his money's worth out of this one, but an action horror fan, at least initially, is not. The first half almost made me consider just dumping the game entirely because I don't take kindly to the idea of having 15-20 minutes of fun after every 2-3 hours.  Then the second half starts and you get to play as Leon almost full time, and if you're smart you just pop a save and then never have to think about Grace's part ever again. Every Resi game at the very least typically has *that* part that makes you not wanna replay it and that's okay.  To me personally, this sets off some Resident Evil 6 alarm bells. A lot of people criticized RE6 for trying to play into two demographics at once (the horror fanbase and the action fanbase) but are now weirdly absent from the debate of RE9 trying to appeal to both classic survival horror fans and action horror fans at the same time, which to me leaves roughly half of the games entire runtime terminally unsatisfying and, worse yet, unavoidable in at least your first run.  The game was also, in general, a little bit easy, but I understand that this may change if or when I decide to play something other than standard difficulty.  Resi 9's second issue is the narrative and the narrative choices, and those narrative choices impacting the gameplay of Leon's part.  Immediately Leon's part is the cool part. The part where you finally get to cut loose and smash some heads. Leon's part in contrast to Grace's feels more adequately paced, contains a broader range of more dispatchable enemies, more ways to answer their attacks and even a rudimentary point-kill system which you can exchange in an automated shop for items, weapons or upgrades. Speaking as someone who lives and breathes for this type of horror this is probably the best Leon as an action horror protagonist has ever played.   Leon's path contains tons of bosses, however some bosses are placed in a way that feels nonsensical: getting to see the RPD again was awesome (when I tell you they preserved everything down to even having the big rig that crashed into Leon and Claire in the cop car at the start of Resident Evil 2 Remake I mean it) and having the chance to see *a* Mr. X again was a cool callback, however, you immediately tell that the police station wasn't quite built for a tyrant to chase you around and you immediately go about leaving it. In total visiting RPD lasts maybe 15-20ish minutes if you're taking your time and the Mr. X chase lasts a grand total of like 1-2 minutes, which I think is pretty bad pacing even if I can relatively understand the reason why. Mr. X, like his chase, is dispatched pretty much within the same hour he is introduced.  The HUNK fight near the very end of the game I will not even try to elaborate on because that in of itself is an actively debated on topic within the Resi community right now. Is it HUNK? Is it not HUNK? No idea.  What both the Mr. X and the HUNK fight both share however is that there's quite little buildup to both events, and they served imo much more as some sort of clippable, high attention moments than they've really added any sort of narrative weight.  Lastly the central theme of RE9's narrative itself rests on this alleged bioweapon called Elpis. It is never directly explained to us, but heavily implied (and something the game kinda expects you to figure out), that Elpis is actually an anti-serum which Oswald E. Spencer (some of you may know him as John Umbrella) made upon reaching a period of regret in his life sometime presumably during the 90s over his hand in proliferating bio-organic weapons. I believe that, on a fundamental level, this is completely contradictory to Spencers character: we know through dialogue exchanges that as late as 2006 (quite a few years after Spencer allegedly had a change of heart according to RE9) that Spencer felt nowhere close to regretful.

This game is excellent, played through 3 times to get all achievements and loved all three runs and cannot recommend enough as a fantastic survival horror.    The downsides first:  - The variety in enemy behaviour is limited,   - The last act of the game falters in story a little bit,  - There's longer slower unskippable sections of the game that are a bit less captivating on replays, and punishing if you try and rush through them  - The new game settings are limited (no "true new game" OR "new game plus", it hits this middleground version where there's no fresh file and no carryover.  Even a 'Chapter Select' would be a nice feature to have)  - There are a few quality of life settings that are missing or confusing (the sensitivity adjustments for kb+m controls are hidden a little, and there's no FOV slider, and the default FOV is extremely tight in first person - to the point that I set both main character's to 3rd person) - Some of the 'upgrade / economy' decisions feel a little meaningless compared to standout prior RE entries  The upsides can be summarized as "everything else", the game is truly exceptional.  But some highlights:  - The character specific gameplay is exceedingly tight as both Leon and Grace, and remarkably unique without being alienating  - The pacing is masterclass - The way it drives the 'horror triller' experience is unmatched - The sound design may be the best in any game I've ever played - The attention to detail in every corner is also probably the best I've ever seen in a game, and the collection of many small visual/audio/animation touches really amounts to an incredible 'vibe.' - The setting is captivating and interesting, and the variation within the locations keeps it feeling fresh constantly - The graphics are exceptional, and the "look" is truly astonishing and is like nothing I've played before. - The animations and voice acting are top shelf - While I noted enemy behaviour is limited, the actual enemy visual design is extremely varied and constantly changing to suit the area, with loads of "scripted / situational" behaviours that make them FEEL unique, especially on a first playthrough. - The creature design is incredible. - The story is very engaging and well presented, with the only critique being some overly heavy nostalgia moments that imho exist only for nostalgia's sake, and the final leg of the game feeling a bit out of place.  - It's actually scary and intense! - The length is perfect (4h playing FAST, 10-12h taking your time and exploring)  There's a million other great things about this game, and while it's not without the odd complaint they are _so easy_ to look past, and hopefully in future updates some of the odd decisions get addressed.   In summary, I absolutely loved it, and it was a delight to do everything the game had to offer.

I've been playing every mainline Resident Evil since the very first one back on PS1, and after all these years, Requiem  absolutely lives up to the hype. This might be my favorite since the RE2 Remake, Capcom really knocked it out of the park. Grace Ashcroft is a great addition to the series, smart, capable and relatable. Her sections deliver tense, atmospheric dread with puzzles and that classic feeling of being outmatched and on edge. Then you get to play as Leon, one of my all-time favorite characters, and it's pure joy – he brings that signature action-hero energy with  moments that feel right at home in the RE universe. Switching between their styles keeps things dynamic and exciting. Gameplay is polished to perfection, tight controls, rewarding gunplay, smart resource management, and some truly memorable set pieces that mix horror and action in the best way. The RE Engine is stunning – the visuals, lighting, creature designs, and overall atmosphere are top-tier. Pacing is balanced well (my playthrough was about 13 hours for the main story), no major issues on PC, and it captures that perfect balance of scares, tension, and fun that longtime fans crave. If you've played the series for years like I have, this feels like a respectful evolution that honors the roots while pushing things forward. No regrets – easily one of the best in the franchise. 10/10 – Strongly Recommended. Capcom, please keep this level of quality coming!

Resident Evil Requiem delivers something I didn’t expect: two completely different flavors of panic, one pure survival horror, the other stylish action… and somehow, a bit of comedy along the way.  Playing as Grace, I went in expecting spooky zombies and the usual questionable inventory management. What I got instead was a full-body workout for my nerves and a deep emotional attachment to the Requiem. That gun feels like the answer to everything, yet I barely used it, constantly wondering, “What if I need this later?” My first playthrough turned into a psychological battle against my own hoarding instincts.  The enemy design is outstanding. It genuinely feels like the developers asked, “What if we took nightmares… and made them faster?” The result is terrifying in the best way. I have never respected a pause menu more in my life.  The atmosphere is immaculate. Every hallway convinces you that you’re safe, and every corner immediately proves that you’re not.  Also, shoutout to Grace for handling situations far better than I ever could. If it were me, the game would end in three minutes, I’d simply leave.  And then there’s Leon.  Do you even need a review?  LEON. IS. BACK.  That’s it. That’s the review.  Leon returns like he never left, cool, sarcastic, and effortlessly making catastrophic situations look like a casual Tuesday.  Inventory management remains a beautifully stressful puzzle: Do I carry ammo, more guns, healing items… or my dignity?  Conclusion: I had an amazing time. Would I play again? Absolutely. Will I turn the volume down next time I play as Grace? Also absolutely.

Review after beating the game (so I can write spoilers), the hype and 100% completion.  RE9 is a game I enjoyed a lot on my first playthrough, but the more I played, the more I started to see problems I have with it. As a long time RE fan, I feel the need to criticize these aspects and not "glaze" the game just because. My main problems are related to three gameplay sections, the lack of content at the moment, and the plot.  Before I start talking about the game, I want to congratulate Capcom for being able to satisfy both sides of the RE community: we have the right mix of action and survival horror, being able to play with or without ink ribbons, changing sound effects, a return of the zapping system (kind of) and more.  As everyone knows, the game lets you play as Grace and Leon, with both having different playstyles. I would have preferred if the game allowed you to play only with one of them once you beat the game but this is not a thing. I'm waiting for an official update or a mod.  Playing as Grace feels like a mix of RE2, 7, and Revelations 2. Exploring and playing the Care Center was amazing because the game is actually survival horror. It makes you think about resources, enemy avoidance, crafting, etc. Even the basement area was fun to play with the girl moving around the area. Unfortunately for us, we don't get any boss fights or additional guns when playing as her. Playing as Leon feels like playing RE4 Remake, but with a lack of unique enemy variety since you mainly fight zombies (with different weapons) and few bosses here and there, or enemy types that appear only once / in one area. While I still find this fun and was not a problem when playing as Grace (due to the zombies having unique behaviors creating interesting situations while exploring / backtracking), I think they could have done more for Leon. This is not a problem when playing on Insanity, though, as you have to use all your guns strategically to be able to kill Blister Heads by using the stun mechanic. I also loved Leon's first section; seeing people in the streets running away from zombies was something I wanted to see in the RE3 Remake. Even with my complaints, I enjoy playing the game, which makes me recommend it.  I was very disappointed, though, when I realized that the game reused the same enemy animations / attacks from previous games. For example, the Licker is the exact same from the RE2 Remake but with reduced movement speed (unless you play on Insanity). The Mutated Victor boss fight is the exact same fight against Final Nemmy in the RE3 Remake, minus the batteries to plug to charge the rail cannon. I wished the Lickers in ark were a mutated version of them similar to RE2 OG, since they were cut from the remake. The Mr. X chase has nothing interesting to make that section memorable, just hold the run button and escape. The Super Tyrant fight is basically the same from the RE2 Remake, apart from the fact that now the Tyrant can throw cars at you and he does not one shot you anymore. However I liked the big spider boss fight, the plants before Ark, and the Hunk boss fight (especially on Insanity). Talking about Hunk, I hope we get a DLC about him escaping Ark. We all know he survived since his body is the only one despawning in the game. And why don't we get to fight Zeno? They didn’t want us to ruin our Wesker boss fight in the upcoming RE5 Remake in the RE Engine?  The intro, the bike part, and the flashback are a pain in the ass to replay on repeated playthroughs. Thank God there is a mod to skip the first and the last, while the bike has something going on at least, but it plays itself; you don't even have to press movement keys to dodge cars or stuff, Leon does everything by himself. You don't even get to fight the dogs outside of the bike section which is a shame.  There are also two endings, but I wished we got two more based on Leon shooting Emily or not. Imagine Grace being angry at Leon for killing Emily and not curing him with Elpis, and her getting a boss fight against Victor too.  As mentioned earlier, while I really like the game, I do have many problems with the plot. The story retcons many things (like Spencer feeling guilty now, which will probably be changed in the RE5 Remake, or Raccoon City not being completely destroyed, etc.). I was also disappointed by the fact that Grace was not Alyssa’s true daughter, and for some reason, she is special and immune to the T-Virus (she gets bitten in the beginning of the game and this thing is not brought up again). I would have preferred if she was Alyssa’s real daughter who inherited T-Virus antibodies due to the Daylight vaccine from RE Outbreak, and this being a key thing to trigger Elpis. Also, the game does not explain how Leon and Sherry got infected and why only them, out of the main characters, are suffering from it. What about Claire, Ada, Chris, Barry, etc.? Why does Chris not show up at the end? Maybe for an upcoming DLC? We will see.  Content wise, you can replay the story many times to get all the achievements / challenges. We really need a free Mercenaries Mode with more characters being playable, such as Hunk and Sherry and fight all the enemies from the game at once. This would fix my problem with enemy variety in the base game.  New Game+ is a little bit of a mess. You can’t turn off a few bonus settings once unlocked, like the upgraded Tactical Tracker for Leon or the additional 50 capacity to the Blood Collector for Grace, and you can’t skip the intro as mentioned earlier unless you use a mod. Also, why can't we change FOV like in previous games?  With all that being said, even though I might sound very critical of the game (which I am because I love the franchise), I consider the game a very good product compared to what we mostly get nowadays from AAA companies. I don’t see it as the best RE game, but it’s for sure a fun game to play.

A fantastic modern era Resident Evil with plenty of the action for those who love the RE4 remake.  Pros: Capcom has pretty much mastered the sneaky, tense first person horror gameplay they started with RE7. You play as a young FBI agent without any combat experience and you can really feel the anxiety and trepidation behind each of her actions. Just like in classic survival horror you will count bullets and healing items, dodge foes to avoid wasting resources, and encounter situations where things get messy and you have to rely on your wits and cunning to survive.  When you play as series favorite Leon Kennedy, you will be treated to fairly classic zombie action against much more powerful foes. In order to challenge you, zombies are now fast and sneaky, climbing up ledges to attack from behind. Some of them even shoot guns and throw projectiles. As in RE4, Leon is more than capable of dispatching any foes put before him so the challenge becomes less about survival and more about overcoming the waves of foes placed in your path.  Cons: As in previous games, replaying the scripted horror set piece levels is beyond tedious. If you played RE:8 and remember the doll mansion, there is a set piece here that makes that sequence seem brief in comparison. Capcom needs to allow these scenes to be skipped on repeat playthroughs. Also "Insanity Mode" is a lame hard mode. Instead of getting a masterfully crafted higher difficulty like "Professional" in RE4, we get bullet sponge enemies that no longer follow stagger rules. Even worse are the badly mangled bosses that feel like some intern just pushed up a bunch of sliders without testing the boss to feel if the changes were challenging and not just terribly tedious. One boss in particular is basically a series of poorly timed quick time button presses, but you can't see the buttons on screen. It results the kind of hilarious "animation sync kills" that you would see in an ancient FMV game or something like Dragon's Liar. It feels goofy and infuriating at the same time and you will hate hearing the same lines repeated over and over during the animation kills against your character. Don't let the length of this section fool you, though, this nitpick is limited to a single mode of play.  If you never touch the Insanity difficulty and just indulge in the other flawless modes, this game is easily a 9/10. It's a new RE classic. I have cleared all content and have all achievements on my profile so I can confidently say as a fan since RE1 on PSX that this is a strong recommendation for series vets and new players alike.

[h3] [b] Mostly spoiler free, assuming you've seen some of the trailers. Spoiler characters briefly described but no names. [/b] [/h3]   ** Received via an Nvidia product promotion at somewhat last minute. As a long time fan of the series, I was as intending to buy for full price otherwise. **  [b] General Info: [/b]  - Played at 4K 60fps, almost everything on Ultra (PC specs should be attached). - One full run completed so far with a run-time of around 14-15hrs, this included exploring and doubling-back for 'side' objectives, extra resources, collectibles etc. - I plan to go back in on Insanity difficulty soon.  [b] Pros: [/b]  - RE Engine does it again, game felt very smooth and looks beautiful. - Loved the option to change between 1st and 3rd person perspective. Default settings are 1st for Grace and 3rd for Leon, I came to prefer this too. - Overall, a good mix of play styles between Grace and Leon. If you enjoyed RE7, you'll likely enjoy the Grace sections. If you enjoyed RE4 Remake, you'll likely enjoy the Leon sections. - Good nostalgic beats through-out, especially in the 2nd half. - Loved the main antagonist. Sinister, intelligent and intriguing, also strangely charismatic. - Enjoyed the collecting and crafting aspect to Grace's sections.   [b] Cons: [/b]  - No additional modes, such as Mercenaries, at launch is rough. - Pacing between each characters' sections feels off at times. - Later Leon section felt like it dragged a bit, admittedly it did then pick up. - Wish we got more of a certain shaded character. Mystery can be good but like, come on. - Final boss was kind of sudden and unfortunately mostly copied from a previous RE game. Could have done with more build-up or foreshadowing.  [b] Conclusion & Final Score: [/b]  Overall a great experience that scratches the itch of wanting more of what RE games have already given us whilst introducing some new lore and advancing the canonical story of the franchise and its main characters. Lots here for RE fans but I do not feel it's the best entry point for a newcomer.  [b] 9/10 [/b] - Highly recommended for fans of the series, well recommended for fans of the genre.

Resident Evil Requiem is, without exaggeration, one of the strongest entries in the series arguably the best so far. From the very first hour, it becomes clear that this is a game crafted with care, passion, and a deep understanding of what makes survival horror truly memorable.  First of all, the technical performance is impressive. The game runs smoothly with very few bugs or errors, which is something fans always appreciate, especially in a modern AAA release. The optimization feels polished, and the experience remains immersive without frustrating glitches pulling you out of the tension.  The horror elements are nothing short of a masterpiece. The atmosphere is dense, oppressive, and carefully constructed. Every shadow feels alive, every sound matters. The developers clearly understood that true horror is not just about jump scares, but about psychological pressure and environmental storytelling. The sound design plays a massive role here distant footsteps, unsettling ambient noises, and sudden silence all work together to keep the player constantly on edge.  Combat is another major highlight. The weapons feel impactful, responsive, and satisfying to use. Whether you're conserving ammo and carefully aiming your shots or engaging in more intense encounters, the gameplay strikes a perfect balance between survival tension and action. Resource management remains crucial, preserving the classic survival horror identity that fans love.  Enemy design is also exceptional. Each type of enemy feels distinct, both visually and mechanically. Encounters require strategy rather than mindless shooting, which adds depth and keeps gameplay fresh throughout the experience. Boss fights, in particular, are intense and cinematic without feeling overly scripted.  What truly sets Resident Requiem apart, though, is how it respects its roots while still pushing the series forward. It captures the essence that made games like Resident Evil 4 and Resident Evil 7: Biohazard so iconic, while refining modern mechanics introduced in titles like Resident Evil Village. The result is a perfect blend of nostalgia and innovation.  The level design deserves special mention as well. The environments are detailed, interconnected, and rewarding to explore. Hidden items, secret paths, and environmental storytelling encourage players to fully immerse themselves in the world. Every location feels meaningful rather than filler.  Looking ahead, I sincerely hope we receive a DLC in the future. There is so much potential to expand the story, explore side characters, or even introduce new missions that deepen the lore. If Capcom decides to continue the experience through DLC expansions, it would be a fantastic way to extend the life of an already outstanding game.  In conclusion, Resident Evil Requiem stands as a triumph in the survival horror genre. With its polished performance, masterful horror atmosphere, satisfying combat, and strong respect for the franchise’s legacy, it sets a new standard for the series. If future installments build upon this foundation, the future of the franchise looks brighter and scarier than ever.

RE9 retreads a lot of old ground, sometimes literally. But in a good way I think.  Gameplay is split between two characters, Grace and Leon, and these two switch periodically. Grace is an FBI analyst who isn't trained for field work, so her sections emphasise the survival horror aspect. Ammo is scarce, enemies are tough and you're often better off avoiding them than fighting them.   Leon's sections are the opposite, emphasising a more action-horror gameplay style. There are more enemies but you have a wider arsenal to deal with them, ammo is more plentifull and you even get money for killing enemies, so you're never incetivised to avoid combat.  And this split works. Grace's sections are tense but you can't maintain that tension forever. Eventually the map opens up a bit more, you get a grip on what you can and can't do and get used to her gameplay. Then the game switches to Leon and you're launched right into the action packed combat. And then when you get used to that you're back to grace for a bit, now in a new area with new dangerous enemies. Its a good balance.  Other than that the usual resident evil quality is here, levels are well designed, enemies are tough but not tedious, my first runclocked in at about 15 or so hours and there's plenty things to do on replay.  Story wise its fairly typical but follows the usual RE formula. Umbrella is up to something, you're trapped in an abandoned hospital for a bit, there's an underground section, a flashback to the orphanage, then you go to a secret lab and along the way you fight a variety of mutant monster bosses. You shoot the final bad guy with an RPG.

Ooooh man where do I start... I'll try to make this review short but BEWARE of spoilers. Wish I could give this review a neutral mark. It is a good RE game. But not GOTY. For me it's lacking. Especially during the 2nd half part of the game.  THE POSITIVE First of all I enjoyed this game. It is a good RE game. The 2 main characters Grace and, ofcourse, Leon felt great in their respective sections. Especially Grace's. Her trauma and "lack" of field experience makes it a great new addition for the "survival horror" side of the game. Her backstory, the way she stutters, gets anxious, trembles while aiming and panics feels "real" so it's easier to empathize with her and it makes sense to stop, breath, check corners, think about what you're doing and how to approach certain situations. The Care Center section, basement and laboratory were perfect. Playing with both Leon and Grace. It's like a good mix between survival horror and lack of resources with Grace and then survival action packed with Leon. Also the crafting system with Grace is top notch. Every tool feel useful in some way or another. So exploration and taking risks feels rewarding.  But after that...  THE NEGATIVE Enter Raccoon City. Don't get me wrong, coming back to RC with Leon hits hard. Nostalgia inducing. But it felt rushed. Most roads are blocked (which is expected) so you end up going towards the main objective pretty fast. Even with some side quests and resources to collect on the side or some buildings.  But the zombies shooting mortars at you, the chainsaw zombie dress all in metal armor like a punk and then the automatic ride with the bike, with infinite bullets, where a "time event" pops at the end against Gideon felt, IMHO so ridiculous and boring. Reminding me, somehow, of RE6. I just wanted to go back to Grace and play some more claustrophobic survival horror. Capcom could've extended some RC streets or buildings to explore or go through it to reach an objective. Maybe even get rid of the whole bike section with a cinematic with Leon reaching the RPD. That section felt so automatic that I was, literally, falling asleep. Then the RPD. Which, overall, was good. Felt way too short but it was ok.  Then the Orphanage which, again, felt too short of a section to even bring it up. Maybe instead of the bike section I would've love to see some fight against the remnants of the little girls that they were cloning back then. Or even solving some puzzles to reach the next section. Then comes the ARK. To enter you have to face Plant 42. That fight offered no obstacle or difficulty whatsoever. You shoot the main root, dodge the left and right roots and then shoot some HUGE RED gas canisters and that's it. I was expecting to find some new bioweapon inside the ARK. Maybe alongside Hunters and/or Lickers. Instead I found myself fighting off mercs. And yes. Leon can "parry" bullets. This part fell short and boring to me.   Overall the game does an incredible job with the first few sections. The Care Center felt amazing and horror inducing. But after that the game falls short. It feels more like a fan service than a proper survival horror experience. I was expecting more with Requiem. I feel a bit disappointed with it. Especially for it's price tag. Feels waaay too expensive for it's current length and content. Capcom already confirmed a DLC and mini games. So we'll see. My recommendation is wait for sale and then get it. I don't feel this game is GOTY as most users seem to think. It's a good RE game but nowhere near R2 and R4 remakes. This feels a bit more like RE3 remake with some RE7 bits. At least for me.  EDIT: Btw this was the "easiest" RE to get all achievements. For the speedrun achievement I would suggest doing it on CASUAL diff. The most difficult achievements to unlock were:  -Finishing the game on insanity difficulty (you need stable frames to parry all the friggin' time with Leon. So practice parrying and timing. Insanity diff relies too much on Hatchet kills and parry) -Destroying all 25 Mr. Raccoon without spoiling myself (this was my last achievement unlocked. I was missing one of them).
Do you like old school RE? If yes you will love this game. Do you love RE 4? If yes you will love this game. Do you like both types of RE bring extra underwear.

I am reviewing this after 100%ing the game. I have never thoroughly enjoyed a game as much as I enjoyed playing parts of RE9. The first part with predominantly Grace was genuinely so enjoyable to play. You can see how they directly took inspiration from every Resident Evil game, and this felt like the magnum opus of the Resident Evil series. With that out of the way, my recommendation? If you like Resident Evil, it might be worth it. If you're not familiar with the series, I can't really recommend this at full price in good faith.   Hunk boss fight was like 2 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ seconds, city section was a running back and forth simulator, and the combat on Leon was just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ RE4R. There are many many more complaints I have like this, but for time's sake I will omit them.  The story is so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ lobotomized (and this is RE we're talking about). Where is Claire? Where is Ada? Where is Jill? Where is literally anybody that would be relevant other than Leon and Sherry???? What the ♥♥♥♥ was Chris doing the whole game????? How are there no political repercussions behind US collusion with bioterrorists? Surely this would instigate WW3? Why the ♥♥♥♥ did Grace decide to hop on a helicopter with Zeno? Grace is an FBI intelligence analyst, a highly selective job that requires strong analytical thinking and logical reasoning; Grace is clearly exhibited to be a paragon of these attributes (sarcasm). Don't even get me started on Leon. He cares about saving lives (which is the reason he joined the RPD), but he lets a woman get mauled by a chainsaw and decides to aura farm instead of trying to save her life? This is brutally inconsistent with his character and its development (although, I think they gave up on his character with RE2R). Sidenote: If the Zeno plotline doesn't continue to RE10, this story is just absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥.   The replay value is absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ horrendous. There is no other content beyond the main story such as Mercenaries (yep, no Mercenaries). Also, there is no legitimate high difficulty mode. You only get Insanity, which is not balanced as a standalone mode; it is explicitly stated that it is balanced around bonus weapons. Capcom? What the ♥♥♥♥!? Resident Evil Requiem is easily one of the best games I've ever played - 10/10 for me.  This is the first Resident Evil game I've played from start to finish, and I almost never touch survival horror games because I don't like being scared. But I do love immersive, polished, well-written games, and this one nails it perfectly.  The pacing is excellent: it keeps you hooked by constantly switching things up. One moment you're feeling helpless, stealthing past terrifying enemies; the next, you're tearing through hordes feeling like an absolute badass. The variety of gorgeous, detailed environments and epic set pieces is amazing—every area feels alive and purposeful. This truly feels like a labor of love from Capcom, blending tension, action, and cinematic polish in a way that's rarely done this well... it almost feels like an interactive movie at times where you're just trying to survive.  I'd highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys high-quality, immersive experiences—even if horror isn't usually your thing.  I'm really looking forward to any story DLC or new modes Capcom adds down the line.

Overall, this is one of the must-play games.  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------  For the first 10%, here's what it is:  The level design during early stages in this game simply failed to communicate with the players.  By communicating, what I mean is, in terms of level design, there are certain factors the designers must take into consideration, including but aren't limited to: 1. Goal: What do you want players to accomplish here 2. Means: How do you expect players to proceed 3. Indications: Subtle implications to remind/warn players of helps/dangers 4. Mechanism Consistencies: If something works before/somewhere/in some way, it should work after/elsewhere/the same way.  The game didn't communicate said factors clearly to the players. An example would be (Spoiler-Free):  [Player finds themselves in front of a hall, they have no other places to go so they must enter. However there are enemies positioned at the center of the hall.] Now, the player wonders: "Do I go in at all? Seems like I should because there's nowhere else I can go. But enemies are right there, how do I sneak pass them? There are no covers to take advantage of."  First, the player feels hesitant because getting too close to enemies triggers them to attack the player. However, in this very scenario, you actually are supposed to simply approach them then walk right past. This is mechanism inconsistency.  Second, in the same scenario, should the player attempts to enter the hall and walk past enemies, more enemies jump out of the shadows and attempt to attack the player, before the player can make it through the hall towards further locations. This is a terrible indication as the message being sent to the player here is "Don't come this way", and this is not even to mention yet another enemy finds its way in the hall, literally positioning itself at the narrow path the player must take, effectively blocking the player's way, but only to - disappear somehow after the player leaves this hall then returning here.  As for goals and means, anyone who's spent two hours or so in this game can tell you that, you come across 7 or 8 locked or jammed doors/containers during early stages, with seemingly no indications as to which one(s) to unlock first, or how to unlock them.  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------  Loved the remaining 90%. So, yeah, this is definitely a buy.

This is, without a doubt, the best Resident Evil game to date. It was the only game I pre-ordered last year.  [b] Disclaimer:[/b] This review contains spoilers and is relatively short.  [h3] Performance: [/h3]  I can run the game at maximum graphics settings with a consistent 60+ FPS, with the only adjustment being a reduction in shadow quality. As long as your PC can handle the game's requirements, you'll be able to enjoy it to the fullest.  [h3] Grace and Leon's Sections, Gameplay, and Story: [/h3]  Grace’s sections are good at making you have a sense of fear and helplessness, particularly on Hardcore difficulty during your first playthrough. For those seeking an even more intense challenge, I highly recommend playing on Insanity difficulty in your second playthrough, without any unlockable items or infinite ammo. Insanity difficulty is, by far, the toughest difficulty I’ve played in any Resident Evil game. Even difficulties like Shadows of Village, Madhouse, and the Ethan Must Die mode don't top the Insanity difficulty. I probably wouldn't have attempted Insanity if I weren’t working toward unlocking all the achievements on Steam for every Resident Evil game.  During my first playthrough, I focused on defeating only the necessary enemies to progress, saving the the rest of them for Leon’s sections.  Leon's sections were by far the most enjoyable part of the game. The bosses were very enjoyable, with my favorites being The Chunk in the attic, The Spider, Mr. X, and Hunk. The moment Mr. X appeared, I had flashbacks of playing the RE2 remake.  Leon's sections ate up most my first playthrough time. The guns he uses look good, and are satisfying to use, especially in combat against both enemies and bosses. I also liked the subtle touches that reflect Leon’s age.  One gameplay element I liked is the impact of Leon’s infection in the very late stages of the game, which slows him down. This gives you more fear if you're on Insanity difficulty.  The ability to parry nearly everything in the game, including rockets, is another feature I loved. However, be on the lookout for the Zombie Soldiers armed with guns, they can stun-lock you and shoot you down in mere seconds, which makes the Insanity difficulty even more PTSD inducing.  [h3] Story: [/h3]  The story is good, and it’s easy to understand what's going on if you've played the previous Resident Evil games. I believe Zeno is not actually dead, as suggested by the post-credits scene, and I believe Zeno will be the main villain in the upcoming Story Expansion.  My only complaint with the story is how Leon gets the Jill Valentine-style treatment when he's cured.    Overall, I highly recommend this game to all Resident Evil fans. It delivers an unforgettable experience, with amazing gameplay, a good storyline, and a good ole challenging difficulty that gives you PTSD.  Rating: 10/10.

Requiem for the dead. Nightmare for the living.  Resident Evil Requiem — 10/10, I really liked the game. Before this, I had only played Resident Evil Village, and I just decided to try the new part. In the end, I liked it so much that now I want to play all parts of the series.  About the technical side — everything is perfect. No crashes, no freezes, no FPS drops. I played on max settings and everything was stable. Big respect to the developers for such good optimization.    I played on the second-to-last difficulty level, which gave a good balance of challenge and fun.  The characters are made really well. Both Leon and Grace are interesting to play, and both feel good from start to finish.  I really liked the idea with two styles.   Leon is more about action — faster gameplay, more shooting, more control.   Grace is like the old games — fewer resources, more tension, you have to play carefully.    And this doesn’t annoy at all — it actually makes the game more interesting.  The atmosphere was very good — yes, it was scary and tense sometimes, but in a good way. [h1]RE9 - Requiem is a solid game for Horror and Action players[/h1]  [b]Graphics: 5/5[/b] It's visually stunning and atmospheric, and ran smoothly on the highest settings.  [b]Characters: 5/5[/b] The main protagonists, Grace and Leon, have playstyles that match their personality and experience. Grace is timid and overwhelmed by the new situation, so while you play her, you play in first person, stealthily trying to avoid the nightmare-fuel creatures that want you dead. Your weapons are limited. Grace behaves like most people would in those moments, and thankfully the writers didn't write her as the StrongFemaleLead™ character, but as a normal, vulnerable person who does what she has to in order to survive.  When you play as Leon, the experience is entirely different. You're a seasoned fighter, cracking dad jokes. In third person, you slice through zombies like butter in action-filled sequences. Having those two different horror playstyles in one game keeps things fresh.  The side characters feel a bit lacking. Except for one guy, the enemies are very "whatever." They are there, they get their task done, but you don't get very invested in who they are, except for one child, maybe.  [b]Story: 5/5[/b] Each of the two characters has their own background story, which weaves together into the main plot. Many strings from previous RE games get picked back up via characters, locations, or files. It's nicely done and feels logical. There are a few twists, and there are two different endings. The game definitely sets us up for a new story/DLC at the end, but our current adventure also leads to a satisfying conclusion.  [b]Gameplay: 4/5[/b] Combat is good, but feels too easy on the standard difficulty. Even the final boss dies surprisingly fast, but I felt similarly about some other RE titles, too. It might be better in Insanity Mode (haven't tried that yet), as even the final boss didn't feel very challenging. Still, it's fun to shoot and sneak your way through Raccoon City. There are many different weapons to play around with, and you find enough ammo or tools to craft equipment in the game to never run dry. As usual, there is a lot of backtracking. The puzzles are neither too easy nor too hard. Exploration is limited, as you'll hit many invisible walls, but it's still possible to a degree and rewards you with extra equipment or the occasional easteregg. I found it overall unfortunately just not very scary compared to RE8.   [b]Replayability: 4/5[/b] The story is linear, so aside from the other ending, your only reason to replay this game would be to try your luck with the challenges. There are new weapons, outfits, and many other things to unlock, and it can definitely be fun to try and beat the game super fast, or in Insanity Mode, or without healing items, etc. So yes, you have reasons to revisit this game after your first playthrough! ______________________________________________________________  [h3]OVERALL RATING: 4.5 / 5[/h3] Really solid, fun game. I liked RE8 Village and RE4 Remake a bit better, but still a really good  game.   [b] Recommendation: YES[/b]    P.S.: The Deluxe version is nice for the bonus outfits, but you'll be fine without it, too. Please note that your base outfits change over the course of the game (get bloody, etc.), whereas the DLC costumes stay as they are. For a first run, it's better to stick to the base outfits.

Resident Evil Requiem – 30 Hours a Hero, 2 Achievements from a Nervous Breakdown By: A Completionist on the Verge of Enlightenment  30.4 hours. 47 out of 49 achievements. If that's not a love letter to the developers, then I don't know what is. Resident Evil Requiem sent me through hell and back, forcing me to scrub every corner of the facility and negotiate with every nightmare-fuel creature I encountered just for a bit of digital recognition.  I felt like a god. I outsmarted the heavy hitters, survived the scripted chases, and took down the final bosses with a single, well-placed shot. The protagonists weren't just characters; they were my extended arms in this bloody symphony of horror. I was ready for the knighthood, the "Platinum" trophy, the holy grail.  Nope.  Two achievements. TWO. They are all that separate me from my sanity and the sweet reward.  Achievement #48: The Paper Trail Apparently, I stomped through the apocalypse, killed tyrants, solved puzzles, and uncovered conspiracies, but I failed to read the right notes. In this playtime, I probably consumed more paper than a librarian on speed. But no. Two tricky files are still hiding like the last nerds in a forgotten corner or folded up in some dusty office. You're more likely to find a needle in a haystack than these damned documents. I’ve probably walked past them a dozen times thinking they were just background decor. I’VE ALREADY READ EVERYTHING ELSE, PEOPLE!  Achievement #49: The Test of Patience (Or "The Why?") Oh, the final hidden challenges. You glorious, absurd, absolutely over-the-top requirements. While the rest of the game prepared me to survive with a mix of firepower and sharp wit, these final goals suddenly demand skills I haven't trained for in 30 hours:  The Waiting Game: One task literally requires you to stand still and watch a repetitive machine do its thing for an eternity. It’s not gameplay; it’s supervised waiting. I could have cleared an entire floor in the time it took for this one "feat" to pop.  The Environmental Obsession: Then there’s the part where you have to interact with a mundane household object over and over again for no logical reason. The water bill in this place must be astronomical. Anyone watching me would think my character had a serious case of OCD.  The Dead Weight: And don’t get me started on the "escort" mission where you're basically babysitting a useless item across the map. We’re fighting for our lives, and I’m worried about a piece of junk!  And then, when you finally input that long, cryptic code you looked up... the game just mocks you. A diabolical laugh from the developers who knew exactly that we completionists are all a little bit insane.  Conclusion Resident Evil Requiem is an absolutely magnificent game. Atmospheric, tough, and exciting. But these last two achievements aren't just hurdles; they're a character study. They don't test your skill; they test your patience, your obsessive-compulsive traits, and your willingness to meditate in front of a meat-processing machine.  So, if you need me: I'm currently back in the facility, looking for that one missing scrap of paper while mentally scheduling my next "pointless interaction" run. The wait for the 100% has begun.  Rating: 47/49 Achievements – or as I call it: "Clinically dead, but too stubborn to fall down."

Resident Evil Requiem is a masterclass in tension, proving that true horror doesn’t come from excess—but from restraint. From the very first moments, the game pulls you into a suffocating atmosphere where every shadow feels alive and every sound matters. It strips the experience down to its essentials, forcing you to think, conserve, and survive rather than simply fight.  What truly sets it apart is its pacing. The game knows exactly when to let you breathe—and more importantly, when to take that breath away. Exploration is slow and deliberate, with environments that feel both hauntingly beautiful and deeply unsettling. Every corridor tells a story, and every encounter feels meaningful rather than repetitive.  The sound design deserves special praise: distant creaks, muffled footsteps, and sudden silences build a constant sense of dread. Combined with tight controls and smart level design, it creates moments that linger long after you’ve put the controller down.  While it doesn’t radically reinvent the formula, it perfects it. The narrative may follow familiar beats, but it’s delivered with enough intensity and polish to keep you fully invested.
