It's a fantastic game, you know that, so I'm focusing on the downsides, not because its bad, but because I think its a modest step down from RE8, and there's enough glazing to go around atm. It tells a much more interesting story, with much better characters, but splitting an already pretty short game between two different gameplay style results in both of them feeling shallow and underutilized in comparison to RE8. I don't really feel like writing a proper review without having explored the side content thoroughly so here's a few things worth noting.  $70 (+tax in the US), is, in fact, alot, I can't make your financial decisions for you. But for most people, this is not an amount of content worthy of that price tag, wait for a sale! It's still awesome  This game was created in the theocratic dictatorship known as Japan, where releasing a good PC port is considered apostasy. In spite of this, I find myself stunned by how lousy this one is. It runs quite badly on anything short of top of the line. With a 3070TI, 32 gigs DDR4, and a i7 10700 I was able to have a strong framerate at medium setting, but burdened with pretty awful lags spike throughout the game. Another thing worth noting, you cannot change your FOV, and it defaults to like 60, for me at least, that is nauseatingly tight, and makes the game way less fun to play, all because they didn't feel like adding a slider, that's really, REALLY stupid. In general the game just doesn't feel like it was ever made with mouse controls in mind, and the shooting feels quite a bit worse than its predecessor as a result.   No better time then now to mention that the variable perspective (defaulting to 1st person with Grace, and 3rd person with Leon), is, unfortunately, more or less cosmetic. It does not change your FOV, it does not change your controls, the best way to think about it is that in 3rd person mode, you're still playing a first person game, but with your character effectively functioning as an enormous weapon viewmodel. It's a total gimmick with effectively zero impact on gameplay, just pick whichever you prefer.   So yeah, it's not a 10/10, or even a 9/10, but it is a really damn good horror game that absolutely lives up to the streak of first person excellence that the series has been building on since RE7. I'm focusing on the bad, frankly, because no one else is, and people ought to know what they're spending a kings ransom on.

The latest mainline RE, splitting gameplay between newcomer Grace and everyone’s favorite hunky cheeseball Leon Kennedy as they return to Raccoon City. Leon’s sections do a good job focusing on action-forward gunplay akin to RE4. Grace’s sections, meanwhile, are the real highlight. They’re low-ammo, high-tension, and deliver some of the best scares I’ve experienced in the series. Roaming mini-bosses force you to move and shoot strategically, and Grace’s VA knocks it out of the park every chance she gets.  The story though… is not great. There are a couple of weird plot threads that I want to say are red herrings. But equally likely, they are seeds for future DLC that feel awkwardly unfinished in the base game. It also bothered me that Leon’s sections contribute almost nothing to the narrative. The longest stretch of his gameplay is literally about getting from point A to point B, nothing more. It would be less egregious if the baddies were as interesting as they are in Grace’s sections, but alas it’s mostly droves of regular zombies with a couple of variants.  Solid, fun addition to the franchise, if a bit over-hyped. I expect to see Grace’s VA a lot next awards season though.

An amazing entry int the Resident Evil franchise that perfectly blends the slow-paced survival horror and campy action that the series is both known for.  For reference, i played on classic (modern) difficulty. The Grace gameplay segments always keep you on edge, while never letting you feel unprepared, nor letting you breathe easy with an abundance of resources. While you can easily get lost or stuck in the facility, modern game design features, for better or worse, always point you into the right direction while not holding your hand. While there isn't a particularly gripping story going on, there's enough of an emotional hook to keep you invested and caring for the characters and in their journey.  Leon's gameplay is simply fantastic, the parrying mechanic deceptively adds a whole new layer to the combat, adding onto the already phenomenal foundation Capcom established in the Resident Evil 4 Remake. The set pieces and environments, while retreading on places already explored in Resident Evil 2, do enough to make them stand out while still providing fanservice that doesn't feel too forced.  The only issue I had with the game is that Leon feels absolutely invincible, I always had around 5 full heals and at least one and a half full magazines for every weapon I had. I never really felt threatened, and most of Leons segments are big cinematic super evil guy boss fights, but Leon is so cool and hot that its really a minor complaint. Leon is just so much fun and is too damn funny with his one liners that i wouldn't trade it for the world. The bad ending is just brutal.  Overall this game is just fantastic and perfectly mixes both gameplay styles found in the modern Resident Evil games, while introducing and elevating new and existing characters that I can't wait to see what DLC or stories they cook up next. I'd put Resident Evil 9 right below Resident Evil 4 (2005) as the second best in the series. A must play for any Resident Evil fan, new or old.

My first ever game is RE2 original one on potato PC but I never finished because I never understand it. But then, I finished RE4 original and man what it was, mind blowing, since then, I am big fan of Resident Evil games, and now this, RE9 Requiem, a perfect blend of action and horror,  In the start, we are introduced with a new character Grace Ashcroft who is having a trauma of her mother Alyssa Ashcroft, death in front of her. I literally relate with this character because of wonderful voice acting by Angela Sant'Albano. She is FBI investigator, she goes to the same hotel to investigate where her mother was murdered. She met with Victor Gideon (antagonist of the game) and Leon one of the OGs has infection, because every Raccoon City survivor is infected. Victor Gideon researches about another virus name Elpis made by Ozwell E. Spencer which enhances and controls the conscious of the infected person. Victor thinks Grace is the only one who can release the virus.  Gameplay: RE Requiem is the perfect blend of action and horror gameplay but I feel like horror is a little bit less than action, but still it was awesome. Horror depends on what perspective you are playing the game, is it 1st person or 3rd, but I suggested play Grace as 1st person and Leon as 3rd person for better action view.  But I think there is one setback in the game horror, game places at 4 to 5 areas, when you as a Grace escape from the center, there is very less chances you will feel the same the horror just like 1st area (Rhodes Hill Center) even playing as a Grace in the 2nd half of the game. In the 2nd half, there is less claustrophobic environment and jump scares than the Rhodes Hill Center except one small sequence in the game. Another reason is Grace is now confident in the 2nd half, you can see it through her aim and firing.  Leon, one of the OGs, is not rookie anymore, he is not scared by zombies, but zombies are scared by him. His action gameplay, OH MY GAWD, you will get goosebumps when he slashes the head of zombies, he literally aura farms by sharpening his hatchet before final blow. But, when Leon jumps from one place to another, it feels clunky when you don’t press jump button, they should remove auto jump or vice versa. For the nostalgia and fan service, this game delivers, when Leon visits RPD, there is so much detailing in this sequence from the banner of “Welcome Leon” to “Marvin’s nameplate”, old typewriter from RE2 to save the game, also some easter eggs from other resident evil games.   Puzzles are here in the good amount and can easily understand by the new players, there is also new mechanic for crafting as Grace. For Leon, there is his trust-worthy hatchet. Developers also give kinda intelligence to the zombies as a new T-virus version infected them, like butler switches off the lights, cleaners literally brush off your face with blood, and much more. For Leon, you can use chainsaw sometimes, literally too much testosterone in this sequence.   They also introduced new mechanics like a different approach to crafting ammo and different. With Leon’s hatchet, you can parry enemies attack. Gameplay never feel boring especially in first play through because of variety of enemies, mini bosses, engaging puzzles, sorting out the inventory, scarcity of ammo especially in insanity mode, some zombies literally have automatic rifles. Length of it is very good, neither less nor more. If you feel length is less, problem is not the game, problem is you, and RE games have never been lengthy games because of achievements, trophies and speed runners. Visuals and details are awesome, you can literally see, patient zombies shat and peed, I don’t know why I am telling this but yeah. They literally changed the cut scenes according to the outfit of the character.  Overall, this time Capcom literally cooks and serves every kind of player, newbies, OG fans, horror fans, action fans and also Leon simps, obviously. First contender for game of the year is here but don’t compare this other titles like RE7. Because RE7 is totally 1st person perspective and serves horror survival genre but this one is different so don’t compare because comparison can kill joy.

This is the 9th game of the resident evil series. You will play as Grace Ashcroft (the daughter of Alyssa Ashcroft, Outbreak character) and Leon Scott Kennedy.  Grace's gameplay is more survival-horror focused, so you will feel powerless against the enemies you face, whereas when you play as Leon, the game is more action focused and you can easily deal with the enemies because the guy has years of experience fighting zombies and bio-organic weapons. I enjoyed both of their gameplay.  The duration of the game is also good enough, not too long, not too short.  The main villain is a guy called Victor Gideon, an ex-Umbrella researcher who considers Spencer (one of the three founders of Umbrella) as his master, and a supporter villan who is a high-ranking member of The Connections, the crime syndicate who created the B.O.W. Eveline from Resident Evil 7.  They added new lore to the game and you will discover hidden things that happened in the past, so if you are interested in the story, you will see good things as well.  A cool guy from the previous games makes his appearance when you play as Leon near the end of the game.  An extra difficulty called Insanity gets unlocked after you beat the game, some new costumes for the characters and new weapons that you can use on your NG+ runs.  Overall it is a really good Resident Evil game that you can confidently purchase and have a good time playing it.

I’ve played RE from 2 to this (remake only, when available).  RE9 imo is the best. Probably has something to do with Capcom rediscovering (and refining) the formula since RE7.  Story is, on paper, nothing special. But what matters is it gets you hooked, and it does that exceptionally well. Grace is a great new character. Leon is OG and they still managed to get you even more attached to the guy.  Can’t tell you how many games I’ve played (both good and bad) where I take away zero from cut scenes because can’t seem to care enough to listen. End up not having any idea what is going on. Never happened here.  Gameplay is great though probably too easy (apart from very early on when resources are scarce). But imo it doesn’t matter because it doesn’t even have to be hard/challenging to be enjoyable. I find myself redoing fights/encounters just because a) I want to do a good run with minimal heals and ammo usage; and b) it’s fun!  From the previews, I was worried that all the melee attacks would make Leon OP. Imo that was part of the downfall of RE6. But they managed to balance it out. Though I think the parry is still OP for standard difficulty.  Graphics-wise, it looks incredible and runs well. The RE engine is definitely one of the best out there despite its age. And the cherry on top is we get path tracing for the first time.  This game well and truly deserves the top user score on metacritic. Will probably be my GOTY.

Grace’s section in the care centre felt like Resident Evil at its best, like a combination of RE2’s RPD and the aesthetics of RE4’s Castle, with some RE7 thrown in. Almost like a celebration of what makes RE great. I honestly didn’t want this part to end.  The soundtrack and sound design in Requiem is absolutely fantastic. Realistic but stylised.  Shooting with Grace felt tense and immersive even in 3rd person. For a game with so few guns it’s weirdly become one of my favourite depictions of gunplay in video games  [b]Bits I didn’t like:[/b] Replayability may be hampered by quite lengthy cinematic intro sequences, it takes a minute to get into the sprawl of the care centre, which is where the game truly opens up. Segments with the ‘Girl’ could also be tedious, as they’re Alien Isolation-esque sequences but mostly scripted. I find these will only be fun to replay if the ‘Girl’ remains scary on subsequent playthroughs, but to be fair the lore & design of the ‘Girl’ is fantastic.  Raccoon City was very bland, after a while I was just trying to rush through it, which is a shame because that takes up a huge portion of Leon’s sections. Leon has really slick and smooth gameplay, basically RE4R on steroids. This kept it fun at least.  Leon’s retorts and one-liners were constant throughout, charming for sure and what you expect from Leon but I was rolling my eyes by the end. His segments mostly felt like aura farming with not that much depth.  Would have honestly preferred if they did A & B campaigns with Leon & Grace similar to RE2, but I appreciate what they tried to pull off here anyways.  My biggest grievance with this game is that I’ll never be able to experience it for the first time again. Requiem hooks you in HARD almost immediately.  A legendary entry in the RE series and a must-play for fans of good horror. Hopefully a GOTY contender at the next VGA’s!

Resident Evil Requiem sits on the upper echelon of the franchise, offering a thrill ride that will delight fans both old and new. Where the game falters, perhaps, is in its pursuit of balancing both sides of the story. The narrative switches between Grace and Leon fairly frequently at the start, only to then dedicate hours on end to one character over the other. Grace gets one section for herself, taking a backseat afterwards for Leon’s one-man show. I like throwing hatchets and delivering roundhouse kicks to zombies as much as the next guy, but Requiem doesn’t strike the delicate balance between that power fantasy and survival horror the way RE4 did. As for its story, Requiem offers a somewhat satisfying, if not overly thrilling, narrative. Like many RE games, the bigger plot reveals all wait for their reveal until the third act. Most of it acts as a coda to the actions of the franchise’s most important players, while the inclusion of some new characters isn’t fleshed out enough to be narratively satisfying. [h2] RE Requiem PC Performance [/h2] On an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Ti, it ran flawlessly at 1440p on the max preset, without path tracing or frame generation. At 1440p output resolution with path tracing turned on, and DLSS on the performance mode, I got frame rates hovering around 150fps. Even with DLAA on the same settings, I was easily cruising above 75fps in intense areas like Raccoon City. The budget-focused, and older, RTX 3060 Ti only has 8GB to play with, and that was the biggest bottleneck in the overall experience. Using “Normal” textures with a mix of high and medium settings would blow past the 8GB buffer in intense scenes. On my Steam Deck OLED, Resident Evil Requiem can be easily run at around 45fps without frame generation. If you’re feeling adventurous, locking the internal frame rate to 30fps at higher settings and using FSR frame generation to double it to 60fps is a viable option.  Full review on [url=https://thescreenzone.com/blog/resident-evil-requiem-game-review] The Screen Zone [/url].

I really wanted to love this game, but unfortunately, it was pretty disappointing. This franchise is at its best when it deftly swings between horror and comedy, but this game has a surprising absence of both (mostly due to the fact that the writing is so needlessly self-serious). There is one great extended horror sequence in the first half, and it's followed up by a moment of genuine emotional catharsis, but the grand majority of this game plays out like the MCU equivalent of a Resident Evil game, with eye-rolling nostalgia-bait and heaps and heaps of unearned emotional beats. The story is poorly written and poorly structured, and it ultimately wastes any good qualities that it starts off with.  Also, maybe it's just me and my filmmaking brain, but I thought that the sound design was really lacking some punch, especially in comparison to what was accomplished in RE8. Sound was used so purposefully and effectively in that game to establish and contribute to atmosphere, but there wasn't a single sound design choice in this entire game that I'll remember a week from now. It's been at least a few months since I last replayed RE8, but I can still hear the sound of my sharp, echoing footsteps in the castle.  For what it's worth, there is still some amount of fun to be had with this game (it is a video game, after all). Some of the gameplay sections are pretty engaging, but it is worth noting that the changes in gameplay between the other RE entries and this one feel rather derivative. The "hide-and-seek" style of horror gets pretty old after a while, especially once you realize how many of the monster encounters are just scripted events. It never really feels like there's any reward to being quiet or clever when the monster is always just gonna hop out of a vent and chase you anyways. There's nothing wrong with using a more scripted horror sequence every once in a while, but that kind of gameplay gets particularly redundant when overused in a horror game because a lot of the terror that is felt while playing them is rooted in a natural fear of the unknown. Once your brain realizes how it works, it becomes less scary.  Not to constantly refer back to RE8, but the dollhouse section works on every playthrough because it complements the previous gameplay so well. In fact, every major section of that game is clearly designed to look, feel and sound unique. But despite that section being the most scripted and "on-rails" part of the game, it still works very effectively because it is tonally surprising and just short enough to not outstay its welcome. Hell, even in great games like Amnesia: The Dark Descent and Alien: Isolation (which, in some ways, mastered the "hide-and-seek" style with its remarkable Xenomorph AI), the gameplay becomes fairly redundant and predictable past a certain point. Maybe RE8 really did do it best.  Anyways, I'm tired of writing about this game. It isn't terrible in the grand scheme of things, but it is kinda terrible as an RE game. I still haven't played RE5 or RE6, but I honestly wouldn't be surprised if I like at least one of those more than this. I guess I'll probably replay this at some point, but it definitely won't be for a while, since it's left a pretty bitter taste in my mouth.

While the RE Engine's technical optimization is so flawless it borders on technological magic, the true weight of the game lies not in its mechanics, but in its profound humanity. The narrative strips away the caricatures of the apocalypse to focus on deeply realistic human anchors. Grace is written with a startling, grounded authenticity, and the entire Emily subplot operates as a devastating emotional core. When the Elpis plot twist finally drops, it doesn't just shock the player ,it retroactively recontextualizes the tragedy of the entire campaign. This emotional weight is anchored entirely by a phenomenal voice cast, with Victor Gideon VA delivering a career-defining performance that carries the gravitas of the script. But the game's greatest achievement is how it mirrors the legacy of the franchise. The thematic parallels between Claire saving Sherry in RE2 and Grace fighting for Emily elevate the narrative from a simple zombie shooter to a meditation on parenthood in the face of annihilation. It is a harrowing, deeply satisfying simulator of what it means to protect the vulnerable when the world falls apart. Absolute peak fiction.

I love resident evil, but I unfortunately cannot recomend this game to anyone who isnt already a fan of the franchise. I think the series is so fun and has an amazing mix of horror and action mixed in with an in-depth story. RE9 feels like it hits a lot of those notes while also leaving you dissapointed at the same time. The game is split down the middle between Leon and Grace.  Grace: Grace had a great introduction and had the bones to be an interesting new character but the script/va left her as a whiny cringey mess. Her gameplay has a lot of amazing horror elements and very cool new mechanics in the beginning, but as soon as that section of the game ends they are hardly ever seen again. Grace then has one of the worst feeling, goofy, linear flashbacks I have ever played. It is only at the very last section where she unlocks a few weapons where the rhythm feels really nice only for her to not be playable for the rest of the game.   Leon: Leon is the standerd action hero we have grown to know and love, but has almost no difference in his gameplay the entire game. The default guns are the same ones you are still going to be using at the end. To the games credit, all the combat is very satisfying and has a few specific sections/mini bosses that make it really shine. That all goes out the window when you get to RCPD the entire scenario is nostalgia bait and is just a worse version of a game we already have. The game was marketed specifically with this as a major seller, but it feels completely shoved in and out of place story wise. The end of the game has a rare shine of real emotion that is immediately followed by a stupid betrayal and a completely unsatisfying boss fight that is a more anti climatic version of RE3's final battle.  Just realizing this right now, but the game also has almost no real puzzles? Every time I was wondering how I could get into an area, I would immediately find the exact tool I needed to get me there.  TLDR:  Grace has cool horror bits, semi interesting story, but and terrible pacing and cringey voice lines. Leon is awesome and very sexy, but has almost no change to his gameplay and has a full section of the game that is nothing but nostalgia bait. The villain might be the worst in the franchise and the end boss fight  is a 1 to 1 of RE3's.   Solid 5.5/10, Not worth 70 dollars, Might be a bottom 2 game in the franchise tbh

[h1]Tasty Little Bits[/h1] - Resident Evil 9: Requiem is by far one of the most graphically impressive games I've experienced as of 2026 and acts as a collage of the "Greatest Hits" that the franchise has to offer: Incredibly atmospheric horror elements (some of the best I've played since Amnesia: The Dark Descent), really intricate but short-lived metroidvania level designs, and some of the most satisfying action-oriented feedback gameplay I've experienced in a while. Despite me having incredibly refined preferences towards anthropomorphic fluffy men, Leon S. Kennedy is the only non-furry fictional character I would permit to father my child, and I'm a male <3  [b]However[/b], I must implore you not to buy this game until you have played the following:  Resident Evil 2 Remake (fantastic metroidvania level-design, and it's story-relevant)  Resident Evil 4 (either the 2005 version or the Remake)  Resident Evil 5 (I wish I wasn't kidding, it's spoiler-related. Do play with a friend, though!)  Resident Evil 7 (This is completely optional; it's an excellent first-person horror game, but you don't need to play it to appreciate RE9)  [hr][/hr] That said, I do recommend waiting for a sale if you just want to play it. The average playthrough ranges between 8 to 10 hours with incentives to replay it (I beat it in 9.5 hours myself).  [hr][/hr]  [h2]The Positives[/h2] - The first opening hours of RE9: Requiem are some of the most fun I've had! Playing as Grace Ashcroft in first-person is a celebration of the horror genre with incredible atmosphere and fantastic metroidvania level design.  Leon S. Kennedy's levels are in third-person, and it just feels so satisfying being so utterly absurd to the point where you ARE the horror genre itself.  It's two different games in one! But because of that, there's a lack of cohesion. It's a lot like ordering a drink where the alcohol is in a separate glass and you have to drink them individually. Like taking a nice hot bath and then dipping into a frozen lake. There simply isn't a unified whole, and I think it's beautiful in its own way, but at a cost.  [h2]The Negatives[/h2] - The metroidvania levels are so much fun, but they disappear way too quickly! Later in the game, it begins to feel like I'm being pulled by a "roller coaster" similar to Doom (2016). It takes away the sense of freedom and control in certain sequences. That's not to say that the sequences themselves are bad, they're very cinematic, but I can't help but feel like I've been given a grand sampler appeteaser of all the strengths of the Resident Evil franchise, but never a complete main course.  And just a side note: I've been running this game on an AMD Radeon 7900 XTX graphics card, and there have been game crashes when loading between levels. If I lower the graphics quality to load the next level, it works perfectly fine and I can set the graphics back to maximum. This is just a heads-up, and it's likely a non-issue for most other gamers.  [hr][/hr]  Overall, Resident Evil 9: Requiem is a collection of the "Greatest Hits" that the franchise has to offer. It's an amalgamation, but I've had a lot of fun!

After getting all of the achievements in this game, making it my 14th Resident Evil platinum, and after all my years playing this series, I can confidently say this is easily one of the top three Resident Evil games ever made.  Resident Evil 9 is honestly one of the best entries we've had in a long time. It feels like the perfect blend of Resident Evil 7 and 8's horror with the action and gameplay of Resident Evil 4 and the remakes.  The balance between horror and action is where the game really shines. Grace's slower, more suspenseful sections ended up being my favorite, while Leon's more action focused gameplay was excellent too. I do wish Grace had a few more weapons. Only having three pistols starts to feel like a drag by the climax. Leon's arsenal also feels a little limited, especially when several of his guns feel very similar to each other. Most of his pistols boil down to, "This one does a little more damage," or, "This one sounds a little different." They never really feel as distinct as the weapons in Resident Evil 4, where almost every gun had its own identity and gave you a reason to actually choose one over another.  The atmosphere is fantastic. The soundtrack, level design, and environments all work together to make every area memorable. The story is also surprisingly strong for a Resident Evil game. Both villains are enjoyable, and I really liked the hidden villain twist, although it's a little disappointing that he only exists in cutscenes. I also wish Sherry had a bigger role, and a few more returning characters like Claire would have been nice. Resident Evil 2 was the tale of two survivors, especially the original 1998 version. Seeing the long awaited return to Raccoon City become almost entirely Leon's cross to bear felt like a missed opportunity.  Enemy variety is pretty strong, with enough new infected to keep things interesting. Grace being hounded by zombie variants and the roaming mini bosses were some of my favorite parts of the game, even if the mutated enemies become pretty annoying on Insanity difficulty. The boss fights are another highlight, especially the final fight as Grace, which felt like a modern callback to Resident Evil 0's ending with Rebecca.  Performance was excellent from start to finish. I experienced very few crashes, no major bugs, and nothing that ever got in the way of enjoying the game.  My biggest complaint is the lack of post game content. Once you finish the 8 to 12 hour campaign, there really isn't much to do outside of achievement hunting. I finished six playthroughs in 55 hours, and while replaying for speedruns and optimization is still fun, sections like the orphanage flashback definitely become a drag. Leon Must Die is a nice addition, but it still feels a little half baked.  Even with those complaints, Resident Evil 9 is one of my favorite games in the franchise. It does a great job bringing together so much of what Resident Evil has built over the years while still feeling fresh, and it left me excited to see what Capcom does next.

[h3] 9.5/10 [/h3]  [h3] tl;dr Review [/h3]  Resident Evil: Requiem is one half survival horror and one half action shooter and somehow manages to pull them both off perfectly without detracting from the other. The game looks great and runs even better. However, the game is not as replayable as other titles in the series, even when parts of the game feel specificially designed for repeat playthroughs. If you like the modern RE titles, you'll love Requiem and it's yet another great addition to the series.  [h3] The Good [/h3]  I'm not sure where exactly I would rank Requiem amongst the entire series but it likely has to be top 5. RE4R is my personal favorite in the series and this game improves on it quite a bit while also lacking in others. The gameplay as Leon is probably the best it's been here and it's only slightly different than RE4R. I thought having two different characters with very different playstyles would cause a whiplash in the fun department but it really doesn't. If you're someone that wants constant action in a Resident Evil game like RE4, RE5, or RE6, you might dislike the Grace sections but can kill all the same enemies that Leon can so either way, the game won't lack for you preferred playstyle.  Performance wise, this is yet another RE Engine game that looks top of the line and yet still runs like butter. There was one section at launch that tanked my FPS down to roughly 20FPS and below but that has since been patched and the game consistently hits 120FPS with FSR4, Ultra settings, and Ray-tracing enabled.  [h3] The Bad [/h3]  The game feels designed to be replayed again and again; more so than RE7, RE8, RE2R, and RE3R but lacks enough challenges and content to make it as replayable as RE4R. For example when it comes to puzzles, the game has next to none. This makes repeat playthroughs easier as you won't need to remember the solution to a complex puzzle and at most, you'll just need to consult with a piece of paper listing the solution a few feet away. This means the game is lacking a core aspect of the series. The only real puzzles in the game are the blood samples you analyze on the computer, which are also entirely optional to do. There's also the [spoiler] organ box puzzle [/spoiler] which has a specific combination you won't figure out without hunting down the solution. A lack of puzzles makes the game feel like Capcom wants you to be able to play it again and again without getting bogged down with complicated puzzles, which I appreciate but does make that first playthrough feel like something is missing.  While on the topic of this game feeling like it was made to be replayable but having odd design decisions counterintuitive to that is [spoiler] the orphange [/spoiler]. Story-wise, it just adds a little background to a supporting character but overall, the game could've shipped without it and added this section as some files to find if you wanted to learn more. Most Resident Evil games have that section that you groan having to repeat on repeat playthroughs and this is Requiem's.  This game only took me about four playthroughs and about 38 hours to get all the achievements which compared to RE4R, is quite a downgrade IMO. RE4R took me 150hrs, but granted a lot of the time there I wasn't even going for achievements and just running through it again for the fun of it. The challenges in this game are really easy, and most are tied to the same achievements on Steam, which again, aren't hard to get. The only ones that could give you trouble are reading all the files, finding the raccoons, and Insanity mode but with infinite ammo, that's not that hard.

Resident Evil Requiem. Capcom has done it again  The story is absolutely brilliant – one of the best narrative arcs in the entire Resident Evil series. The fact that an FBI rookie, Grace, crosses paths with a DSO agent, Leon. The game gets off to an incredible start; you begin in the rehabilitation centre and suddenly find yourself in Raccoon City – my goodness, what a shock! I love how the game captures the development of both characters, adding a layer of emotion between these two protagonists that’s far deeper than I ever imagined. It’s a story of fear, growth and survival that leaves a lasting impression the first time you play it (well, actually, every time you play it, you’ll find yourself thinking, ‘What a masterpiece I’ve just played!’ :)  I don’t think I need to comment on the graphics, because OH MY GOD, they’re gorgeous! Every location you visit with either Grace or Leon is just mad. They manage to create that tense, scary, and even nostalgic atmosphere.  Little is said about the music. When you finish the game and the credits roll, and you’re left speechless watching them whilst the music echoes in your ears? What satisfaction is there in that? SO MUCH. And not just the credits song—all the music in the game is so well chosen and perfectly placed. I have to say there is one track that really broke me emotionally (even more than I already was)   I played using a controller: the controls are very easy to get the hang of  The character development – well, this is incredible. Grace, who starts out as a scared rookie haunted by her past traumas, shows throughout the game that she’s rising above herself, overcoming the fears that life has left her with. Leon is a masterpiece: he’s back as his usual self, but with a touch of vulnerability that left me absolutely heartbroken. Seeing him so broken creates an even deeper connection than in previous games (I just want to tell Leon it’s OK to cry every now and then <3). Emily is a new addition to the series who leaves a lasting impression once you get to know her better. You very quickly feel the urge to protect her.  The only thing I have to add about Requiem is that there are several questions left unanswered, which I imagine will be addressed through DLCs ;)  If you had any doubts about bugs: I haven’t encountered any in my 10 playthroughs.  So yes, if you’re still thinking about buying it, go for it. You’ve got nothing to lose (except your emotional stability).

I find myself on the opposing side of much of the fanbase on this one. While I don't hate the game or think it is bad per say, I wouldn't rate it higher then 7 or 8.  Perhaps it is because, though I've been a fan of the series for awhile, I haven't played the earlier games and so I don't have much nostalgia for parts of this game. I know enough to understand it and connect things, but now emotional weight to it. And maybe having missed that, I am able to be more critical of this title.  To start, I don't connect with Grace. I find the way she acts to be more alien then Ethan who I grew to love. The way she treated Emily, either cold in the beginning and then way too attached for someone you met today very odd. I also have anxiety so I get aspects of her character, but I think they went too far with it. I think a big thing for me, is if they made her a nobody like Ethan I'd be a lot more forgiving. This woman would not have what it takes to work at the FBI, and they have to make so many contrived things happen because of her profession that make no sense (she has no standard issue gun, she was sent there with no partner, her anxiety and ptsd seem to be unmedicated which I doubt would fly there, etc). If she was just a regular reporter or was just going back to investigate her mom's death before the building was torn down I would be more forgiving.   I didn't play the 4 remake, so I am not as used to this version of Leon. I played the original and I miss the snarky, more energetic version of him. I get this Leon is older and so his profession has worn him down some, but to me he now seems too similar to current Chris in personality. I found him to be quite boring in this game.   The plot also has alot of weirdness to it (pretty typical so it is something I can get over), but some things really stood out in this one for me. I have no idea why they are trying to redeem Spencer if that is what they are doing. The man was very evil, and is dead now, no reason to try and give him a turn around. I hate that they took a veteran woman of the series and killed her off so easily. Zeno had no purpose in this game at all, I really have no idea why he was even included in this. We already know about the Connections, honestly most of his stuff could have been in letters or video tapes we got so little. Way to waste a Wesker clone/sibling. Gideon by far was the best part of the game. He was menacing, but in a unique way for him and I enjoyed every bit with him. Oh, and I still don't know what made Grace special by the end. I'm assuming this will be dealt with in a dlc or future story I guess, but as far as we can tell she's just a person, so it makes some things confusing with Gideon getting her blood and all that.   Other negatives to me include: -needing to sharpen the axe was dumb, seems like a nerf to how good the knives were in 7/8 -dodging the cop's gun in Insanity mode is way too hard, had the most deaths to that then anything else -locations, devoid of the nostalgia factor, weren't interesting enough to look at or memorable (issue with going hard into realism but not enhancing it with style) -need an ability to turn off the sounds of them panting and breathing constantly, it gets annoying given how fast and how much they do it -the lack of a merchant was a damn shame -soundtrack was boring  Points I loved:  -the motorcycle bit was a highlight for the spectacle and humor -Gideon is a treat -had no bugs on launch day and that is very impressive -I love a map that updates as you find things or needed to leave things behind  I could ♥♥♥♥♥ more, but I'll spare you. I would give this game like a 7. It is good, plays well and not too bad to 100% and also I noticed no bugs. But, I wont be replaying it for fun like I do with Re7-8. I will return for any dlc they add, but sad to say I am not taken with this game.

This review is meant for people in the same boat. Not specifically RE fans, but people seeking a genuine game. For the last couple years, we've been getting sh♥t on a platter. This game was through and through refreshing. The plot, graphics, performance, and even the atmosphere they aimed for were beyond my expectations. I can't expect much from most game industries, we know why. However this was strangely nostalgic, even made me hopeful. Now for the RE fans regarding the duality they went for with including both horror and action, it was executed perfectly. My opinion means nothing to you of course, but faithfully i assure you it really did strike a great median between both sides of the fanbase. There's exceptionable customization available as well, so even if you aren't someone who likes both sides as i do, you can lean either both horror or action completely. I had no bugs, although I'm sure they exist, I didn't run into a single one which was quite nice. This game did come out polished, and playable. The difference between games that have those two qualities as well remains the fact this game was also enjoyable. It made me want to play again, simply for the fact we haven't had games that were actually finished for such a while.   Starting my replay soon, as there is still so much to do and appreciate even after my first run. So thank you for reading this, and thank you devs for hitting that bar that we held back then. -Redj approval: 9.6/10

A great showing from Capcom! While this games focus on shifting between both the horror & action gameplay styles the series is known for might not work for some people, I felt that it worked perfectly to build tension creeping around as Grace, to relieve that tension by roundhouse kicking zombies as Leon. This game is easily in my list of top 3 RE Games easily. Beware spoilers below!  Though, like most games, Requiem isn't perfect & I never expected it to be, but after 4 playthroughs on Classic difficulty I still feel it would be useful to discuss the few parts that I, personally, found could have been improved.   [spoiler] Firstly, I feel like the game could have done well with more Grace sections, or really any Grace sections during the Racoon City section. I know this might require some rewriting of the plot, but I feel like it would've helped with a lot of peoples initial annoyance with that section just being nothing but Leon running around the ruins from point A to point B (This is something a personally don't agree with, but its an opinion I've heard enough, so I'm using it to help with my point) by cutting to Grace in the RPD. This would 1. give us  more fanservice lol 2. Let Grace's gameplay evolve more(possibly letting here get an additional weapon.) & 3. Gives us more time with this games one character who needed more screen time, Zeno. Overall, I feel like this one change could've done wonders for the game, but not to say it would be easy, just that it would've fleshed out the middle of the game for the better in my opinion.  [/spoiler]  [spoiler] Secondly, I feel like Grace could have done with more boss fights. Now this not to say I wanted FBI Desk Jockey Grace Ashcroft to be doing insane set pieces like old Mr. Kennedy, but I would've loved to see more stealthy, puzzle-like encounters similar to the climatic encounter with The Girl. Again, this could work with my previous change of giving Grace the ability to explore the ruins of the RPD, maybe even give her that bootleg Mr. X wannabe as a chaser enemy since this games identity from my interpretations seems to be a sendoff to the classic trilogy of RE games what with the rampant references, fanservice, talks of clones, legacies, & mirrored scenarios from the past. This would also give Grace more of an impact on the middle section of the game, but this is just an example I thought of on the spot.  [/spoiler]  [spoiler] Lastly, I felt like the bad ending could have been more fleshed out. And, my suggested remedy works with one of the reasons of my second complaint, I think the bad ending should have given Grace a stealth boss fight against Zeno. This could've mirrored the Gideon Final boss with Leon in the good ending, Given Zeno & Grace more character development (Even it would've still been non canon) allowing Zeno to actually have appeared in gameplay & letting Grace get the win in this timeline instead of Zeno just dying after killing Leon from choosing to aura farm & grace just walking out. & again, given Grace another boss fight other than her only encounter being The Girl.  [/spoiler]  While all of these complains/ideas are merely dreams of my perfect Requiem that could never happen & might even convince you that I secretly hate this game (Trust me, I don't,  this game is like crack I swear to god,) The only reason I've written all of this is because of how deeply I love this game. I Feel like its natural for people to see the smallest flaws glaringly in what they loved the most & if my only real complain is "I wish there was more", then I feel like that speaks enough on its own about how good this game is. Its always good to discuss how our favorite pieces of art could've been better as that is were new masterpieces can be born from. This game truly was a Requiem for Resident Evil.  TLDR: Peak gaming, 9.5/10, needs more Grace, lol.

Honestly, this is a very good game overall. Having played some of the OG Resident Evil (1,4) and 2/4 Remake, I knew what the franchise is about and what players want. The addition of Grace is spectacular. She is a really cool character  and has definitely found a place in the franchise. She is definitely worth exploring in future games. Her part is pure Resident Evil and Rhodes Hill brings us back to the OG dynamic of tight hallways, backtracking, scary times etc. My main critique about her part is the puzzle aspect...well in my opinion there are none; they are all pretty straightforward or in your face which made me a little sad to be honest. Also i wish there was still  more of the "Girl" in Rhodes Hill or other form of chaser to emphasise the horror aspect a bit more (the initial sequence is amazing but short). Of course I know that a huge reason why this game has been so successful is because of Leon. His gameplay feels smooth and satisfying (although regarding this aspect, the 4 Remake is still superior in my opinion) and makes us feel powerful; it is the perfect contrast to Grace's part and there are basically no scary parts anymore. However, despite loving Leon as a character from the earlier games, his part in this game has some design flaws. The part where you have to find the detonator pieces is a little bit annoying, long and repetitive (also just too much action idk...). I realised this during my first run and can confirm it after having finished the game 4 times. I'd much rather shorten this part and add a bit more to the RPD or even parts of RE 3 Nemesis (since the remake was... interesting lol :D). The RPD part felt a bit short and rushed and obviously was interrupted by the annoying orphanage sequence which could honestly be cut (first time was ok, afterwards it is just a pain in the ass). The story is okayish still some question marks but hope to see more about it in the DLC or RE X (Zenon is kinda ass, Wesker from Wish). Of course the fanservice is a big reason why people loved this game so much, but considering I'm not a hardcore fan, to me it was cool to see but not a deciding factor for my "grade".  Again, I loved this game mainly due to Grace's part and her character. I honestly feel like Leon was not needed in this game and Grace could have carried the game as the protagonist. I'm aware though that the popularity of the game and success of Grace's character would have suffered if Leon hadn't been part of it (which in the end helps Grace's character and  her acceptance in the fandom)  ps: love you Leon please come back still...   8.25/10 --> Grace's part(9.5) Leon's part (7)

As a fan of the Resident Evil series, the extreme lows on display in this game are really disappointing. In particular, the second half of the game absolutely nosedives in quality compared to the first. There are many others commenting on how uninteresting the game becomes past a certain point and so I know I'm not alone in feeling that way.  So much of the plot and writing is uninspired fanservice that grossly retcons established characters and ideas. It's lazy, it takes itself too seriously and it's forgettable. In many ways — especially throughout Leon's sections — the game seems far more concerned with looking cool and being cinematic than it is with actually being interesting and enjoyable to play.  Requiem has some great moments and sections, but they're too few and far between to redeem the overall experience for me.   Many people will enjoy this game just fine, but I'm personally recommending against it because I do not want the Resident Evil series to continue in this direction.

[Intro]: Sometimes a company needs to fail to understand its creative direction. With the massive backlash of Resident Evil 6, the success of Resident Evil 7 's horror and the action of Resident Evil Village, Capcom has cleverly blended a survival horror and action aspect to attract both sides of fans for Resident Evil Requiem.   [Pros]: What I like most about this game is the small attention to detail of realism throughout the story. When it comes to videogames, this attention to detail matters because it shows the developers put passion into their game. Some notable examples are Grace, the new female protagonist, experiences shakier hands when aiming, considerably more recoil than Leon when firing, can only push a zombie away when they are stunned. Leon, on the other hand, has less sway aiming weapons, easier recoil control when firing, more melee attacks when a zombie is stunned, gun finishers and the ability to throw weapons from enemies. This game does a great job at making you feel weak as Grace and a juggernaut as Leon. Grace is not the stereotypical "girl boss" (Think Ada Wong) but more of an underdog character with massive physical disadvantages in a zombie outbreak where she finds ways to survive the best she can.  **Warning Story Ending Spoiler**  [Cons]: The story was interesting but I felt the final arc could of been done much better. The game really builds up Victor Gideon and Zeno. How they were handled at the end seemed oddly forced and rushed. After Grace makes her decision on what to do with Elpis, she does nothing to contribute further for the final arc. Zeno mistakenly takes Elpis which ends up being an anti-viral to all the current Resident Evil Viruses. He loses his "Wesker like powers" then gets betrayed and decapitated by Victor Gideon. In classic Resident Evil fashion, Victor Gideon transforms into a giant monster and you have to shoot or use explosions on its weak points. My biggest gripe is they continue to recycle the same creative formula for end of story boss fights. I would like if they did a back-and-forth fight utilizing different aspects of Leon and Grace against Zeno or Victor. I believe this was a missed opportunity that really overshadows Grace's efforts of character development from a stuttering, terrified FBI desk analyst to someone that is still very much scared but more confident in their abilities towards the end of the story. Lastly, there were times in cutscenes where subtitles and character's audio didn't sync up with each other. This only happened about 2-3 times throughout the whole game.   [TLDR]: Great game, definitely worth the purchase. Grace and Leon's parts are uniquely fun. The story is interesting but the ending could of been improved. Some cutscenes have out of sync subtitles and audio. Overall a solid game. Definitely deserves the praise and hype its received. Congrats, Capcom.   [Verdict]: A solid 9/10

Peak Game.   In my opinion, this is the best RE game I've played so far (yes I'm relatively new to the franchise). Anyways, what I like the most is the level design, the pacing, the gameplay and of course the storyline.  I never felt like a part of the game was dragging or that it was boring. It was constantly tensive and enjoyable. I couldn't stop myself from playing because I really wanted to see what will come next. The switch between Grace and Leon is always timed well and changes the feeling of the game. It's refreshing to play the other perspective, especially in the Care Center. Capcom managed to combine horror from RE Biohazard/Village and action from RE4 and RE3. Overall, this was done pretty well. In fact, I enjoyed Grace's gameplay more than Leon's oftentimes.  The pacing is also great. You have three major sections of the game and none of them feel too short nor too long. They are also quite distinct from one another, offering a great amount of variety. Each section feels really immersive. The enemies are diverse, scary, interesting and also funny. The zombies who keep their old habits, such as cleaning the ground or shutting light switches off are quite something xD Their voicelines are funny and give them some personality which I enjoyed.  As for the gameplay, obviously this RE is superior to all others. The character movement feels really smooth; it feels like you are controling a real person. The animations are a chef's kiss. When you have a fully reloaded gun, Grace and Leon will check the magazine; a nice attention to detain. When you do a tactical reload, they will put away the magazine instead of dumping it. The animations overall are really clean and realistic. Fighting with Leon feels controlable and satisfying. Gore and blood from the enemies persist for a long time and look very real. Guns also feel powerful and satisfying to use. A personal highlight for me is the flashlight. I don't know why but it just feels good and cool to use, especially with Leon and a pistol in the other hand. That being said, they did make a couple of gameplay changes. For instance, there are no more red or yellow herbs anymore; only green. You have maximum health as Leon from the start. There is no rank anymore after you complete the game (e.g. C, A, S+). None of those really bother me and I think those choices were valid.  Graphics and optimization: The game looks gorgeous, and it is VERY well optimized thanks to the RE Engine. Ray tracing makes a huge difference and I recommend turning it on if your GPU can handle it. I was able to play the game with maxed out settings, and FSR 4.1 set to quality mode (although it probably wasn't even necessary, but I like the extra frames). I was at a constant 100+ fps 90% of the time. Some dips would occur in the city (second section) but it didn't affect gameplay at all. The game looks beautiful and runs perfectly fine. However, there seems to be a bug currently in which the game is bloating your memory if you have "mesh quality" set to standard instead of low. The bug causes you to lose frames slowly but surely until you reach an uplayable level. You can fix this by restarting the game, but the bug will occur again. You need to set "mesh quality" to low and you can set it back to standard later. This was the only fix that worked for me so far. I've seen people from both NVIDIA and AMD GPU's report this issue. But I don't see this as a huge negative because I assume the developers will fix it soon.  Story (no spoilers): Great storyline which uncovers the events before the Raccoon City incident and what happened afterwards. You learn the secret behind Umbrella Corporation and why they did the things they did. It was very captivating, especially the last section of the game.  I would give this game a 10/10, because it is basically flawless. I can't think of something that the devs could have done better, nor about something that I feel like is missing. So I think this title deserves a perfect rating.

There are people who will say that this part of Resident Evil is the weakest and most overhyped; then there are those who consider it one of the best in the series. I’d personally place myself in the second group, because I liked this entry a lot—so much so that for the first time ever, I got the Platinum trophy in Resident Evil and played through it four times in a row.  Where does the game’s strength definitely lie? The first thing that catches the eye is the graphics. While they aren't perfect in some moments, overall they are at a very high level. The same can be said for the optimization: the game will run and behave well on most modern systems. The only thing that might have raised questions was the Nvidia drivers—an older version of which showed a significant FPS boost in certain segments—but that’s not Capcom's fault, which is more than can be said for Nvidia lately.  The next thing that stands out after the graphics is how Capcom brought back horror in its best form, far surpassing RE2 Remake and RE7, which were also good at times. The segments with Grace are one of the strongest parts of the game, offering an unforgettable experience during the first playthrough. Unfortunately, as with all "stalkers" in horror games, this experience is a one-time thing; a purely script-based enemy won't evoke that same fear and tension twice. Capcom simply didn't stray from the formula here—it’s neither good nor bad—but in the future, I’d like to see smarter enemies like the Xenomorph from Alien: Isolation, where the hunter is actually hunting you. Well-placed scripts are a great tool for a first impression, but a smart enemy is an endless generator of stress and unique situations in every playthrough.  Overall, the gameplay as Grace follows the classic Resident Evil formula we all love: limited resources, survival, and a location full of loot and puzzles that you want to explore. The only thing is that the upgrades don't feel significant. Percentage boosts to HP or damage aren't the most ideal way to motivate a player to get a new stabilizer, as they don't really feel what the old one gave them. I much prefer weapon upgrades or something like the body armor in Leon’s campaign; those would give the player a clearer sense of reward for exploration.  Regarding exploration, the situation is a bit mixed. On one hand, the puzzles here are far more unique than those in RE2 Remake, but they lack any real difficulty. They exist, they’re cool, and they aren't annoying, which is good—but there are very few of them. I’d like to see more puzzles and more depth to them. What didn't please me much was the complete absence of puzzles for Leon. While the reasoning behind this is perfectly clear, I would have liked to see more than one or two real puzzles during his segments.  Otherwise, Leon’s gameplay is top-tier. At times, the gameplay even reminds me of The Last of Us Part 2, where Leon acts as the one inspiring fear rather than the zombies. Overall, you could call it a return to the RE4 Remake style and a refinement of an already well-working formula.  I think for the downsides, I can only mention that while both concepts are sewn together competently, they feel somewhat incomplete. What I mean is that stories from previous entries felt more finished and deep than here. Playing as Ethan in parts 7 and 8, you got a full experience from both the story and gameplay. The same goes for RE2 Remake and RE4 Remake—you felt the climax you were building toward and could breathe out at the end. Here, the story rushes toward the finale, and you don’t have time to truly feel the journey before you're told it's already over. I understand that doubling the campaign for both Leon and Grace likely wouldn't have ended well, but I don't think they quite managed to fit two concepts perfectly into such a short game. Does this ruin the final impression? No. I understand why the developers went this route, and in this case, it’s better to "under-deliver" and then supplement it with DLC than to just throw two full games into one and hope it works without boring people. I probably wouldn't have minded a 20-hour campaign, but I think not many would agree with me.  Overall, for me, this is definitely one of the best games of the year—or rather, the best so far. Thanks to Capcom for such an experience, looking forward to the DLC!

[h1]“Coming home… but someone left a chainsaw in the hallway.”[/h1]  [b]I haven’t spent time in the Resident Evil universe for years, but this felt like slipping right back into it. Familiar in all the right ways… just with significantly more things trying to kill me.[/b]  The balance between classic horror and going full gun-wielding maniac is a real treat. One moment you’re creeping through shadows, the next you’re solving problems a lot more directly.  [b]Grace's sections lean hard into tension,[/b] like classic RE. Tight spaces, low light, and that constant feeling that you really shouldn’t be there. You move carefully, listen more than you shoot, and second-guess every door you open.  My “oh ♥♥♥♥” moment was running through narrow, pitch-black hallways with a 2.5 meter tall witch right behind you, breathing like she’s already decided how this ends.  You’re fumbling. You’re turning corners blindly. And at some point you’re just thinking:  WHERE IS THE LIGHT SWITCH?!  [b]Then you switch to Leon,[/b] and suddenly the mindset changes from “avoid everything” to “it’s time to kick ass and chew bubble gum… and I’m all out of gum.” More control, more firepower, and just enough confidence to make bad decisions feel intentional.  There’s a moment where everything just clicks, and you end up splitting a zombie clean in half with a Chainsaw. It’s brutal, slightly unnecessary, and completely satisfying.  That balance carries through perfectly in how the game switches between Grace and Leon. It keeps the pacing fresh and stops the game from ever settling into one rhythm.  Honestly, my only complaint is that I went through the game over a weekend. Didn’t really plan to, just kept going. The story pulls you along without dragging its feet, and before you know it, you’re at the end. Like a good book you didn’t mean to finish in one sitting.  [b]Visually, it’s absolutely stunning.[/b] From tight halls in a rundown hotel to the more open feel of the decayed remains of Raccoon City, it’s a great contrast. Everything feels well crafted, with Umbrella’s influence dripping out of everything… and yes, there’s a lot of dripping going on.  Inventory and upgrades are handled cleanly. Nothing overcomplicated, just a steady progression that feels natural as you go.  [b]Conclusion[/b] Resident Evil Requiem shows what years of game progression, done right, actually look and feel like. The balance between tension and action, between Grace and Leon, and between slow-burn storytelling and moments where you’re just trying to keep up, keeps it engaging from start to finish.  10/10 – Played for the horror, stayed for the chainsaw.

Resident Evil Requiem shows a lot of promise in its opening hours. Promise which it squanders in the back half, leaving players with a disjointed mess of a game that never lives up to its potential.  You start the game as Grace Ashford, an FBI technical analyst who is sent to investigate a hotel that has been the site of gruesome murders. The hotel also happens to have been the location of Grace's mother's murder 8 years prior. Why would the FBI send a young technical analyst alone to a location that has deep personal trauma for her? It's never explained and after the first hour or so, won't even be brought up again.  These sequences with Grace though are a strong point for the game. By default, they take a first-person perspective very similar to Ethan Winters in Resident Evil 7: Biohazard. While playing as Grace, the game is tense, requiring you to hide and avoid enemies, only shooting as a last resort. Add an unkillable enemy that's chasing you throughout the facility and you've got a recipe for a great Resident Evil game.  To make things better, at certain times, you take brief control of Leon Kennedy, who plays more in the style of Resident Evil 4, giving a strong feeling of catharsis as he mows enemies down by the dozens and faces off against bosses in a few fun setpieces.  If Requiem had stayed this way, it would have been a solid entry in the series, but it doesn't. Halfway through the game, you shift to play almost exclusively as Leon and the gameplay tanks. The RE4 gameplay continues but escalates even further as you are given a money system that tracks your kills. Any attempts at stealth that don't end in enemy kills are punished.  For the first time, zombies are given guns, which turns into an exercise in frustration as they can shoot you with perfect accuracy from nearly anywhere, turning the game into a weird shooting gallery of "find them before they hit you". Grace does make a brief reappearance once more before the end of the game, reminding us of what the game could have been before one of the worst final bosses in RE history closes out the game on a real whimper.  The story is nearly incomprehensible and directly contradicts itself and former games over and over again. Anime elements are cranked up to 11 as characters throw around meaningless terms like Elpis and The Connections without explaining what those mean until far later. As a consolation prize for getting through this mess, you're given a 60 page report meant to explain some of what happened and it fails even at that.  This would be fine if the gameplay held up but it really doesn't. Grace's sections are too short and linear to give the joy of exploration from RE7 and Leon's sections aren't fun enough to reach the highs of RE4. Not even close. The game tries to mash these two styles together and fails at both of them. Requiem as a game surpasses RE3make but the story is the worst the franchise has seen by far.

I’ll start with something important: I hated the first-person perspective in Resident Evil 7 and Resident Evil Village. It just never clicked with me for a Resident Evil game. So one of the best things about Resident Evil Requiem is that it gives you the option to play either in first-person or third-person. Fans of the newer style can keep it, while those of us who prefer the classic over-the-shoulder perspective can switch to third person. That alone made me happy.  The game centers around Leon S. Kennedy and a new character named Grace Ashcroft. Longtime Resident Evil fans may recognize that last name — Grace’s mother appeared in the Resident Evil Outbreak games, which is a really nice nod to the deeper lore of the series.  You switch between the two characters throughout the story, though Grace feels like the main protagonist, since you control her more often.  Their gameplay styles are very different: [list] [*]Grace handles the stealth and survival horror elements, and this is where the game gets genuinely terrifying. Her sections are easily the scariest parts of the game.  [*]Leon, on the other hand, is treated like the legendary government agent he is. His sections are more action-oriented.[/list]  There’s also a funny side effect of this: if you manage to eliminate most of the enemies while playing as Grace, when Leon passes through the same areas later he’s basically just walking through empty hallways looking sad, which honestly made me laugh.  The game itself is incredible and genuinely terrifying at times, and I loved playing through it.  Now, do I love it more than the Resident Evil 2 and Resident Evil 3 remakes? No. Those are iconic classics that helped define the series, and their stories have stood the test of time. A brand-new entry really can’t be expected to surpass those legendary titles.  But I will say this:  Resident Evil Requiem comes surprisingly close.  Overall I’d give the game an [b]8/10[/b] and it’s an easy recommendation for anyone who loves survival horror.

The level design deserves a special mention too, every area feels intentional, like it wants to mess with you, and usually succeeds.  What really hooked me though was the parallel storytelling between Leon and Grace. Switching between them kept things fresh, and also kept my stress levels perfectly balanced between “manageable tension” and “why am I doing this to myself.”  This series somehow keeps reinventing itself without losing what makes it great and this game is another example of that. I went in expecting a solid survival horror experience and came out emotionally attached, slightly traumatized, and already wondering when I can justify a second playthrough.

It was good, but Village was definitely better out of the modern Resident Evil games.  Requiem does have Victor, and he is one of the best villains in the series. He has that Joker-like energy, but he is more reserved and calm, which makes him even more dangerous. He feels like the type of villain who stays collected right up until he rips your face off. Grace is also an amazing character she is well developed and likeable.Leon is always a fan favorite to play as. Leon’s gameplay is more fun because he can tear through enemies, while Grace plays in a much stealthier way.  My biggest problem with the game is that it feels hollow. The layered puzzles are mostly gone. In the older games, you had to manage your weapons, crafting, navigation, and remember locations that might matter later, all while checking every corner for puzzle pieces and extra rewards. That whole survival-horror puzzle mystery loop is nerfed to hell. It feels like they made the game more "Mainstream".  The game feels very scripted and linear, and a lot of the locations feel like nostalgia bait thrown into the story. The maps are barely a challenge to explore, and the puzzles are much simpler than they used to be. It feels more like an action-horror story than a true Resident Evil game. The mystery is gone.  The opening with Leon in the city and the hospital was amazing and started the game off strong as hell, but it fizzles out pretty quickly into mediocrity. That is what makes it disappointing, because the game had the potential to be something special if they had let it bake longer and put more effort into it like they did with Village.  It is still a top-tier game, do not get me wrong. But after playing every Resident Evil game leading up to Requiem, my ranking from best to worst is: RE3, RE4, Village, Requiem, RE2, then Biohazard.

But the overall reaction to this game has been pretty confusing and has me feeling like Im living in an alternate universe where we DIDNT just get the denser, better paced, and consistent to its own internal logic and tone of RE4 Remake. RE9 however just feels like a side game experiment of RE7 interspersed w/ RE4 Remake but lacking the good transitions between areas  or even the better weapon advancement of RE4. While Grace's vulnerability makes for a more tense sneaking set piece she just doesnt get enough advancement in her toolset to feel like she grows in any tangible way. The one strength I can see the game has is the semi immersive sim aspects through the zombies in the care center.  I know people dont treat the RE game's story seriously but this just feels like a lazy reuse of nostalgia. Enemies that havent changed in 30 years, returning to locations that boil down to "oh neat I remember that" and retconning ---err I mean ---"REVELATIONS" that dont feel like they align with the logic or knowledge that either the remakes or the OG games set up. Just like the Gears of War-esque scripted explosive barrel areas you can see your heading into from blocks away you can really see where the plot is going about half way through the game.  This just doesnt feel like a step up from RE4R or Village to me. If the reactions were more tempered Id feel less like theres some mass psychosis going on but if I had to guess the nostalgia of RE4 and Leon, the streamer level giddiness of simple thrills of RE7 through Grace's parts and the glut of underwhelming AAA games that have left audiences wondering if publishers even like games has coalesced into overly generous reviews.

I enjoyed it, but it doesn’t have the character of the old Resident Evil games. If anything, it kind of steps on them. It leans hard into nostalgia while at the same time rewriting or undermining what made those games work in the first place.  This felt like a decent dose of member berries without really doing anything bold. There are callbacks, familiar faces, and recognizable locations, but a lot of it feels more like obligation than celebration. For a game tied so closely to the franchise’s legacy, it ends up feeling surprisingly safe and “business as usual” instead of something meaningful or definitive.  Gameplay-wise, it’s solid. The moment-to-moment experience is genuinely fun. Leon’s segments are a blast, leaning into that action-heavy style the series has used before, while Grace’s segments are where the game actually feels like classic Resident Evil. Limited resources, slower pacing, tension in every room, and that constant feeling that things could go wrong at any second. That contrast works well on paper, but the game seems to lose confidence in it halfway through and shifts more toward Leon’s run-and-gun style.  That’s part of the bigger issue. It reminds me a lot of RE7 and Village in the sense that it starts strong and atmospheric, then gradually becomes more linear and action-focused. The early environments feel detailed and intentional, but later sections start to feel more generic, like the creativity ran out before the game did.  The story is where things really fall apart. It starts simple enough, but the more it builds, the less it holds together. The villains are bland, forgettable, and lack any real presence. They feel like half-developed ideas rather than actual characters. Their motivations don’t make much sense, and the more you think about their plan, the weaker it gets.  Grace’s situation is a good example of this. If she’s supposed to be so valuable, it makes no sense that she’s left alone, unguarded, and basically allowed to escape and wander around. There’s no real urgency from the people who are supposed to be after her, even though they clearly know where she is. It just feels like the plot moving forward because it has to, not because it’s earned.  Leon’s return is cool, and there are moments where his character shines, especially when revisiting parts of his past. But even that feels undercut. He’s stuck dealing with weak villains, and instead of building something new around him, the game leans on copying or reworking old ideas. It doesn’t really add anything to his character, and in some ways it makes him feel flatter than he should.  The retcons are another problem. Changing established characters and events, like trying to reframe Spencer, just doesn’t land. It feels forced and inconsistent with what we already know. Instead of expanding the universe, it ends up making it feel less coherent.  At its core, the biggest issue is that the game doesn’t seem to take the Resident Evil universe seriously. It treats its own history more like a toolbox than something worth respecting. There are glimpses of what made the series great, especially in the slower, more methodical horror segments, but they’re surrounded by safe decisions and weak storytelling.  It’s a good game in terms of gameplay, and I had fun with it. But narratively, it’s messy, forgettable, and a bit of a missed opportunity, especially for something that’s supposed to celebrate the franchise. It feels like it played it safe when it should have taken a risk.

Resident Evil Requiem absolutely rules.  This feels like Capcom finally figured out how to fuse the two sides of modern Resident Evil into one game without it feeling stitched together. The Grace sections are tense, intimate, and properly nerve-wracking. The Leon sections let you cut loose and feel like a wrecking ball. That contrast works really well, and it kept the whole playthrough feeling fresh instead of repetitive. I especially liked that the horror side actually feels like horror, while the action side feels heavy and satisfying rather than mindless.  Visually, this game is ridiculous. The lighting, reflections, environmental detail, animation work, all of it looks absurdly good. Even early on I was saying it was running extremely well at max settings and looked better than pre-rendered cutscenes from older eras. By the end, that opinion didn’t change. It is one of those games where you keep stopping just to stare at the scene composition.  As a Resident Evil game specifically, this landed high for me. I liked it more than Village, and it ended up roughly tied with RE7 for my favorite. RE7 still has the edge in grounded, close-quarters dread, but Requiem has bigger spectacle, stronger variety, and a really good overall rhythm. I also thought the bosses were genuinely fun, which is not always something I say about horror games.  It is not perfect. The inventory friction can be annoying, some item gating and backtracking got on my nerves, and there were a few moments where I thought the game was being a little too pleased with its own puzzle logic or enemy setup. I definitely had stretches of “what exactly do you want me to do here?” and a few systems felt more cumbersome than they needed to be.  Still, the highs are much higher than the lows. The atmosphere is excellent, the pacing keeps changing in smart ways, the horror works, the action works, and it actually feels like a meaningful Resident Evil instead of just another entry wearing the name.  If you like Resident Evil, play it. Easy recommendation.
