I feel like this came exposes the flaws in steam’s review system.  It is overall a very good game, and I could in no way justify giving it a thumbs down. It has broad appeal, it looks good and it runs well, therefore it will get glowing reviews across steam, as evidenced by the overwhelmingly positive marker it has on steam. And yet, I feel that it’s the 2nd worst modern post 2017 Resident Evil single player game, and my least favourite of those games from RE7 onwards.  To explain further, RE7 was a massive leap forward for the series, radically changing gear from a series that was occupied with cheesy monster action, to a tight, horror focused experience. I feel like every game after that, while perhaps not revolutionary, has built upon the previous games and brought something new.  The RE2 remake showed the same horror formula could be applied to the 3rd person remakes as well. The RE3 remake, while a poor remake, showed that the series could do thrilling action without descending into the extreme cheese of the older games. RE Village showed that the first person games could do horror and action, and bring the wider story of the RE verse to the Ethan games. Finally RE4 did pitch perfect action horror, that was perfectly paced and had amazing gunplay and set pieces.  In contrast I just feel that Requiem doesn’t bring much new to the table. It essentially merges the slow first person horror of the Ethan games with the action of the 3rd person games, though you can change perspective for either Grace or Leon, the two playable characters. It does this very well, but both elements have been done extremely well in previous games anyway.  It still must be emphasised despite all my griping, this is a very good game, on all levels. Part of the ‘issue’, such as that it is, is that Capcom have managed a golden age of Resident Evil Games the last decade (aside from a couple of crap weird multiplayer spin offs). The RE devs are clearly at the top of the game when it comes to action horror, and that’s the case here again that there is clearly a very competent dev team working on this.   The horror is done so well, and the monsters have great personality, even down to the zombies this time. It’s tense and exciting. I found the gunplay of the Leon sections great, and I personally enjoyed that the late game introduced some human enemies in moderate amounts. To be honest I’d love a game with the gunplay of RE focused on fighting human enemies, I find it really grounded and satisfying. As for this game, again combat is paced excellently, with memorable set pieces, and a feeling of being pushed to your limits, but never unfairly.  The game looks pretty good and runs great. I would say that the game isn’t the best looking any more. In many ways I think it looks similar to the other RE games going back to RE7, it is the same engine after all, and there were a couple of textures that I found were dated and muddy. I’m not going to mark this down as a failure overall, I would rather have a game that runs great, looks decent, focuses on atmosphere and doesn’t take years to develop and require a super computer on release, and that’s exactly what you have here.  Storywise, it’s not revolutionary either, though I found myself engaged and entertained. After an excellent opening section, where I thought we might see in detail how the early stages of an outbreak goes, the game instead switches to standard Resident Evil Pattern. You are in a spooky old building and need to explore it to find three keys to open a door to another area so you can escape. While bits of the story are drip fed to you, I felt this bit was very similar to previous Resident Evil titles and the story wasn’t going anywhere fast. I’ve heard that other people dislike the Leon Raccoon city sections later, but I really enjoyed these more, finding the environment something a bit fresher for an RE9 game, and enjoying that the plot really picked up pace, with plenty of callbacks.  Overall the voice acting is pretty good here, and the writing decent enough, though I can’t help but feel that the story also feels like a diversion away from what was being set up at the end of Village.  Like I said, this is a lot of griping. Overall I did thoroughly enjoy the 16 hours it took me to finish the campaign, it’s another banger of survival horror from Capcom. I early await story expansions and future games, I just hope that it’s not a sign of a start of treading water in the future, and that further games do bring something more.

10/10 -  A Love Letter to Resident Evil Fans  Resident Evil Requiem is more than just another entry in the series, it feels like a heartfelt tribute to everything that made Resident Evil legendary in the first place. From the moment you start the game, it’s clear this was made by developers who truly understand what fans love about the franchise.  One of the best design choices in the game is how it balances two very different styles of gameplay through its characters. Grace’s sections are pure horror. They are filled with tension, and that constant feeling that something terrible could happen at any moment. The environments feel claustrophobic, resources are scarce, and every sound keeps you on edge. It captures that classic Resident Evil fear where you’re never quite comfortable moving forward.  Then there’s Leon, whose sections shift the tone toward high-intensity action. His gameplay feels fast, and incredibly satisfying. Fighting through enemies, pulling off stylish combat moments, and pushing through dangerous situations gives you that adrenaline rush fans loved in some of the more action-heavy entries of the series. The contrast between Grace’s terrifying vulnerability and Leon’s confident action makes the pacing feel dynamic and refreshing.  What makes Requiem special is how it celebrates the history of the franchise without relying purely on nostalgia. There are subtle callbacks, familiar design philosophies, and moments that remind you why Resident Evil has remained iconic for decades.  Visually, the game is stunning, the sound design is phenomenal, and the atmosphere is some of the best the series has ever had.  But above all else, Resident Evil Requiem feels like it was made for the fans. It respects the past, refines the present, and shows that the heart of Resident Evil is still alive and well.  10/10 -  A must-play for survival horror fans and a true love letter to the Resident Evil community.

RE9 can best be described as a Resident Evil Greatest Hits album made by an intern who didn't actually play Resident Evil before.  It isn't a bad game by any means but it's not a great game.  Requiem starts out solid with a prologue that feels a lot like RE7s beginning - classic horror elements including, unfortunately, being completely predictable down to the developer tricks used for jump scares. Once the prologue is over and the real game starts, the feel of more traditional horror continues while embracing modern, though unpopular game mechanics (stalker enemy.)    The Rhodes Hill facility oozes with charm that should be familiar to gamers who actually played the original Resident Evil games. Whether it's the architecture or the interior design itself, or the claustrophobic environments, the game feels like traditional Resident Evil and plays like traditional Resident Evil. Item boxes and typewriters adorn the save rooms, although the player inventory doesn't play nearly as crucial of a role. It's entirely easy to upgrade inventory capacity long before it could ever be an issue like it was in the original games, because the game throws upgrade coins at you even on Insanity.   Once you get outside is when I felt the most nostalgia - it looked and felt as close to RE1 as any game ever has up until this point. Without spoilers, there hasn't been another game in the franchise that felt this close to RE1 remake.  That's also where it basically fell apart. The game seemed to go the "Welcome to Raccoon City" route by cramming both RE1 and RE2 into one package. Just like the movie, that means both segments were hurting for substance. Where the first half was quite good, the second half can only be described as disappointing.   There's way too much RE6 in this game which sucks to say because it's no where near as bad as RE6, but there's still way too much of it. The visual design is way too similar to RE6. The open melee combat from 6 and the ridiculous parrying from RE4 combined make for responsive combat, but the lack of weapons (there are 22 but not really, and Leon can use maybe 16 including the knife, but none of them really stand out like say the Red 9 did) also feels like RE6.  At some points, even the atrocious camera lurching from the RE6 Tall Oaks university chapter returns.   Capcom is completely incapable of telling story after 4.5 decades of experience so this game is entirely retcon. But even so, they left out key story elements that would explain why Leon is even in his game,. The story isn't the worst, but it's barely serviceable compared to earlier titles before all the retcon started.  It's not a bad game but until the DLC is released it's hard to say if it's as great as people think.

Recommended if you like ALL or almost all of the flavors of RE games to date.  - RE9 is a mixed bag of styles and genres, you can't skip or reorder any of it - Play RE Village instead if you want a more coherent experience with similar genre bending variety - RE2 Remake is still the gold standard for characters, stotytelling, nostalgia, and strategic survival horror - RE4 remains the king of action-packed zombie slaughter - RE7 continues to define the intimate first person RE horror story  Personally what I want from a Resident Evil game is smart playstyle and resource management, and RE9 was a bit tough to work with.  - characters, gameplay styles, timelines, bossfights come and go as they please without a warning - there's no reading where and when to bring in your big resources - many areas that contain less resources than you need to plausibly spend to access them discourage exploration - dull segments where there's no player choice at all, only 15-45 minutes of forced waiting and walking into designated spots, in the designated order  Ultimately you'll be much happier just using your big guns first, and stumbling onward one chapter after another. I think this goes well for modern audiences that are not looking to worry if playing the game in a certain way is complete resource wasting or not.  In the end the game is also quite a fun adventure when you don't take it too seriously. - goofy zombie archetypes that are rich in character - Totally appropriate one-liners - Packed full of nostalgic locations, characters and fights for fan service - Over the top cinematic moments just because - Visual celebration with graphics fidelity and brilliant mocapped acting

Resident Evil 9 / Requiem is the newest game in the timeline. So as you'd expect, there are newer plot elements introduced to carry the story and to establish newer issues for the future. However, this is not a story review. So, all I'll say is the story was good and I enjoyed it. My issues lie in the gameplay, so if you don't want gameplay spoilers, don't read. Well, I guess if you were looking at reviews you were expecting that.  You play as both Grace Ashcroft and Leon Kennedy in this game. Grace's side of things are more horror focus, while Leon's side is more action focused. Grace's side of things is focused on more original and traditional Resident Evil play style. "Explore this, find this item, where does this go? Run from big scary monster, use your resources wisely." While Leon's gameplay is more akin to the action of RE4, but unfortunately, that is all Leon's side of things are, action and lackluster substance. I do think Grace's side of the game is much better designed, and Leon suffers as a result, but I don't think it's a make or break for the game. I do, however, think the game is much better played in 3rd Person compared to First Person as a first time experience, because even if the Third Person isn't as immersive as First Person is, my god Grace's characterization and her constant stumbling and fear have way more animation attention in third person compared to first. I swear they tortured that woman in the studio.   My feelings on the game are complicated, and i can't go into it without spoiling the game too much, but I do think the game is worth trying if you're a fan of the series as a whole. Whether you grab it full price or not is up to you, personally I'd recommend it on sale, but if you intend on replaying the game and learning to speed run the game, then sure, gnab it full price.

I just finished Resident Evil Requiem and honestly — wow. This is, in my opinion, the scariest entry in the series. The atmosphere is relentless: every corridor, sound cue, and shadow felt designed to keep me on edge. The game does an incredible job of using silence and sudden, brutal tension to build dread, and the enemy encounters hit hard because you never feel fully prepared.  What surprised me most was how the final action-heavy sequence didn’t just serve spectacle — it actually deepened my connection to the characters. The pacing shifts from creeping horror to full-on chaos, but the stakes feel personal. Seeing the characters pushed to their limits, making desperate choices, and finally revealing small moments of vulnerability made the action emotionally satisfying rather than just flashy. It made me care about who survived and why.  Gameplay-wise the mechanics are tight: resource management, limited saves, and smart enemy placements keep the tension high throughout. Visuals and sound design are top-notch — voice performances nailed those quieter, tense beats. If you like Resident Evil for both scares and character-driven drama, Requiem delivers on both fronts and left me buzzing long after I shut it off.  Final Score: 8.5/10  Resident Evil Requiem delivers a strong survival-horror experience with tense atmosphere, engaging exploration, and memorable encounters. The game succeeds in capturing the classic feeling of the series while still introducing some fresh ideas.  However, there are a few areas that could have been improved. Some sections of the pacing feel uneven, with certain parts dragging slightly while others move too quickly. A bit more variety in enemy encounters and deeper character development could also have made the experience even more impactful.  Overall, it’s a very solid entry that fans of the series will definitely enjoy.

Resident Evil 9 Requiem is easily one of the best entries the series has received in years. It feels like a confident step forward while still respecting everything that made the franchise legendary. The atmosphere, tension, and pacing are excellent and the game constantly manages to keep you on edge. Every new area feels carefully designed and the sense of dread never really leaves you.  The visuals are absolutely stunning on PC. With path tracing enabled the lighting and reflections can look almost photorealistic at times. Dark corridors, flickering lights, and environmental detail combine to create one of the most impressive looking survival horror games available right now. Even without path tracing the game still looks fantastic thanks to Capcom’s excellent engine work.  That said, the PC version does have a few technical frustrations. One of the most noticeable omissions is the lack of a proper FOV slider. For players who prefer adjusting their field of view this can feel restrictive and it is surprising that such a basic option is missing.  Another issue some players are experiencing is the DXGI Error Device Removed crash when alt tabbing out of the game for more than a few seconds. This can be particularly frustrating if you like to multitask while playing and hopefully it is something that gets addressed in a future patch.  There are also moments where Grace’s constant stuttering dialogue can start to wear thin after extended play sessions. While it adds character at first, the frequency can become distracting and occasionally breaks the flow during tense moments.  One of the most interesting aspects of the game is the difference between playing as Leon and Grace. Leon’s sections feel more confident and action driven. His combat abilities and experience make encounters feel controlled and tactical while still maintaining the survival horror pressure. Grace on the other hand plays very differently. Her sections lean far more into vulnerability and tension. Movement feels more cautious and encounters often rely on stealth, avoidance, and careful resource management. The contrast between the two perspectives adds variety and keeps the campaign feeling fresh.  Despite a few technical issues and minor design annoyances, Resident Evil 9 Requiem delivers an incredible survival horror experience. The atmosphere is outstanding, the visuals are breathtaking, and the dual character approach keeps the gameplay engaging throughout.  If you are a Resident Evil fan, this is absolutely a must play.

STORY – AN ATMOSPHERE THAT RECAPTURES CLASSIC TERROR  The narrative of Resident Evil Requiem brings a very familiar feeling to those who experienced the first chapters of the franchise. The focus returns to terror, mystery, and survival, something that directly recalls the heavy atmosphere of Resident Evil. Instead of relying solely on explosive action, the game works with tension, discoveries, and that constant fear of not knowing what lies in the next room. It's the kind of atmosphere that made the series a true survival horror.  SETTING – THE FEAR OF THE UNKNOWN  Just like in the classics, the setting is not just a backdrop; it's part of the terror. Dark corridors, abandoned areas, and places full of secrets are very reminiscent of the feeling of exploration that players felt in Resident Evil 2. Each open door can bring a scare, a puzzle, or a new danger. This slow build-up of tension is something that longtime fans immediately recognize.  EXPLORATION AND PUZZLES – THE SERIES' DNA  One of the coolest things is how the game rescues classic elements of the franchise: careful exploration, resource management, environmental puzzles, a constant feeling of vulnerability. These pillars were the soul of the first games and remain present here, creating that experience where every bullet matters and every decision weighs.  ACTION VS. HORROR – FRANCHISE BALANCE  After the more action-focused phase initiated by Resident Evil 4, many fans always wanted to see the series return a bit to its darker roots. Requiem seems to be heading exactly in that direction, less exaggerated spectacle and more psychological tension, atmosphere, and survival.  WITCHCARE – THE ESSENCE OF SURVIVAL HORROR  The game's greatest merit is recovering that feeling that old fans know well: solitude, constant danger, mystery about what is really happening. It's the kind of experience that makes the player advance slowly, listening to every sound in the dark.  NOSTALGIA THAT SPEAKS LOUDER (SPOILER ALERT)  [spoiler]Returning to a legendary place, going back to the iconic Raccoon City Police Department brings a wave of nostalgia. The corridors, the main hall with the statue, and the rooms full of secrets make the player feel like they are revisiting a piece of Resident Evil history. A shaky thumbs down.   My opinion is not always popular, but maybe you are someone who thinks like me. For quick context, I played RE6 after the blowback, on mouse and keyboard too (way better than controller) and I honestly didnt see why everyone was hating on it. So they came out with 7. Which I thought was so-so. Mostly because there are very little enemies, you kinda wander from boss fight to boss fight.   So that brings us to RE9. I truly loved RE2, RE3, RE4 remakes as well as RE8. Maybe they thought they were drifting too much into action territory again, so they decided to cut up Leon (action) and Grace (horror) into different segments. I feel like in trying to please everyone, they kinda pleased no one.   I think I can speak for some fans when I say we dont want either or. We dont want to jump between them either. We want both to live a little seamlessly together. Tone down both the action and the survival horror one notch and you get something like RE4. Fans want a little of both. The fear is a huge driver in these games. Wandering a villageof infected Spanish people can be scary. Having mastery to work crowd control with your weapons and developing your own style can be like an action movie. We just want both seamlessly. You do that by combining them in just the right doses.   Other CONS? I miss the money system used by RE4 and RE8.  I also miss finding treasures. They really nerfed that in this game.  I also didnt like that Leon's backdrops were so drab and gray. Almost like they were catering to action heads that love military inspired games, trying to look like they are in the desert somewhere in the middle east. I get it, were in a desolate town where a nuke fell. But as someone who works in film there ARE ways to address the color pallet.  Inventory sucks. Story seems half baked. The Doctor and Wesker were also just... not fleshed out (pun intended)  PROS I didnt really like Grace at first. She was a little TOO timid for me. Again, by one notch. BUT the character did grow on me and it became kind of a redemption. I enjoyed the CQC updates to Leon.  I enjoyed a more mass deployment of charms.  I enjoyed the weapons available in this one. I enjoyed enemy movement updates, they can be very difficult to hit at times, I found myself going for more leg shots than head shots because of it.  I enjoyed the new enemies in the sanitarium.  I also enjoyed the feel of the sanitarium too.   Overall, I think anyone that loves the series will enjoy it enough. If you're new to RE, this is probably not a good first impression. I say if its on a super sale, its totally worth it. If you jump on every RE release the second it comes out like me, well... its a lot of money for not a lot of content.

This review is an excerpt of most of my Medium review for Requiem, unfortunately I hit Steam's character limit near the end of the review. [url=https://medium.com/@lukehthomas/resident-evil-requiem-review-fcd1b576ef88]You can read the full review here.[/url]  A few years back, in a video essay on the now decrepit “The Escapist” YouTube channel, video game critic Yahtzee Croshaw proposed that the “Resident Evil” franchise was stuck in a cycle: it would make one great game, then proceed to ruin it in the following entries by repeating the motions, chasing its own tail. Yahtzee’s final, perhaps frivolous, prediction was that the franchise would go through the entire cycle next in just a single entry, in “a game that starts really good, and then Chris Redfield shows up halfway through and the final boss is multiplayer-only.” And while the franchise’s ninth mainline entry, “Resident Evil Requiem,” never reached the trenches of co-op mandated gameplay, Yahtzee’s prediction for the franchise seemed to be prophetic, as the brilliant opening hours of “Requiem” were followed by a rehash of “RE:4R” without the gameplay merits that made it a hit, while being sunken too deep in the established canon.  “Resident Evil Requiem” is mainly separated into two halves, one centered around series mainstay Leon Kennedy’s action gameplay and the other around division I stutterer and newcomer Grace Ashcroft (she’s great). Grace, a data analyst for the FBI, is investigating a murder case at the hotel where her mother was murdered years ago (rough job) when she’s kidnapped by former Umbrella Corporation researcher Victor Gideon. Coincidentally, a now middle-aged Leon, who’s searching for the same guy in order to find a lead on curing his unidentifiable illness, happens to arrive right as Gideon is hauling Grace away.  Gideon, of course, escapes, but Leon follows his tracks to the Rhodes Hill Chronic Care Center and after an opening interlude that teases the two’s gameplay mechanics, the care center gets put on lockdown as Grace and Leon are split up, and the real meat of “Resident Evil Requiem” begins. Poorly equipped with a dinky pistol that only stuns the undead, throwable bottles as distractions, and a punchy last-resort “Requiem” revolver initially filled with only one bullet, Grace is at the mercy of the environment as you must find three hidden quartz emblems throughout the treacherous hallways to get out of the care center. It’s this three-hour long section of the game that I adore.  The care center is brimming with hostile forces, and since the most Grace can do is stun an enemy with a couple of pistol shots and shove them away, as I found more and more rooms and pathways littered with the infected, all with slight differences to their behaviors along with a handful of particularly specialized zombies, learning the best ways to deal with the onslaught became vital as backtracking through the halls is necessary, and the need to confront or hide from the many threats of the center stayed a very effective thrill through the many treks.  But the dead can die, with enough shots or stabs expended or a stealthy puncture from a craftable hemolytic injector that’ll gorily blow the target up, most of the standard infected will be dealt with, but your capability of doing so is only as large as your limited capacity resources, letting expending extra resources to take down a particularly harrowing foe be a meaningful choice.  I initially overlooked Grace’s crafting system, which allowed her to create more healing or combat tools, eventually even bullets for the coveted “Requiem” revolver, using the multitude of scraps collected and the splattered gore Grace can siphon with her Blood Collector. But as the crafting palate expanded, it became an essential part of clearing out the care center. The crafting design really aided the game’s already brilliant transition from starting you completely disarmed and afraid to letting you hold your own through the corridors you’ve memorized. But the center still manages to hold tricks up its sleeve throughout its runtime and continued to engage me with more additions to its already packed halls.  But while it’s a very well-oiled machine, if you do try to bend things too far, you’ll find that it won’t budge much. One annoying example was once the zombie chef shifted from guarding his kitchen to patrolling a hallway leading to a specific room I needed to get to. When I attempted to lure Chef Gusteau back to the kitchen, despite him having formerly stalked the location, his updated pathing wouldn’t let him back into the area, forcing me into one of the “correct” ways of getting around the chef.  Fortunately, “Requiem” seemed to do a good job at subtly directing the player to the intended ways of dealing with getting around in most cases, so that annoyance didn’t come up much. Running through the corridors of the care center managed to stay thrilling, even as it took a detour underground with a new threat to strategize against, all the way up until Grace’s main segment ends, leaving me delighted but wanting more, especially when the rest of the game revealed itself.  After a far too long interlude swapping between Grace’s and Leon’s gameplay, giving Grace two sequences that lacked the previous meaningful threats and exploration, the brunt Leon’s gameplay actually begins and, unfortunately, it doesn’t live up to the fantastic precedent set by the care center. At this point, the story also starts revealing its grander ambitions, zooming away from the interpersonal stakes of Grace’s story to the wider scope of the “Resident Evil” franchise as Leon embarks into the series’ mainstay location, Raccoon City. I’ve never played a “Resident Evil” prior to this release (losing some of my credibility here), so I didn’t come to “Requiem” for the story, but as it steadily became more outlandish and referential (in accordance to Yahtzee’s proposed cycle), it felt mishandled overall.  A polar opposite to Grace’s methodical explorations of freakish corridors, Leon’s segments replaced the fear with gun-toting third-person action gameplay. But once Raccoon City pivoted to its main quest of retrieving a set of, yet again, three detonator parts to blow up a gate that he probably could’ve found a way to climb over, the level design takes a noticeable hit and exposes the combat’s lack of depth.  The city is mainly out in the open, which often lacked structures to work around with while having a severe lack of verticality, and the enclosed arenas don’t meaningfully choreograph the undead’s locations, leading to some awkward and annoying fights. And while the combat has a lot of juice on paper — Leon is equipped with a variety of powerful artillery, an axe that can be infinitely sharpened, and the dreaded parry mechanic that can block seemingly everything — it never feels quite as powerful as it should. Every weapon has a very obvious preferred range, and the pistol’s meager firing speed and power kept it feeling sluggish. It’s still not bad (barring a couple of very poorly designed areas), but the combat’s lack of flair is exemplified by the generally bland level design.  Leon also gets equipped with a “Tactical Tracker” wristband that rewards him with credits for every kill, which you can use to purchase an array of items and weapon upgrades, but the only upgrades that actually matter are an inventory size upgrade you can get immediately — which removed all need for inventory management, I never once ran out of space — and a bulletproof vest. Spending the rest of the credits then just comes down to buying out random menial weapon buffs and extra items with no real thought to it... This game is not the 10/10 masterpiece that everyone is making it out to be, however, it is still a really really good game that is at least top 5 out of all Resident Evil games.   The first half of the game is one of the best things that the RE Engine has ever given us in Resident Evil games. The tension, the atmosphere, the horror, it is all there and it is amazing. Grace has the best part of the game by far and no one else can tell me otherwise. There are some issues I have with it though. There are sections within the first half where you switch to Leon. These sections are short. One is quite literally 10 minutes long at most. It really breaks up the pacing because you go from this beautiful scary part of the game to Leon kicking ass. It is such an immersion breaking switch up; especially since after you do this section, you are back to horror that is unmatched anywhere else once again. After the first half of the game is over, the second half has you playing as Leon for the majority of the time. This part has some issues. Leon's part has him looking around for some macguffins and this searching lasts for what feels like forever. The visuals in this part become very one note and bland and the game starts going very action focused which doesn't feel as well part together as the survival horror of the first half. The game has two endings which feels like it was put there for the sake of giving the player an illusion of choice. It is pretty obvious which ending is the canon and good ending. I am rambling at this point but I just feel like this game could have been a lot better if the 2 gameplay styles had been separated into 2 different campaigns. The way it is right now leaves Leon's section feeling half-baked whilst Grace's section ends way too early for my liking. I wish we had more survival horror aspects throughout the entire game. This game very much so peaks in the opening half and it only goes downhill from there. I am not saying I hate the game after the first half, I just wish that the game had as stronger a second act as it did the first.  Overall, this game is amazing and definitely deserves to be praised. It isn't the perfect game everyone seems to be  making it out to be though.

[h2] 9/10 (A Near-Perfect Horror Experience) [/h2]  Resident Evil 9: Requiem proves that Capcom still knows how to evolve survival horror without losing its identity. Once the story finds its rhythm, the game becomes a gripping mix of tense exploration, sharp combat, and oppressive atmosphere. Every area feels handcrafted, every encounter demands focus, and the emotional weight lands harder than in most recent entries.   It’s polished, confident, and strong enough to stand as a genuine Game of the Year contender. Despite being the ninth mainline entry, it’s surprisingly approachable for newcomers with a mostly standalone plot, but veterans will appreciate the callbacks and deeper lore threads. In terms of quality, it ranks as one of the highest in the series.  The slow early pacing, bugs, and lighter post-game keep it from absolute perfection, but once Requiem opens up, it delivers some of Capcom’s best horror sequences, boss fights, and character moments in years. By the end, you feel like you’ve survived something intense and meticulously crafted.  It’s a bold, haunting entry that earns its place near the top of the franchise. New players will find it a strong starting point, veterans will find plenty to chew on, and its production values and length justify the AAA price tag, though the patient gamer may still prefer to wait for a sale.   [b] Full Review Available at: [/b] https://mobalytics.gg/news/guides/resident-evil-requiem-review
